11383-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Scientific American Supplement number 531, dated March 6, 1886, covers chemistry, machines, electricity, plants, and odds and ends for skilled readers. Articles treat annatto and aluminum, the metal of the future, iron in forts with chilled and rolled cupolas, high speed on the ocean. compressed air power, the Berthon collapsible canoe, steel-making ladles, water gas, Japanese rice wine and soja sauce, the Colson telephone, and the meldometer.

Sibley College lectures on balancing forces in moving bodies add weight. The weekly, five dollars a year alone, served engineers, inventors, and curious mechanics. Its range shows American technical culture in the 1880s, sure that new materials and machines would reshape industry.
13399-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
This February 27, 1886 issue of Scientific American Supplement gathers the practical science and engineering of its week. Articles cover the decomposition and fermentation of milk, the ethics of engineering practice in an address by James C. Bayles, and the lifting of a large water main.

Readers also find the inter-oceanic canal question, the Mersey Tunnel, an improved revolver, motors for street railways, and notes on chemical compounds for building work. Short reports sit beside engravings and figures, giving mechanics, builders, and curious readers a working picture of new machines, materials, and methods in the late nineteenth century.
16360-scientific-american-supplement-no-:
Dated October 2, 1886, this Supplement number opens with botany: a century plant in bloom at Auburn, New York, and alpine flowers of the Pyrenees. Chemistry follows, with Moissan's work toward isolating fluorine and a new method for measuring nitric acid. Notes on water of crystallization round out the science pages.

The issue serves the practical reader of the 1880s, with short, illustrated pieces that explain new work in plain terms. Later sections, as was the journal's habit, would carry engineering and trade news. As a whole it shows Victorian popular science at its busiest: curious, useful, and keen on the newest discovery.
18195-the-girl-s-own-paper-vol-viii-no-3:
Rosa Nouchette Carey's serial Merle's Crusade leads the October 2, 1886 number of The Girl's Own Paper, volume eight, number 353, priced at one penny. Carey also wrote Aunt Diana and For Lilias, and her new serial heads a weekly paper for girls. An illustration shows a scene captioned with a line of dialogue from the tale.

The first chapter, The Valley of Humiliation, finds Merle reading carelessly on a snowy Sunday afternoon while her motto, Laborare est orare, rings in her ears. Aunt Agatha reproves her old-fashioned notions, and Merle climbs a steep hill with Christiana and her boys. Readers get a Victorian girls' paper in full: a moral serial, home scenes, and the steady values of work, duty, and patience.
18293-the-girl-s-own-paper-vol-viii-no-3:
Called Away, a poem of a widowed mother at her stitch work, opens the October 9, 1886 number of The Girl's Own Paper, volume eight, number 354, priced at one penny. An illustration shows a mother and child beside the verses. Its verses picture a woman in a heartless town. She toils at dreary stitch work for a small wage. Her strength ebbs as her pale boy weeps at her feet for his mother's woe.

The poem tells of a widowed life, a mother's love, and the fear of an early death, in plain, sentimental verse meant to move young readers to pity and duty. Fiction follows in the same number, with a baron hurrying up an oak staircase to the nursery wing. Girls get a weekly paper of feeling and story: a poem of poverty and love beside tales of households and children.
18395-the-girl-s-own-paper-vol-viii-no-3:
Volume eight, number 356 of The Girl's Own Paper, dated October 23, 1886, cost one penny. Its leading story is A Dream of Queens' Gardens, a story for girls in two parts by Daniel Dormer, author of Out of the Mists. Part two, A Queen's Dream, opens this number, with an illustration of lilacs and laburnum trees blooming abundantly around.

Hazel, the heroine, muses on a lecture whose tender closing writing may soften her heart, growing calmer and happier as she wonders whether she might be of some use in the world. Exhausted, she stoops to throw coal on a fire, piling large and small blocks and a handful of matches in strange chaos. Girls get a moral tale of a girl's dream and waking: pride, softening, and the hope of usefulness, told across two numbers.
18414-the-girl-s-own-paper-vol-viii-no-3:
Volume eight, number 355 of The Girl's Own Paper, dated October 16, 1886, cost one penny. Its leading piece is The Brook and Its Banks, by Rev. J. G. Wood, author of The Handy Natural History. Wood opens with Burns on a burnie playing over a linn, straying round a rocky scaur, and glittering under the nightly rays below the spreading hazel.

Wood's first chapter treats the many aspects of a brook: the eye sees only what it can see, and each brook keeps its own character. Hill burnies, lowland brooks, Oxford fresh-water brooks, and Kentish tidal brooks all swarm with life. An afternoon's walk, ditches against hedges, and a brook in Cannock Chase follow. Girls get nature study in a weekly paper: a brook as a world to watch.
18501-the-girl-s-own-paper-vol-viii-no-3:
Volume eight, number 357 of The Girl's Own Paper, dated October 30, 1886, cost one penny. Its serial, The Shepherd's Fairy, a pastorale by Darley Dale, author of Fair Katherine, reaches chapter five, The Chateau After the Loss of the Baby. An illustration shows the poor little baroness, asleep, starting up in alarm.

The chapter picks up the baron's guess from an earlier number: a housemaid called from the nursery to fetch Leon's cane lingered talking with servants for a quarter of an hour. Returning, she found the baby gone, supposed the nurse had taken the child, and searched in vain. Marie grows fearful as the footman says the nurse is not expected back till late. Girls get a serial at its tensest point: a missing child, a careless quarter hour, and a household on the edge of grief.
18980-the-girl-s-own-paper-vol-viii-no-3:
The November 6, 1886 number of The Girl's Own Paper was a penny weekly for girls. Its lead serial was Merle's Crusade by Rosa Nouchette Carey. Chapter five finds a young woman taking a post caring for a small boy. The boy lives in a grand London house.

Merle meets a fretful child, a tired mother, and household staff. The staff hold strong views on nursery work. The mother's joy at holding her son softens the strain of social duties. Readers get a slice of Victorian girls' reading, where duty, kindness, and home life carry the story.
19923-the-ontario-readers-the-high-schoo:
The Ontario Readers served Canada's public schools for decades. The High School Reader of 1886 gathers prose and verse for older pupils. Its editors admit limited space prevents a complete anthology. They aim instead to show each author in characteristic moods. A fair perspective of the world of authorship is the goal. The selections present authors as a schoolbook can.

Provincial readers standardized English-Canadian schooling. Pupils from many small schools read the same set pieces. British and Canadian authors share these pages by design. The 1886 reader preserves that shared canon. Education historians trace taste and values through such books. A single volume shaped thousands of classroom hours.
21778-donahoe-s-magazine-volume-15-no-1-:
Irish Catholic America speaks in this January 1886 number of Donahoe's Magazine, a Boston monthly journal. The issue opens with an encyclical letter of Pope Leo XIII, then ranges across tales, biography, poetry, and history. A serial story, Dead Man's Island, promises the tale of an Irish country town. An affecting incident at sea and a valiant soldier of the cross fill out the fiction.

History and argument share the pages: chapters of Irish history, pieces on capital and labor, strikes, and Chinese labor. There is church news, council decrees, and word of Father Ryan's death. The magazine served readers who held Ireland and the Church together in one loyalty. This volume gathers the run from January to July 1886.
26439-the-quarterly-review-volume-162-no:
The Quarterly Review for April 1886, number 324, holds ten long articles in the review's grave Victorian manner. Matthew Paris's great chronicle leads, followed by the Christian Brothers and religious schools in France and England, the archives of the Venetian Republic, and yeomen farmers in Norway. Travels in the British Empire and the Bishop of Durham on the Ignatian Epistles widen the survey.

The Cromwell article tests the Protector's character not through his whole career but through a single train of events where his hand stayed visible throughout. Books and reading, the characteristics of democracy, and the Gladstone-Morley administration close the number. Published in Philadelphia by Leonard Scott, the issue shows the quarterly essay at its most weighty.
2657-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
Abraham Lincoln's fifth volume in the Constitutional Edition covers 1858 to 1862, edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley. The years run from the close of the Douglas campaign through his election, secession, and the first hard years of civil war.

Letters, messages, and orders show Lincoln learning to be a war president, choosing generals, holding border states, and shaping emancipation. The prose is plain, careful, and often moving in its restraint. The volume gives readers Lincoln at work, day by day, as crisis turned into a struggle for the nation's life. Through it all, Lincoln's humor and patience hold the pages together.
2658-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
Abraham Lincoln's sixth volume in the Constitutional Edition covers 1862 to 1863, edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley. It opens with a message to Congress of May 14, 1862, on naval officers, and the promotion of efficiency in the navy.

Through emancipation, military appointments, and the politics of a war government, Lincoln's papers show a president balancing law, army, and public feeling. The volume captures the middle of the war, when victory was still uncertain. Readers see Lincoln's judgment forming under fire, in documents rather than speeches alone. The Emancipation Proclamation falls squarely in these months.
2659-the-papers-and-writings-of-abraham-:
Abraham Lincoln's seventh volume in the Constitutional Edition covers 1863 to 1865, edited by Arthur Brooks Lapsley. It opens with an opinion on the loss of General Milroy's division in October 1863, and runs through the war's final campaigns.

Gettysburg, emancipation in practice, reconstruction plans, and the second inaugural all pass through these pages. Lincoln's letters show a president weary but steady, reasoning his way toward a just peace. The volume closes the set with the voice of a leader who did not live to see the peace he shaped. His final letters carry the weight of a war nearly won.
26682-donahoe-s-magazine-volume-15-no-2-:
Donahoe's Magazine, volume fifteen, number two, dated Boston, February 1886, opens with an epigraph from Right Reverend Doctor Ireland of St. Paul, Minnesota, on the Irish race assuming an independent attitude in American politics. Its first article gossips for half an hour on the Columbian Abbey of Derry, mother-house of Iona.

The Derry writer rambles the city walls, recalls Macaulay's siege, muses in the Protestant Cathedral, and admires Casino College on St. Columb's old monastery site. Derry stands on Lough Foyle in the north of Ireland, its streets coiling round a hill to St. Columb's Cathedral. Walls, gates, and a rusty cannon keep the Maiden City's 1689 No to James. Later pages turn to Fenian writers, including bitter speaker Mat Blake and the Ballybay elections.
acts-pilate-walker-1886:
The Acts of Pilate, also called the Gospel of Nicodemus, is an early Christian apocryphal text, presented here in Alexander Walker's translation for the Ante-Nicene Fathers series. It is not part of the New Testament. Instead, it imagines an official account of Jesus' trial before Pontius Pilate, written from inside the events the Gospels report more briefly.

The narrative expands the trial, death, and resurrection story with speeches, hearings, and testimony that the canonical accounts do not contain. Its best-known part tells of Christ's descent into hell, the harrowing, and the release of the righteous dead. The text shaped later Christian storytelling for centuries, and Walker's version is the founding English translation in its series.
aeschylus-dramas-swanwick-1886:
Anna Swanwick translated all seven surviving plays of Aeschylus into English verse, and her fourth revised edition appeared in 1886. Aeschylus, the earliest Greek tragedian whose work survives, fought at Marathon and reshaped the stage of Athens. Swanwick's volume holds the whole of what time has left of him.

The Oresteia trilogy follows Agamemnon's murder and Orestes' revenge to its trial in Athens. The Persians mourns Athens' beaten enemy, while Prometheus Bound chains its Titan to a crag for mankind's sake. The Seven Against Thebes and the Suppliants complete the seven. Swanwick, a scholar of note, kept the verse stately and clear. Her Aeschylus was the standard Victorian rendering of the poet.
allbutt-wifes-handbook-1886:
The Wife's Handbook, published in 1886 by Dr Henry Arthur Allbutt, was a cheap medical guide for married women. It gave working-class women practical advice, including contraceptive advice, at a price they could afford. That content made the book notorious: the General Medical Council struck Allbutt off the medical register for publishing it.

Struck off and prosecuted in spirit, the handbook still circulated, passed hand to hand as contraband of the era. Its pages told wives what respectable medicine refused to print about their own bodies and family planning. The book survives as a landmark in the history of birth control, and as evidence of the price one doctor paid for writing it.
allibone-critical-dictionary-english-lit:
Volume Three of Allibone's Critical Dictionary, published in 1886, closes the set with authors from R to Z. It ends with Allibone's own colophon, dated 1870, a sign of how long the work took. The dictionary had grown alongside its maker for decades.

The final volume adds later authors the first volumes missed and corrects earlier entries. Quoted reviews let readers hear the period's own critical voices. Allibone died in 1889, his life's work complete. Later bibliographers built on his foundation, and his three volumes still serve anyone tracing a minor Victorian author's books and reputation. His prefaces explain how he gathered notices from sales rooms and private shelves.
arxiv-2412-00586:
Fred Heiding, Simon Lermen, Andrew Kao, Bruce Schneier, and Arun Vishwanath test if large language models can run fully automated spear phishing drives, checked on human subjects. Spear phishing crafts personal lure emails for each target. Their work came out in twenty twenty-four.

Four email groups went to a pool of over a hundred people. Plain lure emails got a low click rate, while expert made lures scored far higher. Fully AI made lures matched the experts, and AI lures with a human in the loop scored a touch higher. A custom tool ran the whole drive, from data gathering to personal risk profiles, which were right and useful in most cases. The authors warn of fast growth in AI lure skill.
arxiv-2412-01686:
Gordon Blower and Simon Malham prove that a family of wave equations with non-commuting terms can be solved by a direct linear method, in a 2024 math paper. The core equation is the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation, a two-dimensional wave model. In the non-commutative case, the order of terms matters, which breaks many classic tools. The pair also derive a lifted partner equation and a log form from which the whole family flows.

Their proof builds a new algebra from the solution of the linearized equation and its derivatives. A special product in that algebra, based on a rule first used for the classic case, does the heavy lifting. Integrability then amounts to one clean expansion in the algebra. Computer runs of soliton-like waves round out the paper. The method opens the family to the same direct tools as the classic case.
arxiv-2412-02186:
Kangsan Kim and co-authors wrote a 2024 paper on teaching video models to handle new tasks from a few examples. Big video models have grown strong at watching and reasoning, yet they drop on tasks rare in their training. Fine tuning on each new task costs too much to be a fix.

Their frame picks the most apt examples by similarity and ranks them for the prompt. The model then answers, and its own confidence is scored. Low confidence sends the frame back to pick fresh examples and try again. That loop stretches the useful context with no retraining. Tests on many benchmarks showed clear gains, above all in niche domains. Code was promised in a public repository.
arxiv-2412-02686:
Nicolas DeStefano, Saeed Pegahan, Aneesh Ramaswamy, and a wider team wrote this physics paper, published in 2024. It reads an electron beam without touching it, by watching how the beam's magnetic field twists the quantum state of rubidium atoms it passes through.

A laser shines through a thin rubidium vapor tuned to an atomic transition. The beam's field nudges the atoms' spins, rotating the laser's polarization by an amount that varies across the beam's width. Mapping that rotation rebuilds a picture of the field, and from it the beam's position, size, and total current. The team verified currents from thirty to one hundred ten microamps. The reading did not depend on the electrons' energy between ten and twenty thousand electron volts. The authors offer the method for accelerator beams in particle and nuclear physics.
arxiv-2412-02886:
Roman Colman and six co-authors present PatchFinder, a tool that pulls data from noisy scanned documents with a vision-language model. Their paper from twenty twenty-four notes that firms and agencies hold vast records as scans. Reading them by old means, character tools plus big language models, is slow and error-prone on dirty pages. High data density pushes costs up as well.

PatchFinder scores the model's own confidence from its top output odds. That score, Patch Confidence, sets a patch size for the page. The page is cut into overlapping patches, each read with its own confidence tag. On a set of noisy scans, a mid-size model with this method beat a flagship chat model by a wide margin. The team works from a national lab setting. The gain comes from letting doubt steer the search.
arxiv-2412-03486:
Anna van Elst and Debarghya Ghoshdastidar published this study in 2024. It builds risk certificates for contrastive learning, a way of teaching models from unlabeled data. Such models learn to place similar items close and unlike items apart. The method is widely used, yet its error theory lags behind. Past bounds were either useless in practice or rested on shaky assumptions.

The authors derive PAC-Bayesian certificates that stay meaningful for the popular SimCLR setup. A subtle point drives the work: SimCLR reuses paired samples as negatives for others, which breaks the independence older bounds need. Their bounds fold in that reuse, plus the role of data augmentation and temperature. Tests on a standard image set show far tighter guarantees than before, for both the training loss and later tasks.
arxiv-2412-03786:
Randall Clark and five co-authors validate the NSFsim equilibrium solver in two thousand twenty four. Plasma shape drives stability and confinement in fusion devices. NSFsim, built on the DINA code, simulates shape and transport. The study tests its Grad-Shafranov solver at DIII-D.

Five plasma shapes span single null, double null, and limited cases. Negative triangularity joins the test set as well in the runs. Simulated flux loops and probe signals face real measurements. EFIT fits and the GSevolve simulator provide cross checks. The solver recreates shape and flux patterns across conditions.
arxiv-2412-04586:
Gadjev, Parvanov, and Uluchev put forth a new tweak in twenty twenty-four to a known math tool that fits smooth curves. The tool, a Baskakov form, fits curves that stay bound on a half line. Their tweak builds on a past fix to that tool.

They prove straight and strong back claims on the fit flaw, tied to a yard stick for curve bend. The new tool is straight-line in its acts but not all-plus in its weights. Still, it fits at a higher rate than the past fix from two decades back. The trade is the loss of all-plus weights.
arxiv-2412-04686:
Simon Florian Koch, Brian Moser, Antonín Lindner, and a wider team wrote this physics paper, published in 2024. It reports the first direct measurement of how much material sits in a pixel detector module built for the upgraded ATLAS experiment at CERN.

Extra material blurs particle tracks, so builders must know the budget precisely. The team fired low-energy positrons through a module at a CERN test beam. As the particles crossed the module, they scattered by tiny angles. A telescope of thin detectors tracked the kinks, with and without the module in place. From the scatter spread, the team derived the module's thickness in standard units: just under one percent, matching the value expected from its parts. The check supports the detector's readiness for the high-luminosity collider era.
arxiv-2412-06286:
Patrick Ramos and colleagues found objects in paintings without any hand-drawn training boxes in a 2024 paper. Finding objects in art helps digital humanities scholars search huge image collections fast, but labeling paintings takes rare expert time. Their pipeline, NADA, borrows the art knowledge already inside diffusion image models instead of training from scratch.

A vision-language model first proposes which object classes might appear, then a diffusion-based detector, conditioned on each class, locates them. Nothing is fine-tuned, and the setup covers both light supervision and fully zero-shot use. On two artwork datasets it beat prior weakly supervised methods and gave the first zero-shot detection results in art. Museums could search collections with far less labeling.
arxiv-2412-06886:
Mahlet Shiferaw, Nickolas Kokron, and Risa Wechsler ask, in a 2024 cosmology paper, how much doubt about galaxy growth clouds what surveys can teach us. Galaxies sit in halos of dark matter, and the link between the two depends on complex growth physics. The team compares galaxy samples built by two very different models of that growth.

They fit the same bias model to samples from an empirical model and from a full fluid simulation. Quiet and star-forming galaxies fell in distinct parts of the bias space, but the spread between growth models was small for matched samples. The work yields prior ranges that should help pull sound cosmic results from red and emission-line galaxy surveys.
arxiv-2412-07286:
Eric Persson and Florian Bernlochner present, in a 2024 paper, a cleaner way to determine a key value in particle physics. The value, written |Vcb|, is an element of the CKM matrix, which describes how quarks change type. It is extracted from decays of B mesons into a D* meson, a lepton, and a neutrino. The fit uses a mathematical parameterization that must be truncated at some order, and that choice can bias the answer.

The pair treat the truncation choice as a model selection problem. They apply the Akaike Information Criterion, which weighs fit quality against the number of terms, and test the approach on simulated data. The method gives unbiased estimates of |Vcb|, though its error intervals run too narrow. A global version that averages across truncation orders fixes the coverage. The authors offer model selection and model averaging as a firmer path to this value.
arxiv-2412-07786:
Rissaki, Fountalis, Vasiloglou, and Gatterbauer propose agentic schema refinement for enterprise databases in twenty twenty-four. Large company databases can be complex and messy. Their structure hides the meaning that analysts need for their work. The authors propose a semantic layer between the database and the user.

That layer is a set of small, easy to read views that act as a refined schema. To find these views, they run a simulation with several language model agents. The agents work together to define and refine views step by step. The process needs only minimal human input. The authors present the approach as a path to AI powered exploration of unwieldy databases. It aims to make hidden data semantics visible and usable.
arxiv-2412-08386:
Some systems jump at random times whose rate itself rises and falls, a pattern captured by Hawkes processes joined with drift. Chiara Amorino and co-authors tackle a statistical question for such systems. From one long observed path, how well can we estimate the stationary density, the map of where the system spends its time? Their system has two parts, the process itself and its jump intensity.

They build a kernel estimator, which smooths the observed path into a density curve, and prove how fast its error shrinks as observation time grows. Oddly, the speed depends on the intensity level being estimated, through the baseline rate of jumps. A change-of-measure trick, turning the Hawkes process into a simpler Poisson one, carries the proofs. They then handle the case where the intensity is unknown, plugging in an estimate and deriving fresh rates. Computer experiments match the theory.
arxiv-2412-08486:
Zijian Zhou, Shikun Liu, Xiao Han, and a large team improve AI-generated portraits of people in this two thousand twenty-four paper. Controllable person generation creates an image of someone from reference photos, letting users set appearance or pose. Prior methods often smear the fine textural details of the reference even when overall quality looks high. The authors blame attention layers that look at the wrong places in the reference image.

Their method, Leffa, learns flow fields inside attention, explicitly guiding each target query to attend to the correct reference key during training. It is implemented as a regularization loss on the attention map of a diffusion model baseline. Experiments reached state-of-the-art results on virtual try-on and pose transfer, with visibly less detail distortion. The loss is model-agnostic, and the authors show it lifting other diffusion models as well.
arxiv-2412-09786:
Yutong Jin, Peter Gilbert, and Aaron Hudson build new statistics tools in 2024 for treatments given as a smooth dose rather than a few set levels. Studies often ask how survival chances change with dose, such as the level of an immune marker after a vaccine. With a smooth dose, the usual math for fair estimates breaks down.

Their methods test whether the chance of surviving to a set time stays flat across all dose levels, without assuming a fixed shape for the link. Computer studies check that the tests behave well. The team then applies them to data from two trials of an antibody meant to prevent HIV. The work helps trial teams judge dose effects with fewer leaps of faith.
arxiv-2412-11486:
Shunta Takahashi condenses exotic anyons inside a wormhole in a proposed new form of three dimensional quantum gravity. The paper came out in two thousand twenty-four. The frame rewrites gravity through Virasoro symmetry, with Wilson lines in the role of anyons. Their label set is continuous, which strains the usual finite rules.

Takahashi first reviews the toolkit and the gauging scheme known as anyon condensation. The scheme is then used on the wormhole, despite the infinite label set. Condensing one special diagonal anyon splits the wormhole's partition function into factors. The boundary theory that comes out is Liouville conformal field theory. The calculation is a rare worked case of gauging continuous non-invertible symmetries. It tests the new form at a point where it might have failed.
arxiv-2412-12486:
Hongjin Qian, Zheng Liu, Peitian Zhang, Zhicheng Dou, and Defu Lian make it cheaper for language models to answer questions over very long documents. Storing the full memory of a long text, its key-value activations, is slow and heavy. Their method, ACRE, keeps that memory in two layers: a compact layer that holds the gist of the whole text, and a full layer that holds the fine detail.

When a question arrives, the model reads the compact layer first. Guided by the question, it then refills that layer with the most relevant entries from the detailed layer, like pulling the right pages back onto the desk. Tests on several long-context question sets showed gains in both answer quality and speed. The authors frame ACRE as a way to match memory to what each question actually needs.
arxiv-2412-13686:
Oliver Sefrin and Sabine Wolk wrote a paper in two thousand twenty-four on a hybrid learning agent that mixes classical and quantum computing. The agent learns tasks in episodes and had been proven to learn faster than classical rivals. But it only worked when the episode length, the number of steps to the goal, was fixed and known in advance.

In real tasks that length is unknown, and classical agents can at least see when they arrive. The authors give the hybrid agent a random strategy for picking episode lengths, removing the need for advance knowledge. In simulations, the adapted agent still learned faster than classical counterparts in some unknown-length scenarios.
arxiv-2412-17486:
Jérémie Sublime and Ilaria Renna surveyed students in twenty twenty-four about their use of large language models like ChatGPT for schoolwork. Generative AI has swept into classrooms, promising help while raising fears about skills and equity. The team questioned three hundred ninety-five students aged thirteen to twenty-five in France and Italy about how these tools fit their study routines.

Use proved widespread across ages and subjects, with older and male students using the tools more often, especially for science. The authors flag a widening gender gap in AI literacy. Most students used the tools constructively, but younger ones rarely proofread or critically checked outputs, risking their critical thinking and core knowledge. The paper urges schools to teach ethical, critical AI use.
arxiv-2412-18686:
Pricopi, Popescu, Rushton, Murphy, Inman, and Toma decode two nearby spiral galaxies by running light through virtual dust until the pictures match. The inverse problem asks where stars, gas, and dust sit inside a galaxy, given only its glow across many wavelengths. Radiative transfer models supply the decoding. Face-on spirals M101 and NGC 3938 are the subjects, imaged from ultraviolet to far infrared by five observatories.

Both fits succeed excellently. Milky Way style dust with standard optical properties explains the data in every galaxy the team has modeled, now a small sample of five. No submillimeter excess appears, and no exotic grain tweaks are needed. Star formation rates, opacities, and attenuations emerge as maps, not just totals. A resolved relation between star formation and stellar density runs steeper than the galaxy main sequence in most components.
arxiv-2412-18986:
Chen Bao and co-authors tackled hand motion forecast in 2024, asking a vision and language model to forecast where a person's hands will go next in a scene. Earlier systems forecast hand paths from video alone. The new tasks add everyday language instructions, stated or implied, so the model must understand the activity and reason about what should happen next.

The team created two benchmarks, one for plain hand forecast from a spoken-style task account and one that demands clear thinking. Their model, HandsOnVLM, answers in natural language conversation while also outputting future hand paths from a first-person view. In doing so it joins the world knowledge of large vision-language models with the step-by-step form of path generation. Tests showed it beat task-certain methods and other vision-language baselines, and used scene knowledge in effect.
arxiv-2412-19686:
Harish Jain, Richard Ho, and Luiza Angheluta study how cell layers start to flow, in a research paper from 2024. Sheets of cells line many body surfaces, and they loosen up when cells swap neighbors. Such a swap is called a T1 transition, and each one looks random when viewed on its own.

Using two computer models of cell sheets, the team found that the swaps are not random in space. Cells that lose neighbors tend to relax their shape, while cells that gain neighbors tend to stretch out. This uneven pattern of swaps builds up across many cells. The result is directed cell movement and shared flow patterns at the scale of the whole sheet.
arxiv-2501-01786:
Qinyi Liu, Ronas Shakya, Mohammad Khalil, and Jelena Jovanovic bring differential privacy to learning analytics with a purpose-built framework. Their paper from twenty twenty-five weighs a live tension. Learner data powers insight, yet laws and public concern demand stronger shields. Plain anonymization fails on rich education data. Theirs is billed as the first differential privacy frame made for this field.

The paper gives hands-on steps for putting the frame to work. A usage scenario walks through a full deployment. An attack test on a known analytics data set checks the shield. The team also maps how utility slides as privacy knobs turn. Settings trade noise against insight in plain view. The work targets scholars and practitioners who must use learner data without exposing learners.
arxiv-2501-01886:
Zhen Tian and co-authors surveyed in 2025 how self-driving cars learn to negotiate with other road users. Interactive driving — merging, yielding, and threading through intersections — is where autonomy is hardest. Deep reward-based learning has become the favored method there. Vehicles can learn self-tuning plans from experience instead of frozen rules. But methods tuned for a highway merge may fail at an unprotected turn, and the literature lacked a review that judged these methods across cases by steady, rational rules.

The survey organizes the field case by case, weighing how varied learning methods are tested for safety, efficiency. And contact quality in each setting. Its aim is useful: to show builders which testing lenses expose a method's real strengths and blind spots. And thereby to guide the design of choice-making systems that can earn large-scale deployment on public roads.
arxiv-2501-02386:
Rafaqat and four co-authors present a 2025 study of predator-prey dynamics using a fractional form of discretization. A continuous model of hunters and hunted is turned into a step-by-step version that keeps the fractional-order character of the original. Fractional steps remember past states, which can change how populations swing. The team studies when the system stays stable and when it splits into new patterns of behavior.

Two kinds of splitting get close attention: period doubling, where cycles stretch to twice their length, and the Neimark-Sacker type, where cycles sprout into rings. The authors mix theory with computer runs to see how parameter changes move the system between calm and complex regimes. Such maps of stability can inform wildlife management and conservation choices.
arxiv-2501-02486:
Gabriel Maher viewed language model prompting through the lens of control theory in a 2025 paper. Model predictive control, a workhorse of engineering, plans by repeatedly minimizing a cost over a short horizon. Prompting tricks have separately made language models better at reasoning, planning, and acting, but the two literatures rarely speak to each other.

Maher argues that, under planning prompts, a language model behaves like an implicit cost minimizer of exactly that kind. He builds a unified framework, LLMPC, that casts prompt design as predictive control design. On several planning benchmarks the framework beat standard few-shot prompting. The bridge may let engineers tune model planners with decades of control insight instead of folklore.
arxiv-2501-02886:
Mohit Gurumukhani, Ramamohan Paturi, Michael Saks, and Navid Talebanfard wrote a 2025 theoretical computer science paper on local enumeration. Enumeration means listing every valid solution to a problem. Their problem asks for all satisfying assignments of a logic formula that have an exact target weight, the number of true variables.

A 2024 paper proposed this problem as a route to breaking a major hypothesis about hard problems, and solved its first non-trivial case. This paper tackles the not-all-equal variant, where each clause must contain both a true and a false variable. Progress on these cases tests whether the hypothesis can fall. The work sits at the frontier of what algorithms can provably achieve.
arxiv-2501-04286:
Bahman Torkamandi wrote a 2025 paper mapping the jagged border between language models that train and those that fail. Training is an iterative process, and small changes in settings like the learning rate can flip it from smooth convergence to blow-up. In tiny networks, earlier work hinted that this border is fractal: zoom in, and the same ragged pattern repeats. The author tested the idea on medium-sized decoder-only transformers, the family behind modern chatbots.

Using a consistent measure of convergence, he charted trainability across learning rates for the attention and feed-forward layers separately. The frontier was no clean threshold. It broke into intricate, self-similar patches of success and failure. The fractal picture matters in practice: tuning near the edge is treacherous, because a hair's change can cross into failure many times over.
arxiv-2501-04886:
Jishen Zhang and co-authors present a 2025 paper on using phones as a sensor fleet. Modern phones carry fine motion sensors and strong connectivity. A fleet of phones can act as one spread-out instrument. The team built an Android app for each phone and a server app to run the fleet. A timing protocol over standard network calls syncs phone clocks to about sixty microseconds. That sync is the hard part: unsynced phones give mushy joint data.

Mechanical tests first grade how exact phone sensors are. Two outdoor test cases then prove the fleet in real field conditions. Science teams get a cheap instrument that is already in everyone's pocket. Earthquake shakes, bridge sway, and crowd motion are natural targets. The method turns spare phones into a coordinated lab without custom hardware.
arxiv-2501-04986:
Na-Na Gao and Jian-Fu Zhang study how cosmic rays spread through turbulent magnetic fields in a twenty twenty-five paper. Cosmic rays are fast particles from space, and both their source and their travel path stay unclear. The team uses a pulsar wind nebula, the glowing cloud around a spinning star remnant, as their test case.

They run three sets of simulations, varying how strong the magnetism is and how the turbulence is spread across scales. Energy losses from radiation are also in the model. They find the rays thin out as a power law with both distance and energy. Near the source the spread is slow, and farther out it turns fast or normal.
arxiv-2501-05186:
Federica Colonnese, Antonello Rosato, Francesco Di Luzio, and Massimo Panella present a 2025 study on detecting ADHD from brain wave recordings. They test hyperdimensional computing, a method that encodes data as very long vectors and learns with simple operations. Their model reads the time and space patterns of EEG signals, the traces of brain activity taken from the scalp. No earlier work had applied this approach to ADHD classification.

The model reached accuracy near eighty-nine percent, beating standard deep neural network rivals on the same task. More striking was its thrift with data: trained on just seven of seventy-nine patients, it matched rivals trained on everyone. That efficiency matters in clinics, where large labeled data sets are rare. The authors present the method as a fast, light route to computer-aided ADHD diagnosis.
arxiv-2501-05286:
Oumarou Oumarou and five co-authors extended a quantum simulation method in twenty twenty-five from energies to molecular properties. Quantum Krylov subspace methods are a leading hope for simulating molecules on early fault-tolerant quantum computers, but work had focused on ground-state energies. Chemists also need density matrices, which yield charges, forces, and other properties.

The authors derive formulas for the derivatives these methods need and show how to extract one- and two-particle density matrices for Krylov states, including excited states. A direct measurement plan would grow quadratically with the subspace size; theirs stays constant by using quantum signal processing to prepare the states. They validate the approach by computing the force on a small molecule's nuclei and estimating its noise level.
arxiv-2501-05386:
Fabrizio Berritta and co-authors wrote a paper from 2025 on a fast way to tune the bits of a quantum computer. Each bit, called a qubit, must hum at an exact pitch. That pitch drifts, so staff must find it again and again. The team built a method that homes in on the pitch the way a binary search homes in on a number.

Each probe step is picked on the fly to split the odds for the pitch into two near-equal halves, so each step adds a full digit of precision. The method needs no repeat probes and allows for setup and reading errors. They ran it live on a tunable chip qubit. The qubit stayed steady, its memory lasted longer, and its gates grew more true.
arxiv-2501-07886:
Ye, Laidlaw, and Steinhardt show tag polish beats pick tune when guides run weak. Post-train for word tools leans on two guide steps in the norm. Show tags train first, then pick pairs train by man picks. As tools grow, their tasks grow too hard to guide well. The team fakes weak guides with small tools and timed men. With weak shows, first train still holds some force in tests.

Pick tune, by DPO, fails to lift past first train in that state. Their swap, ILR, uses pick pairs to polish the show set. Pairs say if a made reply should swap a man show tag. Fresh first train then runs on the polished set in the loop. That loop beats pick tune on math, code, and safe tasks. Weak-guide worlds may thus spend picks on tags, not tune.
arxiv-2501-08086:
Garmaev and Fink wrote in twenty twenty-five about finding the equations behind data when effects are not local. Many discovery tools only try simple local terms and point-by-point formulas. Real systems may involve spread-out effects, extra field equations, or memory of the past. Their frame, called NOMTO, places trained neural operators inside a symbolic network. Those operators stand in for complex terms that formulas alone cannot easily write.

Candidate equations are drawn as sparse graphs that mix algebra with the operator blocks. Tests covered spread-out spatial effects, coupled fields, and time-memory terms. NOMTO recovered compact equations that included the nonlocal parts. The result widens symbolic discovery beyond local derivative libraries. It could help scientists read governing laws from messy measured data.
arxiv-2501-08586:
Weibin Zhang, Sean Preins, and others report the first run of a new detector tile design inside a collider in a 2025 experimental study. Their iron and scintillator calorimeter reads light with silicon photomultipliers mounted on tiles, a scheme planned for future detectors. The prototype rode along, parasitically, during a proton collision run at a New York collider facility.

Placed meters from the collision point near the beam line, the small prototype sampled the forward spray of particles. Running in a real collider hall tests noise, timing, and survival that bench tests cannot. A successful parasitic run builds confidence for full detectors at future machines.
arxiv-2501-09686:
Fengli Xu and a large team of co-authors surveyed reinforced reasoning in large language models in twenty twenty-five. The field has shifted from plain text generation to models that produce explicit 'thoughts' — intermediate reasoning steps — and learn them through reinforcement learning's trial and error. Letting models think longer at test time boosts accuracy further, sketching a path toward what the authors call large reasoning models.

The survey reviews the foundations of language models, then the technical components of the reasoning stack: how trajectories are generated, rewarded, and scaled. OpenAI's o1 series is treated as the landmark that made the direction concrete. The authors map open problems and the research frontier where train-time and test-time scaling meet.
arxiv-2501-09786:
Gabriela Sato-Polito, Matias Zaldarriaga, and Eliot Quataert model how the largest black holes grew by eating gas and by merging. Their 2025 paper uses a newly detected background of gravitational waves. That hum is dominated by the heaviest black holes known.

Quasar light data trace growth by gas intake, while today's black hole counts set the end point. The authors find a two-step history: gas intake peaked early, and mergers took over later. The strong wave background implies many mergers happened. That, in turn, implies quasars fed at higher average rates than a no-merger story would allow. The team lay out a tension among the three data sets. Resolving it will sharpen the story of how giant black holes reached their size.
arxiv-2501-11486:
Hamid Mousavi works on a conjecture in group theory about how elements of a finite group combine. His paper appeared in 2025. For a chosen element, one can collect all partners that generate a soluble group together with it. That collection is called the solubilizer. The conjecture says the size of a related symmetry set, the normalizer, divides the size of the solubilizer.

Mousavi gives an equivalent form of the conjecture, which may be easier to attack. He then proves it in a special case where the normalizer has a tidy two-part structure. He also classifies the finite simple groups in which some element's solubilizer is a largest subgroup of a simple two-prime size. Solo work of this kind helps map a conjecture before a full proof is in reach.
arxiv-2501-11686:
Antonio Garufi and a large team report radio views of planet-forming disks in Taurus, in work from 2025. Most past work probed these disks at short waves, while the longer centimeter range stayed thinly mapped. The team used the VLA array to catch light from twenty-one disks picked from prior ALMA surveys.

A two-part model split the glow into charged gas and dust parts. The gas part scaled with how fast each star pulls in matter, not with disk shape. Dust still shone at two centimeters, and its slope hinted that much of the inner disk stays opaque. Grain traits looked alike across disks of unlike size and shape.
arxiv-2501-12886:
Marija Mitrović Dankulov and co-authors release a large shared data set of online communities across four platforms, in a paper from 2025. Social science online has been hurt by tighter access to platform data. Comparing how groups behave across sites is hard when each site shares data in its own form.

The data set, called MADOC, gathers posts from Bluesky, Koo, Reddit, and Voat from 2012 to 2024. It holds close to nineteen million posts, hundreds of millions of comments, and tens of millions of users, all in one standard form. User names are replaced with codes for privacy. The set supports studies of toxic behavior, of what happens when groups are banned, and of users moving between platforms. Toolkits for two common analysis languages are included.
arxiv-2501-13186:
Hannah Leary, Evan Schneider, and Helena Richie test how grid detail affects simulations of gas clouds hit by wind in a 2025 paper. Such cloud-wind setups model how interstellar clouds are shredded or pushed by fast flows. The team ran wind-tunnel simulations at two wind speeds, one below and one above the speed of sound, each at five levels of detail.

In the slower wind, the cloud's fate changed sharply at a threshold detail of sixteen cells per cloud radius. The trend was not smooth, which surprised the authors. In the faster wind, results changed more steadily with detail, matching the different balance of forces early on. The study warns that simulation detail can change conclusions, not just sharpen them.
arxiv-2501-13686:
Francesco Morri and two co-authors study games where several leaders move first and one follower responds, in a 2025 theory paper. Classic treatments assume leaders know just how the follower will react. In real markets and grids, they rarely do. The team lets each leader form a guess, called a conjecture, about the others' best replies, and update play from those guesses. The frame stays open about how the guesses are formed.

They define a new balance point, the conjectural Stackelberg equilibrium, with the classic balance as a sharper case inside it. A two-stage algorithm learns the guesses from training data, then updates strategies with a promise to converge. Worked examples show the method in action. The authors aim the work at energy and market settings where rivals must guess each other's moves.
arxiv-2501-13986:
Vivek Bharadwaj, Austin Glover, Aydın Buluç, and James Demmel speed up a core math step in geometric deep learning in a 2025 paper. Networks that respect rotations lead their field on spatial tasks such as atom modeling, and their key step joins two feature sets through a sparse tensor named for Clebsch and Gordan. That step runs millions of times and had become the bottleneck.

Their graphics-chip code generator plans memory use at build time, keeps working data in fast registers, and fuses the step with the graph operation that follows it. The kernels beat both the best open package and a vendor package, with the largest gains on a chemistry model at high precision. Code for the step's gradients is included.
arxiv-2501-14986:
Pulsar timing arrays have picked up a nanohertz gravitational wave background, and one candidate source is a supercooled first-order phase transition in a hidden sector of physics. Jinzheng Li and Pran Nath model that transition in a sector with a broken U(1) gauge symmetry and fit it to data from three pulsar timing collaborations. Earlier studies struggled to get a strong enough signal from such transitions.

The authors show the missing piece is thermal history: how the hidden and visible sectors heated and cooled changes the predicted spectrum a great deal. With it included, the transitions match the array data and look promising for future detectors. Bubble collisions dominate the signal, with sound waves and turbulence suppressed, and all fitting events are detonations. The paper offers a framework for reading the early universe in these signals.
arxiv-2501-15086:
Savita Gahlaut wrote a solo cosmology paper in two thousand twenty-five testing a basic rule about distances in space. The rule, called the cosmic distance duality relation, ties two ways of measuring how far away an object is. If the rule failed, it would shake basic ideas about how light travels across the universe.

Gahlaut tests the rule without assuming any model of the cosmos, beyond its standard overall shape. Data from strong gravitational lensing give one distance measure. Data from exploding stars, the Pantheon+ set, give the other. The rule held within tight limits in both flat and curved versions of the test.
arxiv-2501-15286:
Zhi-Song Liu, Chenhang He, and Lei Li present a faster way to fill in 3D point clouds. A point cloud is a set of dots that maps a shape or scene. Sparse clouds lack detail, so tools add more dots. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, uses a method called flow matching for this task.

Their system, PUFM, starts from a mid-step fill rather than pure noise. It lines up sparse and dense clouds with a distance rule so the path stays smooth. Tests on lab data show better quality with fewer steps. Tests on room scans and road laser data show the method works on real scenes too.
arxiv-2501-16586:
Joey Lakerdas-Gayle wrote this logic paper in 2025 on how hard it is to tell when two computer-built copies of a structure are truly the same shape. The set of skills needed for that call is called an isomorphism spectrum. A base result from past work says some structures have copies whose spectrum cannot be built from finitely many parts.

Lakerdas-Gayle adds a new class of structures, called computably composite. In them, matches between copies split cleanly into matches between their parts. With that class, any blend of spectra formed by a computable union is itself a spectrum. That yields fresh cases of spectra with no finite build. The work ties a question about single structures to a tidy algebra of their parts.
arxiv-2501-16686:
Shubham Chakraborty and a team of co-authors measured how single raindrops break into size spreads. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with the raindrop size distribution. Radar reads of rain scale with the sixth power of drop size, so break up paths set how true rain gauges run. The team ran lab tests of one drop splits under many upward air flows. A two term gamma law frames the math side.

They gauge mean drop size from the theory's key sizes, which rain models oft take as set inputs. Lab spreads were set next to in air reads from flight gear. Readers who model rain get a ground link between one drop's break and the sky's full spread.
arxiv-2501-16886:
Juan Diaz Schneider, Eduardo Martínez, Pablo Levy, and Cynthia Quinteros wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It reports odd resistive switching in dense webs of silver nanowires, with an eye to brain-like computing.

A fuse-like step reshapes the web's switching in ways not seen before. By reading the electrical marks before and after the fusing, the authors propose how the effect works. That tale joins two past views of such webs: as clear electrodes, and as matter that computes. Past work showed synapse-like states in these webs. The new work adds neuron-like traits, such as sparsity and nonlinear response, when the web's density and the drive are tuned right.
arxiv-2501-17586:
Text based person search asks a computer to find a photo of a person from a written description alone. The task is hard because training data are scarce and the clues are fine details. Akshay Modi, Ashhar Aziz, Nilanjana Chatterjee, and Subramanyam note that most methods treat all correct image and text pairs as equal, yet some pairs match only weakly. Training then leans on the easy pairs, and some hard ones get thrown out as noise.

Their fix borrows from classic boosting. During training, the method spots the weak pairs, those whose top-ranked match is the wrong person, and raises their weight in the loss. The network must then work harder on exactly the cases it gets wrong. Tested on four pedestrian datasets, the add-on improves search results across the board. The authors present it as a general module that can lift existing systems without a redesign.
arxiv-2501-17686:
Kolter Bradshaw, Ammar Hakim, and Bhuvana Srinivasan simulate how rust and dirt on lithium walls change the plasma layer that hugs a fusion device wall, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Lithium coatings improve fusion plasma behavior, but lithium oxidizes fast, and the oxide sprays out far more electrons when struck. That spray reshapes the thin sheath where plasma meets wall.

Their model ties emission to particle energy and tracks both emitted and bounced-back electrons on its own. With oxidation, the sheath flipped from a smooth form to a crowded, space-charge-limited one. More electrons flowed into the wall, fewer ions arrived, and the energy dumped on the surface rose sharply. The results matter for how fast fusion walls wear down.
arxiv-2501-18486:
Lajos Diósi argues for a healthier way to join gravity with quantum matter. His paper from twenty twenty-five reviews semiclassical gravity, where gravity stays classic while matter is quantum. The standard join uses mean values only. That choice has two flaws. It skips the spread of matter, and it breaks the straight-line rule of quantum change.

Diósi sums up a fix drawn from the measurement problem. A postulated watch-and-feedback step tracks matter on its own and feeds back on it. This step kills so-called cat states, counts the spread, and keeps quantum change linear. The fix works in the slow, weak-gravity limit. Its lift to full relativity hits a wall. The author stresses that the block lies in quantum foundations, not in the gravity side.
arxiv-2501-19386:
Dao Lin, Jian Zhang, and Martin Benning sharpen images from a rotating aperture camera in a twenty twenty-five paper. A rotating synthetic aperture system turns a rectangular opening as it shoots, which blurs each frame in a distinct way. Rebuilding one sharp image from many blurred frames is an ill-posed puzzle.

Past methods guess both the blur and the image by maximizing a posterior score. The new method adds a geometric insight: the true image lies near a low-dimensional manifold inside the vast space of all images. Fitting to that manifold, with a penalty, guides the rebuild. Simulations show sharper pixel values and better kept detail than standard methods.
arxiv-2502-01686:
Rémi Tailleux and Guillaume Roullet rebuild, in a 2025 physics paper, the theory of available potential energy for use on local patches of the ocean. That energy concept cleanly splits reversible from irreversible change in layered fluids, and it guides how ocean models handle eddies and mixing. Trouble is, its classic form rests on a global reference state, which makes local use murky.

Past fixes used ad hoc local references that can drift far from the global one. The authors argue the sound route is to split the energy density into mean and eddy parts, and take the eddy part as the local form. That eddy part barely depends on the global state, as intuition wants. The frame ties modeled transfers to true dissipation rates.
arxiv-2502-02786:
Cornelis and three co-authors ask if giving a model personal data truly helps its forecasts and its reasons, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. In health care, users share private facts and expect sharper diagnoses in return. That hope had not been tested with care. The team builds a frame to measure gains in both forecast skill and clarity of reasons.

They show the two gains can move apart. A model can stay just as accurate yet give worse or better reasons. They study a standard test for group-level gains from personal data. They bound its error rate from group sizes and trait counts. On real data sets, some gains prove impossible to test at all. The work urges joint checks of skill and clarity.
arxiv-2502-03686:
Kushagra Pandey and co-authors published this machine learning study in 2025. Diffusion models generate high-quality images and other samples, but steering them is awkward. Existing guidance tricks often need extra training or work only for one task. The authors revisit guidance through the lenses of variational inference and control theory. Their framework, Diffusion Trajectory Matching, steers a pretrained model's sampling path so the final output meets a chosen cost.

The framework turns out to cover many known guidance methods as special cases. It also suggests new ones. Within it, the team built a method that reached state-of-the-art results on several inverse problems. These included linear, non-linear, and blind tasks, where the corruption itself is unknown. The method needs no extra training and works for models in pixel space or latent space alike. Code is promised in a public repository.
arxiv-2502-04486:
Jennifer Yee and Andrew Gould present a faster way to fit models to data in a 2025 paper. Fitting often means minimizing chi-squared, a score of how far model predictions sit from measurements. Their algorithm, shipped as the sfit_minimize package, estimates the curvature of that score from first derivatives alone. The same derivatives also yield each parameter's uncertainty.

They tested the method on microlensing events, brief brightenings when one star passes before another. Fits used light curves from a 2018 Korean telescope network survey. Against standard tools in a common Python library, their method beat the Nelder-Mead simplex on speed. It proved more reliable than a popular gradient method. A third standard method failed to fit these events well at all. The authors offer the package for likelihood fitting in general.
arxiv-2502-04986:
Hachem Tarif, Abdallah Slaoui, and Rachid Ahl Laamara explore a two-qubit system that can switch between acting as a heat engine and a refrigerator. Earlier work showed work extraction from a single bath using entanglement; this study adds a second bath and direct environmental dissipation, modeled with both local and global master equations. Different initial quantum states push the system into different operating modes.

The authors track entanglement and coherence through the cycle and connect them to regime transitions. They also follow information flow and how individual versus collective decoherence affects efficiency. Optimal parameter regions are identified for engine and refrigerator performance. Coherence located outside the system also turns out to influence thermodynamic quantities.
arxiv-2502-05386:
Charles Cheung, Marianna Safronova, Piet Schmidt, and a team of co-authors find a clock transition in a nickel ion. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, targets an ultra-narrow jump between two states. The natural width is so tiny that the line could anchor a superb optical clock. Finding the exact energy by trial alone would take far too long.

Two heavy calculations pinned the energy to within a hair. That small error bar let the lab team find the line in a few hours. Theory and measure agree to a rare degree for a sixteen-electron system. The method can now serve other complex ions. A nickel-based clock is the long-term prize.
arxiv-2502-05486:
Davide Batic and Denys Dutykh test the stability of phantom wormholes in two thousand twenty-five. The wormholes are static and massive, held open by phantom matter. Past work may have missed some of their ring modes. The pair use a spectral method to find those modes.

They find purely imaginary modes that past studies did not report. For scalar shakes, instability starts when a key size ratio passes one. For axial shakes, it starts at smaller ratios. Gravity waves thus press on stability sooner. When the throat far exceeds the Schwarzschild radius, the wormhole stays stable. Results fit past work but add new bounds.
arxiv-2502-05786:
Sergey Sushkov and Rafkat Galeev wrote this cosmology paper, published in 2025. It studies whether the universe can bounce, shrinking to a minimum size and re-expanding, in a gravity theory where a scalar field's motion couples directly to curvature.

The authors scan uniform, isotropic universes with flat, open, or closed spatial geometry. Bounces prove impossible without positive curvature. With it, both a turning point and a bounce exist. The minimum size depends only on the coupling strength and the curvature term, not on the matter contents. Near the bounce, the size, expansion rate, and all geometric measures stay smooth, and matter densities stay finite. Yet the scalar field itself races to infinity there. The authors conclude the full system is singular at the bounce, despite the tame geometry.
arxiv-2502-05986:
Ohav Barbi, Ori Yoran, and Mor Geva study how one rogue agent can sink a whole team of cooperating AI agents. In multi-agent systems, members share information and any one of them may end the task with a final answer, even when unsure. A wrong move by a single agent can then fail the entire system.

The team proposes watching agents as they form their answers and stepping in when an error looks likely. To test the idea, they built WhoDunitEnv, a collaboration setting where task complexity and communication structure can be tuned. Experiments there, plus tests on code writing and a resource sustainability simulation, showed gains of up to about 17, 2.5, and 20 percent. Their monitors caught the moments when agents grew confused, and the interventions stopped errors from spreading. The authors argue that guarding against rogue moves should be a standard part of multi-agent design.
arxiv-2502-06286: Botti and co-authors prove firm and fit marks for Hellinger-Reissner ghost part spaces used in stress-strain work. The marks' fixed parts rest just on the shape's girth share and the plan's grade mark, not on the mesh size. The team also probes how those fixed parts act in runs on ill-shaped forms and as the grade mark climbs step by step.
arxiv-2502-06486:
James Cotton and Fabian Sinz wrote a 2025 paper on a way to track body movement with no markers on the skin, and to say how certain each measurement is. Camera systems that watch from many sides can now capture movement well, with no dots or suits. Clinics need more than a good average measurement, though. They need the uncertainty for this joint, in this trial, on this camera setup.

The pair's earlier tool reads a whole movement through a body model that can bend in code. The new work learns the full spread of poses that fit the observed points, not just the single best one. That spread gives confidence bands for each joint at each moment. For simulated joint positions, the bands sat near ten to fifteen millimeters of space. Joint angles had bands of just a few degrees, wider at the joints farther from the body center.
arxiv-2502-06986:
Shubhayan Sarkar studies entanglement in quantum measurements in a 2025 paper. Entanglement, where linked parts of a system act as one, is a key edge that quantum tools hold over classic ones. Much is known about entanglement in quantum states, but far less about how to spot it in combined measurements, where several measures act together.

Sarkar sorts such measurements into two groups, those that are entangled and those that can be split apart. He defines a test, called a witness, that can reveal entanglement without trusting the device itself. He then shows that any entangled measurement gives an edge in a network task. For one common class, the gain holds even when no device is trusted at all.
arxiv-2502-07686:
Paras Patel and co-authors revisit how the rare-earth metal yttrium changes form under pressure in two thousand twenty-five. The metal passes through distinct crystal forms as pressure rises, and why each change happens is a basic open question. The team studies the low-pressure range with computer models based on density functional theory.

Two levels of model were compared against lab data. The simpler one badly underrated the pressures at which the forms change, while the finer one matched the lab values well. Shaky vibration modes appeared in two of the forms, and elastic softening showed at the borders as well. The authors argue that such soft modes drive the changes in this metal and may do so in its rare-earth kin.
arxiv-2502-07986:
Italo Santos and four co-authors present OSSDoorway, a game-like tool that guides students through their first contributions to open source software, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Coursework that sends students into real open projects teaches real skills, but many students get lost in the process and stall. The tool was built to scaffold that first climb.

Twenty-nine students tried the tool, answering confidence surveys before and after, plus open feedback questions. Students reported stronger confidence after using it. Clear instructions, instant feedback, and a quest system helped them learn steps like sending pull requests and working with project communities. The authors suggest that structured, game-like support can carry more students into open source work.
arxiv-2502-08186:
Weibing Zhang led a team that wrote, in two thousand twenty-five, on a warp in maps of galaxies. Each galaxy flies away as space grows. That flight shifts its light and makes its range look off. The warp is called redshift-space distortion. Maps are cleaned of a known wave mark first, in a step called BAO reconstruction, which too can bend the warp.

The team built a maths model for one neat check. They set the galaxy field from before the clean step next to the field from after it, and read the cross-power spectrum of the pair. From that cross read, they pull out the size of the warp. They tried the model on high-grade N-body runs that fake a full cosmos in code. The model held up well in all runs. The check gives surveys a fresh gauge of growth.
arxiv-2502-09386:
Sam Cohen and Ravi Chugh put forth styling program code the way web pages are styled, in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Code editors show programs with font choice and syntax highlighting, and not much more, set the same for all, no mind to the program or the task. Code style sheets, like cascading style sheets for HTML, set rules that pick parts of a program's abstract syntax tree and style how those parts show. The selector language stretches CSS constructs to fit languages with algebraic data types.

Styling can rest on meaning: syntax structure, types, and run-time values, plus author and reader tastes. As programs nest, the system adds a layout method showing nested blocks tighter than web-style box layouts. Built for a subset of Haskell, the system shows visualization tasks and hints at one frame for how editors might show programs in task-specific ways.
arxiv-2502-10186:
Jesper Nielsen, Anders Johansen, Komal Bali, and Caroline Dorn argue that the famous gap in planet sizes may be stamped in at birth, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. Close-in exoplanets cluster at two sizes, with few worlds between about one and a half and two Earth radii, a dip called the radius valley.

The usual explanations strip atmospheres away later, by starlight or by heat leaking from the core. Recent work hints the valley could instead grow out of how planets accrete gas in the first place. The authors model the whole formation path: cores grow by pebble accretion, gather atmospheres, and cool after the birth disc disperses. They ask under what conditions a primordial valley forms from those first principles. Their goal is not to fit every detail of the observed dip. It is to test whether planet formation alone can dig it.
arxiv-2502-10986:
Nam Van Tran presents a method to solve equilibrium problems that lack the usual bend toward a low point. The paper from twenty twenty-five works in optimization, where an equilibrium asks for a point that no shift can improve. The method is a relaxed proximal point scheme. It adds two inertia terms, which carry past steps' push into the next one.

Tran proves the step sequence meets a solution from any start, under stated terms. Some past results fall out as special cases of his. A numeric test backs the proofs. Double inertia aims to speed the walk while the relax step keeps it stable. Such problems arise in games, traffic, and market balance. The work gives users a proven tool for the nonconvex case, where guarantees are scarce.
arxiv-2502-12286:
Yinfeng Li, Emiliano Lorini, and Munyque Mittelmann add a notion of rational choice to the formal study of multi-agent games, in a 2025 paper. Their games unfold over time with several agents acting at once, each with likes and dislikes over how a play turns out. Earlier frameworks described what coalitions can force, but not what they can force while acting sensibly.

The authors define a minimal idea of rationality based on dominance: never pick a move another move always beats. They then extend two known logic languages with a way to say a coalition can rationally bring something about. For each language they work out how hard it is to test statements and models, and they give complete rule systems for reasoning. The paper is the long version of a conference paper, with proofs included.
arxiv-2502-14486:
Long and co-authors dig into how defenses against jailbreak attacks on language models actually work in a 2025 study. A jailbreak is a crafted prompt that tricks a model into giving answers its safety rules should block. Many defenses exist, but how they trade safety against helpfulness was not well understood.

The team reframes the task as a simple sorting test: does the model refuse a harmful prompt, and does it refuse a harmless one? From that view they find two core effects. Some defenses just raise refusal across the board, while others sharpen the model's sense of which prompts are truly harmful. They then build combined defenses that mix the two effects, both across and within each kind. Tests extend to models that also take images.
arxiv-2502-14886:
Ufaq Khan and others review how foundation AI models are changing the software that watches surgery and names what it sees. Keyhole operations make video that algorithms can parse for instruments, anatomy, and phases of the procedure. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the survey covers convolutional networks, vision transformers, and general foundation models, including a leading segmentation model, as they are woven into surgical workflows. Gains include sharper segmentation, steadier tool tracking, and better phase recognition.

The hurdles get equal billing: variable data, heavy compute, ethics, and the friction of clinical uptake. The authors map where the tools' abilities meet actual clinical needs. Their closing agenda asks for adaptability, efficiency, and ethical fit before these systems earn a routine place in the operating room.
arxiv-2502-15786:
Qiu and five co-authors read brain waves into words with a model that fits all heads in this twenty twenty-five paper. Brain-to-word tools oft fail on new heads whose wave shapes split far. A tool that takes any head shape is the core need in this field.

Inside, a brain coder with brain-led focus takes waves of any shape a head gives. A drill step then teaches it to hold rich sense marks from those waves. A stock tongue model reads those marks out as plain words at the end. Tests beat past tools on word tasks, new heads, and new tasks alike. Its focus maps can be read back to see how the call was made.
arxiv-2502-16486:
Caixiong Li and five co-authors boost open-vocabulary detection in twenty twenty-five. Such detectors must find objects from any category, even ones never seen in training. They struggle when visual and textual features misalign. Long-tailed category imbalance also drags their accuracy down in hard scenes.

Their paradigm, MQADet, is a plug-and-play add-on for existing detectors. It uses the cross-modal reasoning of multimodal large language models. A three-stage question answering pipeline guides those models to localize objects precisely. The design fits pretrained detectors without heavy extra training cost. Readers get a way to lift a detector they already have, rather than rebuilding it. The approach targets exactly the complex cases where plain detectors falter.
arxiv-2502-16586:
Pei Fu and co-authors present a 2025 review of models that read images full of text. Large models that join vision and language have changed this field fast. Their speed of growth makes the work hard to track. The review gives a full map of models built for text-rich images, such as forms, charts, and signs.

The authors lay out the timeline, build, and steps of nearly all such models. They then compare scores of picked models on standard tests. Last, they set out open problems, limits, and paths ahead. New researchers get one place to learn how the field grew and where it stands. Teams picking a model can see trade-offs before they build. The review is a guide, not a new model, and its value lies in clear order over a crowded field.
arxiv-2502-17586:
Geraldo, Katchekpele, and Kpanzou wrote in twenty twenty-five on stretching chance curves. Their topic is cubic transmutation of probability curves. New data are complex, and classic curves often fit them poorly. The method reshapes a base curve's summed shape by adding knobs. The cubic form is popular, yet it lacks one agreed meaning. Many rival forms sit in past work, never compared.

The team weighs the rival forms in theory and on data. They map how the forms relate to each other. New tweaked forms widen the allowed knob ranges for more flex. A Pareto curve serves as the worked base case. Results show where the forms agree and where they part. The study helps statisticians pick a form with eyes open. It also tidies a split corner of chance theory.
arxiv-2502-19386:
Ziqiao Weng, Weidong Cai, and Bo Zhou propose a faster way to classify autism from brain scans. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses resting-state functional MRI data. Earlier methods used either averaged signals or full moving data. Averaging loses place information, while full data costs heavy computing.

The new framework builds features at two levels for each brain. Voxel-level features keep full spatial detail from time-based changes. Region-level features capture links between brain areas. Tests on the ABIDE dataset beat earlier methods in accuracy. The approach also stayed efficient in computing cost. The authors offer the design as a guide for later autism imaging studies.
arxiv-2502-19486:
M Fournier and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on turbulence in the hot gas of a galaxy cluster, driven by its central black hole. The team used a large magnetohydrodynamic simulation with cooling and black hole feedback. They then measured velocity structure functions in both hot and cold gas phases. These statistics show how gas motion varies with scale.

The hot and cold phases showed no clear shared pattern in their statistics. The cold phase's power-law slope also swung widely across the four billion years simulated. Mock telescope views showed that projection, viewing angle, and atmospheric blur all shift the measured values. The authors warn that such biases shape what observers infer.
arxiv-2502-19786:
Zhu-yao Jin and Jun Jing propose a control strategy that corrects errors in a quantum system's Hamiltonian while the evolution is running. Large-scale quantum processors need error correction, but their method needs no extra control fields or painstaking design. It works for arbitrary error types in real time.

The idea is to open several error-resilient paths for the system, switched by projection operators on an ancilla that follow the von Neumann equation. A path-dependent global phase, varying faster than every other parameter, cancels the transitions errors would cause between paths. The corrected paths double as approximate solutions of the perturbed Schrödinger equation. A three-level population transfer test showed stronger resilience than the parallel-transport condition.
arxiv-2502-21086:
Özgün Turgut and three co-authors test foundation models on brain data in twenty twenty-five. Foundation models transformed language and vision work, and time series models have followed. Their worth for medical tasks with little data is less clear. EEG, the recording of brain signals, is the test bed here.

The team ran general-purpose time series models on three EEG tasks. Those were age prediction, seizure detection, and classification of clinical events. They compared scores against specialized EEG models and judged the quality of extracted features. The general models proved competitive. They captured features tied to age and disease markers. Readers learn that big pretrained models may cut the need for large task-specific data sets in this field.
arxiv-2503-00586:
