Zhang and colleagues present a study from twenty twenty-five on spotting Alzheimer's disease from brain scans. Early spotting matters, since brain loss cannot be undone once it sets in. Standard scans show light and dark tissue patterns, but early shifts are subtle. A second map type shows where the brain has shrunk or grown in shape. The team mixes both map types with a method that lets each guide the other. They test it on a large public dataset for this disease.

Their mix beat two other ways of joining the maps. It did best at telling disease cases from healthy ones. It also used far fewer parts than two big rival models. The authors say shape maps add real value to standard scans.
arxiv-2503-01486:
Wei-Han Li wrote this physics paper, published in 2025. It shows that faint long-range tails of interaction between particles are enough to make a quantum lattice settle into equilibrium, by scrambling its energy landscape into randomness.

The setup is a one-dimensional chain where particles cannot overlap. Li shows that with interaction tails present, any falloff rate lets the particles' arrangement imprint itself on the system's Hamiltonian, making it behave like a random matrix. The proposed test bed uses dipolar particles in optical lattices, a standard laboratory platform. Quenched systems were shown to relax to equilibrium, and the link to eigenstate thermalization was confirmed. The paper names inter-particle forces, rather than disorder added by hand, as the engine of quantum settling, offering a fresh angle on a classic problem.
arxiv-2503-01886:
Umair Zakir and three co-authors compare deep learning tools for reading earnings call transcripts. Their 2025 study asks how well machines can gauge the mood of company calls. Investors and risk managers mine such calls for signs of strength or trouble. Picking up tone at scale is hard to do by hand.

The team tests three models: BERT, its finance-tuned kin FinBERT, and ULMFiT. They weigh the models on data cleaning needs, computing cost, and tuning effort. Scores for accuracy, precision, recall, and overall balance decide the ranking. The authors also suggest upgrades that could sharpen each model on money text. The comparison helps practitioners choose a model for real financial decisions.
arxiv-2503-03386:
Soukaina Ezzeroual and Brahim Sadik use symmetry to pin down the first Maxwell time in a geometric control problem on the group SH(2), in work from twenty twenty-five. Maxwell points mark where rival optimal paths tie, and they shape the study of sub-Riemannian control. Finding them is usually hard.

Tiny symmetry motions of the system leave its structure unchanged. Reading those symmetries through the group's Lie algebra exposes quantities that stay fixed along motion. The fixed quantities and constraints cut the Maxwell point computation down to size. The authors present the symmetry route as a cleaner path to the first Maxwell time than brute force checks.
arxiv-2503-03486:
Maresa Schröder, Valentyn Melnychuk, and Stefan Feuerriegel build a way to estimate who benefits from a treatment without leaking private patient data, in this 2025 arXiv paper. Drug effects vary from person to person, and learning that variation from health records is valuable. Those records, though, hold some of the most sensitive data there is.

Their framework, DP-CATE, estimates person-level treatment effects under a strong privacy standard called differential privacy. It keeps a fairness property that guards against bias from the helper models used along the way. The recipe works with any two-stage learner of the right form and any machine learning model inside. A variant can even release the whole effect curve privately. Tests on made-up and real data show the method works.
arxiv-2503-03586:
Alperen Yildiz and five colleagues benchmark language models and agents at finding real software vulnerabilities in whole code repositories. Function-level benchmarks miss that real flaws emerge through multi-hop call chains. The team introduces JitVul, which links each function to the commits that introduced and fixed its vulnerability, covering 879 known vulnerabilities across ninety-one types.

Their results show agent systems using thought-action-observation loops with interprocedural context outperform plain language models at separating vulnerable from benign code. Chain-of-thought prompting helps the plain models, while the agents still need refinement. Both approaches sometimes miss flaws or over-analyze harmless security guards. The authors conclude there is significant room for improvement.
arxiv-2503-04586:
Yue Tan and co-authors present a 2025 theory paper on odd proton and particle states. Three states are in question, two built around the proton family and one around a lighter cousin. The team tests whether each state is a plain three-quark state. They use a quark model with a standard spread method for the math. A five-quark picture is tested as well.

One state fits the plain three-quark picture well. The other two do not fit their plain slots. In the five-quark picture, one pair forms a shallow bound state and another does not. A channel study found six resonance states plus one bound state in a set energy range. Particle theorists get a sharper view of what these states are made of. The work shows why some states need more than three quarks in the model.
arxiv-2503-05786:
Nobin Sarwar proposes FedMentalCare, a private way to tune language models for mental health reads. His paper is from two thousand twenty-five; the pack row gives no title or year, so the text head is the source. Chat tools for mental health are in wide reach, but health data are guarded by strict laws, which bars pooled training.

Federated learning trains the model across sites while data stay put, and a low-rank tweak method keeps the cost down. He tests how client data size and model shape, such as compact transformer builds, shift results in that shared setup. The frame aims at a scale-ready, privacy-aware path for real clinics, that meets both safety and cost bars.
arxiv-2503-06486:
Chen and co-authors cut made-up text in rich photo word runs from big chat models. Dense word runs oft slip in things the shot does not show. No fine score yet grades such runs at the thought grain. Their new score, HalFscore, builds on a word graph for that grade. It scores both truth and full span of each dense run. The root fault, they hold, is lean on word odds past sight.

Their fix, PerturboLLaVA, trains with warped text thrown in the mix. Warped text breaks the lean and forces weight on the shot. Sight weight lifts, made-up bits fall, and cost stays flat. Runs beat past fixes on made-up text and broad test sets. Word runs stay true to the shot at less strain cost.
arxiv-2503-07586:
JaeWon Kim and co-authors wrote this workshop paper in 2025 on design for hope. Designers often aim at cutting harm, worthy work that can still shrink what people dare to want. The one-day, in-person session, built on a first run at a 2024 meeting, teaches ways to aim higher. It ties design craft to hope theory, which sees hope as goals plus paths plus the will to walk them.

Hands-on tasks anchor the day. Attendees reframe a problem, build a shared shelf of design methods that fit hope theory, and reflect on how to keep hopeful lines of work alive. The aim is skill for handling tangled social ills without losing nerve. The authors offer the plan as a way for research groups to set bold goals and map real paths toward them.
arxiv-2503-08886:
Kristian Barajas and Wesley Campbell present a theory for modeling quantum gate dynamics without the usual rotating-wave shortcut, in a physics paper from 2025. That shortcut drops fast-oscillating terms and fails when drives are strong. Real devices increasingly work in that strong regime, where several timescales act at once.

Their quantum averaging theory builds a rotating frame tied to the fast motion, leaving an effective description for the slow part. Fast effects are kept, not discarded, so high-fidelity two-qubit gates remain within reach. Applied to a standard trapped-ion entangling gate, the theory's numbers converged quickly to exact simulations even at strong coupling. The authors offer both accuracy and a usable intuitive model.
arxiv-2503-10686:
Anzhe Cheng and colleagues improved image segmentation for low-resolution pictures in 2025. Robots, augmented reality, and large scene systems often get only small, blurry images, yet they still must outline what is where. Classic U-shaped networks lose detail in clutter, while big transformer models cost too much for the job.

Their MaskAttn-UNet adds a mask attention step that spotlights key regions and quiets busy backgrounds, balancing fine detail with wide context. On three benchmark sets shrunk to small squares, it handled meaning, instance, and full-scene labeling about as well as leading methods, at far lower cost than transformers. Cheap, sharp outlines suit devices with little power to spare.
arxiv-2503-12486:
Carro, Carlos Pérez, and Rodolfo Torres extend compactness extrapolation to weighted mixed Lebesgue spaces. Their paper from twenty twenty-five proves a Fréchet-Kolmogorov style theorem fit for those spaces, where norms mix across variables. Compactness of operators is the currency: which maps squeeze bounded sets into tight ones. A Rubio de Francia style extrapolation theory then carries compactness from one weight setting to many.

Several applications round out the work. Extrapolation is prized because a hard proof at one exponent or weight can seed results across a family for free. Doing it for compactness, not just boundedness, is the delicate part. The paper supplies analysts with a transfer machine for the mixed-norm world, where classical tools often stall.
arxiv-2503-12686:
Jacqueline Mitchell and three co-authors asked how language models reason when they check code, in a paper published in 2025. Models now draft loop proof facts for verification tools, but their thought path was a black box. Two prompt styles were built to draw out a set style of step-by-step thought, the kind that proof craft uses. The team ran top models on 22 small programs from a known verification set.

Each invented proof fact was graded for soundness: would it hold if the code ran? The wrong ones were sorted by theme to find the kinds of slips that recur. The readings show where model reasoning parts from true step logic. The authors aim the findings at two fronts: safer use of models in verification work, and training that fixes the recurring slips.
arxiv-2503-14186:
Mehdi Testouri, Gamal Elghazaly, Faisal Hawlader, and Raphael Frank put a car driven from afar on a live 5G net. Such far drive is a human back-up for self-drive cars stuck in hard spots. Its fate rests on lag and on how sound the link is. The team fit a stock electric car with a far-drive rig.

Glass-to-glass lag, the full path from lens to screen, came to a mean of 202 ms. Round-trip time for commands had a mean of 47 ms. The gap points to video, not control, as the tight spot. The wheel work was still mostly true and quick. The paper ends with tips for safer use in the field. Real bench scores, not sims, ground the talk. New work aims at the video path.
arxiv-2503-14686:
Ferraiuolo and co-authors published this gravitational-wave study in 2025. Merging black holes and neutron stars ripple spacetime, and those ripples carry a measure of distance. To turn distance into cosmic expansion rates, astronomers need each source's redshift. The spectral siren method infers redshift from the population's mass pattern instead of from light. This paper asks what the background hum of all unresolved mergers adds to the method.

Using a simulated five-detector network at upcoming sensitivity, the background tightened limits on low values of the expansion rate and the dark matter share. It sharpened knowledge of where merger rates peak in cosmic time. Most precision on the expansion rate came from individually resolved events. A real-data check with fifty-nine mergers from the third observing run confirmed the pattern: at current sensitivity, adding the background changed little. Future detectors should make the hum speak louder.
arxiv-2503-15586:
Zeqi Gu and four co-authors teach a model to rig drawn figures of many body shapes so they can be posed and moved. Past image moving methods lean on human body maps and large sets of marked real video. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

Given just a few frames of a new figure with its bone map, the model infers a rig that can pose it in fresh ways. A made up data pipeline builds varied shapes and skins on the fly for training, with a new bone map form. The team also built the first video set of this kind with both human like and non human figures, each frame marked with key points.
arxiv-2503-15986:
Zeqi Zheng, Yanchen Huang, Yingchao Yu, Zizheng Zhu, Junfeng Tang, Zhaofei Yu, and Yaochu Jin add a brain-like brake to spiking transformers in two thousand twenty-five. Spiking networks send sparse pulses and save energy, and transformer forms of them top many tasks. Their attention blocks, though, are copied from standard models and waste focus on off-topic tokens.

Their design copies lateral inhibition, the brain trick where active cells quiet their neighbors. Attention thus leans toward apt tokens and away from noise. Scores rose on image sets, event camera sets, and a large image bank. On the biggest set, the model beat a top rival with far fewer parameters and half the time steps.
arxiv-2503-16486:
Aamina and five co-authors present Accodemy, an AI platform to help new programmers beat the fear of coding. Their twenty twenty-five paper notes that beginners often quit from anxiety: fear of failure, complex topics, and pressure from peers and parents all pile up. Standard course platforms do little about that fear.

Accodemy pairs coding lessons with support for the learner's state of mind. It makes custom practice questions, offers mindfulness quotes and tips, and adds a chatbot that acts as a motivator. Personal roadmaps and game elements keep users engaged. Progress is tracked so the plan can adapt to each learner.
arxiv-2503-17186:
The ATLAS Collaboration reported searches in twenty twenty-five for sleptons, hypothetical partner particles of electrons and muons. In some theories, each slepton decays into a normal lepton and a stable neutralino. The team focused on a hard region where the two particles have close masses, long a blind spot.

They used proton collision data from the ATLAS detector at thirteen teraelectronvolts. Events needed a high-energy jet, missing momentum, and two leptons of the same type with opposite charge. Results mostly matched standard expectations, with small deviations in both searches. The work largely closed the sensitivity gap. It ruled out selectrons up to three hundred gigaelectronvolts and smuons up to three hundred fifty in the models tested.
arxiv-2503-17486:
Zhengqing Gao and a team of co-authors slim down 3D Gaussian splatting by teaching scenes a small set of prototypes. Their work appeared in twenty twenty-five. Splatting renders new views beautifully but needs millions of blobs, too many for light devices.

Instead of compressing finished blobs, ProtoGS learns shared prototypes that stand in for clusters of them. Camera-derived anchor points group the primitives, and clustering inside each group seeds the prototypes. Anchors and prototypes then train jointly under the rendering loss. Gaussian counts fell sharply on real and synthetic scenes. Rendering speed climbed while image quality held or improved. The authors frame prototypes as the natural vocabulary of a splatted scene.
arxiv-2503-19186:
Parisa Mollaei and Amir Barati Farimani use machine learning to find which motions matter most for a protein's job. Their 2025 paper links protein shape to protein function. Proteins move as they work, and a few key paths, called reaction coordinates, drive those changes.

Their model blends a kernel method with a classic tool that shrinks data to its main patterns. It learns from computer simulations that track atoms over time. Applied to a well-known receptor protein, the model picked out the right coordinates. A network view also showed which protein units move together for a given trait. The authors offer the model as a tool for seeing structure and function at once, which can guide drug work.
arxiv-2503-19586:
Hanlin Wu and co-authors published this comparison study in 2025. Hearing a voice tells us who is speaking, and listeners fold that knowledge into understanding words. The team asked whether large audio-language models do anything similar. They compared two such models with human brain recordings. Their tests used sentences that clash with the speaker, either against social stereotypes or against basic biology. A man saying he gets manicures was one social example; a man claiming pregnancy was a biological one.

One model, Qwen2-Audio, showed surprise at speaker clashes, and its surprise scores predicted a known human brain response. The second model, Ultravox 0.5, barely reacted to speaker traits. Neither model copied the human split between the two clash types, which trigger different brain signals in people. The authors conclude that current models partly track speaker context but process it through different mechanisms than the human brain.
arxiv-2503-21386:
Alex Altland and four co-authors revisit a key statistic of random matrix theory, a tool for describing disordered and chaotic quantum systems. Their paper came out in 2025. The statistic, the spectral form factor, tracks how energy levels of a system repel and correlate over time.

Its average behavior is roughly bell-shaped, but small corrections matter for modern applications, and earlier studies disagreed about them. The authors attack the problem with two independent methods: one based on kernel functions, one on a supersymmetric field theory. Both give the same next-order corrections, and both match computer simulations. Their kernel analysis also exposes where previous work went wrong. The paper is written as a guide, pointing out new paths and pitfalls for these fine-grained statistical questions.
arxiv-2503-22886:
Ron Vainshtein, Zohar Rimon, Shie Mannor, and Chen Tessler introduce Task Tokens, a 2025 method for steering humanoid behavior models toward a chosen job. Behavior foundation models imitate broad human-like control and can produce many motions on command, but coaxing one exact task out of them takes fiddly prompt craft and often lands short. Their method leaves the big model frozen and trains a small new encoder beside it.

The encoder reads the scene and emits extra tokens, which the frozen model takes as added input, like a learned prompt written in the model's own language. Training uses reinforcement learning, so builders can blend reward goals with their own priors. Across varied tasks, including ones outside the training spread, the tokens steered performance up while the model's range of motion stayed intact. The approach also mixes with other prompt styles, the authors report.
arxiv-2503-23186:
Vishnu Vardhan Baligodugula and Fathi Amsaad compare strategies for training neural networks across many machines in a 2025 paper. Big models exceed one device, so training splits the work. Data parallelism copies the model and splits the data; model parallelism splits the model itself; hybrids mix both.

The authors benchmarked the options on image classification with the CIFAR-100 data set, measuring time, convergence, and accuracy. The hybrid approach trained 3.2 times faster than a single device at similar accuracy. They also propose a scheduler that switches strategy as conditions change, gaining a further 18 percent in efficiency. Such scheduling helps labs get more from limited hardware.
arxiv-2503-24186:
Souvik Dey, Jian Liu, Yuki Mifune, and Yuya Otake wrote a math paper in 2025 on rings and their module theory. A ring is a set with addition and multiplication rules. The authors study a category that captures where a ring fails to be smooth. They ask when that category can be built from a single object.

They prove that strong building power and one measure of the category are tightly linked. For rings that are domains with dimension at most one, one holds exactly when the other is nonzero. They also study sets where a module needs endless resolution steps. That set turns out to be closed, with a clean ideal that defines it. A last result links building power for all modules to the dimension of the ring.
arxiv-2504-00486:
Kurt Polzin and Giovanni Dematteis study how ocean eddies feed internal waves in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Mesoscale eddies are vast swirls that stir the ocean. Internal waves are ripples that travel inside the water column. The two exchange energy in ways that shape ocean mixing. This paper, the third in a series, tests a forecast formula for that exchange against data from the Sargasso Sea.

The formula updates a theory from the nineteen seventies with a relaxation timescale. The match with observations is strikingly good. It suggests eddy-wave coupling rules the region's wave energy budget. The authors also address where the cascade of swirling energy ends. Their work helps climate modelers, since ocean mixing steers heat and carbon uptake.
arxiv-2504-03586:
Antonakoglou and four co-authors present CAMINO, a system that runs network services across cloud and edge sites on its own, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Modern services must scale fast and need little hands-on work. CAMINO takes high-level goals from users, called intents. It turns those goals into real setups without manual steps.

The system is built from small modules that can be swapped or grown. It stores setups as data, not scripts, so changes stay clear and safe. It watches live resource use to place work where it fits best. It handles the full life of each service, from launch to removal. The team shows it works well for telecom tasks that span many edge sites.
arxiv-2504-05486:
Thomas Body and co-authors fix a simple model for safe plasma exhaust in fusion machines, in work from 2025. Future tokamaks must shed heat in the exhaust zone to shield the wall plates, a state called detachment. A classic model is fast and clear but overstates the impurity load needed to reach that state by about fivefold.

Their extended model matches a scaling law drawn from running machines. Three added effects drive the fix: sideways drift in the exhaust, losses from neutral atoms near the plates, and turbulent spread of the heat channel. The new model also lands on the measured impurity load, so control tools can trust it.
arxiv-2504-05986:
Konstantinos Bampouras, a solo author, examines two classic results in a 2025 math paper. The setting is a family of function spaces tied to a bounded region. A recent result showed that a famous theorem about certain operators fails when the region has many extreme points. He asks whether the theorem can survive under a stronger demand on the operator.

He proves it still fails for a broad class of smooth curved regions, once the demand passes a threshold. For box-like regions called polytopes, he proves a related inequality for all suitable functions. A consequence is that a stronger class of operators on polytope spaces is always generated by a bounded function, as the classic theorem would wish.
arxiv-2504-06886:
Chen and three co-authors introduce a way to compute how temperature fluctuates inside hot quark-gluon matter. Their new thermodynamic function links those fluctuations to the spread of particle momenta seen in heavy-ion collisions. The team computes temperature fluctuations of several orders for the first time.

The fluctuations drop sharply as matter changes from a hadron gas to quark-gluon plasma. The drop traces back to the much larger heat capacity of the plasma phase. The skew of the fluctuations also turns negative. The authors propose these patterns as a signal experiments could measure. That would open a new route to mapping the phases of strong-interaction matter.
arxiv-2504-07086:
Headlines about language models learning to reason have raced ahead, but the tests behind them may be shakier than they look. Andreas Hochlehnert and co-authors audit those tests in this 2025 paper and find that small choices, from decoding settings to random seeds and even hardware, swing the scores.

Re-running recent methods under one strict, shared protocol, they find most reinforcement learning gains shrink to modest size and often overfit small benchmarks. Plain supervised fine-tuning generalized better in their hands. The team releases all code and outputs, urging the field to adopt tighter reporting standards before claiming breakthroughs.
arxiv-2504-07386:
Fang-Fang Du and three co-authors propose a scheme for high-dimensional quantum entanglement in a 2025 paper. Most quantum systems use two-level units, but units with more levels, called qudits, offer larger state spaces and better resistance to loss. The scheme links a flying photon with stationary emitters through waveguides.

By choosing which input port the photon enters, the setup heralds a random maximally entangled state of two four-level qudits. The design extends to three or more qudits using standard gate steps. Error detection built into the emitter-waveguide system keeps the states faithful. The authors note the scheme can scale to still higher dimensions, widening its use in quantum information work.
arxiv-2504-08386:
Khaledian, Ghadiridehkordi, and Khaledian test in twenty twenty-five whether shrinking number vectors keeps search quality while slashing cost. Systems that ground chatbots in outside texts store long vectors for each passage, which strains memory and speed on huge finance corpora. They compressed vectors with a classic method that keeps the main axes of variation, then compared search metrics.

Cutting vectors from thousands of numbers to about a hundred sped retrieval up to dozens of times. The index also shrank by a similar large factor. Agreement with human similarity scores dipped only modestly. The authors say the trade suits real-time finance platforms where speed, memory, and accuracy must hold together.
arxiv-2504-10086:
Bağcı and Hoggan present a paper from twenty twenty-five on new atomic orbital functions tested on helium-like atoms. Standard equation sets for two-electron atoms are solved by a self-consistent loop. The basis uses new exponential-type orbitals that are complete and orthonormal. Unusually, the quantum numbers may take fractional values. The orbitals solve a Schrödinger-like equation the authors derived. For hydrogen, the fractional scheme matched the known ground level. This study extends the test to the simplest correlated systems.

Helium-like ions carry the first real electron correlation effects. The team examine how fractional quantum numbers affect the results. The work probes whether the fractional basis helps atomic calculations. It continues their program on non-integer orbital sets.
arxiv-2504-11586:
Nicholas Barth and six co-authors test how well stars can be traced back to their birth clusters by their motion and their chemistry at once. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-five.

This tag method has been put forth as a strong tool, but its true worth is still in doubt. The team uses motion data from one big sky survey and chemistry data from the next. Their set holds known open clusters plus fake field stars. They run a boot-strap test of each mix of motion terms and element shares. Each mix is scored on how well it finds the true clusters back. The work weighs a hyped method on hard counts.
arxiv-2504-12086:
Mohammadali Moghimi, Sharu Theresa Jose, and Shana Moothedath design decision algorithms that learn from late feedback in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Contextual bandits choose actions using side information and learn from the rewards that follow. In recommendation systems and clinical trials, those rewards arrive only after random, unknown delays, because outcomes take time to appear. Their algorithm, Delayed NeuralUCB, explores using an upper confidence bound strategy adapted to neural reward models.

Assuming delays are independent draws from a sub-exponential distribution, the authors derive an upper bound on cumulative regret over a finite horizon. A second variant, Delayed NeuralTS, swaps in Thompson sampling exploration. Experiments on real datasets, including MNIST and the Mushroom dataset, plus comparisons against benchmark methods, showed the algorithms coping well with varying delays. The setting targets real deployments where feedback lag is unavoidable.
arxiv-2504-12586:
Gustavo Alves Bezerra, Andris Ambainis, and Renato Portugal speed up search on special graphs in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Quantum walks can find marked items faster than classical random walks. The team targets two-tessellable graphs, a wider family than ordinary bipartite graphs.

They adapt two quantum walk styles to these graphs and plug in a known fast algorithm for balanced bipartite search. The result finds a marked vertex with a quadratic speedup in oracle queries over classical chain-based search. Generalizing the walk models widens where quantum search helps. The authors present the speedup as a step in mapping which graph shapes suit quantum methods. Classical search pays a square penalty by comparison.
arxiv-2504-13186:
Yassine Habchi leads a team reviewing how deep learning and large language models are used to detect cancer. Their review appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Deep learning now beats older machine learning, and often human readers, at spotting disease. Many reviews cover single slices of this field. A broad account of cancer detection has been missing. The authors aim to fill that gap.

They survey transfer learning, reinforcement learning, and federated learning. Transformer models and large language models get their own treatment. Each approach helps with a known pain point. Transfer learning eases data scarcity, while federated learning guards privacy across hospitals. Accuracy gains run through the survey. The paper maps where the methods stand and what blocks wider use.
arxiv-2504-14186:
Tian-Fang Ma, Jia-Shu Niu, and Hui-Fang Xue measure how the pulse periods of four bright variable stars drift over decades. These stars, high-amplitude delta Scuti stars, swell and shrink in a single steady mode. Their beat slowly speeds or slows as they age. Timing the brightest moment across many years reveals that drift.

New timings came from a space telescope and two amateur-professional observer networks. Combined with records in the older literature, they trace each star's observed-minus-expected curve. Three stars show periods lengthening at tiny yearly rates. The fourth is shortening instead. The authors weigh what stage of life each star sits in. They also discuss what inner changes could drive the drift. Such long baselines turn bright stars into clocks for stellar aging.
arxiv-2504-14686:
José Suárez-Varela and Andra Lutu wrote a 2025 paper on spotting faults in mobile networks. A modern network has thousands of cells across several generations of technology. Faults hide among normal swings caused by crowds and travel. Their tool judges each cell against its neighbors, so local odd behavior stands out from city-wide patterns.

The system, called c-ANEMON, uses a graph neural network that learns from cells and their surroundings over time. It was trained on three months of data from a large European city with nearly eight thousand cells. The model carried over to areas it had not seen, which suggests one model can serve a wide region. The team then read the flagged faults by hand and graded their severity for repair crews.
arxiv-2504-15186:
Therrar Kadri, Rahil Omairi, Khaled Smaili, and Seifedine Kadry work out the math of adding up independent random quantities that follow the XGamma distribution, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-five. That distribution blends the exponential and gamma families and often bends to fit data better than the exponential alone.

The authors consider sums where each term has its own parameters. They show the density of the sum can be written as a sum of Erlang densities, a tidy closed form. From it, the other standard statistical functions follow exactly. They then study how to estimate the parameters from data by maximum likelihood. A real dataset test rounds out the paper. There, the new sum model fits better than rival sums built from exponentials. Such sums arise wherever waiting times or lifetimes are pooled.
arxiv-2504-15486:
Chan, Begelman, and Dexter model polarized X-rays from black holes in twenty twenty-five. Gas falling into a black hole scatters X-rays, and that scattering can polarize the light. Heat driven motion of electrons is the usual source studied. Inside a zone called the plunging region, gas free falls at near light speed, and that bulk motion may also polarize light.

The team traces rays through a thin falling plasma in a relativistic model. For a black hole seen near edge on, total polarization could reach about seven to eight percent. Resolved maps show much higher local values, but signals from zones cancel in part. The authors say the bulk effect could exceed the heat driven effect. Future X-ray polarization data could thus reveal the plunging region directly.
arxiv-2504-15986:
Yu Gao and colleagues mapped the hidden peer network of the Monero cryptocurrency in a 2025 study. Monero's privacy design deliberately hides who connects to whom, which protects users but blinds researchers trying to judge the network's health and decentralization. A recent protocol update removed timestamps, closing the easiest inference route, so the team built a new method that works from peer lists gathered in network traffic flows.

Validation shows the inference is accurate and improves with longer watching. The resulting map, the first for the updated protocol, reveals connectivity patterns and outsized supernodes that hold the network together. Findings suggest concrete protocol and security improvements for privacy coin networks.
arxiv-2504-17786:
Daniel Salib and Bitan Roy explore how disorder changes a topological crystal in a 2025 paper. Topological insulators conduct on their surfaces while staying insulating inside, and they resist mild randomness. Strong disorder, though, can drive them into a plain insulating state. The authors study what happens near that turning point.

As the change nears, small droplets of the plain phase appear inside the topological material. On the other side, tiny pockets of the topological phase survive inside the plain one. Near the transition, maps of local markers show these islands forming fractal patterns with detail at many scales. The authors suggest this behavior may be generic across dirty topological materials of many kinds and dimensions.
arxiv-2504-18686:
Mustafa Musab, Joseph Chege, Arie Yeredor, and Martin Haardt estimate probability densities by compressing them, in the spirit of minimum description length. Real data are often mixtures with sharp local structure that uniform histograms flatten. Histogram steps also break the smoothness that gradient methods and clustering want. Their framework chooses bins by quantile cuts under a description-length criterion.

The joint density becomes a probability tensor, factorized by a canonical polyadic decomposition. Binning and factorization are unified rather than staged. Synthetic tests and a dry bean classification data set exercise the method. The result is a nonparametric estimator that adapts its resolution to the data's own complexity. Description length acts as the referee: structure is kept only when it pays for its own encoding. The approach targets the many applied problems where the density itself is the object of interest.
arxiv-2504-18786:
Anup Agarwal, Venkat Arun, and Srinivasan Seshan argue that congestion control design should start with what they call contracts. Their paper from two thousand twenty-five notes that these algorithms work half-blind. They cannot see link capacity or rival flows, so each one signals its fair share through cues like loss or delay.

The choice of contract, they show, fixes key traits at steady state. Those traits cover how well the method copes with cue errors, how fair it is, how much congestion it allows, and what link rates it suits. No choice wins on all fronts, so tradeoffs are built in. The frame also flags design traps that starve some flows, and tests back the claims.
arxiv-2504-19386:
Ziad Ismaili Alaoui and Nikhil S. Mande study a puzzle about winners in directed graphs in a 2025 theory paper. A king is a point that can reach every other point in at most two steps. It is well known that round-robin contests, where each pair has one directed edge, always hold at least one king. The pair ask how many edge checks are needed to find one in wider graph classes.

For general directed graphs, they show the check count must grow with the square of the size, so no fast shortcut exists. They prove the same hard limit for a stricter winner type, the strong king, even inside round-robin contests. That result settles an open question from earlier work in the negative. Their graph designs may help future work on contest winners.
arxiv-2504-19686:
Alessandra D'Alise, Giulia Muco, and Francesco Sannino study, in a 2025 paper, what happens along a charged line defect inside quantum electrodynamics when a scalar field is tied to the electrons. A Wilson line, an infinitely heavy charged probe, reshapes the theory near itself, and four-fermion couplings can grow strong there. The paper works out that local dynamics in detail.

There is a window of parameters, where the electron charge shrinks while the line's charge grows so their product stays fixed, in which four-fermion terms take over the behavior near the line. The authors uncover the fixed points of this regime and chart their critical behavior. The result maps a corner of defect physics where interactions usually treated as small become the main story. It speaks to theorists studying how defects reorganize quantum fields around them.
arxiv-2504-20086:
Gehrmann and a large team map safety risks of generative AI in finance and test current guards, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. Banks face strict laws on what advice and content they can give. Most AI safety work looks at broad harms like bias or toxic speech. That misses risks tied to finance rules and duties.

The team builds a risk list shaped for finance products and laws. They weigh what a breach would mean for clients, firms, and markets. Then they test open-source guard tools on data from red-team probes. The guards missed most risks on the finance list. The gap shows that general guards are not enough. Firms need checks built for their own rules and products.
arxiv-2504-21186:
Xu and eight co-authors tackled out-of-distribution detection for graph data in twenty twenty-five. Graphs model networks of linked items, from citations to social ties. Detection means flagging items that do not belong to the known classes, a safety need in open settings.

Zero-shot detection needs no labeled training examples, only class names. Using a graph foundation model, a large pre-trained system for graphs, they showed class names alone can drive detection well. Their method often beat supervised rivals that use many labeled nodes. When names for the odd classes are missing, GLIP-OOD asks a language model to invent informative fake labels from unlabeled data. Tests on four benchmark datasets matched leading supervised performance without any labeled nodes.
arxiv-2504-21786:
Yu Wang, Zhangyu Yang, Xingyao Wu, and Christian Mendl improve a classic eigenvalue method for tensor-network states, in this 2025 arXiv paper. The Lanczos method can find several low-energy states of a quantum system at once and avoids the local traps of its main rival. But squeezing states into a matrix product form forces cuts that blur accuracy.

Their modified thick-block version fights that blur. They tested it on two standard one-dimensional models, the Fermi-Hubbard model and the Heisenberg model in a field, aiming at the five lowest states of each. In every test the method reached the best accuracy the chosen state size allows. The authors present Lanczos as a dependable route to many-state spectra in this format.
arxiv-2505-01186:
Saeid HaghighiFard and Sinem Coleri design a defense for shared learning among moving vehicles. In this setup, cars train a joint model without sharing raw data. Layers of servers group the cars into clusters to save bandwidth and handle motion. Bad or faulty cars can send false updates that poison the joint model.

Their defense scores each car's past accuracy, work rate, and odd records to judge trust. Checks flag updates that stray in size or in direction from the group. Trusted cars earn more weight in the merged update, and clusters are cross-checked for joint attacks. Tests show the method cuts the time to reach a good model next to rival defenses. It holds for both near and far server layouts.
arxiv-2505-01386:
Irene Wang and eight co-authors present CATransformers, a framework that designs neural networks and their computer chips together with carbon emissions as a goal. Their paper came out in 2025. Artificial intelligence carries a lifetime carbon cost: energy burned in training and use, plus the footprint of manufacturing the hardware.

Their framework counts both costs early, while the model and chip are still being designed. Searching that joint space reveals trade-offs that speed-only or energy-only design misses. Across a range of transformer models, the method cut total emissions by up to about a third while holding accuracy and speed. A case study on models that mix text and images shows the approach extends beyond language. The code is released openly.
arxiv-2505-02286:
Allen Zang and four co-authors asked what entanglement purification in quantum networks is sure to buy. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with a fix step for shared quantum links. Raw links spawn by chance and fade in memory, so a network must weigh if a fix run is worth its time. The team studies a CNOT based loop method, known to be best in many cases. They ask what gain is sure, for any mixed set of inputs.

When a sure gain exists, they also find the best time to run the fix. Past that point, fade eats the gain. Readers who build quantum networks get a rule for when to purify and for how long to wait.
arxiv-2505-03186:
Detao Bai, Zhiheng Ma, Xihan Wei, and Liefeng Bo wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five, with two names swapped in order between the catalog and its text. It learns audio-visual codes from the natural sync of lips, voice, and words.

One training aim pulls matching sound and sight traits together. The other asks the model to guess the text. Both ride on the lips' lockstep with speech. With just a few hundred hours of marked data, the codes prove broad in use. They set a best mark in audio-visual speech reading on the LRS2 set. Lip-only reading scores well too. In noise the codes lift scores by over seventy percent. Speech cleanup, parting, and speaker spotting all gain as well.
arxiv-2505-03786:
Md Fahim Anjum tests a small reasoning model as a judge of answers in a paper from two thousand twenty-five, written alone. Planning systems often pair a generator that proposes answers with a discriminator that ranks them. Whether reasoning models judge better than larger plain models was unclear.

Anjum benchmarks a distilled reasoning model of one point five billion parameters against several larger non-reasoning models on a text-to-SQL task. A new method extracts soft scores from the reasoning text for fine ranking. The small model beat a seven billion model by wide margins and edged a thirteen billion model on execution accuracy. More context or thinking time did not always help. Reasoning models also proved weaker as generators than as judges.
arxiv-2505-04186: Meng Yang, writing alone in 2025, gives a direct proof of a key inequality on the Sierpiński gasket. The gasket is a famous fractal, a triangle endlessly pierced by smaller triangle holes. The cutoff Sobolev inequality is a tool that helps estimate how heat spreads on such rough shapes. It had long been seen as very hard to prove directly on the gasket. Yang's paper presents that direct proof. The result supports the wider study of heat flow on fractals, where smooth calculus tools do not apply.
arxiv-2505-04286:
Denis Zelent studies time-frequency concentration in a symmetric function space in two thousand twenty-five. Concentration operators ask how much of a signal can sit inside a set window in both time and frequency at once. His space weights a function and its Fourier twin alike, a setup past the classic band-limited case.

He shows the Bargmann transform maps the space cleanly onto a weighted Fock space, a known arena for such problems. The space's reproducing kernel is then pinned down. A surprise follows: for a two-sided concentration operator, the eigenvalues plunge from near one to near zero over a range as wide as the near-one range itself. That wide plunge breaks the classic pattern Zelent contrasts it with.
arxiv-2505-05386:
Aifei Zhang and six colleagues probe charge flow, in a 2025 preprint, in a quantum Hall sample built to order. Quantum Hall systems can carry current along edges in opposite directions at once. How those counter-flowing channels mix decides the measured transport, and past results looked messy and size-dependent. The team built a sample where the number of channels and their mixing length can be tuned.

Special reservoirs along the path force the channels to share charge over a set length. When the counts of up- and downstream channels differ, flow stays ballistic, meaning clean and direct. When the counts match, flow turns diffusive past a mixing length that grows sharply. The setup lets the team mimic exotic states using well-understood ones, with full control of the settings. The authors say this control can clarify a range of odd quantum Hall effects.
arxiv-2505-05786:
Xiangzhe Yuan, Jiajun Wang, Qian Wan, and Siying Hu let people live a day inside stigmatized jobs through language model driven interactive fiction, in work from twenty twenty-five. So called dirty work draws social scorn that harms workers and fairness. Stepping into another's shoes can soften that bias.

One hundred participants played through stories from four such occupations. Understanding rose clearly, and players reported strong empathy and connection with the workers. Interviews with fifteen players praised the immersion and emotional pull. They also flagged thin context in the generated scenes and moments where stereotypes crept back in. The authors call the approach a scalable stigma fighter with known limits.
arxiv-2505-06386:
Donghao Ren and co-authors (2025) present Embedding Atlas, a tool for exploring the maps that machine learning makes of data. Embedding projections turn large data sets into scatter plots, but existing tools fight their users. Loading data is tedious, big sets crawl, and results do not flow back into other work. Metadata views sit in separate programs. The authors built their tool on modern web technology to remove that friction.

Density-based clustering and automatic labeling help users read structure at a glance. Linked views show metadata beside the map, inside the same tool. Benchmarks show the tool rendering millions of points in real time. A competitive analysis against popular rivals found its feature set aimed precisely at the friction points. The authors release the tool as open source. They hope easy, fast maps become a default step in how teams inspect models and data, not a specialist chore.
arxiv-2505-06586: Baghaei, Frassu, Tanaka, and Viglialoro asked in twenty twenty-five how a plus total flow changes a known model of cells that chase a chem cue. Most work on that model sets the total flow of cells and chem to zero. Their work lets that flow be plus, by edge rules of the Robin kind that let stuff pass at the bounds. The pick is drawn from real acts at cell bounds in life, and new traits of the system show up in that frame.
arxiv-2505-07486:
Huiyun Tang and Anastasia Sergeeva argue for a vaccine-style approach to fighting false information online, in this 2025 arXiv position paper. The usual response, debunking, corrects false claims after they spread, but it is slow and limited. The authors favor prebunking: training people ahead of time to spot weak reasoning and reject false claims on their own.

Their design pairs an opening intervention, the shot, with later booster sessions meant to keep the protection from fading. Artificial intelligence tools support each stage, from spotting likely false content to tailoring practice material. The paper lays out the combined design and how it could build lasting critical thinking, rather than chasing one false claim at a time.
arxiv-2505-07686:
Muzhi Dai, Chenxu Yang, and Qingyi Si wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It tackles overthinking in reasoning models, which spin out long chains of thought even when a short one would do.

Their method, S-GRPO, trains a model on a single chain of thought and lets it stop at varied points along that chain to answer at once. Right answers earn less reward the later the stop comes, so the model learns to quit once its thought is ripe. Tests on math and science benchmarks, with top models such as Qwen3, cut output length by a third to three fifths. Accuracy rose at the same time, by a few points at most.
arxiv-2505-08386:
Xiaokai Hou and colleagues propose a new quantum method for the shortest vector problem, a hard math task behind lattice-based codes. Their paper from two thousand twenty-five targets near-term quantum machines with few usable qubits. Older methods map the task onto a full network of linked qubits, which grows too hard at large sizes.

Their method, called VQKZ, splits the task into smaller parts on projected sublattices. This cuts the qubit count a great deal. In tests, it handled lattice sizes well beyond what older methods could reach. It also found shorter solution vectors than those older methods, which matters for testing how safe lattice codes are.
arxiv-2505-09186:
Yuichi Harikane and ten co-authors combined Webb and ALMA observations in twenty twenty-five to measure electron densities inside early galaxies. Density shapes how emission lines form, and getting it wrong distorts the metal abundances astronomers infer. Their integral-field spectroscopy targeted three galaxies at redshift six to seven, catching the key optical oxygen lines.

Optical lines indicated densities near a thousand particles per cubic centimeter. Far-infrared line ratios from ALMA, by contrast, pointed to densities at most half that — matching values from the nearby universe up to redshift fourteen. No single density fits everything: the far-infrared lines shine too brightly for the dense gas the optical lines trace. A two-zone model, dense and diffuse regions side by side, reconciles all the lines and cautions metallicity estimates.
arxiv-2505-09486:
Seyed Roozbeh Razavi Rohani, Khashayar Khajavi, Wesley Chung, Mo Chen, and Sharan Vaswani fight a quiet failure of lifelong learning: networks slowly lose the ability to learn at all. Plasticity fades as tasks stream in, and deep linear networks resist that fade. Their method, AdaLin, borrows the resistance by letting each neuron blend linearity into its own activation.

Every neuron carries a learnable dial and a gate driven by its gradient flow. When signal weakens, more linearity flows in to keep learning alive. No new hyperparameters and no task boundaries are needed. Across shuffled and relabeled image benchmarks, class-split tasks, a deep residual network, and off-policy reinforcement learning, AdaLin clearly helped. Ablations show the per-neuron adaptation is the crucial part. The authors also probe which internal metrics track plasticity loss.
arxiv-2505-11786:
Dinh Van Le extends two classic results in geometry and algebra to settings with endless symmetry, in a 2025 paper. The Minkowski-Weyl theorem links two ways of describing cone shapes. Gordan's lemma concerns finite generation in ordered counting systems. Here the shapes and systems stay unchanged when their parts are swapped by the infinite symmetric group. Earlier work covered only the nonnegative case.

The author proves a local version of the cone theorem under symmetry. He also gives principles that pass between local and global finite generation. A full proof of the symmetric Gordan's lemma follows. The paper further sorts the odd cases: cones that are not pointed, and systems that are not positive. These cases bring difficulties absent in the classic theory. The work suits readers in algebra and discrete geometry.
arxiv-2505-12086:
The BESIII Collaboration reports a distorted particle signature that betrays a hidden rescattering loop. The team studied a charm meson decay into a pion and two eta mesons. In that channel, one light particle's spectral shape, a scalar resonance, came out altered. A triangle-shaped loop of intermediate particles explains the warp.

In the loop, the decay products scatter off each other before flying free. That final-state interaction reshapes the resonance's line in the data. Seeing the effect confirms a mechanism long predicted but hard to isolate. Amplitude analysis of the full decay pattern separates the loop's mark from plain resonance behavior. The result warns analysts that naive line shapes can mislead mass and width readings. It also gives theorists a clean case where rescattering cannot be ignored.
arxiv-2505-12886:
Zhongxiang Sun and co-authors study a deceptive error type in large reasoning models: reasoning that reads well but is wrong. Their 2025 paper calls it reasoning hallucination. Unlike plain factual slips, these errors hide inside structured chains of thought, which makes them harder to spot and more persuasive.

The team propose a reasoning score that measures depth by comparing late-layer outputs to the vocabulary. Shallow pattern matching scores differently from deep reasoning under this lens. On a truth-focused data set, they find two failure patterns: depth that wobbles early, and backtracking to a flawed earlier step. Their detector built on these signs set new best results across domains. A tuned training method then reduces the errors themselves.
arxiv-2505-13186:
Philipp Scholl and co-authors learn robot joint friction with a method that outputs readable formulas in a 2025 paper. Friction in robot joints is hard to model: hand-built models take expert effort, while neural networks are opaque and hard to trust near people. Symbolic regression searches for compact formulas that fit data, offering a middle path.

The team fit friction torque data from a KUKA lightweight robot arm. The found formulas were about as simple as hand-built ones but more accurate. They could also be extended to include load effects and other dynamic factors without starting over. The authors argue the approach suits safety-critical robotics, where engineers must inspect and trust the model that runs the machine.
arxiv-2505-14186:
Guéret, Schill, and Schmidt add in twenty twenty-five household solar behaviour to energy system models that usually ignore it. Households with rooftop panels and batteries aim to cut their own bills, but flat tariffs give them no signal to help the wider grid, so their timing can clash with system needs. The team inserted a rule that mimics bill-driven self-use into a standard expansion model.

Tuned so the household bill came out lowest, the rule matched household choices well across many tariff designs. In a German twenty thirty case with electric cars, ignoring such households skewed results badly: ideal battery capacity rose up to threefold once they were included. Home and big batteries, they note, do not swap one for one.
arxiv-2505-15386:
Yiming Huang and co-authors wrote a 2025 paper on a method that flags made-up answers from language models and can say why. False but fluent output is a key block to trust in these models. Past detectors gauge doubt, yet they cannot point to which input words breed the error.

Doubt lives in two places: how sense builds up across layers, and how words get picked at output. Their method rescales the classic perplexity score by doubt from both spots. It hands a doubt score to each token, then rolls them into one total in log average form. Tests on question and answer sets gave the best all round detection among rivals. Token scores double as an account of each flag.
arxiv-2505-16086:
Ming Shen and colleagues optimize teams of language model agents by reading their failure reports and rewriting the worst performers' instructions. Multi-agent systems split software work among role specialists, but tuning them is unsolved. Writing in twenty twenty-five, their pipeline runs in two steps. First, textual feedback from evaluations identifies underperforming agents and explains their failures. Second, those explanations drive prompt revisions for the flagged agents only. The team then compares settings: online versus offline optimization, and individual versus group tuning. Group tuning itself comes in one-pass and multi-pass flavors.

Software development tasks were graded on several dimensions. The method improved the role-based systems, the authors report. The comparisons also revealed how each setting changes group behavior. The study is framed as practical guidance for builders of agent teams.
arxiv-2505-16386:
Ahmed Kadhim and co-authors build word embeddings from a fully readable learning machine in a 2025 paper. Big language models give strong embeddings, vectors that place words by meaning, but they are black boxes. The Tsetlin Machine learns by logic rules and stays interpretable, yet its embeddings were limited. Their Omni TM-AE uses the machine's full state, including literals earlier designs threw away.

One training pass yields embeddings that can be reused across tasks. Tests covered meaning similarity, sentiment classification, and document clustering. The model matched or beat mainstream embedding tools on those tasks. It did so while keeping its reasoning inspectable. The authors argue scale, reuse, and transparency can coexist in language technology. Opaque architectures, they suggest, are a choice, not a necessity.
arxiv-2505-16586:
A Rota and co-authors link inflow and outflow in young stars, in an astronomy paper from two thousand twenty-five. Young stars draw gas from a disk around them, and winds or jets push gas back out. The team studied thirty-one disks, split between full disks and disks with gaps.

Radio glow from hot gas near each star gave a clue to the outflow rate. That rate rose and fell in step with the inflow rate. Glow did not track X-ray light or one known wind line in the same way. The match hints that the glow comes from the same wind or jet in both disk types.
arxiv-2505-18186:
Nikhil Singh, Manuel Cherep, and Pattie Maes set out to find the hidden concepts inside a large music-generating model, in a 2025 paper. The head title adds that these concepts can also steer what the model creates. Such models learn the structure of music from data alone, which may reveal how musical ideas can arise from patterns.

The team used special decoder tools to pull clear features out of the model's inner activity, with automatic labeling to check them at scale. Some features matched known ideas like chord movement. Others formed coherent patterns with no name in music theory. By pushing on a feature, they could steer new music in that direction. The method offers a new way to study both the model and music itself.
arxiv-2505-18986:
Zhiwei Lin and Yongtao Wang build a detector for the open world, where the things to find are not known in advance. Closed detectors see their training categories. Open-set systems accept categories typed in at test time, which still needs a human in the loop, while open-ended systems must discover objects unaided and usually perform worse. Writing in twenty twenty-five, the team's framework merges both query styles. General queries from the open-ended side and specific queries from the open-set side are fused so each corrects the other, with a switch that lets the model run in either mode.

Ranked learnable queries, sorted to match proposals, add diversity, and a denoising point training strategy steadies learning. On the LVIS benchmark the method passed earlier open-set and open-ended systems, with the clearest gains on rare objects, the long tail where open-world perception is weakest.
arxiv-2505-19186:
Rushiraj Gadhvi, Priyansh Desai, and Siddharth present PosePilot, an edge device system for correcting exercise posture. Their twenty twenty-five paper uses yoga as the test case. Yoga demands precise alignment held over time. Home users often practise without a teacher watching them.

PosePilot recognises poses and gives feedback at every moment. One recurrent network tracks how movements unfold over time. A second network with attention focuses on key limb angles. That focus improves error detection while keeping computing light. The team also built a video dataset for testing. The design aims at home and outdoor use on small devices, not large servers.
arxiv-2505-19886:
Bernardo Castro Valerio and co-authors present a planning model for offshore wind power linked through a multi-terminal direct current grid, in work from 2025. Sea-based wind farms in the North Sea are set to grow, and links between price zones can move that power to where it is valued. The model extends the standard power flow framework used by grid planners.

Their version adds price zone rules so it can forecast how the future grid will run. A case study based on the planned 2030 North Sea network shows the model in use. One case treats prices as fixed inputs, while two let prices respond to flows between zones. The authors show that for large flows, extra rules beyond line limits are needed to capture price effects well.
arxiv-2505-20786:
Habibullin and Khakimova build clear forms for a coupled wave law from a chain trick in this twenty twenty-five paper. Such laws stand for deep water waves that run in two cross ways. Clear forms for them are prized, since most wave laws hide their waves well.

Inside, a dress chain of linked steps turns a plain start into rich wave forms. The chain here is a broad Toda grid tied to a known Lie form. Their build gives a new class of clear forms for the law in scope. Two free funcs ride in those forms, which widens the class a lot. The route can serve kin laws of the same clan, they note.
arxiv-2505-20886:
Byon Jayawiguna and Piyabut Burikham test how a neutron star bends and spins in nonlocal gravity. They use an exact changed Tolman model for how dense the star is. They work out its spin weight, its quadrupole warp, and its tidal Love number. The maths is the standard even-parity route. The tidal bend is then held to real bounds: two merger events seen in waves, and two pulsars weighed well.

Fit with the tidal bounds needs the model's range term past a set mark, when the nonlocal term is small. That term moves the star's size a lot on its own. Down one path in the terms, the famed I-Love-Q links hold firm. Shift the nonlocal term, and that oneness breaks. A map of where they fail turns them to a test of nonlocal gravity.
arxiv-2505-21186: Eper and Szabó present a math paper from twenty twenty-five on solution spaces tied to the Painlevé equations. Those equations are a famed set of six nonlinear equations in math physics. The paper treats rank three solution spaces for these systems, called wild character varieties. It gives explicit cubic equations that define those spaces. It then compares them with the known equations for rank two cases. The work is the first part of a planned series on rank three cases.
arxiv-2505-22386:
Dinesha Hegde and co-authors model the solar wind across the inner solar system in a 2025 paper. The solar wind is the stream of charged gas flowing out from the Sun, and it sets the backdrop for space weather near Earth. Their model starts from maps of the solar surface magnetism and runs many versions to capture doubt in those maps.

They check the results against data from several probes, plus records taken near Earth, for the years 2020 and 2021. The match with real data was good overall. The study shows how surface map errors spread through forecasts. It also points to ways to sharpen space weather prediction, which matters for satellites and power grids.
arxiv-2505-23886:
Bowei Chen and co-authors present a 2025 arXiv paper on making full-body fit check videos from a handheld phone. Such fashion videos usually need mounted cameras and practiced framing. The team's method takes two mirror selfies, front and back, plus a motion recording from the phone's own sensors as the user performs a reference move.

A video diffusion model then renders the person doing a similar target motion, placed into a new scene with matched light and shadows. A parameter-free frame strategy and a dual-reference attention step feed both selfies into the model. A fine-tuning pass sharpens frames and improves shadows and reflections.
arxiv-2505-24286:
Jonathan Morgner and a large team of co-authors wrote this atomic physics paper, published in two thousand twenty-five, on the magnetic moment of a tin ion. The ion is lithium-like, with three electrons, and its g factor is a sharp probe of how electrons tug on each other inside an atom.

The team measured the g factor to half a part per billion. Their theory calculations treat the inter-electronic pull with fresh care, and they sharpen the prediction further using a known result for hydrogen-like tin, which has just one electron. Measurement and theory agree. That agreement confirms the revised theory at a nuclear charge of fifty, far higher than past tests, where quantum electrodynamic effects swell large. The paper marks a new reach for precision tests of bound-state theory.
arxiv-2505-24486:
Falih Gozi Febrinanto and five colleagues improve audio deepfake detectors that must keep learning as new fake-audio attacks appear. Continual learning with rehearsal replays a few old examples while training on new ones, but naive sample selection captures audio diversity poorly, biasing memory and causing forgetting. Their method, RAIS, uses a label generation network to produce auxiliary labels.

Those auxiliary labels guide diverse sample selection for the memory buffer. Across five sequential experiences, RAIS beat state-of-the-art rehearsal methods, reaching an average equal error rate of about 1.95 percent. The authors release the code. The work targets a moving security problem where detectors face attack types that did not exist at first training.
arxiv-2505-24686:
Enrico Caprioglio, Pedro Mediano, and Luc Berthouze answer a basic question about complex systems: when does information live in the whole rather than in the parts? Such high-order synergy is easy to measure but hard to explain, above all in systems whose parts interact only in pairs. The team solves the question for Gaussian systems in the weak-interaction regime.

They prove that frustrated, antibalanced correlation patterns are enough to make synergy dominate, and that in a standard class of random processes such motifs are also necessary. Tests beyond the gentle regime, in spin models, oscillators, and real networks, back the theory up. The moral is sharp: pairwise rules alone can brew genuinely high-order information, no group mechanism required. Structural balance theory, imported from social science, turns out to be the right lens.
arxiv-2506-01086:
Mateusz Baran and Ronny Bergmann give Kalman filters a new geometric foundation in this 2025 arXiv paper. Kalman filters estimate a moving system's state from noisy readings, and the shape of the state space matters greatly in robotics and motion tracking. Two schools handle that shape differently, one through Lie groups and one through curved-space geometry.

The authors show how the two schools relate, then build a description based on affine connections that covers both. That wider view gives users more freedom in choosing the state space shape, and it still works with standard tools like parameter fitting. They test the idea on a rigid-motion problem and on tracking a point on a sphere, using a software library they built for the purpose.
arxiv-2506-01486:
Jelke Wibbeke, Sebastian Rohjans, and Andreas Rauh review ways to fight data imbalance in regression in a 2025 paper. When most training cases cluster in a common range, models learn that range well and fail on the rare cases that often matter most, such as extreme events. Fixes either resample the data or charge rare errors a higher price.

The authors add two scoring rules that weigh a case by both its rarity and its value to the user, plus two sampling methods that refine a known synthetic technique. On fifty-two data sets, most fixes helped rare cases but hurt common ones. Pairing a fixed model with a plain one in an ensemble softened that trade. Their best sampler led for neural networks.
arxiv-2506-02486:
Baodi Shan, Mauricio Araya-Polo, and Barbara Chapman present a framework for running parallel programs across clusters of graphics processors, in a 2025 paper. Supercomputers increasingly mix many-core chips with accelerators, and the classic programming models force developers to juggle distributed memory by hand.

Their system extends OpenMP, the shared-memory standard, with a global address space model, so offloading work to remote accelerators looks like ordinary parallel code. A communication layer built on fast network libraries moves data, and a portable collective library matches vendor tools. Tests on three flagship accelerator families, in micro-benchmarks and real applications like matrix multiplication, showed better scalability and simpler code than traditional approaches. Portability is the selling point: one program, many machines.
arxiv-2506-02586:
Valentina Abramenko studies the magnetic field at the surface of the Sun in a 2025 solar physics study. She follows one mature active region as it crossed the solar disk and produced flares. Her data come from magnetograms taken by an imager aboard the Solar Dynamics Observatory.

Abramenko tracks turbulence through magnetic power spectra and multifractality through structure functions over time. Neither measure jumps sharply before or after single flares. Instead both shift smoothly and line up better with the region's overall complexity and flare productivity. The result suggests the surface layer organizes itself on its own track, apart from the more burst-like corona above it.
arxiv-2506-04686:
Nicolas Borchard and Gerd Wachsmuth wrote a 2025 mathematics paper characterizing Hilbert spaces among the wider world of Banach spaces. A Banach space is a complete space with a notion of length; a Hilbert space additionally has an inner product, like ordinary geometry. Knowing which Banach spaces are secretly Hilbert spaces, up to isomorphism, is a classical question.

The authors answer it with convex functions. If a Banach space carries a strongly convex function whose derivative is Lipschitz continuous, then the space must be isomorphic to a Hilbert space. The same conclusion follows if both a function and its convex conjugate are twice differentiable. Such criteria let analysts recognize Hilbert space structure from the functions a space supports.
arxiv-2506-04786:
Thore Gerlach, Sascha Mücke, and Christian Bauckhage link two classic ways of shrinking data to a few representative points. One way, k-medoids clustering, picks actual data points as centers by distance. The other grows out of density estimation, matching how points are spread. Both can be written as binary optimization problems with no constraints, the form known as QUBO.

The surprise is that the density-based problem turns out to be a special case of the medoid problem, under mild assumptions about the kernel's feature map. That result gives a geometric reading of the weights inside such formulations and reframes density matching as a kind of center picking. The authors say the link offers fresh insight for vector quantization, a basic tool in learning and data compression.
arxiv-2506-04886:
Paul and colleagues build in twenty twenty-five a shape-based pipeline to spot hip dysplasia, a shallow hip socket that raises arthritis risk. Early detection matters because surgery can lower that risk, but standard checks rely on hand-measured angles from flat scans. Their method learns a statistical shape model from full three-dimensional scans, guided by a few marked landmarks.

Trained and tested on nearly two hundred hip scans, the model separated dysplastic hips from healthy ones more accurately than angle methods. It also highlights the surface regions where dysplastic hips differ most. The authors say the pipeline can save clinicians time by removing manual angle work while improving accuracy.
arxiv-2506-05286:
Lijie Hu and co-workers stabilized concept-based medical image models in a 2025 paper. Concept narrow point models route a diagnosis through human-readable concepts, like lesion shape or density, so doctors can audit the thinking. Forcing all information through concepts usually costs accuracy and the explanations wobble when inputs are slightly perturbed. Their Vision Concept Model fuses concept traits with the image's own feature embeddings inside a vision model. Recovering the lost utility instead of choosing between them.

A stabilized successor adds tool set to keep explanations faithful under perturbation, the paper's second concern. The design targets the twin demands of medical AI: results a health worker can use and explanations a health worker can trust twice, on the same image, slightly changed.
arxiv-2506-05486:
Jordan Barrett and co-authors present a 2025 paper on fake networks for testing community finders. Real networks hide their true communities, so tests need models with known groups. The ABCD model builds random graphs with community structure. Degree and community sizes follow power-law patterns, like real networks. It runs faster than the classic LFR model, stays easier to read, and allows exact analysis.

A past variant added outliers, nodes that belong to no group. The new variant also allows overlapping communities, where a node joins several groups at once. Overlap is common in real social and work networks. Finder tools can now be graded on graphs that mix groups, outliers, and overlap in known amounts. Honest grading matters: a finder that shines on clean graphs may fail on the messy overlap of real data.
arxiv-2506-06086:
Nathan Pagliaroli counts a broad class of planar maps by building a bijection to trees with added marks. A planar map is a graph set in the sphere. A stuffed map loosens the faces. It allows parts that are spheres with several boundaries in place of simple discs. To count such objects straight is hard.

Pagliaroli builds a bijection between bipartite planar stuffed maps and sets of integer-labelled trees. The trees are joined by hyperedges into hypertrees, called hypermobiles. The bijection extends the classic Bouttier-Di Francesco-Guitter match between bipartite planar maps and mobiles. He shows the generating functions of these trees meet an algebraic equation. They also meet a new functional equation. As a case, he counts a class of stuffed quadrangulations in full. The work extends the study of map counts.
arxiv-2506-06186:
Julien Renaudeau, Pierre Lidon, and Jean-Baptiste Salmon devise a microfluidic method for measuring how solutes cross a membrane. Two numbers describe that transport: the solute permeability and the reflection coefficient. Both are usually hard to pin down precisely.

Their setup uses the tight confinement of a microchannel so that a passing osmotic flow reveals both coefficients at once. They tested the idea on hydrogel membranes formed inside the chip by light-based crosslinking. Flows induced by osmosis were measured in place for solutes of different sizes. From those readings they estimated both coefficients and located the membrane's molecular weight cut-off.
arxiv-2506-06486:
Umit Yigit Basaran, Sk Miraj Ahmed, Amit Roy-Chowdhury, and Basak Guler present a method for removing data from a trained model in two thousand twenty-five. Privacy rules now ask that private or protected data be erased from models. Most older methods need the full set of data used to train the model, which is often no longer at hand.

The team uses a stand-in data set that is close in form to the source data. Noise is scaled by the gap between the two sets, with set bounds on how the model acts after removal. Tests on made-up and real data show the method works well while the model stays useful.
arxiv-2506-06986:
Austin Snyder, Ryan Gallagher, and Boris Kovalerchuk build class models that a human can read in full, in work from two thousand twenty-five. Their tool is the hyperblock, a block that sorts a case by the low and high bounds set for each trait. Experts can look at the rules and see why a case got its label.

They add ways to trim blocks, drop traits that add nothing, and merge blocks that overlap. A nearest-neighbor back-up sorts cases that fall in no block, so all data is covered. On test sets, from a small nine-trait set to the large MNIST image set, the trimmed models stay close in score while they grow much simpler.
arxiv-2506-07986:
Lv and a team including Pan and Si put forth a fix in twenty twenty-five for image tools that build pics from text prompts. Top tools can still fail to match the words to the pic in fine ways. They trace the flaw to how text and pic parts weigh each other in the tool's focus step.

Pic parts far out-count text parts, so text gets drowned out, and the tool lacks a sense of time step. Their fix scales the heat of that focus and shifts it by step. With a light tune step it lifts text-pic match on a known test set. Gains show in look, trait binds, and place links.
arxiv-2506-08786:
Brax and Valageas propose using pulsar timing arrays to probe clumps of ultralight scalar dark matter. Such scalars could replace particle models like WIMPs, mainly at very low masses. At those masses, quantum effects grow large on galactic scales.

Timing pairs of pulsars in sync could reach masses from 10^-23 to 10^-19 electron volts. The top of that range beats standard analyses and rises if the time lag shrinks below one hour. But only very dense clouds would register at high masses. Neutron star capture rates are too low, so detection may need direct matter links or black hole-pulsar pairs.
arxiv-2506-10286:
Park, Kim, and Kim build HalLoc in twenty twenty-five, a data set for spotting made up details in AI image answers word by word. Vision language models often invent objects or facts that are not in the picture. Past detectors give a flat yes or no and run slowly. HalLoc holds a large set of samples with each token marked and typed.
