Samples span question answering, instruction following, and caption writing. A light model trained on it flags suspect words as the text is made, with graded confidence. It plugs into live models without slowing them much. The authors release the data and code for open use.
arxiv-2506-11286:
Phu Khanh Huynh, Francky Catthoor, and Anup Das present ways to place and schedule spiking neural networks on a shared bus architecture, in a paper from 2025. Brain-like chips split work across tiles that send spikes over shared links. Spike traffic is sparse but bursty, so links must stay cheap at rest and cope with bursts.

A segmented ladder bus fits that need, but poor placement floods it with traffic and loses spikes. The team's three-step plan first groups the network to cut cross traffic and energy. It then sets spike schedules from the traffic pattern. Last, a routing method reduces path crossings. In a cycle-accurate simulator, the plan removed spike loss while keeping energy low.
arxiv-2506-11486:
Namhun Koo and Soonhak Kwon study a family of math functions used in code making in a paper from 2025. The functions act on finite fields, which are number sets with a fixed size. Designers care how such functions respond to small input changes, since weak responses can aid attacks. The pair examine a two-part function built from a power term and a sign-like term.

They work out full tables of how the function reacts to changes and to a second test called boomerang analysis. In one case the function reaches a rare perfect score on the second test. They also cover settings beyond the two simplest choices. The results add a rare example to a short known list.
arxiv-2506-12186:
Haoyu Dong and six co-authors built a foundation model for MRI scans. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with magnetic resonance imaging in deep learning care tools. New models need vast labeled data, which is dear and bound by privacy. Their model, MRI-CORE, learned from more than six million slices. Those came from more than one hundred ten thousand scan sets across eighteen body sites.

The model was then tested on thin data tasks. It beat top past methods on thirteen segmentation tasks with scarce labels. It also won on image class calls and on zero shot segmentation. Readers who build scan AI get a base that cuts label needs at the start.
arxiv-2506-12986:
Yang, Huang, and Li present a study from twenty twenty-five on improving spliced alignment of RNA and protein sequences to genomes. Such alignment underpins gene annotation and function studies. Current aligners model splice sites, the cut points in genes, too simply. Errors grow when sequences differ across species. Their tool learns splice signals with a small convolutional network. Training spans vertebrate and insect genomes with thousands of parameters. The learned model captures shared signals and mammal-specific intron traits.

The model scores every candidate splice site in a genome in advance. Two known aligners are patched to use those scores while aligning. Tests on human long reads and cross-species proteins show sharp gains. Junction accuracy improves most for noisy reads and distant proteins.
arxiv-2506-13386:
Zhendong Li speeds up quantum simulation of molecules, in a 2025 preprint, by choosing a smarter starting basis. Quantum phase estimation can find a molecule's ground energy, but needs a starting state close to the true one. For hard cases like iron-sulfur clusters, that closeness fades fast with size. Li's fix is to rotate the orbitals so the ground state becomes less entangled. A compact classical method finds those orbitals using small matrix product states that respect spin.

In the new basis, the ground state packs into a much simpler form. For a four-iron cluster, the starting overlap grew by nearly tenfold over earlier orbital methods. For the bigger nitrogen-fixing clusters in enzymes, gains ran to hundreds and even a hundred thousand times over local orbitals. Hard, strongly correlated molecules look more reachable than past estimates suggested.
arxiv-2506-14186:
Anselm Paulus and five co-authors fix gradient errors in contact simulation in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Simulators that soften contact let robots learn by gradient methods, but stiff, realistic contact settings corrupt those gradients. Soft settings, in turn, drift from real physics.

The team pinpoints why gradients degrade, then builds DiffMJX, which pairs adaptive time stepping with penalty contact to restore accuracy. A second trick supplies gradients before contact happens, applied only in the backward pass so the forward physics stays honest. That pre-contact signal solves the vanishing gradient problem when bodies are apart. Together the methods let learning and control use hard contacts without lying about the physics.
arxiv-2506-14486:
Devoto, Jezo, Kallweit, and Schwan present a software link from twenty twenty-five for particle physics sums. The link joins two tools, PineAPPL and MATRIX, so users can save results as grids. Grids let others redo sums for new input sets without running the full hard sum again. The sums reach a high level of care in two kinds of theory at once. The authors call it the first public tool of its kind at that level.

Such grids help world fits of the proton parts that go into collider sums. Exact sums replace rough scale factors that can skew the fits. The new code and the grids made for the work are posted for free public use. The tool should sharpen later fits and their stated doubt ranges.
arxiv-2506-17286:
Luoyang Sun and co-authors slim the attention step in large language models by sharing maps and compressing values, in work from twenty twenty-five. Attention drives model quality but eats memory and compute, and the stored key value cache grows fast with text length. Much of that storage is redundant.

Their method, grouped head latent attention, reuses one attention map across several heads, shrinking the key cache. A learned decoder squeezes the value cache into a compact latent form. Against a common grouped query baseline, compute fell by up to about sixty percent and the cache by up to seventy percent. End to end generation ran about twice as fast, with no extra machinery.
arxiv-2506-18086:
Ning Bao, Keiichiro Furuya, and Joydeep Naskar settle a question, in a 2025 preprint, about the standard tool for proving holographic entropy inequalities. These inequalities bind how entropy can be shared among regions in a gravity dual. The usual proof builds a contraction map between bit-string spaces. Having one is enough to prove an inequality. The open question was whether every true inequality has one.

The authors answer yes for all linear inequalities with rational coefficients. When a map fails to contract, its input set is not a full cube but a cut-down shape. That cut shows up in the gravity side as a change in the geodesic web. Geometries following the standard entropy formula then break the inequality in question. So any true inequality of this class must admit a contraction map, and the method is complete for this family.
arxiv-2506-20186:
Tianshi Yu and five co-authors check an open-source ship motion predictor against a real Antarctic voyage, in a 2025 paper. Forecasting how a vessel heaves, pitches, and rolls guides safety and routing, and the free solver NEMOH is widely used but rarely validated at sea.

The team computed the ship's response operators with the solver, then fed in wave spectra measured by the ship's own marine radar during the Antarctic Circumnavigation Expedition. Predictions were scored against inertial sensors aboard the research vessel. Heave matched observations strongly, pitch reasonably, and roll acceptably, with the worst gaps under specific conditions the authors identify. Honest field benchmarks like this separate trustworthy open tools from hopeful ones for ocean operations.
arxiv-2506-20486:
Salvatore Milite, Giulio Caravagna, and Andrea Sottoriva present mixtures of neural cellular automata in two thousand twenty-five. Neural cellular automata model self growth with learned local rules. Their fixed nature misses the chance that marks real tissue and physics. The new frame blends rule sets with built in noise.

Each cell picks rules by chance, so local acts can vary. Tests span fake tissue growth, image morphing, and microscopy cuts. The mixture stood up better to knocks than the plain form. Growth patterns matched real biology more closely as well. Rule based image cuts stayed clear and readable.
arxiv-2506-21086:
Guillem Cortès-Sebastià and co-authors build PeakNetFP, a neural system that identifies songs from spectral peaks even after extreme speed changes. Their paper appeared in 2025. Audio fingerprinting matches a clip to a database by its pattern of bright frequency peaks. Classic peak systems are light but brittle; neural ones are sturdy but heavy. The new system borrows point-cloud feature methods from computer vision and trains with contrast checks, like the leading neural fingerprinter.

Across stretches from half speed to double speed, it kept top-one accuracy above ninety percent. It matched the leading neural system's skill on stretched audio while using one hundred times fewer parameters and eleven times smaller inputs. The authors call it a practical path for apps that must recognize sped-up or slowed-down tracks cheaply.
arxiv-2506-21786:
Lan Wen and Glen McGee tackle causal estimates when key data are missing. Their twenty twenty-five paper asks for the average effect of a treatment, but in real studies the exposure and the confounders are often partly unrecorded. Their case study asks whether prescription opioid use raises the risk of death.

Standard fixes work when data are missing at random, but can bias the answer when they are not. The pair sets out several stated assumptions for the harder case. Under each, they show the effect can still be pinned down from the seen data. They build doubly robust estimators that stay valid if one of two model parts is right, and test them in simulations and survey data.
arxiv-2506-22486:
Ming Cheung, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, proposes detecting hallucinations in language model answers using committees of small language models. Hallucinated answers undermine retrieval-augmented systems, and errors are hard to spot without ground truth.

The framework splits a generated answer into single sentences. For each sentence, several small models judge it against the question and the retrieved context, and the probability of a yes verdict is aggregated. Experiments use over one hundred real question-answer-context sets, including fully and partially correct responses. The committee improves F1 for separating correct responses from hallucinated ones by about ten percent, offering a scalable verification method.
arxiv-2507-01986:
Balitactac and Rodriguez present a 2025 study of a thick liquid flowing down a sloped plane, in a model where the liquid's thickness itself depends on pressure. Many real liquids barely compress under pressure yet flow much more stiffly, and the classic flow equations cannot capture both traits at once. The authors study a newer extended model that adds higher-order terms, an exponential rule for how stiffness rises with pressure, and matching boundary rules.

They focus on steady flow down the slope, with weak grip at the lower surface and fixed air pressure at the top. Computer simulations show how the flow profile changes with the slope angle. They also vary the outside pressure, the pressure sensitivity, and an internal length scale. The work is the first test of the extended model on this basic flow.
arxiv-2507-02186:
Zahra Ashktorab and co-authors showed EvalAssist in 2025, a human-centered tool for the more and more common practice of letting a language model judge outputs. Practitioners drowning in likely models and prompts need tests, and model judges are cheap, but ad hoc judging rules produce untrustworthy verdicts. EvalAssist slows the human down in the right place: deciding what good means, in writing, before any scoring begins.

The system provides an online setting where users build testing rules interactively, test them against sample outputs, refine them, and share them in an ordered, portable format. Behind the rules sit testing pipelines built from off-the-shelf language models through prompt chaining, a method the team developed and contributed to the ecosystem. The design treats the judge's rubric, not the judge's model, as the artifact worth engineering carefully.
arxiv-2507-02886:
Thi Kim Nhung Dang, Benedikt Peterseim, Milan Lopuhaä-Zwakenberg, and Mariëlle Stoelinga wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gives a firm frame for fault tree analysis when the input odds are fuzzy, not crisp.

Fault trees map how small failures join to break a system, and their inputs are often vague. The authors show any algorithm for crisp unreliability can be lifted to the fuzzy case in full and at low cost. Two facts do the heavy lifting: the alpha-cut form of fuzzy numbers and the coherence of fault trees. Tests on a standard bank of fake trees show the methods run well in practice. The title's fast and formal pair both land.
arxiv-2507-03586:
Matthew Butler, Benjamin Walker, Thomas Montenegro-Johnson, and Panayiota Katsamba model thin active filaments moving in fluid in a 2025 study. Such filaments bend, swim, and stir their surroundings depending on flexibility, the strength and kind of internal forcing, and the fluid itself. Their case is chemical propulsion: surface reactions create slip flows that push the filament along.

Two existing models are combined, a local slender-body theory for the chemistry-driven slip and a computational treatment of the elastic response. Together they predict three-dimensional shapes and motions. Filament swimmers model sperm, cilia, and synthetic micro-robots, so the coupling rules have wide use.
arxiv-2507-04486:
East and four co-authors give a full shape map of twisted pair sets in this twenty twenty-five paper. A twist bends how two set parts merge, by a count the pair's own past sets. Such sets first showed up in chart clans where the count tracks loose parts.

Inside, the team picks out a tight kind of twist and maps its pair sets in depth. Their map spans kin links, fair parts, rest-state parts, and top sub-groups of the sets. Dual terms for the twist let them shift claims from one side to the next. Worked cases start from rank rules in plain matrix math and branch out. Some of those cases are new to print, the team notes.
arxiv-2507-04886:
Bochkov, a solo author, challenges where meaning lives inside a language model, in two thousand twenty-five. Standard models learn their input embeddings from data, and those vectors are taken to hold word meaning. Bochkov instead freezes the embedding layer, filling it with fixed vectors drawn from the visual shapes of Unicode characters.

A new tokenizer built around Unicode ensures all text can be covered. Despite the frozen, non-semantic start, the models trained well and produced coherent text. They even beat identical models with learned embeddings on a reasoning benchmark. The author argues that learned embeddings suffer interference from serving two jobs, and that meaning emerges from the transformer layers themselves.
arxiv-2507-06186:
Pierre Yves Gaudreau Lamarre and Yuanyuan Pan study noisy quantum models on flat bounded regions. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. The Anderson Hamiltonian adds white noise to a particle's motion. Its parabolic cousin tracks mass spread over time. Both sit on a planar domain with fixed edges. The authors compute how things behave at very small times.

They find precise expansions for the model's trace and total mass. The proofs lean on how Brownian paths cross each other. One payoff is geometric: eigenvalues alone can reveal the region. A single spectrum gives back both the area and the boundary length. For fractal boundaries, the spectrum can expose the boundary's dimension. The work links noise, probability, and shape.
arxiv-2507-06286:
Eliezer Rabinovici and co-authors review a new measure of how fast a quantum operator spreads, in a paper from 2025. The measure is called Krylov complexity. It grew out of the study of quantum chaos, where it tracks how a simple action spreads into complex ones over time.

The measure rests on a classic algorithm that builds a ladder of states step by step. Its appeal is that its definition needs no free choices, and its values react sharply to chaos, even at very late times. The review states and proves general facts about its behavior in both chaotic and orderly systems. It also shows how the measure takes geometric form in theories tied to gravity and black holes. Open problems close the review.
arxiv-2507-07086:
Wenjie Wu and a team of co-authors measure the working life of a custom chip for a giant neutrino experiment, in two thousand twenty-five. The chip turns signals into numbers and must run cold, inside liquid argon detectors deep underground. Tens of thousands will be installed and cannot be replaced once the detectors are sealed.

The chip was built with special methods for long life in cold conditions. Lifetime matters because failures would hurt data quality and the experiment's reach. The team's measurements point to a lifetime far longer, by orders of magnitude, than the planned run time. That margin supports the design for the first two large detectors.
arxiv-2507-08186:
Gomez and Terhesiu study walks on groups that are driven by maps with strong mixing traits, in a paper from twenty twenty-five. For plain random walks, it is known how ratios of return odds settle over time. The authors ask if the same holds when steps come from a fixed map, not chance. The hard part is that fixed steps lack the smooth blend that random steps have.

They prove a broad form of the ratio result for these driven walks. They also study group extensions of the same maps. For finitely built groups, they pin down how the pressure function behaves. They do this with no need to assume the walk is symmetric. The work widens tools used in ergodic theory.
arxiv-2507-08686:
Stern, Corn, and Weinshall name a local form of over-fit in deep nets and fight it. Over-fit strikes less oft than math would call for in deep nets. That gap is a puzzle, since big nets should bend to noise. Their claim: over-fit does strike, but in lone zones of the data. A new score marks how fast a net drops past facts in zones. That drop is the local over-fit mark in their text.

Local over-fit can rise with no whole over-fit in sight. It ties close to the twin-fall shape in train runs. A two-step fix draws on one net's own past saves. Saves merge in a crew, then squeeze back to one net. Size stays the same, so run cost stays flat in the fix. Tests cross sets, builds, and train forms for the fix.
arxiv-2507-09186:
Minhaj Uddin Ahmad, Akid Abrar, Sagar Dasgupta, and Mizanur Rahman weld three sims into one open platform for linked car research. Work on road safety, car flow, and cyber risk needs three things at once: traffic flow, true-to-life sensors, and radio nets. No one tool does all three well. OpenCAMS joins them: a fine-grain traffic sim, a high-grade drive sim, and an event-led net sim, locked in step.

A two-way link, synced in time, keeps the three worlds in line. The drive sim draws the cars that need fine sensors and control. The traffic core runs flow and lights for the whole net. The net layer sets talk nodes on cars and road-side posts for car-to-all chat. New sims can join the core. It is open source, and work can be rerun.
arxiv-2507-09386:
Kitichotkul and five co-authors showed in twenty twenty-five that free-run lone-photon lidar beats clock-tied lidar in bright light. Stock sense says such lidar needs dim light to dodge dead time in its counts. Free-run builds dodge chart bend from dead time but had thin fix tools.

Their joint guess step reads light flow, back glow, and depth from count charts alone. A learned cloud score then cleans the reads up. Sims and lab runs both gave lower errors for free-run gear. The clean step cut the error more, they report.
arxiv-2507-09486:
Fusheng Deng, Gang Huang, and Xiangsen Qin extend smooth-shape inequalities from plain functions to twisted forms on Kähler spaces, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Heat kernel bounds for bundle-valued forms come first, built over the compact spaces. Those bounds power the wider inequalities.

Side gains include a vanishing result and size bounds for a key operator on the twisted forms. The work grows out of function-level results proved earlier by two other teams. Forms, not just functions, are what geometry problems often hand us. Readers in complex geometry get form-level tools where only function-level ones stood before.
arxiv-2507-10786:
Henry Bell, Jabari Kwesi, Hiba Laabadli, and Pardis Emami-Naeini wrote a 2025 study on privacy worries about social robots in the home. These robots can see, hear, and move, and they often look friendly and human-like. That makes their data gathering feel different from a smart speaker's. The authors asked American users what concerns them while such robots are still new to the market.

The team ran nineteen in-depth interviews. People worried that a robot's data could be linked together, shared without permission, or even affect safety at home. For robots used in teaching, false information was the top fear. For medical uses, people feared the robot might simply be wrong. Participants wanted clear signs when the robot is collecting data. They also wanted real, touchable controls, such as switches, and features that fit each setting. The authors draw design lessons for makers of home robots.
arxiv-2507-11786:
Simon Portegies Zwart and Erwan Hochart present a 2025 astronomy paper arguing that wide Jupiter-mass binary objects cannot form by the route proposed for them. Telescopes found about 40 such pairs, alongside 500 lone Jupiter-mass objects, in the Trapezium cluster. An earlier proposal held that close encounters strip planet pairs from their stars, yielding the binaries. The authors accept the stripping math but reject the conclusion for crowded clusters.

In a dense cluster, later encounters would tear the fragile pairs apart. The proposed route also ignores that break-up step. So the observed pairs either formed some other way or need firmer confirmation as real pairs. The paper is a short, sharp challenge to a surprising claim, of the kind that keeps a young field honest.
arxiv-2507-12286:
Anouk Oudshoorn, Magdalena Ortiz, and Mantas Šimkus study what happens when two web data standards with opposite instincts are forced to work together. SHACL checks data against constraints, treating the record as complete. OWL instead infers new facts from incomplete data, assuming the world stays open. Combining them is appealing but semantically treacherous.

The authors ground validation in core universal models of the ontology. They give a construction for such models in a rich but tractable description logic. A finite stand-in for the model then powers a rewriting trick: validation with an ontology becomes ordinary validation. Complexity results close the paper. Even simple ontologies push the problem to exponential time in general, though it stays polynomial in the data itself. The work gives the combined standards a firm footing.
arxiv-2507-12586:
A team from the ATLAS group stress tested detector strip modules by heat cycles. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with parts for the new Inner Tracker at CERN. Five pre production modules went through long heat cycles once the test rigs were leveled and locks set for lone runs. Shape checks tracked how each module bowed over time. All five bowed more as the top heat rose.

Four modules cracked their sensors when cycled to deep cold. A soft gel and film layer was then added to three more modules as a stress shield. Those showed near no bow shift and passed full checks. Readers who build particle detectors get a fix for a fail mode that kills scarce parts.
arxiv-2507-12886:
Kengo Anzai, Hiroaki Matsueda, and Yoshihito Kuno study how uneven noise across space changes a cleaning phase shift in mixed quantum circuits. Noise in real circuits falls unevenly, and cleaning shifts mark when a mixed state can still be purified. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The team uses a linked measure of quantum ties in mixed states to spot the shift and grade its sharpness. When the chance of measurement varies across space, the shift's key exponent moves past a line set by a known rule for messy systems. When the gates themselves vary across space, a new pure phase with short range ties appears.
arxiv-2507-12986:
Sepeedeh Shahbeigi and five co-authors set out a frame to write sturdiness needs for vision based AI in cars, using a situation coverage plan. Such cars must stay safe as cameras degrade, but listing needs for every decay case explodes in size. Their work came out in twenty twenty-five.

The frame pairs a camera noise factor hunt with coverage of set driving situations. Experts in the field, in sensors, and in safety extend a decay model with noise factors that matter for AI. The planned drive domain bounds where the system must work. Coverage checks then pick telling test cases. The authors call it a first step toward full sturdiness needs.
arxiv-2507-13386:
Zhang and colleagues wrote in twenty twenty-five about erasing unwanted concepts from image-generating models with minimal damage. Models trained on huge unlabeled sets can produce unsafe or copyrighted content. Past erasure methods often change the model too much and hurt its quality. Their minimalist objective measures only the distance between final output distributions. From it they derive a loss that trains through all generation steps. They also analyze links between their approach and other methods.

Instead of full fine-tuning, they mask selected neurons to lock in erasure. Tests on leading flow-matching models showed robust concept removal. Overall generation performance stayed intact after erasure in their trials. The balance of safety and utility is the core advance. The authors frame it as a step toward more responsible generative models.
arxiv-2507-15086:
Ioannis Diamantis, Louis Kauffman, and Sofia Lambropoulou wrote this paper in two thousand twenty-five. It gathers the theory of bonded knots, classic knots with extra arcs that stand for physical or chemical bonds, into one frame.

Bonded knots are sorted by bond type and by the moves allowed on them, with invariants for each sort. The authors then build bonded braids, their algebra twin, with a monoid and the bonded forms of the Alexander and Markov theorems. A richer build adds two bond kinds, for pull and push, and lifts the monoid into a group. Bonded knotoids cover open chains. The models suit the sorting of large biological molecules.
arxiv-2507-15386:
Juntao Wang and five co-authors built a way to grid space by radio channel, not by map. Their paper, from twenty twenty-five, deals with gridization: to split a zone into cells whose users share like channel traits. That split backs big network tuning. Old ways lean on map spots, oft not in hand. Or they trust that like signal strength means like channel, a false step.

Their frame, channel space gridization, joins channel reads and the grid split in one task. It works from beam level power reads alone. Readers in wireless nets get cells drawn by the air it self, not by where folks stand.
arxiv-2507-15886:
Tim Tian Hua, James Baskerville, and colleagues combine several safety monitors for AI systems under a cost budget in a 2025 study. Runtime monitors watch a model's outputs and trigger intervention on harmful ones, but each check costs money and delay. Stacking monitors blindly either blows the budget or leaves gaps.

Their protocol treats each monitor's accuracy and price as given, then schedules them to catch the most misaligned outputs within an average budget. The goal is maximum recall of bad behavior per unit cost. Principled monitor scheduling turns AI oversight from an art into an engineering trade-off.
arxiv-2507-16986:
See and co-authors map the magnetic fields of slow, fully convective M dwarfs. They used Zeeman-Doppler imaging, which reads field patterns from starlight. Such stars have been mapped far less than partly convective stars. The sample joins new maps of slow rotators with older maps. The team split each field into dipole, quadrupole, and octupole parts.

For slow fully convective stars, field strength did not follow the Rossby scaling seen in partly convective stars. The two groups also split into two clear tracks of poloidal and toroidal energy. Past spin-down torque values for these stars may be too low by ten times or more. Winds and rotation loss rates may need a fresh look.
arxiv-2507-17586:
Vimalesh Kumar Vimal and Jorge Cayao study, in a 2025 physics paper, how entanglement grows and fades inside the smallest possible chains that host Majorana particles. These two- and three-site chains lack full topological armor, yet their edge particles are spread out in space, which may still serve quantum tasks. The authors track pair and group entanglement over time.

In the two-site chain, fully entangled states arise often, and their rhythm is tuned by the pairing strength and site energies. At the special sweet spot, the system swings between plain and entangled states. In the three-site chain, edge particles suppress edge-to-edge pairing at the sweet spot, while a slight detune restores it. Certain starts grow prized three-way entangled states.
arxiv-2507-19086:
Steffen Kionke and four co-authors show that in a broad class of analytic groups, an identity that holds with high probability must hold on whole cosets for structural reasons. Such identities generalize ordinary group identities. They demand that the equation hold for most choices of elements. The groups treated are sigma-compact analytic groups over non-archimedean local fields.

Their theorem converts any such identity into a coset identity in that setting. As an application, compact analytic groups and many pro-p groups from free constructions satisfy a probabilistic form of the Tits alternative. A second thread uses Lie theory to study torsion probabilistic identities in virtually free pro-p and compact p-adic analytic groups. The work links probability, Lie theory, and profinite structure.
arxiv-2507-21586: Weronika Buczyńska, Jarosław Buczyński, and Maciej Gałązka study the Grassmann cactus variety in two thousand twenty-five. The variety blends Grassmann secant and cactus varieties in one frame. Both are built from fixed size spaces inside spans of finite schemes. They prove low socle dimension schemes suffice to pin the variety down. That fact drives study of parameter spaces for such schemes. It also eases worked examples of these varieties.
arxiv-2507-22086:
Honghua Dong and six co-authors built a benchmark for how well language models infer types in raw Python code, in a paper published in 2025. Type hints help tools catch bugs, but most Python code lacks them. Earlier tests judged one snippet at a time. Their benchmark spans fifty complete, high-quality code repositories.

Two new scores drive the test. One grades how close an inferred type is in meaning to the true type. The other checks whether inferences agree across a whole repository. Large models did well on the first score. They often failed on nested types and on consistency across a repository. The authors say the field should pursue consistency next, not just nearly correct guesses. They release the benchmark as a base for that work.
arxiv-2507-22386:
Darij Grinberg, a solo author, studies special sums in the algebra of permutations, in a math paper from 2025. For two sets of positions, he defines an element that adds up all permutations sending the first set to the second. A second element adds those that send it inside the second set. Such sums are named after rook placements on a chessboard.

Grinberg shows that the minimal polynomials of these elements split into simple linear factors with whole-number coefficients. He also gives a formula for multiplying two such elements as a whole-number mix of the same kind. The idea extends to ordered partitions of the full set. There the clean splitting fails, but the span of the elements forms an ideal with a partner ideal. The pair links to known bases and modules in representation theory.
arxiv-2508-00786:
Bimal Chhushyabaga and Behrooz Ferdowsi simulated how saturated sand and gravel fail in 2025, a process behind submarine landslides and possibly earthquake starts. Wet granular material behaves differently in air and under water because deformation, grain friction, and fluid pressure all interact. The team coupled a fluid dynamics solver with a discrete element model of individual grains to watch collapses of dense and loose piles in both settings.

Pore pressure proved to govern the failure mode in saturated cases, choosing between fast and slow sliding, in line with earlier laboratory work. Dense piles dilated as they sheared, letting fluid in and stabilizing themselves, while loose piles compacted, spiked their pore pressure, and briefly fluidized. By averaging grain contacts and fluid fields at an intermediate scale, the authors organized the behavior using apparent friction and pressure measures and found strain-rate-dependent responses throughout.
arxiv-2508-00886:
Etienne Buehrle and Christoph Stiller recast the control of noisy systems as a convex math problem, in a paper from 2025. Steering a system buffeted by chance is a core task in robotics and beyond. Standard fixes lean on worst-case guards or sampled scenes, and both strain over long horizons. Their route works with occupation measures, which tally how much time the system spends in each state.

Over those tallies, the control task turns into a convex problem, a class with fast, reliable solvers. They show the method on made-up and real-world cases. Cost rules are learned from data with a special polynomial tool. The code for the tests is shared in public. The authors pitch the frame as a way to keep control planning tractable. It may suit long tasks where chance cannot be ignored.
arxiv-2508-01686: Julius Stricker, writing alone in two thousand twenty-five, puts forth a claim on how whole counts can be built from prime powers. A prime power is a prime raised to a whole power of at least two. He claims each count past a small bound is a sum of at most five such powers. Counts by computer back him: all counts to a large cap were checked in full, and big ones by sample, with no case in need of more than five.
arxiv-2508-01986:
Rui Xue, Jia-Chun He, Dingrong Xiong, and Ze-Rui Wang hunt the source of a hard gamma-ray feature in the galaxy M87. A large observatory recently hinted the emission hardens near twenty trillion electron volts, suggesting a new radiation component. The team assembled average spectra across wavelengths from two space telescopes, matched to the detection period. Four candidate mechanisms then faced the data.

Proton-proton collisions, whose pion decay yields gamma rays, fit the feature within a single emission zone. An analytic proof rules out proton synchrotron light, which cannot stay hard above a lower threshold. The photomeson option needs a zone squeezed implausibly near the black hole's edge, against broadband limits. A two-zone electron model also survives as an alternative. The study narrows a fresh observational puzzle to two live explanations.
arxiv-2508-03886:
Mayank Gupta and colleagues used advanced computer models in 2025 to study a puzzling effect in twisted, spiral-shaped materials. When charge flows through such a chiral material, the current can come out spin-polarized, even with no magnets present. Scientists still debate what causes the effect, called chiral-induced spin selectivity.

Their simulations track electrons, vibrations in the crystal, and spin together over time. A plain, steady response grows in direct proportion to the field, unlike the real effect. Once vibration-driven scattering between valleys is added, the response turns nonlinear and builds with length, matching lab signs. The work points to that scattering as the likely source.
arxiv-2508-03986:
Yuan Xun and co-authors published this AI safety study in 2025. Reasoning models that see images and serve people can be swayed by user emotion. The authors found strong emotional cues during a model's deep-thinking stage can push it past its own safety checks. They built EmoAgent, an automatic attacker that crafts exaggerated emotional prompts. Its goal is to hijack the reasoning path even when the model spots the visual risk.

Experiments on advanced models confirmed the weakness. Models sometimes produced harmful output while their visible reasoning looked safe. To measure such failures, the team defines three scores. They track hidden harmful reasoning, unsafe answers despite recognized risk, and unstable refusals across prompt variants. EmoAgent proved effective across systems tested. The authors argue emotion-driven misalignment hides below the surface of outputs. Content filters alone will miss it, so safety work must inspect reasoning behavior.
arxiv-2508-04486:
Yanming Che, Clemens Gneiting, Xiaoguang Wang, and Franco Nori link circuit complexity to learning quantum phases in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. Topological order hides in quantum matter in ways local probes miss. The team asks whether the cost of building one state from another can serve as a distance between phases.

They prove ties between that circuit cost and two workable measures: a fidelity-based distance and entanglement growth. Both become kernels for unsupervised learning. Tests on a spin chain, a toric code ground state, and random states sorted the phases cleanly. The entanglement version shrugged off local noise better. The authors frame complexity as an interpretable ruler for topological matter.
arxiv-2508-04586:
Nuo Chen and five co-authors argue that the main AI conference model is broken, in a 2025 position paper. Big meetings such as NeurIPS anchor the field, sharing new work and building community. Yet rapid growth has strained that model on several fronts at once.

The authors back their claim with data. Papers per author have more than doubled in ten years, and one meeting's carbon output can top its host city's daily total. Online talk about the meetings skews unhappy, and top venues are running out of room. As a fix, they propose splitting review, talks, and networking into linked local hubs under one shared program. The paper asks the field to rethink how it gathers.
arxiv-2508-04686:
S. Laznevoi and co-workers modeled how a young star's outburst heats its planet-forming disk over time in 2025. FU Orionis type stars flare hugely as they gulp disk stuff, and the extra light rewrites the disk's heat and lab science. Because the disk warms slowly, its response lags the flare, so a snapshot model misses the story.

They used time-dependent radiation transfer tuned to the real FU Orionis system, which flared decades ago. They tried two flare shapes: heating confined to a tiny inner zone, or spread across the whole disk. Thick regions needed several years to heat fully. The lag matters for reading lab science and dust changes in disks caught mid-flare by telescopes.
arxiv-2508-05086:
Robert Horton and Viktor Holubec simulate flocking with delayed reactions in this 2025 paper. In the Vicsek model, moving agents align with neighbors like birds in a flock. Real agents react late, since sensing and actuation take time. Delay is added to the model at large fixed system size.

The same three phases survive delay, ordered motion, phase separated bands, and disorder. Their boundaries move in uneven ways, though. Short delays stabilize the ordered phase, while long delays favor banded coexistence. The noise range for phase separation widens with delay. Bands also form faster and in greater number. Swirl patterns emerge from the lag itself. Delay, often ignored, reshapes collective motion forecasts.
arxiv-2508-06086:
Kojiro Tanaka, Keiichi Sato, Masahiko Mikawa, and Makoto Fujisawa wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It builds a faster way to simulate how a grass display changes color, a living screen made of grass whose shade shifts with light and viewing angle.

Grass displays are eyed as landscape-friendly interfaces, but their color behavior must be measured in real settings. Older studies took hours for a single measurement, and full trials on real rigs are slow and costly. The authors' interactive simulation runs in a virtual setting fed by real-world conditions. They checked simulated colors against real ones across viewpoints and environments. The match was close to prior careful work, at a fraction of the time. The team offers the tool for designing with living materials before planting anything.
arxiv-2508-06786:
Amy Rae Fox and co-authors measure the social vibes that data charts give off, in this 2025 paper. A chart tells readers more than its numbers: style hints at who made it and why, and readers judge trust on those hints. The authors call this the socio-indexical side of visualization. They build a framework for naming the guesses readers make about a chart's social origins.

Surveys that ask people to attribute charts to makers show the effect is real and studyable at a distance. It appears across cultural groups and does not vanish with data skill. Design choices, topic, and message combine to steer the reading. The authors argue visualization research should widen to these social signals, since public trust rides on them.
arxiv-2508-09186:
Abdolazim Rezaei, Mehdi Sookhak, and Mahboobeh Haghparast proposed a privacy method in 2025 for camera-based intelligent transportation systems. Traffic cameras gather rich visual data, but sending raw images puts people's privacy at risk. Older fixes such as blurring or encryption either fail against modern reconstruction attacks or destroy the data's usefulness.

Their framework, RL-MoE, converts images into written scene descriptions, so no picture needs to be transmitted at all. A mixture-of-experts design breaks the scene into aspects for detailed description, while a reinforcement learning agent tunes the text to balance accuracy against privacy. In tests the method cut successful replay attacks sharply on a face dataset while producing richer descriptions than baseline methods.
arxiv-2508-10586:
Birgit Nierula and co-authors study personal space in virtual reality in a 2025 arXiv paper. People guard their personal space, and avatars can trigger the same reactions as real people. The team asked how threat cues and the phase of an encounter shape body responses.

Sixteen participants faced avatars that either intruded on their space or kept distance, with neutral or angry faces. Personal space limits were set for each person in advance. Skin conductance, heart rate measures, and discomfort ratings were recorded. Standing close after intrusion aroused people more than the approach itself. Angry faces lowered heart rate variability and raised discomfort.
arxiv-2508-11286:
Che Rin Yu and five colleagues wrote a 2025 robotics paper on helping embodied agents replan before things go wrong. People adjust their actions to the state of the room almost without thinking: if a drawer is shut, we open it before trying to put something inside. Many robots instead follow a fixed plan and miss such changes, so their actions rest on outdated assumptions.

Most replanning systems react only after a failure, when recovery may be costly or impossible. The authors propose proactive replanning guided by a scene graph, a structured map of objects and their relations. Watching the scene graph lets the agent spot a mismatch early and revise its plan in time. The goal is agents that fail less often in everyday tasks.
arxiv-2508-11386:
Ryan Chan and eight co-authors pair a small reasoning model with retrieval so it can answer expert questions privately. Their technical report appeared in two thousand twenty-five. Big retrieval systems lean on huge models and outside APIs. Secure or low-resource settings cannot allow either. Demand for lean, local assistants keeps rising. Their test corpus is the NHS health information collection.

A dense retriever joins fine-tuned small Qwen models. Synthetic questions and reasoning traces come from a frontier model. Those traces teach the small model how to reason. Deployment needs no external calls. Complex domain queries still get careful, sourced answers. The report shows a workable recipe for private expertise on modest hardware.
arxiv-2508-13986:
Benjamin Hanson, Carlos Rubio, Adrián García-Gutiérrez, and Thomas Bewley move a probability-tracking algorithm onto graphics processors and make it fly. Tracking how uncertainty spreads through a nonlinear system is vital and expensive. A recent grid method places grid points only where probability actually lives. In high dimensions, though, the original design still crawled.

The team first re-architected the method for ordinary processors, then ported it to a single graphics card. Accuracy and convergence were checked before timing began. Tests pushed a three-dimensional cloud through the classic Lorenz model from nineteen sixty-three. A six-dimensional cloud then rode the larger Lorenz model from nineteen ninety-six. Across several graphics cards, the new code ran more than a thousand times faster than the original. High-dimensional uncertainty work that once waited can now run interactively.
arxiv-2508-14186:
Nicholas Crawford, Maya Sankar, Carl Schildkraut, and Sam Spiro prove a coloring result about hypercubes in a mathematics paper from two thousand twenty-five. A hypercube is a graph with corners linked by edges in many dimensions. In a proper edge coloring, edges sharing a corner get different colors.

The authors show that any such coloring of the n-dimensional hypercube contains a rainbow copy of every tree with at most n edges. Rainbow means every edge of the tree carries a different color. The bound cannot be improved, since a coloring with only n colors can avoid rainbow cycles entirely. The result settles how much color variety is forced by the cube's structure.
arxiv-2508-14886:
Omar French, Gregory Werner, and Dmitri Uzdensky study particle injection in relativistic magnetic reconnection, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. Magnetic field lines snap and rejoin, and some particles are flung to high energies. The flung particles form a power-law spectrum, and the low-energy entry point is called the injection energy. Yet that entry step had drawn far less study than what follows it.

The team runs fully kinetic particle-in-cell simulations in two and three dimensions. They count the share from each of three entry routes: direct electric field push, Fermi kicks, and pickup acceleration. They also measure how the magnetization of the inflow shifts the entry energy, and they build a theory to explain the patterns. Comparing the two- and three-dimensional runs shows what the flux-rope kink and the drift-kink instability do to this step.
arxiv-2508-15186:
Yu, Jiang, and Zhao wrote a theoretical physics paper in twenty twenty-five on Dirac monopoles in non-Hermitian systems. A Dirac monopole is a point-like source of magnetism, long studied as an idea. Non-Hermitian systems can gain or lose energy, unlike closed systems.

The authors show that small non-Hermitian changes can spread a point monopole into an extended pattern of charge. Three forms of a geometric quantity give three distinct patterns. They confirm the patterns by tracking complex geometric phases as the system changes slowly. One neat result links tiny summed energy differences directly to phase shifts. They also propose measuring these signs using solitons, stable wave packets, in a special cooled gas.
arxiv-2508-15686: Renan Isneri, Josias Baca, and Lucas Fernandes explore norms in infinite dimensional Banach spaces in two thousand twenty-five. Distinct norms can shape distinct topologies on one space. Their study weighs how those norms interact and clash. Norms induced by bijective linear maps get close study first. The team then asks when non-equivalent norms can exist at all. Hamel bases, the algebraic spine of such spaces, enter the account. The note is brief and maps the core questions of the topic.
arxiv-2508-16286:
Hao Zhu, Ding-Zu Wang, Shi-Ju Ran, and Guo-Feng Zhang fold disorder into an extra layer so quantum spin chains become tractable. Simulating many-body dynamics with random disorder is a standing challenge. Their statistics-encoded tensor network stores the disorder distribution in an auxiliary layer. Averaging then happens separately, restoring translational invariance and a clean transfer matrix.

A universal criterion ties the needed discretization to disorder strength and evolution time. Encoding pays off most in the weak-disorder, typically chaotic regime. Applied to the disordered transverse-field Ising chain, the method shows the spectral form factor is ruled by the leading transfer-matrix eigenvalue. That contrasts with the kicked Ising model's behavior. The framework opens disorder-driven dynamics to tensor network tools. It gives chaos in dirty systems a new computational handle.
arxiv-2508-16386:
Hortence Nana and Christos Dimitrakakis study fair cohort selection when the end results are not yet known, in a two thousand twenty-five paper. The case that drives the work is university admissions. Staff must pick a class while they can see just part of what each applicant will go on to do. A fixed rule may go stale as the pool shifts year by year.

The team builds a frame that joins outcome models with policy gradient methods. It can use both logistic and neural network rules. In the step-by-step form, the rule and its models change side by side, fed by data from past years. Tests on a simulator built from real admissions data favor the rules that adapt. They beat fixed ones on the gain staff can expect, most when the cost of a place runs high, and they keep fair play in good shape.
arxiv-2508-16486:
Kilian Seibold, Greta Villa, Javier del Pino, and Oded Zilberberg published a 2025 physics paper on whether the topology of classical flows survives in a quantum device. Their system is a driven Kerr oscillator, a nonlinear resonator fed with energy and leaking it away. Such systems settle into non-equilibrium steady states. Classically, the pattern of flows in its phase space decides which states exist and how they connect.

When the number or handedness of those steady states changes, the system undergoes a topological transition. The authors solved the quantum version with a master equation and trajectory methods. The quantum dynamics kept clear fingerprints of the classical flow topology, readable in quantum measurements. That survival is not guaranteed; quantization often washes classical structure away. The result suggests driven-dissipative devices can be designed, and diagnosed, using the classical flow map as a guide, a bridge between two descriptions of one machine.
arxiv-2508-17686:
Video-capable language models chew through huge numbers of image tokens, and long videos make the cost grow fast. Yogesh Kumar proposes a pruning method that lets the words of the user's question steer which tokens survive. Segments that the question points to keep a dense set of tokens, while less relevant stretches are thinned. The approach is not tied to one model and plugs into existing systems such as TimeChat and LLaVA-Video.

In tests, the method cut computing cost by about 65 percent while keeping 97 to 99 percent of the original scores. On the QVHighlights set it raised the top-hit score by 9.5 points, and on Charades-STA it kept 99.6 percent of the top-score result. Gains were largest on questions with clear time markers, such as asking when an event happens. The author argues that question-guided pruning is a practical route to longer, cheaper video understanding.
arxiv-2508-17986:
Karel Bartunek, Lukas Rustler, and Matej Hoffmann wrote a 2025 paper on a robot arm that finds and grasps objects by touch alone, with no cameras. Most robots lean on vision to locate things. Touch, if used at all, plays a small part. This team covered the whole arm in sensitive skin that feels contact anywhere on its surface.

The search runs in two phases. First the arm sweeps the workspace broadly, noting every touch across its skin. Then its gripper, fitted with a force sensor, pinpoints the object for a grasp. In tests on a real robot, single objects were found, grasped, and dropped in a basket with a success rate of about eighty-six percent. The whole-body method worked six times faster than gripper touch alone. The authors point to smoky, dark, or dusty settings where eyes fail but touch still works.
arxiv-2508-18686:
Basak, Kumar, and Bhattacharjee lead a long author list on this paper from two thousand twenty-five. It reports a second band of nuclei in samarium-152 that spins with tetrahedral symmetry.

The band was made by fusing a neodymium target with alpha particles at a Kolkata cyclotron. The new sequence shows mixed parity, no E2 links, and strong signs of E3 links. Those marks fit the known tests for a tetrahedral band. This band lacks the octahedral side its first-found twin showed. Group theory and the Bohr model of shared nuclear motion back the read. The find backs past theory claims and throws new light on symmetry breaking in heavy nuclei.
arxiv-2508-19786:
Han Jiao, Jiakai Sun, and colleagues rebuild moving scenes in three dimensions with a motion-aware split in a 2025 computer vision study. A popular method stores a scene as soft three-dimensional blobs and learns one deformation field to move them all over time. In busy regions that single field blurs detail and drops fine motion, since one rule must serve still and rushing areas alike.

Partitioning the scene by how much motion each part carries lets separate handling fit each zone. Quiet areas stay crisp while fast areas get dedicated deformation capacity. High-fidelity dynamic reconstruction serves film, telepresence, and robot perception.
arxiv-2508-20086:
Youwei Huang and co-authors present a model that spots hidden bad intent in smart contracts. Smart contracts are programs that run deals on a blockchain, and bad code inside them has caused large losses. An earlier model flagged unsafe intent with fair scores. The new model adds a language model pre-trained on code, tuned on sixteen thousand real contracts. It keeps a two-way memory network to sort each contract's intents.

On ten thousand real contracts across ten intent classes, the new model scored far above the old one. Its F-score rose to about 0.93, with high marks for exactness and coverage. It also beat a top general AI model by a wide margin on this task. The authors present it as the new best tool for this check.
arxiv-2508-21686:
Matthew Brunet and co-authors improve a quantum algorithm for hard choice problems by rewriting its constraints, in work from 2025. The algorithm, QAOA, tackles problems such as picking the largest set of unlinked nodes in a graph. Rules that forbid some choices are usually added as penalties in the goal function, which can blur the search.

The team instead writes each constraint as a Boolean formula in a special form before adding penalties. They tested the method on graphs with three to twenty nodes. The rewritten form gave better approximation scores than the standard penalty route, with gains up to about thirty percent. It won after a single algorithm layer on about two thirds of the graphs. The work offers a practical step for near-term quantum hardware.
arxiv-2509-00086:
Rodrigo Tertulino, working alone, compares pooled and federated learning for student performance forecasts in Brazil in 2025. Data mining could personalize learning and flag at-risk students early. Brazil's data law, the LGPD, bars pooling sensitive student data in one place, which blocks the standard route.

Federated learning trains a shared model while data stay at each school. Tertulino trains a deep network with the FedProx method across a simulated set of fifty schools. Its scores are benchmarked against a pooled XGBoost model, a strong tree-based method. Data come from SAEB, the national basic education assessment system. The study tests whether privacy-safe training can still forecast well enough for school use.
arxiv-2509-00286:
Rakshitha De Silva, Shiva Raj Pokhrel, Jonathan Kua, and Sithamparanathan Kandeepan survey intelligent spectrum management in satellite communications in 2025. Satellite networks are a pillar of global connectivity. Demand for bandwidth keeps rising, and mega constellations crowd the sky, so fixed exclusive spectrum grants waste a scarce resource.

Cognitive radio lets gear sense its setting and adapt, and dynamic spectrum management applies that idea to satellites. The survey reviews how smart dynamic methods adapt to satellite networks, with gains in flexibility and performance. It also covers hurdles in regulation and standardization that slow real use. Smarter sharing could ease spectrum scarcity as constellations grow.
arxiv-2509-00386:
Edric Matwiejew leads a team of six authors who realize quantum walk-based variational ansätze on neutral atom hardware in 2025. Continuous-time quantum walks offer provable speedups for set problems, but porting those gains to near-term hardware is hard. Variational ansätze are trial quantum states tuned by classical feedback to solve a target problem.

For unentangled targets, closed-form expressions give near-optimal control parameters that transfer to hardware with minimal calibration. On QuEra's Aquila processor, the team observes the super-quadratic convergence of efficient walk algorithms at low circuit depth. For entangled targets in the Rydberg-blockaded subspace, a protocol exploits spectral traits of the walk, with time scaling inversely with the spectral gap.
arxiv-2509-00486:
Shahrukh Salim and one co-author, Poornima Shakya, use shot noise, the grainy flicker in current caused by charge moving in discrete packets, to study Andreev reflection. That process occurs at a graphene and superconductor join, where an electron reflects as a hole, a missing electron state.

Salim and Shakya compute reflection in three junction layouts, with one or two superconductors around graphene. They find retro reflection, where the hole retraces the path, lowers noise, while specular reflection, where it mirrors away, raises it, with patterns that shift with Fermi level, an energy reference. The work suggests noise measures can tell these reflection types apart beyond what conductance alone shows.
arxiv-2509-00886:
Duaa Abdullah and Jasem Hamoud investigate the density of Fibonacci words. Fibonacci words are built by joining earlier blocks in a Fibonacci pattern. They define a word's density through counts of zeros and ones. Their ratios are analyzed across the sequence of words. The ratios converge to powers of the golden ratio, phi.

This illustrates the exponential growth rates intrinsic to Fibonacci words. The density of the words approaches unity over time. That matches classical results on Fibonacci number distributions. Generating functions are derived for general terms of the words. Combinatorial formulas are derived as well. Numerical data and graphs confirm the theoretical findings. They reveal both early transient behavior and long-run behavior of the densities.
arxiv-2509-00986:
Darko Sasanski and Riste Stojanov review food data in the Semantic Web. The review covers key resources, knowledge graphs, and new applications. It examines resources such as USDA, FoodOn, FooDB, and Recipe1M+. Their roles in representing nutrition data are emphasized throughout.

Special focus goes to food entity linking and recognition methods. Those methods join mixed food sources into cohesive resources. Food knowledge graphs are discussed for data enrichment and extraction. They also help systems work together across formats. Applications include personalized nutrition and ingredient swaps. Food-drug and food-disease links are covered as well. The review sums up current advances and notes open challenges. It aims to guide future work in this domain.
arxiv-2509-01986:
Ziyun Zeng, David Junhao Zhang, Wei Li, and Mike Zheng Shou rebalance roles inside unified models that both read and make images. Such models ace text to image work but stumble on precise edits. The reading side mostly translates instructions, while the making side must design the layout and paint the result alone. Yet the reading side trains on far more reasoning data.

Their Draw-In-Mind data give the reader explicit design duties. One set holds millions of long context image text pairs for instruction grasp. Another holds hundreds of thousands of step by step edit plans from a leading model as blueprints. A small linked model trained on this data tops edit benchmarks despite modest size. Assigning design to the reader clearly pays off.
arxiv-2509-02086:
Roman Okatev, Oleg Zikanov, Dmitry Krasnov, and Peter Frick study a new instability in Hartmann channel flow with varying conductivity. Hartmann flow moves conducting fluid through a channel under a crosswise magnetic field. In liquid metal applications, conductivity and viscosity can vary across the channel width. That variation, absent in the classic setup, reshapes the base velocity profile.

Linear conductivity change makes the profile asymmetric and creates inflection points. Strong enough change triggers instability at far lower flow rates than the classic threshold. The instability shows long axial waves and growth centered in the channel core. Its traits echo the classic inviscid inflection point mechanism. Direct simulations confirm the resulting transition to turbulence.
arxiv-2509-02186:
Phani Sahasra Akkinepally leads four co-authors in building fault tolerant decentralized federated learning without a central server. Federated learning trains shared models across clients while data stay private. Central servers create bottlenecks and single points of failure, so decentralized designs remove them. Synchronous rounds wait for stragglers, while asynchronous updates let clients move independently.

Phase one builds the asynchronous decentralized framework itself. Phase two adds fault tolerance for client failures and dropped messages. Two new techniques let each client judge convergence and decide termination on its own. All active clients conclude meaningfully despite faults and async chatter. The design targets heterogeneous, unreliable real deployments.
arxiv-2509-02386:
Niels de Graaf Sousa and three co-authors wrote a 2025 active matter physics paper on materials made of many self-moving units, such as migrating cells or swimming bacteria. Standard theory treats such systems as either polar, with shared direction, or nematic, with shared alignment only.

The authors add self-propulsion, each unit pushing itself forward, into the nematic framework as a minimal model. Stability analysis shows propulsion shifts when disorder breaks down. Simulations then reveal unusual patterns: density fluctuations opposite to uniform spreading, long-range order in swirling motion, and energy cascades that break standard scaling. Ordered states appear well before full flocking. Order also peaks at a middle propulsion strength, a clue for designing synthetic active materials.
arxiv-2509-02586:
Esha Sadia Nasir and three co-authors wrote a 2025 paper for the MIDOG 2025 challenge. The task is to find dividing cells in tissue images. Such cells are called mitotic figures. The system must also flag abnormal ones.

Their MitoDetect++ pipeline splits the job in two. Detection uses a U-Net style network. It has an EfficientNetV2 backbone and attention modules. Combined segmentation losses train it. The atypical class uses a large vision transformer. Low-rank adapters tune it at low cost. Strong augmentation, focal loss, and group-aware cross-validation fight domain shifts between labs. Test-time augmentation adds robustness at run time. Balanced accuracy across domains stayed strong. That supports use across varied clinical image sources.
arxiv-2509-02686:
Mengjie Yang and Ching Hua Lee wrote a 2025 physics paper on the non-Hermitian skin effect. In that effect, waves pile up at a boundary. The systems have one-way couplings. Intuition says the pile-up follows the coupling direction.

The authors show the pile-up can flip. The flip needs no change to the couplings. Adjusting system size is enough. So is changing boundary conditions in a sideways direction. Suppressing amplification along the first direction makes the reversed behaviour robust. A designed Kagome lattice shows the effect in wavepacket simulations. Kagome is a pattern of corner-sharing triangles. The switch is controlled non-locally, from the transverse direction. The mechanism exploits how spectral loops from distinct boundary choices intertwine. It suggests new sensors and lasers.
arxiv-2509-02786:
Jackson Morris wrote a 2025 solo algebraic topology paper computing the ring of cooperations for very effective hermitian K-theory over finite fields. That ring records how the theory interacts with itself, and it feeds spectral sequence calculations across motivic homotopy theory.

Morris works over every finite field whose characteristic is not two. The computation runs through the motivic Adams spectral sequence. All of its differentials turn out to be determined by the integral motivic cohomology of the field, which makes the calculation tractable. As an application, the first page of the kq-resolution is computed. Results of this kind supply raw algebraic data that other researchers use to resolve further motivic spectra.
arxiv-2509-03086:
Georgy Lukyanov wrote a 2025 economics paper on member-owned lenders that pool returns and hand surplus back as patronage. Such mutual credit pools insure borrowers against bad luck, but each member's stake depends on who else belongs. Alongside the mutual sits ordinary market debt that anyone can seek.

At first, market access helps the mutual by funding borrowers it had to ration. Once the mutual's capacity grows wide enough, though, high-return members do better borrowing alone than subsidizing the pool, so they leave. Their exit frees room for low-return members yet destroys shared insurance. Welfare therefore rises with market access at low capacity and falls near full capacity. The pattern survived even when pooling was incomplete.
arxiv-2509-03286:
Prachi Bagave and 3 co-authors built an accountability framework for AI systems in healthcare in a 2025 paper. As AI helps practitioners make health decisions, who answers for a bad outcome becomes a pressing question. European rules state what should be achieved but say little about how, leaving hospitals and developers unsure of their duties.

The authors reviewed how different actors understand accountability, since the word means different things to regulators, builders, and clinicians. Their framework places healthcare AI rules and each actor's mechanisms under one consistent regime. A three-tier structure sorts those mechanisms by conduct. The paper argues that accountability in medical AI is shared across actors, not owned by one. Clear explanation of system reasoning helps the communication that joint accountability needs.
arxiv-2509-03786:
Xinxin Huang and four co-authors devote a 2025 research paper to detecting camouflaged objects underwater, a task they argue is both important and underexplored. Marine animals blend into their surroundings, and finding them matters for marine ecology. Optical distortion, turbid water, and the complex bodies of sea creatures make accurate detection unusually hard.

The team introduces the task formally and builds DeepCamo, a benchmark dataset for the domain. Leading camouflaged object detection models are first benchmarked on it, exposing their weaknesses. Their proposed network, SLENet, then adds two supports: a gamma-asymmetric enhancement module that strengthens multi-scale features, and a localisation guidance branch that draws a location map rich in global meaning. That map guides a multi-scale supervised decoder toward more accurate masks. Experiments on DeepCamo and three general camouflage benchmarks confirm stronger performance than leading methods. The gains also carry over to the broader camouflage detection task.
arxiv-2509-03986:
A 2025 research paper by Mohamed Insaf Ismithdeen and two co-authors measures how sensitive large multimodal models are to the wording of their prompts. On multiple-choice question answering, changes in phrasing can swing accuracy by up to fifteen percent for some model and prompt combinations. That variability undermines evaluation, since reported scores often come from chosen best-case prompts.

Their framework, Promptception, systematises the test: sixty-one prompt types grouped into fifteen categories and six supercategories, each probing one aspect of prompt formulation. Ten models are evaluated across three multiple-choice benchmarks, with GPT-4o, Gemini 1.5 Pro, and open-source systems among them. Proprietary models prove more sensitive to phrasing, a sign of tighter alignment with instruction wording. Open-source models are steadier, though they struggle more with nuanced and complex phrasing. From the analysis, the authors propose prompting principles tailored separately to proprietary and open-source models.
arxiv-2509-04086:
Yaru Chen and six co-authors present a system for finding events in videos using both sound and images in a 2025 computer science paper. The task, called audio-visual video parsing, must name each event and mark when it starts and ends. Training data usually labels whole clips only, not each moment, so systems learn from rough guesses. Those guesses can mislead attention-based models and blur event timing.

Their design first uses sights and sounds to clean up the word descriptions of events. A graph module then links moments at several time scales, with timing rules fitted to each event type. On two public benchmarks, the system beat earlier methods across standard measures.
arxiv-2509-04986:
Glasses absorb more heat at very low temperatures than simple sound-wave theory predicts. Walter Schirmacher and one co-author explain that anomaly using frozen-in internal stresses in a 2025 theoretical physics paper. Their approach applies a recent theory of nonphononic vibrational states, the extra vibrations in glasses beyond ordinary sound waves.

Within a fully harmonic description, local excitations hybridise with waves to create an excess density of states. That excess produces a specific heat whose apparent temperature exponent falls between one and two, matching experiments. The authors discuss using the findings to characterise glassy materials, and contrast their harmonic account with theories needing tunnelling.
arxiv-2509-05186:
Models that learn to solve equations from examples can also express uncertainty about their answers. Benjamin J. Zhang, lead author with three co-authors, give such models a chance-based reading in a 2025 paper. In-context operator networks learn solution maps from pairs of conditions and solutions across many equations.

The authors show the network in effect does Bayesian inference. It computes the mean of a posterior distribution over such maps. A generative version can sample from that spread instead, capturing uncertainty in the map itself. That gives principled uncertainty estimates for predictions. The framework, built on random differential equations, also makes other multi-map learning methods clearer.
arxiv-2509-05386:
Machines replace workers not by their price tag but by their ability to do work like workers, Vladimir Pokrovskii argues in a solo 2025 economics note. Output rises when equipment enters production, and standard theory describes that rise as capital substituting for labour.

Pokrovskii's proposed mechanism counts three factors: equipment, human labour, and the substitutive work the equipment itself performs. Two technical coefficients state how much labour and energy a unit of equipment needs to engage. From these he builds production functions of several forms. None of them matches the popular Cobb-Douglas form, which he claims is flawed at its core. The note is a theoretical challenge to a textbook staple.
arxiv-2509-05486:
Languages whose words split into many tokens pay a hidden tax, Jessica M. Lundin and six co-authors document in a 2025 paper on multilingual tokenisation. Tokenisers chop text into pieces before a model reads it, and morphologically rich, lower-resource languages need far more pieces per word.

Testing ten large models on a question set in sixteen African languages, the authors show token fertility, tokens per word, reliably predicts accuracy: higher fertility means lower scores everywhere. Newer reasoning models beat non-reasoning peers and narrowed some gaps. They also translate token inflation into money, arguing doubled tokens can quadruple training cost and time. Fairer tokenisation and pricing are their remedies.
arxiv-2509-05586:
Checking whether a shared data structure behaved as if used by one program at a time can be done efficiently when few processes are involved. Lee Zheng Han and Umang Mathur show this in a 2025 computer science paper. This linearizability check is hard in general, even for simple registers.

Their result covers stacks, queues, priority queues, and maps. The algorithm's cost grows exponentially only in the number of processes, not in the history size, so it stays fast for small process counts. The method reduces the check to a reachability question on labelled graphs. An implementation beat existing algorithms, whose worst-case run times are exponential in the history, by a wide margin in their tests.
arxiv-2509-06286:
Recommendations that blend what people say with who clicks what are built in RecMind, a 2025 system from Chang Xue and three co-authors. Consumer platforms fight sparse interactions, fast content churn, and mixed textual signals. RecMind treats a language model as a preference prior rather than the ranker itself: a frozen model with light adapters reads titles, attributes, and reviews into embeddings.

A graph network learns collaborative embeddings from the user-item graph in parallel. A symmetric contrastive objective aligns the two views, and gating inside the layers lets language dominate for cold, long-tail items while graph structure steadies popular ones. On Yelp and Amazon-Electronics data, RecMind tops all eight reported metrics, and ablations credit both alignment and gating.
arxiv-2509-06886:
How stars are born, mass by mass, across the universe is reviewed in a 2025 white paper led by Tereza Jerabkova, with twenty-one co-authors. The stellar initial mass function describes the distribution of masses formed in one star-forming event. It underpins galactic chemical enrichment, habitable zone estimates, and black hole growth, yet whether it varies with environment is unsettled.

The review links the core mass function in star-forming clumps, stellar multiplicity, and dynamical processes to the galaxy-wide version of the mass function. Evidence for dependence on a clump's metallicity and density is weighed, alongside galaxy-scale evidence from gravitational lensing, kinematics, and spectral diagnostics. Theory adds further perspectives on variability. Beyond summarizing, the authors set out a shared framework and strategies for studying a variable mass function with coming telescopes and space observatories.
arxiv-2509-06986:
Cell images from different laboratories are unified by a transformer model in a 2025 computational biology paper by Cedric Caruzzo and one co-author. Cell painting assays photograph cells under many treatments, and consortia like JUMP have produced massive datasets. Batch effects and poor generalization across datasets block large-scale discovery.

Their model, CellPainTR, learns representations of cell shape and structure that resist batch effects. Source-specific context tokens let it adapt to each dataset's quirks while sharing the core representation, so it can generalize to entirely unseen datasets without fine-tuning. On the JUMP data it beat established correction methods at both batch integration and keeping biological signal. On an unseen dataset from another group, performance held up despite major domain and feature shifts. The authors frame it as a step toward foundation models for image-based profiling.
arxiv-2509-07186:
Tiny particles that assemble themselves into crystals pose a sorting problem: how can researchers label each particle's local pattern? Alptuğ Ulugöl and 6 co-authors compare three unsupervised machine learning methods for that job in a 2025 research paper. The methods shrink complex particle data into simpler maps. They are principal component analysis, autoencoders, and UMAP, a popular nonlinear mapping tool.

The team first tests the methods on fluids and crystals of hard and charged spheres. They then try an icosahedral arrangement, a twenty-faced pattern, formed by spheres packed inside a round container, using both simulations and experiments. UMAP captures the complex structural features most reliably in every test. The comparison gives soft matter researchers a grounded pick when no one knows the right patterns in advance.
arxiv-2509-07286:
Santhoshini Velusamy and 1 co-author study how to spot the most frequent items in a data stream with as little memory as possible in a 2025 paper. A heavy hitter is an item whose count stands out against the total stream energy, a standard target in network monitoring and databases. Streams can be huge, so algorithms must summarize them on the fly rather than store them.

Earlier methods, CountSketch and BPTree, set the memory benchmarks, but one leaves a gap when the frequency threshold is very small. The new work targets random-order streams, where items arrive in uniformly random order even if an adversary picked them. For that setting, the authors aim at the optimal memory bound that earlier work reached only in narrower cases. Tight memory limits decide whether stream monitors can run on small, fast hardware.
arxiv-2509-07386:
Rafi Hessami and 5 co-authors simulate Unruh radiation in laser-electron collisions in a 2025 paper. The Unruh effect predicts that an accelerating observer feels empty space as a warm bath of particles, but no one has observed it directly. Smashing electrons with intense lasers accelerates them hard, which may make the effect large enough to hunt for in near-term experiments.

Using three-dimensional Monte Carlo simulations, the team models facilities like FACET-II and LUXE, treating Unruh emission as scattering from a heat-like spectrum. They map where the Unruh signal stands out most against ordinary Compton radiation, the usual glow from such collisions. For current setups the best windows sit at small angles and mid-range energies, though the signal stays tiny. A future LUXE phase improves the ratio by over a hundredfold, which motivates dedicated off-axis measurements.
arxiv-2509-07486:
Zichun Hao and 6 co-authors propose RINO in 2025, a way to pre-train particle physics models on real collision data without labels.
