Supervised models in high energy physics usually learn from simulations, which can mismodel real collisions and detector responses, a mismatch called domain shift. RINO instead uses self-supervised learning, where the model invents its own training signals from raw data.

The method teaches embeddings, numeric summaries of jets, that stay invariant under renormalization group flow, a change of the energy scale at which a collision is viewed. A transformer model is pre-trained on a QCD-dominated dataset that mimics real data, then fine-tuned on simulated data to spot jets from top quark decays. RINO generalizes across the two datasets better than training from scratch. The authors see a path to pre-training on abundant real data and fine-tuning on small, trusted simulations.
arxiv-2509-07586:
Patricia Hu, with 3 co-authors, asks in 2025 whether state-of-the-art piano transcription can run fast enough for live music. Piano transcription turns audio into notes, and online systems currently lag by 128 to 320 milliseconds. Most real-time musical uses need latency under 30 milliseconds, so the authors adapt a leading online model toward that goal.

They remove all non-causal processing, steps that peek at future audio, share computations across model components, and vary model size. Different preprocessing, postprocessing, and label encoding schemes are compared for real-time suitability. On the MAESTRO dataset, strictly causal processing costs some accuracy, and preprocessing choices trade latency against prediction quality. The team releases the adapted system as a baseline so others can design toward minimum-latency transcription.
arxiv-2509-07686:
Faizuddin Ahmed and 1 co-author study light bending around a modified black hole in a 2025 paper. The spacetime is a Schwarzschild black hole corrected by holonomy. Holonomy is a quantum gravity-inspired change drawn from loop approaches. A cloud of strings surrounds the hole. Strings are one-dimensional objects that alter gravity around them. The authors ask how these two ingredients change lensing and the photon sphere.

They work in the weak-field limit. They derive the deflection angle in analytic form and extract lensing observables from it. Each parameter moves the predictions away from the classical case in its own way. A normalized vector field reveals the topological structure of the photon sphere. It shows how strings and holonomy reshape that sphere. Thin accretion disk traits are also examined in this background. Such signatures, if ever observed, could hint at quantum gravity effects in strong gravity settings.
arxiv-2509-08086:
News text mentions thousands of companies and people, and linking each mention to the right knowledge graph entry is error-prone. Michael Kishelev and 3 co-authors present JEL in a 2025 research paper. JEL is an entity linking model built from several neural networks working end to end. The authors report that it beats the current state of the art while staying computationally efficient.

The work grew out of news analytics needs inside JPMorgan, where many teams track news for business decisions. Spending on outside news vendors runs into millions of dollars yearly. Reliable entity linking bridges raw news and curated knowledge graphs. That bridge gives analysts fast access to structured facts about the firms and people in a story. The authors present JEL as a faster, more accurate foundation for such analytics platforms.
arxiv-2509-08286:
An open conjecture about how much classical information two measurements can extract from shared quantum states is advanced by Hasan Iqbal in a solo 2025 quantum information paper. The CQC conjecture, posed in 2014, caps the sum of classical mutual informations from measuring each side in two unbiased bases by the pair's quantum mutual information. It remains unproved in general.

Using a result of Coles and Piani, Iqbal derives a sufficient condition under which the conjecture holds. The condition validates the conjecture for a wider class of states than the original work covered. Conjectures like this police the border between classical and quantum correlations; each enlargement of the proven region tells physicists where quantum advantage in information tasks can and cannot hide.
arxiv-2509-08486:
Helpful, harmless, and honest pull language models in three directions, and Gautam Siddharth Kashyap with 2 co-authors build one framework to balance them in a 2025 alignment paper. Tuning for a single virtue in isolation produces trade-offs and inconsistent behaviour. Mixture-of-experts designs promise modularity, but poorly calibrated routing blunts them for alignment work.

TrinityX installs a mixture of calibrated experts inside the transformer, so routing decisions carry trustworthy confidence. Each expert can lean toward a different alignment dimension while the calibration keeps the blend honest. Assistants deployed to millions need all three virtues at once; a model that is honest but unhelpful, or helpful but unsafe, fails its users just the same.
arxiv-2509-08586:
Prashant Singh Basnet and 1 co-author test a hybrid image model for finding pneumonia in this 2025 paper. The model joins a CNN, which scans local patterns, with a vision transformer, which looks at wider structure. Training uses limited data from scratch, with no pretraining.

Experiments vary how much data is used and whether sick and healthy cases are balanced. The hybrid reaches strong recall and steady scores, and it beats each part alone on uneven data. Training time stays close to transformer models. The work matters where medical image sets are small and uneven.
arxiv-2509-08786:
Valerio Belocchi and 3 co-authors calculate two-particle two-hole effects in neutrino scattering on nuclei in a 2025 paper. When a neutrino hits a nucleus, it can knock out two particles and leave two holes. That process affects how experiments read neutrino energy.

The work uses a relativistic Fermi gas model with meson exchange currents, including pion exchange and a Delta resonance. It first matches known inclusive results, where only the muon is observed. It then extends to a new case, semi-inclusive scattering, where a knocked out nucleon is also seen. Results are given at fixed energy and folded with the T2K experiment flux.
arxiv-2509-08986:
Optimization contests often crown algorithms that secretly spend more computing than their rivals. Junbo Jacob Lian argues the scoring itself is rigged, in a 2025 research paper written alone. Many improved metaheuristics claim wins based on equal function evaluations. Yet costlier iterations, preprocessing, and tuning hide inside that count. Lian proposes wall-clock time as the main budget instead.

His restart-fair protocol gives every algorithm the same time per problem. Restarts, early stopping, and internal adaptation remain free choices within that budget. He advocates anytime performance curves and time-based profiles aimed at fixed targets. A short reporting checklist accompanies the protocol to expose hidden overheads. The aim is credibility: comparisons that reflect what practitioners actually pay. Benchmark reform is unglamorous work, but fields that skip it end up optimizing for the scoreboard instead of the problem.
arxiv-2509-09286:
Bohao Tang and 8 co-authors propose Visual Programmability for chart understanding in a 2025 paper. Charts test the reasoning of vision language models. Code as thought represents chart information in verifiable symbolic form, but a fixed code only approach fails on complex charts.

Visual programmability is a learnable property that decides if a chart question suits a code based route or direct looking. A model learns to choose between the two pathways. Reinforcement learning uses a dual reward: one for data accuracy, one for choosing the right strategy. That prevents defaulting to a single mode. Experiments show strong, robust performance across diverse chart benchmarks.
arxiv-2509-09386:
Measuring a telescope's side lobes, its faint off-axis responses, demands a brightness range that saturates ordinary detectors. Haruaki Hirose and 7 co-authors demonstrate a feedback-controlled measurement method in a 2025 research paper. Their target instruments are cosmic microwave background telescopes. The method uses an artificial microwave source whose power varies under feedback from the detector being tested.

Feedback keeps the detector in its honest range while the source sweeps widely. In a lab proof of concept, the team measured a horn antenna's beam pattern coupled to a diode detector. The feedback added a large chunk of dynamic range to the measurement. Reference readings with standard methods confirmed the result. The technique suits any optical measurement hunting subtle imperfections, where the signal of interest hides far below the peak and detector nonlinearity usually buries it.
arxiv-2509-09686:
Fei Huang and 6 co-authors present a 2025 technical report on GeoGPT, an open large language model system built for geoscience research. To make its answers more exact, they added retrieval augmented generation, which lets the model pull facts from an outside library while it writes. Here that library is a curated store of geoscience material.

Users can also upload their own publication lists and have the system answer from those papers. The team fine-tuned an embedding model and a reranking model to sharpen retrieval, and they released both parts, GeoEmbedding and GeoReranker, as open source. The report frames the work as open science meant for researchers and professionals worldwide.
arxiv-2509-09886:
Daniele Celoria and 2 co-authors prove a formula describing how a topological counting series changes when a cusp in a three-dimensional shape is filled in during a 2025 geometry paper. The 3D index, born in physics, packs deep information about cusped manifolds into a q-series and can be read as a tally over special surfaces inside a triangulation. Filling a cusp, the Dehn operation, is how closed shapes are built from cusped ones.

A relative version of the index for triangulations with exposed boundary lets the authors state and prove a relative Gang-Yonekura formula by gluing pieces and inducting through layered solid tori. Certified computer checks back the theory. Large fillings behave as the formula predicts, supporting a well-defined index for closed manifolds as well.
arxiv-2509-10086:
Xin Wang and 2 co-authors ask whether a deployed speech deepfake detector can notice the world drifting away from its training data in a 2025 machine learning operations paper. A frozen detector weakens as new synthesis engines appear, and nobody may realise until fakes slip through. Watching for drift, a widening gap between fresh traffic and the reference data, could raise the alarm early enough to act.

On a small toy set and on the large MLAAD collection, distance measures between data distributions did flag drift caused by fresh text-to-speech attacks. Better still, fine-tuning the detector on examples from the new generators shrank both the measured drift and the detection error rate. Maintenance, not just accuracy on day one, becomes the paper's measure of a detector.
arxiv-2509-10386:
Junichi Takahashi, Hiroshi Ohno, and Akio Tomiya extract the spectral fingerprint of charmonium, bound states of charm quarks, from lattice simulations in this 2025 nuclear physics paper. The raw data are correlation functions over imaginary time, and recovering a spectrum from them is an ill-posed inverse problem, especially at high temperature where quark matter melts.

Their tool is sparse modeling, which assumes the true spectrum is mostly empty and solves accordingly. Tests on fake data mimicking charmonium show resonance peaks come back well, while broad transport peaks resist recovery without extra assumptions. Applied to real lattice data below and above the critical temperature, the method agrees qualitatively with the established maximum entropy approach. The value: a leaner set of assumptions still captures the main physics.
arxiv-2509-10786:
Long Chen and Cong Zhao redefine the mass of a heavy quark in this 2025 paper. The textbook pole mass carries a hidden flaw. An infrared renormalon ambiguity limits its precision, no matter how many loops are computed. Their candidate, the sigma-mass, is built by subtracting the trace anomaly contribution. They argue it is free of that leading ambiguity, and stays scheme- and scale-independent.

The authors show the offending divergence lives entirely in the trace anomaly part of the energy-momentum tensor. They derive a formula linking the sigma-mass to the pole mass. It uses only the beta function, the mass anomalous dimension, and a rewritten conversion factor. They push the relation to five loops. They also chart how lattice QCD could extract the sigma-mass directly, analyzing the matching through four loops. The case is for a cleaner shared standard.
arxiv-2509-10986:
What do electrons look like the instant a laser frees them from oxygen? Edward L. Ruden models that moment in this solo-authored 2025 plasma physics paper. His semi-empirical model predicts the thermalized temperature of the freed electrons. It also predicts their mean momentum along the laser's direction. A focused ultrashort pulse at eight hundred nanometers frees them from oxygen molecules, across peak intensities. Plasma simulations need exactly such starting conditions.

The work starts from theory: energy spectra for the most probable ionization path, under a nonadiabatic strong-field approximation. Two adjustable parameters, fitted to measured spectra, stand in for effects the scheme omits. The electron may recombine with its parent ion, or scatter off it, during the optical cycle after ionization. Classical kinematics of that elastic rescattering, together with the Lorentz force, then yield the mean forward momentum.
arxiv-2509-11086:
Rong Yang and Xiangling Zhu wrote this 2025 paper in complex analysis. That branch of mathematics studies functions of complex numbers. The authors introduce a new function space. It is called the derivative tent space. They ask how it sits inside a family of logarithmic Bloch-type spaces.

The main result describes the closure of the new space. The closure is taken in the logarithmic Bloch-type norm. Roughly, it tells which functions in the bigger space can be approached by functions from the smaller one. The approach can be as close as desired. The authors also obtain fresh characterizations of two related closures. Those closures were studied before. Results like these help analysts sort out how growth scales fit together.
arxiv-2509-11286:
Spacecraft flying through collisionless shocks measure very strong electric field fluctuations. Simulations produce much weaker ones. Vadim Roytershteyn and four co-authors chase the mismatch in this 2025 plasma physics paper. Without matching amplitudes, models cannot explain shock energy conversion.

The team ran one-dimensional particle-in-cell simulations. They used the true proton-to-electron mass ratio. One case had upstream electrons hotter than the ions. There, fluctuation size grew with a key frequency ratio. It reached realistic strengths once that ratio passed a few dozen. The big fluctuations came from electrostatic solitary structures. Ion phase-space holes were among them. With the temperature order reversed, fluctuations stayed small.
arxiv-2509-11686:
Jian Wang and 4 co-authors test whether execution traces actually help code language models reason in a 2025 study. Such models impress at writing code, yet they struggle to reason about what programs do at runtime, and semantic information like traces is represented inconsistently across existing methods.

The authors introduce a generic framework for adding trace-based semantic information to task prompts in a consistent way. They then study its usefulness for supervised fine-tuning and for inference-time scaling. Surprisingly, results disagreed with previous work. Semantic information showed limited usefulness in both settings studied. That negative finding matters because it redirects effort: simply feeding models execution traces does not reliably fix their weak runtime reasoning.
arxiv-2509-11786:
Dongyang Zhan and 5 co-authors detect anomalies in industrial control systems by joining network and sensor evidence in a 2025 security paper. Such systems run physical processes from afar, and attacks on them can cause serious damage. Most detectors examine only one domain at a time.

Network traffic and physical sensor behavior are linked, so single-domain study misses anomalies that cross domains. The authors build a cross-domain graph that stands for behaviors from many domains. A graph neural network learns their joint features. Because anomalies show up differently per domain, a multi-task setup detects them domain by domain while training jointly. Tests showed better results than past approaches at spotting anomalies. The method targets the security and stability of industrial work.
arxiv-2509-11886:
M. Paola Vaccaro examines how far Newtonian-style gravity can carry the study of merging black holes. This 2025 astrophysics paper is a single-author study. Stellar-mass binary black holes form by two main routes. One is the isolated evolution of massive binary stars. Uncertain stages mark it, like core-collapse supernovae and common-envelope episodes. The other is dynamical formation in dense stellar settings.

Newtonian gravity models large-scale encounters cheaply and well. Close passes and mergers demand general relativity. Vaccaro's focus is the middle ground, post-Newtonian gravity. It is assessed as a bridge between the regimes. The bridge stays physically insightful and cheap to compute. In the gravitational-wave era, observed mergers make such approximations testable as never before.
arxiv-2509-11986:
Something is lost when a vision-language model squeezes an image into words. The picture first becomes vectors from a vision encoder. A connector then projects those vectors into the language model's space. Wenyan Li and five co-authors measure what survives that handoff in 2025.

One test tracks nearest neighbors among image codes before and after the projection step. The neighborhood reshuffles by about half. That loss tracks weaker retrieval scores. A second test rebuilds the first visual vectors from the projected ones, patch by patch. The result is a map of where the detail vanished. Those high-loss patches match the spots where the model later fails on visual questions. Builders get a clear warning sign, not just a bare score.
arxiv-2509-12086:
Search over huge vector collections runs faster when the vectors are squeezed. Compression trades a little accuracy for large savings in space and in distance math. Hui Li and four co-authors push that squeeze further in 2025 with a method called SAQ.

SAQ first splits each vector into segments along its dimensions. A PCA step comes first. More bits go to the early segments, which carry larger values. A dynamic program picks the split and the bit budget to keep error low. Each dimension is then quantized on its own. A coordinate-descent-style pass repairs the result. That avoids an exhaustive search. Against classics like product quantization and newer rivals, the gains are large. Quantization error fell by up to four fifths. Encoding ran more than eighty times faster than one leading method.
arxiv-2509-12186:
Algebraic cycles are the shapes cut out by polynomial equations inside a variety, and their study links geometry to cohomology. Pedro Montero and one co-author examine such cycles in 2025 on smooth complete intersections whose Hodge structure has level one, a family classified decades ago by Deligne and Rapoport.

With special attention to five-dimensional cases, they move the known results into an etale motivic setting and recover a matching finite-dimensionality statement in Kimura's sense. Cycles on other smooth Fano manifolds of the same type get the same treatment. As a payoff, they prove the integral Hodge conjecture for smooth quartic double fivefolds.
arxiv-2509-12386:
Fixing one weakness in a machine learning model can quietly open another. Asim Waheed and two co-authors release Amulet in 2025, a Python library for measuring those cross-effects among defenses and risks across security, privacy, and fairness.

Earlier defenses were each built against a single threat, with side effects on other threats rarely checked. Amulet bundles representative attacks, defenses, and metrics behind one consistent interface, and its modular layout accepts new pieces easily. The authors present it as the first shared foundation for systematically testing both the intended and the unintended interactions in this space.
arxiv-2509-12786:
Adrian Nachtwey, Fabian C. Moss, and Anna Viktoria Katrin Plaksin propose a sampling method for comparative musicology in a 2025 paper. Encoding whole corpora of musical sources is time-consuming, which limits large-scale studies of historical prints. Instead of digitizing everything, they suggest sampling bars from the sources.

The challenge is selecting samples that represent the sources well with respect to differences in edit operations, the changes editors made. The authors evaluate three sampling methods using Beethoven's Bagatelles Op. 33 as a case study. They identify which method best finds representative samples. The approach could enable statistically sound, large-scale analyses and deepen understanding of nineteenth-century editorial practices and scholarly editing of historical musical works.
arxiv-2509-12986:
Anne Broadbent, Upendra Kapshikar and Denis Rochette give in 2025 the first broad treatment of tamper detection against any quantum attack. Tamper codes must flag any illicit change to a stored word before decoding. Classic codes handle huge attack sets with a few banned maps.

Quantum work before this covered only unitary attacks. Random Haar codes now reach tiny error against any attack set that meets plain size and rank bounds. A sharp split from classic codes is shown: quantum codes can allow reject-or-recover where classic codes cannot, even for constant maps. Signs point to universal quantum detection for vast attack sets.
arxiv-2509-13286:
L. Olifer and 22 co-authors put forth a new route by which slow waves in space may drive rain-like falls of electrons in a 2025 paper. A huge geomagnetic storm in May 2024 gave a rare chance to watch strong wave and particle effects at work. In this setting, precipitation means fast electrons that fall from space into the air above Earth.

Data came from a balloon-borne X-ray sensor, ground tools, and the Arase satellite, all in step. They saw bursts of falling electrons in a near rhythm, in time with very low frequency waves. The satellite also saw trapped electron flows rise and fall in a key energy band. The team argues that when those flows pass a known limit, they spark intense chorus waves, which then push the electrons down in pulses. Tracing the drift pointed to a source just past noon in space terms.
arxiv-2509-13486:
Shaobo Zhang and 4 co-authors describe a helium-neon Ramsey comagnetometer in a 2025 paper. A comagnetometer compares the spins of two kinds of nuclei, and does it with great precision. Such devices hold steady over long runs. Physicists use them to hunt for spin-dependent effects that the Standard Model does not predict.

This device pairs helium-3 with neon-21. A rubidium magnetometer sits inside the same cell. While the nuclei precess freely, every laser is switched off. A microwave field steps in instead, quieting the influence that rubidium atoms would otherwise exert back on the sample. The authors also show a geometric trick: shape the polarized sample rightly, and two kinds of interaction between the nuclear spins cancel out. Scalar and dipolar interactions both go. The gains add up to a measurement free of bias. After several hours of integration, its frequency sensitivity is very fine indeed.
arxiv-2509-13686:
Bingsheng Peng and five co-authors upgrade wireless channel modeling in a 2025 wireless networks paper. Optimizing a cellular network needs accurate local predictions of how signals spread. Those predictions are summarized by an angular power spectrum. The standard modeling framework infers that spectrum from received-power measurements. But it handles only one cell, one grid area, and one carrier frequency at a time.

Their framework, RF-LSCM, represents signal loss and multipath inside a radiance field. It borrows machinery from computer graphics. A frequency model built on physics supports predictions across frequencies. Point-cloud environment data extends coverage to many cells and grids. A low-rank tensor method with a new angular modeling algorithm cuts memory and training time. Real-world tests cut coverage prediction error by up to about thirty percent.
arxiv-2509-14086:
Qianlong Duan and four co-authors schedule tasks on vehicle computers in a 2025 real-time systems paper. Multi-core controllers in intelligent vehicles run many parallel tasks that share resources. Blocking while tasks wait on each other degrades whether schedules hold. Standard allocation algorithms ignore blocking. Under heavy load, their schedules fail at high rates.

Their algorithm, BR-WFD, estimates blocking time directly. It also analyzes resource similarity between tasks. It gives scheduling priority to tasks most sensitive to sync delays. It packs tasks that share resources onto the same core, shrinking global blocking overhead. In simulations, it needed roughly a tenth to over a quarter fewer processor cores than older methods. Its success ratio stayed fifteen to twenty points higher under heavy, contested loads.
arxiv-2509-14186:
Patrick Vincent N. Lubenia and Taposh Banerjee study how to spot a sudden change in a random process as fast as possible in 2025. A watcher must pick, at each step, among tests that differ in quality and cost. The aim is a short delay, with few false alarms and a controlled budget.

Lubenia and Banerjee first build a method for the case of two tests, then extend it step by step to three or more. Their method can meet the stated limits and comes close to the delay of the best single test. They also cover the option of running no test at all at some steps, which they frame as saving data and cost when watching can pause.
arxiv-2509-14386:
Arjun S. Nair and Kristina P. Sinaga claim in 2025 that a popular hope for neural network confidence is impossible under binary training signals. A calibrated model should be right about as often as its stated confidence suggests. Training often gives only right or wrong labels.

Through maths and wide experiments, the authors argue networks cannot learn both calibrated confidence and varied, meaningful confidence from binary labels alone. Negative reward training drove extreme underconfidence and crushed confidence spread. Symmetric losses stayed stuck at averaging the binary signal. After the fact fixes reached calibration only by squeezing confidence into a narrow band. The claim, framed as claimed proof in the study, recasts calibration failure as an information limit, not a tuning failure.
arxiv-2509-14486:
Agus L. Soenjaya, Ping Lin and Thanh Tran analyse errors in 2025 for a finite element scheme that simulates tumour growth with a diffuse interface. The model couples a Cahn-Hilliard equation for tumour phase with a reaction diffusion equation for nutrients. Its energy should decay in a controlled way.

Their fully discrete method uses a scalar auxiliary variable trick with mixed finite elements in space and simple Euler steps in time. The scheme is unconditionally energy stable and preserves mass, matching the continuous energy law. The error analysis proves how accuracy depends on mesh and time step sizes. Structure preserving schemes matter in medicine models because a solver that gains fake energy can invent tumour growth.
arxiv-2509-14786:
Konwoo Kim, Suhas Kotha, Percy Liang, and Tatsunori Hashimoto ask how language models should be trained when data stays fixed but computing power keeps growing, in a 2025 machine learning paper. Simply training for more epochs or adding more parameters eventually overfits the limited text. The team looks for a better recipe under that fixed-data, unlimited-compute limit.

Careful tuning of regularization turns out to matter greatly, with the best weight decay far larger than standard practice. With that recipe, loss falls along a simple power law as parameters grow, letting the authors estimate best possible performance. Combining models trained separately works even better. Their full recipe reaches the same loss with far less data, and the scaling laws predict the gain holds at larger budgets.
arxiv-2509-14986:
David Alonso-Gutiérrez, Eduardo Lucas, and Javier Martín Goñi give a discrete route to Zhang's projection inequality in a 2025 convex geometry paper. The inequality relates a convex body's volume to the volume of its shadow in one direction, through an integral measuring self-overlap at every shift. Gardner and Zhang proved it, and it implies Zhang's classical projection inequality.

The authors first reprove the overlap bound with a fresh approach. They then build discrete analogues where counting lattice points replaces measuring volume. Those counting versions imply lattice forms of both the overlap inequality and an equivalent statement. Finally, the continuous inequality is recovered from its discrete counterparts by a limiting argument. The detour through counting shows the result is not an artifact of continuous measure but a robust feature of convex shapes.
arxiv-2509-15086:
Isaac Goldbring and Thomas Sinclair ask whether tensor product norms for C-star algebras can be defined inside the algebras' own logic, in a 2025 mathematics paper. C-star algebras are the abstract backbone of quantum theory, and combining two systems requires choosing a tensor norm. The minimal and maximal norms are the two extreme choices, and they can differ.

Working in continuous model theory, the authors prove neither norm is definable uniformly across all C-star algebras. The minimal case leans on a deep theorem of Kirchberg about exactness, and the maximal case on a recent characterization by Pisier of the lifting property. Further negative results cover particular algebras and stricter, computable forms of definability, drawing on quantum complexity breakthroughs. A question of Fritz, Netzer, and Thom falls along the way.
arxiv-2509-15186:
Alessio Cela and Alberto Landi complete a three-part computation of Chow rings for moduli stacks of hyperelliptic Prym pairs in a 2025 algebraic geometry paper. A moduli stack organizes a family of geometric objects into a single space whose own geometry can then be studied. Prym pairs arise from double covers of hyperelliptic curves, a classical construction in curve theory.

For each genus, two stacks parametrize these pairs, one a rigidified version of the other, and each splits into many components. The authors give quotient stack descriptions of the remaining components for even genus and compute their integral Chow rings, finishing all components of the first stack. They also present every component of the second stack as a quotient and determine when the rigidification map between the two stacks behaves well.
arxiv-2509-15286:
Yun-Peng Zheng and a large team study how spinning nuclei line up in heavy ion crashes. When two heavy nuclei hit off center, the hot matter they make can swirl. That swirl can line up the spins of small particles, an effect seen before with other particles. The team asks whether it also lines up lithium-4, a short lived nucleus.

They model lithium-4 as built from spinning protons and neutrons that merge as the matter cools. Their math shows the helium-3 it decays into flies out in a pattern tied to the swirl and the spin. If labs can measure that pattern, it would give a new way to probe the hot matter made in such crashes.
arxiv-2509-15486:
Isaac Huidobro-Meezs, Jun Dai, and Rodrigo Vargas-Hernández cut the cost of measuring quantum states of molecules. To know a molecule's energy to chemical accuracy takes a huge count of measurements. A common trick groups terms that can be measured together. The usual greedy way to form groups leaves better trade offs unseen.

The trio recast grouping as a search game with rewards. A flow based generative model colors a graph of the molecule's terms to propose groups that do not overlap. The reward can weigh shot count, circuit count, and gate count at once. On test molecules, their groups need about a fifth fewer measurements than the greedy start. Fed into a later step, they cut estimates by up to two fifths.
arxiv-2509-15686:
Partha Ghose revisits a 1924 dispute between S. N. Bose and Einstein about light and matter. Bose proposed a new count for photons and a chance based law for how matter and light trade energy. Einstein praised the count and extended it to matter, but he faulted the chance law. He cited balance rules and the need to match classical physics at high light levels.

Ghose argues the clash fades once two kinds of chance are kept apart: chance of meeting and rate of change. Modern quantum optics backs Bose's core hunch. So called spontaneous emission stems from the atom's link to the field around it, not from the atom alone. The field's local shape sets the rate. Random walk models fit Bose's view too.
arxiv-2509-15786:
Nan Li, Bo Kang, and Tijl De Bie build job taxonomies straight from job postings. A taxonomy of occupations guides job matching and labor market study. Hand made versions are slow. Top down auto versions miss local markets, while bottom up ones can tangle on noisy data.

Their builder, CLIMB, starts with global meaning based clustering to distill core jobs. A team of software agents then reflects and revises, step by step, to grow a coherent tree. On three real data sets from varied places, the trees are more coherent and scale better than past methods. They also capture traits unique to each region. Code and data are released.
arxiv-2509-16386: Daniel Lazarev gives an information-based reading of Stokes' theorem, a classic rule that links a region's interior to its boundary. He looks at all surfaces inside a given shape that obey the Stokes relation and scores each with an entropy measure. The shape's own boundary turns out to be the unique surface that makes that entropy as large as possible. In his terms, the boundary is the least informative subset that still satisfies the relation, which recasts the theorem as a duality driven by entropy.
arxiv-2509-16486:
A 2024 paper that offered a tool for microbiome intervention analysis comes under sharp fire in this comment. Travis E. Gibson argues the work is marred by errors at many levels, from wrong inputs fed to rival methods to starting values given in the wrong units. Score calculations lacked proper unit conversion, the comment says, and data leakage taints the tests.

Claims about false discovery rates and power are said to lack support from both theory and the paper's own tests. Equations and terms are also flagged as wrong. The comment asks readers to treat the tool's reported gains with caution.
arxiv-2509-16586:
Yukuan Wei, Xudong Li, and Lin F. Yang settle how much data a learner needs in a hard setting, in a 2025 theory paper. Their setting is a Markov decision process, where an agent acts over time for average reward. Extra rules cap what the agent may do on average. Past work left the data cost of this capped case unclear.

The team prove upper bounds on the needed samples. They also prove a matching lower bound for the strict case. That match makes their bounds the first that cannot be improved in this setting. The gap in theory for capped average-reward learning is now closed. Such bounds guide how much trial data a safe learner will need.
arxiv-2509-16786:
Tung Nguyen, Alex Scott, and Paul Seymour refine a width measure for endless graphs in a 2025 math paper. Path-width sums up how tree-like a finite graph is. Extending it to infinite graphs in the obvious way breaks down. A nicer extension indexes the parts by any total order, giving line-decompositions and line-width.

The team ask whether the order can always be a well-order, which is easier to use. They show a graph with line-width at most k has such a decomposition with width at most twice k. That bound is the best possible. The result tidies a tool used in graph structure theory.
arxiv-2509-17186:
Dehao Zhang leads a team of eight co-authors on a 2025 arXiv paper about artificial neurons for long data sequences. Sequences keep growing, and models face ever longer inputs at rising cost. Resonate-and-fire neurons ring at set frequencies, which suits them to long inputs, but they remember little and trade energy savings against training speed.

The team's design gives each neuron several dendrite-like branches plus a body, copying the shape of real nerve cells. Each branch picks up its own frequency band, so the branches together cover the signal in full. The body adjusts its firing threshold from past activity, which cuts waste spikes. Tests show accuracy on par with rivals, with sparse firing and training that stays fast. The authors see promise for small edge devices.
arxiv-2509-17286:
David Rowe and Tibor Bece present a 2025 arXiv paper on sending clear speech over land mobile radio. Work and emergency services still lean on these radio systems, where analog FM and digital sets now work side by side. Many digital radios keep the old analog FM modulator, fed by a pulse train instead of a voice wave. The authors call that setup baseband FM.

Their method, RADE, trains an autoencoder to pack wide-band speech into a form the baseband FM channel can carry. The speech spans eight kilohertz, twice the width of classic narrow voice channels. In simulated land mobile channels with fading, the decoded speech beat analog FM on quality. The team also shows the system running live on off-the-shelf UHF radios. The result hints that machine learning can refresh a radio base that changes only slowly.
arxiv-2509-17386:
Stefano Baroni, writing alone, revisits a subtle point in the theory of heat flow. His 2025 arXiv paper asks why thermal conductivity does not depend on how one defines energy density. Two definitions can differ from place to place inside a material, yet both must give the same heat conductivity if the theory is sound.

Baroni shows that invariance in the simplest and most general terms he can find. He states the minimal conditions under which any two energy densities lead to the same conductivity within the Green-Kubo framework. That framework prices heat flow from the way energy currents fluctuate at equilibrium. The paper closes with a note on why the point matters now: simulations with machine-trained neural network potentials lean on these definitions every day, and loose handling can quietly spoil results.
arxiv-2509-17486:
Lvzhou Luo, Yixuan Cao, and Ping Luo trim the context fed to language models in a 2025 arXiv paper. Retrieval-augmented generation grounds answers in outside documents, but the retrieved stack often holds irrelevant text that drags quality down. Compression can strip the chaff, yet fixed rates fit some queries badly and multi-document facts can be lost.

Their framework, AttnComp, lets the model's own attention scores judge what matters. A Top-P rule keeps the smallest set of documents whose total attention clears a set threshold, so the rate adapts to each case. The method stays fast and merges facts across documents. It also estimates answer confidence from the overall relevance of what was retrieved, so users can gauge how far to trust a reply. In tests, AttnComp beat rival compressors and even uncompressed baselines on accuracy.
arxiv-2509-17886:
Sunder Ram Krishnan sharpens a classic bound on how well a stats guess can do. His 2025 paper works on the Cramer-Rao bound, a floor on the spread of any fair estimator. The bound comes from the shape of the model as a curved surface in a large space.

Krishnan adds curve-aware fixes based on how that surface bends in its outer space. For bounds that use higher steps of the score, he spells the terms with neat classic tools. Worked cases show the fixes can tighten the floor by a fair amount. That hints at wider use for judging how good a guess can be.
arxiv-2509-17986:
Nikolaos Bozikis, Dilara Ozev, and Nicolas Noiray predict the whistle of air over a deep hollow. Their 2025 paper deals with turbulent flow that grazes a rectangular cavity at low speed. The flow's shear layer and the cavity's sound modes feed each other, and the whistle settles into a steady cycle.

Their model splits flow parts in three and solves linked sound-flow equations in rounds. Each round updates the sound task with stress from the growing mode, till growth hits zero. Wave shapes match past large sims well. Whistle tone and strength also match a tuned low-order model.
arxiv-2509-18086:
Shrihan Agarwal leads a huge team that confirms far-off galaxies bent by strong lensing. Their 2025 paper reports spectra for lens systems found by a neural net in survey images, then checked with space telescope views. A lens bends light from a back galaxy into arcs, and spectra give the key distances.

Two tools did the work: a Keck infra-red unit and the DESI survey spectrograph. For most of the targeted sources, they pinned the source distance, across a far range. Full lens and source distances for six systems are now in hand. The set helps train the next round of lens searches.
arxiv-2509-18386:
Odd trips on a road network can signal fraud, danger, or a system fault. Jonathan Kabala Mbuya, Dieter Pfoser, and Antonios Anastasopoulos present GETAD, a framework for spotting such trips. Their 2025 paper notes that older methods treat trips as plain point sequences. That view ignores the roads and links that shape real travel.

GETAD weaves road shape, segment meaning, and past travel patterns into one model. A graph attention network learns road-aware codes for each segment. A transformer then reads the trip as a sequence of those codes. Training mixes next-step guessing with link guessing to keep trips realistic. A new scoring rule weights confident oddities more heavily. On real and fake data sets, GETAD beat prior methods, above all for subtle odd trips. The gains come from using the map, not just the points.
arxiv-2509-18586:
Quantum attackers can query random shuffles, called permutations, in ways that classic security proofs do not cover. Joseph Carolan builds a new proof tool for that setting in this 2025 paper. Random oracles have a famous compressed simulation trick, due to Zhandry, that tracks only what an attacker has learned. Permutations resist that trick because they must stay invertible.

Carolan develops a compressed permutation oracle and proves it sound. Its memory is just a short list of input-output pairs, mirroring the attacker's real knowledge. With it, he shows a seven-round Feistel construction is a strong quantum-secure pseudorandom permutation. That settles an open question from 2012. He also re-proves nearly all known quantum lower bounds in the permutation model. New bounds cover cycle finding and a one-more problem. The tool may unlock proofs for many shuffle-based designs.
arxiv-2509-18686:
Assembling parts is one of the hardest jobs for a general robot, since contacts are fiddly and noise can ruin a fit. Ziyi Xu, Haohong Lin, Shiqi Liu, and Ding Zhao present the Query-centric Diffusion Policy in this 2025 paper. Robot assembly is usually split into high-level planning and low-level control. The two levels often mismatch in practice.

Their framework bridges the levels with queries that bundle the object, the contact point, and the skill to use. A query-centric step finds the task-relevant parts and guides the low-level policy. Point cloud views add robustness against noise. On the FurnitureBench benchmark, in simulation and on a real robot, the method improved skill precision and long-run success. For insertion and screwing, skill success rose by over fifty percent versus baselines. The queries, the authors say, are the bridge that was missing.
arxiv-2509-18886:
Firms with secret data hesitate to run language models on shared cloud machines. Marcin Chrapek, Marcin Copik, Etienne Mettaz, and Torsten Hoefler test a hardware answer: trusted execution environments. Their 2025 paper runs full model inference inside these sealed zones, on both CPUs and graphics chips. The zones promise that even the machine's owner cannot peek.

On the CPU side, they ran three sizes of a Llama model inside two Intel sealed-zone systems. Throughput overhead stayed under ten percent, and latency under twenty, with matrix hardware help. On a top NVIDIA confidential chip, throughput penalties ran four to eight percent. Those penalties shrink as batches and inputs grow. Comparing cost and security, the team finds CPU zones can beat graphics ones on price or safety. They call the study the first full map of sealed-zone model serving.
arxiv-2509-18986:
How much longer will a warehouse order take to finish? Erik Penther and two co-authors compare four ways to predict the remaining time of orders still in progress. Their test bed is a real outbound warehouse process from a logistics firm in the aviation business. The firm shared an event log with about 170,000 case traces, which the team can release in public.

Deep learning models gave the most accurate forecasts, as the authors expected. Simpler boosting methods, though, came close in accuracy while needing far less computing power. The study gives warehouse teams a clear trade-off: top accuracy from heavy models, or nearly the same quality from light ones. Work like this sits inside process mining, where event logs are used to forecast live cases.
arxiv-2509-19086:
Michal Konopa and two co-authors present a concept for running jobs on shared graphics processors more efficiently. On clusters built from sliced-up graphics processors, jobs are usually treated as rigid blocks that hold a fixed slice until they finish. Sizing each job by its peak memory use wastes capacity and turns jobs away. Their proposal, scheduler-driven job atomization, opens a two-way talk between scheduler and jobs.

The scheduler advertises open time-and-capacity slots, and jobs signal when they could carve out a subjob that fits. The scheduler picks among signals by its policy, such as fairness or deadlines, and only then does the chosen job build its subjob. Because subjobs are shaped before they run, no costly migration or interruption is needed. As a concept paper, the work defines the pieces and future research directions rather than reporting experiments.
arxiv-2509-19286:
Be stars, hot stars that shed glowing disks of gas, are widely thought to be spun up by a companion, yet whether every Be star needs a partner is unknown. V. M. Kalari and eleven co-authors searched 76 Be stars for companions with speckle imaging from the two Gemini telescopes. The technique resolves pairs from very tight to wide separations, down to faint brightness gaps. They found eleven binaries in that range, six of them unreported.

Archival data added more multiples outside the imaging window, including three triple systems, for twenty-four multiple systems. Within the speckle range and detection limits, the findings rule out a multiplicity fraction above about twenty-seven percent at high confidence. That cap pressures the idea that all Be stars form through binary interaction. The authors call for spectroscopic and interferometric follow-ups to cover the tight separations imaging misses.
arxiv-2509-19486:
Dodging a fast object takes split-second planning that small robot brains struggle to supply. Kieran S. Lachmansingh and four co-authors test whether a distant supercomputer can plan fast enough. Their system, SHARP, sends the planning work to a high-performance cluster. The test task is harsh: a robot arm must dodge foam shots fired at high speed.

Planning took about twenty-three milliseconds on a local cluster and about thirty on one far away. The arm dodged most shots in both setups. Those times sit well below human reaction time. The authors suggest a split design: quick reflexes stay on the robot, while heavy planning bursts go to the cluster. They report timing for each stage so other teams can repeat the test.
arxiv-2509-19586:
Drug hunting often works with fragments, small molecule pieces that can later be joined or grown. Alexander Ho, Sukyeong Lee, and Francis T. F. Tsai trained a foundation language model just for fragments. Their model, FragAtlas-62M, learned from over sixty-two million fragments drawn from the ZINC-22 library. That set is the largest fragment collection used for such training so far.

Nearly all fragments the model invents pass chemical validity checks. Their measured traits closely match the training set across a dozen descriptors and three fingerprint styles. The model recalls about half of known fragments and adds a fifth that are new yet plausible. The team released weights, code, and data in public. A shared fragment model could speed early drug screening across many labs.
arxiv-2509-19886:
Sparse solutions keep only the few components that matter, but the standard penalty shrinks big components too much. Natsuki Akaishi, Koki Yamada, and Kohei Yatabe design a new penalty, ULPENS, that suppresses small elements while sparing large ones. It is smooth, non-convex, and non-separable, so components are judged together rather than one by one. A formula borrowed from ultra-discretization lets one dial slide between the classic penalty and the selective one.

Smoothness allows fast gradient methods to do the optimization. The authors prove the penalty's key properties and test it in practice. Ordered weighting schemes inspired the design but lacked this smooth control. Sparse recovery runs under signal processing, imaging, and model selection. A penalty with a tunable temperament could serve all three more faithfully.
arxiv-2509-20086:
Johannes Wirth wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on speech technology. Its subject is phonemization, the step that turns written words into sounds for text-to-speech systems. Good phonemization matters most for rare words that dictionaries miss. Wirth presents OLaPh, a system built for this task across many languages.

OLaPh mixes large multilingual word lists with language processing tools and a statistical way to split words into parts. On the WikiPron benchmark it beat established baselines in overall accuracy. Strong fallback rules keep it reliable on words outside the dictionary. Wirth also used the system to build training data for a large language model. The model learned sound patterns well but stayed less accurate than the rule-based system overall. Both tools are released as an open resource for grapheme-to-phoneme research.
arxiv-2509-20186:
Liang Wang and four co-authors wrote this 2025 arXiv paper on training large language models. Training compute keeps growing fast, while high-quality text stays limited. Getting more value from each training token is therefore a central problem. Some valuable tokens are hard to learn because the reasoning behind them is deep.

Their method, Thinking Augmented Pre-training, adds generated reasoning traces to ordinary text. The added traces break hard tokens into step-by-step reasoning that is easier to absorb. It also enlarges the effective volume of training data. The team applied the method across many setups, up to one hundred billion tokens of training. It improved models of several sizes and families. For data efficiency, the gain was about threefold. Post-training scores on hard reasoning benchmarks also rose by more than ten percent for one mid-size model.
arxiv-2509-20286:
Teaching a two-armed robot from one human video is the goal of a 2025 arXiv paper by Georgios Tziafas, Jiayun Zhang, and Hamidreza Kasaei. Collecting robot demonstrations by teleoperation is slow and costly. Human videos are plentiful but hard for robots to use directly. Their framework, PAD, bridges that gap in three steps.

First, it parses the video into a keypoint-action path a robot can execute. Next, task-and-motion planning multiplies that single demonstration into many variants, with no simulator needed. Finally, the augmented paths are distilled into a policy that acts on keypoints. PAD beat leading augmentation methods on success rate and cost in their tests. Deployed tasks included pouring drinks, clearing trash, and opening containers. The learned policies handled new layouts, objects, and background clutter.
arxiv-2509-20486:
Self-driving systems locate themselves better when they know what surrounds them. Sven Ochs and three co-authors add that semantic knowledge to laser-based localization in a 2025 arXiv paper. Two routes supply the semantics: segment the laser data directly, or borrow labels from camera images. Diverse sensors make the direct route brittle, so the authors pursue the camera route.

Their method projects laser points into the camera's segmented image, attaching object labels to each point. A state-of-the-art depth network produced the camera segmentation, while an adaptive network handled the laser side. Satellite positioning with real-time corrections provided ground truth. Validation included a fifty-five kilometer drive through Karlsruhe, Germany, spanning city streets, multi-lane roads, and rural highways. The fused approach improved the precision and reliability of the localization pipeline.
arxiv-2509-20586:
Borrowing control patients from outside a trial can backfire statistically. Chi-Shian Dai and three co-authors show the trap and escape it in a 2025 arXiv paper. External controls are plentiful in records and registries, and doubly robust estimators promise safety: one of two models must be right. Yet folding external controls into the standard estimator for the treated group's effect can lower efficiency instead of raising it.

Their new estimator guarantees better efficiency than ignoring the external data, even when models are misspecified. When every model is correct, it matches the efficient estimator that uses the controls. The theory covers high-dimensional confounders, the norm with electronic health records. Simulations and a real data application support the method. The double safety of the title means robustness and efficiency are both protected.
arxiv-2509-20786:
Noisy labels and mixed-quality data make neural network training unreliable. Abhishek Moturu and three co-authors introduce LiLAW in a 2025 paper on learning sample difficulty. LiLAW stands for lightweight learnable adaptive weighting, and it uses only three learned numbers.

Each training sample gets a loss weight based on its current difficulty, classed as easy, moderate, or hard. Three global parameters control that weighting. After each training batch, one step on a validation batch updates those parameters. The method needs no clean, unbiased validation set. The authors test it across general and medical image datasets, many noise types and levels, loss functions, and network designs, reporting steadier training than fixed weighting schemes.
arxiv-2509-20886:
Videos often hide moving content behind a steady, structured background. Tristan Stevens and three co-authors propose Nuclear Diffusion, a 2025 method for pulling that background out. They test it on cardiac ultrasound, where haze obscures the beating heart.

Classic robust principal component methods split video into a low-rank background and a sparse moving part. Real video breaks the sparsity assumption, since moving content is rich and varied. The new method pairs low-rank temporal modeling with diffusion posterior sampling, borrowing the generative power of diffusion models. On heart ultrasound dehazing, the authors report better contrast enhancement and signal quality than the classic approach. The hybrid design aims at medical and other videos where backgrounds are stubborn.
arxiv-2509-20986:
Vision transformers power today's image foundation models, but their features carry high-norm artifacts that pollute downstream learning. Geunhyeok Yu and four co-authors present SiNGER, a distillation method that cleans those features, in a 2025 paper accepted for ICLR 2026. The goal is students that learn signal, not artifacts.

When a teacher's features are distilled into a student, artifact components can dominate the training objective. Students then overfit to artifacts and underweight the informative parts. Earlier fixes traded artifact removal against signal loss. SiNGER uses a singular nullspace-guided energy reallocation to suppress artifacts while keeping the teacher's useful energy. The authors report that distilled students gain more of the benefit that larger teachers should provide.
arxiv-2509-21086:
Moving a concept, such as a character or style, from one video into another demands control over separate parts of the scene. Guojun Lei and six co-authors present UniTransfer in a 2025 paper for NeurIPS 2025. Their architecture decomposes both the video's space and the diffusion process's time.

Spatially, each video splits into foreground subject, background, and motion flow. A dual-to-single-stream transformer design then gives fine-grained control over those components. Progressively, the transfer proceeds stage by stage, in a manner the authors compare to chain-of-thought reasoning. A self-supervised pretraining strategy with random masking strengthens the decomposed representations from unlabeled video. The result is video concept transfer that is both precise and controllable, the authors report.
arxiv-2509-21186:
Dhananjay Singh and Arvind Kumar wrote a physics paper in 2025 on quark matter. They study matter made of quarks under strong force. In heavy ion crashes, this matter can flow unevenly in different directions. The paper asks how that uneven flow changes heat, pressure, and flow traits.

The authors use a model that tracks how quark mass changes and how quarks become free. They add a small stretch to the spread of motion. Then they work out pressure, energy, heat, and the speed of sound. They also work out how thick the matter flows and how well it carries charge. The results help readers link crash data to the state of hot quark matter.
arxiv-2509-21386:
Shipwrecks mark key chapters of maritime history, but finding them in sonar data takes expert time. Multibeam sonar maps the lake or sea floor in detail. Manual review of those maps is slow. Anja Sheppard and 7 co-authors built a tool in 2025 to automate the search. Their software runs inside the open source QGIS mapping platform.

ShipwreckFinder preprocesses bathymetry data, runs a deep learning model, and thresholds its outputs. It returns pixel masks or bounding boxes for predicted wrecks. Training data came from the Great Lakes and the coasts of Ireland. Synthetic data added size and diversity to the training set. The team reports stronger segmentation than a comparable deep learning baseline.
arxiv-2509-21486:
Short video platforms need one system that can flag many kinds of inappropriate content. Training a small classifier per issue needs much labelled data and generalizes poorly. Zixuan Wang and 8 co-authors propose a unified multimodal approach in a 2025 paper. Domain smart pre training reshapes a large multimodal model for short video governance. Three targeted pre training tasks drive the adaptation.

Caption tasks sharpen perception of video details. Visual question answering deepens understanding of issue definitions and annotation guidelines. Chain of thought tasks strengthen thinking about hard cases. A distribution gap separates short video content from first pre training data, and complex definitions add difficulty. Tests show the paradigm improves unified detection across issue types, with thinking as a core part.
arxiv-2509-21686:
Galaxy cluster mass maps reveal dark matter substructure when shear and flexion signals are combined. Jacob Shpiece and David Goldberg present a lensing pipeline for that task in a 2025 paper. ARCH, short for Adaptive Reconstruction of Cluster Halos, applies joint shear flexion analysis to JWST imaging. Past joint approaches used forward modelling or Bayesian inference with strong priors. ARCH instead uses staged optimization.

Candidate halos are generated, locally optimized, filtered, and forward selected in stages. A global strength refinement finishes the fit, with a combined metric weighted by per signal uncertainties. Applied to Abell 2744 and El Gordo, the pipeline recovers convergence maps and subcluster masses consistent with earlier work. The staged design keeps reconstruction tractable and flexible for testing signal combinations.
arxiv-2509-21886:
Teaching a graph network to compute what a circuit does is a basic challenge in graph learning. Ziyang Zheng, Jiaying Zhu, Jingyi Zhou, and Qiang Xu present TRACE in this 2025 paper. Standard message-passing networks treat a graph as an unordered bag of neighbors. Circuits are not like that: computation flows step by step, in a fixed order and hierarchy, so the standard design misses the structure.

TRACE replaces that design with a hierarchical Transformer that mirrors the step-by-step flow of computation. Its training goal is also new. Instead of predicting the circuit's whole function at once, the model predicts only the shift: the gap between the true function and a simple local guess. The system was tested on several circuit forms, from design-level graphs to mapped netlists. Across a broad benchmark suite, TRACE beat all earlier designs by a clear margin.
arxiv-2509-22786: Peter Garnavich, Jordan Tweddale, and Colin Littlefield refine the orbit clock of the magnetic binary FO Aquarii. They combined more than forty years of eclipse timings for this intermediate polar, a system where a magnetic white dwarf accretes from a companion star. A second-order polynomial fits the eclipse times best. That fit gives an eight-sigma detection of a period derivative: the orbital period is currently increasing, at a small but firmly measured rate.
arxiv-2509-22986:
Tiny internet devices need secure links, but moving data to and from memory wastes time and power. Jingyao Zhang and Elaheh Sadredini compute crypto math inside the memory chip itself. Their design, CryptoSRAM, turns a microcontroller's standard SRAM array into a parallel compute fabric. That kills the shuttle between memory and processor. The chip's direct memory access style makes the fit smooth.

For common crypto kernels, speed rose sharply over software versions. AES ran up to seventy-four times faster, and SHA3 up to sixty-seven times faster. The design also beat dedicated crypto hardware on AES by up to six times. The pair pitch it for next-generation small devices.
arxiv-2509-23186:
Planning needs transitive reasoning: if A links to B and B to C, then A reaches C. Qimin Zhong and 6 co-authors study how multi-token prediction teaches that skill. Their theory uses a transformer whose output head is shared, plus a separate transfer layer. The transfer layer slowly learns multi-step adjacency data. The backbone then infers reachability links never seen in training.

Some noise in adjacency estimates is unavoidable, they show. Two upgrades sharpen the transfer layer: next-token injection and a transformer-based design. Tests on synthetic graphs support the theory. On the Blocksworld planning benchmark, path planning improved a lot. The work names the transitivity bottleneck and a route past it.
arxiv-2509-23286:
Diffusion language models can write tokens in any order, which also opens any-order attacks. Wonje Jeung and 6 co-authors built A2D, a token-level defense for that risk. Harmful spans can surface at any position or step. Prefilling attacks like DIJA slip past response-level refusals. A2D trains the model to emit an end-of-sequence refusal signal when harm arises.

Randomized masking during training covers varied decode orders. The same signal allows live monitoring and early cutoff. On safety benchmarks, DIJA success fell from over eighty percent to near zero. Thresholded signal scores also sped safe termination a lot.
arxiv-2509-23686:
Code benchmarks can reward a model that matches surface patterns instead of truly following program logic. Yifeng He and 3 co-authors built TF-Bench to test program semantics reasoning through type inference in System F. Verified transformations strip out natural language that carries no semantic weight, yielding a pure variant of the benchmark. Models must then reason from the code's formal structure alone.

State-of-the-art models struggled: the best, Claude-3.7-sonnet, reached only about fifty-six percent accuracy on the pure set. Two new metrics probe robustness and the value of test-time reasoning. The authors say the gaps mark where current models still fake understanding, and where work should go next.
arxiv-2509-23986:
Building a computational method for a scientific problem usually means weeks of reading, testing assumptions, and coding by hand. Alistair Turcan and 3 co-authors built TusoAI, an agent system that takes a task description plus an evaluation function and develops the method itself. Domain knowledge is organized into a knowledge tree. The system then iterates: optimizing candidates, diagnosing failures, and improving over a pool of solutions.

Across benchmarks in single-cell RNA denoising and satellite earth monitoring, it beat expert methods and other AI agents. Applied to two open genetics problems, it improved known methods and reported new disease associations. The code is public.
arxiv-2509-24186:
A test score can rank medical language models, yet the ranking may say more about the test than the model. Zhimeng Luo and 3 co-authors built MedIRT, a scoring frame borrowed from psychometrics. It models a model's hidden competency and each item's difficulty and pull apart, instead of treating all questions as equal.

The team tested seventy-one models on a licensing-style benchmark across eleven medical topics. MedIRT predicted held-out answers well and its rankings held up better on outside benchmarks than plain accuracy rankings. Topic profiles exposed sharp gaps that a single score had masked. Some models also proved sensitive to difficulty while others were not, a split that calls for different fixes.
arxiv-2509-24286:
Synth sounds are shaped by knobs that control tone color and the attack-decay envelope, which makes copying a synth style onto new audio hard. Jeng-Yue Liu and 4 co-authors built SynthCloner, a codec model that splits audio into three parts: envelope, timbre, and content. That split lets users steer each part on its own during transfer.

The team also built SynthCAT, a data set rendered for this task with hundreds of timbres, envelopes, and note sequences. SynthCloner beat rival methods on both measured scores and listener judgments. Independent control of envelope shape is the feature past spectral or implicit methods lacked.
arxiv-2509-24386:
Robotaxis must spot people crossing the street, including crowds that merge and split, to stay inside their approved operating area. Junyi Gu and 4 co-authors built PCICF, a framework that identifies and classifies pedestrian crossing scenes for incident analysis. It starts from a synthetic data set with lone pedestrians and extends it into a structured dictionary of multi-pedestrian cases.

The framework turns scene features into characteristic patterns with space-filling curves, then matches them to dictionary entries. On a real data set of over a hundred and fifty annotated crossing videos, it classified complex crossings well. Its light compute parts could even run onboard for out-of-domain detection.
arxiv-2509-25686:
Suhail, Anand, and Sethi make short whys for image model calls that also map its paths in this twenty twenty-five paper. A trained model holds scores of rules that could back one call it makes. In vast image space those rules are hard to spot and read by eye.

Inside, a light code net learns masks that keep just the zones a call turns on. Drill goals span layer match, call keep, mask thinness, and faith to the true call. Those masks then feed a path hunt that scores links by weight times spark. Path graphs at the wire scale show which wires drive the call in the end. The pair of tools bridges short whys and deep how-it-works reads.
arxiv-2510-00086:
Nemanja Antonic and four colleagues published this 2025 paper on reading the behavior of a tiny roundworm. The worm, called C. elegans, is one millimeter long and serves as a model animal in biology. Older tools need a clear view of the whole body to sort its movements into units. That view fails when many worms crowd together, which is exactly when social effects show.

The team instead tracks a single point, the worm's body center, over time and space. An automatic pipeline then cuts the motion into behavior units with no preset list. The authors compared those units with hand-designed ones and tested both in a simulated worm. Clear movement patterns emerged even from the single tracked point. The automatic method matched the real worm better, which frees studies of crowded worms from hand labels.
arxiv-2510-00386:
Ayush Jain, Andrea Montanari, and Eren Sasoglu published this 2025 paper on picking fine-tuning data when target examples are scarce. Fine-tuning works best when training samples mirror the target task's distribution. Usually teams hold the few target samples back as a validation set for scoring candidate data. The authors flip that arrangement in a method they call Train on Validation.

Their procedure fine-tunes on the small validation set, then re-scores the whole training pool. Samples whose predictions moved the most under that fine-tune get selected for real training. The insight is that samples most affected by the target data tend to help most on the target task. Experiments covered instruction tuning and named entity recognition benchmarks. In most cases the flipped method reached lower test loss than leading selection approaches. Theory in the paper backs why the signal should work.
arxiv-2510-00686:
Anisha, Biermann, Englert, and Mühlleitner explore a kinetic Higgs portal in this 2025 arXiv preprint on particle physics. The Higgs portal is a leading idea for linking known matter to a hidden sector that could hold dark matter. Their version adds non-standard momentum dependence, which arises naturally when the hidden sector interacts strongly.

The authors derive limits on this setup from four-top-quark production data and from precise measurements of Higgs couplings. Those limits matter most where destructive interference hides invisible Higgs decays from direct searches. They show the portal can still explain the observed dark matter abundance while evading current direct detection bounds. Future machines such as the high-luminosity LHC and a proposed FCC-ee collider could probe the remaining space.
arxiv-2510-00786:
Fedida strengthens a family of no-go theorems for pointwise quantum fields in this 2025 arXiv paper on mathematical physics. Textbook quantum field theory treats fields as operator-valued functions defined at each spacetime point. Classic results by Wightman and Wizimirski showed that this pointwise picture clashes with basic physical demands, but those results were proved mainly for scalar fields. Spinor fields obey different algebraic rules, so Fedida rechecks the obstructions for them.

Weak continuity of the fields turns out to be the decisive assumption. In globally hyperbolic spacetimes it rules out equal-time canonical commutation and anticommutation relations alike. In two-dimensional Lorentzian spacetimes it also kills fermionic microcausality, extending Wightman's theorem. Finally, a Poincaré-invariant vacuum precludes pointwise spinorial covariance altogether. The ban covers Weyl and Dirac fermions, photons, and gravitons, which underlines how hard pointwise quantization of gravity remains.
arxiv-2510-01186:
Shen and co-authors edit videos by swapping the appearance of chosen subjects while leaving everything else untouched. Editors often need several subjects changed at once, and earlier tools tangle masks at boundaries or demand retraining. Their framework, IMAGEdit, works training-free on any number of designated subjects.

Large pretrained models first supply rich descriptions and rough mask motion for each subject. A retargeting step sharpens those masks before a mask-driven generator renders the final video. The design plugs into any compatible generator rather than replacing it. On a new multi-subject benchmark, the method consistently beat current state-of-the-art editors. Time-consistent masks keep edited subjects coherent frame to frame. Prompt-side conditioning was the usual weak point this design strengthens. Non-target regions stay untouched by construction, not by luck. Benchmark clips stress crowded scenes with overlapping subjects. Editing power grows with subject count here.
arxiv-2510-01286:
Cebrian, Kito, and Castro Fernandez map a split personality in the language-model ecosystem, where making models decentralizes while judging them concentrates. Thousands of organizations now build models across many countries and licenses. Benchmarks, the shared yardsticks, tell the opposite story.

A small top slice of the benchmark network carries most of the influence paths. Three countries produce the overwhelming majority of benchmark outputs, and authority inequality is extreme. Simulations show new benchmark entry dilutes concentration, while anti-overfitting penalties barely help. The authors read concentrated yardsticks as useful coordination infrastructure with real, bounded costs. Two curated registries supplied the ecosystem data for the study. Betweenness centrality exposes which benchmarks act as bridges. Rapid inflows of new models can temporarily scramble coordination. Path dependence is the standing risk of shared yardsticks. Concentration and quality are entirely different questions.
arxiv-2510-01386:
Knowles, Ceballos, and Pena reduce the question of how a neuron computes to the sign and size of one number. Neurons switch between spotting matched inputs and summing them over time. Those two operational modes frame much of neural coding theory, yet their boundary stayed loosely drawn.

A stripped-down model captures the quiet dynamics of real membrane behavior. Its smallest curved term alone predicts which mode a driven neuron occupies. Transitions between modes follow from that term's value, not from simulation detail. The sorting may clarify disorders where the cell's firing itself breaks down. In vivo pulse patterns anchor the analysis in real drive. Scaling strips the units and yields the standard form being sorted. Potassium and calcium channel stand-ins supplied the two worked cases. One number replaces a shelf of simulations. Channel diseases are the medical shadow over the theory in the background.
arxiv-2510-01586:
Pan and co-authors train multi-agent systems to defend themselves by sparring with attackers that learn alongside them. Teams of language-model agents face jailbreaks, injected prompts, and unsafe teamwork that single agents cannot spot alone. Bolt-on guard modules add cost and become single points of failure when compromised.

Their framework co-trains attackers and defenders through adversarial reinforcement learning. Agents internalize safety through practice rather than obeying an external policeman. A shared baseline mechanism keeps the joint training stable while both sides improve. Defenses grown this way should generalize to fresh attack styles instead of memorizing yesterday's tricks. Cross-agent attack chains are the blind spot this training directly exercises. Co-evolution keeps pressure honest because yesterday's defense meets tomorrow's attacker. Northwestern-led authorship spans four universities on the author list. Safety practiced becomes safety retained. Public baselines steady the shared learning signal for all.
arxiv-2510-01686:
Xu, Mei, Zhang, and Patel present FreeViS in this 2025 computer vision paper on video stylization. Stylizing a video means redrawing every frame in a chosen artistic style. Doing that frame by frame causes flicker and uneven style. Training a dedicated video model avoids flicker, but it needs paired videos and heavy computing.

FreeViS needs no training at all. It feeds several stylized reference frames into a ready-made image-to-video model. Using many references curbs the error spread that single-reference methods suffer from. High-frequency compensation pins down layout and motion during generation. Flow-based cues keep style textures alive in plain, low-detail regions. In wide evaluations FreeViS beat recent baselines on style fidelity and smoothness over time. Human viewers also preferred its results, which makes the approach practical for creators.
arxiv-2510-02086:
Behnam couples a vision transformer with a diffusion process to segment brain tumors in this 2025 paper. Accurate tumor outlines on MRI scans guide diagnosis, treatment planning, and follow-up. U-Net style models remain the standard tool, but they see only local context. Long-range structure across a whole scan volume escapes them, and complex tumor shapes suffer.

The proposed model, VGDM, places a transformer at the core of an iterative denoising process. Global reasoning from the transformer steers each refinement step. That pairing improves volume accuracy and sharpens boundary precision. Voxel-level errors get corrected across rounds, recovering fine tumor detail. The design targets robustness on the irregular boundaries that trouble purely convolutional systems. Diffusion refinement, borrowed from image generation, turns out to suit medical imaging well. The paper offers a hybrid route for high-stakes clinical tasks.
arxiv-2510-02286:
Guo and co-authors automate the search for chat attacks that unfold over many turns. Their 2025 safety paper treats red-teaming as a planning problem. A red team tries to make a model break its own safety rules. Single prompt attacks miss how real attackers adapt. Skilled attackers steer a conversation step by step. The authors frame each dialogue as a tree of choices. Their system, DialTree-RPO, learns by reinforcement while searching that tree. It prunes weak branches and rewards paths that reach the goal.

Tests ran against ten target models. The method beat both single-turn and multi-turn baselines. It found varied attack routes without human templates. Results confirm that current models stay exposed in long conversations. Automated search gives safety teams a practical stress test. The authors flag the dual use risk plainly.
arxiv-2510-02386:
Wang and co-authors show that cheating on reasoning benchmarks is easy to hide. Their 2025 paper studies contamination in large reasoning models. Contamination means test questions leaked into training data. Scores then flatter the model unfairly. Many detectors hunt for memorization traces in outputs. The team contaminated models at two different life stages. Early contamination during fine-tuning was detectable at first. A short round of reinforcement learning erased the traces. The clipping style objective of that training caused the erasure. Late contamination with worked solutions left barely any trace at all.
