Explanation quality and formatting were usually decent, and open-weight models competed evenly with closed ones. The authors warn against treating chatbots as oracles in this field while noting real value for simpler, well-grounded tasks.
arxiv-2510-20386:
Shaltiel Shmidman, Avi Shmidman, and Moshe Koppel introduce NeoDictaBERT, a family of BERT-style language models built for Hebrew with a modern architecture. Classic BERT models perform well despite modest size, but their design predates newer transformer advances that extend context and improve benchmarks. Their models follow the NeoBERT architecture, with a dedicated focus on Hebrew text, plus a bilingual variant.

The new models outperform existing ones on almost all Hebrew benchmarks and give a strong foundation for downstream tasks. The bilingual version also posts strong retrieval results, beating other multilingual models of similar size. The authors describe their training process and benchmark results in detail and release the models openly to advance Hebrew natural language processing research and development.
arxiv-2510-20586:
Muhammad Atif Butt and five co-authors present GenColorBench, the first comprehensive benchmark for color precision in text-to-image generation. Modern image models produce high-quality pictures but still fail at fine-grained color control, often missing the exact color a prompt names. Existing benchmarks test composition and prompt adherence while neglecting color or judging it only coarsely, including no treatment of numerical color values.

The benchmark grounds its tests in established color systems and contains forty-four thousand color-focused prompts covering more than four hundred colors. Perceptual and automated assessments evaluate popular models and reveal wide performance variation across color conventions. The authors identify which conventions models understand best and where they fail, offering the benchmark as a guide for improving precise color generation.
arxiv-2510-20786:
Deeksha Adil and three co-authors develop optimization methods that trade off gradient queries against Hessian queries when hunting critical points of non convex functions. Gradients give slope, Hessians give curvature, and each costs differently depending on the system, so the best mix matters.

For any smooth function with Lipschitz Hessian, a bounded starting gap. A chosen accuracy, their method reaches an approximate critical point with a stated gradient budget that falls as the Hessian budget grows. The result improves known gradient complexity and makes the exchange rate between first and second order information precise. Such trade offs guide algorithm design when curvature calls are cheap for some variables but costly for others.
arxiv-2510-21086:
Jiaqi Xue leads seven co-authors on DictPFL, a federated learning framework that trains across institutions on fully encrypted gradients with low overhead. Sharing gradients leaks privacy through inversion attacks, while encrypting everything with homomorphic methods is usually prohibitively slow.

Prior systems either encrypt all gradients at high cost or encrypt part and leave openings. DictPFL encrypts every transmitted gradient while keeping overhead minimal, aiming at full protection without the usual penalty. Practical private federation would let hospitals and banks pool model gains without pooling the sensitive signals inside their updates.
arxiv-2510-21186:
Benoît Collins and Sho Matsumoto work on Weingarten calculus, a set of formulas for averaging polynomial functions over groups of matrices. The classic method struggles with high-degree integrals because the matrices involved in the formulas cannot always be inverted, which limits direct calculation.

They rebuild the method using virtual isometries, picturing random matrices that follow the Haar distribution as products of simple complex reflections. From that picture they gain a clear calculus for reflections, a way to compute moments of related rank-one matrices. A formula linking one dimension to the next through new functions in the symmetric group algebra. Examples show how the approach unifies results for unitary groups.
arxiv-2510-21486:
Marco Belli reframes a canonical identification in topology. The singular cohomology of a space, computed from maps of simplices into it, matches the cohomology computed from a cover by overlapping patches, organized into a structure called the Čech nerve.

He shows the matching map is nothing mysterious. It evaluates singular cohomology classes on the simplices of the nerve itself, using a homotopy equivalence between the nerve and the original space. Applied to real tori, spaces shaped like multi-dimensional donuts built as a vector space modulo a lattice, the picture sharpens. Two natural maps, one from the universal cover and one recording how loops twist the cover, turn out to be exact inverses of each other.
arxiv-2510-21686:
Raheem Karim Hashmani and four co-authors manufacture multimodal data sets whose shared information content is known exactly. The field has lacked such a measuring stick. Mutual information between data channels drives how estimators are judged. It also drives how self-supervised learners are tuned. Real data never reveal the true value to check against.

Their generator pairs a flow-based model with a structured causal scheme for the hidden variables. Those variables correlate the channels. The result is realistic data at any chosen level of true mutual information. A suite of estimators is benchmarked across those levels. A sanity law is verified too: prediction improves as true shared information rises. The authors sketch uses from multi-detector astrophysics to self-supervised learning in the strongly multimodal regime.
arxiv-2510-21986:
Dogyun Park leads an eight-author team cutting the training cost of diffusion Transformers, the image generators whose price grows steeply with the number of image tokens. Dropping tokens saves money, but careless dropping damages what the model learns, and earlier fixes either added heavy machinery or broke down at high drop rates.

Their method, SPRINT, splits the work by depth: early layers see every token and capture fine detail, deeper layers run on a sparse subset, and residual links fuse the two streams. Training runs mostly in the cheap sparse mode, then finishes briefly with all tokens. On a standard image benchmark the recipe saved nearly tenfold on training while matching quality scores, and a related inference trick almost halved computing at generation time.
arxiv-2510-22086:
Pau Juan-Bartroli and José Ignacio Rivero-Wildemauwe ask why people reject money in the Ultimatum Game, where a proposer splits a sum and a responder who says no leaves both with nothing. Rejections of positive offers have been blamed both on social preferences, such as spite toward an unfair partner, and on moral concerns about the split itself.

Their model combines the two motives and delivers a sharp answer. A pinch of spite turns out to be both necessary and sufficient for rejecting a positive offer, so social preference does the driving. Morality is not irrelevant: stronger moral concern raises the threshold at which people reject, acting as an amplifier on the social motive. Estimating both traits from earlier experimental data, the authors find two distinct types of rejecters, separable by how the same people behave in a second game with no rejection option.
arxiv-2510-22186:
Nadav Dym, Matthias Wellershoff, Efstratios Tsoukanis, Daniel Levy, and Radu Balan study a disarmingly simple way to fingerprint a cloud of points. Project the points onto several lines, sort each list of shadows, and stack the sorted lists into one vector. Shuffling the points changes nothing, which makes the trick attractive for graph learning, where node order is arbitrary.

Earlier work showed that with enough well-aimed projections the fingerprint is unique and distorts distances only within fixed bounds. Two gaps remained: how many projections are truly needed, and how large the distortion can get. The team improves the upper bound on the required number and adds a lower bound, then constructs projection sets whose distortion can be estimated concretely. The results turn a neat existence theorem into engineering numbers.
arxiv-2510-22386:
Gabriel Nivasch studies how complex the free space can be for a box shaped robot that slides without turning among still polyhedral obstacles in three dimensions. Free space means all placements where the box touches no obstacle interior. Earlier work set looser upper bounds for general polyhedral robots and for box robots.

Nivasch proves the bound for a box is on the order of n squared, where n counts obstacle vertices. He proves the same bound for convex polygons whose edges come in parallel pairs. These results settle the worst case growth question for boxes and for all convex polygons.
arxiv-2510-22486:
Light reflected from a metal can twist slightly when an electric field is applied, an effect called Kerr rotation. Farzad Mahfouzi, Mark D Stiles, and Paul M Haney examine that effect on metallic surfaces in a 2025 paper, combining quantum based calculations with optical modeling.

Their work finds two separate causes acting together near the surface. One comes from electrons piling up with orbital motion, and the other, a surface Pockels effect, comes from the field changing electron wave patterns. In thin platinum films the two contributions are similar in size, but they act differently on two kinds of polarized light.
arxiv-2510-22786:
Some equation families resist any simple one parameter form. Benson Farb and Jesse Wolfson prove that fact in 2025. They work with finite groups and their Galois symmetries. Galois groups track how equation roots permute. The result holds even after adding one low degree root.

In geometric terms, they build special group varieties. No low degree branched cover helps. From any such cover, no dominant map reaches a group curve. Their proof method is new. It applies where older methods fail. Cases vary by group and by degree bound. The work concerns essential dimension, a measure of equation complexity.
arxiv-2510-23086:
Jin Li, Kexun Wu, Qi Hao, Yan Chen, and Jiawei Wang demonstrate an on-chip platform that steers quantum light emission with a special optical singularity. Bound states in the continuum trap light without leaking, and chiral versions favor one handedness. The team uses two coupled microring resonators linked to waveguides.

A reflector feeding back into one ring merges two plain bound states into a single chiral quasi-bound state on an exceptional surface. That higher-order singularity gives strong, tunable control of emission. The fully integrable design could serve quantum photonics chips that need precise, reconfigurable single-photon sources.
arxiv-2510-23386:
Alvaro Paz and three co-authors present a control method for heavy-duty hydraulic manipulators, the large powered arms used on big machines. Such arms are huge and strong, so motion must respect strict limits on force, speed, and position. The team's 2025 aim is to track a planned path while staying inside those limits at all times.

Their method uses nonlinear model predictive control, which looks ahead and picks moves that obey the arm's full nonlinear dynamics. It runs in real time at one thousand cycles per second, guided by live sensor feedback and a multiple shooting plan. A robust low level controller, built on virtual decomposition control, keeps each joint close to its target. Tests on a full size machine show the plan holds the actuator limits at the joints. The arm tip also stays within its allowed space motion, and tracking stays accurate.
arxiv-2510-23486:
Alex Ayoub and four co-authors question a common belief about large reasoning models: that longer answers are better answers. These models often burn through huge numbers of tokens, which raises cost and slows replies. The team treats reasoning as a goal-reaching task where reaching the goal fast matters, much like taking the shortest path that still succeeds.

They train the models with a discount method from reinforcement learning, which works like a small fee charged for each reasoning token. Theory about best-possible policies in limited policy classes supports the approach. In their tests, the trained models produced shorter chains of thought while keeping accuracy about the same, which supports the claim that brevity need not cost correctness.
arxiv-2510-23786:
Joohwan Ko and four co-authors present Relaxed Sequence Sampling, a method for designing proteins with more variety than gradient descent gives. Design pipelines that lean on structure predictors like AlphaFold2 have scored wins, but the standard relaxed optimization follows a single downhill path. It also ignores constraints from real protein sequences, so results cluster tightly and often fail to fold as hoped.

Their framework samples instead, using Markov chain Monte Carlo in a continuous logit space. Gradient guidance steers the walk, while jumps suggested by the ESM2 protein language model keep proposals biologically plausible. The energy being sampled mixes AlphaFold2 structural goals with ESM2 sequence priors. On a binder design task, the sampler produced five times more designable structures than the baseline method, with two to three times the diversity, at the same computing cost. The authors offer it as a way to explore design space widely.
arxiv-2510-24086:
S. M. Al-Marzoug and three co-authors study a single impurity atom held in a double well made by a pair of linked solitons. The setting is a thin, quasi one dimensional system with dipolar forces. Solving for the atom's energy states, they find the two lowest states sit well apart from all higher ones.

That gap lets the atom act as a clean two level system, the basic unit of a qubit. Simulations show the atom swings back and forth between the left and right wells in a regular way. A simple two mode formula matches those swings well, which supports the idea of using this setup as a controllable quantum bit.
arxiv-2510-24386:
Robert G. Radloff and twenty five co-authors show three dimensional X-ray imaging with no need to rotate the sample. Lensless X-ray imaging gives element level detail at tiny scales in thick samples. Light and electron scopes cannot reach that depth. Standard diffraction methods can rebuild a 3D form, but they need many turns of the sample, which makes tests complex. One scattering shot, on its own, gives only weak depth data.

X-ray fluorescence, in turn, is sent out in all directions. The team uses links in fluorescence strength to pull 3D data from a single view. This beats the coherence limits that had confined such imaging to single crystals. The method could make nanoscale imaging of thick, mixed samples far simpler to run.
arxiv-2510-24486:
Tinsae G. Dulecha and four co-authors speed up neural reflectance transformation imaging through knowledge distillation. Reflectance transformation imaging lets users relight a surface interactively from a few dozen photos taken with a fixed camera and varied lighting, revealing fine detail. Classic methods are compact and fast but struggle with complex reflectance, causing artifacts on shiny or shadowed areas.

Neural approaches learn a compact function of light direction and give superior quality at similar storage. The authors distill that neural knowledge into a faster form, keeping accuracy while cutting the cost of evaluating each pixel. The result aims at practical, high quality surface inspection for cultural heritage and materials work.
arxiv-2510-24586:
Michal Botur, Ivan Chajda, and Helmut Länger, three authors, study complemented posets. A poset is a set with a partial order, like a family tree of rank. A complement of an element fills what that element lacks. Each element gets a set of all its complements. The trio study the operator that maps elements to those sets.

They ask when the complement set forms an antichain, an unordered set. They also ask when the operator reverses itself or flips order. Applied to top and bottom cones, it yields four paired operators. Those pairs show traits close to adjointness, a near-mirror link. One example has unique complements yet fails to be Boolean. They close with orthogonality in the Dedekind-MacNeille completion.
arxiv-2510-24686:
Hari Padma leads a team with nineteen co-authors who found a new charge mode in a copper based ladder solid. Light shone in the plane of the ladder drove the solid to a long lived state with a changed charge pattern. The old charge order in the solid partly melted at the same time.

With fast X ray probes, they saw a wave like mode rise from the charge order point and climb in energy. Its speed was close to the speed of single charges in the solid. The mode hints that bound charges can move more freely when lit. That state may help probe how light can stir pair states.
arxiv-2510-24786:
Avinay Bhat, Mun Jung Jung, Gray Putnam, and Haiwang Yu use deep learning to clean signals from a big tank of liquid argon used to catch neutrinos. In such tanks, true hit zones are hard to spot, since wave forms can cancel and gear flaws blur the read. They cast the hunt for hit zones as an image cut task.

A deep net with skip links was trained on fake and real like samples that span many gear setups. It marks hit zones far better than past hand rules, and holds up when gear traits shift. The method is now used in a known short range neutrino plan. It also sets a base for a much larger deep site to come.
arxiv-2510-25086:
Guibin Sun, Jinhu Lu, Kexin Liu, Zhenqian Wang, and Guanrong Chen review a new way for robot swarms to form shapes with no task gives at all. Swan like joint acts in the wild let groups work with more speed and grit. The old give based way hands each bot its post, but scales poor and breaks as swarms change.

A mean shift search plan sits at the heart of the new way, and lifts joint speed by large folds, the team reports. The gain grows as the swarm grows, not less. The piece is a teach review that lays out the math and its uses. Three open tasks for the field close the tour.
arxiv-2510-25186:
Surojit Ghosh and Ankit Kumar give a fresh proof of a broad form of the Nandakumar and Ramana Rao guess, for the prime case. The guess sits in a part of math that tracks how spaces act under group moves. Their proof leans on one tool: a graded form of Bredon cohomology, a way to read such spaces by their group marks.

The key move is to view the cohomology of shape spaces for point sets as a module over the graded cohomology of a lone point. No other frame is used. That lean path is the point of the work: a hard guess falls to a clean group graded read of those spaces alone.
arxiv-2510-25386:
Kumar Manas, Mert Keser, and Alois Knoll survey automated driving methods. Their 2025 survey integrates legal and logical specifications. Self-driving systems must perceive, predict, and plan safely. They must also comply with traffic law. Dynamic and uncertain roads complicate that goal. Decisions need justification beyond technical quality alone.

The survey analyzes methods across perception, prediction, and planning. Methods range from logic approaches to computational law. They aim for regulatory compliance and interpretability jointly. A central challenge sits at their intersection. Perceptual reliability and legal compliance can conflict. The authors present a taxonomy for current methods. It sorts methods by foundations, architecture, and validation. Logic-driven rules and norm-aware prediction are covered. Open questions and useful trade-offs are highlighted. Insights span engineering, logic, and law disciplines.
arxiv-2510-25486:
Peter Krack discusses neutrino event generation at the LHC. His 2025 contribution paper covers next-to-leading order methods. The LHC produces an intense forward neutrino beam. Its scientific likely went unexploited for many years. FASER and SND@LHC began operating in 2023 there.

Modern parton shower methods also improve predictions greatly. Future tests at the Forward Physics Facility are considered. Neutrino energy and rapidity distributions are encoded in grids. Realistic acceptance and choice cuts can be applied. As first use, fast-interpolation grids are computed. LHC forward neutrino fluxes are determined from FASER data. The NNPDF fitting methodology supplies that determination. Flux readings test particle physics in forward region.
arxiv-2510-25586:
Hernando Maldonado Colman and Michael E Mueller present a rush-to-equilibrium concept. Their 2025 paper minimizes reactive nitrogen outputs in ammonia combustion. Ammonia is a zero-carbon fuel. It suits power generation and transportation. It is less explosive than hydrogen and easier to store.

Yet ammonia has poor flammability and flame stability. Rich-quench-lean strategies have shown promise for outputs. Largest outputs come from unrelaxed fuel-rich stage gases. Equilibrium overshoot within reaction zones causes that problem. A decaying mixing rate acts as particle transits flame. That mitigates mixing effects blocking equilibrium method. Gas turbine setting models show order-of-magnitude reductions. Useful implementation settings look reasonable for modern combustors.
arxiv-2510-25686: Subarsha Banerjee computes the Szeged index of power graphs of finite groups, in a 2025 mathematics paper. A group's power graph has group elements as vertices, joined when one is a power of the other. Banerjee first derives a formula for the Szeged index of a generalized join of graphs. Applying it, he obtains the index for the power graph of the cyclic group for every order above two. He also relates that case to the dihedral group, and he provides SAGE code for both computations.
arxiv-2510-25786:
Yaniv Nikankin led six co-authors improving circuit faithfulness. Dana Arad, Itay Itzhak, and Anja Reusch helped. Adi Simhi, Gal Kesten-Pomeranz, and Yonatan Belinkov joined. Their 2025 paper tackles circuit discovery in mechanistic interpretability. Determining which model parts perform tasks is challenging. The Mechanistic Interpretability Benchmark supplies their testing setting. Three key improvements to circuit discovery are proposed.

Edge choice is central to circuit discovery quality. Second, a ratio-based choice strategy prioritizes strong edges. Positive-scoring edges are balanced for results and faithfulness. Third, integer linear programming replaces standard greedy choice. Their methods yield more faithful circuits overall. Faithful circuits help explain how models compute answers. Code is ready publicly for other scholars.
arxiv-2510-26086:
Zheng Zhang, Haonan Li, Xingyu Li, Hang Zhang, and Zhiyun Qian use large language models to find the commit that introduced a software bug. Bug bisection identifies the bug inducing commit, which sets the range of versions at risk. Older patch based methods assume the bad commit and the fix touch the same functions, lean only on code changes, and use simple heuristics. Commit messages often hold rich clues that they ignore.

Their pipeline, LLMBisect, uses the model ability to read both text and code. It extracts full patch information, compares several candidate commits in context, and narrows the field in stages with logical analysis of the vulnerability. The comparative design is meant to break the barriers that limit earlier tools.
arxiv-2510-26186:
Jinho Choi, Hyesu Lim, Steffen Schneider, and Jaegul Choo present a tool that finds hidden biases in visual data sets without costly hand labels. Dataset bias means examples are skewed toward certain concepts, such as backgrounds, which can teach models shortcuts. Their framework, ConceptScope, discovers human readable concepts by applying sparse autoencoders, networks that force a few active features, to representations from vision foundation models.

Concepts are sorted into target, context, and bias types by meaning and by correlation with class labels, which enables class level data portraits and robustness checks by subgroup. Validation shows the method captures objects, textures, backgrounds, facial traits, emotions, and actions, and its spatial maps align with meaningful image regions. It reliably detects known biases such as background bias.
arxiv-2510-26286:
Rakesh Arora leads three co-authors in a study of equations driven by the logarithmic p-Laplacian. That operator is nonlinear, with a log based kernel. It models diffusion with long range effects. The team derive a new Sobolev bound for the log case. The bound controls a function by its gradient.

They also prove optimal placements into Orlicz type spaces. Those spaces are broad forms of the usual power spaces. With these tools, the team tackle boundary value problems with critical growth. The Nehari manifold method then gives a nonzero weak solution. A final part tracks least energy solutions of a fractional problem. It follows them as the fractional parameter tends to zero.
arxiv-2510-26486:
Dipak Meher, Carlotta Domeniconi, and Guadalupe Correa-Cabrera build a tool to map human smuggling networks from court files. Legal case documents hold rich facts about these secretive, shifting networks. But the files are long, loose in form, and full of names and pronouns that point to the same person in changing ways.

Meher and his two co-authors present LINK-KG, a framework that first resolves those shifting references with a three-stage, language-model-guided process. A type-specific prompt cache tracks each reference across chunks of text, so the story stays clean. Then the system draws a knowledge graph, a map of people and links, from the cleaned text. Against baseline methods, node duplication fell by about forty-five percent and noisy nodes by about thirty-two percent. The graphs came out cleaner and easier to analyse.
arxiv-2510-26686:
Steffen Bollmann, with four co-authors, maps the phases of hybrid structures that join fractional quantum Hall states with superconductors. Such hybrids may host parafermions, exotic excitations prized for quantum computing. The team focuses on a filling factor of two-thirds, which leads to parafermions with a threefold character, and they include fluctuations of the superconducting order.

Bollmann and the team first sketch the phase diagram with a phenomenological field theory. Then they map the system onto a chain of topological Josephson junctions holding lattice parafermions, and simulate it with a powerful matrix method. The diagram holds insulating phases and two kinds of Luttinger liquids, whose basic excitations carry full or fractional charge. Transitions match conformal field theory predictions, and the authors extract hints about ground state degeneracy and edge stability.
arxiv-2510-26786:
Cheng Zheng, William Koch, Baiang Li, and Felix Heide teach computers to learn how motion is organised in layers. Complex dynamics, from a swinging arm to a deforming scene, arise from simpler motion parts acting together. Existing methods rely on hand-defined hierarchies with fixed motion pieces, which limits how widely they apply.

Zheng and his three co-authors present HEIR, which learns a graph-based hierarchy straight from data. Observed motion is split into patterns inherited from a parent motion plus local residuals. Vertices hold elemental motions, and directed edges, learned by graph neural networks, hold parent-child links, all in a differentiable setup. Tests on one-dimensional translation, two-dimensional rotation, and dynamic three-dimensional scenes rebuilt the true hierarchy in the simple cases. On three-dimensional scenes, the deformations looked more realistic and interpretable than the baseline's.
arxiv-2510-26886:
Tiannian Zhu, Zhong Fang, Quansheng Wu, and Hongming Weng built MaterialsGalaxy, described in 2025. It is a platform that joins lab data and theory data on solid materials. Such data often sit apart in silos, closed stores that do not link up.

Links rest on structure similarity, how alike the atom layouts of two records are. Records span diffraction, crystal growth, computing, and written papers. Built-in AI tools pull facts from text, guess new crystal forms, and predict traits. Tests show the joined data can reveal hidden links between records. Those links can guide the design of new materials with wanted traits. The platform aims to close the long gap between lab work and theory.
arxiv-2510-26986:
Tobias Blickhan, Julianne Stratton, and Alan Kaptanoglu introduce MRX, a solver for three-dimensional magnetic equilibrium in fusion devices. Finding such a balance, where magnetic pressure and plasma pressure offset each other, is hard when the field lacks neat nested surfaces. Older solvers also struggle with keeping the field divergence-free, meaning free of false sources, and with strongly shaped chambers.

MRX relaxes a starting field toward lower energy through allowed changes, built on the JAX software framework for speed and automatic derivatives. Tests cover crafted vacuum cases and a stellarator field, plus shape tuning for near symmetry. A fast Newton method yields detailed equilibria with islands and chaos in minutes on a single graphics processor.
arxiv-2510-27086:
Tian-Yang Sun, Tian-Nuo Li, He Wang, Jing-Fei Zhang, and Xin Zhang apply a conditional learning model to the cosmic microwave background, the faint glow left from the early universe. Its power spectra summarize temperature and polarization patterns and test cosmological models. The team seeks compression that stays interpretable and supports fast diagnostic checks under weak assumptions.

Their parameter-conditioned variational autoencoder aligns a learned latent space with cosmological parameters while keeping likelihood-style tests available. Five latent dimensions suffice for high-fidelity reconstruction of the main spectra, including cases beyond the standard model. One diagnostic run drops from about forty hours on CPUs to about two minutes on a graphics processor. The latent space also mirrors known parameter links and flags anomalous spectra.
arxiv-2510-27286:
Fei Han and Yuanchu Li construct differential models for twisted Spinc-bordism and its Anderson dual. Bordism classifies manifolds up to cutting and gluing equivalence, and differential refinements add geometric data like metrics and connections. The degree-three twisted setting involves extra background structure that the models must encode carefully.

Their model for the differential Anderson dual builds on the Yamashita-Yonekura framework. With both models in hand, they define a twisted anomaly map from differential twisted K-theory with inverse twist into that dual. The construction is geometric, using bundle gerbes, gerbe modules, and reduced eta-invariants of Dirac operators tied to the twisted data. The map is expected to capture anomalies of twisted supersymmetric field theories in the Stolz-Teichner and Freed-Hopkins pictures.
arxiv-2510-27386:
James Kirk and James Owen determine when stacking transmission spectra from different exoplanets is meaningful. Astronomers co-add spectra to boost signal and reveal population traits, valuable for long-period planets where repeat visits are costly. The question is what a stacked spectrum of distinct planets physically represents across the Webb telescope near-infrared range.

Comparing stacked spectra with geometric-mean spectra across forward model grids, they show the geometric mean of abundance ratios reproduces the stack when two dominant species have self-similar ratios across planets. Adding a third species makes temperature critical, and stacking fails across the carbon monoxide to methane transition. Surface gravity matters little within comparable regimes. They also count how many cloudy sub-Neptunes must be stacked to rule out a flat spectrum confidently.
arxiv-2510-27486:
Junkang Liu, Fanhua Shang, and six other co-authors adapt a top training optimizer for federated learning in this 2025 paper. AdamW is a workhorse for training large models on one site. Spread across many sites, it wobbles: uneven local data makes its variance estimates noisy. Local overfitting also pulls each site's copy away from the shared model.

Their FedAdamW adds a local correction that keeps site updates aligned with the global one. Decoupled weight decay, a shrink term handled apart, curbs overfitting too. Sites average their second-moment estimates, the variance trackers, to steady them before reuse. The team proves a fast convergence rate with no assumption that site data look alike. That makes FedAdamW a candidate for training and fine-tuning large models across fleets of devices.
arxiv-2510-27686:
Seungjae Son, working alone, measures how fast a classic swirling flow mixes fluids in 2025. The flow, set out by Pierrehumbert in 1994, swaps shears whose position shifts at random on a torus, a donut-shaped surface. Prior work showed mixing is exponential, which means a gap shrinks by a fixed share in each time span.

Son asks how that rate depends on the flow's amplitude, which is its strength. The proof builds an explicit Lyapunov function, a gauge that tracks how far the system sits from mixed, plus a paired path for a two-point chain. A quantitative Harris theorem then turns those parts into a clear rate bound. Exact rates help predict mixing in fluids and gases.
arxiv-2511-00486:
Pooja Singh, Shashwat Bhardwaj, Vaibhav Sharma, and Sandeep Kumar address machine translation for Bhili, a tribal language of India with almost no digital resources. They introduce the Bhili-Hindi-English Parallel Corpus, the first and largest of its kind. It holds one hundred ten thousand carefully curated sentences across the three languages, built with expert human translators. The topics span education, administration, and news.

The corpus anchors a full Bhili translation benchmark. Proprietary and open multilingual models were tested on translation both ways between Bhili and English or Hindi. A fine-tuned distilled variant of the NLLB-200 model performed best, showing multilingual models can serve very low-resource languages. The team also probed generative translation with in-context learning, measuring how well models generalize across domains. The resource opens a path for inclusive language technology.
arxiv-2511-00686:
Alex Inch, Passawis Chaiyapattanaporn, Yuchen Zhu, Yuan Lu, Ting-Wen Ko, and Davide Paglieri want image generators to surprise us on purpose. Text-to-image diffusion models paint beautifully but repeat themselves, a real limit for exploration and ideation work. Prompt tricks that chase beauty scores do not fix sameness. Their system, WANDER, imports novelty search, an evolutionary method that rewards difference itself.

WANDER evolves natural language prompts with a language model as the mutation engine, while CLIP embeddings measure how novel each image is. Special emitters steer the search into distinct regions of prompt space, widening the variety further. With a leading image model generating and a compact model mutating, WANDER beat existing evolutionary prompt optimizers on diversity metrics, and ablation studies confirmed the emitters carry much of the gain.
arxiv-2511-01086:
Vladimir Martirosyan and Rachit Kamdar compare employer reviews on two platforms with opposite credibility rules. Glassdoor allows fully anonymous reviews, while Blind verifies employment but keeps reviewers anonymous. The question is how that verification step changes what reviews say about company culture.

Using the Competing Values Framework, which sorts culture into clan, adhocracy, hierarchy, and market types, and a language model built for culture analysis, they study over three hundred thousand ratings. Blind reviews stress clan and hierarchy, while Glassdoor skews more positive and highlights clan and market. Verification, they conclude, does not remove bias; it shifts the cultural signal, so job seekers reading different platforms receive systematically different impressions.
arxiv-2511-01286:
Sivaram Krishnan and colleagues predict connectivity in flying ad hoc networks, swarms of drones that form their own wireless network while moving. Most machine learning for communications assumes static settings, but a drone network's topology changes constantly, so links appear and vanish.

They use data driven Koopman operator methods, which lift nonlinear dynamics into a space where they behave nearly linearly, to model drone trajectories and forecast link quality. Both centralized and distributed versions are proposed. In a surveillance scenario with drones on predetermined paths, the methods accurately predicted signal quality between drones and the isolation events that cause communication outages. Such forecasts could let drones schedule transmissions for moments when links will hold.
arxiv-2511-01686:
T. C. Dorlas revisits a theorem at the heart of quantum statistical mechanics: the quantum version of Varadhan's theorem from large deviation theory, proved earlier by Petz, Raggio, and Verbeure. The theorem turns questions about rare fluctuations in a quantum lattice system into a variational formula. That formula is an optimization over states on an operator algebra. It can collapse to a formula in a single real variable.

Dorlas gives a new proof built from a quantum large deviation analysis together with the Trotter product formula, rather than the standard techniques of the original. He then extends the argument to several non-commuting variables at once. This recovers the variational formula for general mean-field quantum spin systems. Raggio and Werner first derived that formula. The paper is a cleaner route to a foundational result.
arxiv-2511-01986:
Marie-Joëlle Gingras and seven colleagues read the recent diaries of three giant galaxies sitting at the centers of cooling-flow clusters: RX J0820.9+0752, A1835, and PKS 0745-191. Keck Cosmic Web Imager observations of their stellar populations reveal rich molecular gas reservoirs and strong Balmer absorption from stars only 30 to 100 million years old, evidence of long-lasting star formation.

In A1835 and PKS 0745-191 the young populations are spatially extended, forming stars at rates near 100 and 8 solar masses per year respectively. A1835 also holds a blueshifted clump of young stars racing relative to the gas, which the authors suggest formed inside an outflow, detached, and is now falling back in. RX J0820.9+0752 instead keeps its intermediate-age stars in a filament outside the nucleus, with no central star formation. Neighboring galaxies are all old and cannot have donated the enormous gas reservoirs.
arxiv-2511-02186:
Kazuki Yanagisawa, Tomoharu Oka, and four co-authors use archival telescope data to peer at the disk feeding the black hole at our galaxy's centre, Sagittarius A-star. They analysed 77 observing epochs from the ALMA radio array, hunting for patterns in the brightness at a frequency of 230 gigahertz. One epoch showed an unusually clean sinusoidal wave with a period of about fifty-two minutes and strong statistical significance.

Modelling the wave as a hot spot orbiting in the disk and boosted by the Doppler effect places the orbit at about four Schwarzschild radii from the black hole. The fitted tilt, only about eight degrees from face-on, matches earlier constraints from the GRAVITY instrument and the Event Horizon Telescope. The result shows millimetre-wave timing alone can reveal the geometry of the innermost accretion flow.
arxiv-2511-02386:
Vít Jelínek and Michal Opler examine how much logic it takes to describe properties of permutations. A permutation can be viewed as two linear orders on the same set, and earlier work by Albert, Bouvel, and Féray studied what first-order logic can say. This paper moves up to monadic second-order logic, which can quantify over sets. It maps its power and its limits.

The authors exhibit permutation properties that monadic second-order logic can express but first-order logic cannot. They also show that having a fixed point escapes monadic second-order logic. On the algorithmic side, model checking a monadic second-order sentence against a permutation can be done in time governed by the formula size and the permutation's tree-width. Hardness results round out the picture: the problem stays hard on any fixed hereditary class of permutations satisfying mild conditions.
arxiv-2511-02486:
Ignacio Ponce, Rodrigo Bernal, and Federico Milano redefine a basic question in power systems: when do two devices swing together? Coherency has traditionally been asked about synchronous generators, grouping machines that move as one during disturbances so engineers can simplify their models. Modern grids mix generators with batteries, converters, and flexible loads, and the old definition does not reach them.

Their definition rests on the difference between the complex frequencies of the current injections of any two devices connected to the same grid. Because it is stated in terms of currents rather than any device's internal model, it applies to any technology. The authors lay out a systematic procedure for checking which device models can be coherent under the definition, and three simulation case studies show it correctly judging coherency across device types.
arxiv-2511-02886:
Ronan Killian McGovern shows how a tiny reasoning model can adapt during a contest without huge compute. The setting is the 2025 ARC Prize, a test of pattern puzzles. The leading open approach, Tiny Recursive Models, used a seven-million-parameter network trained on altered ARC tasks, but it needed far more compute than the contest allows at run time.

McGovern pretrained a small recursive model on 1,280 public tasks, over more than 700,000 training steps on four high-end graphics cards, reaching about 10 percent on the public test set. During the contest, full fine-tuning in just 12,500 steps lifted it to 6.67 percent on semi-private tasks, inside the allowed limits. The 2025 paper stresses that plain full tuning, not light adapters, did the job.
arxiv-2511-02986:
Giovanni Palla and seven colleagues built scLDM, a generative model that creates realistic single-cell gene expression profiles. Such data are counts across thousands of genes, with tangled dependencies, and cells have no natural gene order. Older generators often force an ordering or use shallow networks. Their 2025 model works in a compressed latent space instead, where a diffusion process does the generating.

The encoder pools genes into fixed-size latent codes with a cross-attention block that ignores gene order, and the decoder unpools in the matching style. A diffusion transformer then learns the latent distribution, guided by conditions when needed. Across observational and perturbation data sets, scLDM beat rivals at generation quality, and its profiles also served well in cell classification tasks. The design scales to large atlases.
arxiv-2511-03086:
Premananth, Philip Resnik, Sonia Bansal, Deanna Kelly, and Carol Espy-Wilson rank people with schizophrenia by symptom severity using speech. The aim is to help clinics decide who needs care first. Many patients wait too long for assessment because expert time is scarce. Their 2025 model compares patients pairwise instead of scoring each alone, using articulatory and acoustic features drawn from recordings.

Pairwise wins feed a Bradley-Terry model, a standard way to turn comparisons into a ranking. On ranking measures, the approach beat earlier regression models that predicted severity scores directly. The authors frame the tool for triage in settings with few clinicians. It is a scalable, remote read of speech that puts the most severe cases first, without claiming to replace diagnosis.
arxiv-2511-03186:
Yiru Chen and eight colleagues report on Summit Concierge, an AI assistant built for Adobe Summit, the company's big user conference. Attendees flood such events with questions about schedules, sessions, and logistics, and the assistant had to work under real limits: sparse data, quality demands, and a fast launch. Their 2025 paper describes the system and what its deployment taught them.

The team kept humans in the loop throughout. Prompt engineering shaped the assistant's behavior, retrieval grounded its answers in real event data, and light human validation caught errors before users did. The authors argue this agile, feedback-driven loop is what made the assistant reliable at scale, even starting cold with no event-specific training data.
arxiv-2511-03386:
Andrzej A Zdziarski and colleagues solve a puzzle about a bright iron line from the black hole binary MAXI J1631-479. In its soft state, the system shows a strong, broad iron glow while its hard tail stays very weak. That weak tail cannot light the disk enough to explain the line, and two earlier fixes each strained belief.

Fresh looks at paired NICER and NuSTAR data point to a third source: disk light boosted by a corona of fast electrons. That boosted glow mirrors the disk shape at low energies and strikes the disk hard enough to raise the iron line. The fit also yields a spin estimate for the black hole. The case shows how reflected light can mislead when the true lamp is hidden in plain sight.
arxiv-2511-03586:
Andrei Ivanov and colleagues introduce PerfDojo, a training ground where language models learn to write fast machine learning libraries for mixed hardware. Modern models must run well across processors, graphics chips, and accelerators, each with quirks of instruction set and data type. Hand tuning is slow, and automatic tools often hide their logic in opaque forms.

PerfDojo frames optimization as a reinforcement game, with a method called PerfLLM guiding language models through it. Scores reward real speed on the target hardware, not code that merely looks right. Sparse and quantized model features enter the challenge set directly. Portable, self-tuning libraries could cut the expert labor now burned on each new chip generation.
arxiv-2511-03686:
Minzhao Liu and Pradeep Niroula are the first two authors of a fifty-two-author collaboration reporting certified randomness amplification across a network, without co-located Bell tests. Cryptography needs truly unpredictable numbers, yet physical sources emit biased or correlated bits, and quantum methods can upgrade weak randomness into nearly perfect randomness.

Gates were streamed in real time to Quantinuum's ninety-eight-qubit Helios trapped-ion processor, holding coherence for about nine tenths of a second. Measurement bases were revealed only milliseconds before measurement, leaving little room for classical spoofing. Random circuits on sixty-four qubits reached a fidelity that supports amplification from a low-entropy source, even if the remote device acts maliciously.
arxiv-2511-03786:
Martin Hoferichter and Gabriele Levati analyse how light new particles could affect the dipole moments of the tau lepton. Testing new physics tied to the third generation is hard. Limits from electron-positron collisions into tau pairs often rely on effective field theory, which only holds when the new scale is large.

Their account covers new light spin-zero and spin-one bosons and explains how asymmetry measurements should be read when extracting dipole moments. Decoupling back to the effective theory limit is checked, and links to other electron-positron constraints are discussed. A tauphilic gauge boson at Belle II serves as a detailed case study of the full approach.
arxiv-2511-03886:
Erdem Sucu, Kuantay Boshkayev, Yassine Sekhmani, Izzet Sakalli, and Mohsen Fathi explore charged black holes in Scalar-Tensor-Vector Gravity and look for signatures that separate that theory from Einstein gravity. Topological analysis, lensing, shadows, and emission are all used as probes.

The gravity coupling strengthens thermal stability while electric charge weakens it, and the two parameters push light deflection and shadow size in opposite directions. Quantum-corrected entropy models reveal phase transitions at microscopic scales. Certain parameter pairs can mimic the radiation pattern of a spinning Kerr black hole, creating an identification trap for observers. The authors map these effects into concrete tests for future imaging and lensing campaigns.
arxiv-2511-03986:
Ahmed A Metwally, Heyjun Park, Yue Wu, Tracey McLaughlin, and Michael P Snyder review how steady glucose monitoring joined with machine learning can split diabetes and its early stage into metabolic subtypes. Fixed glucose thresholds hide differing causes, chiefly insulin resistance, beta-cell dysfunction, and incretin deficiency, and those causes call for different responses.

Home glucose-tolerance tests with wearable sensors feed models that predict standard measures of muscle insulin resistance and beta-cell function. How each person responds to foods, sleep, activity, and meal timing link to specific faults, and dietary aids work differently by body type. The review argues that rich glucose traces can guide tailored lifestyle changes rather than one-size advice.
arxiv-2511-04086:
Qingfeng Chen, Haojin Zeng, Jingyi Jie, Shichao Zhang, and Debo Cheng propose DeNoise for spotting anomalous whole graphs when even the training data are contaminated. Most graph neural methods quietly assume training sets contain only normal graphs, an assumption that fails in critical real domains and badly distorts what the model learns.

An encoder with attribute and structure decoders trains under an adversarial objective for noise-resistant embeddings. An anchor-alignment step fuses informative node embeddings from normal graphs into all graph embeddings, dampening anomaly interference. Contrastive learning then pulls normal graphs together and pushes anomalies away. Tests on eight real datasets showed reliable detection despite dirty training data.
arxiv-2511-04286:
Matteo Cercola, Valeria Capretti, and Simone Formentin propose a hybrid way to learn from human preferences that joins the scale of reinforcement learning from human feedback. It joins that scale with the query efficiency of preferential Bayesian optimization. Preference data are costly and slow to collect, yet such judgments steer models toward subjective human goals.

An acquisition-driven module inside the feedback pipeline chooses which comparisons to ask for, instead of gathering preferences passively. Tests cover high-dimensional preference tuning and language model fine-tuning. Both sample efficiency and overall performance improved steadily in its experiments. For alignment work, smarter questions can be worth as much as bigger answer sets.
arxiv-2511-04486:
Wayne Chi leads eleven authors with EDIT-Bench, a benchmark for instructed code editing. AI assistants now often change a developer's existing code from a plain instruction. Few tests measure that skill with real material rather than artificial tasks.

EDIT-Bench holds five hundred forty problems drawn from real use in the wild. Instructions and code contexts span several human and programming languages. Tasks range from fixing errors to adding features, and many hinge on cursor position or highlighted code. The set gives model builders a realistic yardstick for one of the most common coding assistant jobs.
arxiv-2511-04786:
Madison VanWyngarden leads five authors testing how missing galaxies bias dark siren cosmology. Gravitational waves give a source's distance directly, like a standard siren. Without a light counterpart, every galaxy in the search volume becomes a candidate host.

Galaxy catalogs supply the redshifts, but real catalogs miss faint galaxies. Mock catalogs let the team measure what that incompleteness does to Hubble constant estimates. For well-localized events, the answer depends on whether true hosts tend to be catalogued. Their results guide how much dark siren cosmology can trust today's incomplete sky surveys.
arxiv-2511-04886:
Ahmad Elallaf leads five authors assessing roadway crash risk with beta distribution learning. Crashes kill over a million people a year and cost many nations up to three percent of GDP. Older studies isolate single risk factors and miss spatial context.

Standard neural estimators also give point guesses with no sense of uncertainty. Their geospatial framework reads satellite imagery as a rich spatial input instead. A beta distribution output carries both the risk estimate and its confidence. Planners deciding where to spend safety money need exactly that pairing of a score with honest uncertainty.
arxiv-2511-04986:
Mohammadreza Saeidi and co-authors study how fast the keepers of npm software packages reply to bug reports. The npm web of shared code is core to modern software, yet a bug in one package can spread harm to many that depend on it.

The team mined 30,340 bug reports across 500 of the most used npm packages, and coded why some reports went unmet. Keepers were in fact quite responsive, with a middle project score near seven in ten reports met. The paper maps the main reasons the rest stall, from scope calls to lack of detail.
arxiv-2511-05086:
Takuro Abe and co-authors study universal derivations for multiarrangements, sets of planes with a count on each plane. The topic was opened in 2024 for arrangements from reflection groups, and this work pushes it to the general case.

The authors give a test for when a derivation is universal, and a full account for arrangements with counts of at most two. They then describe universal derivations for several cases, among them the deleted A3 arrangement. That case is the first known non-reflection example with a universal derivation apart from the Euler one.
arxiv-2511-05186:
Akash Das and co-authors compare a plain neural network with a physics-informed one at counting charged particles made in heavy-ion collisions. Both nets train on one million simulated zirconium collision events from the HYDJET++ model.

The physics-informed net has known physics rules built into its training, while the plain net learns from data alone. The authors score each net's count of charged hadrons against the test data. The contest shows when built-in physics helps a model guess right on new events, and when raw data skill is enough, in nuclear collision work.
arxiv-2511-05386:
Charlie Dworaczek Guera, Ronan Memin, and Michel Pain prove a central limit theorem for beta-ensembles with Freud weights. In those weights, the weight grows as a power of the state, with power at least two. Past proofs fail when that power sits just above two, since the weight is not smooth enough there.

Their route sets an optimal local law in the style of recent work on such gases of points. The theorem covers linear statistics for general test functions. As a use, they give a consistency check of the KLS conjecture for uniform laws on Schatten balls, a known open claim in convex geometry.
arxiv-2511-05586:
Jannis Brugger and co-authors offer a post-processing step that improves equations found by neural-guided discovery systems. Such a system reads a data set and proposes an equation for it in one go. If the result disappoints, users have few cheap ways to get a better suggestion.

Their method, RED, studies where the first equation misses the data. It breaks the equation into a tree, computes the leftover error for each part, and asks the system to propose a better part using that error as a new target. Better parts are swapped in only if they win on held-out data. On fifty-three physics equations, RED improved every neural and every classic system tested.
arxiv-2511-05986:
Xing-Peng Yang and Wen-Cong Chen model how some X-ray binaries become millisecond pulsars paired with helium white dwarfs. Magnetic braking, the slow theft of orbital angular momentum, drives much of this evolution. Under the standard braking law, only a razor-thin range of starting periods yields the observed short-period pairs, a puzzle called the fine-tuning problem.

Using a detailed binary evolution code, the authors compare the standard law with a newer one boosted by convection and rotation. The newer law drives systems toward compact detached pairs across a wide range of starting periods, and also yields long-period pairs. They map the starting parameter space for these systems. The results feed future population studies and a new relation between orbital period and white dwarf mass.
arxiv-2511-06086:
Saurabh Page, Advait Joshi, and S Sonawane extend the Muon optimizer so it can fine-tune every weight of a language model, not just some. Muon has shown strong results in pretraining, but fine-tuning public models with it was unexplored. Normally Muon runs beside AdamW, which handles the leftover parameters.

Their variant, MuonAll, reshapes all parameters into two-dimensional matrices so Muon can take them all. They ran extensive fine-tuning tests on public models up to half a billion parameters. Muon and MuonAll matched AdamW across the major benchmarks used. The authors present both as credible alternative optimizers for fine-tuning. They open-sourced distributed implementations of both, aiming to make adoption easy for other teams.
arxiv-2511-06186:
Lakshmi Priya Bodepudi and colleagues examined why building Android apps so often fails. They studied 200 open-source Android projects written in Java and Kotlin, running builds and sorting the failures they found. Complex dependencies, varied setups, and a fast-changing platform make reliable builds a lasting headache for developers.

Four failure families emerged: environment issues, dependency and Gradle task errors, configuration problems, and syntax or API mismatches. Of 135 projects that failed at first, their repair strategy fixed 102, about three quarters of the cases. They also tested a large language model as a diagnostic helper, which suggested workable fixes in just over half of its attempts.
arxiv-2511-06486:
Andrei Arhire, Matei Chiriac, and Radu Timofte compute twin-width, a measure of how close a graph sits to the simple structure of a co-graph. Coined in 2020, twin-width has quickly driven progress in graph theory and algorithm design. The 2023 PACE Challenge gathered benchmark graphs plus heuristic and exact solvers for the problem.

The team offers two solvers, one exact and one heuristic, built for graphs of arbitrary structure. Their entries performed strongly in the contest, with the exact solver taking the best student result and fourth place overall. Public source code accompanies the work so others can apply the methods and extend the research.
arxiv-2511-06586:
Lewis Bowen and Michael Chapman settle a reversed question about surjunctive groups, but in a randomized generalization where the answer becomes reachable. A group is surjunctive when every injective cellular automaton on it is automatically surjective, and sofic groups are known to qualify. Whether every surjunctive group is sofic stays open for groups themselves, since no non-sofic group is known.

Working with invariant random subgroups of free groups, where non-cosofic examples were recently shown to exist, the authors construct one that is surjunctive yet not cosofic. The proof leans on complexity theory and on Rokhlin entropy methods. Their example even satisfies a stronger maximal-entropy condition than surjunctivity requires.
arxiv-2511-06686:
Heshan Fernando and co-authors rebalance training when a control system learns from several senses at once. Vision, audio, and language channels learn at different speeds, and the fast channels hog the optimization while slow ones stay undertrained, leaving the system fragile when a sensor is disturbed. Heuristic balancing tricks exist but can be costly and ad hoc.

Recasting the problem as multi-objective optimization lets the method explicitly favor the worst-performing modality while keeping the overall fusion goal. Their gradient method, MIMO, carries convergence guarantees. On standard multimodal benchmarks it improved balanced performance over leading rivals and cut subroutine computation time by up to about twentyfold.
arxiv-2511-06886:
Neelesh Kumar Shukla and Sanasam Ranbir Singh study entity role detection: recognizing not just that a text mentions a person or organization, but what role that entity plays in context. Roles act like domain-dependent subtypes, and many applications need to retrieve entities by role rather than by name. The difficulty is that roles and their entities are usually described only indirectly.

The paper frames the problem two ways: as named entity recognition, where roles are mutually exclusive labels for sequence tagging. As retrieval, where a role is a query and entities form the collection. The authors learn representative words and phrases for roles and entities automatically, in sentence and document contexts. Their approach is built to work from small data sets without domain-certain knowledge bases.
arxiv-2511-07086:
Marcel Pehlke and Marc Jansen present a modular pipeline that makes language-model decision support auditable instead of opaque. The system externalizes reasoning into artifacts by running the model through three established systems: Vester's sensitivity model, with its factor sets, signed impact matrices. Feedback loops; normal-form games with payoff matrices and equilibria; and sequential games solved by backward induction. Deterministic analyzers, not the model, compute equilibria and role classifications.

Every module can be swapped, and GPT-5 serves as the default language part. In a real-world logistics case run one hundred times, factor alignment with a human baseline averaged about fifty-five percent overall and higher on the transport core, while role accord reached fifty-seven percent. A language-model judge scored the runs on par with a reconstructed human baseline.
arxiv-2511-07186:
Juno C L Chan and five co-authors speed up the search for gravitational waves distorted by gravity itself. Massive objects between a source and Earth can lens gravitational waves, imprinting frequency-dependent modulations that encode the lens. Standard Bayesian inference on such signals takes weeks, and judging significance needs thousands of simulations, which standard samplers cannot supply. Their method, DINGO-lensing, extends a neural posterior estimation system to lensed events.

Benchmarked against standard samplers, the neural approach cuts parameter estimation from weeks to seconds while matching posterior accuracy and evidence ratios. Trained on LIGO noise at design sensitivity, it recovers time delays with millisecond precision and can also flag signals diffracted by point masses. Simulations of thousands of events map how detectability depends on source features, preparing the method for upcoming observing runs.
arxiv-2511-07786:
Hanwen Huang writes Schrödinger bridges in closed form. Bridges transport one probability distribution into another along the most likely noisy path, extending the maps generative models learn from noise to data. Solutions usually need repeated simulation that is slow and sometimes unstable.

A unified framework states bridge dynamics directly for arbitrary starting and ending densities. Earlier scattered cases fall inside the same formulation. Closed forms remove simulation error and speed computation. Modeling, control, and sampling all use such transports; formulas that can be written down cleanly are valuable wherever repeated solvers strain.
arxiv-2511-07886:
Dechuang Chen, Sibo Wang, and Qintian Guo process graphs too large for memory without stopping at every step. Out-of-core systems page graph data from disk, but strict iteration-by-iteration execution wastes bandwidth through read and work amplification and stalls on synchronization. Disks sit idle while processors wait.

ACGraph runs asynchronously, letting computation proceed as data arrives. Sustained disk use replaces bursty access, and redundant reads shrink. Social networks, recommendation graphs, and knowledge bases keep outgrowing single machines, so efficient external-memory engines decide which analyses stay feasible. The design targets throughput on commodity hardware rather than exotic clusters.
arxiv-2511-08286:
Hoang-Hung Vo gives a unified sorting of Liouville type results for fractional elliptic rules with Henon type weights and gradient growth. The rules pair a nonlocal diffusion rule with a power of place, a curved term in the answer, and a factor depending on its gradient. A single critical balance between the weight exponent and the nonlinearity separates three regimes, and the paper spots that balance precisely.

Above the balance, diffusion dominates and global answers with mild growth must be constant. At the balance, bounded positive answers are still constant. Below it, a unique positive radial answer with explicit algebraic decay exists. New nonlocal estimates, a fractional Bernstein transform, and integral moving plane methods drive the proofs.
arxiv-2511-08386:
Markus Kirchweger, Tomas Peitl, Bernardo Subercaseaux, and Stefan Szeider sharpen bounds on Norin conjecture using SAT solvers, attacking both finite cases and asymptotic estimates. The conjecture concerns two colorings of hypercube edges where opposite edges always differ in color, claiming a fully one colored path must join some pair of opposite vertices. Earlier work verified dimensions up to seven by SAT and bounded color changes along forced paths asymptotically.

A more compact SAT encoding with symmetry breaking and cube and conquer parallelism extends verification to dimension eight. Recasting part of the asymptotic argument as SAT improves the color change bound from the earlier constant to a smaller one. The work shows SAT methods can deliver asymptotic progress, not only finite checks.
arxiv-2511-08686:
Arthur Hutsalyuk and three co-authors attack a hard class of problems: two-dimensional quantum field theories that cannot be solved exactly. Their test case is the quartic Landau-Ginzburg model, a basic theory whose finite-volume energies and particle mass are hard to compute at general coupling strength.

The trick is to borrow exact results from a solvable cousin, the sinh-Gordon theory, whose vacuum expectation values and form factors are known analytically. Those quantities anchor a variational ansatz for the unsolvable model. Combined with Hamiltonian truncation and a summation formula, the method yields controlled estimates of ground-state energy and mass as the coupling varies. Detailed numerics in the weak-coupling regime check the spectrum and even parts of the scattering matrix.
arxiv-2511-08786:
John Hitchcock, Adewale Sekoni, and Hadi Shafei revisit a classic question in computational complexity: how do the classes P and NP behave when algorithms can consult a random permutation as an oracle? Bennett and Gill showed decades ago that a random permutation separates P from the intersection of NP and coNP with probability one.

The new work strengthens that almost-everywhere statement to individually random permutations. Permutation martingales and betting games define what randomness means for a single permutation under resource bounds. The main theorem then separates the classes for every polynomial-time betting-game random permutation. A quantum separation from the nineteen nineties is also strengthened. The authors further show random oracles can be built from random permutations, while the reverse direction stays open.
arxiv-2511-09086:
S. Beuchler and four co-authors optimize a non-Newtonian fluid flow by solving everything at once: space, time, and the optimization loop itself. Their five-dimensional concept discretizes the optimality system with finite elements in three space dimensions, one time dimension, and one dimension for the optimization iteration. It replaces the usual time-stepping wrapped around spatial elements.

The test problem is a simplified Carreau flow, a shear-thinning model used for fluids like blood and polymer melts. Treating the Karush-Kuhn-Tucker system as one large space-time problem lets the solver exploit smoothness in every direction at once. The authors present the framework as a proof of concept for optimal control problems where the physics is time-dependent. The control must be shaped globally there, a setting where step-by-step methods can struggle to see the whole trajectory.
arxiv-2511-09286:
Amir M. Mansourian and two co-authors enrich knowledge distillation. Their student model learns from two kinds of teachers at once. Distillation compresses expert models into a small student, and multi-teacher versions usually rely on visual information alone. Their method adds CLIP, a vision-language model, as a second source of supervision.

The framework fuses logits and features from a conventional teacher with CLIP's, guided by multiple text prompts. The fused teacher makes more confident correct predictions and fewer confidently wrong ones. It also produces more meaningful probabilities for non-target classes, improving consistency across categories. Across benchmarks, their RichKD beats most existing baselines and holds up better under distribution shifts and corrupted inputs.
arxiv-2511-09586:
Yuchen Huang and seven co-authors survey how to scale up the environments where language-model agents learn by doing. Static datasets built from human knowledge are expensive and lack dynamism and realism, they argue. Agents instead need interactive worlds that generate tasks, respond to actions, and grade the results. The authors formalize that cycle as generation, execution, and feedback.

The survey organizes existing environment-scaling methods along those three stages, from an environment-centered viewpoint. It also reviews implementation frameworks, open challenges, and applications. By consolidating fragmented advances in one map, the authors aim to guide future work on agent intelligence. Environments, in their framing, are not scenery but the producers of experiential training data.
arxiv-2511-09786:
Jarett LeVan and Scott D. Baalrud use mean force kinetic theory to compute how a two-component plasma of ions and electrons carries heat and electric current. They evaluate five transport quantities, including electrical and thermal conductivity and shear viscosity, and check them against molecular dynamics simulations. The simulations are made feasible by assuming a repulsive Coulomb force for every interaction.

The theory matched the simulations for all five coefficients up to a Coulomb coupling strength near twenty. That range is more than a hundred times beyond where traditional theories break down. The authors conclude that mean force kinetic theory can extend fluid-style plasma models into the dense regime, where older formulas fail.
arxiv-2511-10086:
Nicklas Ramberg and Daniel Schmitt study how axion-like particles, candidates for dark matter, can fragment when they escape a temperature-dependent trap in the early universe. In trapped misalignment models, a finite-temperature barrier holds the field in place until cooling releases it. As the field is freed, spatial inhomogeneities grow exponentially through an instability, and the axion field breaks apart.

That fragmentation, they show, is a new source of gravitational waves, similar to the zero-temperature version but with a distinct spectral shape. The signal can be up to a hundred times stronger than in the standard fragmentation scenario, and the authors map its peak frequency and amplitude. The catch is that the region producing both strong signals and the right dark matter abundance is limited.
arxiv-2511-10186:
P. I. Pavlova, S. A. Khaibrakhmanov, and A. M. Sobolev analyze magnetic fields around massive young stars using methanol maser observations in three star-forming regions, including NGC 6334I. Masers in the disks of these objects trace conditions close to the star, and the team estimates distances to the masing gas, the magnetospheric radius, and the field strength there. Special attention goes to whether fields connect with maser flares.

The masing regions sit a few hundred astronomical units from their stars. The stellar and disk fields at the magnetosphere boundary are comparable, in the range of several hundred to nearly two thousand gauss. With fields that strong, the authors argue magnetic effects matter locally, and that observed luminosity bursts and maser flares may come from magnetic reconnection near the stars.
arxiv-2511-10486:
Tamara Koletic, Rachel Pillsworth, and Ralph E. Pudritz use a detailed simulation of the galaxy NGC 628 to ask how star clusters inherit their properties. Real JWST images of this galaxy show clusters forming along its spiral arms, inside a web of interstellar filaments that spans many scales.

In the simulation, the team identifies filaments with a finding tool and tracks star clusters that form between 268 and 278 million years, following them for another 60 million years. The mass distribution of newborn clusters matches the filament mass distribution exactly, both following the same power-law slope. That match shows young clusters get their masses from the gravitational fragmentation of their host filaments. As clusters age, they expand, lose mass, and their distribution steepens.
arxiv-2511-10686:
Tiago Machado and seven co-authors ask a methodological question about jailbreak testing: how much do attack success rates move when the attack prompt itself is slightly reworded? They compare open-source models aligned by the three most common methods, supervised fine-tuning, direct preference optimization, and reinforcement learning from human feedback.

Applying systematic prompt perturbations and statistical tests, they find even small modifications significantly change the attack success rate. Models look more or less vulnerable depending on wording. The direction and size of the effect depend on the alignment method. Their conclusion is cautionary: running existing attack benchmarks as-is is not enough to expose the vulnerabilities of a model or its alignment recipe. They argue for statistically grounded evaluation of prompt variation.
arxiv-2511-10786:
Kirill Khoruzhii, Patrick Gelß, and Sebastian Pokutta find faster ways to multiply structured matrices, the kind with symmetry or triangular patterns that appear throughout scientific computing. Their schemes are explicit low-rank bilinear algorithms for small matrices, which serve as building blocks that recursive methods amplify into better long-run scaling.

A flip graph search over tensor decompositions discovers the schemes over small finite fields, which are then lifted to the integers and rationals. The haul covers general, triangular, symmetric, and skew-symmetric inputs, plus products of a matrix with its transpose, improving the constants for thirteen of fifteen structured formats. One new scheme even beats a result from DeepMind's AlphaTensor, multiplying a small skew-symmetric matrix by a general one with one fewer multiplication.
arxiv-2511-11086:
Alexander Kagan, Peter MacDonald, and their colleagues introduce a model for sets of networks that share nodes but split into groups. Brain scans across patients and trade links across goods are classic cases, where layers may share some structure only within a subgroup, such as treated and control groups. Older methods capture what all layers share, plus some per-layer quirks, but miss those group patterns.

Their GroupMultiNeSS model pulls out shared, group-specific, and individual latent structure at once. They prove the model can be identified, fit it with convex methods plus a rank penalty, and argue group structure matters for testing and low-dimensional views of such data.
arxiv-2511-11286:
Ruoqi Wang, Haitao Wang, and their colleagues present D-GAP, an augmentation method that helps vision models stay accurate when test images come from a new domain with unlike backgrounds, styles, or instruments. Generic image tweaks give uneven gains under such shifts, while tailored tweaks need expert study of each data set. Networks also lean too hard on domain-specific frequency parts, which hurts transfer.

D-GAP needs no data set expertise. It builds sensitivity maps in frequency space from task gradients, showing which frequencies the model leans on, and blends amplitudes between source and target images under that guide. A dual-space step also adjusts pixel values, jointly curbing spectral bias and keeping spatial detail.
arxiv-2511-12286:
Khyati Kiyawat and seven co-authors present Sangam, a memory system designed to speed up inference for large language models. As models and context lengths grow, inference becomes limited by memory, especially the key-value cache used during decoding. Processing inside memory can help, but putting compute inside DRAM chips costs area and limits capacity.

Sangam splits logic and memory into separate chiplets, made in different processes and linked on an interposer with a standard interconnect. The logic chips reach the DRAM banks at high bandwidth and carry stronger processors, such as systolic arrays and fast buffers. The design targets the memory-bound matrix work that dominates decoding.
arxiv-2511-12686:
Stefano Bianchini, Aldo Geuna, and Fazliddin Shermatov measure what happens when artificial intelligence meets supercomputing in science. Both tools are spreading fast, but their joint effect on discovery, and who gets access to them, was poorly documented. The authors draw on metadata from more than five million publications across twenty-seven fields, published between 2000 and 2024. Track where AI and high-performance computing were used together, separately, or not at all in the work behind each paper.

They find the combination is strongest at the frontier: work using both is more likely to introduce novel ideas and reach top-cited status than work using either alone. Access, though, is concentrating in a few regions, led by the United States and China, with the European Union still competitive in combined output. The authors argue that future discovery depends on policy that widens access, not only on better algorithms and machines.
arxiv-2511-12786:
Kristina Bukina and Dima L. Shepelyansky model how opinions spread through a scientific collaboration network using the Ising model from physics. Each researcher is a spin pointing up or down, red or blue, standing for one of two opinions. A few elite nodes hold fixed, opposite opinions. Everyone else flips by majority influence of neighbors, only when it passes a conviction threshold.

The simulation shows a phase transition. While the crowd's influence amplitude stays low, the elite opinion dominates the network. Past a critical strength, the crowd's own opinion takes over and the elite can no longer impose its view. The paper reads the network as a model of elite influence on public opinion. It was published in the journal Information, and it gives a crisp, physics-style account of when prestige stops being persuasive.
arxiv-2511-12986:
Abdelouahed Ben Mhamed, Assia Kamal-Idrissi, and Amal El Fallah Seghrouchni teach a solver to choose its own branching decisions by trial and error. Branch-and-bound is the standard exact method for mixed integer linear programs, the workhorse model behind scheduling and logistics optimization. Its speed hinges on branching choices, and learned policies usually imitate an expert's decisions, which overfits the training problems and falters on new structures. TGPPO instead trains the policy with proximal policy optimization, a reinforcement learning method, letting it learn from consequences rather than demonstrations.

A parameterized state representation tracks the evolving search tree.
