The projection gives a one-dimensional alternating process whose peaks and valleys mark sign changes in the projected step. That reduction preserves first-return and first-passage events and leads to a Motzkin polynomial form. Boundary return terms appear as high-order integrals, handled with one truncation factor fit from Monte Carlo data. The factor follows a Cauchy distribution. Resulting first-return probabilities match full three-dimensional Monte Carlo within 2% for anisotropy up to 0.7.
arxiv-2512-14286:
Samuel Cruz Alegria and four coauthors present an additively preconditioned trust region strategy for machine learning in a 2025 paper. Training deep networks means solving large, highly nonconvex problems with rough objective landscapes, where plain methods can crawl.

Their method borrows additive Schwarz ideas from parallel solvers for large linear systems. The parameter space is split into subdomains, local nonlinear subproblems are solved in parallel, and their corrections are added together at each step. A classical trust region frame controls the step size. The authors report fast convergence and, thanks to the trust region design, much less need for hyperparameter tuning. The approach aims to scale network training across many processors.
arxiv-2512-14486:
Hiddo Algera and thirty-seven co-authors report the first systematic search for a key oxygen emission line in galaxies seen as they were within six hundred million years of the Big Bang. Using the ALMA telescope array, they observed four bright, gravitationally lensed galaxies that the Webb telescope had picked out. The line comes from ionized oxygen and traces star formation and gas conditions.

Two galaxies showed the line clearly, glowing about as expected from nearby-universe patterns. The other two, even more distant, showed none, and no dust appeared anywhere. One detection carried a broad extra component, the signature of gas blasting outward faster than star formation alone would suggest.
arxiv-2512-14586:
Muhammad Waseem studies a subtle optical effect that microwaves might switch and steer. When light reflects at an interface, its two polarizations shift sideways by slightly different amounts, the photonic spin Hall effect. Waseem models the effect inside a closed-loop atomic system of the lambda type, where a microwave field joins the optical controls.

At some settings the shift's size stays fixed while the microwave slides its angular position, which suits measuring microwave fields by comparison. At other settings the shift fades exponentially as the microwave grows, or peaks with the phase tuned just right. Phase changes even flip the effect on and off, pointing toward microwave sensors and optical switches.
arxiv-2512-14686:
Stochastic optimization drives most modern machine learning training, and its noise is often heavy-tailed rather than gentle. Recent work has pushed first-order methods from the classic bounded-variance setting toward noise that may not even have a finite mean, with gradient clipping as the key control.

The bias-variance trade-off of those clipped methods is the subject here: clipping tames wild gradients but also biases them, and the balance decides how fast a method can converge. Understanding that trade-off helps practitioners set clipping levels on principle instead of by trial. The analysis extends guarantees toward the messy noise that real training actually produces.
arxiv-2512-14886:
Jing Huang and a coauthor extend a classic family of graphs to the signed setting. Chordal graphs are prized because they admit neat descriptions: by forbidden subgraphs, by orderings of vertices and edges, by separating sets, and by tree like pictures. Signed graphs add a plus or minus label to each edge.

The authors define chordal signed graphs and chordal signed bigraphs, and describe each by the subgraphs they forbid. Signed graphs of this kind turn out to match strict chordal digraphs, a class studied by Hell and Hernández-Cruz, so old results translate over. For signed bigraphs the forbidden list looks similar, but the proofs are far harder and more intricate. The work completes the chordal picture for signed structures.
arxiv-2512-14986:
Carlo Bellingeri and a coauthor define a new integral for random processes that are rougher than Brownian motion. The Wick integral is built for processes with bounded p-variation for p below 2, which need not be Gaussian. The integrand can be a class of entire functions tied to the process itself.

For fractional Brownian motion with Hurst index above one half, the new integral agrees with the divergence operator of Malliavin calculus. It obeys a correction formula against the Young integral and an Itô formula, both with endless correction terms. Those terms come from integrating against the cumulant functions of the process, and they shrink to the familiar identities in the Gaussian case. The proofs grow from diagram formulas for Appell polynomials. The theory covers processes in the second Wiener chaos, such as the Rosenblatt process.
arxiv-2512-15086:
Hongjin Mi and three coauthors strengthen a neural method that learns to solve whole families of partial differential equations. Operator learning predicts full solution fields for new inputs fast, but models like DeepONet can demand huge datasets and wobble in their inner features. The authors borrow an old stabilizer: partition of unity, which blends local pieces into a whole.

Their network, PIP2 Net, adds a simplified physics informed partition penalty that keeps the trunk outputs of DeepONet coordinated and expressive. The penalty grows from a fresh take on an earlier partition based framework. They test it on three nonlinear equations: the viscous Burgers equation, the Allen-Cahn equation, and a diffusion reaction system. In each case PIP2 Net beat DeepONet and its physics informed and partition based variants in accuracy and robustness.
arxiv-2512-15486:
Mohammed Lalou and co authors study completely independent spanning trees in split graphs in a 2025 paper. Such trees share no edges and no internal vertices, so they give disjoint backup routes through a network. Split graphs, whose vertices divide into a clique and an independent set, are the setting here.

The authors link the existence of these trees to coloring problems on a related hypergraph, which yields bounds on how many such trees a split graph can hold. They prove that deciding whether two such trees exist is NP complete. The paper ends with a conjecture about the bipanchromatic number of the linked hypergraph.
arxiv-2512-15586:
Benjamin Minixhofer and co authors introduce Bolmo, a family of byte level language models, in a 2025 paper. Most language models read text as word fragments, which hides fine detail that matters in code or biological sequences. Models that read raw bytes avoid that loss but have lagged in performance until now.

Bolmo starts from existing subword models and converts them in two stages, with little extra training. The resulting fully open models beat prior byte level systems and shine on character level reasoning tasks, while staying competitive on standard benchmarks. Inference speeds are practical, and the low conversion cost lets others reuse the ecosystem around the source models.
arxiv-2512-16086:
Saeed Mahloujifar and three co-authors audit a common privacy trick in their arXiv paper from 2025. Photos shared for research often show faces and license plates, which must be hidden before release. The industry standard is Gaussian blur, but the team shows practical blur settings can be reversed enough to expose private details.

They compare four ways to hide image content: blur, pixelization, pixelization plus noise, and cropping. Privacy was tested with reversal and discrimination attacks, while usefulness was tested by training vision models on the cleaned data. Blur proved the least private of the four. Pixelization, with or without added noise, gave both privacy and utility at the right grain size. The authors released their methods and suggested settings in a software package called Privacy Blur.
arxiv-2512-16286:
Cassandre Lebot reviews a limit in fluid theory in their arXiv paper, posted in 2025. When flow speeds are far below the speed of sound, the Mach number is tiny, and compressible flow equations should simplify to nearly incompressible ones. Taking that low-Mach limit cleanly is a classic mathematical problem.

Lebot first surveys what is known for single-phase flows governed by the compressible Navier-Stokes or Euler equations. The focus then shifts to two-phase flows, mixtures like gas bubbles in liquid. Several model families are compared: pressure given by an algebraic rule or by its own equation, one shared velocity or two separate ones, and versions with or without entropy. The paper is a formal map of which limits have been justified and how the choices interact.
arxiv-2512-16586:
Shaohua Wu and three co-authors upgrade text-to-image generation in a 2025 paper on arXiv. Diffusion models build images inside a U-shaped network whose convolutional blocks see only local neighborhoods, which can blind them to long-range meaning in a scene. The team swaps those blocks for Swin transformer blocks in both encoder and decoder.

Text conditioning gets equal care, through a well-chosen text encoder and a careful way of feeding text embeddings into the network. An adapted time step search across diffusion stages improved inference performance by a further 10 percent. The model reached an FID score of 1.37 on the ImageNet generation benchmark, state of the art at the time, with no auxiliary models at any denoising stage. In side-by-side tests, people struggled to tell its images from human-painted ones.
arxiv-2512-16686:
Xinqun Mei, Guofang Wang, and Liangjun Weng study a prescribed curvature problem for convex capillary surfaces, which meet a flat wall at a set angle. They ask which such surfaces have a given Lp curvature, a blended measure of how the surface bends.

Using the support function, the task becomes a Hessian quotient equation on a spherical cap with a Robin edge rule. For p of one or more, they prove solutions exist under fit conditions on the data, with uniqueness in matching ranges. At the borderline exponent an eigenvalue problem appears, unique up to scaling. The results also cover capillary Christoffel-Minkowski and quotient curvature tasks in one frame.
arxiv-2512-17086:
Cole Wyeth and Marcus Hutter extend the AIXI agent, a flagship design in universal artificial intelligence, to a wider class of utility functions. A snag appears with hypotheses that predict only a finite history prefix, often read as a chance of death, the semimeasure loss.

The pair argue the same math reads as naturally as total ignorance, in the sense of imprecise probability. That view leads them to compute expected utilities with Choquet integrals and to chart the computability level of the result. The standard recursive value function returns as a special case. Yet their broadest utilities under the death reading cannot be written as such Choquet integrals, a split worth noting.
arxiv-2512-17486:
Luka Matijević and a large team weigh two forces tugging at the spiral galaxy NGC 2276. As the galaxy plows through thin group gas, ram pressure can strip and squeeze its own gas, like wind on a moving car. At the same time, gravity from neighbors can pull it out of shape by tides. Which force sculpts this galaxy's lopsided look was unsettled.

The team presents the first Hubble images of the galaxy and pairs them with hydrogen glow maps and infrared views. Young stars, up to about 100 million years old, crowd the leading edge and smear out behind it, the signature of gas being compressed by a headwind. Spiral arms also unwind with radius in a matching way. Ram pressure leads, though tides may still play a part.
arxiv-2512-17586:
Mahesh Keswani and Raunak Bhattacharyya test whether a safety method built for controlled settings survives contact with real driving data. The method, called SRPL, gives a learning agent a model that predicts future safety violations, so the agent can weigh reward against risk before it acts.

On the Waymo Open Motion Dataset and on NuPlan, SRPL improved the balance between reward and safety, with large gains in success rate and lower costs, both statistically significant. The benefit depends on the optimizer beneath it and on the data mix, and the method also held up better when sensor input grew noisy. Agents trained with it transferred to a fresh dataset without retraining better than agents without it, a sign the approach may carry toward real roads.
arxiv-2512-17686:
David Luce and three co-authors film the inside of a draining grain silo and find a wave running the show. As grains pour out, the bulk does not slide smoothly: a pulse of slowing starts near the outlet, beside the stagnant dead zone, and climbs toward the top of the pile. Acceleration maps of the flow make the pulse train plain to see.

Two traits surprised the team. The pulses come slower when the grains are stickier, a cohesion effect no simple model predicted. Yet widening or narrowing the outlet changed the pulse rate not at all. Engineers who design hoppers for grain, sand, and powders care, because such waves set the rhythm of discharge and the risk of jamming.
arxiv-2512-17886:
Laksha Pradip Das and four coauthors revisit particles that rain down when cosmic rays smash into the upper air. The IceCube detector, buried in Antarctic ice, sees more high energy muons than older models predict. Part of the excess may come from charm particles born inside the incoming cosmic ray itself.

Adding that charm source raises the predicted muon flow, but it also raises the flow of related neutrinos above a limit IceCube has set. The team tests several charm models and tweaks the share from plain mesons to ease the clash. The mismatch tells builders of air shower models where their physics still needs work.
arxiv-2512-18086:
J. López-Santiago leads a six author team reporting a steady beat in the light of GJ 3512, a small red dwarf star. The TESS space telescope caught a wobble with a period of 70 to 100 minutes. The signal lasted for weeks in one run and showed up again across three years of data, with no fade between big flares.

That long life rules out the usual flare echoes, which die in minutes or hours, and the star is too old for the known pulsing class. The team favors a corona based cause, such as repeated magnetic snapping in large active regions. No late type star has shown a sustained beat like this before.
arxiv-2512-18486:
Rajavardhan Talashila proves a uniqueness theorem for time-harmonic fields, the steady oscillating fields of electromagnetism. His paper, posted to arXiv in December 2025, asks what boundary data pin down the field inside a spherical volume. The volume holds only perfect conductors and uniform lossless materials. The driving currents are given.

He shows the solution is fixed uniquely by two sets of data. The first is the radial parts of both fields, E and B, on the outer spherical surface. The second is the tangential part of either field on inner surfaces. The proof leans on the uniqueness of the multipole expansion outside the sphere. The result also frames the classic lossless theorem as a limiting case, as dissipation in lossy materials shrinks to zero.
arxiv-2512-18886:
Rhea Fernandez and six co-authors organize the young field of quantum education for school students. Quantum ideas are entering classrooms, but teachers face a scatter of approaches with no map. Drawing on a literature review and expert interviews, their framework, posted to arXiv in December 2025 and presented at a symposium on teaching Einsteinian physics, sorts the methods into seven categories.

The seven are Defamiliarization, Quantum Picturalism, the Spin-First and Einstein-First approaches, the Many Paths approach, the Historical Development approach, and Game-based Quantum Learning. For each, the authors summarize how it works and weigh strengths and weaknesses, stressing which concepts stay mathematically accessible to primary and secondary students. The result is a practical menu: an educator can pick a route that fits their class instead of improvising one.
arxiv-2512-19086:
Byung Gyu Chae models networks that feed their own output back in as input, a loop found in biological brains. His network is kept in balance by homeostasis, an internal control that resists drift. The goal is a clean theory of when such a system settles, reacts, or keeps reflecting on its own state.

The population dynamics collapse exactly to a one-dimensional radial flow, which reveals a fixed threshold for sustained reflective activity. A renormalization-group analysis then tracks how gain, stiffness, and reentry strength flow. All paths are drawn to a critical surface where leak and reentry balance. Three regimes appear, with a universal onset pattern.
arxiv-2512-19286:
Sameera M., Serena Nicolazzo, Antonino Nocera, and Vinod P. defend federated learning against poisoned updates. In federated learning, many clients train a shared model without sharing raw data. A malicious client can slip in crafted updates that drag the model down or bend it toward chosen errors.

Their shield, GShield, first learns what honest gradients look like, using clustering and Gaussian models in an opening round. Later updates are kept only if they fit that trusted pattern, which sidelines attackers and junk updates alike. The design targets the hard case where client data differ widely. A broad test campaign backs the defense, the authors report.
arxiv-2512-19586:
Diego Marques and Pavel Trojovsky mix geometric progressions with the Zeckendorf writing system, where every integer is a sum of non-consecutive Fibonacci numbers. The work is prompted by an Erdős conjecture about ternary expansions and by recent results on progressions meeting Cantor-like sets in ordinary bases. Forbidden digit patterns are the heart of the question.

Fix any finite set of forbidden binary patterns and any window onto the last digits. The authors prove the exponents for which a progression term's Zeckendorf expansion avoids those patterns in the window form a set that is either finite or eventually periodic. Wild avoidance, in other words, cannot continue in a chaotic way.
arxiv-2512-19686:
Zixuan Ye and seven co-authors fix a blind spot in AI image tools that think before they draw. Chain-of-thought prompting made such tools follow text prompts better. But the thinking mostly checks words against words. When a guide image is in play, the results often lose key traits. A face changes, an object shifts, or the style drifts.

Their method adds two habits. First, the model writes a checklist of visual traits that must stay fixed. Then it checks its own output against the list and refines it, round by round. Training teaches the routine, and a reward based on the visual check sharpens it. Tests show stronger visual consistency than plain models. They also beat models that reason with text alone.
arxiv-2512-19886:
Fawad Kirmani and six co-authors teach a neural network to spot a rare sight. The sight is a supernova split into two images by gravitational lensing. Such events fade fast. They are most often found because lensing makes them look too bright. This proof of concept reads the bent shape of the doubled image instead. It works from a single difference image. The split it hunts is under six tenths of an arcsecond.

Real cases are too rare to train on. So Hubble archive images fed made-up training and test sets. Priors from astrophysics set the splits, brightness ratios, and colors. Fake traps, like artifacts and plain supernovae, were added too. The network recalled 99 percent of the fake lensed events. It also split plain and empty images with care. The method aims at wide-field space surveys like the Roman Space Telescope.
arxiv-2512-20586:
Humza Nusrat and a clinical team test whether reasoning makes an AI planner safer for brain radiosurgery. Stereotactic radiosurgery sculpts dose tightly around metastases while sparing structures like the cochlea. Black-box automation has stalled clinically because planners cannot audit it. Their agent, SAGE, plans with a language model in the loop.

Forty-one patients with brain metastases, each treated with a single eighteen-gray fraction, were replanned by reasoning and non-reasoning variants. The reasoning planner matched human dosimetry on coverage, maximum dose, and conformity, while lowering cochlear dose below human benchmarks. Its traces show hundreds of prospective constraint checks and trade-off deliberations, behaviours absent in the standard model. Auditable reasoning, the authors argue, is the road to clinical trust.
arxiv-2512-20686:
Michael A Jones, Brittany Ohlinger, and Jennifer Wilson watch legislatures fill seat by seat. Divisor methods apportion seats by rounding scaled vote shares; because they satisfy house monotonicity, seats can be handed out sequentially as parties earn them. The authors focus on stationary divisor methods, defined by one rounding cutpoint.

With integer votes, the resulting apportionment sequences are periodic. For two parties, the authors characterize exactly which sequences can occur and tie their lexicographic ordering to the cutpoint's value. Pairwise sequences then extend systematically to any number of parties, and the count of distinct sequences is determined. A reframing of size bias emerges: large parties do not simply get more seats, they get their seats earlier. The Adams and D'Hondt extremes turn out to be intimately related.
arxiv-2512-20786:
F. Yusef-Zadeh and seven co-authors watched the black hole at our galaxy's center flare in three kinds of light at once. On 5 April 2024, the JWST, NuSTAR, and VLA telescopes monitored Sagittarius A* together. Its brightness changes reveal processes in the disk of gas swirling under strong gravity.

A strong X-ray flare arrived alongside a bright near-infrared flare, with radio brightening about an hour later. The team argue the X-rays came from infrared light scattered to higher energies. They propose an ejection much like a solar coronal mass ejection, with a magnetic rope and reconnecting sheet. One picture then explains the flaring across all three bands.
arxiv-2512-21186:
Tieguang Zi and Chang-Qing Ye forecast whether the future LISA observatory could detect a scalar charge on a small body spiraling into a massive black hole. A scalar charge is an extra field charge that some extensions of gravity predict. Real inspirals are messy: the small body plows through an accretion disk and a dark matter halo, not empty space. Both the environment and any scalar charge distort its gravitational waveform. The authors fold the charge into the energy fluxes and orbital evolution and compute its signal.

Under suitable parameters, the scalar-charge imprint stays distinguishable from the vacuum prediction amid the environmental effects. LISA could then pin the charge down with a relative error near ten percent. That forecast matters because a measured nonzero charge would falsify general relativity, while a tight null bound would discipline its rivals; the study shows astrophysics need not blind the test.
arxiv-2512-22286:
Ernest Fokoué develops a general theory of how ensemble weights should be chosen, arguing the usual story is incomplete. Textbooks credit groups with reducing variance, but that cannot explain why groups of already-stable methods, like smoothing splines or Gaussian process regression, still help. Fokoué formalizes groups as linear operators on a hypothesis space and puts geometric and spectral constraints on the weight sequences themselves.

A refined bias-variance decomposition shows structured, non-uniform weights can beat uniform averaging by reshaping approximation geometry and redistributing spectral complexity, even when variance barely moves. Optimal weights emerge as solutions of constrained quadratic programs. Plain averaging, stacking, and the author's Fibonacci ensembles all appear as special cases of the unified theory.
arxiv-2512-22686:
Kumar Sai Bondada, Daniel J. Jakubisin, and R. Michael Buehrer design a multistatic radar that syncs itself wirelessly instead of relying on GPS. Separate senders and receivers must share precise time and frequency references to locate targets jointly. Their protocol exchanges a two-tone waveform for frequency synchronization and a two-way exchange for time sync, keeping the network self-contained.

A Bayesian Cramér-Rao lower bound system gauges how leftover sync offsets degrade delay and Doppler estimates, and with them target position and velocity accuracy. Simulations from the analytical formulas show how much damage residual offsets do. With the sync-link parameters tuned, the multistatic layout can beat a single-unit radar and approach the ideal perfectly synced case. The required link parameters look feasible in practice.
arxiv-2512-22986:
Siyi Wang, Zifan Wang, and Karl Johansson study learning algorithms that must stay risk-averse while the world, and the right level of caution, keeps changing. Their setting is online optimization in a shifting environment, where risk is measured by Conditional Value-at-Risk, a statistic that focuses on the worst outcomes rather than the average. Two kinds of drift matter: the objective functions change, and the risk level itself moves.

The authors measure the first drift with a function variation metric and introduce a new metric for risk-level variation. They design algorithms for two information settings, one where gradients are observable and one where only function values are sampled, both under a limited sampling budget. Dynamic regret bounds are proved in terms of the two variation measures and the sample count, showing the methods adapt to non-stationary, risk-sensitive problems. Numerical experiments confirm the theory's predictions.
arxiv-2512-23086:
Teng Liu and a large team introduce eigen microstate entropy, a complexity measure meant to flag phase transitions before they fully arrive. The measure is built from the probabilities of statistically independent eigen microstates extracted from data. Its scaling behavior is first established in equilibrium systems and tested on classic critical models, the mean spherical, Ising, and Potts models, where transitions are well understood.

The payoff comes in nonequilibrium settings. Across very different systems, the entropy rose significantly ahead of the main transition, acting as a precursor rather than a symptom. It climbed before biomolecular condensates formed by liquid-liquid phase separation inside living cells. It also rose months ahead of El Niño events in climate data. The authors position the measure as a general framework for detecting and interpreting phase transitions in complex systems that never reach equilibrium, where traditional order parameters are hard to define.
arxiv-2512-23386:
Sunghun Ko and Jinsuk Park study bidding in Arbitrum's Express Lane Auction, a mechanism that sells speed on a blockchain network. The winner of each ahead-of-time, second-price auction gets a latency advantage lasting one minute, an edge for time-sensitive transactions. Building on a single-round model with risk-averse bidders, the authors hypothesize that priority access is worth less than a risk-neutral calculation suggests. Short-horizon volatility is hard to forecast, and bidders dislike that uncertainty.

They test the hypothesis by matching Express Lane bid records against high-frequency prices of Ether, the network's currency. The evidence lines up with the model: bids behave as if the value of priority is discounted for volatility risk. The study connects auction theory to a blockchain market. It shows how a one-minute advantage gets priced when the asset can jump before the advantage is used.
arxiv-2512-23586:
Marcin Markiewicz, Łukasz Pawela, and Zbigniew Puchała study twirling, the averaging of a quantum channel over a symmetry group until only its symmetry-respecting part remains. Twirling is a standard simplification tool, but doing it for channels rather than states is technically awkward. The arXiv record's title replaces the catalog's different working title, and the record governs here.

Working through the Choi representation, which turns a channel into a state, they give a constructive description of the averaging map for arbitrary input and output symmetries. A partial-transpose trick converts the hard mixed twirl into an ordinary Schur-Weyl twirl, yielding explicit formulas built from permutations. They also extend twirling beyond compact groups to reductive non-unitary ones, and give two finite constructions that realize channel averaging with designs.
arxiv-2512-23686:
Deepak Babu Piskala releases ProfASR-Bench, a benchmark for speech recognition in professional settings where mistakes carry real costs. In finance, medicine, law, and technology, speech is dense with specialized terms and formal registers, and an error on a critical name or number is far worse than an average word error. Existing benchmarks underplay those pressures. The arXiv record's title and framing govern over the catalog entry.

Each test item pairs a natural-language context prompt, a domain cue or speaker profile, with an entity-rich utterance to transcribe. Scoring covers ordinary word error plus entity-aware measures, reported by accent and gender slices. Testing Whisper and Qwen-Omni families under several context conditions, Piskala finds a context-utilization gap: even perfect oracle context barely improves recognition, meaning today's promptable systems underuse side information they are given.
arxiv-2512-23786:
Ankan Aich and five co-authors improve depth estimation for surgical cameras, a capability autonomous robotic surgery depends on. A single camera must infer three-dimensional shape, but models trained outside the body fail inside it: real operations bring mirror-like reflections off wet tissue and constant deformation. Training on noisy labels from real surgery causes boundaries to collapse. The arXiv record's title governs over the catalog's shorter one.

The team instead adapts the strong synthetic priors of a foundation depth model, Depth Anything V2, using a low-rank adaptation scheme with dynamic vectors. On the public SCARED benchmark they report a new state of the art, with squared relative error cut by over seventeen percent in the most reflective conditions. They also introduce ROCAL-T 90, the first validation set from real operations, with ninety endoscopic sequences and sub-millimeter ground-truth trajectories from CT alignment.
arxiv-2512-23886:
Sylwia Antoniuk, Andrzej Dudek, and Andrzej Ruciński ask how much randomness completes a dense graph's structure. Their graphs satisfy the Pósa-Seymour condition, a minimum-degree requirement slightly above a threshold fraction of the vertices. The target is a power of a Hamiltonian cycle: a cycle through all vertices. It is strengthened so each vertex also connects to its near neighbors along the cycle, up to a chosen power m.

Adding random edges one by one eventually forces such a power to appear, and the paper finds how many are needed. Two threshold types govern the answer, with the so-called over-threshold dominating once m grows. For each fixed degree parameter and all large enough m, the authors prove tight bounds, in the limit, on these over-thresholds, show the bounds coincide for infinitely many m. They also determine exact thresholds for several small parameter pairs.
arxiv-2512-24186:
Felix Zahner and five colleagues report a first sighting. Topological spin textures appear inside an intrinsic antiferromagnet. The setting is a single atomic layer. Skyrmions are whirl-like spin patterns prized for spintronics. Antiferromagnetic versions should move better in devices. Until now they were seen only in synthetic stacks.

The team used spin-polarized scanning tunneling microscopy. Manganese layers sat on a tantalum surface. The monolayer showed a spiraling antiferromagnetic pattern. The double layer showed a straight, collinear state instead. Half-skyrmions formed at the boundary between the two. Calculations and simulations backed the reading. The layout of the structure thus switches the film's state. Plain states and topological ones are both reachable. That control matters for future devices.
arxiv-2512-24386:
Gur-Eyal Sela and four colleagues cut the cost of live video analytics. Camera fleets run vision models around the clock. Inference with modern models is expensive. Choosing model size dynamically per segment could cut cost tenfold. The catch is judging accuracy without ground truth at runtime. Existing systems sample a few models, read their confidence statistics, then pick a size.

Prior systems generalize poorly to new workloads. Mobile videos and lower accuracy targets expose the failure. Sampling often costs more than it saves. Per-segment accuracy prediction is also unreliable. RedunCut answers with a measurement-driven planner. It weighs the cost and benefit of sampling before doing it. A light, data-driven model improves accuracy prediction. Across vehicle, drone, and surveillance videos, compute fell by wide margins at fixed accuracy. Robustness held under scarce history and drifting content.
arxiv-2512-24586:
Xian-Peng Zhang, Xiangrong Wang, and Yugui Yao build a small-scale theory of magnetoresistance, how the resistance of a magnetic material changes in a magnetic field. They treat free electrons and local magnetic moments as one open quantum system. Their method solves the governing formula with a projection method that tracks loss of spin order over time.

Both ferromagnetic and antiferromagnetic cases emerge from heat and field dependent spin decoherence, meaning the fading and dephasing of spins. Resistance linked to decoherence follows the magnetic order of the material. Readers get guidance for learning about and designing magnetic materials where this effect matters.
arxiv-2512-24886:
Tyler Hanks, Cristian Nino, and Joana Bou Barcelo track multiple unknown targets with a varied team of agents using cellular sheaves. Sheaves generalize graph theory and allow other state spaces on other nodes. Nonlinear motion and mismatched dimensions defeat standard graph Laplacian methods. Their work extends sheaf teamwork methods from cooperative consensus to non-cooperative target tracking.

Tracking is cast as a harmonic extension problem over the sheaf, letting varied agents share information in matching forms. Robotics and estimation readers get mathematics built for mixed teams. Sheaves let a camera, a drone, and a ground sensor cooperate without forcing a common state format.
arxiv-2601-00086:
Xiang Gao, Yuguang Yao, Qi Zhang, Kaiwen Dong, Avinash Baidya, Ruocheng Guo, Hilaf Hasson, and Kamalika Das address a practical problem. Language models often use tools badly in specialized settings. The tools may be odd, poorly documented, or built for private work. Their 2026 paper presents RIMRULE, a method that teaches models through short rules. It does not change the model's weights. The rules are drawn from records of past failures.

Each rule is kept in both plain words and a structured form. It is then pulled into the prompt when needed. A measure that favors short, general rules guides which ones survive. Tests on tool-use benchmarks show better accuracy on both known and new tools. Rules learned from one model can also help others.
arxiv-2601-00186:
Moirangthem Tiken Singh and coauthor Adnan Arif protect meaning, not just bits, when bandwidth is tight. Their 2026 system sends quantized semantic embeddings over a noisy channel. Plain uniform protection treats every dimension alike. Meaning, though, is not spread evenly. Some dimensions carry entities that must survive. Their framework learns where extra care pays off.

A reinforcement learning agent assigns repetition coding per dimension. A composite score guides it during training. That score balances whole embedding closeness with entity level survival. Tests beat uniform protection by clear margins. Text quality and entity keeping both rise at low signal strength. Classic codes cannot match this fine grained fit. Their structure ignores semantic granularity by design. The authors aim at edge and sensor networks. There, bandwidth is scarce but meaning still matters.
arxiv-2601-00586:
Klaus Heinemann and a ten-author team give a detailed account of the kinetic approach to spin polarization in electron storage rings. Synchrotron radiation gradually polarizes the spins of circulating electrons and positrons, but it also depolarizes them, and predicting the balance matters for precision experiments. The kinetic approach, introduced by Derbenev and Kondratenko in nineteen seventy-four, describes this with distribution functions.

Unlike the older non-kinetic method, the kinetic version does not center on the invariant spin field, so it applies more generally. It covers the classic Sokolov-Ternov effect, its correction, and the kinetic polarization effect, and it can estimate how reliable the older formulas are. The account extends earlier work by the team and applies from a few giga-electronvolts upward.
arxiv-2601-00686:
Thomas Orrière and David Z Pai report, in 2026, how a laser pulse can boost plasma waves on a surface. The waves are called surface ionization waves. They run along a barrier in air. When part of the barrier is a semiconductor, the waves run in a smooth, even sheet. The team used the light sense of silicon, the semiconductor in their barrier.

They fired a short laser pulse at the surface before each discharge. If the pulse came more than three millionths of a second early, it had no effect. That span matches the time free charges take to drift away from a key layer. When the pulse came within that span, the wave ran farther and glowed more. The discharge also gained up to about seven in each hundred in energy. The tight timing shows the boost comes from freed charges, not from charge wiped off the surface.
arxiv-2601-00786:
Teng Ee Yap and Konstantin Batygin offer a new explanation for why Jupiter's moon Callisto never joined the orbital resonance of its siblings. Io, Europa, and Ganymede orbit in a neat four-two-one rhythm called the Laplace resonance, usually explained by their slow migration through the gas disk around young Jupiter. Callisto, the outermost, sits outside the chain, and the standard story blames its late or slow formation.

Yap and Batygin instead blame structure in the disk itself. Their N-body simulations, which include the moons' interaction with the disk, show a pressure bump can act as a migration trap, parking Callisto away from the others. That mechanism relaxes the awkward timing constraints on when Callisto must have formed.
arxiv-2601-00886:
Elohan Veillon and three co-authors argue, in 2026, that new materials from AI must be judged by chemistry, not just by scores. AI models can dream up vast numbers of candidate materials. The gold check is a physics method called DFT, which is slow and needs expert hands. The authors build a friendlier frame that bakes DFT checks into the score.

Their frame pairs stability checks from DFT with the usual stats that AI work reports. They test it with both small tweaks to known materials and fresh AI-made ones. The usual stats, they show, can rate unfit materials as if they were sound. That gap is the heart of the paper's warning. With the chemistry checks in place, weak candidates are caught early. The authors urge the field to adopt such checks as standard. Their frame is meant for both experts and newcomers to use.
arxiv-2601-00986:
Chunmei Wang and Shangyou Zhang present, in 2026, a simple finite element method for flow-and-spread equations. Such equations mix three effects: drift with a flow, spread, and local growth or decay. The method is of weak Galerkin type, which loosens how the trial shapes must join. That looseness lets it run on meshes of many-sided cells, even ones that bulge inward.

The authors prove error bounds in a norm fit to the problem. Their bounds say the method's error shrinks at the rate theory hopes for. Computer tests then back the bounds. The runs also show the method is cheap for the accuracy it gives. Mesh freedom matters in real domains, which are rarely neat grids. A method that takes cells as they come saves hours of mesh repair. The paper adds a flexible tool for engineers who model spread in odd-shaped regions.
arxiv-2601-01186:
Alexandre Baigol and six colleagues build artificial synapses whose strength can be tuned with tiny pulses of energy. Their devices store the strength in the conductance of a ferroelectric film, a material whose inner domains shift under a pulse. Shorter pulses cost less energy, but a device cannot respond faster than its own self-loading time allows.

By shrinking the device area below one hundred square micrometers, the team made that response fast enough for twenty-nanosecond pulses, costing at most three picojoules each. They then measured the update rule directly, across pulse strengths and starting states. The final weight turned out to depend on the pulse strength alone, not on where it started, which makes control simple. The devices are built with a process that fits standard chip production. Such cheap, predictable updates are a step toward hardware that learns with brain-like efficiency.
arxiv-2601-01286:
Fatiha Chouaou and Abbes Benaissa study a degenerate Schrödinger equation fitted with fractional damping at the boundary. The degeneracy means the equation's main coefficient can vanish at a point, which complicates both the math and any physical reading. Working on a unit interval under mixed boundary conditions, they first prove the problem is well-posed, so solutions exist, are unique, and depend sensibly on the starting data.

They then ask how fast solutions settle. Using the multiplier method, a classic energy-based technique, they establish both exponential and polynomial decay rates, depending on the setting. Results of this kind matter for quantum systems and control problems where damping acts only at the edge. Knowing the exact rate tells engineers and theorists whether the damping is strong enough for the job. The paper adds a careful case to the stability theory of damped wave and Schrödinger equations.
arxiv-2601-01386:
Twelve authors led by Xiaobao Wei build the first system for reconstructing parking lots in three dimensions from a car's surround cameras, aimed at autonomous parking. Parking is cramped and often underground, where GPS fails. Prior work reads painted slots in flat images, but full spatial geometry has gone largely unstudied.

The team curates ParkRecon3D, a benchmark with data from four fisheye cameras, calibrated positions, and dense slot labels. Their method, ParkGaussian, rebuilds the scene with three-dimensional Gaussian splatting, a fast modern rendering technique. A slot-aware strategy uses existing slot detectors to sharpen the reconstruction exactly where parking decisions happen. On the benchmark, the method reached top reconstruction quality and kept downstream slot detection more consistent than rivals. Code and data will be released. The work links pretty rendering to a concrete driving task, rather than treating reconstruction as an end in itself.
arxiv-2601-01586:
Li and 3 co-authors study flat stretches, called plateaus, in the fading glow after gamma-ray bursts. These bursts are the brightest explosions known, and a plateau may mean fresh energy keeps feeding the glow. The team gathered 124 bursts with known distances and glow records in both X-ray and visible light.

Bursts split into four groups by where plateaus appear. For bursts with plateaus in both bands, many match the checks expected if extra energy is injected, which supports that reading. Bursts with a plateau in only one band mostly fail the same checks in the other band. The team also weighs a spinning magnetized star as the energy source.
arxiv-2601-01786:
Language models trained on personal data may memorize names, addresses, and other identifying details that privacy law, including Europe's GDPR, can require deleted. Intae Jeon, Yujeong Kwon, and Hyungjoon Koo argue that standard machine unlearning forgets uniformly, ignoring that some personal attributes are far riskier than others.

Their approach, UnPII, ranks personal data with a risk index. The index combines how easy a fact is to identify, how sensitive it is, and how well it links to other facts. It also weighs how permanent and exposed the fact is. The riskiest items are forgotten first. It plugs into known unlearning methods without changing how they work. Tests used a synthetic dataset of seventeen hundred personal records. Results showed gains in unlearning accuracy. Retained utility and general use also improved. The extra fine-tuning cost was modest. The work offers a risk-aware template for compliance tasks.
arxiv-2601-02486:
Paola Pinilla models how dust is kept, or lost, inside the discs where planets form. Dust grains drift inward fast, so a disc should lose its solid material in about a million years unless something traps it. Pressure bumps in the gas can act as traps. The study varies key dust evolution settings in models with and without such bumps, then turns the results into simulated telescope images at millimeter wavelengths.

Without bumps, large dust masses survive for millions of years only when grains fragment at low speeds. And viscosity takes one specific moderate value, and the images show bright inner emission with shallow outer glow. At higher fragmentation speeds most dust is lost to drift unless traps are present, in which case retained mass rises by orders of magnitude and clear structures appear in the images. Viscosity strongly shapes the outcome as well.
arxiv-2601-02586:
Daeun Hwang and Hyeonbin Hwang study how people actually judge music plagiarism, which in real disputes rests on audience perception rather than on any single similarity algorithm.

Their study isolates the musical features listeners use, focusing on melody, rhythm, and chord progression. Those are the three features most similarity systems also use. The study also asks how much variation in each feature listeners tolerate before calling two works alike. From those findings they propose a framework where a large language model acts as judge. The judge applies a systematic step by step procedure. Its modules extract the high level attributes listeners rely on.
arxiv-2601-02886:
Leonardo Giani and four co-authors introduce a new way to measure the scale on which the universe becomes smooth and uniform. Their velocity coherence scale marks the radius where the average motion of galaxies along the line joining them switches from flowing together to flowing apart. It is a velocity-based cousin of the count-based methods long used to find the homogeneity scale.

The authors show the new scale shares the same large-scale behavior as the standard correlation dimension, so both can locate the turn toward uniformity. In the standard cosmology it also ties closely to the matter and radiation equality scale and stays fixed in comoving coordinates, making it a potential standard ruler. A proof of concept uses galaxy velocity data from the Sloan survey.
arxiv-2601-03186:
Debajyoti Biswas studies whether the SND@LHC detector, a scattering and neutrino experiment in the far-forward region of the Large Hadron Collider, could spot a family of hypothetical dark particles. These sub-GeV dipolar dark states interact with ordinary matter only through photon-mediated dipole couplings, a minimal portal for feebly interacting particles. Their large momenta in the forward region let them scatter off electrons and nuclei inside the detector's target.

Production of the dark states through meson decays is limited by measured invisible decay widths, while the Drell-Yan process offers a production route in the GeV range. Biswas presents sensitivity plots for magnetic and electric dipole interactions and compares them with limits from direct detection, beam dump, fixed-target, and collider experiments. The paper also checks the effective theory's validity under conservative coupling bounds.
arxiv-2601-03286:
The NAVER Cloud HyperCLOVA X Team presents HyperCLOVA X 32B Think, an open vision-language model built with particular care for Korean language and culture. The model is pre-trained with a strong focus on reasoning, then post-trained to add multimodal understanding, stronger reasoning, agentic behavior, and alignment with human preferences. It is released as open source.

Evaluations against comparably sized models show strong performance on Korean text-to-text and vision-to-text benchmarks, as well as on agent-oriented tasks. The report positions the model as a foundation for Korean-language AI that can reason, see, and act. By open-sourcing it, the team aims to support wider adoption and further research across both academic and industrial communities.
arxiv-2601-03386:
Zongyang Lv and five co-authors model and control a drone carrying a load on a cable, when the cable is not attached at the drone's center of mass. Slung-load transport is a classic system, but real missions and mechanical constraints often force the suspension point off-center. That offset couples the load's swing to the drone's motion in a complicated nonlinear way, and earlier models, built around the center of mass, handle it awkwardly.

The authors instead model the system around the suspension point itself. Their cascade controller uses the middle loop to regulate the load's swing angle through the suspension point's acceleration, sidestepping the coupling, while an inner loop tracks attitude without simplifying the coupling away. They prove local exponential stability with a Lyapunov argument, and validate the design in simulations and real experiments.
arxiv-2601-03686:
Lina Zhu and three co-authors design a coordination system for robot teams searching an area for targets, such as people needing rescue. The core tension is balance: robots must explore unknown ground while also covering known points of interest. Earlier methods used uniform graph representations that could not model those two jobs distinctly, so the balance suffered.

Their network, DA-HGNN, builds a mixed graph with robot nodes, frontier nodes marking the edge of the known, and interesting nodes for targets, plus their history. Two attention stages first capture spatial and temporal relations, then weigh each robot against each goal type separately. Deep reinforcement learning trains the system. Decoupling exploration from target coverage in the model itself could make search-and-rescue swarms faster where minutes matter.
arxiv-2601-03786:
Loris Schoenegger and Benjamin Roth study how to pick the few training examples that best explain a language model's output. Influence methods can estimate which training documents shaped a prediction, but people can only read a handful, so selection matters. Earlier evaluations largely ignored selection strategy, even though it directly controls explanation quality.

The authors propose a selection relevance score that needs no retraining and predicts whether a chosen set supports or undermines the model's prediction. Fine-tuning experiments validated the score. Surprisingly, common selection strategies often did worse than picking examples at random. Guided by that finding, they propose a strategy balancing influence with other factors. Honest example-based explanations could help auditors trace a model's answer back to the data that taught it.
arxiv-2601-04086:
Jinbo Hao, Kai Yang, Qingzhen Su, Yifan Li, and Chao Jiang target made-up answers that come from the prompt itself. Their framework grows out of chain-style knowledge distillation, where a strong model's reasoning is taught to another. They add a programmable module that steers search through a knowledge graph.

That module sits inside the reasoning prompt as runnable code, so the model can consult outside structured facts while it reasons. The five authors test the method on public benchmarks with GPT-4 and LLaMA models at the larger scale. Hit rates at the top ranks rise by double-digit margins, with several settings scoring above ninety-five percent. They read the gains as a sign that guided, checked steps curb false reasoning.
arxiv-2601-04286:
Niklas Kueper, Kartik Chari, and Elsa Andrea Kirchner work on reading movement intentions from brain signals in a 2026 arXiv paper aimed at stroke rehabilitation. If a robot is to help a patient move at the moment they intend to, surface EEG must be decoded online and continuously. is far harder than classifying tidy recorded trials after the fact.

Using two datasets from fourteen healthy volunteers making self-initiated arm movements, they test ensembles of three classifier types together with a sliding-window postprocessing step. In realistic pseudo-online tests, pairs of models beat the best single model once enough postprocessing windows were used, and false early detections fell. Offline tests showed little ensemble advantage, a gap the authors stress when judging systems meant for live therapy.
arxiv-2601-04386:
Alexander C. Kruse, Pavlos G. Aleiferis, and Andrea Giusti simulate what a magnetic field does to the air between two plates, in a 2026 arXiv paper. Oxygen and nitrogen differ sharply in magnetic susceptibility, so a field gradient pulls the two gases differently. Their quiescent binary mixture, held between parallel walls with a uniform gradient of the field's square pointing through them, is tested across pressures, field strengths, and starting compositions.

In a uniform mixture the species separate and gather at opposite walls, and the effect strengthens as pressure falls. A starting composition gradient tilted against the field gradient does more: it sets the whole mixture moving, because the average susceptibility gradient and the field gradient pull out of line. That induced flow speeds species transport, and the authors suggest engineered fields could exploit it for targeted mixing.
arxiv-2601-04886:
When an AI coding agent opens a pull request, its written summary is how human reviewers learn what changed. Jingzhi Gong and 3 co-authors check whether those summaries match the code in a 2026 study. They examine more than twenty thousand agent-authored pull requests from five agents, measuring message-code inconsistency, and they hand-annotate nearly a thousand cases to classify the failure types.

High inconsistency appears in a small share of requests, and the most common type is a description claiming changes that were never implemented. Eight inconsistency types are catalogued in all. For teams adopting coding agents, the study shows review cannot rest on the agent's own words; the diff itself still needs reading.
arxiv-2601-05186:
David Delepine and Shaaban Khalil test whether the universe's matter excess could arise without thermal equilibrium processes in a 2026 paper. They work in a gauged extension of the Standard Model with an inverse seesaw mechanism for neutrino masses. In that framework, right-handed neutrinos couple strongly, causing washout effects that render ordinary thermal leptogenesis, one route to creating matter over antimatter, ineffective.

Their alternative produces right-handed neutrinos from the decay of the heavy Higgs boson tied to the new gauge symmetry, a non-thermal route. They analyse whether this scenario can still generate the observed baryon asymmetry. Keeping viable origin stories for matter matters, because any successful theory must explain why the universe was not annihilated at birth.
arxiv-2601-05686:
Zhenqiao Cheng and 3 co-authors develop, in a 2026 paper, secure multiuser beamforming for movable antenna arrays. Beamforming aims radio energy toward intended users. Movable antennas can also shift position, adding a physical way to strengthen secrecy against eavesdroppers at the physical layer.

The authors derive expressions for the achievable sum secrecy rate using secure channel coding results. They then optimize digital beamforming and antenna placement together to maximize that rate. Their method mixes fractional programming with block coordinate descent, and each step has a closed-form or simple search update. Numerical results show higher secrecy rates than fixed-position arrays, backing movable antennas as a real-world security upgrade for multiuser wireless systems.
arxiv-2601-05786:
Michele Cogo and 3 co-authors examine in 2026 whether the Reynolds analogy survives in high-speed turbulent flow over rough walls. The analogy links momentum and heat transfer in a boundary layer, letting engineers predict one from the other. Roughness disrupts that coupling near the wall, which matters for vehicles and turbines at Mach speeds.

Mining direct numerical simulations at Mach two and four, with adiabatic and cooled surfaces, the authors find the breakdown confined to the roughness sublayer. Above it, velocity and enthalpy fields recover smooth-wall-like similarity, and the generalized analogy becomes valid again once roughness-enhanced stress and heat flux are included. They propose a wall model built on that recovery, coupled with a drag prediction method for prism-shaped roughness.
arxiv-2601-06286:
Stepping stones and narrow beams leave a humanoid robot no room for error. Min Dai and 4 co-authors present a physics-guided learning framework for that terrain in a 2026 paper. Pure optimization needs exact terrain models, while pure reinforcement learning rarely discovers precise footholds and step sequences on its own.

Their PLANC approach lets a reduced-order stepping planner supply motion targets that are consistent with the physics. Those targets steer reinforcement learning through rewards based on Control Lyapunov Functions, which certify stability. The learned policy combines structured planning with data-driven adaptation. Tested on real hardware, the robot crossed stepping stones accurately and agilely, with far better reliability than conventional model-free learning baselines.
arxiv-2601-06586:
Telling machine-written text from human writing matters for fighting fake news and academic misconduct. Hongyi Zhou and 3 co-authors train a detector with statistical guarantees in a 2026 paper. Existing detectors often lean on watermarks or knowledge of which model wrote the text, and rarely support formal statistical inference.

Their classifier needs no auxiliary information at all. It distinguishes human from machine authorship more effectively than existing detectors in their tests. It also controls the false-positive error rate while maintaining high detection power and computational efficiency, the inference guarantees missing from most prior work. The detector runs on a public CPU-based platform. The authors frame reliable detection as a statistical problem, not just a pattern-matching one, which strengthens trust in its verdicts.
arxiv-2601-06686:
Darius Jakobeit and Oliver Wallscheid teach one brain-like net to run many power boxes in 2026. Control of such boxes is now tuned box by box, they point out. That blocks reuse when the shape of the box changes from job to job.

Their plan does not care what shape the box has, by design. The box's wire list is writ as a graph of two node kinds. A graph net reads that graph, shaped by the task at hand. Small heads spread through the box then act on what the net finds. One frame could run a whole line of box shapes with no fresh tuning. They show this as an early proof that the thought can work. If it holds, design time drops for whole fleets of such boxes.
arxiv-2601-07086:
Osama Yousuf and four co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on a tool called XBTorch. XBTorch helps teams model chips that learn in a crossbar layout. In such a layout, rows and cols of tiny parts store weights and do math in place. The tool lets teams design the chip and the model as one task.

New kinds of memory parts have drawn much note in the past few years. They can do math right where the data sits. The parts are built at a tiny scale and hold their state when power is off. Their conductance can be tuned in fine steps. Chips of this kind can cut energy use by a wide margin. They can also cut wait time, when set next to classic von Neumann designs. XBTorch gives teams a way to test such chips before they build them.
arxiv-2601-07586:
Jerome Droniou and colleagues design a numerical scheme for contact problems with friction on fractures. Their 2026 preprint uses a higher order polytopal method, which works on meshes with general polygon or polyhedron cells. The mechanics problem involves fractures along which Tresca friction acts. Contact conditions must hold where surfaces press together.

The approach rests on a mixed formulation with two fields. One is the displacement field; the other is a Lagrange multiplier that represents traction at the fractures. The scheme belongs to the Discrete de Rham family. Higher order accuracy on rough meshes matters for rock mechanics and reservoir modeling, where fractures shape the response. The authors both design and analyze the method. Numerical analysts and geomechanics scholars are the readers.
arxiv-2601-07686:
C E Lopetegui-González and coauthors build one shared route to Bell tests from contextuality with smooth, unbroken values. Bell tests check whether nature allows the local realism Einstein favored. The original EPR paradox used position and momentum, which are continuous. Most later studies, though, used tests with only a few split outcomes. Their 2026 preprint returns to the continuous case.

The scheme does not hinge on system size, the authors state. It can probe pure smooth cases, pure split cases, or mixed nonlocality in one language. That unity helps compare experiments across very different physical platforms. Contextuality is the broader idea that measurement results can depend on what else is measured alongside. The paper serves quantum foundations scholars who want one framework for many setups. The team writes for those who test the deep rules of the small scale world.
arxiv-2601-07786:
Abdullah Al Mujahid and Mia Mohammad Imran study the technical debt that developers admit AI tools created. Their 2026 preprint examines code comments where programmers flag problems left by generative AI. Tools like ChatGPT, Copilot, Claude, and Gemini now sit inside daily development work. Some comments name both the AI involvement and the shortcoming it left behind. The paper's title quotes one such comment: TODO, fix the mess Gemini created.

Self-admitted technical debt is a known research topic; AI-induced debt is its new branch. Cataloging these comments shows where AI assistance creates cleanup work. That evidence can guide tool design and team practice. It also gives managers a realistic view of AI coding gains. The study is empirical, based on real open-source traces. Software engineering scholars and development leads are the readers.
arxiv-2601-07886:
Abhishek Yadav, Uaday Singh, and Feng Dai extend a neural network approximation method to several variables. Max-min neural network operators approximate functions using maximum and minimum operations inside the network. Recent advances built such operators for one variable. Their 2026 preprint proposes and analyzes multivariate versions. The operators are activated by sigmoidal functions, the smooth S-shaped curves common in neural networks.

Multivariate approximation is the real-world case: most functions depend on many inputs. A method proven only for one variable has limited use. The authors develop the framework and its analysis together. Approximation theory supplies guarantees about how fast these operators converge. Such guarantees help engineers choose methods with known error behavior. The paper serves scholars in approximation theory and neural network mathematics. It carries a newer operator family into higher dimensions.
arxiv-2601-07986:
Haorui Yu and colleagues release Vulca-Bench, a benchmark for cultural understanding in vision-language models. Existing benchmarks mostly measure basic skills: object recognition, scene description, and factual questions. Higher-order cultural interpretation is under-evaluated. Vulca-Bench holds 7,410 matched image and critique pairs. They span eight cultural traditions, with Chinese and English bilingual coverage. Their 2026 preprint introduces the resource.

Matched critiques let evaluators check whether a model reads an artwork's cultural meaning, not just its content. Bilingual coverage tests whether understanding survives language change. Eight traditions guard against benchmarks that quietly center one culture. The resource gives model builders a fair test they can rerun. The paper serves the multimodal AI community. It extends a companion line of work on cross-cultural art critique into a full benchmark.
arxiv-2601-08486: Chengqian Zhang and seven co-authors wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on models of atoms and how they fare on new ground. A structure-property model must work past its training range, for new molecules and materials. Pre-trained models score well on their home range after fine-tuning. How they fare off that range was less clear. The authors find a flaw in the plain way of fine-tuning. It makes the model's inner forms collapse, and wipes the chemical priors it learned. Multi-task fine-tuning is their fix.
arxiv-2601-08586:
Tao Zhou studies superconductivity in strain-engineered graphene with a self-consistent Bogoliubov-de Gennes approach. His 2026 arXiv paper challenges a common expectation about flat bands. High density of states in flat bands is often assumed to enhance pairing universally.

Zhou identifies a kinetic blockade instead. Strain-induced sublattice polarization segregates electronic states and renders the singularities inert. Superconductivity then emerges as robust filaments at geometric nodes, forming a pair density wave. The picture redirects the search for strong pairing in graphene devices. Strain patterns, not just flatness, may decide where superconductivity lives. Where strain acts thus shapes where pairing can survive at all.
arxiv-2601-08686: Matthias Carosi wrote a 2026 arXiv paper on ways to compute a value called a functional determinant. Such values sit at the core of field theory sums that rest on a saddle-point expansion. Many ways to find them skip the need to know the full spectrum of the operator. Two named ways are the Gel'fand-Yaglom theorem and the Green's function method. Carosi sets out how these ways match, as equal routes to one value. That helps users cross-check results and pick the cheapest route.
arxiv-2601-08786:
Guido Lagos, Jorge Navarro, and Hector Olivero study fix plans for systems that can fail in groups. A system here is a set of parts where the whole works or fails based on its parts. In real life, parts can fail at the same time, as in a storm or a power surge. Fixing a part should never make a sound system fail.

The team looks at plain fix rules for such systems. They split a system into parts that can be read on their own. That split makes it clear which fix rule is cheap and safe. A reader who keeps key kit gets math for a hard case. Group fails are the norm in the field, not a rare edge case.
arxiv-2601-09286:
Hanze Guo, Jianxun Lian, and Xiao Zhou ask why pick tools fail on items few folk have tried. Pick tools learn a dense code for each item from past picks. For a rare item, that code is built from few marks. The team shows a hard cap on how much true sign such a code can hold. Past that cap, more marks add noise, not sign.

They give a dual view fix. A sparse view, based on plain counts, can serve rare items well. A dense view serves rich items. Join both, and each item gets the view that fits its marks. A reader in pick tools gets a cause for a known flaw, and a split fix.
arxiv-2601-09486:
Ismail Huseynov, Arzu Ahmadova, and Agamirza E. Bashirov ask how fully an operator can steer a heat exchanger. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies two semilinear systems, one for a single-tube exchanger and one for a two-stream design. Neither system can be driven to every possible state.

For each system, the authors single out a subspace of states that can be reached exactly. That property is called partial exact controllability. Knowing the reachable subspace tells plant designers which temperature profiles they can truly command. The rest must be left to the physics of the device.
arxiv-2601-09586:
Said Yasin and Torsten Zesch want handwriting learners to see their mistakes, not just read about them. Their 2026 arXiv paper tackles visual error feedback on handwritten documents. Handwriting is still a core skill in school, yet feedback tools for it are little studied.

Going from a photo of handwriting to correctly placed, helpful marks is hard. The authors compare modular pipelines with end-to-end systems. They find that neither approach yet reaches acceptable overall quality. The honest verdict maps what must improve before such feedback can truly help in real classrooms.
arxiv-2601-09686:
Ha Nguyen and Sumanta Basu improve a standard method for learning networks from data. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents LARGE, a locally adaptive regularization approach for Gaussian graphical models. Such models encode which variables depend directly on which others.

The graphical Lasso is the usual tool: it estimates the precision matrix by maximizing likelihood with an L1 penalty. One global penalty treats all edges alike, which can misfit varied data. LARGE adapts the penalty locally instead. Adaptive penalties should recover truer networks in finance, biology, and other fields where dependence maps are the goal.
arxiv-2601-09886:
Sathvik Nair and Byung-Doh Oh ask why model surprise predicts reading effort better than human guesses. Their 2026 arXiv paper compares language model surprisal with cloze surprisal. Word predictability can be measured two ways: by asking people to fill blanks, or by reading a model's probabilities.

Both scores can predict how hard a word is to process. Language model scores win in practice. The authors dig into why the machine measure beats the human one. The answer matters for psycholinguistics, where surprisal is a main link between language statistics and the reading brain.
arxiv-2601-09986:
Cheng Zhang and co authors speed up checks for a class of programs. The programs are GKAT automata. They mix tests, loops, and acts. A check asks if two such programs act the same on all traces.

Checks of this kind can be slow. The team gives fast checks that work on the fly. They use SAT tools to search for a gap. To show use, they built a tool for code flow checks. It tests if a change to code flow keeps the acts the same. Fast checks of this sort help keep code changes safe.
arxiv-2601-10286:
E. A. Kokin sorts the twist groups of a class of contact shapes. Such shapes have a frame that twists as one moves. The twist group is named the holonomy group. It tells how a vector turns on a loop trip. Kokin's shapes have a metric of mixed sign.

Mixed sign breaks the plain tools. Past proofs split space by sign, which can fail here. Kokin adapts the proof to dodge that flaw. He shows the flat twist group is the full group, or sits in it one step down. The work fills a gap for these shapes.
arxiv-2601-10686:
Daniel Barake, Owen Chuchman, Cameron Franc, Geoffrey Mason, and Brett Nasserden connect vertex operator algebras to modular curves. A vertex operator algebra encodes the symmetries of a two-dimensional field theory. Each one can be tied to a vector bundle over the elliptic modular curve. The authors describe that bundle in detail.

They treat quasi-vertex operator algebras as well, a broader class. The stated aim looks ahead: using this bundle picture to study the characters of these algebras. Characters are the key functions that count states by weight. A firm geometric base could pay off across math physics, where these algebras link number theory, geometry, and string theory.
arxiv-2601-11086:
Chenlu Liu and co-authors convert qubit relaxation into erasure errors with a single fluxonium qubit. Qubits whose main error is erasure, a loss at a known place, are easier to correct than qubits with hidden errors. Dual-rail designs in cavities and transmons already make this trade, but they cost extra hardware and circuit complexity.

A single fluxonium could make the same trade leaner. Fluxonium is a superconducting qubit known for long coherence. If its relaxation can be recast as erasures, error correction gets a cheaper input. The work matters for fault-tolerant designs, where the type of error can matter as much as its rate.
arxiv-2601-11186:
Donato Bini and Giorgio Di Russo work on gravity in the strong-field regime. Their 2026 preprint studies a particle that falls straight into a black hole. The hole is of the Schwarzschild kind, with no spin or charge. The particle starts at rest and falls in along a radius.

The team counts the energy shed as waves to first self-force order. Self-force is the push a body feels from its own field. They treat two cases side by side for the fall. One is a scalar particle that sheds scalar waves. The other is a mass that sheds waves of gravity. Post-Newtonian checks back the results at weak field strength.
arxiv-2601-11486:
M. Idris and J.-M. Sac-Epee study which polynomials divide Newman polynomials. Their 2026 preprint gives algorithmic results on that question. Newman polynomials have coefficients of just zero and one. Their roots and measures link to deep number theory.

The team first treats the 8438 known cases of low measure. Those have Mahler measure less than 1.3 in the count. Mahler measure sizes a polynomial by its roots' growth. They then list polynomials that divide no Newman polynomial. A degree-10 case of small measure is singled out in the list. Such lists bound where small-measure polynomials can arise. The work aids the hunt for Lehmer-type minimal cases.
arxiv-2601-11586:
Shan Zhang and four coauthors trace how students replay problems in games. Their 2026 preprint studies latent problem-solving pathways in learners. Game-based learning logs each move a student makes. Pathways through problems reflect understanding and procedural skill.

Flexibility in approach also shows in those pathways. Replay behavior is the paper's special focus. Replaying may signal productive struggle or broad exploration. Both can foster deeper learning when they pay off. Little is known about how pathways unfold across problems. Timing of replays and strategies is also unclear. The team links those patterns to near and far learning outcomes.
arxiv-2601-11986:
Mingjie Feng, Yiming Li, and Hua-Sheng Shao weigh the odds of finding a new tetraquark state at LHCb. Tetraquarks are parts made of four quarks. The state they study holds both a bottom and a charm quark, with spin-parity 0+.

They model proton-proton crashes at 13 TeV at LHCb. They focus on states that decay strongly, so they are short lived and hard to spot. Rate checks show if a search is worth the effort. The work gives a target for LHCb teams to test.  Such rates set the scale for a search at the LHC.
arxiv-2601-12086:
A. A. Zheltukhin studies a spinning string with no tension. The action he uses is unchanged by reparametrization, local supersymmetry, and scale shifts. He builds the density of the energy-momentum tensor for this string.

He proves that its covariant divergence is zero. That zero comes from a mutual cancel of bosonic and fermionic parts. He also sets out how worldsheets of tensionless strings differ in geometry from normal strings. The work adds to the theory of strings at zero tension.  The string case is a clean test for field maths.
arxiv-2601-12186:
Vatsal Venkatkrishna, Indraneil Paul, and Iryna Gurevych ask what makes code verifiers trained with verifiable rewards work. Such verifiers grade and rerank model outputs in post-training. They are now a fixture for general tasks, but code use has been sparse.

For code, run feedback has been the main signal. The team's study, named in the work, probes which parts of reward-led training drive code verifier skill. That map can guide teams to train verifiers that catch bad code with less waste. It joins reward design to code quality.  Code verifiers could rerank code as they do prose.
arxiv-2601-12286:
Jonathan Pan sorts conversational context with a representation engineering route. As language models spread, guards must catch replies that stray out of context. Strays span topic shifts, false facts, and hallucinated claims.

Classic anomaly tools do not map well to context sense in text. His method works on the model's inner representations in place of surface text. Inner signals may flag a stray before it is full-blown. The work aims for more sound LLM guards.  Inner flags could warn before a bad reply is sent.  Topic drift is one clear stray kind the tool must catch at once.
arxiv-2601-12886:
Christoph Wittner surveys communication methods in multi agent reinforcement learning. This field extends reinforcement learning to systems with many interacting agents. Communication methods have multiplied in recent years to solve hard multi agent problems. Those problems include partial observability, non stationarity, and action spaces that grow exponentially.

When agents can talk, they can share what each one sees alone. Communication further enables efficient cooperation among all agents in an environment. A survey of methods helps researchers pick the right channel design. It also maps which problems each method really solves. The work serves robotics, games, and distributed control research.
arxiv-2601-13186:
Diego Gosmar and Deborah A. Dahl harden language models against prompt tricks in agent chains. A prompt trick hides a bad order in text a model reads. In chains of agents, one bad out put can pass the trick on and grow it. That risk is a top block to safe use.

Past work by the pair set a four part score for how weak a set up is to tricks. The new work grows that score. It adds a cache that reuses past checks by sense match, to cut cost. It adds a fourth agent that judges by fixed rules. It also adds a fifth part score for how clear the chain is to watch. The aim is guards that stay strong while they stay open to view.
arxiv-2601-13486:
Anderson Anrrango and co-authors teach a self led learner to guess power flow answers that stay safe. The task is security constrained DC optimal power flow. It picks cheap power dispatch that still holds if a line fails. Solve in full is slow, so a fast guess has worth.

Their guess is a linear model with tuned parts. The parts shift with demand and scale line caps. That form keeps the true physics shape of the DC task in view. Self led teach needs no solved cases to learn from. For grid teams, a fast and form true guess can run where a full solve cannot keep up.
arxiv-2601-13786:
Mozib Bin Awal and Prabwal Phukon study constant-entropy processes in a class of black holes in 2026. These are Anti de Sitter black holes tied to nonlinear electrodynamics. An isentropic process keeps entropy fixed while the hole changes. The pair ask if such a process can happen at all.
