For cusp forms unramified everywhere, the formulas give new evidence toward conjectures of Wan-Zhang and Gan-Gross-Prasad for GSpin6 times GSpin3, linking L-values, periods, and arithmetic conjectures in one framework.
arxiv-2602-14786:
Achraf Badahmane, Issa Ezzagouri, and Xian-Ming Gu develop a randomised global GMRES method for large linear systems with many right-hand sides. Their algorithm builds on a randomised global Gram-Schmidt process, where sketched Frobenius inner products stand in for exact ones in high dimensions, cutting cost while keeping the solver's structure.

New convergence results support the method, and for diagonalisable coefficient matrices the authors derive upper bounds for the randomised residual norm. Matrix sketching thus enters a classic iterative solver without breaking its guarantees. Large-scale linear algebra gains a faster, still principled route.
arxiv-2602-14986:
Nzongani and colleagues attack the scaling problem of the Quantum Approximate Optimization Algorithm. QAOA leads near-term quantum optimization, but tuning twice as many variational angles as layers grows painful as circuits deepen. Recent work hints that optimal angles concentrate and transfer across problem sizes. The team turns that hint into a schedule-learning method that carries spectral-gap-informed adiabatic control from small instances to larger ones.

Their method reads the gap profile of small problems and builds a smooth schedule from the instantaneous gap with two global hyperparameters. Discretizing that schedule yields closed-form angles for every layer, shrinking the classical tuning task from twice the layer count to just two values at any depth. Tests on random QUBO and 3-regular MaxCut cases show the learned schedules transfer well with competitive approximation ratios.
arxiv-2602-15086:
Barman and Das derive the hyperbolic Sombor index of a graph from its M-polynomial. Topological indices are numbers drawn from a graph that reflect its shape, and degree-based indices can be computed through the matching graph polynomial. The hyperbolic Sombor index, proposed in 2025, already shows chemical use for octane isomers and sensitivity to structure across octane, nonane, and decane isomers.

The paper establishes a closed derivation formula for the index from the M-polynomial. That formula is then used to compute the index for several standard graphs and chemical families. Numerical and graphical displays of the M-polynomial and the computed index for those families complete the work, giving chemists a direct route from polynomial to index.
arxiv-2602-15186:
Tong and colleagues define and study lending games for the interbank money market, where lending banks strategically allocate cash to borrowing banks. Each borrowing bank offers an interest rate inside the central bank's interest rate corridor, ultimately shaped by cash demand and supply in the market. Lending banks aim to maximize income from interest repayments. In its purest form, the game has infinite strategies, yet the team shows it is an exact potential game with a unique pure strategy Nash equilibrium.

Next they set up and solve a constrained optimization problem, then put forward an algorithm, strongly polynomial in time, for computing that equilibrium. The team also looks at variants of best-response dynamics, which reach the Nash equilibrium under both discrete-time and continuous-time settings. The paper thus gives the interbank market a tractable game-theoretic footing with computable equilibria.
arxiv-2602-15786:
Bick works alone on charged null fluids in general relativity. He studies the bouncing continuation proposed by Ori in 1991. In that model, charged massless particles may instantly reverse direction after losing all 4-momentum to charge repulsion. He studies timelike bounce surfaces in spherical symmetry: an incoming beam of charged null dust reverses along a timelike surface B, the free boundary of an interacting two-dust region.

A decoupling of the motion equations is found there. Every timelike curve segment in the quotient of Minkowski or Reissner-Nordström spacetimes arises as the bounce surface of a beam from past null infinity. The built spacetime glues to Reissner-Nordström and Vaidya regions, with metric smoothness C-two-one across B and Einstein equations satisfied. A free boundary problem for a given incoming beam is then formed and solved conditionally, in the exterior Reissner-Nordström region under a technical rule.
arxiv-2602-15986:
Misiak and Dziubinski clock how fast best response dynamics settle in network public good games, where players react in random order and each choice substitutes for neighbours choices. Mixing proofs with simulations, they hunt for the structures that drag convergence out.

The main culprit is a late awakening. Part of a network settles while neighbouring nodes sit idle. Those nodes then switch on near the end and force a fresh round of adjustment, possibly more than once. The authors pin down graph features that make such restarts likely, features that reach beyond the graph spectrum. Comparing co spectral mates, graphs sharing a spectrum yet converging at different speeds, proves the spectrum alone cannot predict the delay.
arxiv-2602-16086:
Idil Bilge Altun leads a team of five researchers improving how images are turned into discrete tokens for generation. Recent collapse-free quantizers like FSQ gain stability by fixing the codebook geometry, trading away learnability. Their method, Learnable Geometric Quantization, keeps a learnable codebook and moves from soft to hard assignment through temperature annealing, guided by two cheap penalties.

A diversity term that punishes concentrated code use does most of the work against collapse, while a peakedness term sharpens each token assignment toward a single code. Under a fixed VQ-GAN backbone, the method tops rival quantizers on reconstruction quality at a mid-size codebook while using every code. It keeps improving as the codebook grows, holding full use at each size, and it also leads on class-conditional generation with a frozen tokenizer.
arxiv-2602-16186:
Masoud Amouzgar models how retail payment outages can shake trust and liquidity long after systems recover. Shoppers and merchants interact through repeated payment attempts, while shoppers also influence one another on a Watts-Strogatz small-world network. Shoppers carry bounded memory variables for accumulated negative experience, called scar, and perceived systemic risk, called rumor. Merchants add persistent broadcast signals that may lag operational bounce-back.

Under mild conditions on memory persistence and threshold rules, the model proves that total withdrawal pressure can peak strictly after the outage nadir, even during recovery. Simulations reproduce behavioral stickiness and confirm delayed outflow peaks. Instant-transfer substitution consistently reduces peak avoidance, yet its effect on cumulative outflows is non-monotonic when merchant broadcast persistence is real. The lesson is that a green status light does not equal resolved risk, and incident response must address perception and messaging as well.
arxiv-2602-16286:
Partha Ghose asks what kind of world supports Darwinian evolution. It requires heritable records, repeatable copying with variety, and routine one-way change. The language of categorical quantum mechanics pins down why copy and delete fail to count as generic quantum operations. Such operations show up only inside a realized data sector, where a preferred basis carries commutative structure. Decoherence explains how a pointer basis can be selected in time, but it does not by itself select a unique outcome.

That gap motivates a neutral presentation of the main basic options: unique-history, decohered multiplicity, agent-relative facts, and a random foundation with variable spread. An agency constraint sharpens the point. In a strictly coherent, basis-unselected regime, minimal agency fails due to no-cloning and linearity. Extended Wigner Friend cases serve as a stress test. A stochastic-mechanics bridge spans between quantum and classical regimes.
arxiv-2602-16386:
Dimitrios Amaxilatis leads four coauthors on data sharing for the next generation of mobile networks. Coming 6G networks are expected to support data-driven services at huge scale and complexity, with strict trust, interoperability, and automation demands. Central to that vision is creating, managing, and sharing high-quality datasets across distributed environments.

The paper presents the data architecture of the 6G-DALI project, a shared dataspace and DataOps infrastructure for secure, compliant, and scalable data sharing, supporting AI-driven experimentation and orchestration. Drawing on GAIA-X and International Data Spaces Association principles, it includes federated identity management, policy-based contracts, and automated pipelines. The authors show how it aligns with and extends the GAIA-X and IDSA reference models for 6G needs like low-latency edge processing, dynamic trust control, and cross-domain federation. A comparative analysis highlights where the models converge and where new ideas are required.
arxiv-2602-16486:
Alessandro De Rosis and Yang Zhou build a fluctuating lattice Boltzmann formulation based on orthogonal central moments. Heat-driven fluctuations matter in fluid flow at small scales, yet numerical schemes must add them in a way that fits statistical mechanics. The authors place random forcing directly in central-moment space, paired with mode-wise relaxation.

Because the basis is orthogonal, the equilibrium covariance matrix of the central moments is diagonal, so each non-conserved mode acts as its own discrete Ornstein-Uhlenbeck process with variance set by equilibrium thermodynamics. The scheme gives exact energy equipartition at equilibrium, keeps Galilean invariance, and stays stable where older fluctuating BGK schemes fail, even near the stability limit. Tests on two standard lattices confirm correct thermalisation and isotropy.
arxiv-2602-16586:
Emily Logan, Ning Qi, and Bolun Xu propose a two-stage framework for behind-the-meter energy storage in commercial buildings. The goal is to coordinate peak shaving with stacked services, cutting electricity costs and lengthening battery life. First, a nonparametric kernel regression model builds state-of-charge trajectory bounds from past data. Those bounds must satisfy peak-shaving requirements.

Second, the remaining capacity is used for energy arbitrage through transfer learning. Case studies on New York City commercial building demand show a strong gain over a forecast-based state-of-the-art method. Cost savings and effective peak control arrive without relying on predictions. Building operators get a practical control scheme grounded in history rather than forecasts.
arxiv-2602-16886:
Ondrej Dyck and co-authors show atomically precise electron beam sculpting of bilayer hexagonal boron nitride. They reveal how crystal orientation and milling plan shape results. The focused electron beam of a scanning transmission electron microscope carves nanoribbons as narrow as six angstroms with atomically smooth edges. Grasping atomic structure, above all in twisted bilayer systems, proves key to that precision.

High-angle annular dark-field imaging plus multi-slice simulations reveal distinct intensity signatures. Those signatures identify varied stacking arrangements within moiré patterns. Math study of moiré lattices predicts optimal cutting directions. Armchair cuts beat zigzag cuts on edge quality. Surprisingly, sequential milling, translating a small beam subscan area during the process, beats parallel milling of the whole target region. A random-run milling model shows sequential milling cuts unwanted exposure to nearby material.
arxiv-2602-16986:
Qin Ding and co-authors present ULTRA-HSTU, a sequential suggestion model bending the scaling law curve in large-scale pick systems. Learning from user interaction history through ordered models has become a cornerstone of large-scale recommenders. Recent advances in large language models have revealed promising scaling laws, sparking research into long-sequence modeling and deeper architectures for pick tasks.

ULTRA-HSTU is developed through end-to-end model and system co-design. It innovates in input sequence design, sparse attention mechanisms, and model topology. Full benchmarking shows remarkable scaling speed gains, over five times faster training scaling and twenty-one times faster inference scaling compared to conventional models, while delivering superior suggestion quality. The solution is fully deployed at scale, serving billions of users daily and driving significant consumption and engagement gains in real-world production.
arxiv-2602-17086:
Xinyu Dai led a three-author team studying what happens to a popular Bayesian learning rule when its model of the world is wrong. Thompson Sampling assumes the true model sits inside its model class, yet real decision problems rarely grant that comfort. The paper first maps a misspecified two-armed Gaussian bandit in full, sorting posterior behavior into correct concentration, incorrect concentration, and persistent belief mixing.

Each regime yields sharp predictions for limiting beliefs, action frequencies, and long-run regret, driven by the direction of evidence and the mapping from models to actions. The analysis then widens to any finite model class through a stochastic stability framework that treats posterior motion as a Markov process on the belief simplex. The result is a first qualitative and geometric map of Thompson Sampling under misspecification, with foundations for sturdier bandit design.
arxiv-2602-17186:
Seulbi Lee led a two-author team fighting language bias in large vision-language models. These models often answer from language habits without truly using the image. Prior fixes through decoding, architecture, or curated data lack a quantitative measure of how much each training sample or token actually gains from visual input. The paper introduces Visual Information Gain, a perplexity-based metric for that drop in uncertainty.

The metric supports fine-grained analysis at sample and token level, spotlighting visually grounded elements like colors, spatial relations, and attributes. A selective training scheme then prioritizes high-gain samples and tokens, improving visual grounding and easing language bias. The approach reached superior performance with far less supervision, simply by training on the visually informative parts.
arxiv-2602-17286:
Callum Barber led a two-author paper on counting diagonal subsemigroups against congruences. For a semigroup, such a subsemigroup is a reflexive, compatible relation, equivalently a subsemigroup of the direct square containing the diagonal. When the semigroup is finite, the DSC coefficient is defined as the ratio of the number of congruences to the number of these subsemigroups. Prior work showed that ratio equals one exactly when the semigroup is a group.

The paper proves that every rational value between zero and one occurs as a DSC coefficient for some semigroup. The construction uses the Rees matrix method, adapting the congruence classification of such semigroups to describe their subsemigroups of that kind. The result completes the picture of which ratios the ratio can take.
arxiv-2602-17586:
Antonio Guillen-Perez tackles a bottleneck in self-driving safety. Rare, high-risk edge cases slip past rule-based checks, so Level 4 cars lack a scalable way to prove they are safe. His framework, Deep-Flow, learns the density of expert human driving with no labels, then flags acts that fall outside normal road conduct.

The method uses optimal transport conditional flow matching, squeezed through a low-rank spectral manifold. That keeps motion smooth and likelihoods stable. A transformer with lane-aware goal conditioning handles tricky junctions. A weighting scheme favors energetic moves in training. On Waymo data, it surfaced lane and junction breaches that standard filters missed, pointing to data-driven safety gates.
arxiv-2602-17786:
Adolfo del Campo unifies shortcuts to adiabaticity through tuning quantum Zeno checks. Starting from a pulsed check routine for a time-shifting projector, he shows the working Zeno rule involves a non-slow shape link. That link takes the form of the Kato-Avron rule for side-by-side transport, stirring change within the time-shifting Zeno subspace.

When projective checks use the at-the-moment energy basis, the motion reduces to counter-driving. The working Zeno rule also emerges from ongoing checks of a time-shifting readout and from non-Hermitian change with a complex soaking field varying in time. Together these routes give a unified frame for making shortcuts via tuning Zeno checks, linking check routines that once looked distinct.
arxiv-2602-18186:
Seohwa Hwang and one co-author built Box Thirding, a method for finding the best option when tries are scarce. Their 2026 paper tackles best-arm identification under a fixed budget, including anytime use, where the budget is not known in advance, and cases with so many arms that full testing is impossible. The method compares three arms at a time.

Each round keeps the current best for more testing, parks the middle arm for later, and drops the weakest. Even without knowing the budget, the method's error rate matches Successive Halving run on a fitting subset, though that rival needs the budget up front. On a New Yorker cartoon caption contest dataset, Box Thirding beat existing methods under tight budgets. The paper offers a flexible tool for ranking many options cheaply.
arxiv-2602-18386:
Mohamed Elgouhary and one co-author let reinforcement learning tune a classic racing controller on the fly. Their 2026 paper targets Pure Pursuit path tracking, widely used in autonomous racing for its speed and geometric clarity, yet sensitive to lookahead distance and steering gain. Standard velocity-based schedules approximate those settings and often fail across tracks and speed profiles.

The team trains a proximal policy optimization agent to choose lookahead and steering gain jointly at each step from compact state features of speed and curvature. Trained in F1TENTH Gym and run in a ROS 2 stack, the policy drives Pure Pursuit directly with light smoothing and no retuning per map. In both simulation and real-car tests it beats fixed-lookahead, velocity-scheduled, and lookahead-only rivals, and even a kinematic MPC raceline tracker on lap time, tracking accuracy, and steering smoothness.
arxiv-2602-18486:
Jean Pinsolle and four co-authors improve radar detection where clutter is heavy. Their 2026 paper notes classic radar detectors estimate noise covariance from target-free secondary data. Those detectors work in Gaussian settings but fail under clutter, which fits heavy-tailed models such as the Complex Elliptically Symmetric and Compound-Gaussian families better.

Robust covariance estimators such as M-estimators or Tyler's estimator help but still falter when thermal noise mixes with clutter. The team tests Support Vector Data Description, plus its deep extension Deep SVDD, for finding targets. These one-class learning methods skip direct noise covariance estimation and serve here as CFAR detectors. Two novel SVDD-based detection algorithms are proposed and shown effective on simulated radar data.
arxiv-2602-18986:
Highly automated AI systems are spreading through finance, healthcare, transport, content checks, and key systems. Yet firms lack principled ways to quantify how machine control amplifies harm when failures occur. Vishal Srivastava, with one co-author, proposes a Bayesian risk decomposition in 2026. Expected loss becomes a product of three terms. First, the chance of system failure. Second, the conditional chance that a failure spreads into harm, given the automation level. Third, the expected severity of harm.

That middle term captures running and oversight risk, not model accuracy alone. The frame adds formal proofs, a harm spread equivalence theorem linking spread chance to observable running controls, risk elasticity measures, efficient frontier analysis, and optimal resource allocation principles. The 2012 Knight Capital incident illustrates the pattern. The work also describes the research design needed to validate the frame at scale, offering foundations for deployment-focused risk governance tools.
arxiv-2602-19286:
Some Hubble observations can never be repeated: a supernova, a kilonova, or a tidal disruption event happens once, inside a fixed window. Getting the science data depends first on centering the target precisely, a job handled by the STIS acquisition sequence, usually placed only at the start of a visit. If the observatory cannot lock onto guide stars in time, that sequence fails and the visit is lost.

Matthew Dallas and Matthew Siebert propose safety acquisitions as insurance for multi-orbit visits. The idea is redundancy: extra acquisition steps placed so a failed first attempt does not doom the whole visit. For one-shot targets, that backup is cheap compared with losing the event entirely. The paper spells out how such safety steps fit into visit planning for the Space Telescope Imaging Spectrograph.
arxiv-2602-19686:
Coroutines can pause mid-run and resume later, generalizing plain functions. Qiqi Jason Gu and two co-authors work with Coroutine Types, behavioral types that model coroutine interplay as one receive followed by one yield. Those types already serve engineering driven by models, smart contracts, and test-case generation, but they cannot yet handle coroutines with several receives and yields.

The authors add a Flow extension covering multiple receives and yields, revising the reduction rules to match. They then map Go expressions to Coroutine Types in a type system. A reduction result of 0 means the two channel operations pair properly and the program holds no deadlocks. The analyzer covers 17 channel and goroutine patterns, using the Z3 SMT solver for conditionals and type inheritance. It beats static and dynamic detectors that crashed or mispredicted on some patterns.
arxiv-2602-19786:
Climate models run many scenarios and configurations, spawning data sets that researchers must hunt down through search tools and metadata vocabularies. A 2026 arXiv paper by Miguel Ceriani and seven co-authors presents the Climate Change Knowledge Graph, built to unify that scattered landscape.

The graph integrates diverse sources about climate simulations into one coherent, interoperable structure, so a single complex query can span models, simulations, variables, places, times, and granularities. Domain experts shaped the design, and the graph and its ontology are published under an open licence. Readers and services gain a framework for exploring climate data more directly, supporting better-informed choices on mitigation and adaptation.
arxiv-2602-20086:
Random multiplicative functions look chaotic. Sums over certain sets behave almost like Gaussian random variables. A 2026 arXiv paper by Besfort Shala, working alone, develops a general framework for the large fluctuations of such sums. The framework extends earlier central limit work by Soundararajan and Xu.

For short intervals with admissible length, the paper shows the sum almost surely exceeds a positive multiple of its natural scale infinitely often. For values of an admissible polynomial, it extends work of Klurman, Shkredov, and Xu, and of Chinis and the author. The same almost-sure lower bound holds even when the polynomial is a product of linear factors over the rationals. A matching almost-sure upper bound is also established, in line with the law of the iterated logarithm. A key ingredient bounds a transport distance, the Kantorovich-Wasserstein distance, using a quantitative martingale central limit theorem.
arxiv-2602-20186:
The Quantum Singleton Bound limits how much quantum information a code can protect. Most proofs route through entropy arguments. A 2026 arXiv paper by Frederick Dehmel and Shilun Li proves the bound with linear algebra for stabiliser quantum error-correcting codes, and gives a Lean4 version of the linear-algebra argument.

The proof works in finite symplectic vector spaces that model Pauli operators. It relies on erasure correctability tied to distance, plus the cleaning lemma. Counting dimensions inside the symplectic framework yields the bound: the number of logical qubits plus twice the distance minus two cannot exceed the number of physical qubits. The approach shows the algebra behind the bound, avoids heavier tools from entropy-based proofs, and suits formal checking.
arxiv-2602-20286:
Kristin DeVleming introduces readers to wall crossing in the theory of moduli of varieties. Her 2026 semi-expository guide follows a decade of progress that largely settled how to build moduli spaces for two key kinds of pairs. They are log canonically polarized slc pairs and K-polystable log Fano pairs. Once such spaces exist, a natural question follows: how do they change when the coefficients of the pair divisor are varied?

That change is wall crossing, a theory developed in several important cases over the past five years. The guide explains the background of moduli of varieties, the tools used in explicit computations, and worked examples, including new ones. It aims to give newcomers both the concepts and the working methods of the field. A reader who works through it gains a path into current research on how moduli spaces shift as their defining coefficients move.
arxiv-2602-20486:
Dialogue systems have long helped learners reflect, with rule-based designs giving ordered support but struggling when engagement shifts. Paras Sharma and eight co-authors present a hybrid system that embeds language-model response inside a theory-aligned, rule-based setup, tested in a culture-aware robot summer camp. The rule-based structure grounds talk in self-regulated learning theory, while the language model decides when and how to prompt deeper thought as chat evolves.

Reading themes across talks, the authors find the hybrid talks aided richer learner thoughts on goals and tasks. The same response brought problems, though: repeats and off prompts reduced engagement. The paper thus maps both the promise and the pitfalls of mixing large language models into theory-based thought support.
arxiv-2602-20586:
The roughly eleven-year jet precession period seen in M87* points to a spinning supermassive black hole with a tilted disk. Tao-Tao Sui and two co-authors use that observation to constrain a rotating black hole in Bumblebee gravity, modeling tilted disk motion with spherical orbits. They compute spherical orbits and innermost stable orbits. Energy, angular momentum, and the Carter constant shift with radius, spin, symmetry-breaking scale, and tilt, with distinct prograde and retrograde trends.

For prograde orbits, the innermost stable radius falls with spin and that scale and rises with tilt, while retrograde orbits reverse them. Using the precession period with a fixed tilt, the warp radius spans a range growing with spin or that scale. Comparison with Kerr limits suggests that a warp radius above sixteen may signal a non-vacuum Bumblebee vector field. Adding the Event Horizon Telescope shadow tightens the range further.
arxiv-2602-21086:
Flaws can probe the hidden order of thwarted magnets. Maksymilian Kliczkowski, Jakub Grabowski, and Maciej Maska study two pinned spin flaws in a thwarted spin-half chain in this 2026 arXiv paper. They join second-order nudge math with large-scale density-matrix rescaling-group math to map the flaw link against gap, coupling strength, and thwarting.

In weak coupling, the host spin response rules the link, which falls as a wavy power law in the gapless phase and fast in the gapped paired-up phase. Stronger coupling crosses into an edge-ruled regime with parity effects tied to the segment length between flaws. Flaw links thus tell gapless phases apart from gapped phases through local probes.
arxiv-2602-21186:
Vision-language models read two-dimensional images well but reason weakly about three-dimensional space. Haoyi Jiang and seven co-authors close that gap in this 2026 arXiv paper with Spa3R, a self-taught builder of one view-steady spatial picture from multi-view images with unknown camera poses. A predictive spatial-field objective compresses context views into a compact latent code and predicts geometric and semantic fields at new viewpoints.

A lightweight adapter plugs the pretrained encoder into a vision-language model, grounding language reasoning in global spatial context. The resulting model scores fifty-eight point six percent on a spatial reasoning benchmark and leads or matches rivals on three more. Predictive spatial learning proves an effective visual foundation for three-dimensional reasoning.
arxiv-2602-21286:
Type-1 active galactic nuclei hide their centers behind host-galaxy light plus accretion-disk and broad-line emission. Miguel Coloma Puga and six co-authors cut through that glare in this 2026 arXiv paper with integral field spectroscopy. They model and subtract quasar light to study both host cores and central engines cleanly. Results are presented for one jetted, gamma-ray-emitting source.

After separating host and active-nucleus spectra, the authors report an unresolved, unidentified variable emission feature: high-velocity, varying on timescales under a year, unlike anything seen in other variable active nuclei. The discovery showcases what careful light subtraction can reveal in galactic centers. Readers get a method plus a mystery emission component awaiting identification.
arxiv-2602-21586:
Joel D. Hartman and 12 co-authors present HATPI pre-perihelion time-series photometry of interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS. HATPI is a recently commissioned time-domain facility at Las Campanas Observatory in Chile, using 64 wide-angle lenses and back-illuminated CCDs to cover 7,100 square arcdegrees at a 45-second cadence.

HATPI first robustly recovered the comet on the night of 2025 July 2, one night after discovery, near magnitude 18 in the Gaia G band. Brightness rose to near magnitude 14 by 2025 September 13, after which perihelion approach hid it from HATPI. Before reaching magnitude 16 on 2025 August 6, it appeared only in stacked nightly observations; afterward single 45-second exposures sufficed. No significant short-time-scale brightness variations appear after August 6. HATPI magnitudes fit a power law in heliocentric distance with index near 5, steeper than the index near 4 from combined literature data.
arxiv-2602-22086:
Weak van der Waals forces shape how molecules bind, drugs dock, and batteries store charge, yet they are costly to model well. Evgeny Moerman and three co-authors present MBD-ML, a pretrained neural network that predicts the atomic inputs needed for many-body dispersion calculations. It reads atomic structures directly and plugs into existing dispersion software, skipping slower electronic-structure steps.

With those predicted inputs, the method yields total energies, forces, and stress tensors that include many-body dispersion effects. The authors pitch it as a practical shortcut: state-of-the-art dispersion physics becomes available inside any electronic-structure or machine-learned force-field code. For chemists, that means better weak-force modeling without paying the full cost of quantum calculations.
arxiv-2602-22286:
Lossless compression saves storage and bandwidth, but most learned compressors serve one modality, forcing redundant deployments for images, text, speech, and more. Yan Zhao and six co-authors propose OmniZip, a unified lightweight compressor for multi-modal data spanning images, text, speech, touch, databases, and gene sequences. It rests on a lightweight backbone with three key components.

A modality-unified tokenizer reversibly turns diverse data into tokens, while a routing mechanism learns flexible multi-modal context. Multimodal language models could in principle unify compression too, but remain too complex for practical use. OmniZip offers the unification without the bulk, giving edge and archive systems one compressor for every data kind.
arxiv-2602-22686:
Satya Ranjan Nayak and two co-authors study non-flow correlations in proton and heavy-ion collisions at RHIC energies. They treat the two-particle cumulant as an event-by-event distribution and track its skewness and kurtosis, the shape measures that reveal jets, decays, and other non-flow effects.

Non-flow sources skewed the distribution in every model tried. By contrast, HYDJET++ produced a smooth bell-shaped curve at wider pseudorapidity windows in fixed-impact collisions. Skewness and kurtosis rose with window width in non-quark-gluon-plasma models like PYTHIA, PHOJET, QGSJET, and DPMJET. In HYDJET++, both shape measures fell with growing separation and reached zero at wide gaps, a clean signature worth chasing.
arxiv-2602-23186:
Volker Ziemann models the time-dependent behavior of superconducting multi-cell accelerating cavities with an equivalent-circuit picture. Such cavities, built from several linked cells, behave differently from the single-cell resonator model that engineers commonly use. The paper sets out to map those differences.

The circuit model tracks how the multi-cell system responds over time. It also takes up the tolerances that arise from manufacturing flaws. For readers working on accelerator design, the value lies in seeing where the simple single-cell picture breaks down. It also shows how much slack real, imperfectly built cavities introduce into the expected behavior.
arxiv-2602-23286:
Sungho Park and two co-authors present SPARTA, a framework that builds large Table-Text question-answering benchmarks automatically. Real tasks demand reasoning across long text and source tables, over several hops, with operations such as aggregation. Yet existing benchmarks are small, hand-built and thus error-prone, and their questions rarely exceed two hops or call for grouping and other advanced operations.

SPARTA enriches each source table with grounding tables of atomic facts drawn from the text, then synthesizes nested queries whose predicate count matches the target hop count. Provenance-based refinement rewrites queries that return empty results, while realistic-structure enforcement limits generation to post-order traversals of the query graph. The pipeline yields thousands of quality pairs at a quarter of HybridQA's annotation time. Leading models that score over 70 F1 on HybridQA or over 50 on OTT-QA drop by more than 30 F1 points on SPARTA.
arxiv-2602-23586:
Kyle Medler and 14 co-authors report optical and near-infrared observations of the interstellar comet 3I/ATLAS before and after perihelion. Interstellar objects offer a unique view into how other star systems form. Spectra were taken between three point seven and one point eight astronomical units on either side of perihelion. Instruments were Keck-I/LRIS, Keck-II/NIRES, Gemini/GMOS, and UH88/SNIFS.

The team reports continued emission of nickel and CN, plus post-perihelion detections of iron and a weak detection of C3. Optical slopes run positive, about 21 to 27 percent in the blue and 6 to 10 percent in the red. Near-infrared slopes run negative, about minus zero point nine and minus two point three percent in two bands. A clear turnover in spectral shape near one point one micrometers corresponds to scattered light from the dusty coma. The near-infrared shape resembles that of 2I/Borisov.
arxiv-2602-23686:
Siddhant Manna and one co-author search for gamma-ray emission from the merging galaxy cluster Abell 119, combining archival data. Data come from INTEGRAL/ISGRI, COMPTEL, and DAMPE.

No significant emission is detected at the cluster position in any band. ISGRI mosaic imaging gives a three-sigma cap of eight point five times ten to the minus eleven erg per square centimeter per second. COMPTEL reanalysis gives ninety-five percent confidence caps from nine times ten to the minus eleven to eight times ten to the minus ten in the same units. The band covers zero point seven five to 30 MeV. DAMPE gives caps from ten to the minus twelve to ten to the minus ten in the same units. The results constrain the reported GeV excess from Fermi-LAT studies, leaving any non-thermal emission tentative.
arxiv-2602-23786:
Yu. D. Fomin reports a solo 2026 computer simulation of liquid carbon, using a machine-learning potential known as GAP-20. The paper is brief, and its core claim concerns the critical temperature of carbon in this model.

The simulation gives a relatively low critical temperature. The author argues that such a low value could shift how lab measurements of the melting point of graphite are read, since the critical point shapes the liquid region near melting. The paper offers a model-based insight rather than a new experiment, and its value rests on how well the GAP-20 potential captures real carbon at extreme heat and pressure.
arxiv-2602-23886:
Joydeep Chandra and two co-authors use persistent homology, a tool from topological data analysis, to map individual mental health journeys in online communities. The 2026 paper argues that community snapshots miss how single users move through distress and recovery over time.

The team models each user's posting history as a path in semantic embedding space, then reads its shape. Loops mark cycling back to similar states, read as stagnation. Flares mark exploration of new coping strategies, read as growth. A new metric, semantic recovery velocity, tracks how fast a user moves away from early distress-focused posts. Across thousands of trajectories from a depression forum, topological features predict self-reported improvement better than sentiment baselines. The work offers interpretable signatures and design ideas for adaptive support platforms with ethical guardrails.
arxiv-2602-23986:
GiBaik Sim and Stephan Rachel identify a microscopic interacting model whose ground state is a p-wave magnet, a newly recognized form of magnetism with odd-parity, time-reversal-symmetric spin splitting in momentum space. The 2026 paper addresses a gap: the phase promises spintronic uses, but the mechanism that stabilizes it was poorly understood.

The authors start from a Hubbard model and derive its low-energy spin Hamiltonian. At the classical level the p-wave magnet is stable yet tied in energy with competing noncoplanar states. Quantum fluctuations break that tie, picking the p-wave magnet as the unique ground state. Its electronic structure shows finite spin accumulation through the Edelstein effect, a handle for spintronic devices. The theory also bears on quasi-two-dimensional honeycomb magnets, supporting spontaneous p-wave magnetism as a real possibility.
arxiv-2602-24086:
Nathanael Jo and two co-authors argue that monoculture in machine learning, the striking agreement of model outputs, is a subjective judgment rather than an absolute property. The 2026 paper shows that claims of excess agreement hinge on two analyst choices that are rarely made explicit.

First, the analyst must pick a baseline null model for what independence should look like, and different null models yield dramatically different inferences about excess agreement. Second, inferences depend on which models and items are included: models that look highly correlated on one question set may look independent on another, or against a different peer group. Tests on two large benchmarks confirm the theory, including a sharp contrast when the null model accounts for item difficulty. Monoculture evaluation, the authors conclude, is a context-dependent inference problem, not a fixed trait of model behavior.
arxiv-2603-00286: Cheng and Basu prove a linear threshold for Oertel's conjecture: some point in a mixed-integer set has every halfspace through it capturing a fixed fraction of the set. Earlier proofs needed an exponential threshold, later cut to polynomial. When the projection holds a box-like ball whose radius grows linearly with dimension, a suitable point exists. Its halfspaces capture nearly a one-over-e fraction. With a larger linear radius, the conjectured fraction follows. Linear scaling is necessary: with sublinear radius, the best fraction can shrink without limit.
arxiv-2603-00386: Fang, Massarenti, and Wu build families for Hilbert quotients of Lagrangian and orthogonal Grassmannians by blowing up the matching isotropic spaces. The result gives smooth toroidal compactifications of maximal rank matrix spaces, symmetric and skew, with simple normal crossing edges that include complete bilinear forms. Over any algebraically closed field they stay smooth and the quotients match complete bilinear form spaces. In characteristic zero they are weak Fano, rigid, and resolve Landsberg-Manivel rational maps.
arxiv-2603-00586: Guo and seven colleagues build WildActor for human video generation that keeps the same person recognisable across shifting shots, viewpoints, and motions, where rivals fixate on faces or freeze poses. Their Actor-18M data set pairs 1.6 million videos with 18 million human images across arbitrary and canonical views. An asymmetric attention design plus viewpoint adaptive sampling reweights reference conditions by marginal utility for balanced coverage. On Actor-Bench the system holds full body identity through varied compositions and large viewpoint shifts, beating existing methods.
arxiv-2603-00786: Singh and five colleagues probe how large scale brain nets reorganise in cognitive decline, where self taught resting state fMRI models learn well but resist reading. BrainInterNet masks set brain nets and rebuilds them from left context, gauging how well nets predict each other and link across nets. Trained on multi cohort data totalling 5,582 recordings and tested on Alzheimer's data, the method finds steady shifts in default mode, limbic, and attention nets. The learned maps also support accurate Alzheimer's spectrum classification.
arxiv-2603-01186: Avram, Adenane, and Halanay analyze multi-strain rumor models with reaction network tools, sorting edge moves through the lattice of fixed faces from minimal siphons. They show calm shifts take relay form. For each distance-one cover, one entry rule governs the home balance's loss of sideways calm and the next one's birth on the next face. The model yields exact ratio rules checked by symbols, while a waning-impulse variant needs Jacobian blocks and Routh-Hurwitz checks for messy cases. This sets relays apart from old cross-critical splits.
arxiv-2603-01486:
A short search term on a food and goods app can mean quite different things at once. Emmanuel Aboah Boateng, Kyle Macdonald, Akshad Viswanathan, and Sudeep Das report a DoorDash case study from 2026 on that puzzle. A word like a flower name might point to a shop chain, a product, or fresh blooms, and a forced single guess often fails.

Their system grounds a large language model in the shop catalog and, for new terms, in live web search. It lists several ranked intents, and fixed business rules then pick how to route the search. On DoorDash search, scores beat both a plain language model and the old live system. The setup now serves most daily searches and can fit other shops that supply their own lists and rules.
arxiv-2603-01586:
Editing one small object in a busy photo is hard when the target is not the obvious focus. Yecong Wan, Fan Li, Chunwei Wang, and colleagues teach an editor to reason about place first in this 2026 work. In scenes with many things, a vague request can point to several spots at once.

Their frame, InterCoG, mixes text thought with visual grounding in turns. It first works out the target place and identity in words, with spatial links spelled out. Next it marks the target with boxes and masks on the image itself. Then it rewrites the edit request to state the wanted result in precise terms. Two training aids sharpen place accuracy and keep the reasoning clear, backed by a new set of annotated edit cases.
arxiv-2603-01786:
Nikita Morozov, Ian Maksimov, Daniil Tiapkin, and Sergey Samsonov find shortest paths with a learning method built to sample good options. Their 2026 work uses Generative Flow Networks, which learn to build objects step by step with odds tied to reward. Shortest paths matter for planning, routing, robots, and many puzzle-like tasks.

The team first proves a key fact for graphs that contain cycles, not just trees. If total flow is minimized, the learned forward and backward routes use shortest paths only. That proof turns pathfinding in any graph into training one such network with a flow penalty. Tests cover permutation puzzles and Rubik Cube solving, a stern test of search. Their solver matches top custom machine learning tools on solution length while using a smaller search budget at test time.
arxiv-2603-02186:
José Liceaga Martínez, Jesús Rodríguez Viorato, and José Carlos Gomez Larrañaga study shape tools on layered spaces in this 2026 paper. Their tool is the discrete Morse function, which tags points of a shape to reveal its form. The best such functions pair off as many points as possible. The spaces here are stratifolds, shapes built from smooth layers of mixed sizes.

The authors give a method that computes best functions fast for a wide class of these spaces. They also pin down when such a function is perfect. A perfect function leaves exactly the points that the shape's core counts demand. No extra critical points remain to clutter the picture. The result links fast computation with a clean test for perfection.
arxiv-2603-02286:
Yaoteng Zhang, Qing Zhou, Junyu Gao, and Qi Wang improve step-by-step object detection in this 2026 paper. A detector must learn new object classes over time without forgetting old ones. Prompt-based methods are cheap and need no replay of old data. Yet linked prompts interfere, drift, and slowly degrade as tasks pile up.

Their framework, PDP, splits prompts into two pools with clear jobs. A shared pool holds general knowledge that transfers across tasks. A private pool holds features that mark each task's own classes. A second module builds class prototypes to label old objects that new data marks as background. That keeps training signals consistent across steps. Scores hit new highs on two major benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-02386:
Caleb Robinson, Nils Lehmann, Adam Stewart, and colleagues present a tutorial on geospatial machine learning in this 2026 paper. Satellite data differs from ordinary photos in ways that break standard workflows. Scenes are huge and georeferenced, and labels come as masks or map shapes. Training and testing also need sampling that respects geography.

TorchGeo is a library built on PyTorch for exactly those needs. It supplies data sets, samplers, transforms, and pretrained models for Earth data. The tutorial walks through its core ideas with code examples. A full case study maps surface water in multispectral satellite images. The trained model is applied to a scene over Rio de Janeiro, Brazil. Predictions are saved as a standard map file for further analysis.
arxiv-2603-02486:
Shadab Choudhury surveys explainable AI for assistive technology in this 2026 paper. People with vision or hearing loss rely on AI to describe images, read documents, and caption speech. Those models are deep networks, so their reasons stay hidden. Explanation tools exist, but they were rarely built for disabled users.

Choudhury reviews human-centered and accessibility-centered explanation research. Almost no work accounts for people with sensory disabilities, the survey finds. Many standard explanations are hard for those users to grasp or even perceive. A visual heat map, for instance, fails the blind users who need it most. The paper maps this perceptual gap in detail. It closes with concrete avenues for accessible, human-centered explanation design.
arxiv-2603-02586:
Hao Li, Huan Wang, Jinjie Gu, and colleagues benchmark AI agents on real-world tasks in this 2026 paper. General agents are spreading into daily use, but benchmarks poorly reflect real user needs. Their benchmark holds just over a hundred scenarios drawn from real requirements. Questions come from social media posts and real products, not synthetic prompts.

A generation method ensures each task is relevant, complex, and verifiable. The full release holds hundreds of tasks split between validation and testing. Models, frameworks, and commercial products were all evaluated on it. Results reveal practical performance levels and clear areas for improvement. The generation process supports continuous updates with fresh real-world queries. Static benchmarks age fast, so that renewal matters.
arxiv-2603-02786:
Noga Alon, Michał Dębski, Jarosław Grytczuk, and Jakub Przybyło ask how short an interval can hold shifted copies of many step-pattern sets. Each set in their 2026 study is an opening stretch of the multiples of some step size, like the even numbers up to a limit. The copies must sit inside one interval without overlapping each other.

They pin down the shortest interval length in two setups: patterns cut off at one shared bound, and patterns each holding the same count of terms. For the full family of steps, the answers grow at rates they determine exactly in order of magnitude. Beyond a threshold family size, a simple linear bound takes over. The results complete the picture for every smaller family size as well.
arxiv-2603-02886:
Guoqing Ma, Xun Lin, Hui Ma, and colleagues hide a face inside a normal picture so fake-face checks can run in private. Their 2026 framework, StegaFFD, responds to a leak risk: face images sent to cloud detectors can be intercepted or mishandled. Blurring or encryption protects privacy but looks suspicious and can erase the subtle traces detectors need.

Steganography instead tucks the face into a natural cover image, and detection runs directly on the hidden version. New modules suppress the cover image's low-frequency bulk and sharpen attention on the faint hidden face features. An alignment step matches hidden-face signals to their raw counterparts. Across seven datasets, the method stayed inconspicuous while preserving detection accuracy better than prior privacy tools.
arxiv-2603-02986:
Alessio Mazzucchelli, Ivan Ojeda-Martin, Fernando Rivas-Manzaneque, and colleagues recolor three-dimensional scenes in about two seconds. Their 2026 system, VIRGi, edits scenes built from 3D Gaussian splats, a fast rendering method that lacks good appearance editing tools. The challenge is keeping view-dependent shine, like specular highlights, correct after a color change.

The method splits color into a flat diffuse part and a view-dependent part, and trains across many viewpoints at once for a cleaner base scene. A user then edits one single image of the scene. Fine-tuning one small network spreads that edit across the whole scene, with a strength control for the shiny effects. Broad tests show clear gains over older radiance-field editors.
arxiv-2603-03486:
Mohammad Alikhani shrinks a network attack detector until it fits the smallest devices. Security monitors at the network edge and in real-time systems have little computing room, so big models are out. His 2026 framework starts from the opposite end: a large Kolmogorov-Arnold Network, a model skilled at capturing complex patterns, is trained first as a teacher on attack data.

Through decoupled knowledge distillation, that teacher trains a tiny plain neural network as its student. The students end up with only a few thousand parameters each, far smaller than the teacher, while keeping high detection performance. On two public testbed datasets, the distilled students beat identical untrained-by-distillation students by several points of F1 score. Alikhani presents the recipe as practical for resource-starved devices and releases the implementation publicly.
arxiv-2603-03586:
Ricardo A Pinto maps the unwanted couplings inside a fully connected star of superconducting qubits. In a star array every transmon qubit talks capacitively to every other, a connectivity that promises faster gates and cheaper error correction. The same web breeds crosstalk: several distinct ZZ-type couplings arise, one per interaction channel, each a path to operating errors. His 2026 analysis studies how two coupling families respond to qubit detuning, the frequency offset that dials interaction strength.

The exchange coupling fades smoothly and steeply as detuning grows. The ZZ couplings behave worse first, spiking where qubit states resonate with states outside the computational basis, then collapsing quickly to zero. That shape defines a safe operational region of near-zero coupling. Pinto derives formulas for both families as functions of detuning, and they agree with direct numerical solutions of the Schrödinger equation.
arxiv-2603-04386: Dembo and McKenzie prove the Gaussian wave is the only typical process on finite cone type trees with mild expansion. Their covariance comes from the Green's function on tree vertices. The result generalizes Backhausz and Szegedy, who proved it for regular trees of degree at least 3. A reduction to inner products with Green's function columns, which are easy to compute, drives the proof. Consequences follow for random bipartite biregular graphs and for generic configuration models including random lifts, where local eigenvector distributions approach the Gaussian wave.
arxiv-2603-04586: Zhuang and colleagues describe NEXUS, a JWST multi-cycle survey near the North Ecliptic Pole. Running across Cycles 3 to 5 during 2024 to 2028, NEXUS holds two overlapping tiers in depth and area. The Wide tier covers hundreds of square arcminutes with NIRCam grism spectroscopy across three annual epochs. The Deep tier covers tens of square arcminutes with NIRSpec spectroscopy for about 10,000 targets over 18 epochs at 2 month cadence, plus imaging per epoch. Primary Deep data, including imaging, spectra, and vetted redshifts, ship in regular Quick Data Releases tracking targeting and status per epoch.
arxiv-2603-04686: Young introduces the augmented van Trees inequality. The augmented form yields tighter minimax squared Bayes risk bounds than the classical van Trees inequality. It also covers priors whose densities need not vanish. The refinement enables elementary minimax lower bound proofs, sometimes with exact constants. As an example, minimax mean squared error for normal-error regression is obtained up to a factor of 1.37 for univariate functions with Lipschitz derivative. Both results escape the classical inequality. The augmented inequality extends beyond Gaussianity and squared error loss.
arxiv-2603-04886: X. Huang and colleagues examine why separating internally generated magnetic fields from external ones grows hard when measurements cover only part of a sphere. With full coverage the split is a standard stable procedure dating to Gauss, but over a subdomain, and without prior assumptions, the authors show no unique separation exists. Assuming exterior sources like magnetospheric and ionospheric currents sit above a source-free shell makes a unique split possible, yet highly unstable.
arxiv-2603-04986: Sirui Huang and team debias step by step recommendation with TIPS, Time-aware Inverse Propensity Scoring. Step by step models guess next contacts from past action order but lean on clear clicks or buys, passing over exposures. Shown, unclicked items read as no care, and unshown items as duds, a picking and exposure bias that links alone cannot crack. Old inverse propensity scoring stays fixed, missing step by step links and time dynamics. TIPS accounts for both, catching tastes better and lifting step by step guides as a plug-in.
arxiv-2603-05186: Nele Callebaut offers master's course notes from the University of Cologne introducing holography, a quantum-gravity approach in which a gravitational theory is described by a lower-dimensional boundary theory without gravity. The course opens with Poincaré and conformal symmetry in quantum field theory, then covers Anti-de Sitter physics and its hints of duality. It then formulates the AdS/CFT correspondence, including finite-temperature cases with black holes and their thermodynamics. It closes with entanglement in AdS/CFT and the idea that gravity emerges from entanglement.
arxiv-2603-05286: Chek-Manh Loi and the rest of the team study minimal-power tracking of objects from stationary locations. The question is how to set individual ranges to optimize energy use. Theoretically, even for straight-line motion at constant speed, no polynomial-time algorithm guarantees optimal reach from a given start. Practically, a geometric algorithm solves the min-max variant minimizing peak power optimally. 500-object, 25-station instances run in seconds for cases playing out over minutes, demonstrating real-time capability.
arxiv-2603-05586: Boyle and colleagues present the TESS All-Sky Rotation Survey, listing periods of variability for 1,046,317 stars with T below 16 within 500 pc. An estimated 93% of these periods are rotation periods, greatly expanding measurements for nearby stars. Half-period alias correction in TESS data reliably recovers 25-day periods from one TESS sector. The survey supports studies of ages, young associations, and Galactic structure, as the biggest homogeneous catalog of stellar rotation periods so far.
arxiv-2603-05786: Jin and colleagues address a trust gap in deployed AI agents, where users must take safety claims on faith. Their answer is proof-of-guardrail, letting developers cryptographically prove a response passed a specific open-source guardrail. Agent and guardrail execute inside a trusted execution environment, which issues a signed attestation any user can verify offline. The authors implement the scheme for OpenClaw agents and measure latency overhead and deployment cost. Guardrail integrity is preserved without exposing the agent, though malicious developers could still jailbreak the guardrail.
arxiv-2603-05886: Das and Sinha describe Casimir-Polder shifts on an excited test atom near a two-dimensional atomic array. Using fourth-order perturbation theory with far-detuned resonance, they derive resonant and off-resonant potentials for the excited test atom. The total potential sums pairwise resonant and off-resonant contributions from array atoms. They analyze asymptotic scaling with separation and dependence on array spacing, size, and dipole orientation. Results bridge a single-atom limit recovering the Van der Waals potential and a macroscopic boundary limit with new tunable scaling laws.
arxiv-2603-06186: Xue and his team put forward SpaCRD, a transfer learning method that fuses histology images with spatial transcriptomics data for cancer region detection across samples, platforms, and batches. Detection leans on morphology in histology images but gives false positives where regions look alike, while transcriptomics adds phenotypes and locations. Current methods fail to join the two sources across platforms. Once trained on source data, SpaCRD works on samples from platforms and batches, built on a fusion network that joins category regularization, variational reconstruction guidance, and bidirectional cross attention.
arxiv-2603-06386: Neau and Falomir build on REACT to propose REACT++, a state of the art scene graph model. Scene graph making encodes visual object links as graphs, promising robot agent reasoning. Real time uses require weighing performance and speed, yet methods target only one objective. REACT++ uses feature pulling plus subject to object cross attention to balance latency and power. It has the highest run speed among older models, lifting relation accuracy while keeping detection scores. Versus REACT, REACT++ is 20 percent faster with 10 percent higher relation scores.
arxiv-2603-06686: Verma and team test w_logCDM, a dark energy model, with DESI baryon acoustic waves, Big Bang forging priors, cosmic clocks, and Pantheon Plus blasts. The joint dataset yields a Hubble constant of 71.02 km per second per Mpc, closer to SH0ES than the LambdaCDM guess, partly easing the Hubble tension. Results show phantom dark energy with mild temporal evolution, while the equation of state remains matching a cosmic constant. The deceleration parameter shifts from slowing to acceleration at mid redshift, and w_logCDM stays strong with it.
arxiv-2603-07086: Kang and colleagues improve cross-domain recommendation by giving each user a flexible profile that adapts to the target domain. Past methods lean on coarse behavior signals and miss how tastes differ within one domain. Their Multi-TAP system captures that within-domain spread through profile modeling, then pulls in source-domain signals only when they fit the target. On real-world data sets, it beats top cross-domain methods, and its code is public.
arxiv-2603-07286: Hsu and colleagues argue that global safety models miss Taiwan-specific risks because their training data lacks Taiwanese Mandarin nuance. Their TS-Bench suite tests models on locally grounded prompts covering fraud, medical falsehoods, bias and political manipulation. Alongside it they offer Breeze Guard, a safety model tuned on human-checked Taiwan-focused data. It beats the leading general safety model of its size on the new suite, with the largest gains on scam detection.
arxiv-2603-07586: Gao and colleagues extend web browsing beyond phone screens with AiRWeb, a phone-plus-AR approach. Users select arbitrary page content and offload it into surrounding space, choosing what to move, when, and how it is arranged. A functional prototype built on standard web technologies covers selection through in-air manipulation. A preliminary study finds the system learnable and usable, while flagging open design challenges around activating offload mode.
arxiv-2603-08286: Wang and colleagues build LAMUS, a sentence-level corpus for argument mining from United States caselaw. The field spots and classifies judicial reasoning parts, such as facts, rules, and analysis, but progress has lagged for want of large annotated sets, for states. LAMUS draws on Texas opinions and Supreme Court decisions, combining case collection, LLM annotation, and checks. As a six-class classification task, it is tested under chain-of-thought, few-shot, and zero-shot prompting, against LegalBERT. It lifts performance. Verification reaches a Cohen's Kappa of 0.85.
arxiv-2603-08386: Bezick and colleagues propose Drone Detection via Harmonic Fingerprinting, a per-pixel temporal framework for real-time drone spotting in event cameras. Spotting fast-moving objects such as drones from event data is hard because the input is sparse and asynchronous. Traditional Discrete Fourier Transforms identify periodic signals from spinning rotors, but they assume uniformly sampled data, which event cameras lack. The method uses analytical techniques that find the frequency signature of drone rotors, marked by frequency combs in their power spectra, beating a YOLO detector on accuracy and latency.
arxiv-2603-08586: Santanu Sinha and colleagues map two-fluid flow in porous rock onto a spin-glass model. Large-scale flow rules have long lacked a firm base in small-scale models, yet droplet patterns turn out to mirror spin patterns. The map yields a phase chart whose glassy side matches flow with hysteresis and wild swings, and its dividing line marks where flow stops rising in step with pressure.
arxiv-2603-08686: Changyan Shi and colleagues derive bright-dark soliton solutions for the coupled Sasa-Satsuma equation. They start from two-bright-two-dark solutions of the four-part Hirota equation, then squeeze them down with parameter limits to the coupled case. The paper closes by mapping and picturing how the one- and two-soliton solutions move.
arxiv-2603-09086: Rongxiang Zeng and Yongqi Dong survey latent world models for self-driving cars and sort a fast-growing field into one shared frame. Their scheme groups designs by what the hidden state holds, from whole worlds and acts to generators, in smooth, token forms, or mixed forms. Five cross-cutting themes link these choices to strength on new roads and safe use. They close with test rules, closed-loop scores, and a cost gauge for slow, careful thought.
arxiv-2603-09386: Lorenzo Mobilia and colleagues test a hybrid gravitational-wave search that joins matched-filtering ideas with convolutional neural networks. Matched filtering stays central for compact binary coalescence signals, but its cost will climb sharply with next-generation detectors like the Einstein Telescope. Their method skips the usual chi-squared rejection test while keeping detection efficiency at or above a standard search. Tests use simulated data with injected signals, Gaussian and transient noise, and effects missing from the template bank.
arxiv-2603-09686: Trambak Jyoti Chall and colleagues summarize the formalism for exclusive dijet electroproduction using generalized parton distributions in collinear QCD factorization. The soft hadronic input is modeled in the double distribution approach, with all leading-order light sea, valence quark, and gluon exchanges included, for light and charm final states. Results cover differential cross sections over a broad phase space. Gluon and sea shapes resemble each other, while the small valence part behaves markedly differently at large momentum fraction.
arxiv-2603-10086: Giancarlo Consolo and coauthors study how inertia shapes vegetation patterns on sloped dry land where plants poison their own soil. Their model extends the Klausmeier equations hyperbolically and adds autotoxicity effects. Near onset, inertia both widens the range where uphill migrating bands appear and slows their travel, and it can flip the regime to subcritical with hysteresis. Far from onset, large travelling pulses take over, traced by simulation and analysis.
arxiv-2603-10186: MengXing Na and coauthors engineer stronger photomagnetism in layered antiferromagnets by doping with nickel ions. Fast optical control of antiferromagnetic spin matters for terahertz spintronic devices, yet strong photo magnetic effects appear in only a few systems. In nickel doped MnPS3, resonant pumping of nickel transitions drives large coherent spin precession while the Néel ground state largely survives. Even modest doping boosts the response over tenfold, with tunable frequency across compositions.
arxiv-2603-10586: Vincenzo Mottola and co-authors speed up tests of how fields scatter from large metasurfaces. These surfaces are arrays of thousands of tiny parts that interact, which makes solvers heavy to run. Their scheme pairs a tailored QR compression with a preconditioner built on the array's geometry. The result is a fast, accurate iterative solver. Tests with surfaces of thousands of particles confirm the method works well, a step toward realistic design studies at full scale.
arxiv-2603-10686: Lukas Mischinger and co-authors review how often, and how well, reviews of diagnostic tests look into why their results differ. They took the hundred most recent published reviews that reported summary sensitivity and specificity. Most did look into the differences, and more did so when more primary studies were at hand. Subgroup checks were the commonest tool, and the bivariate model was used most where a model could be told. Few write-ups set out the plan in full beforehand, so clearer reporting may cut spurious findings.
arxiv-2603-10886: Xing Liu and Axel Gandy propose kernel-based tests for a question standard goodness-of-fit testing cannot answer: whether two distributions are close enough to count as equivalent. Failing to reject a difference may only mean weak power, so their tests flip the setup, treating a meaningful gap as the null hypothesis. Discrepancies come from the kernel Stein discrepancy or maximum mean discrepancy, with critical values from an asymptotic normal approximation or bootstrapping. Simulations gauge how the tests perform.
arxiv-2603-10986: Sumit Kumar Birwa and coauthors build a quantitative theory of why eyeless mutants of the alga Chlamydomonas swim toward or away from light with the opposite sign to wild-type cells. Without a pigmented eyespot, the spherical cell body acts as a lens. It delivers a strong, fast-varying focused signal to the photoreceptor from behind, competing with the slower direct signal. The model shows the flagellar response follows the signal with the higher time derivative. This explains the reversal and predicts bistability in direction choice.
arxiv-2603-11186: Alexander Fagerlund, Christopher Ekman, and Rodrigo Arouca show that Hall physics can appear in an open system that is only weakly time-reversal symmetric, with no magnetic field applied. Both the quantum Hall and anomalous Hall effects normally demand broken time-reversal symmetry. Here a fermionic subsystem breaks it locally, through a self-energy from interactions with bosonic degrees of freedom and a reservoir. The fermions develop a non-quantized Hall conductance. The authors stress that wavefunction renormalization, not just a mass term, is key for the effect.
arxiv-2603-11286: Xiurui Zhao and coauthors probe the hot coronae of active galactic nuclei. Redshift slides the corona's high-energy cutoff into the observable X-ray band. Local studies struggle because the cutoff often sits beyond instrument reach. The team gathered simultaneous NuSTAR and XMM-Newton observations of thirteen radio-quiet nuclei beyond redshift one. Their coronae run cooler, with higher optical depth than local counterparts. Cutoff energy potentially anti-correlates with luminosity and black hole mass. This hints non-thermal electrons may not drive these coronae.
arxiv-2603-11386: Anamika Avinash Pathak and Swastik Bhattacharya study how the temperature of a Schwarzschild black hole fluctuates from place to place near its horizon. They work within Euclidean quantum gravity. They present evidence tying these fluctuations to near-horizon supertranslations, the horizon's symmetry modes. Temperature-dependent corrections to the free energy become polynomial functionals of a supertranslation field at every order. The leading term is proportional to the supertranslation charge. It also drops out of a microscopic state counting. This recasts low-energy horizon physics as a sum over all supertranslations.
arxiv-2603-11686: Mosolova, Candito, and Ramisch argue that word sense induction is still unsolved, even in the LLM era. The task asks systems to discover a word's senses with no labeled data. The team first faults current evaluation: scores can hide weak methods. They build a SemCor-derived test set that keeps the source corpus's polysemy and frequency shape. Embeddings, clustering methods, and a new LLM-based approach all face that test. No unsupervised method beats the plain one-cluster-per-lemma heuristic, though augmentation and Wiktionary data help.
arxiv-2603-11786: Matassa shows that any quantum irreducible flag manifold satisfies an analogue of the Einstein condition. The condition ties the Ricci tensor to the metric with one fixed factor. He proves this at least for a small open interval around the classical value of the quantization parameter. The proof leans on standard constructions tied to these algebras, such as differential calculi and bimodule connections. Those tools were built by earlier authors.
arxiv-2603-11886: Magbool and co-authors survey flexible intelligent metasurfaces, bendable surfaces that reshape their own geometry to steer electromagnetic waves. Rigid arrays tune only the signal; these surfaces add shape itself as a design lever. That lever can sharpen beamforming and focusing and help systems adapt to changing conditions. The article lays out hardware designs, integration paths, and use cases. Case studies pit flexible surfaces against rigid arrays in communication and sensing, showing gains from the added freedom.
arxiv-2603-11986: Zyuzin and Zyuzin study phase stiffness in flat-band superconductors that have nodal pairing. Their model mixes a dispersive band with a flat band in a two-band system. That mixing can open a parabolic node in the flat-band quasiparticle spectrum. At low temperatures the phase stiffness then falls with the square of temperature. The authors also note that plain disorder creates deep subgap states, a sign that such superconductors react strongly to dirt in the material.
arxiv-2603-12086: Bilen and Akyildiz design a knowledge-driven framework for picking small cells in dense 6G networks. Signal-strength rules often leave loads uneven, with more lag, loss, and wasted radio resources. Their setup links knowledge, control, and data planes for adaptive, data-driven choices. Queue-based measures of load and waiting time feed a joint cost tied to latency and packet loss. A light learning model then applies the guided policy at the edge. Simulations show large latency and loss cuts under heavy traffic.
arxiv-2603-12486: Gekhtman, Shapiro, and Vainshtein build a generalized cluster structure on GLn through birational Poisson maps. Earlier work used such maps when aperiodicity held for the Belavin-Drinfeld data at hand. This paper pushes the method into cases where that condition fails outright. Two Cremmer-Gervais solutions to the classical Yang-Baxter equation, linked by conjugation, define the target bracket. A birational map ties that bracket to two others, one on GLn-1 and one on rational functions. New notions of regular pullback and almost-cluster structure support the construction.
arxiv-2603-12586: Yi Xu and co-authors tackle a basic flaw in click-through rate models: features differ wildly in sparsity and content. Item IDs are sparse, while prices are dense, yet most models mix all features at once. Early entry of weak features can add noise and hide strong signals. Their MGDIN groups features by information density at several scales. A masking scheme then holds sparse groups back in early layers. Deeper layers admit them once a firm base is set.
arxiv-2603-12686: Zhikai Zhang and co-authors teach a humanoid robot to play tennis from imperfect human motion data. Full, precise match motion is hard to collect, so their data hold only fragments of basic skills. Those fragments still carry useful priors on how people move. Their LATENT system corrects and composes the fragments into a policy for the robot. On a Unitree G1, the robot struck balls under wide conditions and held multi-shot rallies with human players.
arxiv-2603-12886: Lydia Schönpflug and co-authors set out a protocol to test how staining variation affects pathology models. H&E stain looks differ across labs, which can shift model predictions in hidden ways. Their three steps pick reference stains, profile the test set, then rerun models under simulated reference looks. They built a reference library from the PLISM dataset. As a case, they tested 306 microsatellite instability models on an unseen cancer dataset. Robustness varied widely and linked weakly, in reverse, to raw performance.
arxiv-2603-12986: Simon Popelier and co-authors improve real estate appraisal by learning how to pick comparable past sales. The sales comparison approach is a standard route, also used in automated valuation models. Most systems impose a fixed rule for choosing comparables. Their method learns the selection policy instead, jointly with the price estimator. A hybrid vector and geographic retrieval module adapts across datasets. Careful picks let lean models with fewer comparables match top performance on five datasets.
arxiv-2603-13086: Dominik Erb and co-authors factorize the position-space photon propagator for QED corrections to lattice QCD correlators. Such sums over propagator endpoints grow with the square of the volume, which is costly. A class of integral forms splits the two volume sums apart. One new route writes the scalar propagator as the autoconvolution of a five-dimensional one. Three choices were compared on a real gauge ensemble for vacuum polarization. The work also points to light-by-light sums for the muon g-2.
arxiv-2603-13386: Yuntao Shou, Xiangyong Cao, Qian Zhao, and Deyu Meng work on controllable pathology image generation. Text-guided diffusion gives only coarse global control and cannot enforce fine structural limits. Paired data are also scarce, since labeling gigapixel slides by hand takes far too long. Their multi-agent framework drafts descriptions and diagnostic steps, then judges quality, with human checks for reliability. On that data they build IC-DiT, a layout-aware diffusion transformer with hierarchical attention. Tests on five histopathology datasets showed higher fidelity and stronger layout control than rivals.
arxiv-2603-13686: Soham Ray, Keshav Dhandhania, Victor Barres, and Karthik Narasimhan introduce a benchmark for full-duplex voice agents on real-world domains. Voice agents that listen and speak at once are moving into production, but evaluations split dynamics from task completion. Their framework extends a prior bench with grounded tasks, domain policies, and environment interaction in voice form. A controllable voice user simulator gives diverse accents, realistic audio, and rich turn-taking. Across 278 tasks, a top text model reached 85 percent while voice agents reached only 31 to 51 percent.
arxiv-2603-13986: Brax and co-authors study screening in multi-field scalar-tensor theories with a dilaton and an axion. Screening hides fifth forces near dense bodies so gravity tests still pass. With planetary and stellar density profiles, they find screening without fine-tuning for a light dilaton. The axion's backreaction cancels the dilaton gradient, which cuts the outside scalar charge. Thin shells, by contrast, need not screen at all in this setting. A thinner shell can even leave the fifth force unchanged or stronger.
arxiv-2603-14086: Kats and Heinrich pretrain feature models on 3D medical images to improve image registration. Aligning scans across patients and scanners is hard for intensity-based methods. Their DINO-style self-supervised training runs on medical volumes, not natural photos. The learned features target deformable registration of abdominal MRI and CT scans. The specialized model beats the big DINOv2 model while using far less compute at test time. It also tops established registration models on out-of-domain tests.
arxiv-2603-14186: Ravishankar and co-authors benchmark one-step image generators against multi-step diffusion and flow models under matched settings. Past comparisons mix step counts and guidance settings, which can move scores in opposed ways. Eight models are tested on ImageNet and two further sets, including a new proofread out-of-distribution set. Scores cover FID, Inception, CLIP, and Pick metrics. The team shows that chasing FID alone can mislead in few-step regimes, since guidance tweaks may lift FID while hurting text fit.
arxiv-2603-14586: Ilyankou, Cavazzi and Haworth warn of deception risks in AI navigation chat. Walking directions are shifting from checked geometry to fluent dialogue. Smooth talk can hide manipulation and breed misplaced trust. The authors sort risks in a two-by-two frame by intent and origin. Willful tricks count as dark patterns. Accidental harms count as explainability pitfalls. Seamful design steps can cut both kinds of harm. A neuro-symbolic build, with checked pathfinding under the chat layer, anchors their fix.
