arxiv-2603-14986: Shin and co-authors clean reverberant speech by estimating deep filters from inter-frame correlations. Distant microphones smear speech with echoes tied to the target voice. Simulated training data often fails on real rooms. IF-CorrNet feeds correlations between neighbor frames at each time-frequency cell. A dual-path Transformer turns those features into multi-frame filters. The pairing echoes the normal equation of linear filtering. REVERB tests give top scores on simulated data across four metrics. Real recordings lead on the SRMR measure as well, they report.
arxiv-2603-15186: Liu and co-authors present NavGSim, a Gaussian Splatting simulator for large-scale robot navigation. Navigation paths often cross many rooms or whole floors, which strains rendering and collision checks. A hierarchical splatting framework gives photorealistic scenes over hundreds of square meters. A slicing trick pulls navigable areas straight from the reconstructed Gaussians. The package ships with APIs for scene building, robot setup, training, and evaluation across GPUs. A vision-language-action model trained on its trajectories handled varied navigation queries in simulation and the real world.
arxiv-2603-15286: Samanipour and Poonawala certify safety for nonlinear systems whose controls face polytopic limits and saturation. They build convex barrier certificates on piecewise-affine surrogate models, then verify them facet by facet on the true system. A two-slope leaky ReLU shape for the class-K function trims conservatism. Several certificates merge through a union of invariant sets. Counterexamples trigger local uncertainty updates. On pendulum and cart-pole tests with input saturation, the method certified larger safe sets than linear designs, at tractable cost.
arxiv-2603-15386: Ropero and co-authors present RieMind, an agent that reasons about indoor scenes through an explicit three-dimensional scene graph. Vision-language models still stumble on metric and spatial questions. RieMind splits perception from reasoning: a module builds the graph, and the agent queries it with geometric tools. Tools report sizes, distances, poses, and relations between objects. With graphs built from ground truth, scores on VSI-Bench beat prior work by up to 16 percent. The agent also topped base vision models by wide margins, with no task-specific tuning.
arxiv-2603-15486: Dortmann and co-authors present Cuckoo-GPU, a fast cuckoo filter library for modern graphics processors. Deletion-capable membership structures usually pay a steep speed penalty on GPUs. Their design leans into random memory access to saturate bandwidth instead of chasing cache locality. A lock-free layout uses atomic compare-and-swap, and a breadth-first eviction rule cuts thread divergence at high load. On high-end NVIDIA cards, insert and delete speeds beat the GPU quotient filter by hundreds of times. Query speed rivals even append-only Bloom filters.
arxiv-2603-16186: He and Cai extend a neural solver to the McKean-Vlasov mean-field Fokker-Planck equation. The hard part is a mean-field term, an average over the solution itself. Their pushforward network estimates that average by Monte Carlo sampling. No change to the network design is needed. For a quadratic interaction kernel, the term shrinks to a plain batch mean. Tests in up to 100 dimensions recovered the exact Gaussian solutions. Training took from 27 seconds to 10 minutes on one GPU.
arxiv-2603-16486: Quantschnig and co-authors map Austria's gas and hydrogen networks toward 2040. Their dataset covers transmission lines down to medium-pressure distribution. Hydrogen plans from the grid manager are folded in. Maps from ENTSOG became a clean graph with matched technical data. A new GIS tool, QGas, edits the network graph. The set holds 586 gas pipeline segments over 5,000 km. It adds repurposed and new hydrogen segments too. Storage, electrolyzers, and demand data complete the package.
arxiv-2603-16586: Kaptein, Khan, and Podstavnychy govern AI agents while they run, not before. Agent behavior is path-dependent and hard to fix at design time. Their framework scores each proposed step along the actual path. A policy maps identity, path, action, and org state to a violation chance. System prompts only shape path odds, they note. Static access control ignores the path entirely. Runtime checks form the general case, they argue.
arxiv-2603-16786: Ben Mazziane and co-authors analyze Elastic Sketch, a hash-based tool that counts item frequencies in a data stream. The sketch keeps exact counts for a few elected heavy items and a Count-Min Sketch for the rest. Its accuracy depends on the stream and on an eviction threshold that sets how easily heavy items are replaced. The authors study random stationary streams and derive closed forms for the limiting counter distribution and expected error. These forms make tuning the memory split and threshold practical.
arxiv-2603-16886: Saidd compares nine deep learning architectures for financial price forecasting at several horizons. In all, 918 experiments cover crypto, forex, and equity index markets at 4 hour and 24 hour horizons. A strict protocol fixes seeds, tunes each model once per asset class, then retrains and validates the results. ModernTCN ranked best overall, with a 75 percent first place rate, followed by PatchTST. Rankings formed three clear tiers and stayed stable across horizons. Directional accuracy stayed near 50 percent for every model, so none showed real directional skill.
arxiv-2603-16986: Buck and co-authors study the Gram matrix of Gabor systems built from B-splines. A Gabor system tiles the time frequency plane with shifts of one window function over a lattice. They show that, with the right ordering, certain submatrices of the Gram matrix have a block Toeplitz structure. That structure lets them import spectral results from the theory of Toeplitz matrices. They derive spectral facts for finite sub blocks of the Gram matrix. They then apply the results to systems generated by B-splines of any order.
arxiv-2603-17086: Wang and co-authors build a topological test for comparing brain networks across groups, and apply it to stroke recovery. Persistent homology summarizes network shape, but its features vary a lot between people. The team uses a scale space form of persistence diagrams, built from heat diffusion and Fourier coefficients. On that form, they build a permutation test for group comparisons. Their lesion symptom mapping then finds network cycles tied to levels of speech impairment in post stroke aphasia.
arxiv-2603-17186: Govindappa benchmarks visual embedding models for product search in industrial settings. Finding the exact product instance from a photo matters in maintenance and procurement, where wrong matches cause costly failures. The benchmark tests open source foundation models, proprietary multimodal systems, and domain tuned vision models under one retrieval protocol. Data come from manufacturing, automotive, DIY, and retail use, plus public benchmarks. Scores isolate raw retrieval skill with no cleanup step.
arxiv-2603-17386: Wang and co-authors build PJB, a benchmark for matching people to jobs. Full job posts serve as queries and full resumes as documents. Labels mark domain families and reasoning types, so users see where systems fail and why. The data span six industries and nearly 200,000 resumes. Dense retrieval varied far more across domains than across model upgrades, they find. Reranking helped steadily, while query rewriting hurt.
arxiv-2603-17486: Xie and co-authors model how bubbles form on catalyst surfaces during electrolysis. Their free-energy model predicts the barrier and the size of the smallest stable bubble. It takes in gas level, temperature, pressure, and how the surface wets. The barrier falls fast as gas level rises, with an inverse-square law, they find. Predicted sizes for hydrogen, oxygen, and nitrogen match lab values well. A linked model then caps gas levels at a set current.
arxiv-2603-17686: Gheorghe and co-authors compute maximal positive invariant sets for rank-deficient linear systems. Such sets come from repeated predecessor steps under state and input limits. Feedback can push some closed-loop eigenvalues to zero, which drops the dynamics to lower dimensions. Their algorithm uses the Schur form to handle that singular case head-on. It returns the set in polyhedral form or as constrained zonotopes. Both forms suit control design checks.
arxiv-2603-17886: Argyros, Gonzalez, and Motakis study subspaces of the James-tree space JT and its dual. Every closed subspace of either space holds a complemented copy of l2, they show. JT also holds uncomplemented l2 copies, which splits the picture. Weakly Cauchy sequences that fail to converge hide subsequences shaped like the James basis. Each non-reflexive subspace thus holds a copy of J. Basic sequences sort into l2 or J types along subsequences.
arxiv-2603-18186: Ulmer's thesis builds open-closed string field theory from Calabi-Yau types to aid work on counting curves. Graph sets, A-infinity types, and Kontsevich's cocycle build are linked in part one. A formality map then extends counts from the closed case to the open-closed case. That map rests on a split of the non-commutative Hodge filter. The last part sketches a type-based form of twisted holography at the level of partition sums.
arxiv-2603-18386: Nijhoff and co-authors build integrable systems with PGL(3) symmetry by splitting linear operators. Third-order spectral tasks give plain forms for the key invariants, a rank-3 take on the Schwarzian and cross-ratio. The splits create dual links among spectral tasks that ground exact discrete forms. Both smooth and discrete PGL(3) Boussinesq systems result. A parent PDE set with a Lagrangian form caps the chain of systems.
arxiv-2603-18486: Oshima, Arai, and Hukushima study phase transitions in a modified Ising spin glass with tensor-network sampling. Correlated random bonds make configuration generation costly in this Nishimori-type model. Their scheme samples bonds and spins in a hierarchical, independent way for high precision up to size 256. Results show spin-glass and ferromagnetic transitions split on the Nishimori line, with a Mattis-like phase between. Critical exponents differ from the standard Edwards-Anderson class.
arxiv-2603-19186: Asiaee and Pal tackle a snag in using large health studies to sharpen trial results. Trials are sound but small, while outside studies track partly different traits for each person. Their CALM method maps both sources into one shared space. It then moves outcome models into the trial space and tunes them on trial data. Bounds split the error into parts for mapping, model size, and tuning. On real data, the neural version gives the largest gains.
arxiv-2603-19286: Liao and co-authors predict stock prices from past prices plus the day's financial news. One shared model is trained to serve many stocks at once. News text is encoded by a pre-trained language model. Three attention pooling styles then filter the news by how well it fits each stock's name. The filtered news joins price history as model input. On test data, mean absolute error drops by 7.11 percent against the baseline. The result backs stock-name cues as a news filter.
arxiv-2603-19386: Rege and co-authors synthesize contrast-enhanced MRI scans from plain scans, skipping contrast dye. Dye adds cost and safety risk, yet tumors show up best with it. Their TuLaBM moves between scan types in a learned latent space via a Brownian bridge. A tumor-focused attention step boosts features in the tumor zone during the trip. A boundary loss keeps tumor edges sharp in the output. Tests on brain and liver data beat top baselines on image and tumor scores. The latent design also cuts compute and run time.
arxiv-2603-19486: Goel and co-authors build one network that can be equivariant to many symmetry groups at once. Equivariance helps on geometric data, but most designs fix one group in advance. Their ASEN starts from a full permutation-equivariant base model. A symmetry-breaking input feature then selects the subgroup to respect. Finding such inputs is hard, so they use approximate breaking and 2-closure algorithms. Tests on graph, image, and sequence tasks beat separate equivariant models and a plain model.
arxiv-2603-19986: Zens and Sigman estimate how many migrant deaths on the Central Mediterranean route go unrecorded. Records from the Missing Migrants Project are known to be incomplete. Some deadly incidents are never documented at all. Their Bayesian model builds on multiple-systems estimation with a time-stratified latent-class design. It allows for missing death counts from unseen incidents. Applied to data from 2014 to 2025, it estimates 31,922 to 41,413 total deaths. Recorded data thus capture only about 62 to 81 percent of deaths. Smaller incidents are the most likely to stay hidden.
arxiv-2603-20286: Guo and co-authors rethink retrieval-augmented generation as merging, not just selecting, retrieved text. Standard pipelines keep only top-ranked chunks and lose key bridging evidence. Their MergeRAG framework scores and merges context in two ways. One path joins weak signals, while the other removes repeats with entropy-guided anchors. A layered parallel scheme limits information loss during merging. Tests show gains of up to 13.7 points in F1 over strong baselines.
arxiv-2603-20486: Ghosh and co-authors present COmPOSER, an open-source framework for automating RF circuit design. It turns target specifications into optimized circuits with layouts. The flow unifies schematic synthesis and layout generation. Placement and routing cover both active and passive parts. Physics-based equations mix with machine-learned electromagnetic models. Post-layout checks covered amplifiers running up to 60 GHz in 65nm. Results matched expert manual designs on performance targets. The authors report productivity gains of 100 to 300 times.
arxiv-2603-20586: Liu and co-authors propose Memory-Keyed Attention for long context language models. Large key value caches make training and use costly. Their design stacks three cache tiers: local, session, and long term. A learned router picks where attention should look. A fused variant, FastMKA, merges sources before the attention step. It matched MLA on perplexity in their tests. Training ran up to five times faster, with lower latency at test time.
arxiv-2603-20686: Jung and co-authors present SNAP, a fix for speech deepfake detectors that lean on speaker identity. Modern speech synthesis can mimic real voices with high fidelity. Detectors built on speech encoders often key on who speaks, not on fake cues. The team calls this flaw speaker entanglement. SNAP finds the speaker subspace in the features. It then projects that part out, leaving artifact signals in the rest. Cutting this reliance gave state of the art results in their tests.
arxiv-2603-20786: Boudreault and Levasseur study symmetric separability for states with a conserved global charge. A separable state may fail to split into parts that each respect the charge. They call this the Symmetric Separability Problem. For random states the answer is almost always no. They use number entanglement as a witness of this failure. Most such states sit far from being symmetrically separable. The witness values cluster in a Gaussian shape around a positive mean. They also discuss tasks with superselection rules.
arxiv-2603-20886: Burungale, Skinner, and Wan prove refined non-vanishing results for p-adic logarithms of rational points on abelian varieties. Their work is inspired by a formula due to Bertolini, Darmon, and Prasanna. The main cases involve abelian varieties of GL2 type. These are tied to Hilbert modular newforms and Heegner points. The key tool is the p-adic analytic subgroup theorem. The results address when non-torsion points stay nonzero under the p-adic logarithm map.
arxiv-2603-20986: Manna and co-authors present AutoMOOSE, an agent system that runs phase-field simulations on its own. Phase-field models track how microstructure evolves, but the MOOSE framework needs expert setup and care. Six agents draft inputs, run jobs, review output, and test results against physics laws. On a twenty five task grain growth benchmark, the system wrote valid inputs for all tasks. It finished nineteen runs, and fifteen passed kinetics checks and skeptic review. A thousand run ensemble recovered the target activation energy to within one percent.
arxiv-2603-21186: Yu and Zhong restore the first law of thermodynamics for nonsingular black holes in 2D dilaton gravity. Prior work suggested these black holes violate the first law. They build a broad class of nonsingular solutions with a simple metric form. With the Iyer-Wald method, they derive the correct energy formula. The earlier violation came from an energy that was not the Hamiltonian conjugate to the time translation in use. Under their boundary conditions, the energy matches the Casimir function of the theory, so the first law holds.
arxiv-2603-21286: Chen and co-authors build ReasonDiag, an interactive system for diagnosing errors in chain-of-thought reasoning. Long reasoning traces can hide logical and factual slips, which makes them hard for users to check. Their detection pipeline pairs external fact-checking with symbolic logic validation to flag errors step by step. ReasonDiag shows step distributions and error spread in an arc diagram, plus a node-link view of the flow. In tests and interviews with sixteen users, it helped people find faulty steps and root causes.
arxiv-2603-21986: A team from SII-GAIR and Sand.ai presents daVinci-MagiHuman, a model that generates video and audio in one stream. A Transformer reads text, video, and audio tokens in one sequence, using self-attention only. That plain design trains and serves with standard tools. The model shines on human content: expressive faces, natural body motion, and tight sound sync. It speaks six languages, from Mandarin and Cantonese to German and French. Distillation and a fast decoder cut 5 seconds of video generation to 2 seconds on one GPU.
arxiv-2603-22086: Deruelle and co-authors prove a curvature result for manifolds in all dimensions. Hamilton had conjectured that complete non-compact 3D manifolds with pinched Ricci curvature are flat. Ricci flow recently settled that case. The team proves the analogue in every dimension: such spaces are flat or compact. Their proof uses a new lifting technique for spaces collapsed at infinity. It also gives a Ricci flow curvature estimate without the usual strong positivity demand. An improved gap theorem follows as a further application.
arxiv-2603-22186: Kim and co-authors tackle document-level machine translation with language models. Such models track context well, which should suit whole documents. Two problems hold them back. Large, clean document-level parallel data is scarce. The models also tend to hallucinate or drop content. The team builds new parallel data by converting summaries with a language model. They filter that data with BLEU, COMET, and LaBSE similarity scores. Training then runs in two stages. Sentence-level data comes first, and the filtered document corpus comes second.
arxiv-2603-22286: Nawaz and co-authors speed up video world models with smarter feature caching. Diffusion transformers render video well but cost much per step. Caching reuses features across denoising steps to save compute. Plain reuse treats them as frozen snapshots. That causes ghosting, blur, and motion errors in dynamic scenes. WorldCache instead adapts reuse to the content. It uses motion-aware thresholds and saliency-weighted drift checks. It also blends and warps cached features for a closer fit. It runs 2.3 times faster while keeping 99.4 percent of baseline quality.
arxiv-2603-22486: Tseng studies Virasoro constraints in Gromov-Witten theory for a product variety. Gromov-Witten theory counts curves on a space, and Virasoro constraints are equations those counts must obey. A product variety is built by combining two simpler spaces. Tseng focuses on the case where one factor has semi-simple quantum cohomology. That special structure is what makes the product case tractable here. The note works out the constraints under exactly that assumption.
arxiv-2603-22586: Saha and Shmakov present iAmTime, a foundation model for time series tasks. The model learns from written instructions plus input and output examples shown at test time. It does not need its weights retrained for each new task. Its design pairs a multi-scope transformer encoder with a task-aware patch decoder. Training covers forecasting, filling gaps, sorting, anomaly spotting, and signal splitting. The authors report that iAmTime beats strong rival models on zero-shot forecasting tests. It also matches or beats them on four tasks that are not forecasting.
arxiv-2603-22686: De Sousa and Soares-Pinto derive a master equation for quantum systems with feedback that has memory. Such feedback is called non-Markovian. Their equation is deterministic, not random. It covers a system with general evolution and measurement, plus feedback applied as signal processing. The size of the feedback signal shows how much memory the processing holds. Worked examples show how the equation models memory feedback. They also show feedback with non-trivial frequency response.
arxiv-2603-23586: Dastidar and three co-authors compute magnetic moments of decuplet baryons inside magnetized nuclear matter. Strong fields in hot, dense matter offer a window on quark behavior. Their hybrid method treats quarks as the basic degrees of freedom. It sums valence, sea, and orbital sea quark parts for each baryon. Landau quantization enters the vector and scalar densities of the matter. Effective masses come from a chiral SU(3) quark mean field model. A chiral constituent quark model then yields the moments under the field.
arxiv-2603-23686: Qiao and six co-authors attack fast 3D Gaussian splatting models with doctored input photos. Feed-forward splatting rebuilds a scene from a few views with no per-scene tuning. That speed rests on neural nets, which invite tampering. Their AdvSplat starts with white-box probes that expose core weak points. Two black-box attacks follow, tuning pixel noise in the frequency domain. One estimates gradients, the other needs none, and neither sees the model's guts. Tiny, unseen tweaks wreck the rebuilt scenes across datasets.
arxiv-2603-23886: Wei and co-authors present AgentChemist, a multi-agent robotic platform for chemical experiments. Most lab automation follows rigid scripts and fails on rare or changing tasks. Their system splits work among agents, schedules tasks dynamically, and adjusts control as reactions evolve. Chemical perception tracks the reaction state in real time, and feedback guides each step. They validate the platform on acid-base titration. It tracks progress on its own, adapts dispensing, and completes the full experiment, they report.
arxiv-2603-23986: Abdurro'uf and co-authors present GalSyn, a Python package that makes synthetic galaxy observations from simulations. It builds data cubes for single galaxies particle by particle, which is far cheaper than full radiative transfer. Users choose the stellar models, isochrones, libraries, and mass functions. Dust dimming is modeled along each line of sight. Separate kinematics shift stellar and nebular light for realistic integral field data. The first release covers IllustrisTNG fields, 290 local massive galaxies, and 259 major mergers in 47 filters.
arxiv-2603-24286: Luo studies hidden weak points in higher-order networks built from simplicial complexes. Robustness is often tracked by the smallest positive eigenvalue of the Hodge 1-Laplacian as simplices are deleted. Luo shows that measure is ill-defined, since eigenvalue branches can switch mid-process. He fixes the first branch of the intact complex and follows it through the damage. This branch-consistent measure shows that deleting few triangles can collapse the tracked mode. Graph-level measures stay blind, because the underlying graph never changes.
arxiv-2603-24386: Chen and Wise clarify what Raman phonons do inside optical frequency conversion. Raman phonons are quantized molecular motions from inelastic light scattering, yet most theory treats only the Raman gain spectrum and skips their dynamics. Within a time-domain framework, they show phonons are the oscillating part of the Raman-induced index change. They expose a phonon-mediated coupling between optical fields, then use it to drive conversion into a chosen Stokes order by tuning wave-vector matching. Simulations with realistic dynamics confirm the approach.
arxiv-2603-24486: Karbasizadeh and co-authors study defects in the layered material 4Hb-TaS2 with first-principles math. In this compound, charge moves between Mott-insulating and metallic layers in turn, giving effects such as the Kondo effect and topological superconductivity. The team studies more than 90 defects with large-scale density functional theory. Sulfur vacancies in the metallic layer, tantalum-on-sulfur antisites, and tantalum interstitials emerge as the likely source of defects seen in microscope images. Antisites shift the interlayer charge transfer most strongly, they find.
arxiv-2603-24586: Mittal and co-authors present TRACE, a framework for comparing developer and language model biases in code evaluation. As models increasingly judge code, they should be tested in realistic settings with partial context and ambiguous intent. TRACE measures how well model judges predict human preferences and extracts rubric items that reveal systematic bias. Across chat coding, IDE autocompletion, and instructed editing, the best of 13 models trail human annotators by 12 to 23 percent. TRACE finds 35 significant sources of misalignment, most tied to known code quality criteria.
arxiv-2603-24786: Gafarov and Ura refine cluster-robust inference for regression. With a small number of clusters, the normal approximation for t-statistics can be poor. Their critical value comes from a conditional Cramér-Edgeworth expansion. It guarantees third-order refinement and needs no resampling, being a closed-form function of score skewness and kurtosis. Simulations show the proposal improves size control with as few as ten clusters. The method keeps standard practice while correcting its small-sample distortion.
arxiv-2603-24986: Chung, Xu, and Pollack argue that health AI should help a whole care team, not one user alone. Most tools serve a patient, a caregiver, or a clinician in isolation. That split view can hide facts and pull goals apart. The authors use a made-up but expert-checked case of a child with kidney disease. In it, missed doses trace back to poor shared awareness, not missing facts. They sketch design rules for AI that shares context and aligns goals while people keep final say.
arxiv-2603-25086: Pramanik links market control math to quantum-style path integrals. He studies best firm behavior in an economy with market clearing, Pareto efficiency, and rival firms in feedback play. His Euclidean path-integral method skips the hard step of building a value function. Best policies come from a smooth Ito process built with integrating factors. This helps when the standard Hamilton-Jacobi-Bellman route is too hard to run. He derives a feedback Nash equilibrium in this frame. Examples contrast it with mean-field and classic maximum-principle results.
arxiv-2603-25186: Jakobsen and co-authors make fake patient data for psychiatry research without touching real records. Privacy rules keep real psychiatric tables locked away, which slows AI work. Their method steers a language model with text pulled from the DSM-5 and ICD-10 manuals. It builds synthetic tables for six anxiety disorders. Rivals trained on real data still win on some traits. But the guided model matches pairwise structure well and posts the lowest pair error in two disorders. Checks show low linkage risk, near the best rival.
arxiv-2603-25286: Mitchell and Wild study negative avoiding sequences, a cut-down form of de Bruijn sequence. These periodic strings over a finite ring never repeat a block of length n in one period. If a block does appear, its negative must not. Such sequences may serve location tasks. The pair sets a simple cap on the period length. Sequences that reach the cap are called maximal. They then prove maximal ones exist for every alphabet size from three up and every block length from two up.
arxiv-2603-25386: Zabel and co-authors map the hydrogen gas in the dwarf galaxy UGCA 320 with the MeerKAT array. The galaxy is the largest of three dwarfs in one group, all gas-bearing. Motion fits show at least a fifth of its gas moves in odd ways. A third of that odd share likely comes from a tidal tug by neighbor UGCA 319. Star birth seems to drive an outflow too. A tenth of the gas floats above the disk in threads. Deep views show how much company shapes a small galaxy.
arxiv-2603-25586: Domingo shows that several families of asymptotically rigid mapping class groups split into clean algebraic pieces. Each family turns out to be a quotient of the fundamental group of a graph of groups. Ordinary mapping class groups sit at the vertices and edges as stabilizers. Building on work by Labruère and Paris, he turns that split into explicit presentations for these groups. Generators and relations are written out in full. The result gives surface symmetry groups a concrete handle.
arxiv-2603-25686: Erzurumlu, Kwag, and Yilmaz present Just Zoom In, a new way to locate a street photo on a map. Most methods match images by retrieval in an embedding space. Their model instead zooms step by step over a city-scale satellite map. It starts wide and picks finer cells until it reaches the target resolution. The method needs no contrastive loss or hard negative mining. The authors also build a benchmark from crowd-sourced street views. They report gains of 5.5 and 9.6 percent in recall within 50 and 100 meters.
arxiv-2603-25886: Bhandari and co-authors study how sweep quality affects AI reading of obstetric ultrasound. Blind sweeps let lightly trained workers record standard fetal scans for AI review. Small protocol slips could skew the AI results, yet this risk was untested. The team simulates reversed sweeps, probe inversion, and incomplete sweeps. They measure the effect on three tasks, from sweep tagging to placenta location. They also train quality models that flag these faults. A feedback loop that re-acquires flagged sweeps improves downstream scores, they report.
arxiv-2603-25986: Morley, Lehmberg, and Kong test how well trait evolution methods cope with hybrid family trees. Standard comparative methods assume a simple branching tree. Hybridization breaks that assumption and can distort results. The team simulates trait growth on many network shapes. They then run tree-based methods for ancestral states, rates, and model choice. Performance is subpar across the board, they find. Frequent or recent hybridization hurts most, above all with fast traits and transgressive events. The authors offer guidance for researchers facing such tangled histories.
arxiv-2603-26086: Liyanage and co-authors present a software tool for working with solar radio burst data. The e-CALLISTO network runs over 150 stations and produces large FITS archives. The data suffer interference, noise, and mismatched frequency setups. Bursts also split across 15-minute frames. Their analyzer merges frames in time and frequency into one spectrum. It subtracts background, lets users mask burst regions, and fits drift rates with power laws. For one Type II burst at Arecibo, it found a shock speed of 449 kilometers per second.
arxiv-2603-26186: Zhang and co-authors segment heart scar tissue in MRI scans with a staged learning method. Late gadolinium scans reveal scar in the left atrium, tied to fibrillation severity. Low contrast and loose labels make automatic maps unreliable. Their three-stage design follows the clinical workflow. A first model learns the atrial cavity. A second learns how cavity shape relates to scar patterns, and a final pass refines the scar map. A weighted loss keeps predictions on plausible wall regions. Scar Dice reaches 0.50, beating a one-stage model.
arxiv-2603-26286: Singh and co-authors propose proofdoors, a new measure meant to explain why CDCL solvers run fast on some hard formulas. A proofdoor splits clauses into chunks linked by a chain of interpolants. Each interpolant acts as a short summary passed to the next chunk. The team proves that small proofdoors yield short resolution proofs that a set form of CDCL can find fast. They show floating-point addition miter formulas have small proofdoors, despite their large pathwidth.
arxiv-2603-26386: Cervantes-Villanueva and co-authors study coherent exciton oscillations in a single layer of tungsten disulfide. They run a first-principles time-dependent GW-Bethe-Salpeter calculation for the coupled A and B excitons. Under a linearly polarised pump, the coupling drives clear oscillatory motion between exciton states. A simple effective model explains the pattern they find. Their work also reads a recent experiment on the same material, and they propose a pump-probe scheme to create and renew the oscillations on demand.
arxiv-2603-26986: Minotti and Modanese couple a scalar-tensor gravity extension to Aharonov-Bohm electrodynamics with bosonic matter. A scalar mode from the vector potential makes the field's energy-momentum trace nonzero. That induces an electro-gravitational coupling, amplified by a second gravity scalar. In superconductors, the large-scale wavefunction creates the scalar already at semiclassical level. The coupled system admits a saturation solution and a threshold for large effects. Scaling laws for anomalous signals match threshold behavior in two discharge setups.
arxiv-2603-27086: Park and co-authors present EFlow, a fast way to train few-step video generators from scratch. EFlow learns a solution flow that jumps a noised state from one time to another. A gated local-global attention block cuts per-step compute and tolerates random token dropping. A cheaper guidance path and a mean-velocity regularizer keep quality at very low step counts. Training throughput rose up to 2.5 times over standard solution flow. Inference latency fell by a factor of 45.3.
arxiv-2603-27286: Wang and co-authors bring prospect theory into pursuit-evasion differential games. Players misjudge uncertainty through risk aversion and skewed probability weighting. Cumulative prospect theory supplies the behavioral models for both sides. Conditions for capturability are derived in terms of bias levels. The resulting CPT-Nash equilibrium is studied with fixed-point logic. Bias helps the pursuer in some regimes and the evader in others. Some captures that rational players cannot achieve become possible for biased ones. The results ground human-machine control design in such terms.
arxiv-2603-27486: Pachika and co-authors gauge how COVID-19 changed travel demand in Houston. They count cars in high-grade satellite images. A Detectron2 model with Faster R-CNN does the counting. Sites include campuses, malls, plazas, eateries, and supermarkets. Counts from 2019 and 2020 are compared site by site. Car counts fell by about thirty percent on average in 2020. The team argues satellite views give rich demand signals. Such signals can guide transport planning.
arxiv-2603-27586: Kim and Lavaei design one estimator that handles two kinds of disturbance. Calm zero-mean noise suits mean-based fits best. Sparse attacks with bias need median-based fits instead. Their Huber estimator bridges the two with one threshold. It learns a system matrix from a single run of data. Error falls as one over the square root of run length. That rate holds for symmetric noise or linear basis terms. Under attacks below half the time steps, error stays bounded.
arxiv-2603-27886: Biryukov and co-authors present Mat3ra-2D for realistic 2D material design. AI models train mostly on ideal bulk crystals. Real devices hinge on surfaces, defects, and interfaces. Their open framework builds slabs and mixed interfaces fast. Disorder and defect complexity are supported throughout. Standards govern data storage and exchange. Builder pipelines keep provenance for each structure. Browser-ready notebooks lower the entry bar.
arxiv-2603-28386: Sygkounas and four co-authors let language models invent both training worlds and the policies that learn in them. Static training sets cap how far agents can generalize. Their COvolve frames world-building and policy-writing as a two-player zero-sum game, each side written as Python code. The duel creates its own rising curriculum. A Nash equilibrium mix over past policies guards against forgetting. Tests span city driving, mazes, and geometric navigation, with worlds growing steadily harder.
arxiv-2603-28886: Bacellar studies how to fuse graph and vector scores for multi-hop question answering. Dense similarity scores and graph scores like Personalized PageRank have unlike spreads, so they are hard to compare. His method, PhaseGraph, maps both to a unit free scale with percentile rank normalization before fusion. On MuSiQue and 2WikiMultiHopQA, calibrated fusion improved held out last hop retrieval. Against the official HippoRAG 2 pipeline, results split by cutoff, ahead at one and behind at another. Ablations suggest percentile calibration is more robust than min-max scaling.
arxiv-2603-28986: Legrand and co-authors introduce Mimosa, a multi-agent framework for autonomous scientific research that evolves over time. Current research systems use fixed workflows and toolsets, which limit adaptation. Mimosa synthesizes task specific multi-agent workflows. A meta-orchestrator generates workflow shapes, and code generating agents run subtasks with tools. An LLM based judge scores each run, and its feedback refines the workflow. The system uses the Model Context Protocol for tool discovery. On ScienceAgentBench, Mimosa reached a 43.1 percent success rate, beating single agent and static multi-agent baselines.
arxiv-2603-29186: Matsuda and co-authors propose SLVMEval, a benchmark for judging text-to-video evaluators. The benchmark checks evaluators on videos up to about three hours long. The team degrades source videos in controlled ways across ten quality aspects. That creates clear high-versus-low quality pairs. Crowd workers kept only pairs where the drop was easy to see. Humans picked the better video with 84.7 to 96.8 percent accuracy. Evaluator systems fell short of humans on nine of ten aspects.
arxiv-2603-29486: Hooft and co-authors improve the Ghent Hybrid model for single-pion production in neutrino scattering. This process adds much to the total neutrino-nucleus cross section in accelerator experiments. They aim for a better Delta-region fit with few free parameters. A multipole breakdown lets them use K-matrix theory on background terms. Watson's theorem is enforced across all multipoles. Delta decay width and form factors are adjusted to match. New rho and omega exchange diagrams are added. The changes improve the Delta peak fit against data.
arxiv-2603-29586: Pinter and co-authors present a stochastic control method for home battery scheduling. Smart scheduling can cut power costs and aid grid resilience. The catch is uncertain home use and solar output. Instead of fixed power setpoints, their method optimizes power intervals. The battery can then respond inside set bounds as conditions change. Mixed random variables, part discrete and part continuous, model the uncertainty. Tests used real data from 15 homes over five months. Their controller posted the lowest costs against benchmarks.
arxiv-2603-29886: Jiao, Murali, and Afroogh warn that AI empathy can erode young users' thinking independence. Mirroring a user's feelings can slide into affective sycophancy. It lends false weight to passing anxieties and cuts needed mental friction. Training rewards shaped by adult raters may deepen the problem. Such rewards can foster emotional dependence instead of healthy reappraisal. The authors propose stoic designs built on functional neutrality. Those designs aim to protect autonomy in younger users.
arxiv-2603-29986: Varner presents ParetoEnsembles.jl, a Julia package for fitting models against several goals at once. A single best fit hides trade-offs when datasets conflict. His package builds ensembles that map those trade-offs instead. Its simulated annealing method needs no gradient data. Fixes include strict Pareto dominance and cheaper ranking steps. Multi-chain parallel runs widen front coverage. Tests cover gene expression and blood clotting models. Held-out clotting data is predicted within ten percent.
arxiv-2604-00086: Lee and four colleagues introduce HIVE, a framework that fuses vision-encoder layers with a large language model through hierarchical cross-attention instead of flattening image embeddings. A three-stage schedule aligns the encoder with the language model step by step, steadying optimization and improving gradient flow. The approach tops self-attention baselines on image classification and vision-language benchmarks including MME, GQA, OK-VQA, and ScienceQA.
arxiv-2604-00186: Gupta and Kumar apply task exposure analysis to agentic AI, systems that complete whole occupational workflows rather than single subtasks. They build an Agentic Task Exposure score from O*NET task data, combining capability scores, workflow coverage, and adoption speed. Across five major United States technology regions over 2025 to 2030, 93.2 percent of 236 occupations cross the moderate-risk line in top-tier regions by 2030. The pair also spot seventeen emerging occupation types gaining from reinstatement effects, centered on human-AI teamwork, AI governance, and domain AI work.
arxiv-2604-00486: Saleh and Maiti build a theory of electronic Raman scattering from two-dimensional metals without inversion symmetry. Losing inversion symmetry breaks SU(2) symmetry, splitting electronic states at the Fermi level by spin-orbit coupling of Dresselhaus, Rashba, or Ising type. That splitting allows spin-flip excitations and chiral-spin modes, and adds a direct spin-photon interaction. The authors show their scattering probe reaches spin excitations with no need to tune the laser to an internal resonance, unlike conventional Raman theory.
arxiv-2604-00886: Wang and colleagues propose PixelPrune, a method needing no training that cuts visual tokens for document work and interface use by dropping repeated pixels. Across benchmarks, only 22 to 71 percent of image patches are unique, with the rest exact duplicates. Pruning redundant patches before the vision transformer speeds the whole pipeline. Tests show competitive accuracy with inference up to 4.2 times faster and training also accelerated.
arxiv-2604-00986: Tang and colleagues ask whether phone-use agents respect privacy on benign mobile tasks, introducing MyPhoneBench, a verifiable evaluation framework built on a minimal privacy contract called iMy. Privacy-respecting use means permissioned access, minimal disclosure, and user-controlled memory, checked by mock apps and rule audits. Across five frontier models on 10 apps and 300 tasks, no model leads on all three: task success, privacy-compliant completion, and later use of saved preferences. The most persistent failure is filling optional personal entries the task does not require.
arxiv-2604-01486: Yildiz studies finite binary algebras, not necessarily associative, where every bracketing on n variables determines an n-ary term operation. This produces arrays of evaluation words. He shows the structure of these arrays is governed by the translation monoid of left and right translations. Context maps are the elements of the translation monoid, so every element occurs as a block map. He proves rank defines a chain of ideals in the translation monoid, that minimum-rank elements form a minimal ideal, and that Green's J-classes lie in rank layers.
arxiv-2604-02086: Dewan, Gupta and Mishra pin down a Ramsey number pitting a complete bipartite graph against even cycles. They prove the Ramsey number for K 2,n versus an even cycle equals that for K 1,n, settling the exact value across the even range. The equality is striking because the denser graph might be expected to force a larger threshold. The result leads them to ask how the pattern extends when the cycle and bipartite sizes vary.
arxiv-2604-02286: Xu and Ma model how microbial interaction networks rewire with host and environmental factors. Their TRECOR framework treats microbiome counts through a latent normal distribution on a phylogenetic tree, with mean and spread both tied to covariates. Covariance splits into a sparse stable baseline plus a low rank covariate shift. Full conjugacy yields efficient Gibbs sampling. In simulations TRECOR beats covariance regression on transformed counts, and in gut data from 531 people across three countries, age emerges as the largest driver of covariation.
arxiv-2604-02386: Salazar derives closed form formulas for coprime counts of even numbers dodging a prime. They use a remainder rule, step functions, and minimal answers of two congruences, with the key answer found via Euclid method. The count proves piecewise affine along arithmetic runs, ruled by residue classes modulo two values. After two residue values are set, each check needs only a handful of steps, against linear counting. Checks match brute force counts exactly.
arxiv-2604-02786: Zhuang and four colleagues present QuadAgent, a training-free agent system steering agile quadrotor flight with vision and language. High-level reasoning runs apart from low-level control in an asynchronous multi-agent design: foreground agents handle live tasks and commands, while background agents reason ahead. An Impression Graph of sparse keyframes holds scene memory, and a vision-based avoidance network keeps flight safe at speeds up to 5 meters per second indoors.
arxiv-2604-02986: Ono and four colleagues attack reward hacking in reinforcement learning from human feedback, where chasing a proxy reward lets true quality stall or fall. They blame flipped advantage signs, which raise a bad response's likelihood instead of lowering it. From an adversarial perturbation of reward-model parameters, they derive a certified sign-preservation radius: the smallest perturbation that can flip a sign. Their SignCert-PO method down-weights non-robust completions in policy updates. On TL;DR and AlpacaFarm benchmarks, it beats baselines on win rate while cutting reward hacking.
arxiv-2604-03086: Rajkumar and colleagues bridge delay dynamics and finite Koopman learning, giving explicit error bounds for the learned predictor. Their method cuts system history into steps, uses kernel-based mode decomposition, and splits total error across history steps, kernel fitting, and regression. A kernel rebuild step recovers states from lifted coordinates, and tests show steady prediction of nonlinear delay systems.
arxiv-2604-03486: Liu and colleagues present VisionClaw, an always-on AI agent that runs on Meta Ray-Ban smart glasses. It watches the world through the glasses and lets wearers start tasks by voice, from adding objects to an online cart to making notes from paper documents. A lab study of 12 people and a field study of 5 found quicker task times and less hands-on effort than non-agent baselines.
arxiv-2604-03886: Arthur Amorim and colleagues built Platum, a framework that turns high-level drone protocol specs into verified runtime monitors. MAVLink lacks checks on whether message sequences make sense in context, leaving autopilots open to stealthy ill-timed commands. Platum needs only five semantic pieces per session type, checks them with reflective procedures in Meta-F*, and compiles them into flat allocation-free C state machines. Tests in ArduPilot simulation cut monitor latency fourfold versus the earlier DATUM system.
arxiv-2604-03986: Anh Dau and colleagues built COBOL-Coder, a domain-adapted language model for COBOL generation and translation. An automated pipeline curated training data with compiler-guided validation and multi-stage similarity filtering. Fine-tuned on that data, COBOL-Coder hit up to 73.95 percent compilation success on COBOLEval, against 41.8 percent for GPT-4o. Java-to-COBOL translation beat general models, which scored near zero, and developer surveys praised its enterprise fit.
arxiv-2604-04186: Sujoy Bhore and team opened the study of Steiner DAG covers, where cover DAGs may include extra Steiner points. Earlier work on general digraphs set the stage for this structured-graph study. The authors showed that any digraph of treewidth tw admits a Steiner cover with stretch 1 using just 2 DAGs, and planar digraphs admit a near-exact cover with 2 DAGs. They also proved a sharp gap: non-Steiner covers for treewidth-1 graphs with stretch below 2 and sub-quadratic extra edges need at least logarithmically many DAGs.
arxiv-2604-04386: Fu, Heddaya and Tan build a pipeline that auto-generates hard math benchmarks from hypotheses about model errors. Most math benchmarks need heavy manual effort and scale poorly. Prior auto-generation rarely targets specific weak concepts and skills. The new pipeline uses AI hypotheses to pinpoint weak concepts and skills, then makes fresh problems for those weaknesses. Problems from the best hypotheses cut Llama-3.3-70B-Instruct accuracy to as low as 45 percent, against 77 percent on the original MATH benchmark. The pipeline also adapts beyond math to probe other capabilities.
arxiv-2604-04586: Balmaseda-Marquez and five colleagues use orbital angular momentum waves to boost a computational imaging system. Adding multiple orbital angular momentum waves to a frequency-diverse system greatly widens its measurement modes and cuts the bandwidth needed for high-quality images. A Ka-band prototype built from two metalized 3D-printed cavities holding fully dielectric transmitarrays validates the approach. Imaging tests show better quality with multiple orbital angular momentum waves, most clearly for complex spread-out targets. Accurate images need only one eighth of the frequency-diverse system's operational bandwidth.
arxiv-2604-04686: Siboni clarifies a step textbooks often rush in policy gradients: the REINFORCE estimator's full return swapped for reward-to-go via causality. The claim is correct, he notes, but accounts leave unclear where the past-reward terms go. His paper isolates that step, deriving it cleanly from the score-function identity applied to prefix trajectory distributions. Reward-to-go then falls out once the objective is split over prefixes. The estimator does not change; causality returns from the derivation, not an extra heuristic added after the fact.
arxiv-2604-04886: Pandey and Adhikari build a neutrino model under Z4 symmetry in a Type I seesaw setting. It uses only three complex Yukawa parameters plus one mass for heavy right-handed neutrinos near the electroweak scale. That spare set reproduces mass-squared differences, mixings, and the CP-violating phase within three sigma. Adding three real parameters from soft-symmetry breaking terms, they make the lightest right-handed neutrino a dark matter candidate through freeze-in. The two heavier neutrinos, decaying, can generate the universe's matter excess through resonant leptogenesis.
arxiv-2604-05086: Lei, Carrasco, and Escudero define sample entropy for graph signals, spreading a conditional measure to data on networks. Permutation entropy was lately extended to graph signals, opening new fields for high-dimension systems evolving on networks. Yet measures remain rooted in Shannon entropy and symbol dynamics. The authors explore whether and how sample entropy can be defined for graph signals. They test whether it can characterize nonlinear dynamics of data. Their SampEnG generalizes sample entropy from one-dimensional signals, including time series, using topology-aware embeddings.
arxiv-2604-05186: Iguro extends the b to c sum rule to include Bs to Ds and Xib to Xic decays, giving more cross-checks. The rule checks b to c tau events for gaps. Both heavy quark rule and SU(3) flavor rule are broken in reality, so the break size must be measured. Chiral theory suggests a small break, and number work finds it smaller than lab error. He therefore constructs more new-physics-free sum rules for checks.
arxiv-2604-05386: Leuenberger and four colleagues study a neglected side of migration: times people choose or are forced to go without phones, information, or connectivity. Interviews with 32 people in migration in El Paso, Texas, from February to May 2025, map device, message, and protective forms of non-use. Non-use shifts across phases of understanding, negotiating, and resolving a transition. It serves as a shield against risk and as a mark of being shut out by systems. The authors close with design principles that treat non-use as normal, not a failure.
arxiv-2604-05586: Xu, Ullah, and Yang boil topological-material hunting down to a physics-informed chemical rule built on makeup, orbitals, and crystal shape. A linear score codes electron fill and orbital settings, letting the rule tell apart twins that share makeup but not structure. The model scores well, stays clear, and spots candidates where symmetry checks fail.
arxiv-2604-05686: Devi and three colleagues study a static spherical black hole wrapped around a global monopole. Strong-field deflection and shadow size grow with the monopole parameters, stable circular orbits shift outward, and electromagnetic ringing damps more slowly as the parameter rises. Matching EHT views of M87* and Sagittarius A* constrains the allowed parameter pairs.
arxiv-2604-05786: Depian and three colleagues study realizing planar linkages inside open polygonal domains. They show XP membership and W[1]-hardness in graph size even with unit edges and no fixed vertices. Path linkages with fixed endpoints stay NP-hard in general, but a linear-time algorithm handles three-edge paths in convex domains.
arxiv-2604-05986: Elhag and Chai test whether fermion density profiles can stand in for entanglement in particle scattering, using Thirring-model fermion scattering as a test bed. Quantum convolutional networks match or beat classical nets of like size, converging faster with less variance. Bigger models do not help, and a compact four-qubit quantum net wins, so trainability and encoding choice matter more than scale.
arxiv-2604-06286: Inoue and five colleagues present CHRONOS, a cryogenic sub-hertz cross torsion-bar detector with a quantum non-demolition speed meter, built to open the 0.1 to 10 hertz band. That band is blocked by seismic, Newtonian, and suspension thermal noise. CHRONOS pairs cryogenic torsion-bar test masses with a Sagnac readout, suppressing quantum radiation-pressure noise and enabling quantum non-demolition measurements below one hertz. This opens a window between LISA and ground-based interferometers, targeting intermediate-mass black hole binaries, stochastic background searches, and macroscopic quantum tests.
arxiv-2604-06786: Wang and thirteen colleagues link an October 2024 geomagnetic storm to sympathetic solar eruptions. Interacting mass ejections often drive big storms yet blur their solar origins. Observations show a quiescent filament and an active-region eruption firing together, producing two of them. A spheroid shock model fits the shock where they overlap in coronagraph view. The pair had finished impulsive acceleration before entering that view. Compressed southward fields drove the storm. The trailing one kept flux-rope character, while the leading one distorted between Wind and STEREO-A.
arxiv-2604-06986: Siebenmorgen and four colleagues report the third part of a large sky survey of starlight bent by dust grains between stars. Dust in thin space is still poorly known in shape, make up, size mix, and how its grains line up, yet those traits shape how starlight dims and bends. The team studied ninety six dimming curves and new bent light spectra for sixty stars, joined with star distance data and heat glow maps. They fit a three part dust model that matches the varied spectra well.
arxiv-2604-07486: Ma and Rajtmajer propose RPSG, a method for making realistic synthetic copies of private text while keeping privacy. Large language models excel at synthetic data, but private-text replication demands a careful balance of privacy and utility. RPSG starts from private seeds and uses privacy-preserving tactics, including a formal differential-privacy rule in picking outputs. Broad tests against leading private synthetic-data methods show RPSG achieves high closeness to private data while providing strong safety.
arxiv-2604-07586: Vakhnovskyi presents IOGRUCloud, a large-scale three-tier IoT platform for auto greenhouse climate control. The design splits field-level sensing and action, site-level planning, and cloud-level tuning. It enables growing self-rule from rule-based to fully self-run use. A Vapor Pressure Deficit control loop governs heat and moist air with GRU-aided PID tuning, cutting manual tuning effort by 73 percent. Deployed across 14 houses spanning 47000 square meters, the platform cuts energy use by 23 percent and lifts climate calm by 31 percent.
arxiv-2604-07886: Sakata and four colleagues study how language models encode hierarchical relations like Japan within Eastern Asia within Asia. Building on linear relational concepts, they train linear maps for each depth and semantic domain and compare them to map representational differences. Unlike prior work, the analysis covers multi-token entities and cross-layer patterns. Across several domains, ranked relations prove linearly recoverable from internal patterns within a domain. The team also tests generalization to unseen data and transfer across domains.
arxiv-2604-08386: Guadagnuolo and four colleagues give a sharp test for whether shrinking a network keeps its dynamics intact. They prove that harmonic morphisms, maps that preserve harmonic functions, are the least condition under which random walks on the fine network project exactly onto walks on the coarse one. Laplacian shrinking, they find, sometimes meets the condition exactly, a fact that a standard entropy based check misses.
arxiv-2604-08786: Rahman defines Script Fidelity Rate, a reference free metric catching a failure word error rate misses: speech models producing fluent output in the wrong writing system. Measuring script collapse across ten languages, six writing systems, and ten models on FLEURS, he finds 21 of 100 model language pairs collapse, 20 involving Whisper and one Gemma 4 on Urdu. Script aware prompting lifts mean fidelity to 97.7 percent in a Gemma probe, fixing Urdu collapse and recovering translation quality.
arxiv-2604-08886: Md Awsaf Alam Anindya and four colleagues propose ToxiShield, a real time browser add on that spots and cleans toxic code reviews in open source work. Three modules handle harshness spotting, argued multi type sorting, and review cleaning. A fine tuned BERT binary sorter reaches 97 percent F1 on 38,761 review texts. Claude 3.5 Sonnet reaches 39 percent MCC and 42 percent F1 on multi type samples, and a fine tuned Llama 3.2 cleaner reaches about 95 percent style transfer score with 97 percent fluency. Checks with ten coders suggest a more welcoming space.
arxiv-2604-08986: Oh and five colleagues tackle persona prompting's robustness-fidelity trade-off. Assigning a character steers a language model, but the best persona costs time to find and its quality effect stays unclear. Prior fixes search prompts at inference, adding compute. Training with verifiable rewards dulls persona sensitivity and flattens expression in role-play. Their PerMix-RLVR method mixes personas during training, preserving robustness to shifts and faithful adoption where needed. It lifts persona stability by about 21 percent on MATH500 and fidelity by about 11 percent on PersonaGym.
arxiv-2604-09086: Datta contrasts chaos in finite and endless systems through the Kuramoto-Sivashinsky equation, the Lorenz system, and a Wilczak Lorenz-type reduction of the former. Tests of that equation show built-in space-time chaos, with mess growing at once in space and time. By contrast, the Lorenz system and the Wilczak version show simple time-only chaos without spatial detail. The contrast splits two kinds of chaos: one woven through space and time, the other kept to time alone.
arxiv-2604-09286: Hird and Livingstone propose an adaptive MCMC method that learns a linear preconditioner dense off-diagonal yet sparse in form. That sparsity yields step cost of order m squared times d, against order d squared for existing methods that capture correlation. Diagonal preconditioning costs only order d per iteration but fails when the target is highly linked. Their version uses target covariance clues inferred via online PCA, built from a diagonal matrix and reflection matrices.
arxiv-2604-09486: Boiardi, Marchello, Santucci, Riccobelli, and Noselli present a 3D model for polyelectrolyte hydrogel threads under an electric field. The build rests on a morphoelastic plan for stiff, unbending rods. Thread motion is coded in field-driven natural bends, while fluid effects use a local Stokes estimate. The plan studies a thread with oval cross-section fixed at its base. Under a steady even field lined up with its axis, the thread flutters past a set strength, with flat or 3D lasting swings in simulations.
arxiv-2604-09586: Rost proposes LLM-mediated computing. In this mode, interaction no longer revolves around fixed applications but emerges live from human intent and language-model reading. His paper offers three contributions. Reflective conversation serves as a design metaphor. Postphenomenology frames the human-model-computer tie. Co-disclosure is the mode itself, where it takes shape through use. They define a new way of computing, a way to analyze it, and a metaphor to design with.
arxiv-2604-09686: Nayak, Shaik, and Wang give vision-language models a way to track belief for human intent inference. Traditional intent models lean on visible states and generalize poorly across tasks and changing environments. Current vision-language systems lack ways to track belief over long horizons. Their framework approximates belief with a vector memory that retrieves relevant multimodal context for reasoning. Decisions are refined with a reinforcement-learning policy over the model's latent space. Tests on public question-answering sets such as HD-EPIC show consistent gains over zero-shot baselines.
arxiv-2604-09886: Vinod and three co-authors estimate object volume from images by fusing stereo vision cues with language priors, tackling single-view ambiguity without heavy 3D reconstruction. Their method reads a stereo pair plus a text prompt naming the object's class and rough volume, merging both through a projection layer into one representation for regression. Tests on public datasets show the text-guided method beats vision-only baselines by a wide margin. Even simple textual priors guide volume estimation well, pointing toward more context-aware visual measurement systems.
arxiv-2604-09986: Kercheval and Sowunmi solve the long-only minimum variance problem under a one-factor model with arbitrary-sign betas. The solution uses the set of active, positive-weight assets, with a computable characterization, resolving a mixed-sign betas question. In the high-dimensional regime, the active ratio converges almost always to F of beta star. Beta star solves an integral equation. With all betas positive, the active ratio converges to zero. When few betas are nonpositive, the rate is on the order of the cube root of that share.
arxiv-2604-10286: Zhang, Yang, Gong, and Wang study skill invocation safety for agents using installable skills. Static auditing cannot judge whether an invocation is unsafe under the current request. STARS treats auditing as risk estimation, predicting triage scores from request, skill, and context. STARS combines a static prior, a risk model, and a fusion policy. On held-out prompt injection attacks, fusion reaches 0.439 high-risk AUPRC, ahead of contextual and static baselines. In-distribution gains shrink, so auditing works best as triage, not screening replacement.
arxiv-2604-10686: Garg and Sarkar study vector-valued de Branges spaces tied to a de Branges operator, a pair of Fredholm functions on a symmetric domain. From a split of a Hilbert space they build reproducing kernel Hilbert spaces and show these are de Branges spaces under assumptions. The spaces serve as models for certain completely non-unitary contractions, with a Fredholm-type test for the claims. They link the Sz.-Nagy-Foias characteristic function to a projection-valued function and the kernel, showing the two coincide on the disc.
arxiv-2604-10786: Bei and three colleagues probe whether BERT embeddings encode story dimensions: time, space, causality, and character. Using a language model to speed tagging, they build a dataset marked with the four categories plus others. A probe on BERT embeddings hits 94 percent accuracy against 47 percent for a probe on random embeddings, confirming real story encoding. With balanced class weights, macro-average recall reaches 0.83, with middling success on rare causality at 0.75 and space at 0.66. Yet clustering lines up near-randomly with the categories, suggesting encoded dimensions that are not separable clusters.
arxiv-2604-11386: Qin and thirteen colleagues generate robot training data at scale with compositional simulation, blending classical and neural simulation. A closed-loop real-sim-real pipeline uses a small amount of real data to produce diverse large datasets, with a neural simulator converting classical simulation videos into real-world-looking representations. Policies trained on this data succeed more often in the real world, narrowing the sim-to-real gap. The approach offers a scalable route to robust training data spanning broader real-world scenarios without heavy manual collection.
arxiv-2604-11486: Löwen inverts the cooling problem: given an internal heat path, what external plan produces it? Forward cooling under given protocols is well studied. He computes the external plan from the Newtonian cooling equation and models. Those models include a two-level system and a Brownian harmonic oscillator with noise. The same inverse question is posed for Newtonian laws covering Mpemba effects, overcooling, heating asymmetries, and delay. Backward-engineered protocols do not always exist and can be non-unique. The results matter for steering cooling with varying external heat sources.
arxiv-2604-11586: Sánchez reviews recent ATLAS and CMS analyses of rare top quark production. Top quark pairs dominate LHC production and enable precise property measurements. Rarer mechanisms, including multiple top quarks and production with electroweak gauge bosons, offer unique sensitivity to top couplings and physics beyond the standard model despite far smaller cross sections. The contribution surveys how these rare channels probe new physics.
arxiv-2604-11986: Han, Zhang, Zhu, and Ning introduce Graph Concept Bottleneck, a new paradigm for self-explainable text-attributed graph learning. Graphs map into a concept subspace where each concept is a meaningful phrase, and predictions rest on concept activations, not subgraphs. An information bottleneck refines the concept space to the most relevant concepts, yielding concise, faithful explanations that guide the model toward correct decisions. Empirically, the method matches black-box graph neural networks on accuracy while beating them under distribution shifts and data perturbations, showing improved robustness from concept-guided prediction.
arxiv-2604-12086: Liu, Sun, and Zheng frame reward hacking, where agents exploit flawed proxy rewards, as robust optimization over all proxies correlated with the true reward. Their tractable max-min formulation makes the agent maximize performance under the worst-case proxy allowed by the correlation limit. For linear rewards it also yields readable worst-case rewards. Across several environments their method beats occupancy-regularized optimization on worst-case returns, with better stability.
arxiv-2604-12186: Mandal and Pfister build a quantum message-passing system for factor graphs over finite abelian groups. From group-covariant pure-state channels, they show the Gram matrix is diagonalized by the dual group's character basis, so each channel is captured by a character-indexed eigen list. Update rules for check, equality, homomorphism, marginalization, and automorphism factors keep messages inside the same class, giving a closed framework for tree-structured graphs. It covers polar, LDPC, convolutional, and turbo codes, extending quantum belief propagation to non-cyclic alphabets.
arxiv-2604-12886: Juan C. Alzate Cobo and two colleagues solve beam warping for hyperelastic beams in Voigt notation. Beam theory long assumed small strains and rigid cross-sections. Cross-sectional warping yields general nonlinear constitutive relations, lifting both limits. Their formulation uses Green-Lagrange strain and second Piola-Kirchhoff stress. Tensor symmetry lets the form collapse into compact Voigt notation for easy coding. Numerical tests confirm the form and give beam stiffness sensitivities.
arxiv-2604-12986: Joel Fokou argues prompt guardrails cannot secure agents that act. Agents now read files, run commands, and change databases. Prompt instructions sit at the same level as the threats. Parallax splits thinking from doing, so reasoners cannot execute. An independent validator checks actions with graduated determinism. Data labels track sensitivity through workflows. Pre-action state capture allows rollback after failed checks. Across 280 cases in nine attack types, Parallax blocks 98.9 percent by default and all cases at maximum security.
arxiv-2604-13286: Dhaliwal and four colleagues run 220 fine-tuning trials on parallel translated data to test how language mix shapes later training of large language models. English-only training usually falls short, they find, while adding even one other language lifts English scores and cross-language transfer. Broader mixes help low-resource languages most, leave high-resource scores flat rather than worse, and allow strong transfer to unseen languages, though distant low-resource languages gain least.
arxiv-2604-13386: Nordby, Pais, and Parrack study linear probes that detect when language models output claims they know are false. Single-layer probes are fragile, since the best layer shifts across models and tasks and some deception types defeat them entirely. Combining probes from many layers into an ensemble restores strong performance where single layers fail. Multi-layer ensembles lift AUROC by 29 percent on Insider Trading. On Harm-Pressure Knowledge the lift reaches 78 percent. Across 12 models, probe accuracy also grows with scale, by about 5 percent per tenfold parameter increase.
arxiv-2604-13786: Zhu, Huang, and Wan introduce QuantileMark, a multi-bit watermark for language models keeping messages symmetric. Word-list watermarks break symmetry at low entropy: some messages grab most mass, others tail tokens. No message gets a head start. QuantileMark embeds messages in the probability range. Each step splits the interval into equal-mass bins, sampling from its bin, fixing a one-over-M budget. Verification rebuilds the partition and gathers evidence. A proof of message-unbiasedness backs the design. Tests on C4 and LFQA show better recovery and detection.
arxiv-2604-14186: Sukhadia and Chowdhury present HARNESS, a family of Arabic-focused speech models trained from scratch with iterative self-distillation. A large bilingual Arabic-English teacher passes knowledge down to compact student models that keep Arabic sound and expressive detail. The students trade accuracy for efficiency on speech recognition, dialect identification, and emotion recognition, beating HuBERT and XLS-R on Arabic tasks while staying strong under heavy structural cuts.
arxiv-2604-14386: Guo, Wu, and Yiu ground coalition formation among language-model agents in hedonic game theory, the first formal treatment of shifting groups. They define the LLM Coalition Formation Game, give conditions for Nash-stable groupings, and prove complexity results, finding agents act with bounded rationality. In 2,400 episodes across three models, their Coalition-of-Thought protocol reaches Nash stability in 73.2 percent of cases, against about 58 percent for chain-of-thought and about 42 percent for plain prompting. The framework offers a footing for building steadier multi-agent systems.
arxiv-2604-14586: Li's team of seven extends CPGRec with two modules fixing its blind spots in video-game recommendation. CPGRec ignores how much player-game ties differ in showing preference, feeding over-smoothing in graph layers. Preference-informed Edge Reweighting assigns signed edge weights splitting strong likes from dislikes and gauging strength. Representation Generation uses large language models to reason what players like from global-versus-own contrasts, writing rich profiles of games and players. On two Steam sets, CPGRec+ beats state-of-the-art models on accuracy and range.
arxiv-2604-14786: Zhang, Cheng, Ye, and Huang built CogEvolution, an educational agent that simulates how a student's cognition evolves during practice, not just fixed persona behavior. A cognitive depth perceptron based on the ICAP taxonomy measures engagement across interactive, constructive, active, and passive modes. Memory recall modeled on item response theory links new and prior knowledge. An update system driven by evolution then tracks real-time shifts in learning behavior and mental state. Tests found stronger behavior fit and learning-curve fit than baselines, plus plausible learning paths matching psychology expectations.
arxiv-2604-14886: Nguyen, Huynh, and Pham introduce CoCoGen+, a coopetitive cross-silo federated learning framework where groups train jointly but compete downstream. Training inputs can improve the model while aiding rivals, and non-IID data skews gains. CoCoGen+ treats each round as a weighted potential game, with groups choosing synthetic amounts by weighing learning gains against compute costs and rivalry losses. They give a tractable equilibrium picture and best-welfare strategies, plus a payoff-sharing incentive for inputs and rivalry damage. Tests validate the approach, with CoCoGen+ beating baselines on efficiency.
arxiv-2604-15186: White and colleagues serve multi-model agentic workflows with Scepsy, a scheduler for GPU clusters. Agentic workflows branch, fan out, and recurse unpredictably, and their models often outnumber available GPUs. Scepsy notes each model's share of run time stays fairly stable across requests, then profiles models under varied parallelism. Combining profiles with those shares yields an aggregate pipeline that predicts throughput and latency.
arxiv-2604-15286: Danchev, García, and Gómez Lozano settle when square matrices over finite fields of characteristic 2 split into a diagonalizable matrix plus a square-zero nilpotent one. They answer yes for every such field with more than three elements, completing the picture for all fields except F2 and F3 with an earlier paper. For F2 itself they prove a variant using a potent matrix of index at most 4.
arxiv-2604-15486: Tapia and seven colleagues probe how device size picks the transport regime in epitaxial hafnia-based ferroelectric memristors for brain-like electronics. Across areas spanning three orders of magnitude, small devices show area-scaled low resistance from spread-out transport, while larger ones show area-free resistance from narrow conductive channels. A nucleation model pins the crossover near 1,000 square micrometers, tied to ferroelectric wake-up in larger devices.
arxiv-2604-16086: Ouattara and four colleagues introduce ST-STORM, a framework treating look and feel as a stream apart from content. Methods chase light- or shape-proof features, suiting object recognition. Rain, snow, scattering, and halos carry weather data, and driving grip and sight hinge on ground. ST-STORM splits two streams: Content seeking meaning, Style catching look and feel. Style isolates look and feel: F1 of 97 percent on Multi-Weather and 94 percent on ISIC 2024 with 10 percent labels, keeping Content meaning at 80 percent on ImageNet-1K.
arxiv-2604-16186: Perles-Ribes offers a way to spot explosive behaviour, and co-explosive behaviour seen in economic time series. It works from the path the data takes, not from a set model of how the data was made. Four checks look at normalised curvature, log-space behaviour, level shape, and growth-rate dynamics. Together, they tell true self-reinforcing growth apart from other moves, with no set rules about spread. Set cut-offs screen episodes first, then one joint score is set. Pairs are judged by joint timing and strength match.
arxiv-2604-16286: Gan, Bhatt, Shlegeris, Stastny and Hebbar built a test for catching hidden sabotage in machine learning research code. Their Auditing Sabotage Bench uses nine codebases with doctored versions that change experimental findings while keeping the stated methods intact. Frontier language models and people working with them both missed many planted flaws, with the best system fixing only 42 percent of cases. The benchmark aims to strengthen checks on research done by autonomous AI systems.
arxiv-2604-16386: Leyva-Sánchez and colleagues turned the EU Data Act into a machine-readable ontology called DAOnt. It lets data-sharing agreements be checked by reasoning rather than reading alone. Built from three established vocabularies, it captures the regulation's core concepts. It also puts three of its articles into working form, covering consumer access, business trade-secret exceptions and government competitive-use bans. Queries over the ontology return obligations, permissions and prohibitions, letting organizations test agreements against the Act, including fair pricing duties.
arxiv-2604-16686: Tao and Agrawal tackle neutral regression, where a model swaps a correct output after seeing a blank context. They formalize it as a do-no-harm rule, gauged by accuracy drops on baseline-correct items. Their NWCAD adapter couples two streams behind a two-stage gate. For blank contexts it falls back to no-context decoding, else it uses context-conditioned decoding with a fallback under uncertainty. On benchmarks splitting reliability from utilization, it stops neutral regression while preserving strong scores on helpful contexts.
arxiv-2604-16786: Sosnova and colleagues in lab tests build magnet-proof insensitive qubit states in metastable electron D-states of trapped ions. Ion trap machines usually store qubits on field-prone ground state Zeeman levels. Coherent operations are demonstrated within the D-state manifold of barium, including coherent flopping between the synthesized states, agreeing with theory. The encoding may allow freer atomic-level use for photonic interfaces, and coherence time improves by a factor of 3.
arxiv-2604-16886: Wang and nine colleagues argue that robot benchmarks miss the step-by-step reasoning of real chores, where each move reveals what to do next.
