Their COIN benchmark offers 50 everyday manipulation tasks plus primitive skills and composed variants. Built from 1,000 teleoperated demonstrations, it finds current methods still stumble between seeing a scene and moving through it.
arxiv-2604-17086: Vaughan models quantum gates with an effective Hamiltonian acting for a characteristic time, tracing gate action to Bloch sphere paths along lines of latitude. Such paths would push a rebit, a real-only bit confined to one latitude line, off that line with a complex phase. Complex phases also drive two-qubit entanglement. He then shows real-only quantum mechanics cannot reproduce this continuous evolution, since gate matrices with determinant minus one cannot come from special orthogonal operators in matching dimensions.
arxiv-2604-17186: Zheng and five colleagues propose a persona-driven scheme for clear multi-agent education systems, built from day one. Personas and stories capture needs of educators, students, a patient agent, and care agents for exams, diagnosis, intervention, supervision, and evaluation. Tested in reasoning training, over 78 percent of students reported better thinking skills, showing persona-based plans link expert needs with non-expert students.
arxiv-2604-17486: Mohtashim, Sajjan, and Kais rank key building blocks of proteins with quantum walks on residue networks drawn from solved structures. A residue's rank comes from its long-run occupation odds, backed by spectral analysis. Across about 150 proteins, the ranking matches the classic eigenvector ranking while adding quantum interference marks and wider spectral gaps. It recovers known functional residues in protein kinase A and oxytocin, with a proof-of-principle run on IBM hardware.
arxiv-2604-17586: Trieschman and Amin show that shortfalls in Financial Transmission Rights can arise structurally, not from bidding. These rights let market players hedge congestion risk in day-ahead trading, but payouts must stay within the surplus held by system operators. When the auction's network model differs from the day-ahead model, payouts can exceed funding. The method yields weights on transmission constraints that pin down misalignment constraint by constraint, with clear implications for uniform derates and surprise outages.
arxiv-2604-17686: Hebbar and three colleagues study online non-random control: steering a linear system under hostile shocks and hostile costs to cut total cost. Recent work reaches sublinear regret against steady states gained with a constant input. The authors extend this line with an algorithm enjoying square-root-of-T regret against richer steady states gained under an affine control. The broader class gives much stronger proofs. Their method pairs a Follow-The-Perturbed-Leader-style tuning approach with batching that keeps balance despite changing policies.
arxiv-2604-17786: Germano and four colleagues model how dendritic cell clustering in lymph nodes shapes T cell activation. The link matters because breast cancer patients with more clustering show better survival. They build a probabilistic agent-based model of T cells meeting dendritic cells. From it they derive a deterministic partial differential equation for activation and motion. The equation estimates expected stimulation from a cell group's layout and grouping. It finds intermediate-uptake T cells gain most from heavier grouping, activating in greater numbers and with wider variety.
arxiv-2604-17886: Yejin Yoon and two colleagues study tool-calling agents that must fill in details users leave out. Their MPT benchmark spans 4,695 instances across 459 multi-session histories, covering preference recall, induction, and transfer. Their PRefine method stores a user's latent preference as a written hypothesis, revised through cycles of generation, verification, and refinement at test time. Across five language models, PRefine beats all baselines and alone tops full-history prompting on preference transfer.
arxiv-2604-17986: Mason Wang and Huang introduce the Latent Fourier Transform, giving generative music models new controls. The method pairs a diffusion autoencoder with Fourier analysis in latent space to sort music patterns by speed. Masking latents by frequency during training yields codes that can be changed smoothly at inference, making variations and blends from examples while keeping traits at chosen speeds. Like an equalizer shaping timbre through audible sound, LatentFT shapes musical structure through latent bands, following prompts and beating baselines on quality.
arxiv-2604-18086: Nasir and ten colleagues survey materials data science across scales, from atom simulations through microstructure study to bulk models. Data methods now support design at each scale, yet trust and transferability vary strongly with scale. They review atomic potentials, mesoscale stand-in models, and lab microstructure studies, stressing data quality, uncertainty, clarity, and cross-scale fit. They also examine data standards, shared terms, and self-run labs, showing what counts as solid today and what blocks broader multi-scale use.
arxiv-2604-18586: de Oliveira and three colleagues present the largest long-run study of Brazil's YouTube vaccine discourse. Using a semi-supervised stance method joining self-tagging and self-training, they sort nearly 1.4 million comments. Mixing stance, time patterns, engagement, and channel types, they map how pro- and anti-vaccine stories spread. That learning boosts stance sorting for tracking views across Brazil's full vaccine schedule. Splits spike during crises, above all COVID-19, but fragment across shots later. Science and digital-native channels are the main pro and anti talk sites.
arxiv-2604-18686: Ghosh and three colleagues show that simple feed-forward neural networks can compute correlation functions of conformal field theories on a line from minimal data. Trained only on crossing symmetry, with the leading operator's scaling dimension and one anchor value, the networks rebuild target correlators to within a few percent across many theories and dimensions. The authors trace the alignment to the training bias toward smooth functions. They also extend the method beyond the diagonal kinematics of the line.
arxiv-2604-18786: Mohammadi, Gaur, and Ferraro frame scientific feasibility assessment as a test: given a hypothesis, a model says feasible or infeasible and justifies its call. They test large language models with the claim alone, with experiments, with outcomes, or with both, and check robustness by removing context step by step. Outcome evidence usually beats experiment descriptions. Outcomes lift accuracy beyond what the model knows alone, while experiment text can be brittle and may hurt results when context is cut short.
arxiv-2604-18986: Ntontin and Chatzinotas derive a tight channel capacity lower bound for the integrated receiver in simultaneous wireless information and power transfer. Most prior work treats the separate receiver; this work targets the integrated design. They approximate the channel transition matrix in closed form using a fourth order Taylor expansion of the Schottky diode current voltage curve. Numerical tests show a gamma input distribution yields a tight bound, unlike Rayleigh or uniform inputs. Keeping the fourth order term notably beats the simpler second order model.
arxiv-2604-19186: Wang and five colleagues show recurring inductive subgraphs act as spurious shortcuts, fooling networks and reinforcing false correlations. Prior work adapted networks through neighbor spread or refinement, but errors stayed unclear. From a causal view, they build a debiased graph blocking confounding and spillover paths behind the shortcuts. Their Causal Disentangled GNN splits spurious subgraphs from true causal ones. Focusing on genuine causal signals, it lifts heterophilic node classification. Real-world tests validate the theory and show it beats baselines.
arxiv-2604-19386: Fu and colleagues propose Air-Know, a network for composed image retrieval that tackles noisy triplet correspondence, where query triplets carry unreliable matches. Most robust learning methods lean on the small-loss hypothesis, but semantic ambiguity in noisy triplets, such as partial matching, invalidates that assumption. It also leads to shaky noise spotting. The learner then falls into a self-fed vicious cycle, tangled with its arbiter, causing catastrophic representation pollution. Air-Know breaks that cycle with an Expert-Proxy-Diversion decoupling design, starting with external prior arbitration.
arxiv-2604-19486: Fraser and Pham study the Falconer distance set problem in Euclidean space. They obtain better dimensional estimates under natural Fourier analytic assumptions. Under mild assumptions, they beat the half-dimension threshold in dimensions 5 and above. A Borel set with Fourier dimension at least 2 has a distance set of full Hausdorff dimension. Sets with Fourier dimension zero can also qualify in dimension 4 and above.
arxiv-2604-19886: Maheshwari, Murali, and Smid study completely independent Steiner trees, a fault-tolerance concept for networks. A set of trees spanning chosen terminals qualifies when, for every terminal pair, the paths in different trees share no inner vertices and no edges. It generalizes the spanning-tree version and the internally disjoint Steiner version. The authors give structural results, connectivity bounds, algorithms, hardness results, and uses for planar and bounded-treewidth graphs, plus a directed variant.
arxiv-2604-20786: Kellerhals, Krebs, Nichterlein, and Schmid study a demand-aware network design task: start from a tree G and build a binary tree H over the same vertices. Their goal is to minimize the total of H-distances between G-adjacent vertex pairs. They give a factor-4 approximation in linear time for this problem. The factor 4 means the produced tree's total distance is at most four times the optimum.
arxiv-2604-20886: Patel presents KinetiDiff, a structure-based design tool for new kinase blockers that pairs a Geometry-Complete Diffusion Model with real-time AutoDock Vina gradient guidance. By feeding physics-based docking gradients into the diffusion denoising loop, KinetiDiff steers molecule generation toward high-affinity shapes for ACVR1 (ALK2), the causative kinase in FOP. From 10,000 diffusion samples, the tool made 9,997 valid molecules. The best candidate hit minus 11.05 kcal/mol, about 19 percent better than the crystal reference.
arxiv-2604-21286: Jon-Paul Cacioli tests whether a K-way energy probe result survives removing cross-entropy training. Across ten seeds on CIFAR-10 with a backbone, the probe sits below softmax for standard predictive coding trained with mean squared error. On bidirectional predictive coding it exceeds softmax on all ten seeds, though a check finds no greater latent movement. Removing cross-entropy alone halves the probe-softmax gap, and about two-thirds of the gap traces to logit scale, with the rest a ranking advantage.
arxiv-2604-21386: Shuya Yamazaki and four colleagues warn that novelty claims in materials discovery can be fooled when a predicted ordered crystal merely orders a known disordered phase. Their order-disorder family trees organize ordered and disordered structures through group-subgroup links, with a fast matcher finding disordered parents and ordered kin. Tests on A-Lab cases recover known parents, and wider checks show many seemingly novel structures belong to known families. Models blind to symmetry err most, while symmetry-aware ones are two to four times less prone to the trap.
arxiv-2604-21486: Jorik Jooken and Denys Lohvynov prove a non-existence result for vertex-girth-regular graphs, where every vertex lies on equally many shortest cycles. Such graphs obey an upper bound on that count, and near-bound graphs interest cage researchers. For every k at least 3 and every positive epsilon up to half of k minus 1, no girth-5 graph has the count equal to the bound minus epsilon. Earlier results had settled all odd girths at least 7 and, recently, girth 3, completing the picture for odd girths.
arxiv-2604-21586: Denis Grebenkov builds a scheme for surface autocatalytic action, where bulk particles meet a wall, vanish or divide through branching, splitting, or fission. A renewal nonlinear integral equation for the population generating function gives the spread and moments. A matching Fokker-Planck equation with nonlinear Robin boundary conditions encodes surface events. Loss and copying there yield distinct regimes and common scaling laws. They predict when surface action leads to die-off or growth, showing catalytic efficiency, metabolic control, and how groups last in mixed settings.
arxiv-2604-21686: Xu and seven colleagues build WorldMark, a benchmark for interactive video world models driven by actions rather than written or picture prompts. A common WASD-style vocabulary, translated by per-model adapters, gives ten unlike models identical instructions across 500 standard cases. The suite scores direction accuracy, purity, delay, and steadiness for each axis, plus memory and visual quality, revealing trade-offs such as speedy responders proving least steady.
arxiv-2604-21786: Prasse and six colleagues benchmark automated visual discourse analysis for climate change on social media. They test six promptable vision-language models and 15 zero-shot CLIP-like models on two X datasets: a 1,038-image expert-annotated set and a corpus over 1.2 million images with 50,000 validated labels, across five annotation dimensions. Gemini-3.1-flash-lite leads on all super-categories and both datasets, though open-weight models of moderate size trail closely. Population-level trends prove recoverable even when per-image accuracy is only moderate.
arxiv-2604-21886: Curtis and eleven colleagues cover the Dyson Minds 2025 Workshop, held at MIT's Center for Brains, Minds and Machines and organised by Penn State, MIT, and The Ultraintelligence Foundation. People from astrophysics, engineering, AI, computing, and philosophy looked at large post-biological minds powered by supermassive black holes. Talks centred on building, behaviour, and observable signs, including swarm limits, power-versus-latency trade-offs, and whether such minds act as one or as loose groups. The key recommendation is anomaly detection in old WISE, JWST, and Event Horizon Telescope data.
arxiv-2604-22086: Bhatia and fourteen colleagues use damascene to replace the sidewall native oxide of a superconducting transmon device with metal touching substrate. Surface oxides cause losses in superconducting transmon devices, degrading performance. The authors mimic sidewall oxide growth by burying an oxide layer while building. They observe a modest improvement between the two types of devices, hinting at less surface loss.
arxiv-2604-22386: Calandriello, Lazaric and Valko tackle kernel ridge regression storage, where the kernel matrix for n samples takes squared space. Nyström approximations cut that space by sampling columns, but uniform sampling needs many columns when coherence is high. Ridge leverage sampling needs only about the effective dimension, yet exact scores also take squared space. An earlier incremental algorithm updates scores on the fly but depends on the largest eigenvalue. Their SQUEAK algorithm uses unnormalised scores, simplifying the method with space only a constant factor worse than exact sampling.
arxiv-2604-22986: Hemmelgarn, Moskovitz, and Vida sort meteoroids by machine learning from 13 observed Global Meteor Network parameters, deepening the three-parameter Kb index. A semi-qualitative study of 28,177 meteor events from 2023 tests normalization, dimensionality-reduction, and clustering methods. Factor Analysis with a Gaussian Mixture Model yields clusters closest to old models, with three factors for kinematics, trigger thresholds, and size and shape effects. The activation factor best splits asteroidal and cometary origin, and the hardness scheme extends the older index from the densest iron ones to the softest cometary material.
arxiv-2604-23086: Azuma studies non-Gaussianity of Pegg-Barnett phase-operator eigenstates from their Wigner functions, confirming negative values in phase space regions. These eigenstates live in a finite Hilbert space, and he tracks how their negativity volumes depend on its dimension. He presents a quantum-optical circuit generating these eigenstates, naming single-photon detection as their non-Gaussianity source. With flawed detectors of non-unit efficiency, he tracks how detection chance, output fidelity, and negativity volume change as detectors vary. He applies the setup to phase gauging with a beam splitter.
arxiv-2604-23286: Campbell builds a method for computing Kronecker coefficients, a central open problem in algebraic combinatorics and representation theory. Joining a Schur function rule of Littlewood, the Giambelli rule for Schur functions, and Blasiak's rule for hook-shaped partitions, the method turns Kronecker coefficients into signed sums over hook-indexed cases. As a use, he obtains counting readings for two-row partitions paired with hook-like partitions under natural conditions. The approach extends hook-based rules to wider families of Kronecker coefficients.
arxiv-2604-23486: Kobler and colleagues measure whether student-AI tutoring dialogues actually serve teaching goals, using six new metrics across hundreds of conversations. They find a basic mismatch: tutors are designed for sustained learning dialogue, but students mostly mine them for answers. How the tool is deployed predicts usage best, with optional tools spiking near deadlines and embedded tools drawing verbatim assignment questions.
arxiv-2604-23586: Ye and colleagues present Talker-T2AV, a talking-head generator that models speech and facial motion together without tangling their fine details. A shared autoregressive backbone reasons over audio and video tokens jointly, while two lightweight diffusion heads render each modality separately. On talking-portrait benchmarks it beats dual-branch rivals on lip-sync, video quality, and audio quality, with stronger cross-modal consistency.
arxiv-2604-23786: Chiang and colleagues study fairness and explainability of vision-language models for wellbeing assessment on lab and naturalistic depression datasets. Performance swings widely by model and setting, with one model near 80 percent on naturalistic data while another sits near 34 percent, and both over-predict depression on lab data. Fairness prompting can equalise opportunity for one model only at a severe accuracy cost, and explainability gains do not guarantee fair outcomes.
arxiv-2604-23886: Xu and colleagues present MUSIC, a data-driven system for muscle-driven dexterous hand control that plays piano pieces beyond its reference data. Low-level policies learn muscle-tendon activations by reinforcement learning, then distil into variational autoencoder latent spaces. High-level piece-specific policies operate in that latent space, coordinating two-handed motions from note events in scores. Tests show accurate key presses, state-of-the-art physics-based piano performance, and muscle patterns matching human electromyography.
arxiv-2604-24386: Kim and Park recast auto chord recognition as segment-level sequence prediction. Instead of tagging frames one by one, their model predicts chord sequences auto-regressively, spotting changes only at segment edges. This design cuts extra segmentation, a key weakness alongside scarcity and skew, especially for complex non-triad chords rare in existing datasets. Two new token codes and encoder pre-training, both built for time-aligned chord work, further support the approach. Tests show gains in chord recognition and segmentation, with lifts for complex and rare chord types.
arxiv-2604-24686: Marin and Chaudhary address a gap in rules for autonomous AI agents: an agent can stay fully authorized yet grow unsafe as behavior drifts and foes adapt, with code unchanged. Their Informational Viability Principle turns governance into a bound on unseen risk. An action is allowed only when its capacity beats that bound by a margin. The Agent Viability Framework grounds this in viability theory, with monitoring, anticipation and monotonic restriction as its properties. RiskGate puts it into practice with stats tools, a fail-secure pipeline and a kill switch.
arxiv-2604-25286: Yousefjani and three co-authors extend time-crystal sensing to nonlinearity, showing it raises sharpness by raising the size scaling of quantum Fisher information. Their analysis splits a seminorm bound from product-state scaling. Quantum Fisher information retains quadratic growth with Floquet cycles, while its system-size exponent grows in line with it. Stronger nonlinearities shrink the stability window and heighten sensitivity. Imperfect pulses can enhance, rather than suppress, signal. A superconducting-qubit implementation is noted.
arxiv-2604-25386: Banerjee and three colleagues study PM2.5 swings in fifty-four Indian cities over six years. Despite varied settings and climates, the swings show shared traits in spread and time patterns. Once slow trends and seasonal parts are out, scaled spread curves of leftover swings fall onto one curve, fit by an exponentially modified Gaussian curve. Scaled leftover series also share decay traits, with matching auto-correlation decay and a similar 1/f fall at the tails. A spare random model explains the shared traits: steady spread, time links, and spectral scaling.
arxiv-2604-25586: Jin and Hong give a clean test for when a transposed Poisson algebra collapses in a nilpotent way. In finite dimensions, the algebra is nilpotent exactly when left multiplication in both its associative and its Lie parts is nilpotent. Behind that test, the lower central series takes a simpler form, and tensor products and derivations yield new nilpotent and solvable examples. For Lie nilpotent cases, the derived Lie part forms a nilpotent ideal, tying the two radicals together.
arxiv-2604-25886: Fang, Chen, and Cai present MarkIt, a training-free framework adding visual markers to video for precise temporal grounding. Video language models grasp open-world video well but struggle to output exact start and end times. MarkIt derives canonical subject tags from the query, maps them to instance masks by open-vocabulary segmentation, and embeds semantic markers plus a frame index in each frame. Long-range temporal reasoning thus becomes explicit visual cues. Tests on moment retrieval and highlight detection reach state-of-the-art results.
arxiv-2604-25986: Gutierrez, Ratnapriya, and Barman analyze RNA-Seq data from age-related macular degeneration patients and controls with robust clustering. Gene co-expression networks group genes into modules beyond single-gene links. The authors generalize the MEGENA framework. They curate quality metrics to pick similarity measures from statistical distance or information theory, not linear correlation. A stability test checks hub-gene robustness under noise. Differential module eigengene analysis tracks upregulation and downregulation per module. They confirm known hubs and modules, and find new hub genes for further research.
arxiv-2604-26586: Pawar and Das studied heat physics of a magnetically charged, slowly spinning Kerr black hole with a cosmological constant in nonlinear electrodynamics. Spin stays at most about a tenth, and the mass curve flattens near the cosmological length no matter the charge and nonlinearity picks. Horizon layout, with inner, outer, and large cosmological horizons, hinges on spin, cosmological length, and mass curve. Listed temperature, angular velocity, and entropy at those horizons show the nonlinear theory markedly reshapes Kerr heat physics.
arxiv-2604-26786: Benetti Genolini, Couzens, and Lüscher introduce equivariant localization for finding the action of probe branes in super-gravity backgrounds. Applied to SUSY probe D3-branes in type IIB spacetimes from lifting the Kerr-Newman-AdS5 black hole over a toric Sasaki-Einstein space, the branes represent non-perturbative fixes to the superconformal index. They also represent defect inserts in the index of a large family of 4D quiver field theories. For wrapped cycles, the final action reduces to equivariant integrals found wholly from toric data.
arxiv-2604-26886: Nasirudin, Bull and Ye predict counts and clustering for hydrogen galaxies that the SKA-MID radio array will list. They weigh three mock catalogues, S3-SAX, GAEA, and IllustrisTNG, and attach modelling-uncertainty bounds to the forecasts. The mocks differ by about a factor of two in counts and about 10 percent in bias near redshift 0.1, giving about 20 percent gaps in forecast cosmological precision. Gaps grow at higher redshifts. A medium-deep survey model fitted to IllustrisTNG patches adds clustering outlooks for near redshifts.
arxiv-2604-26986: Adewumi and three colleagues introduce BatteryPass-12K, the first public benchmark for digital battery passport conformance classification, built synthetically from real pilot samples. They test 22 language models zero-shot, from small models and mixture-of-experts to dense large models. Thinking models perform best, with GPT-5.4 leading, while few-shot examples help markedly and prompt-injection attacks hurt scores. Merely scaling parameters does not guarantee gains, since small models beat some large ones, and even strong frontier models find the task hard. The dataset is released under a permissive licence.
arxiv-2604-27086: Kalari and Vacca present a K-band spectral atlas of massive stars at high resolution and high signal-to-noise. It covers 81 stars, including known optical standards, spanning spectral and luminosity subclasses from O2 to O9, plus supergiant subclasses from O2 to B1. The telluric-corrected reduced spectra are publicly available and discussed here. The atlas gives a reference set for massive-star spectra at resolution near 45000 and signal-to-noise above 100.
arxiv-2604-27586: Mazhar, Suri, and Galhotra study how uncertainty contaminates multi-agent workflows that reason over PDFs, spreadsheets, and slide decks. They inject structured perturbations into artifact representations, run fixed workflows under full logging, and measure contamination as trace divergence in plans, tool calls, and middle states. Over 614 paired runs covering 32 GAIA tasks and three language models, they find workflows can diverge yet recover correct answers, or stay similar yet produce wrong outputs. They identify three manifestation types and show why common verification guardrails fail to catch contamination.
arxiv-2604-27786: Qian and Morris ask how much graph-net power it takes to recover answers for linear semidefinite programs, a strong convex optimization frame. They first prove that standard graph nets fall short on these programs, then pin down a richer design mirroring the programs' shape. That design can even mimic a standard first-order solver's steps, and on made-up and SDPLib tests it beats weaker baselines on forecast error and goal gap. Feeding its forecasts into the solver as a warm start speeds it by up to 80 percent.
arxiv-2604-27886: Liu and Wu study StoqMA(2), a proof system class using unentangled proofs built on sign-problem-free physics. They show NP fits inside it with short proofs and near-perfect completeness, matched by an exponential-time upper bound from a sum-of-squares algorithm under a standard hardness assumption. With logarithmic-size proofs the class sits inside MA, so quantum-inspired randomness can shorten unentangled proofs sharply.
arxiv-2604-27986: Dal Lago, Fiorillo and Pistone tackle whether probabilistic higher-order programs stop with probability one, a question that cannot be decided in general. They translate the problem through the weighted relational semantics of linear logic into computing generating functions for the program. For a class extending affine recursion schemes with bounded exponentials, those functions are always algebraic. That gives a working test for stopping.
arxiv-2604-28086: G. Díaz and J. I. Díaz study whether solutions exist, and whether they are unique, for a nonlinear evolution equation driven by an m-accretive operator in a Banach space. Its extra term breaks the Lipschitz rule, which normally caps how fast a term can change with its input. The paper asks what existence and uniqueness results survive without that cap.
arxiv-2604-28186: Liu, Farina and Ozdaglar study equilibrium ideas that survive coordinated deviations by coalitions, not just single-player moves. Nash and correlated equilibria ignore coalition gains. Strong Nash and coalition-proof versions often fail to exist. The authors instead cut average group gain, so it always exists, and extend the idea to weighted and worst-member gains. For average and maximum gains they prove a matching complexity lower bound and method, then solve the exploitability welfare frontier, the best welfare at a given exploit level.
arxiv-2605-00286:
Mingrui Yuan and Nikolay V. Golubev unify the theory behind two ways of filming ultrafast change in matter: x-ray diffraction and ultrafast electron diffraction. Both tools can probe quantum dynamics as it happens, yet they are usually treated in split schools, each with its own shortcuts. That split makes it hard to compare what each one truly shows.

The authors present a single quantum-field account that covers both probes in one frame. Within it, the match between the two methods becomes clear, and what the two share, and where they part, can be told apart cleanly. The frame also absorbs extra effects, such as current couplings at near-light speeds, in a simple way. As a test, they simulate the scattering pattern from laser-driven electron motion in graphene, showing how the imaging can untangle complex quantum events.
arxiv-2605-00386:
Louis Shuo Wang offers an introduction to mathematical programs with equilibrium constraints, known as MPECs, and to the closely related bilevel optimization problems. These are optimization problems with a twist: part of the feasible set is defined by another problem. That inner problem might be an optimization, a variational inequality, a complementarity system, or an equilibrium model.

As an introduction, the paper explains the objects before judging them. It motivates MPECs through applications, so readers see why a leader's choice might be constrained by a follower's best response. It then presents the main equivalent formulations of equilibrium constraints, which recast the tangled feasible set in workable forms. Finally, it summarizes the basic existence theory, the conditions under which an optimal solution is guaranteed to exist at all.
arxiv-2605-00686:
Byungsoo Oh and Rachee Singh find and remove a hidden bottleneck in running mixture-of-experts models across many machines. Megakernels, which fuse expert computation and fine-grained communication into one persistent graphics-processor kernel, beat collective-based designs on a single node. Across nodes the advantage collapses: communication-bound models slow by up to tenfold on eight nodes, worsening as nodes are added. The authors trace the regression to serialization inside proxy-based network transports.

Each tile transfer must be fenced before its completion signal, and that fence drains the network pipeline. Their system, Perseus, decouples signaling by batching fences per destination, cutting their count eightfold, and moves ordering into hardware flags so the proxy never stalls. On proxy transports Perseus speeds end-to-end inference by up to about tenfold. It even matches or beats direct GPU transports, showing serialization was the true limit.
arxiv-2605-00986:
Paulo Luz presents general series solutions to the Tolman-Oppenheimer-Volkoff equations, which govern the structure of compact stellar objects such as neutron stars. An algorithm computes the power series coefficients directly from the equation of state and its derivatives with respect to thermodynamic variables. From those results, general properties of analytic solutions are set out. They link to how regular that law is.

Using Padé approximants, Luz derives series forms for meromorphic functions whose convergence domains may include isolated poles. These then yield closed-form approximations for a star's radius and mass. Uses on affine and polytropic fluid models agree with numerical integration. The formalism also extends to piecewise state laws matched across change surfaces.
arxiv-2605-01286:
Ibuki Okuda and two co-authors propose inverse design of inorganic crystals by jointly generating crystal structures and local electronic descriptors. Making structures for a target property is harder than unconditional generation, because that conditioning can degrade structural quality. Their diffusion framework denoises structure variables and site-resolved descriptors together through a shared score network. It uses Bader charge and atomic density of states.

When band gap and formation energy are fixed, joint models achieve higher success rates than a structure-only baseline in most conditions. They also increase the share of structures that are unique, novel, stable, and physically valid. A dummy-variable control confirms gains come from electronic content, not from extra inputs. Generated charges agree closely with reference calculations on stable ones.
arxiv-2605-01386:
Hung Pham Van and six co-authors build a memory system that lets a language model agent recall users across long chats. Plain models forget, and earlier graph-based memories thin out facts, lose track of where facts came from, and search the same way for every query.

MemORAI adds three parts. A filter with two compression layers keeps only facts tied to the user's profile. A rich graph stores relations between facts and tracks each fact's origin down to the chat turn. Retrieval adapts to the query, weighting graph links by what is asked and ranking with a tuned PageRank method. On the LOCOMO and LongMemEval benchmarks, the system tops prior work at both recall and tailored replies, which the authors read as proof that selective storage and adaptive search both matter.
arxiv-2605-01586:
Luc Devroye and Joe R Hill build fast random number generators for the Pearson IV distribution, a skewed family from Karl Pearson's system of curves. Simulation and Bayesian work both need streams of draws from such laws, and a generator that crawls, or only works in part of the parameter range, limits what can be tested.

Their generators are uniformly fast across the whole range of both shape parameters, so no corner of the family is left slow or unserved. Uniform speed matters in practice: a sampler inside a large Monte Carlo loop cannot afford rare slow cases, and Bayesian posteriors may wander into any part of the range. The paper pairs the algorithms with applications in a Bayesian setting, showing where Pearson IV draws earn their keep. It is a tools paper in probability computation, in the exact style of its senior author's simulation work.
arxiv-2605-01986:
Ahmet Bahaddin Ersoz asks whether twelve language model agents, cast as jurors from the film 12 Angry Men, can change each other's minds. Each agent takes a persona faithful to the film and debates the same murder case. Two models are tested, GPT-4o and Llama-4-Scout, under three prompt conditions, with three runs in each setting.

Seventeen of eighteen runs ended with a hung jury. The steady shift from a lone dissenter to a shared verdict, central to the film, almost never happened, which points to anchoring as a strong failure mode. The two models also behaved quite differently inside the debate, in vote changes and in how discussion moved.
arxiv-2605-02086:
Baobing Zhang and Wanxin Sui shrink 3D Gaussian splatting scenes, which can take hundreds of megabytes to several gigabytes for one scene. That size exceeds what mobile, immersive, and volumetric video systems can handle. Past compression split pruning, quantisation, and coding into separate steps with hand-tuned rules, which limited use across scenes and budgets.

Their method, GETA-3DGS, jointly prunes and quantises in one automatic, end-to-end process. A dependency graph built for 3D Gaussians treats each primitive as a group with attribute and spherical harmonic sub-nodes, aware of degree. Users can state a target rate or quality budget. The authors present it as the first such joint framework for this representation.
arxiv-2605-02286:
Maksym Nechepurenko evaluates a deadline-aware version of the Information Leakage Score on documented insider cases from Polymarket, a prediction market. The score aims to detect trading that front-loads information before a public event. Deadline-resolved contracts, which settle by a set date, are the dominant form among publicly documented insider cases on the platform.

The study anchors on a 2026 United States-Iran conflict cluster, the largest documented deadline cluster in the inventory used. Parts cover hazard-rate fitting by category, a single-case score computation, cross-market wallet analysis, and method refinements. Military-geopolitics markets fit an exponential hazard well, with a half-life near three days. A corporate-disclosure fit is preliminary, and the regulatory-decision category is rejected as bimodal.
arxiv-2605-02386:
Jilie Zhang gives network synchronisation a fresh treatment from control theory, rather than from graph theory and network structure. The key object is the inner coupling matrix, which is not bound by limits such as distance or communication strength among nodes. If local states can be measured or observed and the communication topology is connected, that matrix can be configured at will to meet a synchronisation target.

Zhang analyses the synchronisation region through that matrix, a route the author calls useful for practical engineering design. A further finding is that network synchronisation and multi-agent consensus are essentially equivalent problems. The paper develops a unified viewpoint in which consensus control and synchronisation share the same essence.
arxiv-2605-02586:
Jintao Guo and seven co-authors present StableMind, a method for decoding brain scans from a new person when data are scarce and older raw data cannot be shared. Models that read functional MRI across people usually need much paired scan and image data for each new subject. Cost limits that data, and privacy or access rules can block reuse of prior subjects' scans.

Two faults drive failure: brain responses vary greatly between people, and fine image details used as targets may not be supported by weak scan signals. StableMind reuses projections from the pretrained model as anchors, and augments brain features in the frequency domain to steady the brain side. On the image side, it tightens which details supervision may claim. The aim is reliable decoding under the limits clinics actually face.
arxiv-2605-02886:
Giorgio Cavicchioli and seven co-authors present CityOS, an operating system layer that governs how applications use a city's growing web of cameras, sensors, and kiosks. Cities observe public space continuously, yet no architecture controls how apps access, combine, and keep that data. Privacy risk and uneven policy enforcement follow from that gap, which CityOS is built to close.

Access is mediated by a three-tier interface. Real-time sensing keeps raw data local, single-place aggregation gives privacy-protected long-term statistics for one site, and citywide analytics aggregate across places, with user devices enforcing per-user privacy budgets. Untrusted apps run in short-lived containers at the edge, and privacy loss is broadcast for transparency. Working apps across all tiers, including pedestrian safety alerts, show the design in use.
arxiv-2605-03186:
Chady Ghnatios and Kazem Fayazbakhsh model how composite feedstock bends and warps during robotic 3D printing of continuous fiber thermoplastics. That deformation drives defects and complicates path planning, so predicting it before printing matters.

Experiments and simulations isolate three drivers: stress relief, drying, and crystallization, plus thermal stress. The team blends a Kelvin-Voigt material model with a stabilized neural differential equation for drying and crystallization, fitted from lab tests. In real robotic printing trials, the hybrid model reproduced prepreg behavior well beyond its training temperatures, showing strong generalization for practical use.
arxiv-2605-03386:
Xiao Zhang, Yafei Li, Ruixiang Wang, Wei Wei, Shuo He, and Mingliang Xu propose LTE-ODE, a traffic forecaster that treats numerical integration error as a signal instead of a flaw. Large road networks mix smooth daily rhythms with sudden shocks, and smooth neural differential models blur those shocks away.

The team shows that forcing error down with rigid penalties causes gradient conflicts and attention collapse. Instead, local truncation error becomes an attention mask: stable regions keep precise continuous evolution, while shock points trigger a discrete correction branch. Trained end to end, the model set leading scores on large benchmarks and adapts to varied hardware limits.
arxiv-2605-03486:
A. Pezo, A. Manchon, Y. Nii, K. Ando, and T. Kato predict from first principles that chiral phonons, lattice vibrations with handed rotation, pile up orbital angular momentum in metals. Chiral phonons can move angular momentum without magnetic order, but electronic responses beyond spin have been poorly mapped.

Evaluating orbital and spin expectations from strain-perturbed ab initio Hamiltonians, they find a clear orbital accumulation plus a smaller spin companion through spin-orbit coupling. Orbital character, near-degeneracies, and electron-phonon coupling control the response more than spin-orbit strength alone. Light transition metals emerge as promising platforms for phonon-driven orbitronics devices.
arxiv-2605-03586:
Wen-Tao Lyu, Luis Roca, and Eulogio Oset examine whether the scalar meson a0(1710) leaves a visible signal in two decays of the J/psi particle. Mesons are short-lived particles made of a quark and an antiquark, and the a0(1710) is thought to be generated dynamically by interactions among other mesons. The team includes those final-state interactions in their calculation.

They predict a clear peak near 1.8 GeV in the invariant mass distribution of the strong decay into rho and omega mesons, tied to the a0(1710). A similar peak appears for the radiative decay. Future measurements at BESIII, Belle II, and the planned Super Tau-Charm Facility could pin down its mass and width.
arxiv-2605-03886:
Suman Cha, Seongchan Lee, Antonin Schrab, and Ilmun Kim challenge a common intuition about Monte Carlo permutation tests, a cornerstone of model-free statistical inference. Practitioners widely assume that sampling more permutations improves a test, in particular that statistical power tends to grow with the Monte Carlo budget. The authors show that intuition is false in general.

Leveraging the saw-toothed structure that power inherits from the discreteness of permutation distributions, they give a simple structural explanation for why power can decrease as more permutations are sampled. They then prove that such decreases occur infinitely often as the Monte Carlo budget grows. The result is a caution for practice: enlarging the simulation budget does not guarantee a uniformly better permutation test.
arxiv-2605-03986:
Kishan Athrey, Ramin Pishehvar, Brian Riordan, and Mahesh Viswanathan present a framework that automates the creation of multi-agent systems from a user's stated intent. Building such systems normally means manually composing a plan, selecting suitable agents, and wiring an execution graph. Their framework replaces those manual steps with software modules and an orchestrated workflow.

The modules include a language-model-derived planner, tasks described in natural language, a dynamic call graph, an orchestrator that maps agents to tasks, and an agent recommender that searches local and global registries. The recommender uses a two-stage retrieval system, a fast retriever followed by a language-model re-ranker. Experiments explore choices of embedders, re-rankers, agent description enrichment, and a supervising critique agent, benchmarked end to end.
arxiv-2605-04286:
Stephen Tivenan, Indranil Sahoo, and Yanjun Qian add uncertainty to climate classification, using the Sahara Desert as their test region. The classic Koeppen-Trewartha system assigns each place one firm label, which hides how close a borderline place is to another climate type.

Their neural network instead gives probabilities for each climate class at each location. Trained on the first eleven years of a thirty-year record with hundreds of thousands of space-time points, the model is checked for accuracy and stability in later years. The probabilistic view gives planners a clearer picture of transition zones between climates.
arxiv-2605-04586:
Ali Fatemiabhari and Maurizio Piai use holography, the duality between gravity theories and strongly coupled quantum field theories, to compute the bound-state spectrum of a family of confining theories. Their gravity side lives in a six-dimensional supergravity with a magnetic flux along a compact direction, and the field theories confine like the strong nuclear force.

A first-order deconfinement transition at zero temperature caps how much flux the geometry can support. Computing fluctuations of the background fields gives the masses of the dual bound states. Two scalar particles are lightest, with suppressed and nearly equal masses across the whole parameter space, while heavier states behave differently away from the transition.
arxiv-2605-04686:
Anton Biryukov, Amir Levinson, and Pavel Abolmasov draw conclusions about neutron star interiors from new polarisation observations of Her X-1, an X-ray binary whose brightness varies on a thirty-five day cycle. The polarisation patterns correlate with that cycle, supporting the idea that the cycle is driven by the neutron star slowly precessing, like a wobbling top.

Keeping such precession going for fifty years would require extreme behaviour from the superfluid inside the crust. That is how long the system has been watched. Its vortices must stay unpinned for centuries. They must also feel almost no friction while crossing the inner crust's lattice of heavy nuclei. Those demands challenge standard models of neutron star glitches.
arxiv-2605-04886:
Arnault Chatelain and nine co-authors argue that language model benchmarks largely ignore the social sciences, and that this gap harms both fields. Benchmarks do more than measure progress, they argue, since they shape reputations, research plans, and commercial outcomes. Social scientists, meanwhile, produce carefully labelled, context-rich datasets every year.

To close the gap, the authors introduce BenCSSmark, a benchmark built from datasets annotated by computational social scientists. Fields from history and sociology to political science and economics stand to gain, they argue. Better inclusion should make models more robust and transparent, and give scholars tools better matched to their actual questions.
arxiv-2605-04986:
Edan Lerner and Eran Bouchbinder explain how wavy phonon behaviour in disordered solids departs from the classic Debye picture of vibrations. In the longest wavelengths, elastic waves in any solid follow Debye's model, but higher frequencies show anomalies, most famously the boson peak. Both curved phonon dispersion and extra non-phonon vibrations can contribute, and their split was poorly understood.

The authors show curved dispersion in many disordered solids, from elastic networks to glasses, stems from a disorder-set length scale that also controls wave fading. Large simulations then separate the two contributions, finding their balance depends strongly on how disordered the solid is, including its cooling history.
arxiv-2605-05286:
Pascal Kettmann and three co-authors define well-behaved meanings for fuzzy logic programs that mix two kinds of negation, in an extended version of their work. Logic programs can treat not-proved as false, or require positive evidence of falsity, and combining both is delicate. Adding fuzzy truth values, where statements hold by degrees, makes the semantics harder still.

The authors use approximation fixpoint theory, a unifying framework for logic program semantics, to formulate their definitions. They show the framework recovers several existing semantics for such programs as special cases. It also gives rise to a host of new paraconsistent semantics, which tolerate contradictory information without collapsing into triviality.
arxiv-2605-05586:
Designing aircraft means running costly flow simulations again and again. Francisco Giral and ten co-authors introduce AeroJEPA, a surrogate that learns compact models of airflow fields instead of predicting every point. Geometry is encoded as context tokens, and the flow state as tokens, both open to direct use in design tasks.

A decoder reads the field only where detail is requested. On large benchmark suites, AeroJEPA gave up some full-field accuracy for reusable models. In selective decoding tests it beat direct-regression rivals while skipping most of the aircraft, and its latent space supported blending and early design tests.
arxiv-2605-05786:
Proving a quantum program correct in Hoare style is sound but rarely automatic. Wei-Lun Tsai, Yu-Fang Chen, and Ondřej Lengál introduce a specification language that makes full automation practical for fixed-qubit programs. Automata-based checking scales well, but translating high-level set-based assertions into automata used to blow up exponentially.

Their set-based language and translation scheme run in time linear in the number of qubits. Controlled building and qubit reordering keep the automata compact. The report presents the language as a practical front end for automatic quantum checking, aimed at fixed-qubit programs throughout.
arxiv-2605-06086:
Niels Vyncke, Pooya Ashtari, and Aleksandra Pižurica handle missing input channels in multimodal image analysis by working in weight space. A medical scan may lack one of its usual sequences, and most fixes engineer features that resist the gap. Such designs often need rework for each new data set or tuning burden.

Their hypernetwork, LARGO, instead models the weights of the many dedicated missing modality models as one compressed network. A tensor decomposition keeps that single network compact across all combinations of present and absent inputs. On two medical benchmarks it ranked first in 47 of 52 configurations, with clear average gains over leading baselines. A small audio visual test hints the idea may travel beyond medical imaging.
arxiv-2605-06186:
Marco Agozzino and four co-authors turn carbon atomic wires into stable nanoparticles through an electrochemical reaction. These wires are finite chains of sp hybridized carbon atoms, studied here as polyynes with alternating single and triple bonds. Applying a reducing potential to a solution of mixed length, hydrogen capped chains produced a black precipitate, which spectroscopy showed was a genuine reaction product, not simple degradation.

The precipitate proved to be amorphous carbon nanoparticles whose diameters can be tuned through growth kinetics at the solid liquid interface. Raman analysis showed an sp-sp2 character, with more than 60 percent of the sp fraction retained. The particles stayed stable in air for over six months. Experiments on size selected chains suggest the starting chain length survives better with this synthesis route.
arxiv-2605-06486:
Mohammad Mamun, Mohamed Gaber, Scott Buffett, and Sherif Saad benchmark language model agents as autonomous red-team attackers. Such agents can plan attacks, emulate adversaries, and chain steps like lateral movement inside a network. The authors map these abilities onto the MITRE ATT&CK framework and weigh strengths, limits, and governance needs.

Two lateral-movement scenarios run in a controlled emulation environment, with tasks checked by explicit validation rules. Three modes are compared: fully autonomous work, self-made plans, and expert-written plans. Expert plans complete the most tasks, but failures stay frequent everywhere, often from brittle commands, unstable environments, and credential or state handling errors.
arxiv-2605-07086:
Houman Safaai and four co-authors separate two questions that vision network pruning often merges into one score. A channel may carry strong information about the task, yet its work might be easily covered by neighboring channels if it is removed. They call that second property local replaceability, and measure both properties on separate axes.

Across three well-known networks trained on an image dataset, the two axes aligned weakly and produced different channel groupings. Replacement experiments showed peer support predicts removability better than task relevance alone. Under a matched computing budget, local measures proved the more reliable guide to which channels can safely be pruned.
arxiv-2605-07186:
Zekai Tong and four co-authors find an uncanny valley in how language models read corrupted text. Breaking words by inserting spaces inside them first hurts detection of target information, then, at heavier corruption, performance recovers. The authors name that U-shaped dip the Text Uncanny Valley and set out to explain it.

Their hypothesis is a mode switch: models read near-normal text word by word, and heavily broken text character by character, with the valley between the two. Several experiments fit that account, and tokenization measures peak just before performance bottoms out. The finding exposes a failure mode that clean-text benchmarks never show.
arxiv-2605-07286:
Kevin Kurian Thomas Vaidyan and Siddharth Rout solve stiff differential laws with sparse random-feature neural networks. Such networks train fast because only output weights are learned, but their dense hidden features produce ill-conditioned, low-rank arrays that limit scale. The authors build structured sparseness into the hidden activations instead.

That sparseness raises the rank, and a sparse singular value split solves the least-squares step well despite its poor shape. They examine the underlying bidiagonalization theory and the need for an orthogonalization step. On a one-dimensional convection-diffusion benchmark with strong advection, the method matched or improved accuracy while gaining substantially in training efficiency and robustness.
arxiv-2605-07486:
Giorgio Di Natale and six co-authors show that one chiplet inside a modern package can spy on a neighboring chiplet through side channels. Chiplet integration builds complex systems from small dies, gaining modularity and yield, but it also creates new physical attack surfaces. A communication chiplet meant for antennas or contactless links can double as an internal observation platform.

The authors formalize the threat with a realistic adversary model and describe the attack principle. Experiments assess feasibility and show that signals captured through the communication interface reveal information correlated with a victim chiplet's activity. The work warns that package-level integration needs its own side-channel defenses.
arxiv-2605-07786:
Caterina Gallegati and four co-authors introduce APEX, a metric for judging how close a generative model's output distribution is to real images. Standard metrics lean on outdated feature extractors with closed vocabularies, or on rigid parametric assumptions about the distributions. Both flaws grow more serious as image generators improve.

APEX extracts features with two open-vocabulary foundation models, CLIP and DINOv2, and compares distributions with the sliced Wasserstein distance, which assumes nothing about their shape. The authors back the design with theory and experiments showing it scales effectively to high-dimensional feature spaces. In benchmarks the metric proved robust to visual degradations and stable within and across datasets, including out-of-domain data, where stable evaluation matters most.
arxiv-2605-07886:
Ziyan Li and Naoki Hiratani expose a hidden distortion in online learning, where a model updates as data streams in rather than training on a fixed set. Studying kernel regression, they derive a closed form for the function that online learning actually produces and compare it with the offline answer.

Online kernel regression, they show, is exactly equivalent to offline regression fed shifted, inaccurate target outputs: an implicit target shift baked into the teaching signal. Correcting for that shift, in closed form or iteratively, makes online learning provably recover the same predictor as offline training. On continual image classification benchmarks, online gradient descent with corrected targets even beat learning with the true targets.
arxiv-2605-08086:
Aizierjiang Aiersilan, Haochen Liu, and James Hahn survey how 3D rotations are written down in computing. Graphics, robotics, and machine learning all need fast, exact ways to store and update a pose. The choices include Euler angles, axis-angle forms, quaternions, matrices, exponential maps, and newer continuous and random forms.

The authors weigh each choice on smoothness, gimbal lock, speed, storage, blending, and how forms combine. They mix algebra with uses such as cartoons, pose tracking, guidance, and shape matching. The evidence favors quaternions, which are small and quick. Six-part continuous forms suit neural networks best. The survey is a hands-on guide to picking a form.
arxiv-2605-08186:
Wei-Ping Huang, Chee-En Yu, Guan-Ting Lin, and Hung-yi Lee unify a scattered practice: adapting generative speech and language models at test time by minimizing entropy. For classification the trick is well understood, but for autoregressive models, methods relied on separate heuristics such as teacher forcing with pseudo labels or policy-gradient reinforcement learning.

The authors derive the exact entropy objective for autoregressive models and show it splits into a token-level policy gradient term plus a token-level entropy term. Earlier methods appear as partial versions of that single formula. Using the Whisper speech recognizer as a testbed, the unified method improved results across more than twenty domains, including noise, accents, and multiple languages.
arxiv-2605-08286:
Hyunmog Kim builds a test for equivariant neural force fields. It finds how much fine angular detail a trained backbone keeps. Such models predict molecular forces while respecting rotation symmetry. A trained backbone may silently drop high angular detail. Fine chemical work needs that detail, so a silent loss is a real risk.

The test injects a controlled angular wiggle into the field. It freezes the backbone. A small prediction network then reports which parts can still be read back. On aspirin, recovery held at one spherical harmonic degree. It collapsed at the next. That cliff matches the predicted boundary. The pattern repeated across four independently trained backbones and a second metric. A finite-degree theorem calibrates the tool.
arxiv-2605-08386:
Ziyang Yu, Yongliang Miao, Liang Zhao, Bowen Zhu, and coauthors organize agent skills so they can be reused at the right size. Skill libraries let language model agents carry procedures between tasks. Flat, one-size prompt blocks create a bind, though. Coarse skills drag in irrelevant context. Rewriting a whole skill for each task is slow and costly.

SkillLens arranges skills in a four-layer graph. The layers hold policies, strategies, procedures, and primitives. Retrieval works at mixed granularity. A random walk over the graph expands the first matches. A verifier then accepts, splits, rewrites, or skips each unit. Compatible pieces are reused as-is. Only the mismatched parts get adapted.
arxiv-2605-08586:
Mamadou Keita and Christopher Homan argue that computer science conferences should require proof that reported experiments really ran. Current practice leans on self reported checklists, optional code sharing, and logs the authors control, none of which tie printed numbers to an actual run. They name the gap experiment nonrepudiation and state the security properties a valid protocol must meet.

Their working system, K-Veritas, written in Go, signs experiment reports without touching training data and already keeps a public registry of sealed records. The authors call for an open shared standard built with the community. Research publishing gains a concrete way to make results tamper evident and harder to fake or later deny.
arxiv-2605-08786:
Christopher Lohse and five coauthors find the root cause of system anomalies with PRIM, a meta learned Bayesian method that skips model fitting at test time. Root cause hunting is hard because errors propagate, causal structure is uncertain, and inference is slow. PRIM trains on a synthetic prior of causal models, learning to spot which mechanism changed between normal and anomalous periods while averaging over structural uncertainty.

Its transformer process attends jointly to normal samples, anomalous samples, and node structure, delivering answers in milliseconds for systems up to one hundred variables. On synthetic and two realistic benchmarks it rivals methods handed the true causal graph, and light fine tuning helps further. Operations teams gain near instant diagnosis.
arxiv-2605-08986:
E. Jafarov, S. Nagiyev, and J. Van der Jeugt solve one clean case of an electron gas in a wire. The wire is not the same in all ways. Its mouth is shaped like a wave spring. The electron mass shifts with how far it sits from the core. That shift breaks the wire's even form. They work the case two ways, the stock way and a non stock way. Wave forms come out in Laguerre terms. The split tone scale comes out with them.

The side part of the mass law also solves clean in the non stock way. Its wave forms use Gegenbauer terms, for both par states. Bound ties and odd cases close the work. Clean cases like this one ground gut feel. They also test the codes used on real wires.
arxiv-2605-09186:
Liding Xu, Yugeng Zhou, and Sebastian Pokutta ask whether language-model agents can speed up research on mixed-integer programming, a core method for hard planning problems. Testing an idea inside a solver normally takes much coding, fixing, tuning, and large test runs. Their 2026 paper places agents inside a harness built around SCIP, an open solver, so they can write, check, and test solver add-ons.

The test case asks agents to spot global patterns hidden in a model's constraints and build handlers that spread known values through them. On a standard benchmark set, the agents recover known patterns and produce working handlers. Inside a safe sandbox they also tune and debug their work. Five extra benchmark cases were solved by new spreading methods the agents found.
arxiv-2605-09386:
Yang and four colleagues improve metric-induced discrete flow matching for discrete generation. It is limited by heuristic schedulers needing hyperparameter search, and by finite-step path-tracking drift from its first-order Markov chain solver. They work out a kinetic-optimal scheduler for prescribed scalar-parameterised probability paths. For metric-induced discrete flow matching it becomes a training-free schedule traversing the path at constant Fisher-Rao speed.

They also add a finite-step moment correction adjusting the jump probability while preserving the Markov chain jump destination distribution. The resulting method, GibbsTTS, is validated for codec-based zero-shot text-to-speech. With one architecture and a large-scale dataset held fixed, it takes the best objective naturalness and is preferred subjectively over masked discrete baselines. Against state-of-the-art speech systems, GibbsTTS shows strong speaker similarity, top on three of four sets and second on the fourth.
arxiv-2605-09486:
Li and three colleagues propose CTQWformer, a hybrid graph learning framework integrating quantum walks with graph neural networks. A trainable Hamiltonian fuses graph shape and node features, giving a physically grounded model of quantum walk dynamics that captures rich graph shape. The extracted walk-based representations feed two modules: a Graph Transformer module embedding final-time propagation chances as biases in self-attention, and a Graph Recurrent Module capturing time patterns with two-way recurrent networks.

Wide experiments on benchmark graph classification datasets show CTQWformer beating graph kernel and GNN-based methods. To the authors' knowledge it is the first hybrid CTQW-based Transformer, joining CTQW-derived bias with time modelling to advance graph learning.
arxiv-2605-09586:
Li and six colleagues present DeformMaster, an interactive physics neural world model for bendable objects learned from videos. Such a model must recover shape and looks plus body motion, contact grounding, and matter traits. That is hard because bendable linear, planar, and volume objects evolve under many axis bending, noisy contact, and complex matter response. The system turns real contact videos into an online hands on model within a unified motion and looks frame.

It keeps ordered rollout while a neural extra makes up for missed effects. It grounds sparse hand motion as a spread compliant driver. It covers matter response with place varying matter experts. It renders high quality 4D looks from forecast growth. Tests on real world bendable object clips show it rolls out future motion and renders looks better than state of the art rivals. It gives novel action rollouts, matter setting changes, and novel view renders.
arxiv-2605-10186:
Chen, Yin and Zhou introduce LegalCiteBench, a benchmark that tests whether legal language models cite real cases correctly. Incorrect citations and invented precedents can cause serious professional harm, yet existing legal benchmarks stress statutory reasoning and question answering rather than citation itself. The central failure mode is closed-book: asked for authorities without outside sources, models return plausible-looking but wrong citations.

Built from one thousand real United States judicial opinions held by the Case Law Access Project, the benchmark holds about twenty-four thousand instances. It spans five tasks: retrieval, completion, error detection, case matching, and verification with correction. Across twenty-one models, exact citation recovery stays brutally hard, with even the best below seven out of one hundred on retrieval and completion. Misleading answer rates exceed ninety-four percent for twenty of twenty-one models on retrieval-heavy tasks, and scale plus legal pretraining barely help.
arxiv-2605-10486:
Maksym Nechepurenko asks how leverage changes rigging in event prediction markets. Leverage on event contracts raises three questions: how it changes rigging incentives, how it interacts with informed trading rents, and how regulation should respond. His 2026 paper develops a framework for the first two and surveys regulation for the third.

Its core move is a two-axis taxonomy. Price rigging moves the contract price without affecting the event resolution. Outcome rigging affects the event itself, such as thrown matches or bribed voters. For price rigging, leverage amplifies profit while cost stays flat. For outcome rigging, leverage shifts the threshold at which influencing an event pays in expectation. Sports and sub-national political markets are where leverage most shifts that balance; large-electorate political and macroeconomic markets stay bounded by cost. Informed trading rents scale with leverage three ways: direct multiplication, Sharpe-ratio preservation, and detection-cost amortization.
arxiv-2605-10986:
R. Pullano and G. Modanese trace a structural link between the Bohm quantum potential and the scalar mode of Aharonov-Bohm electrodynamics in a bosonic Schrödinger model. The model, recently proposed by Minotti and Modanese, couples the electromagnetic field to a conserved current with an extra source term.

In the Madelung picture, the Bohm potential tracks the relative curvature of the wave amplitude, while the scalar mode's source tracks the amplitude's density and gradient content. The two quantities therefore probe different differential aspects of the same profile rather than sourcing each other directly. Once boundary and normalization data are fixed, the link becomes precise. Quantum-foundations researchers get a clean map between two faces of one amplitude.
arxiv-2605-11486: Yamaguchi and nine colleagues analyze the large planet-forming disk V1094 Sco and its multiple ring-gap pairs. ALMA continuum and carbon monoxide emission plus VLT scattered light show four narrow dust ring-gap pairs out to about 380 AU. Gas extends to about 760 AU in orbital rotation. Dust ring widths cap stirring near one thousandth or less, implying weak turbulence. A double gap near 100 AU fits multi-gap driving by a low-mass companion, while outer rings fit secular gravity instability, supporting a hybrid origin.
arxiv-2605-11986: Arthur Siqueira and four colleagues test, in 2026 work, large language models as support for database design with Entity-Relationship diagrams drawn from plain-language needs. Three models faced three prompting styles on one task of growing size, judged against the needs for shape and meaning fit. Models did fine on simple cases, but trust fell as tasks grew harder, with more errors, vague spots, and broken constraints, so checking costs may erase time savings.
arxiv-2605-12386: Huang and five colleagues argue that robot success scores hide unsafe behaviour, since a robot can reach the goal while contaminating objects, releasing too early or acting out of order. Their SafeManip benchmark judges safety over time from low-level action traces across eight physical and semantic categories. Symbolic predicates become reusable temporal properties, organised through the ManipVerse ontology for rules that transfer across objects and tasks. Per-trigger metrics then score violations against the chances each safety duty actually arose.
arxiv-2605-12586: Liu and ten colleagues show that 3D geometric primitives can serve as a spatial language for vision-language models. These models can generate code that rebuilds a 3D scene from cubes, spheres and cylinders with correct counts, classes and rough positions. Yet they fail simpler spatial questions on the same image. Their SpatialBabel benchmark tests fourteen models on primitive-based reconstruction across six scene-code languages, finding one model's detection F1 varies by up to 5.7 times across languages. A training-free Code-CoT strategy routes spatial reasoning through primitive code.
arxiv-2605-12786: Rogel, Yadollahi and Laban study how people perceive emotional expressions from Reachy Mini, a low-degree-of-freedom robot with a non-human repertoire. Emotion expression matters in human-robot interaction, yet affect is little known on sparse, non-anthropomorphic robots. In an online study, one hundred participants viewed ten short clips of Reachy Mini expressing emotions. For each clip, they identified the emotion, rated valence and arousal, and evaluated social-perception traits. Exact recognition was modest and varied, with anger, sadness and interest recognised more than love.
arxiv-2605-13086: Bae and four co-authors present a manipulation strategy for the Variable Topology Truss, a truss robot of actuated members joined by passive spherical joints. Truss robots promise rapid deployment, yet manipulation strategy has barely been studied. Their hybrid control framework regulates position and force together without explicit decoupling, using sensor-based force feedback at each member despite high friction. Tests on a single module and the full system confirm consistent, reliable object manipulation.
arxiv-2605-13386: Daniel Matsui Smola proves that conditioning a generative model on a small support set amounts to kernel smoothing. Under a Gaussian optimal-transport path, the exact velocity field is a Nadaraya-Watson smoother. Its bandwidth shrinks as flow time advances, moving from broad averaging to nearest-neighbour behaviour. A single Gaussian-kernel attention head computes this field exactly. The theory predicts three failure regimes, including collapse at high dimension. Experiments confirm that learned conditioning helps precisely in those regimes.
arxiv-2605-13586: Zini Chen and six colleagues propose HetScene, a heterogeneity-aware diffusion framework for dense indoor scene generation. The authors revisit layout generation through structural heterogeneity, splitting objects into primary and minor kinds by their own roles in a scene. HetScene splits layout work into two stages: Structural Layout Generation and Contextual Layout Generation. The first stage builds tidy layouts from primary objects only, guided by text notes, room masks and spatial link graphs.
arxiv-2605-14186: Cao and four co-authors build a metacognitive harness turning language models' self-monitoring signals into test-time control. Before solving, models can estimate their odds of success. After solving, they can judge whether an answer is right. Yet those signals are measured in isolation rather than used to steer inference. Borrowing Nelson-Narens theory from cognitive psychology, the harness separates monitoring from reasoning. Each problem starts with a pre-solve feeling-of-knowing signal. Each solve attempt ends with a post-solve judgment-of-learning signal.
arxiv-2605-14286: Matsumoto proves mixed-characteristic versions of two degeneration theorems, due to Connes and to Feigin and Tsygan, for varieties over Witt vectors. When the variety is smooth and proper, and its dimension stays below a bound tied to the prime, the de Rham-to-periodic-cyclic spectral sequence splits. It also degenerates under that bound. He extends the result to rings of integers with a ramification bound. He also covers a related topological sequence, and adds a q-de Rham analogue after inverting an explicit factorial.
arxiv-2605-14386: Taebong Kim and colleagues present the Darwin Family, a training-free way to improve language-model reasoning by evolving merged models in weight space. Darwin uses a fourteen-dimensional merge genome, MRI-Trust Fusion balancing layer-importance signals against evolutionary search, and an Architecture Mapper for breeding across model families. Its flagship Darwin-27B-Opus scores 86.9 percent on GPQA Diamond, ranking sixth among 1,252 evaluated models, and beats its fully trained foundation model. Across four-to-thirty-five-billion-parameter models, evolved models consistently beat their parents.
arxiv-2605-14586: Chirolli, Brosco, Vool, Catelani and Amico propose a superconducting circuit that hosts several low-lying states, kept well apart from the rest of the spectrum, as a qudit protected from leakage errors. The states are fractional fluxons, dubbed fraxons, trapped in minima of a Josephson potential shaped by Fourier engineering. Spectra for four- and five-level systems are given, and a non-Abelian STIRAP protocol for single-qutrit gates is proposed.
arxiv-2605-14786: Lugoloobi, Marro, Magomere, Wright and Russell ask whether websites can passively identify which language model powers a browsing agent. Across fourteen frontier models and four web environments, an agent's actions and interaction timings, caught by a passive tracker, identify the model with up to ninety-six percent F1. Classifiers generalise across model sizes and families and need only few traces. Randomised timing delays degrade performance, but retraining on delayed traces largely restores it.
arxiv-2605-15186: Kaixin Zhu and eleven others introduce VGGT-Edit, a feed-forward framework for editing 3D scenes natively from text instructions. Older methods edit views in 2D and lift them back to 3D, blurring textures and breaking geometry across viewpoints. VGGT-Edit injects text in sync with depth and spatial poses for stable grounding, then a residual head predicts geometric displacements that deform the scene while holding the background steady. A multi-term objective keeps geometric accuracy and high-fidelity appearance.
arxiv-2605-15286: Andreas Crivellin, Paul H. Frampton, and Ahmed Hammad assess discovery prospects for doubly-charged bileptons at the High-Luminosity LHC. Two channels complement each other: direct bilepton pair production, sensitive mainly to bilepton mass, and production through heavy-quark decays, sensitive mainly to heavy-quark mass and often enhanced. The four-energetic-lepton signature is nearly background-free. Run-2 data allow discovery only below about 1 TeV in heavy-quark mass, while the HL-LHC reaches 2.5 TeV there and 2 TeV in bilepton mass.
arxiv-2605-15486: Swayamjit Saha, Subhabrata Das, Haonan Duan, and Xiao-Yang Liu use large language models to plan tasks for building robots. One model drafts the plan from task facts, agent skills, and the goal. A second model checks it. A plain-language link lets site staff reshape plans as site facts change. The pair was tried on a plain test case. Scores back the approach. The team says such models count for robot work on building sites.
arxiv-2605-15886: Daria Blinova and six colleagues introduce a dataset of interlinked multimodal political messages from the Russian government. It covers official speeches by Kremlin and Foreign Ministry actors over multiple decades. Each speech carries Russian- and English-language texts, linked images and captions where present, and matched data on dates, speakers, locations and content tags. Unique IDs link images to speeches and align Russian and English versions. Checked topic labels from transformer-based mixed-media topic models, refined by a Russian politics expert, support multilingual, time-based and place-based studies.
arxiv-2605-15986: Ömer Faruk Çoban and five colleagues mine 16 years of Fermi telescope data on the microquasar SS 433, whose jets wobble on a roughly 162-day cycle. They confirm a gamma-ray source, 4FGL J1913.2+0512, and a western-lobe excess, while gating out a bright nearby pulsar. Its 162-day rhythm stands out in the first decade of data but fades later, suggesting the gamma-ray output of the SS 433 environment shifts over years.
arxiv-2605-16186: Nagura, Terasawa, Terawaki, and Takada compare analytic methods for the Gaussian covariance of the cosmic shear two-point correlation function, allowing for finite survey geometry. With HSC Year 3 survey-mask convergence fields as a test case, they find the improved narrow-kernel approximation fails to match simulation covariances. Leftover errors in off-diagonal harmonic-space parts leak through the Legendre transform and distort real-space results. The weighted quartic-counts method matches better, showing off-diagonal modelling is crucial for sound estimates.
arxiv-2605-16286: Alexander and six others propose homoglyph tweaks to protect first-year CS theory problems from AI solvers. Students using AI tools to solve tasks can defeat a course's learning goals. Their method first rewords a question without changing its meaning, then tweaks a few letters with twin glyphs. Tests show theory problems can be tweaked well, and the authors also offer a hands-on tool for easy use of the method.
arxiv-2605-16386: Zhang and nine others audit multimodal language-model raters scoring Clock Drawing Test images on the Shulman rubric.
