Fine-tuned Vision Transformers calibrate best, yet zero-shot language models stay competitive on tolerance-based agreement, with GPT-5 reaching 92 percent within-1 accuracy. Per-score analysis reveals a central tendency effect: predictions compress toward the middle, over-predicting at the low end and under-predicting at the high end. The effect hits extremes hardest and survives few-shot exemplars and terminology removal, demanding calibration-aware evaluation before high-stakes use.
arxiv-2605-16786: Wang and colleagues present Lever, a system for flash-backed language-model inference on smartphones. Large models exceed phone DRAM, and flash storage is slow because decoding repeatedly calls the target model with costly I/O. Lever keeps a small draft model in DRAM while a larger flash target checks several candidate tokens per call. It tunes drafting with token trees, verification with early-exit pruning, and execution across phone CPU-NPU hardware. Tests show latency down 2.93-fold versus flash-offloaded baselines and 1.50-fold versus standard speculative decoding.
arxiv-2605-17086: Garg, Crosta and Baier map how exposed jobs are to automation in 124 economies, using a language model to grade nearly nineteen thousand work tasks. Exposure shifts with local conditions, not just job type, and ranges from about three percent to over sixty percent across countries. Poorer economies lean toward rule-based, worker-replacing automation, while richer ones show more worker-aiding uses. Women face more replacement-facing jobs, the authors report.
arxiv-2605-17186: Chang introduces an operator-splitting method for infinite chains of linear differential equations indexed by counts. When coupling grows linearly with the index, an exact transform closes the chain on finite windows with no top boundary value. Strang splitting handles the rest with a standard capped solver. Tests on branching, predator-prey, chemical and gene-expression models show memory and time savings at accuracy rivaling finite-state projection.
arxiv-2605-17486: Lin and colleagues present DyGRO-VLA, a two-stage frame that stops reinforcement-learning optimizers from shrinking vision-language-action models into narrow task specialists. It first captures cross-task latent representations on information-based principles. It then dynamically refines policy optimization through a mixture of RL residuals. The design exploits task-relevant latent information while limiting harmful interference. Tests on LIBERO, RoboTwin2 and real robots show consistent gains under multi-task training and distribution shift.
arxiv-2605-17786: Shogo B. Kobayashi and colleagues report XRISM looks at M82 X-2, an ultraluminous X-ray pulsar. XRISM watched M82 for 207.7 kiloseconds with X-2 in view. A search found a candidate pulse near the known 1.38727-second period at 3.15 sigma. If that pulse is real, the iron K-alpha line looks wider at pulse peak than elsewhere, hinting some of the line comes from the pulsar system. The width points to gas too fast for a companion star atmosphere and to a source under 63,000 kilometers wide, likely in the accretion flow.
arxiv-2605-17986: Lei Zhao, Abhay Bhaskar, and Edgar Dobriban introduce LivePI, a benchmark for indirect prompt injection risk in agents. Agents like OpenClaw work locally, where harmful instructions hidden in email, files, webpages, or chats can trigger actions. LivePI covers seven surfaces, twelve attack families, and five goals, run on a virtual machine with controlled interfaces. Across five models, success ranges from 10.7% to 29.6%, group-chat injection always succeeds, and a two-layer defense intercepts all malicious completions for GPT-5.3-Codex while keeping benign utility.
arxiv-2605-18486: Bin Li and three co-authors study, in a 2026 paper, a multi-UAV integrated sensing and communication system with movable antenna arrays. They simulate roaming ground users and three-dimensional UAV deployment, aiming to maximize total data rate. The problem splits in two: HDBSCAN clustering handles ground-to-air association, while a soft actor-critic algorithm optimizes trajectories, antenna positions, and beamforming. Movable-antenna UAVs beat fixed-antenna ones on rates while preserving sensing performance.
arxiv-2605-18886: M. W. AlMasri builds a quantum framework for open systems changing on fast and slow clocks. Translating classical asymptotic-preserving schemes into quantum channels and Lindblad dynamics, the paper proves layered protocols converge uniformly to the slow limit with a stiffness-free error bound. Superlinear gate savings appear exactly when fast motion is handled by native analog evolution or analytic elimination shrinking the working space. A cavity QED setup in the bad-cavity limit and a kinetic model settling into fluid behavior show the theory at work.
arxiv-2605-19086: I. A. Aleksandrov, M. A. Dorodnyi, and E. D. Akimkina show that spectral fringes in Schwinger pair creation need not come from structured driving. Two nearly identical bell-shaped pulses, a Gaussian and a deformed variant, give different momentum spectra near the crossover. The Gaussian stays smooth. The deformed pulse develops fringes as the Keldysh parameter nears one. Numerical solutions match a turning-point account tracing the effect to a shift in the saddle. The same mechanism appears in a Dirac model for graphene on silicon carbide.
arxiv-2605-19286: Amirmehran Mahdavi and Ehsan Roohi study how wall heating steers nitrogen flow through a converging-diverging nozzle. Using simulation Monte Carlo, they test cooling, neutral, and heating walls across a flux range. Heating stratifies the flow, with wall temperature passing fivefold the inlet level while the bulk warms more slowly. It narrows the mass-carrying core, so mass flow falls. Yet specific impulse climbs from 156 seconds to 201 seconds because thermal and pressure thrust gains outweigh the loss, and two flow modes capture over 97 percent of the variation.
arxiv-2605-19386: Yang and colleagues present MatPhys, a system that predicts spring-mass physics settings for bendable objects from a single video. Earlier methods assume one uniform material and refit each scene, giving clashing values for the same material. MatPhys splits objects into parts using image features, assigns each part its own material behavior, and ties values together through a shared material codebook. The result matches per-scene fitting on reconstruction and forecasting while generalizing better to new objects and interactions.
arxiv-2605-19586: Mori and team study links between anti-blocking lattice polytopes and their unconditional counterparts, formed by reflecting across all axis hyperplanes. They prove the toric ring of an anti-blocking polytope is normal exactly when the toric ring of its mirror partner is normal. Also, the toric ideal is built from quadratic binomials on one side exactly when it holds on the other. They also obtain a graph-based characterization of such generation for symmetric stable set ideals.
arxiv-2605-19886: Zinihi and Ehrhardt present a constraint aware physics informed neural network for SEIR reaction diffusion epidemic models with vital dynamics. Disease data are scarce, so synthetic benchmarks are made with structure preserving finite difference schemes that keep values positive and bounded and the scheme stable. The network loss combines PDE errors, data, edge rules and constraints, including values at or above zero and allowed values. Forward runs and inverse fitting in 1D and 2D rebuild space and time spread and pin down values well from sparse noisy data.
arxiv-2605-19986: He-Yang Xu and seven co-workers argue that pass-or-fail scores hide what embodied robots actually get wrong in fine hand work. Their MetaFine scheme splits skill into grasp of the task, sight, and controlled motion, and rebuilds varied tests into diagnostic cases on one shared set of rules. Tests of leading vision-language-action models show faults that differ by skill area. A targeted fix pinpoints how well the visual encoder keeps local spatial detail as a key choke point.
arxiv-2605-20086: Nico Pelleriti and six co-workers ask what coding agents actually evolve, beyond their benchmark scores. A score can reflect new algorithmic structure, retuning, reusing ideas already in the model, or overfitting to the evaluator. EvoTrace gathers coding traces across four frameworks, both kinds of models, and sixteen tasks. EvoReplay replays search states behind top scores, testing changes to constants, removal of parts and model swaps. Most gains come from a small set of edit types, and about thirty percent of added lines bring back lines deleted earlier.
arxiv-2605-20186: Dan Hooper, Gordan Krnjaic and Gabriele Montefalcone show WIMP-like dark matter need not thermalize at freeze-out to match the relic density. Dark matter stays in equilibrium with Standard Model radiation until freeze-out, with cross sections near ten to the minus twenty-six. Hidden-sector models decouple dark matter from the Standard Model at high temperature. Both sectors share similar temperatures at freeze-out, giving relic abundance. Coupling can be small, putting direct detection and collider signals far below what experiments can reach.
arxiv-2605-20286: Junxi Chen, Junhao Dong and Xiaohua Xie present adaptive probe-based steering for robust LLM jailbreaking. Contrastive steering can jailbreak large language models, but current methods use limited, biased prompts and need manual tuning of steering strength. They use model extraction to guide steering vectors toward the ideal vector, and tune steering strength adaptively from activation statistics. Tests show the method improves effectiveness and robustness, without extra prompts or manual tuning. It reveals breakdowns of fortified models, raising the harmfulness score from six percent to seventy percent.
arxiv-2605-20386: Qi and two co-workers build Music of Changing Lines, an interactive system that treats the I-Ching as a meaning-bearing frame, not a bare chance device. Users cast coins by the Wen Wang Fa method, and that reading becomes a prompt for a generative music model. The Lyria model then renders a musical reply, keeping ritual, reading and participation at the centre. The work shows generative AI can back participatory, meaning-led music without fixing structure or displacing human choice.
arxiv-2605-20586: Kevin Carlson and Ea Thompson resolve Arkor's conjecture on exponentiable virtual double categories by giving equivalent characterizations in terms of cell decompositions. Virtual double categories provide a framework for formal category theory, and recent work asked about higher morphisms between them. Exponentiable ones are those whose outgoing morphisms can themselves be enriched to a full virtual double category. The authors also prove that virtual double categories of cospans are always exponentiable, as are those arising from pseudo double categories or exponentiable multicategories.
arxiv-2605-20686: Eiko Kozaki and seven colleagues study dust in early-type galaxies using AKARI near-infrared spectra of 30 galaxies. Dust origins there are debated, with candidates including mass loss from old stars, mergers, and grain growth in space. They focus on silicon monoxide and carbon monoxide absorption lines tracing old stellar photospheres. Dust mass tracks the summed strength of those lines, pointing to mass loss from evolved stars as a major source, with no strong link to X-ray plasma.
arxiv-2605-21086: Seogyeong Jeong and six colleagues present LoCar, localization-aware evaluation of in-vehicle assistants. Large language models are increasingly integrated into in-vehicle chat systems, yet identifying the optimal model remains challenging for lack of domain-specific standards. Their design focuses on Korean-language tuning, and analysis reveals notable patterns in model behaviour. Fine-grained Korean honorific control stays unstable in current models, so exact speech-level realization must be explicitly evaluated.
arxiv-2605-21286: Maja Franz and colleagues present a software framework that takes quantum machine learning down to pulse-level modeling, inside the QML-Essentials package. Gate abstractions hide hardware detail and may curb what hardware can do. Direct pulse-level work is richer and truer to physics, but harder to build. Their framework embeds quantum optimal control in a machine learning setting, joining gate-based and pulse-level views. The gain is tailored error mitigation and optimization, with structured tools to tame the added complexity.
arxiv-2605-21386: Ruslan Mushkaev, Francesco Petocchi, and Philipp Werner investigate strange metallicity in the Kagome metal Ni3In with dynamical mean-field theory. Strange metallicity, a linear temperature link for resistivity, appears across correlated materials and recently in Ni3In, where almost trapped and moving charge degrees coexist from a partly flat band. Work on a minimal single-band Hubbard model shows non-Fermi-liquid-like self-energy pattern and local magnetic moment growth even at modest repulsion. With more hole doping, a crossover to a heavy Fermi-liquid regime appears.
arxiv-2605-21486: Dayal Singh Kalra and Maissam Barkeshli quantify hyperparameter transfer and the role of embedding-layer learning rate. Hyperparameter transfer extrapolates optimal optimization settings from small to large scales, critical for training large language models. This is done by fitting a scaling law or by a choice of parameterization, such as Maximal Update, that renders optimal settings roughly scale invariant. They develop a framework with three metrics: scaling-law fit quality, robustness to extrapolation errors, and asymptotic loss penalty from parameterization choice.
arxiv-2605-21586: Chul Chung and co-authors re-examine age-bias correction in supernova cosmology. They re-examine Wiseman et al. (2026), who claim progenitor-age bias has negligible impact on Type Ia supernova inferences. They show Wiseman's inferred host-age-Hubble residual slope is severely underestimated. Their sample spans a wide redshift range, zero point zero four to zero point four two, over which mean host age evolves by about three gigayears. Supernovae spanning large host-age differences are thus assigned similar residual values before regression, flattening the relation.
arxiv-2605-21786: Jacob Bedrossian, Tom Schang, and Franziska Weber prove Leray-Hopf type weak solutions exist for a whole-core model of Earth's field dynamics. The model joins magnetohydrodynamic laws in the outer core to physics for the conducting inner core, with a perfect insulator outside under Maxwell's laws. The proof uses Galerkin approximations, which require a tailored function space for the field and a Biot-Savart result. The hard part is a math setup handling fluid-solid coupling with the inner core plus the transmission problem at the core edge.
arxiv-2605-21986: Karol Fulat and co-authors simulate nonrelativistic high-Mach-number oblique shocks moving through turbulent gas with PIC methods. Collisionless shocks commonly accelerate matter in astrophysics, and at oblique shocks some fast electrons escape upstream, forming a foreshock where reflected charges drive instabilities. Their runs show upstream churn boosts whistler waves, boosting magnetic ripples and larger structures. That shortens and heats the foreshock, and prior churn yields non-thermal ones that are more numerous, faster, and carry more total energy.
arxiv-2605-22086: Zhiqing Hong and co-authors present GenHAR, a framework for generalizing cross-domain human activity recognition for last-mile delivery. It works well in many applications, yet distribution shift across sensor data domains degrades performance in real deployments. GenHAR mitigates the domain gap, beating state-of-the-art methods by 9.97 percent in accuracy and reducing floating point operations by 6.4 times on real-world datasets. The team also deployed GenHAR at a leading logistics company in 4 cities, detecting 2.15 billion real-time events, and they release their code.
arxiv-2605-22186: Senyan Xu and co-authors present EIC-LIE, an event-illumination collaborative framework for low-light image enhancement. Event-based methods exploit high dynamic range from events but overlook global illumination and event noise in real scenes. Their EICI module gathers HDR features across lighting conditions and injects complementary content into illumination and event representations. An illumination-aware event filter then cuts event noise using brightness statistics from images. The team also builds a beam-splitter-based hybrid imaging system for real-world data collection.
arxiv-2605-22286: Wu, Li and He present EmoTrack, a model that gauges depression severity from counselling transcripts. It predicts the total score on the eight-item Patient Health Questionnaire, known as PHQ-8. The model joins structured clinical feature scores with sentence-level meaning. It links each clinical feature to the utterances that support it. It can also carry a compressed form of the prior session as memory for longitudinal assessment. On the DAIC-WOZ benchmark, it cuts mean absolute error from 2.82 to 2.47 against the strongest baseline.
arxiv-2605-22586: Fu and Wang write a unified tutorial on diffusion theory, joining views apart: diffusion probabilistic models, score based modelling, stochastic differential equations and numerical sampling. Starting from a conditional Gaussian noising process, they derive ODE and SDE forms and reach the reverse time equations that make generation possible. They explain the marginal score as the central unknown in reverse sampling and show score matching as the standard denoising aim. DDPM and DDIM, flow matching, and score based SDEs all land in one framework.
arxiv-2605-22786: Asif and four colleagues present LCGuard, a guard for multi-agent language systems that share key-value caches instead of plain text. Those caches carry reasoning and private context, so one agent can leak sensitive input to another without any words changing hands. LCGuard reshapes shared caches through adversarial training, cutting how much an attacker can rebuild while keeping task performance close to unguarded sharing.
arxiv-2605-22886: Thomas and Calvanese Strinati propose the Topological Resilience Index, a real-time gauge of how deep-learning wireless receivers hold up as channels shift. Bit error rate alone, they argue, says little about resilience. Their index blends loss-landscape stability, drift in channel impulse responses, and channel manifold shape. In simulations across ten environment changes, it warned of degradation more than one symbol ahead of baselines and cut post-shift errors by 80 percent when guiding re-adaptation.
arxiv-2605-23086: Davis and Park define integer valued invariants gamma^k for three component links. They prove they hold under concordance and more generally weak cobordism. The invariants lift certain Milnor invariants of three component links. The proof introduces h(L), a three component version of the Kojima-Yamasaki eta invariant, which gives the gamma values. As uses they obtain weak cobordism classes when the chosen component has trivial Alexander polynomial. They also describe knots bounding smoothly placed disks in 4D balls whose outsides have fundamental group Z.
arxiv-2605-23186: Imaykin studies global pull, in the energy norm, for finite energy states of a classical particle joined to a scalar wave field. Pull could head toward still solutions under a holding field, or toward the soliton set under zero field. By an energy saving argument, he shows that in both cases no global pull occurs.
arxiv-2605-23286: Van Regemortel and five coauthors present a setup for guessing and testing quantum photon stats in light-matter circuits, using device values for (Al)GaAs guide platforms. Strong light-matter link between a guided light mode and an exciton chip shift gives rise to exciton-bits. By mapping the pulsed curved guide moves onto a bosonic quantum circuit model that adds loss, they find quantum signs in labs across two circuit setups.
arxiv-2605-23486: Shen and Wang propose a high-order finite element method for linear fourth-order elliptic problems that preserves nodal bounds and mass, built on a variational inequality form. The method also has an equivalent strictly convex minimization form, which secures well-posedness and an optimal error estimate under regularity. They extend the frame to nonlinear fourth-order parabolic problems with space-time discretizations, and to second-order parabolic problems via a consistent fourth-order regularization. Numerical tests with singularities and low regularity confirm stability, efficiency, and high-order accuracy.
arxiv-2605-23686: Xu and colleagues present pilot results from the FAST HI Deep survey, mapping a DESI DR1 region. The pilot covers a 10 deg² field overlapping HSC-SSP and DESI EDR SV3, at 7.3 minutes per beam. They identify 339 HI sources below redshift 0.09, about 34 per deg², nearly six times the wide-field rate. Optical counterparts come mainly from DESI redshifts, above 90 percent matching and correctness for galaxies brighter than 19.5 mag. Gas fraction relations versus stellar mass, surface density, NUV-r, and star formation rate match previous surveys, supporting a complete HI census.
arxiv-2605-23886: Ishige and Marieni study heterotic string models compactified on Enriques surfaces, a special class of geometric spaces. They sort the inequivalent shift vectors for the E8-times-E8 and Spin(32)-over-Z2 lattices. They examine the light particle spectrum of the resulting models and read them as ten-dimensional non-supersymmetric string theories wrapped on these surfaces. For some shift classes, projection removes the tachyons, unstable particles inherited from the parent theories that do not depend on moduli.
arxiv-2605-23986: Chen and eight co-authors rework agent memory as a write-efficient data problem. MemForest breaks the sequential bottleneck with parallel extraction, splitting memory building into concurrent, independent jobs. Its MemTree index orders memories as time-ordered trees and swaps global rewrites for local dirty-path refresh, refreshed in parallel across nodes and trees. On LongMemEval-S with Qwen3-30B, it hit 81.8 percent pass at 1 while building 6.0 times faster than EverMemOS, and on LoCoMo it nearly matched EverMemOS while building 9.5 times faster.
arxiv-2605-24286: Jia, Benton, and Easley study chain-of-thought faithfulness as information flow. Faithful reasoning should route answer information through the reasoning path, not a direct prompt-to-answer shortcut. Their frame rests on sufficiency, completeness, and necessity, measured with entropy, masked-KL, and gradient diagnostics. The metrics recover judged faithfulness gaps in hinted reasoning and expose a low-entropy mode where gradient measures stay stable. Update-time interventions for on-policy reinforcement learning shift behaviour toward stronger reasoning mediation and cut wrong-hint susceptibility.
arxiv-2605-24486: Yuyang Hu and colleagues ask whether peer agents on one long task can gain from each other rather than from bigger single agents. Their AgentFugue framework links agents through a shared hub. The hub records what each agent has established, tried, or ruled out. Each agent can draw on peers' findings in a form suited to its own search, with no central planner. Across demanding long-horizon tests, the collective approach beat strong baselines, suggesting that scaling out peers is its own source of gains.
arxiv-2605-24786: Yubo Li and Yidi Miao present CONF-KV, a cache manager that sets the key-value budget at each step from model uncertainty. Long chats make the cache the main memory cost, yet most eviction rules use fixed windows or past attention. CONF-KV turns the next-token distribution into a confidence score. It keeps more context when unsure and prunes hard when sure. Paired with mixed-precision storage, it reaches 91 percent retrieval accuracy on a needle-in-a-haystack test.
arxiv-2605-24986: Moyu Zhang leads HeteGenCTR, a click-through-rate model fixing uneven field training. Generative pre-training via discrete diffusion supervises all fields, easing sparse-data collapse. Yet generative click models weight each field equally, ignoring wide difficulty gaps across ID, sparse, numeric, and behavior fields. Easy fields hog gradients. HeteGenCTR learns per-field difficulty in denoising. That signal drives a self-balancing loss shifting gradients to hard fields and attention muting easy fields. Five benchmarks and a week-long live test show gains, strongest for cold-start users.
arxiv-2605-25186: Julius Vernie and Matthias Grabmair compare rival formalizations of the same legal provision by the decisions they encode, not their structure. Their method matches formalizations at node level, builds a shared interface per pair, and uses a SAT solver to list edge cases where they disagree. Those cases are then turned into concrete factual scenarios a legal expert can judge. Applied to ten EU provisions from nine frontier language models, behavioral divergence proves essentially unrelated to structural agreement, and disagreements include genuine controversies from legal commentary.
arxiv-2605-25286: Aagashram Neelakandan, Karsten Albe, and Bernhard Eidel couple atom-level models to continuum mechanics for larger systems. Their two-scale scheme drives small atomistic cells with deformation from a nonlinear finite-element problem, then returns averaged stresses and stiffnesses. The handoff follows Hill-Mandel energy equivalence, with no preset law imposed on the small scale. Tests on single-crystal copper show tension-compression asymmetry, sudden defect formation, and rapid settling under cyclic loads. The coarse solver stays robust throughout, recovering near-quadratic convergence in its final steps.
arxiv-2605-25386: Chen-Hao Zhao and colleagues extend non-Hermitian band theory to open and disordered systems. The skin effect piles states at boundaries, but its Brillouin-zone description only works for repeating lattices. The team builds a site-by-site theory with a local scaling transformation, introducing a twisting measure for metric-operator nontriviality. That measure exposes a multi-channel skin effect and defines a zone for nonperiodic lattices. Unifying the metric with Brillouin-zone geometry yields a correspondence principle for localization, plus a skin index for phase changes.
arxiv-2605-25486: Hengjun Jiang and eight colleagues improve search relevance judgment for knowledge-heavy queries, where ranking needs background grounding, multi-step reasoning, and set boundaries. Existing models lean on direct labels or shallow similarity, missing implicit intent, factual equivalence, and fine-grained distinctions. Their RAG-Match framework runs in three stages: knowledge pretraining to strengthen query-centered grounding. Reasoning alignment and preference calibration then fix boundary errors. On a real-world search benchmark it beats strong language-model baselines across multiple ranking metrics.
arxiv-2605-25686: Marmonier, Bawden and Sagot test the deliteralization hypothesis for modern machine translation: translations grow less literal through drafting and revision. Using WMT24++, they compare human translations and post-editions with two neural systems and six language models across 54 pairs and three tasks. Human translations stay less literal than all machine systems, though recent language models narrow the gap. Prompted to revise their own output repeatedly, language models deliteralize monotonically, the first such evidence for models. As post-editors, models invert human triggers, tolerating literal drafts and targeting idiomatic phrasing.
arxiv-2605-25786: Zeng and colleagues present NPSolver, a neural Poisson solver trained without labels via physics guidance. Older solvers stall on ill-conditioned systems, while neural nets need labeled data or unstable training. NPSolver refines its predictions with preconditioned conjugate gradient steps, giving a training signal. Theory confirms this guidance is a sound error proxy, and a stop-gradient design is vital. Its Boundary-Aware Transolver separates interior and boundary tokens, and tests on irregular geometries beat baseline families.
arxiv-2605-25986: Tian, Hu, Wu and Shi generate images and text with quantum mechanics and no training at all. Current generative models demand heavy compute and behave like black boxes. The authors instead build a local parent Hamiltonian, an energy operator whose lowest-energy state encodes the target distribution. Solving the full Hamiltonian then yields samples. Superposition and entanglement, the quantum traits that let states combine and correlate, keep the output globally consistent. The result is a new route to generative modelling rooted in physics.
arxiv-2605-26286: Maxim Mednikov and Oren Gal add a plug-in estimation layer that shields pre-trained multi-agent reinforcement learning policies from stale observations and delayed messages. The layer pairs a learned gated transition model with recursive Kalman filtering to estimate current states from asynchronous measurements. Because it sits at execution time, the 2026 layer needs no changes to training, architecture, or rewards. Across multi-agent and continuous-control benchmarks, it hardens policies against latency and packet loss, most in coordination-heavy and unstable tasks where timing matters.
arxiv-2605-26386: Jorge Ananias Neto and Ronaldo Thibes ask how black hole areas can take only spaced, set values. They apply Landauer's rule, which ties erasing one bit to a fixed disorder cost, to gaps between successive area levels. For the standard Bekenstein-Hawking measure, the method returns the known Bekenstein-Mukhanov spacing. Tests of Barrow, Rényi, and Kaniadakis measures then show unlike spacing behavior as levels grow large.
arxiv-2605-26486: The Meituan LongCat Team and twelve colleagues present LongCat-Video-Avatar 1.5, an open-source audio-driven video avatar system tuned for production, not novelty. A Whisper Large audio encoder and scaled training recipes yield accurate lip-sync, full-body stability, and long videos with strict identity hold. Careful data curation and RLHF training extend it to anime, animals, multi-person scenes, and object handling. Step distillation cuts inference to 8 function evaluations, balancing serving speed with visual quality. Tests on over 500 cases rival leading closed systems like HeyGen and Kling Avatar.
arxiv-2605-27286: Yiding Liu and colleagues present Falcon-X, a forecasting model for multivariate time series with mixed physical quantities. It maps each variate into a shared latent prototype space, weighs both positive and negative affinities, and rebuilds each series through a routing step. The design supports zero-shot transfer across structures and tops its benchmarks for forecasting.
arxiv-2605-27386: Supriya Khadka and Sanchari Das review augmented reality for preschoolers who move constantly. They find camera tracking fails during motion, screens distract children into safety hazards, and crowds gather around markers, alongside privacy risks from always-on sensing. Their AnchorPlay AR concept separates walking from visual tracking, using audio cues while moving and visuals only when still.
arxiv-2605-27486: Khayyam Nosrati and colleagues introduce a federated learning dataset for multivariate factory time series anomaly spotting. Older sets lack scale, good labels, and freedom from common flaws, while cyclic factory behavior stays little studied. Their dataset builds in cyclic dynamics from repeat factory runs, and they test chosen methods on it and on a public benchmark.
arxiv-2605-27586: Nicole Summer Hsing, Asuka Yuxi Zheng, Yi Zhao, Haoqin Tu, and Jen-tse Huang show that one aligned seed agent can spread cooperation through a multi-agent population by talk alone. Placed among four unmodified teammates in the Red-Black Game, the seed more than doubles cooperation from about 25 percent to about 62 percent. The same seed transfers to Sugarscape with about 92 percent trade success against a baseline near 22 percent.
arxiv-2605-27686: Kabir Swain, Sijie Han, Daniel Karl Weidele, Mauro Martino, and Antonio Torralba propose Tensor Memory, a fixed-size recurrent 3D memory tensor for Transformers. Tokens write into a voxel grid as Gaussian-weighted volumes around predicted locations, and read back context by continuous sampling with gated residual fusion. Constant-size memory unties state capacity from input length while preserving spatial bias for long-horizon video understanding.
arxiv-2605-27786: Yun and colleagues tackle wasted capacity in large language models, where neighboring layers often encode the same information. Their training-free method, LoRP, measures how similar each layer's inner states are, groups layers that resemble each other, and trims depth where overlap inside a group is highest. Tests across several model families show better perplexity and task scores after pruning.
arxiv-2605-27886: Wu and colleagues teach robots gentler handling by combining sight, touch, and language with live force feedback. Their Tabero suite turns existing robot trajectories into tasks that score both success and how softly the robot grips. The resulting model kept high success rates while cutting average grip force by over seventy percent on gentle instructions.
arxiv-2605-28086: Fangzhu Shen, Amir Gilad, and Sudeepa Roy price each seed user's contribution to influence spread before diffusion happens. Their Shapley-value framework gives fair ex-ante credit for budget and pricing decisions without relying on single observed cascades. Fast algorithms cover single-step activation, hardness is proven beyond one step, and approximations carry guarantees for standard diffusion models.
arxiv-2605-28386: Camille Jorge and Denis Bartolo study flat assemblies of spinning disks at high Reynolds number, where inertia reshapes what active matter can do. At low density, competing attractions and sideways Magnus forces break and remake bonds, yielding a sparse, hole-filled fluid that still percolates. At high density, spin alignment locks particles into a dense crystal with ordered spins, showing that fluid motion can build order rather than destroy it.
arxiv-2605-28586: Farrokh Labib and Vincent Russo bound stabilizer ranks for Clifford orbits of magic states in qutrits. The single-qutrit Clifford group shows four inequivalent magic-state orbits, but a nontrivial exponent bound was known only for the T-state. For the Strange, Hadamard-eigenstate, and Norrell orbits they give explicit decompositions, yielding per-copy asymptotic exponent bounds below the T-state baseline. They also prove first nontrivial lower bounds for two orbits and show two-qutrit circuits converting two copies into an injectable phase state, enabling constant-overhead gate injection.
arxiv-2605-28986: João Pedro d'El-Rey, Raúl Vallejos, and Fernando de Melo compare classical simulation with learning from measurement samples. Using one fixed deep energy-based generative model, they tune entanglement via matrix-product-state bond dimension and non-stabilizerness via T-gate counts in Clifford circuits. For both resources, harder simulation tracks sharper loss landscapes and worse reconstruction under limited capacity, judged by Hessian eigenvalues and random subspace tests. Within the regimes studied, learnability follows known simulation complexity, so training dynamics can probe quantum hardness in practice.
arxiv-2605-29286: Qian Wang and colleagues introduce CrossAlpha, a public annual-report benchmark for cross-market factor research. Existing benchmarks do not support evaluating whether firm signals from one market predict returns in another, partly because filings differ across languages and regulatory systems. CrossAlpha standardizes filings into ten-category English business descriptions, builds cross-market firm-pair scores from schema-level disclosures, and pairs the graph with eleven years of daily market data. It covers about 3,600 firms and 10,700 firm-year reports across five markets.
arxiv-2605-29386: Dmitrii Korshunov gives a simple example of a polynomial contraction map of complex d-space, in 3D or more, with endless degree growth. With the Poincaré-Dulac theorem, it gives an algebraic map of complex d-space, in 3D or more, which is linearizable by holomorphic means but not by algebra. The build is plain, but its degree growth has no bound. This sets holomorphic apart from algebra linearizability here.
arxiv-2605-29486: PhoneWorld, from Yuxuan Liu and colleagues, turns recorded use of real phone apps into runnable, resettable Android test environments for phone-use agents. Real apps are hard to reset and check automatically, while screenshots and traces alone cannot create new experience. PhoneWorld therefore distills observed pages, moves, and state changes into app specifications built through an automated build, inspect, and repair loop. The suite covers 34 consumer apps across 16 domains with programmatic checks, and its trajectories complement existing supervision and improve results on real phones.
arxiv-2605-29686: Marcus Weber and five colleagues develop a logical system based on Boolean rings for sepsis testing. The method builds an ideal of choice rules fencing empty patient subsets, giving clear rules from marker readings. Analysis finds distinct septic and non-septic patterns: high GLP-1 and MyD88 mark septic states, while high TRAIL and low MyD88 suggest non-septic cases. A new way to fold in expert knowledge filters out overfit or dataset-own quirks. The findings highlight logics making open, plausible rules for data and expert insight.
arxiv-2605-29786: Omar Benjelloun and ten colleagues offer Croissant Tasks, a metadata format for reproducible machine learning evaluations. Vague execution details and brittle software environments still break reruns, and manual checklists demand heavy effort without scaling. The declarative, machine-actionable format abstracts low-level details into high-level specs, splitting task problem from solution. A language-model pipeline converts existing benchmarks into the format, and agents can ingest the specifications to build working rerun pipelines from scratch. The format aims to ground automated, conceptual reruns in the field.
arxiv-2605-29986: Michael Sullivan and Alexander Koller speed grammar-constrained language model decoding by shrinking the token search space. Grammar engines force each next token to fit a context-free grammar, but scanning the whole vocabulary each step costs dearly, worst for complex grammars where engines help most. Their CFGzip method compresses the token space offline, slashing engine overhead. Batched tests cut latency up to seventy-five times, leaving overhead near one to two times on the hardest grammars. Constrained decoding for complex grammars thus turns practical at scale.
arxiv-2605-30086: Mao and Wu construct canonical extensions of p-adic shtukas, arithmetic objects, on integral models of toroidal compactifications of abelian-type Shimura varieties. With a log diamond defined as a v-sheaf tied to a log scheme, they build a p-adic log shtuka over the compactification's log diamond by studying its degeneration at the boundary. They define integral models of toroidal and minimal forms in the sense of Pappas and Rapoport, checked in that generality. Uses include canonicity and functoriality, plus well-placed stratifications on the special fiber.
arxiv-2605-30186: Fabrice Nonez studies a process giving another proof of the Spectral Embedding Theorem. It shows every densely defined symmetric operator extends via a multiplication operator, embedding the Hilbert space into an L2 space. The process targets specific operators, where natural spectral embeddings or matches may be found. Considered in two earlier arXiv papers, the process was introduced through nonstandard techniques; this work recasts the theory through classical analysis, without them or ultraproducts.
arxiv-2605-30686: In a 2026 study, Rashidi tests indirect prompt injection in ReAct agents, which mix reasoning with tool calls. An attacker controlling any tool's return value can plant orders steering the agent from the user's goal, yet benchmarks test fixed points. Across four studies and 460 trials, success against one model falls from three-fifths at the first step to zero by the fourth, while another resists throughout. Framing swings success widely, turn caps do not matter, and cleaning only the first observation would catch two-thirds of successes.
arxiv-2605-30786: Lin and colleagues propose AbstainGNN, a theory-driven design for graph classification with abstention, letting networks reject unsure guesses. Old networks are forced to predict even under high doubt, producing unreliable decisions. AbstainGNN models both the predictive function and the refusal function, using graph structural information. Unlike heuristic methods, the authors characterize the trade-off between errors and rejection costs, deriving a unified learning objective. Training runs in two stages: predictive warm-start, then refusal calibration. On five benchmark datasets, AbstainGNN beats existing refusal methods at the same rejection rates.
arxiv-2605-31186: Komorniczak asks a plain question about streaming data: when the data pattern shifts, does a classifier's accuracy score tell us how good the drift detector is? The field has no one shared way to judge drift detectors, and accuracy blends many effects beyond detection alone. The overview compares eight drift-quality measures with classifier scores across seven synthetic stream makers, mapping which measures truly inform. Drift dynamics are also weighed as a factor.
arxiv-2605-31586: Scivetti and team test whether small open-source models grasp rare Paired-Focus constructions in English, such as let alone and much less. Grasping rare constructions has proven hard, once thought solved only by the largest models. The team builds a dataset testing meanings through scalar adjectival semantics and world knowledge. Testing many models, they find several small models grasp both forms and meanings of Paired-Focus constructions. Models trained on human-scale data fail all meaning evaluations. For checkpoint models, Paired-Focus understanding emerges later than syntactic knowledge.
arxiv-2606-00686:
Hashemzadeh and co-authors rethink AI safety in this 2026 paper. The standard path erases unsafe data or trains models to refuse all risky prompts. That cuts harm, but it also shrinks what a model knows. The result can be bland refusals to mild, lawful questions.

Their frame, SafeMoE, keeps unsafe knowledge but locks it in small expert parts. Each expert trains on harmful texts from one domain. A light routing network then steers these experts at run time. It trains on a small, well-picked set of safe and rich replies. The authors report over 20 percent relative gain in safe reply rates on strict tests. Replies also carry more real content, they say. The router works on new domains with no fresh training.
arxiv-2606-00786:
Xu and co-authors set a baseline for the hunt for a QCD critical point in this 2026 physics paper. In heavy-ion collisions, swings in conserved charges may flag that point. Proton counts are a key proxy. The team studies gold-on-gold collisions at four energies, from 3.2 to 4.5 GeV, in the JAM model.

They compute high-order cumulants of proton counts, plus factorial cumulants and their ratios. A new method, CIGAR, removes swings from the starting volume without tying results to centrality bins. They compare CIGAR with the standard bin-width fix, step by step. They also test how much spectator matter warps the counts. The point of the work is a clean, non-critical baseline at high baryon density. Searches for the critical point need such a baseline. Without it, a real signal and a plain model effect look much the same.
arxiv-2606-01286:
Wu and co-authors evolve coding tasks to test frontier models harder. Top models now saturate many benchmarks. On LiveCodeBench easy splits, they pass over 99 percent. New hard tasks take huge human effort to build. BenchEvolver grows tasks from existing coding problems. It evolves reference solutions through structured changes. New statements and tests derive from those solutions. Correctness stays verifiable by design.

They apply it to LiveCodeBench and SciCode. A new set, LiveCodeBench-Plus, holds 91 problems. Frontier Pass@1 there spans 27 point 5 to 62 point 6 percent. Clear gaps between strong models return. Training on evolved tasks also lifts held-out coding scores.
arxiv-2606-01386:
Jimenez-Gutierrez and co-authors build a privacy-preserving chatbot for Italian offices. GuidaPA serves the Italian Public Administration. It trains via federated learning, so data stay on site. Source texts come from two national PA platforms. SIGESON and SIDFORS manuals and FAQs form the corpus. Public documents act as a safe proxy in this study. Real deployment would extend to restricted internal sources.

Role-based access control guards who can query what. Secure client-side preprocessing adds another layer of care. Parameter-efficient federated fine-tuning adapts the language model. QLoRA runs over 15 federated rounds in their tests. Scores on ROUGE and BLEU near private centralized training. Data never pool centrally, which suits regulatory limits.
arxiv-2606-01586:
Kawarabayashi and Yu prove connectivity bounds for knitted graphs. A pair (G, S) is knitted if each split of S can be honored. For any partition of S into nonempty parts, disjoint connected subgraphs must cover them. A graph is l-knitted if this holds for every S of size l. They prove every 8l-connected graph is l-knitted. The result then feeds into Hadwiger's Conjecture. That conjecture says every k-chromatic graph contains a K_k minor.

They bound the vertex connectivity of any minimal counterexample. It is at least the ceiling of k over 8. This improves the prior bound of ceiling of 2k over 27. Their proof also corrects a gap in a 2013 argument. A claim stated without proof in 2019 is now established.
arxiv-2606-01886:
Borjigin and co-authors design an agent harness that absorbs finance complexity. Finance agents often fail by shifting work to users. Users must restate goals, risk taste, and portfolio facts. The agent answers, acts, and then forgets it all. In finance, lost context can cause unsafe choices.

Their InKH harness turns events into structured knowledge. Events come from users, markets, portfolios, and tools. Passive injection builds a bounded context before each step. A temporal graph memory serves fast retrieval needs. A wiki surface gives humans a clear audit view. Background extraction handles growth, decay, and maturity. The aim is fewer repeated errors and safer decisions.
arxiv-2606-01986:
Kwaśnicki and Wszoła study the spectral theory of infinite Toeplitz matrices. A Toeplitz matrix has constant entries along each diagonal. The entries here form monotone sequences on both sides. One side is absolutely monotone, the other completely so. Such structure shapes the matrix's spectral behavior strongly.

The pair derive forms for generalised eigenvectors of the matrix. They then prove a generalised eigenvector expansion for it. The matrix need not be normal for the result. Even so, only real entries appear in the expansion. Eigenvalues and eigenvectors both stay real throughout. The work extends classic Toeplitz theory to this class. It gives a firm basis for later analytic use.
arxiv-2606-02186:
Kimura and Sharma compute spectral flow for Dirac operators on a warped cylinder. The cylinder is finite and carries an O(2) symmetry, and the Dirac operators are equipped with regularized APS boundary conditions. The twisting bundle is a real higher rank orthogonal bundle, and reflection symmetry is implemented by a fiber involution. That setup shapes how the spectral flow is defined and tracked.

After the twisting bundle is complexified and the orthogonal twist is diagonalized, the Dirac equation splits into a scalar Fourier mode radial equation. Moving rotating blocks and stationary neutral blocks appear in that split. Once conjugate and reflection paired blocks are regrouped, the crossing contributions define real classes in the RO(O(2)) group. The team obtain an explicit blockwise formula for the resulting spectral flow. Standard hypotheses on self-adjointness and crossings support the derivation.
arxiv-2606-02386:
Rahman and Rahman present AgentPLM, a protein design system that can check its own work. Normal protein language models emit a sequence in one pass. They cannot ask outside tools for feedback mid-stream. They cannot steer away from a flawed candidate. AgentPLM adds that loop.

One part, Reasoning-Augmented Decoding, mixes generation with tool calls. The tools are ESMFold, FoldX, and AutoDock Vina. A second part, CAPO, trains the policy on whole paths. It learns when oracle feedback truly helps. Tests cover enzyme design, antibody tuning, heat stability, and interface design. Zero-shot fitness prediction is also tested. The authors report top results across the suite. Antibody hit rates beat the strongest passive baseline. The gains show online error repair at work, with no backtracking step.
arxiv-2606-02486:
Syed and co-authors help robot arms catch moving objects. Vision-language-action models handle static tasks well. Moving objects break them. They map the current view to an action and assume the scene is frozen. At any real object speed, the delay eats the time left to grasp. AHEAD predicts instead of reacting.

A small world model forecasts future patch tokens in the model's feature space. Optical flow supplies per-token velocity and acceleration, and a saliency mask focuses prediction on key patches. The model rolls ahead adaptively, halting when uncertainty crosses a threshold. The frozen decoder then acts on the predicted future view. AHEAD adds just 4.9M parameters. Success runs 79 to 97 percent across 20 dynamic tasks, against 31 to 58 percent for the best baseline. On a real arm, conveyor and rolling-ball tasks score near perfect. Every baseline scores zero on projectile catching, where AHEAD reaches 19 of 30.
arxiv-2606-02686:
Liu and co-authors build a bootstrap method for loop-level cosmology correlators. Correlators encode the statistics of early universe fluctuations. The new strategy is called spectral dispersion. A correlator can be rebuilt from its on-shell data by analyticity. Local counterterms are the only ambiguity. For loop processes, the on-shell data form a discrete sum. Quasinormal modes supply the terms.

The method joins the de Sitter spectral decomposition with dispersion relations. New results come out in simple forms. Three-point and four-point correlators with one-loop massive exchanges are computed. Scalar and vector bosons are covered. Couplings can be direct or derivative. Extensions look straightforward. Higher spins and higher-loop banana graphs fit the same frame. The authors present the tool as a simpler route to loop cosmology.
arxiv-2606-02886:
Miñoza, Laylo, and Ibañez tackle a gap in AI weather forecasting. Deep learning models now match numerical forecasts and run far faster. But they give single deterministic forecasts with no uncertainty estimates. That gap matters most during extreme weather, when choices carry high stakes.

The team proposes NTK-UQ, a method based on neural tangent kernels and last-layer features. It needs no retraining and adds uncertainty at inference with one matrix-vector product. Their analysis shows quality depends on the model's design. When a truncation rank nears the effective rank, uncertainty estimates lose their edge. A data-driven rule picks between two decomposition methods based on the spectrum. Across four model designs, the rule picked the better method each time. NTK-UQ gave prediction intervals 31 to 37 percent sharper than split conformal prediction at 90 percent coverage. Its intervals also widen as events grow more severe.
arxiv-2606-02986:
Maleki and Palma ask how much about a quantum system's metrological power can be learned from a few accessible measurements. Quantum Fisher information sets the ultimate precision of parameter estimation through the quantum Cramér-Rao bound. But computing it directly needs full knowledge of the density matrix. That cost grows steeply with Hilbert-space dimension.

The team tests support vector regression for predicting Fisher information in multipartite systems from limited features. They compare physically motivated feature sets. Collective spin moments alone lose predictive power as system size grows. The dominant signal comes from the interplay between collective covariance and low-order spectral moments of the density matrix. Using a restricted set of accessible quantities, the team still achieves accurate estimates of metrological sensitivity. No full quantum-state tomography is needed. The work maps which information sectors govern Fisher information, and it points to cheaper routes for assessing quantum sensors.
arxiv-2606-03186:
Boroun studies how higher-twist corrections change a key ratio for the future Electron-Ion Collider. The ratio compares the reduced cross section to the structure function F2 for light and heavy nuclei. It is taken at the smallest x value for a given energy. Higher twists add terms that grow as the momentum transfer falls.

Boroun works in the color dipole model. Bounds for the ratio are found in the linear region. Twist-4 terms matter at small x in that region. Their inclusion matches lab data from JLab for the FL to F2 ratio. Twist-6 and twist-8 terms are summed by non-linear methods where the variable grows past one. The deuteron ratio is checked in the low momentum, small x zone against JLab data as well. The match lets Boroun probe non-linear QCD effects as FL tends toward zero.
arxiv-2606-03886:
Bousige and co-authors simulate borophene growth to find windows for chosen phases. Making borophene to order is hard, since many polymorphs compete as layers form. A reactive learned potential drives the runs. Grand-canonical Monte Carlo runs on silver surfaces, both the 111 and 100 faces. A data-driven sorting step tracks growth from early nuclei to full layers.

Growth maps over heat and pressure come out of the runs. Vacancy motifs, phase mixing, and seed shape govern which polymorph wins. The runs match lab trends, with two phases on top and a heat-linked rivalry. Kinetic paths link short-lived nuclei to long-range order. Conditions that suppress rival motifs are named. Growers get workable windows for targeted phases. The frame extends to phase control in other thin materials.
arxiv-2606-03986:
Cavada and co-authors build NewtPhys, a data set for low-level physics sense. Past tests used fake or half-fake scenes with question answering. Those tests stressed high-level events, not fine physical detail. NewtPhys uses multi-view images of real scenes. Physics-based simulation adds dense labels over time.

Labels include 3D forces and per-pixel measures of motion and form. They also cover tracking, semantics, and geometry at each step. The team tests 56 vision-language models on the set. Ten vision foundation models were tested as well. Results reveal clear limits in low-level physics reasoning. The set also aims to guide future physics-aware tests and models.
arxiv-2606-04086:
Chang-Yan Wang and Xue-Feng Zhang study in 2026 how two quantum strings, extended objects in a many-body system, interact when they are simply forbidden to cross each other. That hard-core rule alone creates an effective attraction or repulsion, but its form is hard to measure because the distance between strings is not a local quantity.

The authors show that full counting statistics, the complete distribution of a measured count rather than its average, captures this nonlocality naturally. They derive an exact formula by isolating the virtual process where the strings touch and hop back. The resulting potential is governed by the entanglement entropy of half a string, a link confirmed by high-precision numerics. They suggest the trick extends to other topological defects.
arxiv-2606-04186:
Nicholas Lee and colleagues report in 2026 a fast quantum chemistry method that runs in a few GPU hours. Their approach mixes a classical selected-configuration solver with quantum hardware, and neither side dominates.

The classical part picks the most important electron patterns. The quantum part then refines the energies for those patterns. For systems ruled by dynamic electron correlation, a regime where quantum methods usually struggle, the mix did well. It recovered over ninety-five percent of the correlation energy given by a trusted classical method. Accuracy matched the best classical tools on the test molecules. The authors argue the hybrid route is the near-term path for useful quantum chemistry.
arxiv-2606-04286:
Linsen Li, Aron Culotta, and Nicholas Mattei present a text-based causal method in 2026. It untangles which aspects of a service truly move its overall rating. Aspects tend to move together, so raw sentiment counts cannot isolate any one factor's effect.

Their method builds on a causal language model. It adds temperature scaling to calibrate who counts as exposed to an aspect. That tuning avoids over-adjusting for confounders, the hidden factors that muddy such studies. Tools to inspect the confounders found come with it. Tests used over six hundred thousand reviews of United States schools, plus semi-synthetic data. The method gave more reliable estimates than prior tools. Views of school leadership and test performance stood out as key drivers.
arxiv-2606-04486:
Zhao proposes a new way to watermark text from diffusion language models, in a 2026 arXiv paper. They do not write left to right like standard models. Watermarks embed a hidden statistical signal. The signal lets generated text be identified later. Most known schemes work locally. They nudge each next word based on the words before it. That design fits poorly when many positions are sampled jointly, as diffusion models do.

Zhao's watermark instead controls a global sketch. This is a compact vector that summarizes statistics of the whole sequence. Diffusion sampling can steer the sketch as text forms. Detection then depends on the global statistic, not on local contexts. The signal is order-agnostic. It is not a simple bias toward certain tokens. The paper analyzes the method's distortion, meaning how much it changes text quality. It also analyzes soundness and robustness against removal attempts.
arxiv-2606-04686:
Vercellino and colleagues test whether a small quantum computer can forecast how much cash ATMs will need, in a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum reservoir computing. Their framework uses parametrized four-qubit circuits as reservoirs, with partial measurement and reset. Only a classical ridge-regression readout is trained.

The quantum models do not beat the classical Prophet benchmark on mean absolute error or normalized mean squared error. They are more competitive on dynamic time warping, a metric rewarding matched temporal shape over exact values, indicating a partial ability to capture temporal structure.
arxiv-2606-04786:
Rossi and co-authors present a 2026 arXiv paper on quantum chemistry, the use of quantum computers to model molecules. Their subject is ADAPT-VQE, an adaptive method that builds a compact trial description of a molecule step by step. At each step, the method scores candidate operators, meaning small changes that might improve the description, and then adds the best one.

The authors rewrite that scoring step using an exact change to the Hamiltonian, the equation that gives a system its energy. Their rewrite gives the same scores as standard fermionic Rotoselect, yet needs about half as many circuit runs on average. That saving brings its cost close to the cheaper gradient-based method. Benchmarks cover lithium hydride, beryllium hydride, and water, each at normal and stretched shapes. For lithium hydride, the weakest case, one pairing built an accurate answer while skipping the usual optimization stage altogether.
arxiv-2606-04886:
Chanda, Das, and Das explain a cosmological observation with friction, in a 2026 arXiv astrophysics paper. Results from the DESI survey prefer dark energy whose equation of state appears to cross the phantom divide in the recent past, behavior requiring phantom dynamics. Their scenario instead invokes dark energy: the quintessence field that drives cosmic acceleration loses a little energy to dissipation as it rolls. That simple ingredient produces both the evolving behavior and the apparent crossing.

The key result is economy: even weak dissipation of the quintessence field suffices to explain the current DESI observations. No phantom field is needed. Apparent phantom crossing becomes an artifact of ignoring dissipation when reconstructing dark energy's history from data. The paper adds a candidate to the rush of models answering DESI, and it makes a methodological point: the dark energy we infer depends on the assumptions baked into the reconstruction.
arxiv-2606-05086:
Chun-E Fu and Wen-Xuan Ma study how fermionic Kaluza-Klein modes mix in thick braneworld models under background perturbations in this 2026 arXiv paper. Braneworld models place our four-dimensional universe on a membrane inside a higher-dimensional space. Fermions spread into the extra dimension as a tower of Kaluza-Klein modes with different masses. For a still background these modes form a clean orthogonal set.

Perturbations vary along the extra dimension. Expanding the Dirac operator in the old basis produces nonzero overlaps between levels, adding off-diagonal couplings to the mass matrix. The authors resolve the states with a singular value decomposition of that matrix, preserving the five-dimensional chiral structure. They find parity-odd perturbations mix only same-parity modes and keep the symmetry. Parity-even ones mix across parity, break the symmetry, and polarize the mode densities toward the brane, lighting up dark modes.
arxiv-2606-05186:
Felipe Chavarro Polania tests staged factorial screening for budget-constrained micro-pretraining in this 2026 arXiv paper. Automated research loops must triage many candidate training recipes on shared accelerators before budgets are spent. Best-so-far searches can find better recipes, but they never reveal which factors, depth, width, batch size, or learning rate, actually drive performance differences.

On an autoresearch-derived single-GPU training loop, Polania ran 613 experiments. These included screens at two, five, and ten minutes, seeded reruns, anchor checks, and baselines, plus a 60-minute bridge package and continuations up to 24 hours. The penalties from batch, depth, and width were largest at short budgets and relaxed as budgets grew. Designed screens retained clear factor attribution after correction where random search offered none. The workflow is bounded and practical: screen briefly to find high-penalty directions, confirm anchors with repeated runs, then refine locally in the reduced space.
arxiv-2606-05886:
Filothodoros rewrites Bragg diffraction as the shadow of a polylogarithm in a 2026 arXiv paper. Diffraction peaks reveal a crystal's lattice, and the classic Bragg law fixes their positions. Real materials blur those peaks through finite coherence and disorder. The usual fix is extra broadening pasted onto the theory. Filothodoros instead sums weighted interference from many planes into one generating function. The polylogarithm's parameters carry coherence length directly.

Perfect coherence returns the standard Bragg law, so the old theory sits inside the new one. Shorter coherence reshapes peaks' positions, widths, and profiles from a single source. Peaks themselves sit at the function's boundary edge as its argument nears a branch point. That view ties diffraction line shapes to complex analysis. partly coherent or disordered materials gain a model with fewer ad hoc patches. The paper appeared in Physics Letters A.
arxiv-2606-06286:
Gianluca Barmina, Peter Schneider-Kamp, and Lukas Galke Poech separate two kinds of memorization in this 2026 arXiv paper on language models. A model can often be forced to recite training data when an attacker feeds it the right prefix. That is capability. Propensity asks a different question: does the model leak such data under ordinary prompting, when nobody is trying to extract it?

Their framework, PropMe, turns standard memorization scores into propensity scores by contrasting attack settings with everyday ones. A tracing tool, SimpleTrace, matches model outputs against full training corpora to find verbatim and near verbatim leaks. Testing two fully open models on corpora in two languages, they found a consistent gap. Prefix attacks drew out far stronger memorization than normal prompts, where leakage stayed rare. Continued training on partly new data also reduced how much of the older corpus the model could reveal.
arxiv-2606-06486:
Mingyang Liu and co-authors rethink what regret means when your opponent learns back in this 2026 arXiv paper on game theory. In repeated games, standard external regret compares your earnings with the best fixed strategy in hindsight. But adaptive opponents react to your history. That comparison misses the what if that matters: what would have happened had you played differently all along, with everyone responding? Their Repeated Policy Regret builds exactly that comparison.

The paper first finds necessary conditions for keeping this regret sublinear: limits on how much the comparator strategy may vary, and on both sides' memory lengths. Then it gives algorithms for a problem that is non convex in the strategy space. The payoff is end state quality. When everyone minimizes Repeated Policy Regret, outcomes can beat classical regret minimization, because the metric respects repeated play's history dependent reality.
arxiv-2606-06586:
Jonathan von Rad and co-authors teach models to remember facts in every language, not just English, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Models trained mostly on English know many facts yet fail to state them in other languages, a flaw called cross lingual factual inconsistency. The team built PolyFact, a parallel question answering dataset of one hundred thousand Wikidata facts in twelve languages. On two seven billion parameter models they compared three fixes: light continued pretraining, supervised fine tuning, and reinforcement learning with GRPO.

Reinforcement learning won consistently. It improved both consistency across languages and recall in languages never trained on, while continued pretraining on parallel text added little. Looking inside the models, the training had reorganized their routing. Language specialization in the MLP layers and attention heads shrank. Shared cross lingual representations grew. The inconsistency, the authors conclude, is less missing knowledge than unreliable access to knowledge already present.
arxiv-2606-07586:
Li and co-authors teach an AI coding agent to deploy language models onto edge hardware by watching a human-guided run, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Spatial neural processing units are energy-efficient chips for on-device inference, but porting a model onto one is labor-intensive. In stage one, humans guided an agent through deploying a 1-billion-parameter Llama model on AMD's XDNA 2 chip. It achieved speedups of 2-fold on prefill and 4-fold on decoding over an optimized baseline, while documenting lessons as structured notes.

Stage two distilled that documentation into an 8-phase agent skill system enforcing numerical correctness at each phase. The agent then deployed 8 models, from 0.5 billion to 4 billion parameters. Each took within 0.5 to 4 hours of wall time with no human guidance. All passed correctness gates; 3 matched or beat the reference deployment's performance. The authors claim several models had never run on this hardware through open tooling.
arxiv-2606-07686:
Rupasinghe and co-authors extend physics-informed neural networks, models that learn while respecting known equations, so they can also learn from written and structural knowledge, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Their test case is microbial communities, modelled with generalised Lotka-Volterra equations that describe how species grow and affect each other. Equations alone miss outside influences that field papers describe in plain text.

The framework feeds in findings mined from peer-reviewed metagenomics literature, plus network structure between species, alongside abundance measurements. On real and simulated data from human and plant communities, the method beat the prior state of the art by up to fifty-three percent, even before knowledge was added. Adding the literature and network knowledge lifted accuracy further, by up to twenty-three percent on one measure and forty-seven percent on another. The inferred interaction networks also matched ecological roles reported in print.
arxiv-2606-07786:
Diao, Ding, Geng, and Liu analyse a spectral problem that arises when an elastic body turns invisible to an incoming electromagnetic wave, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The frequencies at which invisibility can occur are called transmission eigenvalues. For coupled elastic-electromagnetic systems the problem is mathematically delicate, since the governing equations are neither elliptic nor self-adjoint in the usual sense.

For general bounded domains with rough boundaries, the team proves the positive eigenvalues form a discrete set whose only possible accumulation point is infinity. For round, radially symmetric domains they prove a whole sequence of eigenvalues exists and derive how it grows. Along that sequence the electromagnetic parts of the vibration concentrate sharply at the boundary, while the elastic displacement spreads through the whole body. Gradient bounds quantify the boundary blow-up. The authors note the effect could seed super-resolution imaging methods for such coupled materials.
arxiv-2606-07886:
Roman, Siddiqui, and Busani study how yttrium iron garnet films crystallise on silicon, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The material, YIG, is prized for magnonic devices, circuits carrying signals as magnetic waves. Its structure supports long-range magnon propagation. The team deposited a film three hundred ninety nanometres thick by RF sputtering onto silicon with a silica buffer. It was then annealed in oxygen between seven hundred fifty and eight hundred fifty degrees.

Two sample sets separated the substrate's role: one had patterned hole pairs etched into the buffer as crystallisation seeds, the other was plain. Analysis showed the film is off-stoichiometry, rich in iron and oxygen, and that annealing changes neither that balance nor the substrate. Diffraction showed full crystallisation at eight hundred degrees for one hour in patterned samples. Plain samples were crystallising at seven hundred fifty degrees after three hours, evidence the seeds speed the transformation.
arxiv-2606-07986:
Navonil Deb, Younghoon Kim, and Sumanta Basu build valid statistical inference for the frequency-by-frequency wiring diagram of many time series, in this 2026 arXiv paper. For stationary series, a spectral precision matrix at one frequency encodes which components are directly linked at that rhythm. Testing those links is hard: Fourier transforms bring truncation and smoothing biases, and the complex-valued matrix breaks standard methods.

Their framework uses the full likelihood of neighbouring Fourier transforms rather than isolated ones. They construct a debiased complex graphical lasso estimator: a sparse precision estimate with its shrinkage bias corrected, at any chosen frequency. Its sampling distribution is pinned down, and covariance estimates pool information across neighbouring frequencies. The key is controlling all three biases at once. In simulations the method kept reliable coverage away from zero frequency and detected links with better power than the benchmark.
arxiv-2606-08086:
Jiannan Chen and Haiping Fu of Nanchang University construct measures that only ever move one way along the level sets of harmonic functions, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The setting is asymptotically flat three-dimensional manifolds with simple topology and nonnegative scalar curvature. Monotone measures are prized there because they underwrite key inequalities and notions of mass.

Their measures are calibrated against the model case. On spatial Schwarzschild manifolds, the geometry of a non-rotating black hole, they stay constant outside round spheres. The derivation follows Miao's strategy rather than the ODE analysis of earlier work. As applications, the authors recover and generalise known geometric and mass-capacity bounds. They also obtain integral formulas for the mass-capacity ratio. Whatever the measure does between two level sets bounds the geometry there.
arxiv-2606-08286:
Chu, Smith, and Pardo present an interface for exploring audio effects by browsing a map, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Audio effects shape sound throughout music production, but most software presents them as separate modules with parameter knobs, a layout that favors targeted adjustment over playful exploration. That separation makes it hard to build intuition about the wider space of possible sound changes. FXplorer instead organizes effects within a two-dimensional space informed by how the sounds are perceived.

In FXplorer, sound transformations become a continuous landscape that users can browse rather than a list of isolated presets. The system combines established spatial interaction techniques and familiar workstation controls with embedding-based methods for similarity and meaning-based search. Users can edit presets and slide between them interactively, moving from one effect character toward another. The authors aim the tool at composition, production, and live performance.
arxiv-2606-08686:
Suman Chabri and Anand predict the crystal structures of disordered alloys with an information-based neural approach, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Chemically disordered alloys, including high-entropy alloys, pose a significant challenge for phase prediction. The number of possible atomic arrangements explodes combinatorially. Exploration of compositions requires an efficient way to search the potential energy landscape, plus a metric for how much of it has been covered.

They demonstrate alchemical Monte Carlo sampling, which swaps atomic identities to explore arrangements. It is driven by a graph convolutional neural network that predicts energies from atomic neighborhoods. Information entropy supplies the coverage metric for the explored landscape. They also evaluate a cheap structural descriptor, the bond disproportion vector, against a state-of-the-art overlap method.
arxiv-2606-09086:
Zhao and colleagues generate realistic citywide travel flows from the calendar alone, without historical trip data, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Origin-destination flows count trips between regions and underpin transport planning, but fine-grained records are often missing. DynaOD builds flows from context. Its key idea is to model time two ways. Discrete directional trends capture shifts in city activity, like the morning rush. Continuous evolution captures how shifts unfold.

Jointly encoding both produces time-varying region profiles. These condition pretrained static flow generators in plug-and-play fashion, so existing models gain dynamics without retraining. The design also supports scale and transfer between cities. On large real-world datasets, DynaOD beat standard baselines on predictive accuracy and fidelity, meaning its synthetic flows match real flow stats, not just averages. The code is available. The work targets planners needing plausible data where sensors and surveys fall short.
arxiv-2606-09186:
Huang and colleagues build an AI that listens, watches, speaks, and thinks at once without freezing mid-conversation, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Humans interact full-duplex: talking while listening, redirecting mid-sentence. Omni models handle speech, vision, and text in one serial pipeline, so deep reasoning or a tool call pauses dialogue, while shrinking the model to stay real-time guts its capability.

DuplexOmni splits into two layers running asynchronously in parallel. The interaction layer takes streaming audio and video and produces streaming text and speech with low latency. The thinking layer is pluggable, any large model or tool agent, consulted in the background, results folded into later responses. A Writer-Director pipeline makes the training data: overlapping speech, silences, interruptions, user supplements, delayed thinking feedback. Benchmarks are strong, behavior natural, with candid limits: video is thin for lack of data, and English lags because training speech is mostly Chinese.
arxiv-2606-09286:
Li and colleagues teach a humanoid to carry boxes, push carts, and ride a skateboard using only onboard depth, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Agile interaction demands whole-body coordination: the object's dynamics change its balance and contacts continuously. Existing controllers lean on dense reference trajectories and perfect state information, collapsing outside the lab. VAIC uses only onboard depth, proprioceptive history, and decoupled commands.

Training uses two-stage distillation. A privileged teacher masters skills using precise object kinematics and exact states, only available in simulation. A student distills them, replacing full-body tracking with velocity targets plus an interaction indicator. A recurrent adaptation module infers unobservable object dynamics from depth and proprioception: what the object must be doing, from how the world responds. One policy then ran box carrying, cart pushing, and skateboarding, beating baselines. Train with omniscience, deploy with senses: a bridge from simulation to real robots.
arxiv-2606-09886:
Yuhao Zhang trims the expert pool of sparse mixture-of-experts models by grading teamwork, not solo acts in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such models route each token to a few experts from a large bench. The whole bench must sit in memory, which makes big models dear to serve. Pruning cuts the bench, but old scores grade each expert alone.

Zhang's SHAPE treats a layer's routing traces as a joint game. A Shapley-style tally, drawn from real top-pick teams, credits each expert for what its team-ups add. A quality-coverage rule then keeps the smallest set that holds a set share of the good mass in each layer. A bisection step matches a set keep rate. On three fresh backbones, SHAPE held accuracy well at twenty and forty percent cuts, with no retraining. Peak graphics memory fell in step.
arxiv-2606-10086:
Battu develops a theory of how AI assistance changes a system's ability to keep exploring, in a 2026 arXiv paper on complex systems and cognition. His central variable is adaptive responsiveness: how well a system can still find new paths when conditions change. Systems evolve over rugged landscapes with many locally reinforced setups. Predictive AI can either replace exploration or amplify it, and the paper models both cases.
