When predictive AI dominates, it substitutes for exploration, cutting responsiveness and causing early convergence, hysteresis, and collapse of exploration: systems grow efficient locally but rigid overall. In other regimes, the same help expands movement across the landscape. The swap effect hinges on starting routines, so weak explorers are most at risk while strong ones may gain. Long-run effects hinge on the setting and the design of use, not on AI power alone.
arxiv-2606-10186:
Das and Sarkar solve a battery of extremal problems for a class of analytic functions defined by an exponential condition, in a 2026 arXiv paper on complex analysis. The class consists of normalized starlike functions, whose images are star-shaped domains, singled out by requiring a certain derivative ratio to be subordinate to an exponential function.

They determine sharp upper bounds for the first three initial inverse logarithmic coefficients and sharp upper and lower bounds for the difference of consecutive ones. They also derive sharp bounds for a second-order inverse logarithmic Hankel determinant and sharp bounds for a third-order Hermitian-Toeplitz determinant. Finally, they fully solve the extremal problem for a generalized Fekete-Szegő functional with two parameters. In each problem the estimates are proven sharp, with extremal functions characterized in full, completing the coefficient picture for this exponential starlike class.
arxiv-2606-10686:
Rigas and colleagues rebuild a neural solver for pulsar magnetospheres in this 2026 arXiv paper on astrophysics. A pulsar's magnetosphere, the plasma-filled magnetic bubble around a rotating neutron star, is governed by equations that resist direct solution. A recent physics-informed neural network solver worked, but needed hours of training and heavy manual tuning. The framework swaps in Kolmogorov-Arnold networks, adds an adaptive training pipeline, and uses a physics-based convergence criterion instead of hand-set cycles.

Equation residuals fall to about a millionth in double precision, two orders of magnitude below the baseline, and convergence takes under twenty minutes in single precision. The solver handles stellar radii shrunk by up to eighty percent, where scale disparities defeat traditional solvers, and corrects the formula linking open flux to a key equatorial point. The framework is released as the open-source library PulsarX.
arxiv-2606-10886:
Nikulov argues that textbook superconductivity clashes with thermodynamics in this 2026 arXiv paper. The standard story says the superconducting state wins when its free energy drops below the normal state's. Nikulov claims that bookkeeping quietly credits a solenoid's power source with creating magnetization energy rather than field energy. Through the closed Gorter cycle, he adds, the Meissner effect implies negative surplus work.

On his reading, the equality of free energies at the transition in a critical field cannot be derived without breaking the second law. The field's faith in that law hid the contradiction for decades. He points to levitating magnets gaining height, and hence potential energy, at the transition as the visible symptom.
arxiv-2606-11286:
Wang and four co-authors present FreeBridge in a 2026 arXiv paper, a model of how single cells change under treatment. Imaging assays measure cell reactions to drug and genetic perturbations, but cells are fixed when imaged, so trajectories are unobservable. Modelers see only separate control and treated populations, the marginals, and must infer the transport between them. Matching endpoints alone does not pin down the intermediate evolution.

FreeBridge formulates this as a Schrödinger Bridge problem under endpoint-only supervision. Atomic states are segmented single-cell representations, defining a fixed cellular manifold. The model learns stochastic transport constrained within that geometry, using latent support regularization to keep intermediate states near observed morphologies. Across the BBBC021, RxRx1, and JUMP benchmarks, FreeBridge kept competitive or improved endpoint fidelity and mechanism-of-action retention under a unified protocol. On BBBC021 it further reduced support violations, evidence that geometric grounding matters.
arxiv-2606-11686:
Sawyer Zhang, Alexander Wang and Sophie Lei propose a sharper way to test software agents in this 2026 arXiv paper. Judging a deployed language model agent by one overall success rate shows that it regressed, but not where. The authors split one production ordering agent into fixed layers, covering routing, intent signals, memory, safety and more, and test each layer separately.

Each layer gets its own assertion slice that runs in a deterministic pure mode with no language model involved. The full suite of 238 baseline cases runs in about two and a half seconds on every code change, against locked per-layer baselines. The team then deliberately breaks one layer at a time. The overall pass rate barely moves, dropping only a few points, while the matching layer's slice collapses by twenty-five to ninety-one points. Damage stays off other slices, and the pattern repeats on a second, different deployment.
arxiv-2606-11786:
Joanito Agili Lopo, Yunita Sari and Guntur Budi Herwanto improve translation for a low-resource language in this 2026 arXiv paper. Kupang Malay, spoken in eastern Indonesia, lacks the large parallel text collections that machine translation normally feeds on. Standard fine-tuned language models degrade badly on such languages.

Their model, Lius, is trained with instructions built from explicit lexical and semantic features drawn from a bilingual dictionary, so the model learns word-level knowledge directly. Training uses Continual Instruction Tuning, an iterative scheme that revisits instruction-based learning in rounds rather than one pass. On several evaluation metrics, Lius beats standard instruction-tuned models by four to six points. It surpasses dedicated neural translation systems and multilingual language models by ten to thirteen points. The model keeps its broader multilingual skills and handles sentiment analysis and question answering competently, though native speakers still rate its output below high-quality standards.
arxiv-2606-11986:
Niklas Elmqvist, Panagiotis D Ritsos and Peter W S Butcher rethink interaction itself for multi-device analytics in this 2026 arXiv paper, presented at NordiCHI 2026. Classic interaction models assume one person, one interface, one stable loop between action and display. Cross-device and ubiquitous analytics break every part of that picture. Their model borrows distributed cognition: thinking and information live across minds, speech, bodies, artifacts and devices.

Interaction becomes the propagation of information state across these substrates, not traffic through a single screen. Generalising data visualisation theory, they define input and output channels that carry state through substrates whose availability depends on context. A voice command, a glance and a hand-off between screens become comparable moves in one framework. The authors demonstrate it by reanalysing several ubiquitous, immersive and situated analytics systems, giving designers a shared vocabulary for systems where the interface is the whole environment.
arxiv-2606-12386:
Éltető and co-authors automate the scientist's hardest choice: which experiment to run next, in this 2026 arXiv paper. Such modeling explains behavior with an explicit mechanism, not just predictions. Progress stalls when tests cannot tell rival mechanisms apart. Their framework, ATLAS, keeps an ensemble of sparse neural networks as living hypotheses about the mechanism. It then designs tests chosen to split those hypotheses as sharply as possible, and iterates.

They test it on recovering reinforcement learning agents, software learners like Q-learning, from bandit-task behavior. ATLAS invents varied experiment sequences with temporal structure tailored to each agent's traits. Models are scored three ways against the truth. Across all metrics, ATLAS needs five to ten times fewer samples than random testing. It also holds up against experiments designed by human experts from the literature. Automated design, tuned to competing theories, could speed such modeling far beyond cognitive science.
arxiv-2606-12686:
Kehoe and colleagues use deep James Webb Space Telescope spectra to study gas flowing into and out of distant galaxies, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The galaxies sit at redshift near 3, so their light left when the universe was young. Outflows expel material and regulate star formation, while inflows supply fresh fuel. The team traces cool gas through absorption lines of iron, magnesium, and sodium in NIRSpec spectra.

Combining 3 surveys gives samples of 176, 197, and 315 galaxies per tracer. Outflow speed shows no significant correlation with galaxy properties, yet galaxies with detected outflows tend to have higher stellar mass and star formation rates. The clearest result concerns viewing angle: face-on galaxies show stronger absorption and faster outflows, while highly tilted galaxies more often show inflowing gas. This first such evidence at this distance matches winds launching perpendicular to galaxy discs, with fresh gas arriving along the plane.
arxiv-2606-12786:
Zhou and He analyse the well-posedness and stability of suspension bridge models coupled with Cattaneo heat conduction, comparing systems with and without viscoelastic memory, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The model couples a vibrating cable and a Timoshenko beam deck through elastic springs representing the suspenders, with thermoelastic damping from the Cattaneo law, which gives heat a finite propagation speed. Operator semigroup theory is the main tool for deciding whether solutions exist, are unique, and decay over time.

For the memoryless system, the authors prove well-posedness and polynomial energy decay. The rate is t to the power minus one half when a parameter ratio matches, and slows to t to the minus one quarter when it does not. They also prove exponential stability is unachievable under specific coefficient configurations. Adding viscoelastic memory changes the picture qualitatively: the memory system is also well-posed, but now achieves exponential decay.
arxiv-2606-12986:
Alenezi reviews the rise of AI-native software engineering and its effects on practice, education, and the workforce, in this 2026 arXiv paper. The paper draws together 48 peer-reviewed publications from 2016 to 2026, found and analysed through a 4-agent research workflow and checked against sources.

The synthesis is organised along 9 themes and 3 arcs covering practice, education, and workforce. A scientometric analysis finds an inflection in which annual papers on language models for software engineering grew 5-fold after late 2022. The paper adds a framework for AI-native practice around intent, collaboration, and verification; a 9-dimension competency model; a 4-phase curriculum roadmap; and an agenda of 11 research gaps. Alenezi stresses that the evidence on productivity effects is contradictory and context-dependent, so training engineers for judgment, verification, and orchestration, rather than code production alone, is the central challenge.
arxiv-2606-13286:
Mitsiou and Krikidis analyse error rates for quantum communication in this 2026 arXiv paper. They study phase-shift keying, a scheme that encodes symbols in the phase of a light signal, using phase-squeezed states. Squeezing cuts phase noise at the cost of more noise elsewhere, suiting a receiver that measures only phase. The authors adopt the Mark-II adaptive receiver, a realisable phase measurement. Their analysis builds on its phase probability operator measure in the Fock basis, the count of photon number states.

They develop routes to the symbol error probability. One derives the phase distribution from the squeezed noise and folds in the receiver's uncertainty through an angular convolution, a mixing of angle distributions. Because that step has no closed form, a second model produces a closed-form answer. Results show phase squeezing lowers error probability compared with coherent light, and the gains grow for larger alphabets.
arxiv-2606-13486:
Smits presents CRAFTIIF in this 2026 arXiv paper, an unsupervised framework for spotting anomalies in multivariate time series. Such data, many sensor channels evolving together, contain at least four kinds of anomaly: isolated spikes, sustained level shifts, changes in rhythm or frequency, and breakdowns in the correlations between channels. Most detectors handle only one or two kinds, and few explain which signals or anomaly type triggered an alarm. CRAFTIIF is designed to cover all four types at once, without dataset-specific tuning, and to stay interpretable.

The method draws hundreds of random analytic wavelet features from four wavelet families, each family targeting a specific anomaly character. Wavelets dissect signals by timescale, so spikes, shifts, and rhythm changes leave distinct fingerprints. An isolation forest then flags points that are easiest to separate from the bulk. Because features are organised by type and channel, a detection can be attributed to its cause.
arxiv-2606-13786:
Ribes Metidieri and colleagues revisit the moment when a small black hole, spiraling around a much larger one, stops circling and plunges inward. Such extreme mass-ratio inspirals are key future targets for space-based gravitational wave detectors. Their 2026 arXiv paper studies tilted, nearly circular orbits in Kerr spacetime, the swirling geometry around a spinning black hole, using catastrophe theory, which sorts the ways smooth systems suddenly change behavior.

The transition still obeys the same Painlevé one equation known from level orbits. The physical starting conditions pick out one special solution, called the tritronquée solution. The authors compare new analytic forms of that solution against direct numerical integration. Accuracy is similar, while the analytic form stays more stable in later steps. Level orbits match a fold catastrophe and tilted orbits a cusp catastrophe. Crossing fold lines slowly explains why the same equation governs both cases.
arxiv-2606-13886:
Chandra, Damodaran, and Wang add a physics safety net around robot control models without retraining them. Vision-language-action models map camera views and instructions straight to robot actions, yet they learn by copying demonstrations and can command impossible moves. Their 2026 arXiv paper presents PhysVLA, a plug-in wrapper that checks each predicted action at run time and corrects it only when needed, adding under one millisecond per step.

Two layers do the work. A phase-aware state machine splits tasks into approach, grasp, transport, and place. A selective Euler-Lagrange gate, based on rigid-body motion equations, switches on only when a dynamics check flags inconsistency. Across four backbones on LIBERO-Spatial tasks with a Franka Panda arm, success rose by up to seventeen points and stability by nineteen. Efficiency improved by up to fifteen percent. On a real Agilex Piper arm, success gains reached fifty percent.
arxiv-2606-14086:
Chen and colleagues make speech emotion recognition explain itself, then fix the noisy labels teaching requires. Explainable systems cite speech emotion descriptors: prosodic features like pitch and volume, plus speaker traits like age. Reliable descriptor labels are scarce, so training data is annotated automatically and imperfectly. Their 2026 arXiv paper adds two post-training tools: a confidence score selecting trustworthy data, and reinforcement learning rectifying descriptors on the fly.

Experiments ran on IEMOCAP and MELD, two standard benchmarks. Systems using either component beat baselines with no selection or rectification. The best system, integrating both, gained two point nine percent absolute on IEMOCAP, three point seven percent relative. On MELD the gain was three point three percent absolute, five point four percent relative. Label quality, handled by selection and live correction together, matters as much as model design for SER.
arxiv-2606-14286:
Van Deyck, Van Acker, Chaffey, and Van Hertem let an optimizer decide how many DC breakers a future power hub needs, and where. Multiterminal high-voltage DC grids will need switching stations joining converters and lines, but a DC fault can cascade into large outages, and breakers are expensive. Current practice picks from pre-defined protection strategies. Their 2026 arXiv paper formulates a mixed-integer linear optimization minimizing protection cost plus fault-impact risk.

It designs the connectivity of external connections and the breaker arrangement inside the station, across many operating conditions. A case study with six external connections used a year of pre-fault power flow scenarios. The method outputs the optimal breaker count, given component failure rates and breaker cost relative to fault impact, and each additional breaker's marginal risk reduction, showing where spending stops paying. Sensitivity analyses show how cable failure rates and breaker costs shift the optimum.
arxiv-2606-14386:
Xia and Wang build a 2026 arXiv theory of why machine aided discovery stalls. Their setup mixes local search with large language models. The models propose bold new hypotheses. The authors argue that fresh ideas stop helping when they add no new information. This can happen even when the idea space still looks large.

They state a search compression claim with three parts. First, the explored ideas must compress. Second, the new idea must escape the span of what was explored. Third, it must still point toward the target signal. Tests support the claim. The team used synthetic setups, Chinese stock factor files, and symbolic regression tasks. Random jumps widened coverage but did not raise yield. Directed jumps helped only in thinly covered spots that held real signal.
arxiv-2606-14586:
Xiang, Zhang, and Mao make self-supervised image representations readable in a 2026 arXiv paper. Self-supervised learning extracts useful features from unlabeled images, but those features stay opaque vectors that people cannot inspect. Their framework, S2COPE, instead describes each image as a set of concepts written in natural language.

A vision-language model proposes candidate concepts for an image. A self-supervised objective then scores how well each concept fits that image while distinguishing it from others, and the feedback becomes preference data that trains the model to propose better concepts. Across eight diverse visual datasets, the concept representations transferred without adaptation and beat earlier interpretable approaches on downstream recognition. In medical imaging, the discovered concepts exposed spurious visual cues and supported a more robust classifier, showing self-supervision can yield human-readable representations.
arxiv-2606-14786:
Fan and co-authors detect copied videos at platform scale in a 2026 arXiv paper. Video platforms must spot reproduced content to protect creators and keep recommendations diverse, beyond filtering harmful material. Their production system, MatchLM2Lite, judges pairs of videos using video, audio, and text signals to produce fine-grained reproduction scores.

A high-capacity multimodal language model, MatchLM, acts as teacher and sets the performance ceiling. Its skill is then distilled into MatchLite, a compact student built for low-latency, high-throughput inference inside real-time recommendation systems. The teacher improved the F1 score by a wide margin over the previous production model, and the student retained most of that gain while cutting computing cost roughly thirty-five-fold. Deployed at scale with end-to-end latency under thirty seconds, the system reduced the reproduced video view rate measurably without hurting engagement.
arxiv-2606-14986:
Biondini and coauthors derive a modulation theory for lump waves in the Kadomtsev-Petviashvili equation in a 2026 study. Lumps are stable, fully two-dimensional localized waves of the KPI equation, unlike its unstable line solitons. A slowly varying mean field can bend and reshape a lump as it travels. No Whitham-style theory existed for such genuinely two-dimensional structures.

The authors derive a system of four hyperbolic equations describing how lump parameters evolve with the mean field. The system passes the Haantjes tensor test for integrability and admits a Hamiltonian form for steady mean fields. A reduction then treats a lump meeting a rarefaction wave in the mean field. Sharp conditions decide whether the lump passes through or gets trapped inside the wave. A lump moving horizontally is transmitted only when its starting amplitude clears a stated threshold. Numerical simulations of the full equation match the predictions closely.
arxiv-2606-15086:
Yu develops a bookkeeping framework for the Navier-Stokes regularity problem in a 2026 analysis paper. The equations govern fluid motion, and whether their solutions can form singularities remains open. A singular point must dodge the smallness regime at every scale, through windows. The paper answers with an audit that tracks critical quantities across windows.

The audit shows persistent badness cannot survive free of charge. It must generate untaxed critical supply or accumulate leakage from cutoffs and pressure tails. A second theorem transfers a clean model's regularity gap back to Navier-Stokes solutions. The transfer needs three structural inputs, including stability of a quotient construction. Every residual that could obstruct it is itemized as a ledger entry. The upshot is a conditional reduction, not a regularity proof. Any surviving singularity must be an organized, reproducible defect cascade, or defeat the controls. That narrows where a proof or a counterexample must aim.
arxiv-2606-15686:
Mannem and colleagues introduce RecurrReason in 2026, a benchmark stress-testing whether sequence models reason through logic puzzles. Language models look strong on symbolic tasks, but benchmarks check only the final answer, not whether solutions stay robust as difficulty scales. RecurrReason covers four puzzles, from Tower of Hanoi to Checkers Jumping, with one difficulty dial and optimal solutions from breadth-first search.

The suite holds nearly eleven thousand puzzles and over a quarter-million moves. Trained on easier settings, tested on harder ones, a fine-tuned T5 reaches about eighty-one percent out-of-distribution accuracy on Block World. Every model scores zero on River Crossing under all conditions. Architecture matters more than scale: T5's bidirectional goal-conditioning supports planning, while decoder-only attention bottlenecks planning. Pre-training transfers only to puzzles whose transitions are locally structured. Reliable multi-step reasoning needs search or constraint checking, not just bigger models.
arxiv-2606-15886:
Baltacı and colleagues introduce the first dataset for text detection in historical astronomical diagrams in 2026, a corner of document analysis that benchmarks had skipped. The dataset holds 948 diagrams spanning the 8th to 18th centuries and seven linguistic traditions, from Arabic and Persian to Chinese, Byzantine, Latin, Hebrew, and Sanskrit. Its 10,940 text regions carry ordered-polygon annotations tracing each boundary and encoding reading direction. The Latin regions also carry twenty class labels.

The team benchmarks strong detectors and proposes Poly-DETR, a simple DINO-DETR extension that predicts ordered polygon vertices directly. Poly-DETR sets the state of the art on two manuscript benchmarks and gives a solid baseline on the dataset, though a fine-tuned TESTR beats it there. The dataset is open access, with code released. For historians of astronomy, such regions are the first step toward reading what medieval diagrams say.
arxiv-2606-16086:
Li, Linghu, and Wang build a Kalman filter in 2026 for tracking evolving physical fields from sparse, noisy data. Data assimilation updates a field governed by partial differential equations as observations stream in. The field is infinite-dimensional in principle, so the filter state must stay finite. Their random-feature approach freezes random basis functions and tracks only their coefficients.

Once features are frozen and the equation is discretized, the coefficient vector obeys a finite linear-Gaussian model. The Kalman recursion then gives the exact posterior for that chosen model. For non-orthogonal draws, a mass-whitened coordinate system removes near-null directions and finds the true posterior dimension. For the heat equation with implicit-Euler stepping, the authors prove posterior contraction and consistency with high probability. The error splits cleanly into feature, time, and estimation parts.
arxiv-2606-16286:
Hamel asks in 2026 whether a learned world model can sharpen robot policies trained by flow matching, without retraining them. Flow matching clones behavior well across multimodal action spaces, but it is not trained to maximize reward directly. Hamel's framework, FlowMPC, keeps the imitation-learned policy and adds planning at test time. A world model built in the TD-MPC2 style predicts how candidate action sequences play out.

Planning uses Model Predictive Path Integral control, which samples action sequences from the policy, scores them in the world model, and favors the best. Tests run on ManiSkill manipulation tasks, picking up a cube and picking a single YCB object. Adding the world model improved performance over the flow policy alone on both tasks, per the report. Gains were clearest in success at the end of episodes, where early small errors usually compound.
arxiv-2606-16386:
Nguyen and co-authors plan drone swarm trajectories in 2026 as a game, because each drone's route taxes every other drone's radio link. In low-altitude wireless networks, cellular-connected drones share ground base stations across many cells. Under 5G's equal resource block policy, a drone entering a cell shrinks the resource share of all drones already served there. Routes and data rates are thus strategically coupled, a link earlier single-cell studies missed.

The team formulates the problem as a cooperative stochastic congestion game with a product-form utility joining communication quality and mission completion. The objective becomes social welfare maximization over the swarm. Their solver, built on multi-agent PPO with centralized training and decentralized execution, lets a central critic see the global congestion state while each drone acts alone at run time. The framework addresses multi-cell, congestion-aware planning directly, rather than assuming interference away.
arxiv-2606-16586:
Tao and co-authors train multimodal language models in 2026 to hunt for small decisive details inside big images, curing what they call visual context rot. Even with high-resolution inputs, models miss fine-grained evidence: the detail is present in the pixels but drowns in redundant context and never gets selected. Their framework, LOCUS, teaches local evidence search through a verifiable proxy task done entirely at training time.

During training the model receives a local crop as a visual cue and must recover that crop's spatial support in the full image, rewarded by overlap with the true region. At inference the cue disappears and the ordinary image-question interface is untouched. Across fine-grained perception, hallucination, general understanding, and reasoning benchmarks, LOCUS improves localization-sensitive understanding while preserving broad capabilities, per the report. Attention analyses confirm stronger focus on the true evidence regions.
arxiv-2606-16686:
Huong, Duy and Dong propose a dark-sector model in a 2026 particle theory paper that tackles two puzzles at once. Neutrinos have tiny but nonzero masses, which the Standard Model cannot explain. Dark matter, the unseen mass shaping galaxies, also needs a stable particle candidate. Their framework links both puzzles through one new dark gauge symmetry.

The model uses an inverse seesaw, where light neutrino masses are suppressed by a small parameter. Instead of inserting that smallness by hand, the parameter arises from corrections by dark fields. When it vanishes, lepton number symmetry returns, so its small size is natural in the technical sense. The same dark symmetry keeps the dark matter candidate stable. The authors map regions that satisfy relic density, direct detection and collider limits. The model also allows observable flavor signals, such as a muon decaying into an electron plus a photon.
arxiv-2606-16786:
Günther and colleagues argue for explanation cards in a 2026 paper on explainable machine learning. Tools that explain algorithmic decisions often mislead quietly: what an explanation seems to say is not what it actually shows. Some popular methods are even uninformative about how a complex decision function behaves, yet users cannot tell from the output alone.

An explanation card would travel with each explanation, adding facts about robustness and validity plus plain reading instructions. That shifts the burden from users, who now must guess the limits, to providers, who must state them up front. Worked examples show how to build cards for counterfactual explanations, which describe what would need to change, and for SHAP, which credits input features. A tiny stability region around a counterfactual, for instance, warns a loan applicant that the suggested change is nearly unreachable. Cards also link to duties under the European AI Act.
arxiv-2606-16886:
Pirzada and colleagues pair local language models with symbolic reasoning for software verification in a 2026 paper. Proving a program correct usually needs loop invariants, statements that stay true on every loop pass, and inventing them is the bottleneck. Cloud-based tools using big proprietary models solve many cases, but private code often cannot leave the building.

Their pipeline, VerIbmc, runs entirely on one local machine with open-weight models. A symbolic phase first proposes invariants, then a model refines them using feedback from the ESBMC verifier. Two prompting styles are compared across five models and five benchmark families. The best setup solves most of the roughly five hundred problems. The symbolic phase alone settles dozens of problems with no model call, and rescues many extra cases for the weakest model.
arxiv-2606-16986:
Researchers at INFN Padova and Kyung Hee University shortcut a hard gravity calculation in a 2026 paper on supersymmetric black holes. The setting is five-dimensional supergravity with vector multiplets. For black saddle solutions, the on-shell action, which weights each geometry in the path integral, is usually painful to evaluate.

The action, they show, equals an equivariant integral of the anomaly polynomial over cones. Splitting the solution's toric diagram into simplicial cones localizes the integral: the action becomes a sum of contributions at each cone's tip. The procedure needs a six-dimensional extension sharing the same fan, a resolution into simplicial cones, then the localized sum. Known results for black holes, black rings and black lenses drop out simply, including a hole in a topological soliton background. It also yields new predictions, among them Wald entropy formulas for extremal solutions, curved or flat at infinity.
arxiv-2606-17086:
Shah, Ashokan, Drummond and Pathak map the phases of electrons and holes in two parallel wires in a 2026 condensed matter paper. Electrons in one wire and holes in the other can bind into excitons, neutral pairs that might condense into a coherent quantum fluid. The wires are mass-asymmetric, and the temperature is zero.

Using diffusion quantum Monte Carlo, which samples the many-body wavefunction stochastically, the team computes pair correlations and condensate fraction across densities and wire separations. The phase diagram shows three regimes: a two-component plasma, an excitonic fluid with quasicondensation, and a Wigner-correlated phase where charges order themselves. One dimension helps the excitons: strong correlations sustain quasicondensation even at high density, where wider systems would ionize into plasma. The map tells physicists where coherent excitonic behavior survives in one-dimensional electron-hole systems, and where plasma or charge order takes over.
arxiv-2606-17286:
Sania, Ziosi, and Barez present a 2026 arXiv paper arguing that artificial intelligence systems can enable authoritarianism by design, and not only inside autocracies. The authors trace the full lifecycles of six deployed AI systems across regimes from the United States to China. Their evidence spans academic studies, investigative reports, third-party evaluations, media interviews, and government procurement notices, compared in a set way for the features that make misuse possible in each setting.

Enabling features included centralised state data being co-opted for law enforcement and political punishment, plus rules too weak to deter misuse. Weak user compliance that nullifies human oversight, and encoded traits marking vulnerable groups, also recurred across the cases. Both centralised and fragmented systems contributed, one by escaping formal oversight and the other by diffusing accountability. The authors close with recommendations for developers and policymakers to cut these design-level risks.
arxiv-2606-17386:
Xiong and colleagues present a 2026 arXiv paper on teaching cars to drive without the costly expert demonstrations that end-to-end methods usually imitate. Their approach, TerraTransfer, splits the job into learning to drive and learning to see, exploiting cheap vectorised simulators for the first part. Self-play there runs millions of steps per second and naturally produces crashes, near-misses, and recoveries no real driving log contains in such density.

A policy pretrained by self-play is then aligned with a pretrained vision backbone through action-based losses, never against a logged human trajectory. Only paired images and scene states are needed, so no curated demonstration set enters the pipeline at any stage. On photorealistic closed-loop scenarios built with three-dimensional Gaussian splatting, the resulting policy matches or beats prior end-to-end methods. The recipe cuts both labelling cost and rendering cost sharply.
arxiv-2606-17686:
Comer and colleagues write a 2026 physics paper on fluids that lose energy as they flow at speeds close to the speed of light. Their model has two parts, a flow of particles and a flow of entropy, set in curved spacetime. The key rule is plain: a flow counts as losing energy when a key measure of its spread is not zero.

From a least-action rule built on that idea, the team derives the equations that such flows must obey. Added terms for bulk and shear drag then appear in those equations on their own. The model also recovers the well known Cattaneo form for heat flow, in which heat moves at a finite speed. The paper closes by listing the extra flow data a full heat result needs.
arxiv-2606-17886:
Krasnov and colleagues make a neural network family respect a simple rule: when an input rises, the output must not fall. Many tabular, scientific, and economic tasks carry such monotone links, and baking them in as a hard guarantee beats hoping the model learns them. Earlier designs forced monotonicity only partly or needed awkward projection steps during training, and spline-based Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks lacked a clean version.

Their model, MKAN, guarantees monotonicity for every parameter value by construction, through exponentiated spline coefficients, positive edge weights, and a monotone base activation, so plain gradient descent does the training. A representation-cost theorem bounds the price: a monotone twin of a given feature extractor needs at most twice the size. Tests on four real classification datasets matched the bound, recasting monotonicity as a priced trade-off rather than a ban.
arxiv-2606-18186:
Molu rebuilds diffusion policies for robots on infinite-dimensional foundations, in a 2026 paper. Diffusion policies plan actions by denoising, but finite-dimensional versions drift over time when deployed on physical systems, thanks to discretization artifacts, and their long-horizon behavior sours. Molu lifts the policy into a Cameron-Martin space, swapping stochastic score matching for a deterministic boundary-value problem drawn from the backward Kolmogorov equation.

Training uses a precision-weighted loss in that space, and a Kolmogorov residual doubles as a built-in failure detector at run time, with no reward signal needed. Convergence guarantees depend on the effective rank of the kernel rather than the action dimension, and spectral weighting smooths the trajectories. On the PushT manipulation benchmark the new loss lifts top episode reward by a clear margin over the standard objective. A second study pairs the policies with reachability checks for certified safety.
arxiv-2606-18486:
Alpay and Başaran reframe the rendering of a scene of convex objects as a communication problem, in a 2026 paper mixing geometry and information theory. What many diagrams carry is not pixel detail but a pattern of separations: which groups of objects stand apart and which overlap, a payload they call the scene's apartness table, or separoid.

With that table as the source signal, they pose rendering as a rate-distortion problem: spend few description bits while faithfully transmitting the certificates that generate the table, weighting errors by consequence. Their differentiable pipeline recovered scenes from the apartness table alone at near-perfect bit accuracy in planar experiments, and the certificate skeleton already determined the whole table. A small rendered image delivered a share of the apartness information, rising with resolution and collapsing with noise like a capacity-limited channel. The best viewpoints certified most separations from one direction.
arxiv-2606-18686:
Lee, Merrill, and Karger build a forecasting benchmark inside a simulated strategy game, so that predictions can be scored quickly and counterfactual questions become answerable, in a 2026 paper on AI evaluation. Real-world forecasting benchmarks resolve slowly, rarely sample tail events, and can never score what would have happened under an intervention, because only one history is realized.

ForecastBench-Sim runs on rollouts of Freeciv, the open Civilization-style game. Forecasters receive a structured world report snapshot and answer binary or continuous questions about hidden future states, after which the simulation continues and scores them. Paired intervention worlds, created by mutating the saved game before rollout, support conditional and causal questions, and disruptive outcomes can be sampled densely with immediate resolution. The authors describe the pipeline and scoring protocol and report validation slices from model runs and an anonymized human pilot.
arxiv-2606-18786:
Qin and the team wrap the RoboCup 2D soccer simulator into a reinforcement learning environment, in a 2026 multi-agent learning paper. Robot soccer is a demanding testbed. It combines partial observability, cooperation and opposition, sparse scoring rewards, and long-horizon tactics. But the competition platform's server-client architecture resists the Python workflows that multi-agent reinforcement learning researchers use.

R2D-RL connects the simulator and HELIOS-based player clients to a Python interface, through shared-memory communication with cycle-level synchronization. It supports full-field and scenario-based training, with configurable opponents, discrete and parameterized hybrid action spaces, action masks, and reward shaping based on expected possession value. It also supports parallel execution. The authors supply front-goal scenarios and an eleven-versus-eleven benchmark with baselines. The results verify trainability on attacks, while exposing how teammate use, passing choices, and credit assignment grow harder at full scale.
arxiv-2606-19286:
Sen and colleagues study how error correction shapes trust in social chatbots in 2026. Social chatbots are prone to convincing but wrong outputs, and the social bond they build makes errors costly. A between-subjects experiment with over a hundred participants compares three correction routes. The error is fixed by a webpage retraction, by the same chatbot correcting itself, or by an expert chatbot stepping in to correct it.

All three routes corrected the error equally well in factual terms. Only self-correction did so without damaging credibility. Participants rated self-correcting chatbots higher in trustworthiness and perceived expertise than chatbots corrected by external sources. The strength of the user's social connection with the chatbot also shapes how corrections land. A chatbot that fixes its own mistakes can keep trust that outside corrections erode.
arxiv-2606-19586:
Chuer Pan and colleagues turn single robot demonstrations into rich training data in 2026. Visuomotor policies learn manipulation from camera views and actions, but small setup changes break them. New obstacles or a shifted start pose push views outside the training set, causing hard failures.

Demonstrations come from a portable parallel gripper carrying one fisheye camera, in an eye-in-hand setup. A Gaussian Splatting method adapted to wide fisheye lenses rebuilds the 3D scene for editing. Editors can insert unseen objects into that rebuilt scene. Trajectory optimisation then crafts smooth, collision-free action paths that suit the new views. Matching fisheye image sequences render from those paths, forming fresh training pairs. Tests in simulation and the real world lift success rates on varied manipulation tasks. Gains hold both in the same scene and in cluttered scenes needing avoidance.
arxiv-2606-19886:
Xiaotong Li, Wei Liu, and Wenjie Xiao analyse long-run behaviour of a numerical method for stochastic equations in 2026. Invariant measures describe where a random process settles in the long run. The stochastic theta method steps such equations numerically, covering super-linear growth in drift and diffusion.

The numerical solution is shown to possess exactly one invariant measure of its own. That measure converges to the true invariant measure of the underlying equation. Simulations illustrate the theory on test problems. Earlier results for a narrower diffusion case are extended by the new proof. The backward Euler-Maruyama method falls inside the theta family as a special case. Its known invariant-measure results thus generalise along with it. Long-time simulation of stiff random systems gains firmer footing.
arxiv-2606-20086:
Alessandro Marino and seventeen colleagues report a deep radio search for two accreting millisecond pulsars caught in their quiet state. Their 2026 paper uses China's FAST telescope, the world's largest single-dish radio instrument, to observe IGR J00291+5934 and MAXI J1957+032 in the L-band. These neutron stars spin hundreds of times per second while feeding from a companion, showing X-ray pulses while active. Whether they switch on as radio pulsars when feeding stops, as transitional pulsars do, remains open.

Swift and Las Cumbres data suggested both targets were dormant during the campaign. The team searched for periodic signals at the known spin rates and across other frequencies, yet found no convincing candidate. Assuming pulses occupy a tenth of each cycle, they set flux limits of 3.3 and 5.6 microjanskys, the tightest yet for persistent accreting pulsars. The silence sharpens the puzzle of why some dormant neutron stars stay radio-dark.
arxiv-2606-20186:
Svante Janson returns to quasi-random graphs, asking which subgraph-count properties truly force a graph sequence to behave like random graphs. His 2026 paper continues a line opened with Vera Sós in 2013. Many restricted counting properties do characterize quasi-randomness: if counts of certain small subgraphs match what randomness predicts, the whole graph must be random-like. But some properties are exceptions, and understanding why matters for the theory of graph limits.

Janson introduces new versions of these properties to probe the boundary. A fresh proof ingredient does much of the work: the space of symmetric functions splits into pieces irreducible under measure-preserving transformations, simplifying some arguments and structuring others. Some earlier cases remain open, and new conjectures are posed. The paper is both a contribution and an invitation to finish mapping which local statistics determine global randomness.
arxiv-2606-20286:
Jiyuan Lyu revisits four long-running arguments about Chinese farm growth between 1949 and 1986, testing each with one dataset and several methods. His 2026 paper tackles the size of the price scissors that squeezed farmers, the effect of heavy industrial investment, and the role of the 1978 reforms. It also asks what the end of collective farming did to irrigation. Using a single dataset keeps the answers comparable across questions that earlier literature studied in isolation.

Several results cut against received wisdom. The years 1952 to 1957 were the only net extraction period; afterward the state channelled a net inflow of about 168.6 billion yuan into farming. Heavy industry investment actually helped agriculture with a lag. Structural breaks point to the 1970 North China Agricultural Conference as a turning point. Disaster prevention capacity fell after household contracting, mainly because collective upkeep collapsed. And after 1979, price incentives faded toward zero.
arxiv-2606-20786:
İsmail Yüksel and three colleagues examine memory-centric computing in 2026, where computation moves into memory instead of data moving to a processor. Today's systems shuttle data between processors and DRAM memory. That movement wastes time and energy. Processing-in-DRAM uses the traits of a DRAM chip to compute where data sits. The shift promises speed and energy gains. It also changes system security in ways that are not yet well explored.

Turning memory from a passive store into an active computing surface cuts both ways. It can support new in-memory security tools and reduce data exposure during movement. It can also open new attack surfaces inside the memory itself. The authors discuss benefits and challenges for processing-in-DRAM in particular. Their analysis helps designers weigh a real tradeoff: less data in transit may mean fewer leaks, but a smarter memory chip must itself be protected.
arxiv-2606-21086:
Ge Wang and many colleagues present ReFPO in 2026, an online reinforcement learning method that adds reflow regularization to flow matching policy gradients for robot control. Flow-based policies generate actions through a learned flow. Their gradient updates, the authors show, can be read as an implicit advantage-weighted reflow process. That view gives a new geometric picture of flow policy learning.

Building on it, an explicit geometric regularizer is added. The change takes a single line of code. No extra compute or distillation stage is needed. Advantage-guided updates join path rectification. Training becomes more stable, with fewer proxy-ratio spikes. One-step inference often matches multi-step quality. Tests span grid worlds, MuJoCo playground tasks, and humanoid control. Stable, fast flow policies matter for real-time control, where a robot cannot spend many sampling steps deciding each movement.
arxiv-2606-21186:
Andrianos Sygrimis and Giorgos Tsironis study plasmonic excitations in 2026 in twisted bilayer graphene within a non-Hermitian framework with gain and loss. Twisting two graphene layers creates a moiré pattern that reshapes electronic bands. Their model extends a standard continuum description to include gain and loss. A biorthogonal formalism computes optical conductivity for that active bilayer.

Non-Hermiticity changes the collective spectrum. Optical and acoustic plasmon branches appear. The acoustic branch shows strong subwavelength confinement. In a parity-time symmetric setup, gain-loss balance can cut spatial damping and lengthen propagation in the ideal linear model. Strongly localized near fields arise in the same regime. The enhancement, they argue, comes from moiré band effects combined with non-Hermitian changes, not from gain alone. Active plasmonics could one day route light at scales far below its wavelength.
arxiv-2606-21386:
Florian Seligmann, Emiliyan Gospodinov, Enes Ulas Dincer, and Gerhard Neumann built VLA-FAIL in 2026, a lightweight guard that watches robot policies for signs of failure while they run. Vision-language-action models manipulate objects well but can act unpredictably on unfamiliar scenes, and existing failure detectors are costly or need examples of failures. VLA-FAIL needs no failure data and adds minimal overhead, using two paired detectors.

One measures how far last-layer features drift from training patterns, token by token. The other checks consistency between overlapping action chunks, which should agree under receding-horizon control. A new metric scores detectors on precision, recall, and detection speed together. Across real and simulated tasks, the combined detectors catch failures early and reliably, often beating far costlier baselines.
arxiv-2606-21586:
Stefano Profumo argues in 2026 that cosmology's success does not settle what the universe really is. The same data, he notes, can be carried by quite different math and concepts, so the data alone cannot fix the underlying picture of reality. What survives across all good descriptions, he proposes, is information structure rather than any one picture.

He names that shared content cross-representational informational invariants. These cover how data correlate, how well states can be told apart, and how much information observers can in principle reach, measured with tools such as the Fisher-Rao metric. On this view, models are compact encodings of what is observed. Progress then means sharpening the information open to observation, not homing in on a final account of what exists. The stance pushes against scientific realism while keeping the field's empirical success fully intact.
arxiv-2606-21786:
O'Rourke, Trisovic, and Bertsimas introduce RocketPFN in 2026, a training-free way to classify time series, meaning ordered sequences of measurements. Their pipeline pairs Rocket, which extracts features using random convolutional filters, with TabPFN, a pretrained model that classifies new cases by comparing them with labelled examples shown in context. No training on the target dataset is needed at all.

Across 92 datasets from the standard UCR archive, RocketPFN matched HC2, the strongest published method, with both reaching mean accuracy of 0.900 under repeated testing. It also beat every single classifier inside the HC2 ensemble, and a median fold took about thirty seconds. On twenty multivariate UEA datasets the gap was likewise not statistically significant. Three recent time-series foundation models, given the same downstream classifier, all scored significantly lower.
arxiv-2606-22086:
Li and Zhang extend, in 2026, the known black hole solutions of revised Deser-Woodard nonlocal gravity, a modified gravity theory where the field equations involve influences from the whole spacetime region. Static, spherically symmetric solutions are the starting point for testing any gravity theory against Schwarzschild. The authors work out how corrections to Schwarzschild behave at first order in this theory.

Because the field equations are linear at that order, different correction modes can be superposed cleanly. Two further asymptotically flat extensions are studied. A logarithmically dressed correction decays slowly with radius, spreading the nonlocal effect far from the hole. An exponentially suppressed correction stays localized near the horizon and, for positive amplitude, shifts the horizon inward. The authors link the two forms to quantum corrections and to finite-range screening mechanisms in modified gravity.
arxiv-2606-22286:
Prosper Mama Assandje and four colleagues, including M. Nguiffo Boyom, compare two cohomology theories, tools that extract global shape information from local algebraic data, in this 2026 paper. They work on three Lie groups, which are groups with a smooth geometric structure: the circle rotation group, the Heisenberg group, and the Galilei group.

The team compares De Rham cohomology with Koszul-Vinberg cohomology, a version adapted to flat affine structures, which are coordinate systems with straight-line changes. They compute the dimensions of both complexes and form a quotient measuring the gap between topological invariants and affine structures. The framework extends to coadjoint orbits of the Heisenberg and Galilei groups, studied under a special foliation. They also prove a vanishing theorem for the second Koszul-Vinberg group. It shows every small deformation of the affine structure is trivial, so these orbits are structurally rigid.
arxiv-2606-22686:
Shivam Ratnakar and Kartikeya Vats probe how safety alignment lives inside language models in this 2026 paper. Aligned models refuse harmful requests, but whether refusal is a deep semantic decision or a shallow, manipulable feature was unclear. Their tool, Contrastive Logit Steering, needs no optimization: it isolates a refusal direction by contrasting model states under safe and unrestricted system prompts.

Unlike activation steering, the method acts directly on the output distribution. Combined with prefix injection to slip past the initial refusal reflex, it triggers a phase transition where guardrails collapse. Across seven model families, safety proved architecturally deterministic. One family with a late-decision topology reached ninety-five percent attack success in about a second, while another integrating safety mid-computation resisted better. Logit steering far outperformed activation methods on two test models. Inverting the same vector hardened models against jailbreaks without retraining, showing one safety axis cuts both ways.
arxiv-2606-22786:
Yuval Banoun, Daniel Sadoc Menasché, and Ori Rottenstreich look for unused information inside a counting Bloom filter in this 2026 paper. Bloom filters answer whether an item belongs to a set, such as the contents of a cache. Hash collisions force them to answer yes when unsure, so they never miss a real member.

A counting Bloom filter replaces each bit with a counter, which supports deletions as well as insertions. Banoun and colleagues show that these counters carry extra signal: they can estimate how certain a positive answer is. A membership claim backed by strong counter evidence means something different from one produced by a single weak collision. The paper shows how architectures that pair Bloom filters with machine learning models can exploit that certainty signal. The model receives not just a yes, but a measure of how much to trust it.
arxiv-2606-23086:
Kissa Zahra and Zaib Un Nisa prune the channels of latent diffusion models in a 2026 paper. Latent diffusion models generate images inside a compressed space built by an autoencoder. That space has many channels, and whether all of them matter was unknown. Their framework, PeLAP-A, adds a small importance predictor to the standard pipeline. The predictor studies pooled latent features and softly masks channels it judges unimportant, before the denoising network sees them. The whole system trains together on the CIFAR-10 image set.

Zahra and Nisa report a striking outcome they call sparsity collapse. Under strong sparsity pressure, the predictor drove nearly every channel toward zero. Yet the denoiser still achieved slightly lower loss than the unpruned baseline, and reconstruction error also improved. Their analysis explains the collapse and what it reveals about how little latent information denoising actually needs.
arxiv-2606-23786:
Baibhav, Metzger, and Hui propose that a famous gravitational wave event was born inside the collapsing disk of a dying massive star, in a 2026 paper on gravitational wave astrophysics. GW190814 paired a twenty three solar mass black hole with a companion of about two point six solar masses, an extreme mismatch standard formation channels struggle to produce. The companion sits in the mass gap between neutron stars and black holes.

Recent work shows that disks around newborn black holes in collapsars can fragment into neutron stars or small black holes. The authors argue one such fragment later merged with the central black hole. They identify a Type Ib supernova seen about sixty days earlier inside the event's sky volume as a possible precursor explosion. Three body encounters among fragments can delay some mergers by weeks to months, matching that gap.
arxiv-2606-24086:
Yang and colleagues build a pronunciation coach for learners of Modern Standard Arabic, a language whose emphatic and throat consonants are hard for software to judge. Their system must spot and diagnose mispronounced phonemes, the smallest sound units, yet real learner recordings are scarce and synthetic speech differs from real voices. The 2026 framework therefore trains in two stages, first on native and synthetic material, then adapting gently to the small set of genuine learner data.

A pretrained encoder paired with temporal convolutional networks preserves fine sound detail that ordinary recognition often smooths away. Several saved model versions vote together at test time, with an N-gram rescoring step steadying the final answer. On the QuranMB.v2 test set the system posts a large relative gain over its baseline and tops the IqraEval challenge. Yang's team presents the result as a new high mark for low-resource Arabic pronunciation diagnosis.
arxiv-2606-24286:
Chen and colleagues help omni-modal language models watch hour-long audio-video content without drowning in tokens. Long recordings overflow context windows and repeat themselves endlessly, so most tokens carry nothing new. Their 2026 framework, AVOC, inserts a learnable compression module between the audio-video encoders and the language model, treating compression as a retrieval problem under a fixed budget.

Three classical information-retrieval criteria guide which tokens survive: relevance to the user's query, general importance, and diversity among the chosen set. Each criterion becomes a tailored mechanism inside one unified pipeline, so the retained subset best supports answering the actual question rather than summarising everything equally. On long-form audio-video benchmarks AVOC reaches state-of-the-art performance, beating the second-best model by several points of average accuracy on OmniVideoBench and a companion benchmark. Chen's retrieval framing turns an engineering squeeze into a principled selection problem.
arxiv-2606-24386:
van Lieshout and van Rossum ask whether the canonical model for planning public transport lines survives contact with national scale networks. Line planning decides which lines to run and how often. Passenger routing is traditionally modelled on a change-and-go network, capturing every transfer exactly, which makes the network balloon.

Three compact rival models approximate transfers differently. The Eindhoven team develops strong solution methods tailored to each of the four models. All are evaluated across nearly a thousand instances, drawn from the Dutch and Swiss railway networks. Contrary to its canonical status, the exact network competes only on small or easy instances. On large ones it often finds no feasible solution at all. The compact model built on direct connections leads overall and wins the most cases. Careful approximation, the authors conclude in 2026, beats exact transfer modelling as the base for large scale line planning.
arxiv-2606-24486:
Karkosova Martinovicova and Pleskot recycle two flagship LHC searches to hunt a particle nobody has aimed them at directly. Monojet and mono-V signatures, one energetic jet or vector boson recoiling against large missing momentum, probe many new physics scenarios at ATLAS and CMS. They range from supersymmetry to dark matter candidates. Reinterpreting those searches means re-reading existing data through a different theoretical lens, rather than collecting new collisions.

The lens here is compositeness: the possibility that quarks and leptons are built from smaller preons. It predicts excited fermions, heavier siblings of ordinary particles. Excited neutrinos are the specific target. The authors assess the prospects for limits on such particles, from the monojet and mono-V final states the collaborations already measured. Their 2026 reinterpretation extracts fresh constraints from finished analyses. Collider data keep yielding results long after the original searches close.
arxiv-2606-24686:
Haizhong Li, Luc Vrancken, Xianfeng Wang, and Zeke Yao classify hypersurfaces with constant sectional curvature inside the product of two hyperbolic planes. Classifying curved surfaces inside curved spaces is a classic problem of differential geometry. The analogous problem for two spheres was settled earlier, and its answer is rigid. Any such hypersurface in the sphere product has product angle function identically zero. The hyperbolic product behaves differently. Its examples show far more diversity, the authors find.

A special example anchors the contrast: a hypersurface whose product angle function is not constant. Nothing like it exists in the sphere case. The classification covers all constant sectional curvature hypersurfaces in the hyperbolic product. As a byproduct, Li and colleagues also classify hypersurfaces there with constant product angle function. That second result holds under either constant mean curvature or constant scalar curvature.
arxiv-2606-24786:
Dimitri Gominski and eight colleagues take on counting individual trees in satellite images. The task matters for environmental monitoring, yet satellite resolution makes it hard. Isolated trees can be spotted, but crown boundaries blur together in dense forest. Hand labelling trees at scale is also far too costly. The team instead derives training labels from airborne LiDAR data. Those labels scale well but arrive noisy, so the counting method must tolerate errors.

Counting is reframed as matching a spatial density, supervised through unbalanced optimal transport. That setup locates lone trees precisely while still estimating density inside dense stands. A self correction step uses transport residuals to clean the noisy labels during training. The new TinyTrees benchmark spans three continents and three satellite sensors. It holds over 216 million tree annotations across some 25,890 square kilometres. The method beats detection, regression, and other transport based baselines throughout, Gominski and colleagues report.
arxiv-2606-24986:
Leutrim Uka, Severino Pinto, Gundula Hoffmann, and Marina Höhne ask whether fusing several sensors helps classify cattle posture. Their systems label animals as lying or standing. Sensors include collar accelerometers, rumen bolus sensors, and environmental measurements. Data come from a pasture based beef herd across two years. XGBoost is the main model, against logistic regression, random forest, and LSTM baselines. Evaluation grows stricter by stages: random splits first, then leaving animals out.

The test is cross year, on animals never seen before. Multimodal models shine within the year, reaching a macro F1 around 0.94, but fall to about 0.49 under the time shift. The collar only model unexpectedly beats every multimodal configuration there, at about 0.54. Explainability analysis shows why: the fused models lean on rumen bolus activity and environmental variables that do not travel across years. Uka and colleagues warn that extra sensors can buy accuracy that evaporates on deployment.
arxiv-2606-25086:
Many language model pipelines return an averaged model, an exponential moving average of the training weights, rather than the final weights themselves. Kwok Chun Au and Adam Block ask how training should change when the average is what gets shipped. They cast optimiser design for the averaged estimate as a problem in optimal control.

In a continuous time stochastic quadratic model, they solve for the control that minimises the error of the returned average under a penalty on intervention size. A practical approximation gives PACE, a light AdamW wrapper that pulls the live weights toward their moving average with a clipped, per coordinate strength. Theory shows standard convergence rates, and strict error improvements in the quadratic setting. In practice PACE beats AdamW on fine tuning of one to two billion parameter models and on GPT-2 pretraining.
arxiv-2606-25186:
Neutron stars of different masses share one equation of state, the rule linking pressure and density in their interiors. Aleksi Kurkela and Tuhin Malik ask what causality alone, the rule that sound cannot outrun light, then forces on their radii. The anchor is chiral effective field theory near saturation density.

The answer is a closed form ceiling: the radius of a two solar mass star can exceed that of a 1.4 solar mass star only within a fixed linear bound. A one parameter family of equations of state, built analytically, saturates the bound exactly. Applied to NICER radius measurements of three pulsars, the ceiling keeps only 7.5 percent of the combined probability and trims the large radius tail of the heaviest pulsar. The construction isolates what generic physics forces, apart from any prior choice.
arxiv-2606-25286:
Consensus bodies announce unanimous decisions, hiding who actually shaped them. Casper van Elteren and colleagues recover the hidden politics in 2026 from a trace consensus cannot erase: the documents actors choose to work on. Borrowing tools from economic complexity, they build a space of concerns for the Antarctic Treaty, where issues sit close together when the same actors repeatedly specialise in both. Six decades of records, over six thousand documents from sixty six actors, feed the map.

Engagement turned out to be structured, local, and persistent rather than random or fleeting. The most specialised actors produced binding law at about five times the baseline rate. The team argues the method travels to any document rich forum run by consensus, since unanimity moves political structure upstream into the organisation of attention rather than deleting it.
arxiv-2606-25486:
If neutrinos are their own antiparticles, certain nuclei should decay in a way never yet observed, splitting off two electrons and no neutrinos. L Coraggio, G De Gregorio, S Lyu, and N Itaco compute the nuclear part of that rate in 2026 within one consistent framework. Both the nuclear Hamiltonian and the decay operator are derived from chiral effective field theory. That is the systematic expansion of the strong force at low energies. Many body perturbation theory then processes them into shell model form.

Three candidate nuclei are treated: calcium 48, germanium 76, and selenium 82, all targets of real experimental searches. Spectra of the nuclei come out alongside the decay matrix elements, giving an internal check on the wavefunctions. A convergence study of those quantities supplies the raw material for an honest uncertainty estimate, which searches need in order to interpret their results.
arxiv-2606-25586:
Approximating an integral by a weighted sum of function values is quadrature. Gauss type rules tuned to spline spaces are known to be nearly unbeatable for smooth integrands. Geno Nikolov and Petar Nikolov revisit the error constants of those rules in 2026 for parabolic and cubic splines with doubled, evenly spaced knots. Earlier work built the rules for both degrees and estimated how large the error constant can be. The machinery goes back to nineteen ninety five results on asymptotic optimality.

For the cubic case the pair refines the error constant estimate. For both degrees they point out alternative bounds that are easier to compute. Some are sharper than the classical ones, which depend on the largest value of a high derivative of the integrand. The new forms run through Peano kernel representations and Bernoulli polynomials, standard tools they deploy to squeeze the constants.
arxiv-2606-25786:
HotNets is the networking workshop for bold early ideas. It is redesigning itself. Paolo Costa and Michael Schapira lay out the new protocol in this 2026 document. Submission volumes have swollen. AI tools have arrived in the research process. Formats built for a smaller community strain under the load. The upgrade widens the scope to perspective and community facing pieces. Technical papers remain welcome. Each kind gets its own judging criteria. Reviewing becomes more of a shared discussion.

How accepted work is presented and debated also changes. The organisers explore careful uses of AI in reviewing and sharing work. Backward compatibility is the stated spirit. The ambition and intellectual risk that made the workshop valuable stay. The document solicits community feedback openly. A follow up report will summarise reactions and lessons once the experiment has run.
arxiv-2606-25886:
Comparing touch sensors fairly is impossible when every lab's test textures are whatever objects happened to be on the shelf. Dexter Shepherd and colleagues at the University of Sussex fix that in 2026 with a texture dataset anyone can fabricate. Six surface patterns are defined mathematically, built from sine wave and Fourier ingredients, varying spatial frequency, amplitude, and direction in controlled steps. Any lab can print the same textures and run its sensor over them. The team first ask how reproducible the prints themselves are, across three popular printers and several filaments.

Print quality, especially peak sharpness and stringing, drove the tactile readings apart. Higher end printers gave far more consistent signatures under an optical tactile sensor. Classifiers generalised strongly within one printer's output but struggled across printers, thanks to small geometric mismatches. The openly shared benchmark gives tactile sensing its first physically reproducible yardstick.
arxiv-2606-25986:
C. Evans Hedges asks whether limit order book prediction, forecasting short-term price moves from the queue of buy and sell orders, obeys a scaling law like those seen in language models. Speed is everything here: a forecast that arrives late is worthless. Using the FI-2010 benchmark and models from small decision trees to neural book architectures, Hedges maps accuracy against the forward computation each model needs.

A power law fits the accuracy-versus-compute frontier well. Trained only on low and mid-range models outside one neural family, the fit predicts that family's high-compute frontier across orders of magnitude with strong accuracy. Latency refuses to follow the same law, showing delay is not just noisy compute. That gap motivates FastBiNLOB, a hardware-friendly mixer architecture that beats published accuracy targets for two forecast horizons at markedly lower latency across five random seeds.
arxiv-2606-26286:
A. Ballester-Bolinches and colleagues carry two classic group theory results into the world of skew left braces. Braces are algebraic structures born from work on the Yang-Baxter equation. Grün's lemma says the first two centres of a perfect group coincide. Baer's theorem ties finiteness of a central quotient to finiteness of a lower central term. Both facts police how centrality and commutators interact in groups.

Analogues now hold for infinite skew left braces. The proofs run through the trifactorised group attached to each brace, a bridge back to group theory. Improvements over earlier brace versions are part of the claim. Centre behaviour in braces matters beyond pure algebra. Braces encode set-theoretic solutions to the Yang-Baxter equation, which feed knot theory and quantum groups. Knowing where brace centres stabilize sharpens every construction built on them.
arxiv-2606-26386:
Joan Montas, Samuel Dodson, Anitha Gollamudi, and Matteo Cimini build programming-language support for a legal duty: data collected for one purpose must not quietly be used for another. Privacy laws like the GDPR demand this, yet compilers rarely check it.

Their language, PurPL, uses typestate, where a type carries a state that changes as the program runs. Here the state is the set of purposes a piece of data may serve, which can grow or shrink during execution. The authors give the formal type system, implement the checker, and test it on scenarios that handle sensitive data.
arxiv-2606-26786:
Henri Riihimäki and Jason P. Smith invent a new homology theory from the sandpile model. In that model, piles of sand on a graph topple when too tall, sending grains to neighbours. Avalanches are the chain reactions that follow. Homology theories count holes and connections in a shape. The authors build a simplicial complex from the sets of unstable vertices during an avalanche.

They compute this avalanche homology for directed paths and directed cycles under set starting loads. Even such simple graphs yield a wide range of topologies. Comparisons with two earlier graph homologies, the directed flag complex and burning homology, follow. The dynamics also filter the complex step by step. That yields a persistent version, tracking features across the avalanche's lifetime.
arxiv-2606-26986:
Xin Lin, Liang Zhang, Guoqi Ma, Hongyao Tu, and Jinsong Su present ReaORE, a reasoning-guided method for open relation mining. The task pulls relationships between named things out of raw text. Open mining must handle relation types never seen in training. Grouping methods cannot name new relations. Asking a language model directly confuses similar relations.

ReaORE reasons from coarse to fine in two stages. Filtering first builds a candidate relation set by reasoning over several aspects of the text. Vector similarity then adds to and prunes the set to keep the true relation inside. The last step compares the surviving candidates with fine-grained reasoning. Easily confused relations get separated by deliberate contrast. The authors report gains in reliability on unseen relation types.
arxiv-2606-27186:
Cantini studies rare fluctuations in a many-species particle system using macroscopic fluctuation theory. The model generalises the symmetric simple exclusion process, where particles swap places on a line at unit rate. Several species, possibly including vacancies, move together here. Keeping all coarse-grained densities, even redundant ones, keeps relabelling symmetry visible throughout. In 2026, current fluctuations between two regions of a general graph are the first target.

Extending an argument of Derrida and Gerschenfeld, Cantini shows the current's generating function depends on boundary data through one scalar variable alone. Saddle-point equations for the infinite line then form an integrable system of Landau-Lifshitz type. A gauge transformation rewrites them in AKNS form, opening the inverse scattering toolbox. Solving that linear problem recovers the known single-species generating function, now for any species count. Conditioned density profiles for a fixed current fluctuation come out as well.
arxiv-2606-27286:
Bazarova and colleagues compare simulation-based inference with the classic sampling workhorse for epidemic model fitting. Mechanistic disease models guide forecasting and public health decisions, but Bayesian fitting by Markov chain Monte Carlo can crawl. Their SECIR model tracks susceptible, exposed, infectious, and recovered groups through German intensive care data from 2020. Neural posterior estimation, that route, learns posteriors from simulated runs instead. During 2026, short windows and a long multi-wave rebuild are both tested.

Across month-long windows, the neural route recovers posteriors in strong agreement with the sampler and reproduces intensive care trajectories well. Runtimes collapse from roughly a thousand seconds to about a minute on one graphics processor in those tests. The long reconstruction preserves the main posterior shape despite wider uncertainty, again far faster. Near-real-time, repeatable fitting becomes realistic for outbreak response.
arxiv-2606-27386:
Lu and Qi propose publishing the know-how behind a paper, not just the paper. Scientific progress leans on tacit knowledge: running the code, reproducing figures, dodging failed paths. Static manuscripts capture almost none of it. Their Agentic Publication Protocol packages a paper with its code, data, environment details, and reproduction instructions in a version-controlled repository. An agent-facing instruction file defines a paper agent able to explain the work and rerun key results. The repository itself becomes the publication object, in a proposal published in 2026.

Design principles keep the format lightweight enough for ordinary research groups. Follow-up research gets direct machine support instead of archaeology through appendices. The authors close with a broader discussion of research in the agent era. Publication shifts from frozen PDF to living, operable artefact. Reproducibility becomes a feature of the object, not a hope about it.
arxiv-2606-27486:
Nazé defines a quantity called counterwork for driven systems and shows that Jarzynski's equality, the exact work relation for driven systems, governs it directly. An imposed driving protocol first passes through an active memory filter that inverts its sign. The counterwork is simply the ordinary work computed along that flipped drive. When the filter makes the new drive swap the original's endpoints, the free-energy difference flips sign too. Their exponential averages are then exact inverses in this paper from 2026.

A kernel choice realising the reversed displacement is derived. Jensen's inequality bounds their product by one, forcing their sum to stay at zero or above. Negative average counterwork is therefore possible only when the original operation's average work compensates. Under incomplete information, the robust move is enforcing endpoint reversal while keeping dissipation low. Work relations gain a mirrored twin.
arxiv-2606-27786:
Retrieval-augmented generation grounds chatbots in external documents. Trouble starts when retrieved text conflicts with what the model already knows. Editing knowledge neurons is one fix, but those neurons are entangled with general skills. Side effects can damage the model's broader abilities. Ruochang Li and seven colleagues propose Shift in 2026 to avoid direct editing. Shift turns neuron modification into learnable gate modulation.

A lightweight gate module is added to the model. Fewer than a hundredth of a percent of parameters are trainable. The backbone stays frozen. During generation, the gate adjusts internal activations. The model can then lean on context or on memory as each case demands. Experiments ran on six datasets against various competing baselines. Shift proved effective across them. The authors present gate modulation as a safer route to knowledge arbitration. It resolves conflicts while leaving the underlying model untouched.
arxiv-2606-27886:
Wearable sensors can recognise human activities automatically. Combining several sensor types usually beats using one. How the streams are fused matters a great deal, though.
