Severin and colleagues built an RNA sequencing atlas of soybean gene activity across fourteen tissues in a 2010 study. Sequencing can measure gene messages over a huge range, and expression patterns hint at what unknown genes do.

Tissue profiles grouped into three families: above ground, below ground, and seed. Longer genes tended to show higher measured expression, a bias worth noting. Seed and root nodule tissues displayed dramatic specialisation, including many legume-only genes. Over two thousand seed-favouring genes were profiled. They pointed to more than a hundred and fifty candidates for the seed-filling process that drives yield.
europmc-pmc3104486:
John Malone and Brian Oliver wrote a 2011 opinion piece in BMC Biology comparing two ways to read which genes are active in a cell. Chip-based tools first made such broad reading possible, while newer direct sequencing of RNA promised finer detail. The authors ask whether older chip work must all be redone.

Sequencing wins, they argue, for tasks such as spotting gene variants used on one side only and finding where RNA pieces join. Chips, though, still measure gene activity levels well and rest on a huge body of past data. Their verdict is that the two methods support each other, so labs can keep trusting sound chip results while gaining new detail.
europmc-pmc3168486:
Yohei Miyagi and colleagues profiled amino acids in blood plasma as an early cancer signal in a 2011 paper in PLoS ONE. Amino acid patterns link every organ system and shift with disease, making them promising screening material from a single blood draw. The team compared about two hundred patients across five cancers with matched healthy controls.

Each cancer, lung, stomach, bowel, breast, and prostate, showed a distinct plasma amino acid pattern, detectable even in symptom-free early-stage cases. Combined statistical models separated patients from controls with solid accuracy for every cancer type, regardless of stage. The authors caution that the case-control design needs follow-up in large forward-looking cohorts before screening use. If confirmed, one blood sample could flag several cancers at once with little burden on the patient.
europmc-pmc3170586:
Paula Goines and colleagues measured immune signals in stored pregnancy blood from mothers whose children later received developmental diagnoses in a 2011 paper in Molecular Autism. Immune oddities are common in autistic people and their families, but whether the mother's pregnancy immune state relates to risk was unknown. Samples came from the middle weeks of pregnancy, years before diagnosis.

Three signals ran high in mothers of autistic children, a profile tied to roughly half again higher odds of autism, regardless of onset type or intellectual disability. A different trio of raised signals marked mothers of children with developmental delay but not autism. The split profiles suggest distinct prenatal immune patterns for distinct outcomes, worth tracing for their effects on the developing brain.
europmc-pmc3238286:
Jun Dong and Steve Horvath laid out a mathematical framework for understanding network concepts in biological modules, in this 2007 paper in BMC Systems Biology. Networks are used everywhere in genetics, from protein interactions to gene co-expression, and graph theory offers dozens of summary measures. The authors asked how those measures relate to one another inside tightly knit modules.

They focus on networks whose connection strengths can be split into per-node contributions, a property they call approximate factorizability. In such networks, simple formulas connect measures that look unrelated, such as clustering, density, and topological overlap, and most measures can be approximated from plain connectivity. Tests on protein-interaction data, co-expression data, and simulations confirmed many module networks behave this way. Free R code accompanies the paper.
europmc-pmc3334586:
Mungall, Torniai, Gkoutos, Lewis, and Haendel introduced a shared dictionary of anatomy spanning many species, in a 2012 paper. Databases for each organism describe body parts in their own vocabulary, which traps information in separate silos. A search for genes active in the lung of a mouse cannot easily reach the matching human or fish data.

Their system, named Uberon, holds more than sixty five hundred entries for anatomical structures, described in species neutral terms. Each entry links out to the species specific dictionaries already in use, so data can flow across them. The system also records how structures vary between groups of animals. The authors report it has already become essential for analyses that compare traits and disease signs across species, a core task in turning animal research into human medicine.
europmc-pmc3459986:
Shpargel, Sengoku, Yokoyama, and Magnuson used mutant mice in 2012 to show that two related proteins can guide development without their famous enzyme activity. UTX and its Y-chromosome twin UTY belong to a family that removes methyl tags from a histone, loosening genes. Test-tube work suggested UTY had lost that cutting power entirely.

Female embryos missing both copies of Utx died mid-pregnancy with brain, yolk sac, and heart defects. Males missing Utx but keeping Uty mostly survived, just smaller, while males missing both matched the females' fate. Mouse UTY indeed showed no tag-cutting in the body, yet it covered for its twin. The pair must steer genes by another route, and the cutting itself is not essential for embryos to live.
europmc-pmc3488186:
First period and last period frame a woman's reproductive years, and the Collaborative Group on Hormonal Factors in Breast Cancer measures how their timing shifts breast cancer risk. Their 2012 meta-analysis pools individual data from 117 studies in 35 countries: 118,964 women with invasive breast cancer and 306,091 without, none using menopausal hormone therapy.

Risk rises by a factor of 1.050 for each year younger at menarche. It rises independently by 1.029 for each year older at menopause. Premenopausal women face higher risk than postmenopausal women of the same age. The links weaken for some tumor types and strengthen with certain features the authors detail. Few single studies could size these effects this precisely.
europmc-pmc3533686:
Nanoparticles promise gains in drug delivery and imaging, and Lara Yildirimer, Nguyen T. K. Thanh, Marilena Loizidou, and Alexander M. Seifalian review their toxic side in 2011. A particle's huge surface for its size changes how it acts in the body, compared with the same material in bulk.

Harm hinges on size, shape, surface traits and charge, on dose, and on the route of entry; the host's immune state matters too. Results from cell cultures carry poorly to living animals, a recurring frustration. The field still lacks one shared protocol for profiling particle toxicity. The review sorts what is known about how harm arises and calls for shared standards before clinic use widens.
europmc-pmc3580286:
Alex Carisey and colleagues dissected how cells grip their surroundings in Current Biology in 2013. Cells anchor through focal adhesions, clusters where receptor proteins cross the membrane and link to the cell's actin skeleton inside. A protein called vinculin sits in these clusters and was suspected of managing their assembly, but how it coordinates the other parts, and how force feeds into that control, was unclear.

Working with altered forms of vinculin, the group showed its link to the talin-integrin chain drives other core parts in and out of the adhesion. Vinculin's own arrival depends on the cell's internal pulling machinery being switched on, so force regulates the regulator. Under repeated stretching, cells needed vinculin's actin-binding tail to re-aim their polarity. The model that emerges casts vinculin as the foreman passing outside mechanical news to the inside skeleton.
europmc-pmc3647286:
Burning away faulty heart circuits gives lasting relief for some patients, Ganesan and eight colleagues find in a 2013 systematic review and meta-analysis in the Journal of the American Heart Association. The treatment, catheter ablation, had become standard care for atrial fibrillation with symptoms in the decade before. Yet proof on results three or more years out was scarce when the team began its search of four data banks.

Nineteen studies with 6,167 patients gave the long view. One round of the treatment left 53.1 percent free of faulty rhythms years later, more in the burst kind of the condition than in the steady kind. With repeat rounds, the share rose to 79.8 percent, at an average of 1.51 rounds per patient. Results swung widely between studies, so the authors frame the treatment as strong but often needing a second pass.
europmc-pmc3652786:
Fungi that eat plant walls carry very unlike toolkits, Zhao, Liu, Wang and Xu find in a 2013 BMC Genomics study. The tools are enzymes that cut plant sugars, and their mix hints at how each fungus lives. The team sorted these enzymes across the predicted protein sets of 103 fungi from four major groups, hunting five enzyme classes in each set.

Great spread showed up in both count and kind. A few enzyme families appear in every fungus checked, and some fungi hold cellulose cutters though never known to digest cellulose. Plant-attacking fungi held the most tools overall. Fungi that feed on living hosts held fewer than those that kill tissue first, and fungi attacking broad-leaf plants held more pectin cutters than grass attackers. In the wheat scab fungus, most wall-cutting genes switched on during infection.
europmc-pmc3688486:
Shu and colleagues traced how the plant regulator ABI4 keeps Arabidopsis seeds dormant. Dormancy is set by a balance between two hormones: abscisic acid, which holds germination back, and gibberellin, which promotes it. Seeds lacking ABI4 held less abscisic acid and more gibberellin, and they germinated sooner after short storage.

The team showed that ABI4 switches on genes that build abscisic acid while directly repressing two genes, CYP707A1 and CYP707A2, that break the hormone down. ABI4 also feeds into gibberellin production genes. The work places one transcription factor at the centre of the hormone balance that decides when a dry seed stays asleep.
europmc-pmc3692086:
Heo, Park, and Seok present GalaxyRefine, a web server that improves the accuracy of predicted protein structures. Models built from templates inherit template errors, and refinement tries to push a model closer to the true structure than its template allows.

The method first rebuilds the side chains of the protein, repacks them, and then relaxes the whole structure with molecular dynamics simulation. In the CASP10 blind assessment the approach performed best at improving local structure quality, and it improved global quality on average for models from leading prediction servers. The server is free for anyone refining template-based models. Better refined models matter because experiments are often planned around the details of a predicted shape.
europmc-pmc3730086:
George Koob wrote a theory paper in Frontiers in Psychiatry in 2013 that frames addiction as a reward deficit and stress surfeit disorder. He describes addiction as a three-stage cycle: binge and intoxication, withdrawal with negative feelings, and preoccupation with getting more. Each turn of the cycle shifts the brain's reward and stress systems further from normal.

As reward function falls, the brain's stress systems switch on and drive drug seeking through relief of bad feelings rather than pleasure. Key players include a stress factor called CRF and the dynorphin opioid system, active in areas tied to emotion and control. Blocking those systems reduced compulsive-like drug taking in animal work. A calming signal, neuropeptide Y, had a similar effect for alcohol, which Koob reads as support for the model.
europmc-pmc3735986:
Lucina Uddin, Kaustubh Supekar, and Vinod Menon wrote a review in Frontiers in Human Neuroscience in 2013 on brain connectivity in autism. Researchers agree that autism involves altered links between brain systems, but studies clash: some find weaker links, others stronger ones. The authors propose that development explains much of the clash.

Looking across brain imaging studies of children, teens, and adults, a pattern emerges. In teens and adults with autism, the resting links between brain systems are usually weaker than in peers. In younger children with autism, the links look stronger instead. The authors argue that future work should record age and puberty stage with care. Doing so may settle the conflict and give a fuller picture of the autism brain.
europmc-pmc3755386:
Thomas Kean, Paul Lin, Arnold Caplan, and James Dennis wrote a review in Stem Cells International in 2013 on delivering mesenchymal stem cells, or MSCs. These adult stem cells are being tested for many diseases, helped by their ability to change into tissues such as bone and cartilage and to calm immune responses. A weak point is engraftment: few delivered cells settle, and only briefly.

The review argues that delivery should be tailored to the lesion and to how the cells act, locally or body-wide. Injecting into an artery beats injecting into a vein, since it avoids cells getting trapped in the lungs on first pass. New targeting methods alter the cell surface by chemical, genetic, or coating tricks to steer cells to set organs. Better targeting should raise efficacy and lower the dose needed.
europmc-pmc3853586:
Michael K. Skinner, Mohan Manikkam, Rebecca Tracey, Carlos Guerrero-Bosagna, Muksitul Haque, and Eric E. Nilsson report a rat study in BMC Medicine in 2013. The pesticide DDT was sprayed on pregnant rats for a short span. The team ask whether effects skip to great-grand-offspring who were never exposed at all.

Directly exposed offspring did not grow obese, though they did show kidney, prostate, and ovary disease as adults. The third generation told a new story. Over half of those rats, male and female, grew obese, along with other linked diseases. Sperm from that generation bore chemical marks on DNA that differ from controls. The work adds DDT to the list of exposures whose harm may pass down by marks on genes, not gene changes.
europmc-pmc3878786:
Harald Breivik, Elon Eisenberg, and Tony O'Brien make a policy case on chronic pain in BMC Public Health in 2013. Long-lasting pain is common across Europe and is widely under-treated. Its costs to people, employers, and health systems rival those of top health priorities, the authors argue from fresh data.

Poor training and scarce team-based pain services block good care in much of Europe. Confusion over opioid drugs, between sound medical use and misuse risk, also warps access by country. Since lost work drives much of the cost, care should aim at full rehab, not pain relief alone. The paper calls on European planners to rank chronic pain with other set priorities and to fund training and services to match.
europmc-pmc3897386:
Aaron E. Darling and a team of co-authors present a phylogeny pipeline in PeerJ, with the record dated 2014. Metagenomic sequencing reads DNA from whole microbe communities, most of which cannot be grown in a lab. Placing those reads on the tree of life can reveal who is there and what they do.

Their open pipeline, PhyloSift, chains known tools to place protein and RNA reads on family trees. It can test, in a formal way, whether a given organism is present in a sample. It can compare community make-up across many samples and link organism levels to sample traits such as place or disease state. It also measures the family diversity of a community. The package turns raw community DNA into evolutionary insight.
europmc-pmc3913786:
Janne Marieke Veerbeek and colleagues take stock of physical therapy after stroke in PLoS ONE in 2014, updating the trial evidence in one large review and meta-analysis. Their search found 467 randomized trials covering 25,373 patients and 53 distinct therapy approaches. Outcomes were sorted by the international framework for function and disability, and trials were checked for bias.

Strong evidence backed thirteen interventions for walking, eleven for arm and hand activity, one for daily-life tasks, and three for fitness. More practice at higher doses worked better, and intensive, repetitive, task-focused training helped in every phase after stroke. Gains mostly stayed within the exact skills trained. The authors close with priorities for the next round of stroke rehabilitation research.
europmc-pmc3916286:
Metodi Dimitrov Metodiev, Henrik Spåhr, and seven colleagues report in PLoS Genetics in 2014 that one mitochondrial protein does two jobs needed to build the cell's protein-making machines. The protein, NSUN4, works with a partner called MTERF4 inside mitochondria, the cell parts that make most of the cell's energy. Building mitochondrial ribosomes requires both small and large subunits to mature in step.

In mice lacking the gene, mitochondrial protein production stopped entirely. The team showed that NSUN4 adds a chemical mark to one spot on the small subunit's RNA, and that it does this alone. The NSUN4-MTERF4 pair is instead needed to join the two subunits into a working whole. The protein thus acts as a final quality check, letting only mature subunits assemble.
europmc-pmc3938686:
Eiko I. Fried and Randolph M. Nesse show that depression symptoms do not weigh alike. Their paper appeared in PLoS ONE in 2014. Standard scales add all symptoms into one score. That habit assumes each symptom counts the same. The team tested that idea with real patient data. They used 3,703 depressed outpatients from the STAR*D study. Each patient rated 14 symptoms. Each also rated how much depression impaired daily life. The domains were work, home tasks, social life, private acts, and close ties.

Symptoms differed sharply in their links to impairment. Sad mood alone explained about a fifth of the gaps. Sleeping too much explained less than one percent. Symptoms also hit domains with unequal force. The authors argue that one lump score hides useful facts. Clinicians gain from knowing which symptoms disable a patient most.
europmc-pmc3994286:
Witold Lasek, Radosław Zagożdżon, and Marek Jakobisiak weigh an immune signal called interleukin 12 as a cancer treatment, in Cancer Immunology, Immunotherapy in 2014. The signal links the innate and adaptive arms of the immune system. It wakes natural killer cells and killer T cells, and drives output of a second signal that fights tumours.

In animal tests the effects looked strong. Early human trials, though, gave weak gains and harsh side effects, which cooled hope for the drug. The review covers a fresh round of approaches now in trials. These use the signal as a boost for cancer vaccines, deliver its gene by shots into or near tumours, or fuse it to antibodies that home to tumours. Whether this second wave helps a select group of patients should soon become clear.
europmc-pmc4022086:
Bradly Shrum and six co-authors build a scoring system for sepsis in mice, in BMC Research Notes in 2014. Sepsis is a body-wide reaction to infection that can end in shock and death. Mouse studies of sepsis lacked a shared score for illness severity. Death as the sole endpoint also raises ethical concerns.

Their score rates seven visible signs. Sepsis was caused by injecting a filtered gut-content mix into the belly. At a set dose, three quarters of mice died within a day. The score forecast decline and death with strong accuracy, held together well as a scale, and agreed closely between raters. A low set score flagged coming shock and death with no false calls. Blood tests confirmed liver strain and a body-wide inflammatory surge that tracked the score. The score offers a shared yardstick and a humane early endpoint.
europmc-pmc4086086:
Tessa G. Montague, José M. Cruz, James A. Gagnon, George M. Church, and Eivind Valen built CHOPCHOP, a website that speeds up design of genome editing experiments. Their paper appeared in Nucleic Acids Research in 2014. Two editing methods, CRISPR/Cas9 and TALEN, had made mutant organisms far easier to create, but picking good target sites remained a slow step.

CHOPCHOP accepts gene names, genome regions, or pasted sequences. Fast alignment methods keep search times short, and off-target binding is predicted rigorously for both guide RNAs and TALENs. Results appear as an interactive picture of the gene, with candidate sites placed along it and colour-coded by quality. Each site also shows restriction sites and primer candidates, streamlining mutant making and checking.
europmc-pmc4095986:
Liara Rizzi, Idiane Rosset, and Matheus Roriz-Cruz reviewed the worldwide pattern of dementia, focusing on Alzheimer's and vascular types. Their review appeared in BioMed Research International in 2014. Reported prevalence varies sharply by region, partly because studies use different methods and populations differ in age.

Even after allowing for those biases, real regional gaps remain. Latin America shows higher prevalence than its age profile predicts, a pattern the authors tie to low average schooling and high vascular risk. Japan appears to show the lowest rates among developed countries, while migration studies suggest lifestyle shifts change the mix of dementia types. Case numbers in the Middle East and Africa will be large by 2040. Tackling schooling and vascular risks, they argue, is central.
europmc-pmc4120086:
Kevin Vanneste, Guy Baele, Steven Maere, and Yves Van de Peer retested the claim that plant genome duplications cluster around the extinction event that killed the dinosaurs. Their analysis appeared in Genome Research in 2014. Whole-genome duplications have been cast both as evolutionary dead ends and as roads to success.

Combining thirty-eight full plant genomes and three transcriptome sets, the team dated duplications inside a Bayesian framework that allows loose molecular clocks and fossil uncertainty. Twenty independent ancient duplications were placed, and the pattern over time was strongly non-random. Many fall near the Cretaceous-Paleogene boundary of about sixty-six million years ago. The authors suggest harsh times favour polyploid survival, echoing studies of modern invasive polyploid plants.
europmc-pmc4177586:
Aimin Li, Junying Zhang, and Zhongyin Zhou built a sorting tool called PLEK in BMC Bioinformatics in 2014. Gene sequencing runs turn up thousands of RNA messages, and researchers must tell protein-coding messages apart from long non-coding RNAs, which do other jobs in the cell. Older tools needed a reference genome or were slow.

PLEK judges each RNA by short letter patterns in its sequence and a trained classifier, with no need to line it up against a genome. On human test sets it sorted the two classes with accuracy up to 95.6 percent, and it held above 90 percent on most other vertebrate sets. It also ran about eight times faster than a rival pattern tool and far faster than the standard alignment tool, which suits species with no finished genome.
europmc-pmc4280686:
Ben G Armstrong, Antonio Gasparrini, and Aurelio Tobias present a simpler way to run case cross-over studies of air pollution and health. Their methods paper appeared in BMC Medical Research Methodology in 2014. The usual approach reshapes count data into a case control form and uses a model that cannot handle some forms of extra variation in the counts.

Their conditional Poisson model works on the counts directly and skips estimating a parameter for every time stratum, which cuts computing load. It gives the same estimates as the standard method while allowing checks for overdispersion and correlation over time. The paper gives environmental health researchers a more flexible route to the same answers.
europmc-pmc4284386:
N. Simon-Delso and a large group of co-authors trace the rise of neonicotinoid insecticides and fipronil, how they work, and what they turn into in the environment. Their review appeared in Environmental Science and Pollution Research in 2015. Since the late 1980s these systemic products spread to crops, animal care, and even fish farming, taking about a third of the world insecticide market.

The review explains their chemistry, their action on insect nerves, and the breakdown products they leave behind, some of which are also toxic. It covers why they first succeeded: no resistance in pests, flexible use, and movement through the whole plant. The paper forms the opening account of a series assessing these insecticides' wider effects.
europmc-pmc4302686:
Hirohisa Katagiri and eight co-authors updated a scoring system that predicts survival for patients whose cancer has spread to bone. Their study appeared in Cancer Medicine in 2014. The earlier 2005 score guided treatment choices, and the update adds lab test results as a factor and tests the system on a fresh group of patients.

Just over eight hundred patients treated between 2005 and 2008 were tracked, most without surgery. Six factors predicted survival: the original cancer type, spread to organs or brain, abnormal lab values, poor physical condition, prior chemotherapy, and multiple bone sites. The revised score helps doctors match treatment intensity, from surgery to comfort care, to a patient's likely course.
europmc-pmc4334486:
Fernanda Palhano-Fontes and eight co-authors scanned the brains of experienced ayahuasca users during the psychedelic state. Their study appeared in PLoS ONE in 2015. Ayahuasca, a traditional Amazonian brew, brings strong introspection, and self focused thought at rest is linked to a brain system called the default mode network.

Ten seasoned users underwent brain imaging after drinking the brew. Activity fell in key hubs of the default mode network, and its internal coupling weakened, while links to task focused networks changed as well. The pattern fits reports of loosened self focus under psychedelics. The authors discuss what the network shifts may mean for the brew's reported effects on mood and for research into depression treatment.
europmc-pmc4343186:
Matthew J. Rogatzki, Brian S. Ferguson, Matthew L. Goodwin, and L. Bruce Gladden argue that lactate is always the end product of glycolysis, the cell's sugar burning pathway. Their article appeared in Frontiers in Neuroscience in 2015. Textbooks long split the outcome by oxygen: pyruvate when oxygen suffices, lactate when it does not, with lactate cast as a waste product of hard exercise.

The authors rest on the chemistry of the lactate dehydrogenase reaction, which runs near balance and at high capacity, so carbon flows to lactate regardless of oxygen. Whether lactate piles up depends on production, burning, and transport rates. They revive a shuttle model in which lactate carries fuel from cytosol to mitochondria. The claim reframes lactate as a central fuel, not a dead end.
europmc-pmc4382686:
Daisuke Asanuma and co-authors built a glowing probe for tiny cancer spread, in Nature Communications in 2015. The target was ovarian cancer spread across the belly lining. Such spread is hard to spot when deposits are small, and ovarian cancer is often found only at that stage. The team targeted an enzyme, beta-galactosidase, which ovarian cancers make in excess. Older probes were too dim or could not enter cells. So they built a membrane-crossing probe with a switch that stays dark until the enzyme cuts it.

Once cut, the probe glows more than 1,400 times brighter. It lit up enzyme activity in several ovarian cancer cell lines. In mice with human ovarian tumors spread in the belly, it revealed deposits under a millimeter wide. The glow was bright enough to see in real time with the naked eye, and through an endoscope as well.
europmc-pmc4383486:
Birk Diedenhofen and Jochen Musch introduced cocor, a free tool for comparing correlations, in PLoS ONE in 2015. Researchers often need to know whether one correlation is truly stronger than another, for example before and after a treatment. That judgment needs a direct statistical test, yet many popular statistics packages lack one. The cocor package fills the gap inside the R computing environment.

It covers comparisons of independent correlations and of dependent ones, whether the two share a variable or not. It also computes a recommended confidence interval for every comparison type. Two friendly front ends, a plugin for the RKWard interface and a web page, make it usable without coding. The platform-independent package is scriptable for larger projects. Proper comparison tests help stop a common error: calling two correlations different when the gap is noise.
europmc-pmc4425186:
Margherita Cantorna, Lindsay Snyder, Yang-Ding Lin, and Linlin Yang reviewed vitamin D and T cells in Nutrients in 2015 and added new data of their own. Vitamin D, made in skin or taken in food, shapes immune cells both directly and through other cells. The active form is written in the article as 1,25(OH)2D.

In mice and humans, that form slows T cell growth. It lowers two inflammatory signals, IL-17 and IFN-gamma. It also raises calmer signals such as IL-4 and IL-10 and favors regulatory T cells. Effects appear late, after cells have been active for two to three days and have built the vitamin D receptor. The pattern, the authors argue, fits diseases such as bowel inflammation and multiple sclerosis.
europmc-pmc4471386:
Luigi Boni and seven co-authors reported their experience with fluorescence-guided keyhole surgery in Surgical Endoscopy in 2015. A dye called indocyanine green glows under near-infrared light, letting surgeons see blood flow and bile ducts through tissue in real time. The team used this imaging during more than a hundred laparoscopic operations at their centers, across several kinds of procedure.

Gallbladder removals and bowel resections made up most cases, with kidney donor operations, a kidney autotransplant, lymph node surgery for melanoma, and a few others besides. A high-definition stereoscopic camera with a scope emitting both visible and infrared light projected the glow during surgery. No problems during operations were tied to the dye in their report. The authors present the technique as a practical aid to surgical decisions, helping identify ducts, vessels, and tissue perfusion before cutting.
europmc-pmc4472786:
Luisa Carbognin and a team of co-authors pooled trials of immune checkpoint drugs in PLoS ONE in 2015 to test whether a tumor marker predicts benefit. The drugs, nivolumab, pembrolizumab, and MPDL3280A, release a brake on immune cells by blocking the PD-1 pathway. Tumors that display the partner protein PD-L1 were expected to respond better, but trial results varied.

From twenty trials in melanoma, lung cancer, and genitourinary cancers, the team extracted response rates and compared PD-L1 positive and negative tumors. Response was clearly higher when tumors expressed PD-L1, in the overall pool and in most drug, tumor, and treatment-line subgroups. Yet a sizable share of marker-negative patients also responded, so the marker enriches for benefit rather than ruling it out. The analysis supports testing PD-L1 while warning against denying treatment on its basis alone.
europmc-pmc4480686:
Weidong Li, Shakir Saud, Matthew Young, Guohong Chen, and Baojin Hua reviewed the energy sensor AMPK as a cancer target in Oncotarget in 2015. AMPK switches on when a cell runs low on energy, restoring balance by boosting energy production and cutting spending. It is already a target in metabolic syndrome and type 2 diabetes, through drugs such as metformin.

Population studies link metformin use with lower cancer rates, and lab work finds AMPK activation opposing tumor growth in several cancer types. The review gathers evidence that AMPK acts as a metabolic tumor suppressor, in part by calming inflammation and reining in the energy-hungry metabolism tumors depend on. It walks through the molecular mechanisms proposed and weighs which cancers might respond. The authors present AMPK activation as a promising strategy for both prevention and treatment, while noting how much remains unproven.
europmc-pmc4489286:
Tilmann Weber and a team of co-authors released antiSMASH 3.0 in Nucleic Acids Research in 2015, a resource for mining microbial genomes. Microbes make many valuable compounds, antibiotics, cancer drugs, insecticides, through gene clusters that encode a whole production line. Finding those clusters in a genome is a key step in discovering new compounds, and antiSMASH, launched in 2011, automates the search and analysis.

Version 3.0 integrates a probabilistic algorithm that can detect clusters of unknown types, not just known families. A new comparison module matches found clusters against more than a thousand clusters whose end products are known, helping judge novelty. At the enzyme level, the active sites of key building enzymes are now pinpointed by curated patterns, and every enzyme gene receives a functional classification number. The authors present the update as a comprehensive genome mining workbench.
europmc-pmc4521086:
Y. M. Arabi leads a twelve-author case report in Infection in 2015 on brain harm in a new virus disease. MERS, a severe lung infection caused by a coronavirus first found in Saudi Arabia in June 2012, had by then topped 941 confirmed cases worldwide with 347 deaths. The illness was known for lung failure, shock, kidney injury, and clotting faults.

Doctors at a Riyadh medical center then saw three patients whose main trouble was in the brain. They ranged from confusion to coma, with unsteady gait and weakness on one side. Brain scans showed broad, striking bright patches in white matter across several lobes. The cases are presented as the first report of nerve injury tied to this virus, widening what doctors should watch for.
europmc-pmc4536786:
Teresa A. Simon and four co-authors update the cancer risk picture in rheumatoid arthritis, in Arthritis Research & Therapy in 2015. People with this joint disease develop cancers more often than the general population. Concern grew as immune-damping drugs, including biologic therapies, came into wide use, raising the question of how much risk belongs to the disease itself.

The team searched five databases for observational studies from 2008 to 2014 that compared cancer rates in arthritis patients with the public. They computed standardized incidence ratios for cancer overall and for lymphoma, melanoma, and lung, colorectal, breast, cervical, and prostate cancers. The update sharpens which cancer sites truly run high in this patient group.
europmc-pmc4611486:
In 2015, a study measuring how the light used in super-resolution microscopy harms living cells was published by Stefan Wäldchen and colleagues. These microscopes need intense light to beat normal resolution limits, yet that light can damage the very cells under study. The team tested cell lines under varied light settings. The work appeared in Scientific Reports.

Shorter wavelengths hurt cells far more than longer ones. Blue-violet light caused fixation, membrane leaks, and skeleton damage at doses cells tolerated easily from red light. Red-emitting labels were much safer for long imaging sessions. The authors also list practical steps to cut harm, such as managing dose and temperature. Their limits and tips help microscopists design live-cell experiments that keep cells alive and behaving normally.
europmc-pmc4673186:
In 2015, a mouse study showing that two gum disease germs can push oral cancer forward was published by Adi Binder Gallimidi and colleagues. Gum disease has been linked to mouth cancer in large population studies, but proof of cause was missing for want of a good animal model. The team built a model that pairs a cancer-causing chemical with long-term mouth infection.

Infection with Porphyromonas gingivalis and Fusobacterium nucleatum sped tumour growth. The germs met mouth lining cells head-on through toll-like receptors and raised signals along the IL-6 and STAT3 path. They also made human mouth cancer cells grow faster and switch on tumour-linked molecules. The authors call this the first proof of a working role for mouth germs in this cancer.
europmc-pmc4717286:
Qian Liu, Weijun Peng, Fan Zhang, Rong Hu, Yingxue Li, and Weirong Yan measured blended learning in health training, in the Journal of Medical Internet Research in 2016. The journal's hosted text opens with an editor masthead; the review is the work of these six authors. Blended learning mixes classroom teaching with online study, and it has spread fast through health education. Whether it actually builds knowledge better than alternatives had never been pooled. The team searched seven databases through September 2014.

Fifty-six studies qualified. Against no teaching at all, blended learning showed a large knowledge gain. Against purely online or purely classroom teaching, the gain was moderate, though an adjustment for publication bias shrank it substantially. Study designs with exercises and objective tests showed bigger effects. Results varied a lot between studies. The authors conclude blended learning works, while urging care about the uneven evidence behind the average.
europmc-pmc4789586:
Adi Sagiv and eight co-authors study how worn-out cells flag themselves for removal, in Aging in 2016. Senescent cells have stopped dividing, a brake on cancer and a help in wound repair, but they linger if the immune system misses them. How they call in their own executioners was the puzzle.

Across three ways of driving cells into senescence, two surface flags, MICA and ULBP2, rose steadily. Both flags dock with the NKG2D sensor on natural killer cells, and blocking them blunted killer-cell attack on senescent cells. A DNA damage alarm starts the flags, and a growth signal path keeps them up. In mouse livers lacking the sensor, senescent scar-driving cells piled up and scarring worsened, proof the system guards tissue in life.
europmc-pmc4819786:
Juan E. Pérez-Jaramillo, Rodrigo Mendes, and Jos M. Raaijmakers review what plant breeding did to root microbes, in Plant Molecular Biology in 2016. Roots recruit soil microbes that defend them, feed them, and steady them under stress. Domestication remade crops for yield and taste and shrank their genetic variety; the review asks whether that breeding also broke the old recruitment skills.

Lines of evidence point that way, through changed root shape, changed root leaks, and farming habits that came with modern crops. Wild kin in their native soils may still carry the lost traits, in both plant and microbe. The authors propose a back-to-the-roots program: scout the wild relatives and their soils, find the traits that rebuild good partnerships, and breed them back into crops.
europmc-pmc4823286:
Ramendra Das and six co-authors review heat stress in dairy animals in Veterinary World in 2016. Heat stress sets in when hot, humid air keeps an animal from shedding the heat its body makes. Breathing quickens, the heart races, and body temperature climbs. Dairy breeds take the hit harder than meat breeds, and the heaviest milkers worst of all, since making milk itself generates heat.

The damage spreads from there. Cattle eat less, so growth slows and milk yield drops. Breeding suffers, and extreme heat can kill. A dulled immune and hormone system leaves animals open to disease they would normally shake off. With the climate warming, the authors treat heat stress as a growing threat to farm income across the tropics and beyond. They survey shade, cooling, feeding, and breeding measures that can soften the blow.
europmc-pmc4855186:
Caroline C. Bell and a large team built liver cell balls, called spheroids, in 2016 as a better lab model of the human liver. Flat liver cell cultures lose their character fast, which limits drug safety tests. The team grew primary human liver cells as tiny 3D balls in defined, serum-free fluid and checked their protein makeup in depth.

The balls matched real liver closely and kept each donor's traits. They stayed stable and working for at least five weeks. Under long dosing, they flagged liver harm from test drugs at doses seen in patients, including a drug whose harm hid in short tests. Drug makers gain a sturdier screen for liver risk.
europmc-pmc4879186:
Gail Davies and co-authors ran a genome-wide hunt in UK Biobank in 2016 for gene links to thinking skills and schooling. Up to 112,151 people took part, with tests of reasoning, memory, and reaction time, plus degree records. Thinking traits run in families, yet few gene hits had replicated before, since each gene adds a tiny push.

The scan found firm hits in 20 regions for single variants and 46 in gene-based tests, naming genes such as ATXN2, APBA1, and CADM2. Several hits matched earlier studies of cognition and schooling, and child data echoed them. Mind traits rest on many genes of small effect, and big biobanks can finally weigh them.
europmc-pmc4977686:
Derrick M. Chu and six co-authors test whether a mother's high fat diet shapes her baby's first gut microbes. Their study appeared in Genome Medicine in 2016. Mouse and primate work had shown maternal diet reshaping offspring flora, with effects lasting past birth. The team enrolled a population based human cohort of more than one hundred and sixty mothers. They sampled newborn stool and first stool, called meconium, at delivery and again by six weeks, and estimated mothers' recent diets by questionnaire.

A maternal high fat diet during pregnancy linked to clear changes in the newborn microbiome. The shifts were present at delivery and persisted at six weeks. The link held apart from the mother's own obesity. The authors say the findings bear on dietary advice in pregnancy. Rules for total calories and micronutrients are firm, they note, while guidance on fat and sugar balance stays vague.
europmc-pmc4996886:
Simon M. Rice and five co-authors review the mental health of elite athletes. Their narrative systematic review appeared in Sports Medicine in 2016. The physical toll of elite sport is well documented; the mental toll is not. The team searched six databases to May 2015 for studies of mental ill health and substance use in elite level athletes. After double screening, sixty studies qualified for the review.

Elite athletes showed broadly the same risk of common disorders, such as anxiety and depression, as the general population. Evidence on eating disorders, substance use, stress, and coping was less consistent. Only a quarter of studies were well reported or methodologically strong, and intervention research was scarce. The authors list elite specific stressors: injury, overtraining, burnout, media scrutiny, and constant performance pressure. They call for mental health care in sport to reach the standard of physical care.
europmc-pmc5127486:
Oscar Venter and eleven co-authors published updated Human Footprint maps in Scientific Data in 2016. The maps score how strongly people press on the land, combining satellite data with ground surveys. The new release gives matching maps for 1993 and 2009, the first pair built the same way so change can be tracked.

Eight pressures feed the score: built areas, population density, electric infrastructure, cropland, pasture, roads, railways, and navigable waterways, covering all land except Antarctica. A check against more than three thousand randomly sampled plots, scored by hand, agreed strongly with the maps. The authors offer the pair as a yardstick for human disturbance, useful for ecology, conservation planning, and watching environmental change.
europmc-pmc5141386:
Niancai Cheng and eleven co-authors made single-atom platinum catalysts, reporting in Nature Communications in 2016. Platinum drives the hydrogen-making reaction in water splitting better than any other material, but it is scarce and costly, and in normal catalysts only the surface atoms work.

Using atomic layer deposition, the team placed isolated platinum atoms and tiny clusters on nitrogen-doped graphene, so nearly every platinum atom sits exposed. For hydrogen production the single-atom catalyst ran up to 37 times more active than commercial platinum-on-carbon and stayed stable. X-ray and computer analyses tie the performance to the electronic state of the lone platinum atoms on the doped graphene, a route to squeezing far more work from far less platinum.
europmc-pmc5364386:
Emad Moeendarbary and co-authors measured the feel of nerve scars in rats, in Nature Communications in 2017. Harm to the brain or spinal cord leaves a glial scar, a dense patch of support cells and web proteins. The scar is thought to block nerve regrowth by chemistry and by force. Its chemistry has been probed for years, but its stiffness had barely been touched.

Using a fine probe that taps tissue at the atomic scale, the team mapped the hurt zones at two set times after injury. In sharp contrast to scars in skin and other organs, the nerve tissue grew softer, not stiffer. Softening tracked rises in two glial fiber proteins and in web parts. Since nerve growth answers to stiffness, a soft scar may mislead regrowing fibers. The find reshapes how the scar's block on repair is understood.
europmc-pmc5410086:
Hiroyuki Itabe, Tomohiro Yamaguchi, Satomi Nimura, and Naoko Sasabe review a family of proteins on lipid droplets in a 2017 paper in Lipids in Health and Disease. Lipid droplets are small fat stores inside cells, each a ball of neutral fat wrapped in a single skin studded with proteins. They are not still depots but busy sites of fat handling, and their size and protein mix differ by cell and tissue type.

The proteins in view, called perilipins, share a short repeated motif and sit on droplet skins. Proof shows all of them help form droplets and shape how droplets work, each under its own states. The review sums what each family member does in mammal cells, from fat tissue to liver, and pairs them with the enzymes that build and burn the fat they guard.
europmc-pmc5419486:
Martin and Van Belleghem present a way to track how family trees change along a genome. Their research article appeared in Genetics. Closely related groups rarely share one clean tree. Recombination and shared ancestry shuffle the pattern from place to place. With many sequences per group, the possible trees explode in number. Counting them all becomes hopeless. Their method, called topology weighting, cuts through that tangle.

Topology weighting asks a simpler question. For each stretch of genome, how much does each group-level tree contribute? Their software, Twisst, samples subtrees again and again to get the weights. The results can be plotted along the genome. Peaks and dips show where relationships shift. The authors test the method on simulated data. They also test it on real genomic data sets. They share the scripts freely online. The tool suits studies of hybrid ancestry and species history.
europmc-pmc5460586:
Topiwala and co-authors link even moderate alcohol drinking to adverse brain outcomes over 30 years. Their cohort study appeared in The BMJ. The Whitehall II cohort supplied the participants. Five hundred fifty adults entered the analysis. None was alcohol dependent at baseline. Drinking and cognition were measured repeatedly for decades. Brain MRI came at the study endpoint. Structural and functional measures were both assessed.

Higher consumption meant higher odds of hippocampal atrophy. The relationship was dose dependent throughout. Heaviest drinkers faced odds 5.8 times those of abstainers. Moderate drinkers, at 14 to 21 units weekly, still tripled their odds. The right hippocampus showed that effect clearly. Light drinking gave no protection over abstinence. Corpus callosum microstructure differed with intake too. Lexical fluency declined faster in heavier drinkers. The authors support the lowered UK guidance. They question current US limits as well.
europmc-pmc5477786:
Gerhard-Herman and co-authors present the 2016 AHA/ACC guideline on lower extremity peripheral artery disease, published in Circulation. It is a report of the American College of Cardiology and American Heart Association task force. The guideline gives graded advice for doctors who treat this circulation disorder. Each claim rests on a formal review of the evidence.

Sections cover testing with the ankle-brachial index and checks of other artery beds. Drug advice covers antiplatelet agents and statins. Further parts cover structured exercise, smoking cessation, and procedures to restore blood flow. Care for claudication, critical limb ischemia, and acute limb ischemia each get guidance. Clinicians use it as a standard reference.
europmc-pmc5489686:
Falin and co-authors report a materials study in Nature Communications on boron nitride sheets. These atom-thin sheets are strong electrical insulators with many uses. Their mechanical strength had never been fully measured, though. Graphene, a close cousin material, loses strength as layers stack up. The team tested single and few-layer boron nitride under indentation.

The sheets rank among the strongest insulating materials known, they report. Unlike graphene, their strength barely changed as thickness grew. The authors credit stronger links between the layers, which resist sliding. That stability makes the sheets attractive as reinforcements in composites. Heat resistance adds to their appeal for harsh settings.
europmc-pmc5516186:
Riva and co-authors report a gut microbe study in Environmental Microbiology on childhood obesity. Altered gut microbes are well tied to adult obesity. Far less was known about children. The team sequenced gut bacteria from 42 obese and 36 normal-weight children in Milan. Ages ran from 6 to 16.

Obese children carried more Firmicutes and fewer Bacteroidetes, they report. Their microbe networks also looked denser and more clustered. Bacteroidetes members predicted body mass better than Firmicutes did. Gut fermentation products ran higher in obese children too. The pattern hints that microbial imbalance helps drive childhood obesity.
europmc-pmc5597586:
Geirnaert and co-authors report a gut study in Scientific Reports. People with Crohn's disease have too few butyrate-making bacteria. Butyrate feeds the gut lining and keeps its barrier strong. The team tested adding such bacteria back, using a lab model of the gut.

Stool communities from ten Crohn's patients were grown in the model. Three single species and one six-species mix were added. F. prausnitzii and the mix raised butyrate output by 5 to 11 percent. They also settled well in the mucus layer. B. pullicaecorum and the mix improved barrier strength in cell tests. The work is proof of concept only. It supports building a probiotic from butyrate producers. Readers see early lab evidence, not a clinical result.
europmc-pmc5654086:
Solini and co-authors ran a pilot study of dapagliflozin in type 2 diabetes. The study appeared in Cardiovascular Diabetology. Sixteen patients took the drug for two days. Ten others took hydrochlorothiazide for comparison. The team measured vessel and kidney function. They also tracked urine output and oxidative stress.

Dapagliflozin lowered systolic blood pressure. It raised daily urine output like the comparison drug. Flow-mediated dilation improved after treatment. Aortic stiffness fell, measured by pulse wave velocity. Renal resistive index also dropped. The comparison drug showed none of these changes. Oxidative stress markers declined as well. The authors say the vessel effects came fast. They did not depend on pressure changes alone.
europmc-pmc5702186:
Nash and co-authors profile the fungal side of the healthy human gut. Their research article appeared in Microbiome. Most gut studies focus on bacteria. Fungi form a smaller, less studied part. The team used samples from the Human Microbiome Project. They sequenced 317 stool samples.

Fungal diversity proved far lower than bacterial diversity. Yeasts dominated the samples. Three genera appeared in most people. Saccharomyces, Malassezia, and Candida led the list. One yeast species appeared in nearly every sample. Variation between volunteers was high. Variation within one person was high too. Still, core species persisted across a year. The authors say ITS2 sequencing gave the sharpest view.
europmc-pmc5748586:
Kandel, Joubert, and Doty review how bacteria settle and spread inside plants. These residents, called endophytes, live in plant tissue without harming the host. They can fix nitrogen, make plant hormones, and fetch nutrients. They also help plants bear stress from drought, salt, and attack.

Getting inside is the key step, and its workings stay poorly known. The review sums up entry, growth, and spread in many plant species. It gives close attention to maize plants colonized by poplar endophytes. The authors see such natural partners as a way to raise crops with less farm impact.
europmc-pmc5793986:
Heidari and co-authors present the SAGER guidelines for reporting sex and gender in research. Such differences are often skipped in study design and reporting. That gap limits how far findings apply, for women and for men. A panel of 13 experts from nine countries built the guidelines.

The group also surveyed hundreds of editors and scientists and searched policy writing. The guidelines give a full procedure for design, analysis, results, and reading of findings. They aim mainly at authors preparing manuscripts. Editors can also use them as a check at the gate of publication.
europmc-pmc5808086:
Choukroun and Ghanaati test gentler spinning for platelet-rich fibrin. Doctors spin a patient's blood to make a healing concentrate. The fluid holds platelets, white cells, and growth factors. Standard spins may throw away much of that value.

Blood from six healthy donors was spun at forces from 710 down to 44 g. Lower force left far more platelets and white cells in the fluid. Growth factors VEGF and TGF-beta1 also rose. The lowest setting gave the richest mix. The authors name this the low speed concept. Readers get a simple tweak that could boost wound care.
europmc-pmc5813086:
Carhart-Harris and co-authors follow psilocybin therapy for hard-to-treat depression. Psilocybin is the active part of magic mushrooms. Early trials hinted at fast, strong relief. This report tracks patients for six months after dosing.

Twenty patients with severe, stubborn depression took part. Each got two oral doses, 10 and 25 milligrams, a week apart. Support staff sat with them through each session. Symptoms fell sharply within one week. Nine patients met response marks at week five. Gains held, though softer, at six months. No one sought standard drugs in the first five weeks. Readers get careful early proof, not a final verdict.
europmc-pmc5827986:
Marotz and co-authors present a cheaper way to clear human DNA from saliva samples. Shotgun sequencing reads all DNA in a sample at once. In saliva, human DNA swamps the microbial share. Most reads then miss the microbes researchers want.

The team tests three commercial kits against a new method. Their trick bursts human cells with water, then tags the loose DNA with a dye. Human reads fell from 89 percent to about 8.5 percent. The method also skewed microbe counts the least. It works on fresh and frozen spit and costs little. Readers get a practical boost for mouth microbiome work.
europmc-pmc5852086:
Møller and co-authors find stray circles of DNA crowding healthy human tissue. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Chromosomes were thought stable outside cancer cells. The team purified circular DNA from muscle and blood of 16 healthy men.

They cataloged some 100,000 distinct circles of chromosomal origin. Half carried genes or gene fragments. Most measured under 25 kilobases, small beside whole chromosomes. Signs of transcription place the circles inside nuclei. Some circles recur across men, hinting at circularization hotspots. The titin gene, a muscle giant, shed the most circles of all.
europmc-pmc5862886:
Wan and co-authors present a bright dye for imaging deep into tissue. Their article appeared in Nature Communications. The dye glows in the second near-infrared window. Light there scatters less and tissue glows less on its own. The team wrapped the dye inside a polymer shell. That kept it bright in water, which suits living tissue.

The authors used the dye to track blood flow in mouse brains. They imaged vessels through intact tissue without surgery. With fixed brain tissue, they built 3D views about 1.3 millimetres deep. Fine detail stayed under ten micrometres across. Two-colour imaging paired the dye with nanotubes to mark tumours. The work pushes fluorescence imaging toward sharper deep views.
europmc-pmc5908886:
Vallée and Lecarpentier review cross talk between two opposing cell pathways in cancer. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. One pathway is led by PPAR gamma, a nuclear receptor. The other is the canonical WNT and beta-catenin route. When one rises, the other usually falls. Both shift during inflammation and oxidative stress.

WNT signalling often rises in cancers and inflammation. PPAR gamma usually falls in those same states. Shared downstream genes then amplify the harmful cycle. Drugs that lift PPAR gamma can slow cell growth. They can also cut inflammation and new vessel growth. Readers get a map of this tangled opposition.
europmc-pmc5920286:
Kingston and co-authors project multi-morbidity in older people in England to 2035. Their study appeared in Age and Ageing. They used a simulation model fed by three large surveys. About 303,589 people aged 35 and over were modelled. The model tracked diseases, behaviours, and ageing traits over time. Prior models had looked at only one or two diseases.

Complex multi-morbidity will expand sharply, they report. The share with four or more diseases nearly doubles. Two-thirds of that group will have mental ill health. Extra years of life will be spent mostly with many diseases. Incoming older cohorts already carry more conditions. Prevention and joined-up services need a new focus.
europmc-pmc5936086:
Taylor reports his own experience with stovain anaesthesia in surgery. He read the paper to the Royal Medico-Chirurgical Society of Glasgow in November 1921. It appeared in the Glasgow Medical Journal. Stovain was given by spinal injection, in the lumbar region. Taylor used only the heavy form of the drug, mixed with glucose. Most of his cases were abdominal operations.

He had used the method in over five hundred cases. He argues that stovain blocks the afferent nerves more fully than other options. That block protects patients from surgical shock, he says. He also notes a drawback: blood pressure falls soon after injection. The paper weighs these gains and risks from first-hand practice.
europmc-pmc5993786:
Yang and co-authors review dynamic m6A decoration of the transcriptome and its roles in RNA metabolism. Their review appeared in Cell Research. N6-methyladenosine, or m6A, is the most abundant mark in messenger RNA. Writers place it, erasers remove it, and readers bind it. Together they tune almost every step of mRNA life. The review sums up current knowledge of these protein groups. Splicing control gets special emphasis throughout.

The mark also steers export, stability, and translation of messages. Isoform dosage control is a highlighted function. The authors trace how reader variety spreads these effects. Physiological processes far beyond RNA are touched as well.
europmc-pmc6004386:
Wang and co-authors review the S100A8/A9 protein pair and its role in inflammation. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. The two proteins bind calcium and usually pair together. Neutrophils and monocytes produce them in large amounts. Inside cells they sense calcium and shape cell structure. During inflammation they are released in active form. They then recruit white cells and stir cytokine release.

Levels of the pair mark many inflammatory diseases, the authors note. They can track disease course and treatment response. Blocking them eased disease in mouse models. The pair thus offers both a diagnostic and drug target.
europmc-pmc6089986:
Ng and co-authors pool evidence on blood inflammation markers in elderly depression and Alzheimer's disease. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appeared in Scientific Reports. The team searched three databases. Thirty-four studies qualified. They covered 2,609 depressed patients and 1,645 patients with Alzheimer's.

Four markers were compared against healthy controls. IL-6 and IL-1β ran higher in depression before adjustment. After a strict correction, only IL-6 stayed clearly raised. Alzheimer's cases showed a raw IL-1β rise only. It faded under the same correction. TNF-alpha and CRP showed no firm differences. Readers get a cautious verdict on inflammation blood tests in older adults.
europmc-pmc6096486:
Croll presents ISOLDE, an interactive tool for rebuilding molecular models into blurry density maps. His article appeared in Acta Crystallographica Section D. Low-resolution maps hide single atoms and whole residues. Builders must guess more, and errors creep in. Large structures make the strain worse.

ISOLDE runs live molecular dynamics as the user works. The model behaves like a physical object inside the map. That realism helps fix strained geometry by hand. Croll tests the results against known problem cases. Error rates in weak maps run far above clear ones. The write-up stresses strict checking of finished models. Readers get both a tool and a warning about weak data.
europmc-pmc6120486:
Hughes and Nibbs wrote a guide in The FEBS Journal to chemokines and their receptors. Chemokines are a large family of small proteins released by cells. They signal through receptors on the cell surface. Their best-known job is drawing cells to move, above all white blood cells.

The guide walks readers through the family and how its members pair with receptors. It explains how this signaling guides immune cells around the body. That traffic matters for defense against infection and for inflammation. Readers get a structured entry point to a system with many similar parts. The guide suits students and researchers who need the layout before the detail.
europmc-pmc6185986:
Méndez-Blanco and co-authors wrote a review in Experimental and Molecular Medicine on sorafenib resistance in liver cancer. Sorafenib is a multi-action drug and the standard first-line treatment for advanced hepatocellular carcinoma. It slows growth, cuts blood supply, and promotes tumor cell death. Long-term success is low because resistant cells emerge.

The review focuses on hypoxia-inducible factors, proteins that respond to low oxygen. By shrinking tumor vessels, sorafenib itself deepens oxygen shortage. Hypoxia programs then select cells that thrive in that setting. High HIF-1 alpha and HIF-2 alpha mark poor outlook in patients. The authors map this feedback loop and what it means for future combination treatments.
europmc-pmc6227386:
The India State-Level Disease Burden Initiative CVD Collaborators tracked heart disease across India. Heart and vessel diseases are rising in the country. Their state patterns were not well mapped. The group used Global Burden of Disease study data. The report appeared in The Lancet Global Health. It covers 1990 to 2016.

These diseases caused about 28 percent of all deaths in 2016. That share had almost doubled since 1990. Burden varied ninefold between states. Ischaemic heart disease and stroke led the toll. The group assessed major risk factors by state. High blood pressure and poor diet featured strongly. The authors stress that national averages hide state gaps. Policy must fit each state's stage of transition.
europmc-pmc6309586:
Sherman and co-authors build a pan-genome for people of African descent. Their study appeared in Nature Genetics. They deeply sequenced 910 individuals. Reads that failed to match the standard reference genome were kept. Those reads were assembled into new DNA stretches. The goal was DNA present in African populations but missing from the reference.

They found about 296 million base pairs of new sequence. It sat in 125,715 distinct stretches. That is roughly 10 percent more DNA than the reference holds. Some new stretches fall inside known protein-coding genes. Most lie between genes, with unknown roles. The work shows how one reference misses whole populations.
europmc-pmc6323986:
Szklarczyk and co-authors announce STRING version 11, a network of protein links. Their update appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Proteins work through webs of physical and functional ties. No single source holds all of that knowledge. STRING gathers public interaction data and scores it. It adds computer predictions to fill the gaps.

Version 11 more than doubles species coverage, to 5,090 organisms. Users can now upload whole genome-wide datasets. The site draws a network from just the uploaded genes. It also runs enrichment tests on the full input set. It uses Gene Ontology and KEGG groupings for that task. New groupings come from text mining and network clustering too. The goal is a fuller picture of how cell machinery connects.
europmc-pmc6324086:
Bao and co-authors present LncRNADisease 2.0, a database of non-coding RNA disease links. The article appeared in Nucleic Acids Research. Long non-coding RNAs misbehave in many diseases. The first release of this database came in 2013. It gathered links backed by experiments. This update expands those links over forty-fold.

The database now holds more than 200,000 associations. Each link carries a confidence score. Regulatory ties among lncRNAs, mRNAs, and miRNAs were added. Circular RNA disease links joined the collection too. Those RNAs form closed loops in cells. The authors expect clinical uses to grow from these data. The resource is freely available online.
europmc-pmc6330386:
Simon and co-authors introduce a special series on host and microbe partnerships. Their preface appeared in Microbiome. The holobiont concept treats a host plus its microbes as one unit. Microbes live on and in nearly every large organism. They shape health, ecology, and evolution. The series gathers work across many kinds of hosts.

The covered hosts range from humans to sponges. Plants and insects feature as well. Some papers use the holobiont idea directly. Others test it or debate its limits. The authors name open problems of theory and method. They propose paths for the field to take next. Health, food production, and ecosystem care all stand to gain. The piece frames why single-organism views now fall short.
europmc-pmc6342986:
Liu and co-authors compare gut microbes in Chinese children with autism. Their study appeared in Scientific Reports. Autism affects social skills, speech, and behavior. Many autistic children also have gut symptoms. Gut microbes and their products may play a role. The team studied autistic and typically developing children.

Stool bacteria were read through a marker gene. Short-chain fatty acids were measured in the same samples. Gut symptoms were scored for each child. Both microbe makeup and fatty acid levels differed. The shifts linked to each other in the analysis. They also linked to gut symptom patterns. The authors say the gut may feed into autism biology. They call for larger studies to test that idea.
europmc-pmc6384686:
Narayanaswamy and Torchilin review hydrogels for drug delivery in Molecules. Hydrogels are water-rich gels, about ninety percent water, with a porous build. They can hold drugs and release them slowly at a target site.

Normal drug dosing can poison the whole body and needs repeat doses. A gel placed at the right spot can protect fragile drugs from breakdown. The authors explain how gel traits can be tuned for control. They also note wider uses, from wound dressings to contact lenses. Worked examples show gels aimed at tumors and other sites.
europmc-pmc6394586:
Hull and co-authors present a questionnaire study in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders. Many autistic adults camouflage their traits in social settings. No self-report measure of that behavior existed, so the team built one from autistic adults' own accounts.

The Camouflaging Autistic Traits Questionnaire has twenty-five items in three groups. It was tested in 354 autistic and 478 non-autistic adults online. Scores were steady over time and matched related measures well. The same structure held across gender and diagnosis groups. Clinicians and researchers can now measure camouflaging rather than guess at it.
europmc-pmc6404286:
Nissen and co-authors review collagens and cancer stroma in the Journal of Experimental and Clinical Cancer Research. A tumor's support tissue, the stroma, changes as cancer grows. Collagens are the main building proteins in that tissue.

Much past work focused on the thin membrane tumors break through. Less was known about collagens deeper in the stroma. The review covers fibrillar collagens and the fibroblast cells that remake them. Those cells, tied to the cancer, reshape the scaffold in ways that help tumors. Targeting that scaffold is a growing idea in cancer care.
europmc-pmc6424886:
Koutsimani and co-authors pool published studies to measure how strongly burnout relates to depression and to anxiety. Burnout involves emotional exhaustion, cynicism, and a drop in felt accomplishment, usually tied to work stress. Experts had argued for years over whether it simply restates depression under another name.

Searching four databases for work from January 2007 to August 2018, the group found a solid link with depression (r = 0.520) and a weaker one with anxiety (r = 0.460). Studies using the standard burnout inventory, and higher-quality studies, showed smaller effects. Overlap fell short of sameness, so the authors treat the three as separate conditions that often travel together.
europmc-pmc6433686:
Fang and co-authors review the two-way relationship between sleep disturbance and depression, and what it means for treatment. Poor sleep was once treated as a side effect that would fade once mood lifted. Longitudinal studies now show insomnia often comes first and predicts new or returning depression at every adult age.

Mechanisms linking the two run through shared brain circuits and stress systems. Treatment sections cover hypnotics and antidepressants alongside non-drug approaches, timed before, during, and after a depressive episode. Treating sleep directly may improve outcomes and lower relapse risk, since lingering insomnia is the most common leftover symptom. The review urges psychiatrists to manage both conditions together.
europmc-pmc6453886:
Zou and co-authors find that clear-cell carcinomas, aggressive cancers of kidney and ovary stuffed with lipid and glycogen, share a hidden weakness: dependence on the enzyme GPX4, whose loss triggers ferroptosis. These tumors resist a broad range of standard therapies, so a state-based vulnerability matters. CRISPR screening and lipid profiling traced the cause.

The hypoxia pathway drives the sensitivity. In kidney tumors, HIF-2α switches on HILPDA, which enriches polyunsaturated lipids, exactly the fuel that lipid peroxidation burns during ferroptosis. Blocking GPX4 with small molecules exploited the state across lineages and genetic backgrounds. Morphology plus metabolism, the authors argue, can reveal drug targets that genetics alone misses.
europmc-pmc6466186:
Fan and co-authors catalog bat coronaviruses in China and assess where the next outbreak strain could come from. Three bat-origin coronaviruses caused major outbreaks in two decades: SARS in 2003, MERS in 2012, and swine acute diarrhea syndrome in 2017, two of them starting in China. That record makes surveillance an early-warning priority.

Known viral diversity, host bat species, and geographic spread are compiled province by province, with southern Yunnan repeatedly rich and the north barely sampled. Many circulating bat viruses remain unclassified. The authors use the map to predict hotspots and cross-species transmission potential, arguing that finding the viruses first is cheaper than meeting them in an outbreak.
europmc-pmc6467886:
Dirkse and co-authors challenge the cancer stem cell hierarchy in glioblastoma, showing that marker-defined stem-like cells are a reversible state rather than a fixed elite. The standard model puts stem cells at the top, generating all other tumor cells. Tracking cells over time told a different story.

Cells carrying stem-associated surface markers shared no distinct functional or transcriptomic identity, and ordinary tumor cells could adopt the state and shed it again. The microenvironment instructed these transitions, and mathematical modeling predicted the shifting proportions. Tumors whose cells reshuffled fastest regrew their diversity and gained an advantage in animals. The authors argue plasticity itself, not a stem cell caste, is the target.
europmc-pmc6521386:
Heinken and co-authors model bile acid metabolism in gut microbes. Their study appeared in Microbiome. The liver makes primary bile acids. Gut microbes then change them into secondary bile acids. That shared process links host and microbe health.

The team compared bile acid pathways across 693 gut microbial genomes. They expanded 232 curated metabolic reconstructions with new reactions. Each microbe could make at most six of 13 secondary bile acids. Pairs of microbes could make up to 12. Personal models were built from metagenomic data. Gut microbiomes of children with inflammatory bowel disease showed much lower bile acid output. Strain roles also differed from controls.
europmc-pmc6559986:
Heiland and co-authors show how astrocytes help glioblastoma hide from the immune system, writing in Nature Communications. Glioblastoma is the most lethal common brain tumor, and its surroundings are oddly cold to immunity. The team purified astrocytes from human tumor samples and profiled their gene activity against astrocytes from non-tumor brain.

Tumor astrocytes ran a distinct program marked by JAK/STAT signaling and the checkpoint molecule CD274. In a human slice model with injected tumor cells, the shift appeared only when microglia were also present. Together the two cell types flooded the area with calming signals such as TGFβ and IL10. Blocking JAK/STAT tipped the mix back toward inflammation, which marks the pathway as a possible lever for waking up anti-tumor immunity.
europmc-pmc6565686:
Park and co-authors build a human blood-brain barrier on a microfluidic chip, writing in Nature Communications. The real barrier keeps most drugs out of the brain, and animal models mimic it poorly. Their chip lines tiny channels with brain vessel cells grown from human stem cells, backed by astrocytes and pericytes — the two partner cell types that coach the barrier in life.

The trick is borrowed from development: growing the vessel cells under low oxygen, as the fetal brain does, before assembly. The resulting barrier stayed tight for at least a week, with proper junction proteins and working efflux pumps. It also ferried selected peptides and antibodies across, matching behavior seen in the body — a platform for testing brain drug delivery.
europmc-pmc6595586:
Fukuchi and co-authors review how walking speed changes gait mechanics in healthy people. Their systematic review and meta-analysis appears in Systematic Reviews. Patients often walk slower than healthy controls. That gap can distort gait comparisons in the clinic. The team searched three databases for studies across age groups. They pooled effect sizes for speed against comfortable pace.

Twenty studies covering 587 people met the criteria. Four covered children, and three covered older adults. Speed shifted nearly every measure they tracked. Step timing, joint motion, joint forces, and ground reaction forces all moved. Values fell at slow speeds and rose at fast ones. The authors warn that speed must be matched in gait studies.
europmc-pmc6636886:
Carey and co-authors map how behavior change techniques are thought to work. Their synthesis appears in Annals of Behavioral Medicine. Interventions bundle techniques such as graded tasks or goal setting. Each technique is meant to trigger a mechanism of action. No shared map of those links existed.

Two coders extracted claimed links from 277 published intervention articles. They logged 2,636 links in total. Of 77 techniques coded, 70 tied to at least one mechanism. Beliefs about capabilities and intention were the most linked mechanisms. Each technique linked to up to five mechanisms. Each mechanism linked to up to eight techniques. The authors offer the map as a base for theory-led design. They note that claimed links still need direct testing.
europmc-pmc6734286:
Abdelaal and co-authors benchmarked automatic tools that name cells in single-cell RNA data. Naming cells by hand is slow and hard to reproduce. As datasets grow, supervised classifiers promise to do the job. The team compared 22 classification methods, both general and single-cell specific.

They tested the tools on 27 public datasets of varied size, species, and complexity. Two setups measured accuracy within one dataset and across datasets. They also checked speed, unclassified cells, and sensitivity to input features. Most tools did well overall, with accuracy dropping on complex datasets. The study gives analysts a guide for picking a classifier that fits their data.
europmc-pmc6743286:
Giuranno and co-authors review radiation-induced lung injury. Radiation therapy for lung and esophageal cancer often damages the lung itself. The two main harms are pneumonitis, an early inflammation, and fibrosis, a later scarring. Injury strikes 5 to 20 percent of patients. It caps the dose doctors can give, which lowers tumor control.

Physical dose and the patient's biology both set the risk. The review traces the chain from radiation exposure to tissue damage at the molecular level. It covers treatment, body, and environment factors, including a curious pattern involving smoking history. Drugs that might prevent or curb the injury are surveyed. Preventing it would let stronger, more durable tumor treatment proceed.
europmc-pmc6755986:
Lassale and co-authors reviewed whether healthy diets protect against depression. Depression carries a huge cost for society in rich countries. Better proof on food could guide prevention. The team gathered studies that scored diet quality with set indices and tracked depressive symptoms or clinical depression in adults.

They included 20 long-term and 21 cross-sectional studies in the review. Diets scored included the Mediterranean diet and healthy eating indices. The strongest proof favored the Mediterranean diet. In four long-term studies, the group that followed it most closely had a risk of 0.67 compared with the group that followed it least. Less inflammatory diets also looked protective.
europmc-pmc6764986:
Götzke and co-authors introduce the ALFA-tag, a designed protein label for life science research. Tags help scientists detect, move, and purify proteins. Existing tags each do only part of the job well. The ALFA-tag forms a small, stable helix that works wherever it sits on a protein. It functions in both simple and complex cells.

A matching nanobody grabs ALFA-tagged proteins with extremely tight binding. It suits super-resolution microscopy, pull-downs, and blotting, and it can flag proteins in living specimens. The team solved the pair's crystal structure. That let them design a gentler nanobody that releases its catch on cue. Whole living cells can be purified in one step this way.
europmc-pmc6784786:
