Kleiner and co-authors studied what drives fibrosis progression in fatty liver disease. Nonalcoholic fatty liver disease is a leading cause of liver illness. Its aggressive form, steatohepatitis, scars the liver toward cirrhosis. The team followed 446 patients who were not on specific treatments. They asked which factors predicted scarring, and which predicted healing.

A high baseline disease activity score predicted worsening fibrosis. Changes in the score moved together with changes in scarring. Weight gain raised the risk of progression. So did a high or rising level of the liver enzyme AST. Of 86 patients with simple fatty liver, 41.9% progressed toward steatohepatitis. The results support using activity scores as trial endpoints.
europmc-pmc6784886:
Messina and co-authors map the current and future global distribution of dengue. This mosquito-borne virus has spread across the tropics in 60 years. It now threatens over half the world's population. It causes an estimated 100 million symptomatic infections and 10,000 deaths each year, in more than 125 countries. The team built the largest database of dengue locations yet.

Statistical mapping predicted where the virus could live in 2015. Climate, population, and economic projections then extended the picture to 2020, 2050, and 2080. The study is the first to fold in the spread of Aedes mosquito vectors. Expansion is likely under all climate scenarios. The maps aim to help officials prepare for shifting dengue risk.
europmc-pmc6833286:
Qin and co-authors review new immune checkpoint targets in Molecular Cancer. Checkpoint drugs block brakes on T cells so they can attack tumours. The first targets, PD-1 and CTLA-4, changed cancer care. Still, most patients gain little, because their cancers resist from the start or adapt. Fresh brakes must be found.

The review profiles candidates such as LAG-3, TIM-3, and TIGIT. Each holds T cells back in its own way. The authors sum up trial results for drugs against each one, alone and paired with PD-1 blockers. They also discuss markers that might show which patients could benefit. Combination treatment is presented as the likely way forward.
europmc-pmc6889286:
Leonetti and co-authors review resistance to a leading lung cancer drug, in the British Journal of Cancer. Osimertinib blocks the epidermal growth factor receptor in its mutated forms, including the T790M form that defeats older drugs. It works in advanced non-small cell lung cancer driven by such mutations. Every patient, though, eventually develops resistance. Clear next options are then lacking.

The review sorts resistance into changes within the target gene and detours around it. A further mutation, C797S, can lock the drug out; rarer swaps such as L718Q answer to older drugs instead. Other tumours wake side pathways or change cell type entirely. Blood tests for tumour DNA help track which route a given cancer took.
europmc-pmc6906186:
Penney and co-authors review stem cell models of Alzheimer's disease, in Molecular Psychiatry. Alzheimer's has no cure, and drug after drug that helped rodents failed in patients. Human induced pluripotent stem cells offer a different test bed. Reprogrammed from adult cells, they can become any brain cell type. Disease features can then be studied in living human neurons.

All major brain cell types can now be grown this way, and mixed cultures grow ever more complex. Using cells carrying Alzheimer's mutations, studies have tested whether the faults act by loss or gain of function; one famous mutation acted by gain. The review maps which disease traits these models reproduce, and where they still fall short.
europmc-pmc6946686:
Oh and co-authors find that a common RNA processing factor can speed or slow cancer cell movement. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. U1 snRNP is the most abundant small nuclear RNA complex in vertebrate cells. It guards gene transcripts, silencing early cut points so full-length messages get made. Cancer cells often show shortened messages.

Lowering U1 activity in lab-grown cancer cells raised their migration and invasion up to five-fold. Raising U1 levels did the reverse. The shift came with wide transcriptome changes, including altered splicing. Levels of cancer-promoting and cancer-suppressing genes moved too. The results point to a balance effect: cells need U1 amounts matched to their transcription load. That balance, the authors suggest, could become a handle for controlling aggressive cell states.
europmc-pmc6966486:
Batista-Gonzalez and co-authors review how fat metabolism steers macrophage behaviour. Their review appeared in Frontiers in Immunology. Macrophages switch roles with their fuel use. Inflammatory M1 macrophages kill pathogens and sustain attack, leaning on fast sugar burning and fat building.

Calming M2 macrophages resolve inflammation and repair tissue, burning fats instead for steady energy. Recent work has blurred that tidy picture. Fat burning also proves essential for triggering the inflammasome in M1 cells. Meanwhile, sugar burning feeds fat oxidation in M2 cells. Lipid handling sits at the centre of both states, the authors argue. Mapping the whole metabolic network during activation could let doctors tune macrophage behaviour. That, in turn, may improve outcomes in metabolic disease.
europmc-pmc6969186:
Wang and co-authors build a self-assembling nanozyme that makes its own oxygen inside tumours. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Light-based photodynamic therapy kills cancer by turning oxygen into a toxic form. Solid tumours, though, are starved of oxygen, which blunts the treatment.

Their agent packs a light-sensitive drug inside a metal-organic framework. Single ruthenium atoms stud the structure and act like the enzyme catalase. They split hydrogen peroxide, which tumours produce, into fresh oxygen on site. That relieves the oxygen shortage right where the light will strike. The particles form by self-assembly with a body-friendly polymer coat. They showed even size, high drug loading, and strong tumour killing in tests. The design, the authors say, is a versatile route to single-atom cancer therapy.
europmc-pmc6978386:
Yang and co-authors uncover a feedback loop that lets melanoma resist an iron-based death drug. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. Ferroptosis is a form of cell death driven by iron and damaged fats. The drug erastin triggers it by binding channel proteins VDAC2 and VDAC3 on mitochondria.

Cells fight back. Erastin treatment switches on a protein called Nedd4, driven by the factor FOXM1. Nedd4 tags the channels for destruction, lowering their levels and blunting the drug. Removing Nedd4 kept channels intact and made cancer cells far more sensitive to erastin. Boosting the channels had the same effect in tumours grown in mice. The loop, the authors say, frames a first plan for defeating resistance to ferroptosis drugs.
europmc-pmc7144386:
Lin, Li, and Lin review computational methods for screening and designing drugs, in Molecules. Computer methods have sharply cut the time and cost of finding new medicines. The review starts with multiscale simulations that locate drug binding sites on target proteins and reveal how drugs act.

Virtual screening techniques come next: molecular docking, pharmacophore modelling, and QSAR, which links chemical structure to activity. Structure-based and ligand-based design, including building molecules from scratch, are covered too. Machine learning methods are reviewed last, as accelerators across all the earlier steps. The authors expect progress to come from combining methods at different scales rather than from any single technique.
europmc-pmc7175086:
Caspi and co-authors follow mental health histories across four decades in a New Zealand birth cohort. Their study appeared in JAMA Network Open. The cohort holds 1,037 people born in Dunedin. Staff assessed them from age 11 to age 45. Most studies judge a patient by one diagnosis at one visit. The team asked how diagnoses change over a full life course.

The authors report that most people's disorders shifted over time. Successive episodes often fell in different disorder families. Internalizing, externalizing, and thought disorders took turns in the same lives. Age of onset, episode length, and disorder diversity described people better. No single diagnosis captured a whole history. The authors warn against building care and research around one diagnosis alone. Their results favor a broader, life-course view of mental illness.
europmc-pmc7178086:
Buratta and co-authors review how cells release material through lysosomes and related pathways. Their article appeared in the International Journal of Molecular Sciences. Lysosomes are best known for breaking down cell waste. Yet they can also fuse with the cell surface and empty their contents outside. A related route releases exosomes, tiny vesicles that carry signals between cells. Autophagy parts can also drive secretion.

The review sets out three linked routes in detail. These are lysosomal exocytosis, exosome release, and secretory autophagy. It explains how fusion choices send cargo to a lysosome or to the cell surface. That choice helps keep cells in balance under stress. When these routes fail, undigested material builds up. The authors link such faults to storage disorders, brain disease, and cancer. Readers get a map of how waste handling and cell signaling overlap.
europmc-pmc7178886:
Meng and co-authors review extracellular vesicles as drug delivery vehicles, with a focus on the cells that produce them. Their article appeared in Drug Delivery. Vesicles are tiny membrane bubbles released by most cell types. They carry proteins and genetic material between cells. Their natural origin gives them traits drug makers value.

Compared with synthetic carriers, vesicles are gentle on the body. They are stable and rarely provoke the immune system. Studies have loaded them with small RNAs, proteins, and gene-editing tools. They have also carried small-molecule drugs and nanoparticles. The source cell shapes what a vesicle can do, the authors stress. Isolation methods differ in yield and purity. The review weighs this promise against the practical hurdles.
europmc-pmc7181686:
Jew and co-authors present Bisque, a tool that estimates cell makeup from bulk gene expression data. Their study appeared in Nature Communications. A tissue sample mixes many cell types, and bulk sequencing blends their signals. Single-cell data can supply reference profiles for each type. The challenge is matching the two kinds of data despite technical differences.

Bisque learns gene-specific adjustments between single-cell and bulk profiles. Those adjustments make the estimates hold up when study methods vary. The team tested the tool on brain data, among other sets. It linked microglia share to Alzheimer's severity stages as expected. The method runs fast enough for very large datasets. Researchers studying mixed tissues gain a more reliable way to count cell types.
europmc-pmc7192386:
Jarvis and co-authors review which metabolic traits predict severe liver disease in fatty liver patients. Their analysis appeared in PLoS Medicine. Non-alcoholic fatty liver disease is a leading cause of chronic liver illness worldwide. Most people with it never develop cirrhosis or liver cancer. Spotting the minority at real risk is the clinical challenge.

The team pooled population studies on risk factors such as diabetes and high blood pressure. Evidence on blood pressure was mixed across studies. Some large linkage studies tied diagnosed hypertension to later severe liver outcomes. Others found weak or negative links after adjustment. The review shows how uneven the prediction evidence remains. Doctors get a clearer view of which patients need closer follow-up.
europmc-pmc7251286:
Liu and co-authors survey anxiety among medical workers in China during the early COVID-19 outbreak. Their cross-sectional study appeared in Epidemiology and Infection. Staff answered the Zung Self-rating Anxiety Scale between February 10 and February 20, 2020. The team looked for factors tied to higher anxiety scores.

Of 512 medical staff, the overall rate of anxiety was 12.5%, mostly mild. Workers who had direct contact treating infected patients scored higher than those who had not. Staff from Hubei province, where the outbreak began, also scored higher. The strongest link was for workers who were themselves suspected cases. Gender, age, education, and marital status were accounted for in the analysis.
europmc-pmc7258486:
Cai and co-authors investigate a cluster of COVID-19 cases tied to a shopping mall in Wenzhou, China. Their short report appeared in Emerging Infectious Diseases. Seven workers in one office on the seventh floor fell ill first. Cases then appeared among staff and shoppers on other floors. Many patients denied close contact with known cases.

The team traced contacts and tested people with PCR. They describe onset dates, floor locations and shared spaces in the mall. Possible routes include touched surfaces, virus in the air of small rooms, and spread by people without symptoms. Restrooms and elevators are noted as shared points. The report shows how hard early outbreak routes were to prove.
europmc-pmc7273686:
Ma and co-authors build a single network showing which microbes tend to appear together across the whole planet. Their study appeared in Microbiome. Microbe communities have usually been mapped one environment at a time. This team used the Earth Microbiome Project catalog, holding 23,595 samples and 12,646 exact sequence variants from 14 environments.

The resulting network split into 8 modules, each tied to particular environments such as soil or animal surfaces. Plant and animal surface communities bridged two larger groupings of environments. Certain microbes acted as hubs in most subnetworks. The share of negative links, suggesting competition, ranged from 1.9% in soil to 48.9% on non-saline surfaces. The map shows that microbe partnerships are mostly specific to their environment, not universal.
europmc-pmc7280786:
Cole measures brain age from several kinds of brain scan at once and tests what a faster-aging brain means. The study, by a solo author, appeared in Neurobiology of Aging. Brain-age models guess a person's age from scans; a brain that looks older than its years predicts worse health. Most models use only one scan type.

Using UK Biobank data, Cole modeled brain age in 2205 healthy people across six imaging types. In a held-out group of 520, the combined model predicted true age with a mean error of 3.55 years, beating any single scan type. Applied to 14,701 new people, an older-looking brain was linked to stroke history, diabetes, smoking, alcohol intake, and some thinking test scores.
europmc-pmc7315286:
Deftereos and co-authors run the GRECCO-19 randomized trial of colchicine, an old anti-inflammatory drug, in patients hospitalized with COVID-19. Their trial report appeared in JAMA Network Open. Severe COVID-19 is driven by intense inflammation, and colchicine calms inflammation without the drawbacks of steroids. The trial enrolled 105 patients.

Clinical deterioration, the primary clinical endpoint, was more common in the standard care group than in the colchicine group, and it arrived sooner. A heart injury marker, high-sensitivity troponin, did not differ between groups. However, D-dimer, a clotting marker, rose less in colchicine patients than in controls. The authors call their findings hypothesis-generating: suggestive of benefit, and a reason for bigger trials rather than a settled answer.
europmc-pmc7373986:
Rubio Gomez and Ibba review aminoacyl-tRNA synthetases in RNA, the enzymes that load transfer RNAs with the right amino acids. That loading step is where the genetic code is physically enforced, pairing each tRNA with its matching building block. The family is essential and found in every living cell.

Accuracy comes from sharp recognition of the right partners and from proofreading that rejects mistakes. Oddly, loosened quality control sometimes helps cells adapt to stress. Beyond translation, the enzymes turn up in many other cell processes, with effects on health and disease. Their versatility also makes them tools for expanding the genetic code in the lab. Readers get a portrait of ancient enzymes with modern reach.
europmc-pmc7453686:
Khalil and co-authors explore how Saudi medical students saw the sudden move to online learning in COVID-19. Schools closed, and teaching shifted at once to digital formats. The study took place at a medical college of Qassim University.

The team ran eight virtual focus groups with 60 students. Four themes came out: teaching impact, time control, problems faced, and hopes for the future. Students liked the time saved and felt their output rose. Problems covered teaching style, hard content, tech faults, and behavior in sessions and online exams. Most preclinical students wanted online learning to stay in coming years. The authors urge steady checks of the model's quality. Online classes, they say, hold real promise for medical training.
europmc-pmc7503386:
Ghemrawi and Khair review endoplasmic reticulum stress and the unfolded protein response in neurodegenerative disease. The ER checks protein quality and keeps cell balance. When unfolded proteins pile up, stress follows.

Cells answer with the unfolded protein response, run through the PERK, IRE1-alpha, and ATF6 pathways. Brief stress brings adaptation, but long stress can trigger cell death. Faults in this system appear in Alzheimer's, Parkinson's, ALS, and prion diseases. All share clumps of misfolded proteins in the brain. The review gathers current proof of response activation in these disorders. It then surveys drugs that tune the response. Such tuning may slow or prevent neuron loss in future care.
europmc-pmc7543886:
Banerjee and co-authors show how SARS-CoV-2 disrupts host cell processes. The virus blocks splicing, translation and protein trafficking. Each block helps mute host defenses against infection.

One viral protein binds splicing RNAs U1 and U2. That binding suppresses global mRNA splicing in cells. Another protein binds ribosomal RNA and halts translation. Two more proteins bind the signal recognition particle RNA. That step blocks protein flow to the cell membrane. Each disruption cuts the interferon response to infection. Together they form a multi-pronged attack on host cells. The results point to targets for future antiviral work.
europmc-pmc7662786:
Chang and co-authors review recent updates on a liver cancer treatment called TACE. TACE, or transarterial chemoembolization, is a standard option for mid-stage liver cancer. It sends chemotherapy into the tumor through an artery and blocks its blood flow.

Two forms, standard TACE and bead-based TACE, kill tumors to a like degree. The bead form risks more artery and bile duct injury but less pain after the procedure. Scores can guide when to repeat the treatment. The authors also cover pairing TACE with ablation, radiation, or drug therapy, plus new models that predict survival.
europmc-pmc7664986:
Griffiths and co-authors ask how hearing loss in midlife could lead to dementia. Studies link midlife hearing loss to about 9% of dementia cases. Hearing loss is treatable, so the link matters for public health. The authors weigh several brain routes that could connect the two.

One route is shared damage in the hearing pathway and in brain areas that serve many tasks. Another is strain: hard listening drains mental resources and leaves less in reserve. The authors add a new idea tied to the medial temporal lobe and its role in sound patterns. They note that which fix helps depends on which route is at fault.
europmc-pmc7675386:
Yanez and co-authors measure how age and sex shape COVID-19 death rates. Case reports had shown high death rates in patients aged 65 years or older. The team wanted rates for whole populations, not just for known cases. They gathered death counts from 16 countries.

Over six weeks, the countries logged 178,568 COVID-19 deaths among about 2.4 billion people. Death rates for ages 55 to 64 were 8.1 times those for younger adults. For ages 65 and older, rates were more than 62 times higher. Men died at rates 77% higher than women. The authors stress the sharp risk that comes with age.
europmc-pmc7682786:
Wilcha reviews how well virtual teaching served medical students during COVID-19. Lockdowns shut medical schools and cut clinical placements round the world. Schools rushed to move teaching online. The author searched two databases for early evidence on what worked.

The search found 201 articles, of which 34 fit the review, plus 5 from reference lists. Strengths included rich web resources and open access talks by experts. New formats let students meet patients from home, and peer mentoring gave support. Weak points included tech faults and privacy concerns. The review maps a fast shift that schools built on the fly.
europmc-pmc7703786:
Lee and co-authors adapt a leading language model for biomedical text. The model is BERT, trained on general text. Medical words differ enough from daily words that plain BERT does poorly on medical tasks. The team retrained it on large biomedical text sets to close that gap.

The result, BioBERT, shares the same design as BERT but knows medical terms. It beat prior top models on three tasks: finding medical names, linking facts, and answering questions. Gains were largest for question answering. The authors release the trained weights and code for free. They argue that domain training is the key to strong medical text mining.
europmc-pmc7732386:
Ma and co-authors test melatonin against bone loss tied to diabetes. In type 2 diabetic osteoporosis, bone-forming cells suffer under high glucose. The team found signs of ferroptosis, an iron-driven cell death, in these cells. Tests ran on cultured bone cells and on diabetic rats.

High glucose lowered key guard proteins and raised fat damage in the cells. Known blockers of ferroptosis reversed these effects. Melatonin at several doses restored the guards and bone-forming power. It acted through the Nrf2 and HO-1 signal path. Silencing Nrf2 erased the benefit. Rat bones also kept better structure on melatonin.
europmc-pmc7809486:
Tian and co-authors test a spike protein vaccine candidate, NVX-CoV2373, in baboons and mice. The vaccine uses the full SARS-CoV-2 spike protein. The protein is held in its prefusion shape. It forms particles of 27.2 nm.

In mice, low doses with the Matrix-M adjuvant raised strong antibodies. Those antibodies blocked the spike from binding its human receptor. They also neutralized the virus. Vaccinated mice resisted virus challenge with no sign of worse lung disease. T cell responses were broad and strong. In baboons, low doses were likewise highly active. Antibodies blocked binding and neutralized the virus there too. The results back the phase 1/2 human trials then under way.
europmc-pmc7846086:
LaMoia and Shulman review how metformin works inside cells and tissues. Metformin is the first-line drug for type 2 diabetes. It lowers blood sugar with a strong safety record. It is also cheap. Its main effect is to cut glucose output by the liver.

Even after decades of use, the exact route stays debated. The drug touches glucose handling in several ways. The authors sort the evidence for each claimed route. Some actions center on the liver's energy state. Others involve the gut and hormone signals. Old models are weighed against new data. The review gives a current map of a very old drug's workings.
europmc-pmc7944786:
This unsigned report describes the presentation of two volumes of essays to Sir William Osler on his seventieth birthday. The record carries no named author. A large gathering met in London on Friday July 11, 1919, for the event. The volumes honoured Osler's arrival at the age of seventy. About 150 writers from both sides of the Atlantic contributed to them.

Sir T. Clifford Allbutt chaired the meeting and made the presentation. Lady Osler attended, along with leading figures of British and Canadian medicine. Names from the Army medical services stood beside university leaders. The report lists the guests in detail, which gives it lasting value as a record. It captures a moment when the profession paused to honour its most loved teacher. Osler's standing on both sides of the Atlantic fills every line.
europmc-pmc7973386:
Amjad and co-authors present a review of NAD+, a coenzyme found in every living cell. It sits at the heart of how cells make and use energy. Levels of it fall with age and disease. That fall is tied to weak stress responses, poor DNA repair, and cell ageing. Raising its levels with precursor supplements helps in many disease models. The review gathers what is known about its roles.

Shifts in the NAD+ pool or its balance with its partner form can derail cell systems. Such shifts feed brain disorders, ageing, and tumour growth. The compound sits in different amounts in different cell parts, which clouds its direct role in people. The authors call for long studies that measure it and its kin over time. Flux through its making and breaking paths needs mapping too. The review is a guide to a molecule with wide reach.
europmc-pmc8061386:
Yang and co-authors engineer a hydrogel dressing built for wounds in hard-to-cover places. Joints and skin folds defeat ordinary gauze, which slips and needs tape. The team grafted cationic polymer brushes onto bacterial cellulose nanofibers. Those fibers were folded into a polydopamine and polyacrylamide gel. Each ingredient was chosen to fix a known weakness.

The brushes stiffen the gel while keeping it stretchable. Tensile strength reached 21–51 kPa, with stretch of 899–1047%. Charged groups on the brushes kill bacteria over long periods. They also encourage skin cells to crawl and multiply. Catechol groups make the gel stick to many surfaces without tape. In rats, dressed wounds inflamed less and closed faster. The dressing stayed put through movement. The authors see a practical answer for mobile body sites.
europmc-pmc8102486:
Ting and co-authors update the picture of infectious keratitis, a leading cause of corneal blindness. Corneal opacity ranks fifth among global causes of blindness. It affects about 6 million people worldwide. Infection drives more of that damage than any other cause. The reported incidence spans 2.5 to 799 cases per 100,000 people each year across regions. Bugs of many kinds can invade the cornea.

Bacteria and fungi cause most infections, with place and season shifting the mix. Viruses and Acanthamoeba matter more in rich countries. Contact lens wear tops the risk list in those settings. Trauma, surface disease, and eye surgery raise the odds elsewhere. Broad topical antimicrobials remain the standard first treatment. Rising drug resistance, including multidrug strains, now threatens that playbook. The review maps where resistance bites hardest. Early culture and tailored drugs grow more vital.
europmc-pmc8125386:
Zhao and co-authors review how plants sense and survive salt stress. Salt invades farmland worldwide and strangles crop growth. About 20% of the world's irrigated land already suffers salinization by the estimates they cite. Plants cannot flee bad soil as animals do. Sodium piles up to toxic levels inside their cells. Water balance collapses under the osmotic strain.

Plants answer with layered defenses, and the review sorts them. Ion transporters pump sodium out or lock it away. Osmotic pathways rebuild the cell's water economy. Hormone signals retune growth to the emergency. The cytoskeleton shifts, and cell walls remodel their mix. Most crops are salt-sensitive glycophytes, unlike tolerant halophytes. Borrowing halophyte tricks is a breeding goal. Each mechanism mapped is a trait waiting to be stacked. Salt-proof crops would feed a warming, drying world.
europmc-pmc8426186:
Elmentaite and co-authors map the cells of the human intestinal tract across place and life stage. The gut lining changes from before birth through adult life. It also varies along its length. A full cell map can explain health, growth, and disease programs.

The team used single-cell RNA sequencing on almost half a million cells. Samples came from up to 5 regions in the developing gut and 11 regions in children and adults. They found BEST4 epithelial cells all along the tract. They also describe nerve cell groups and genes tied to Hirschsprung's disease. Programs that build lymphoid tissue early in life reappear in bowel inflammation.
europmc-pmc8450986:
Aiyegbusi and co-authors review the symptoms, complications, and care of long COVID. Most people recover from COVID-19, but a large share keep having problems after the acute illness. These patients face wide physical and mental symptoms.

The most common complaints were fatigue and shortness of breath. Muscle pain, joint pain, headache, and cough also ranked high. Chest pain, changed smell and taste, and diarrhea were common too. Memory loss, poor focus, anxiety, and sleep problems filled out the picture. Many people reported worse quality of life and trouble at work. The authors call for team-based care and long-term follow-up.
europmc-pmc8597086:
van der Zanden, Qiao, and Neefjes give a fresh look at doxorubicin, an old drug still used against cancer. The drug harms both DNA and chromatin in tumor cells. Its chromatin harm drives much of the benefit. The DNA harm adds long-term risks such as heart damage and new tumors.

The review sorts the two kinds of harm and what each one causes. It covers cell death signals, histone loss, and effects on the immune response. The authors argue that new forms of the drug could keep the chromatin harm and drop the DNA harm. Early work shows such forms are possible. That path could cut side effects while keeping the drug strong.
europmc-pmc8748686:
Tsaban and co-authors harness protein folding networks to model how peptides dock onto proteins. AlphaFold2 and its peers predict protein shapes with high accuracy. They were built for single proteins, not pairs. The team asked if the same tool could model peptide-protein pairs.

Their simple use of AlphaFold2 gave quick, accurate models of such pairs. It needed no alignment data for the peptide partner. It also handled shape changes in the receptor on binding. Examples showed where the tool matched or beat a top docking protocol. The authors see it as a strong start for studying peptide interactions in detail.
europmc-pmc8811286:
Gallo, Volpe, and Savoia review endothelial dysfunction in hypertension and its clinical weight. The endothelium lines blood vessels and sets their tone. It makes nitric oxide and other relaxing factors. When it fails, vessels tighten and shift toward inflammation and clotting.

This failure helps start vessel inflammation, remodeling, and plaque buildup in hypertension. It also marks higher cardiovascular risk on its own. Triggers range from poor flow forces to oxidative stress. Vesicles released by vessel wall cells have emerged as regulators of vessel health. Some may carry drugs or gene signals to protect vessels. The review sums up current concepts for care.
europmc-pmc8958186:
Haddaway and co-authors present PRISMA2020, a free tool for drawing systematic review flow diagrams. Flow diagrams show how records shrink through a review's stages. Reporting standards ask for them, yet quality is often poor. Standard templates could lift that quality. The team built an R package and a Shiny web app. Both produce diagrams matching the PRISMA 2020 standard. No coding skill is needed for the app version.

Users can export diagrams in several formats. A first for this tool class is interactivity. Readers can click a diagram box to reach methods or data. The authors supply an interactive example to try. A case study shows the workflow in action. The tool is open source and free. The authors expect wider, better diagram use. Transparency in evidence synthesis is the goal.
europmc-pmc9004186:
Stovner, Hagen, Linde, and Steiner update the world picture of headache and test why estimates vary so much. Headache disorders rank among the most common and disabling conditions. The team gathered every population study they could find up to 2020. Clinic-based samples were shut out. In all, 357 publications fed the work. Most came from rich countries. Prevalence figures were pulled for each headache type. Methods were coded with equal care.

Active headache disorder touched 52.0% of people in the pooled estimate. Migraine alone reached 14.0% in the same pooled work. Tension-type headache and near-daily headache followed behind. Each day, a large share of the world has a headache. The numbers matched global burden figures for migraine. Method choices explained part of the spread between studies. How questions were asked mattered. So did sample size and who was sampled.
europmc-pmc9014886:
Shahan and co-authors built a single-cell atlas of the Arabidopsis root, mapping gene activity cell by cell. The root's fixed cell layers make it a clean model for tracking how identities form over time. The team charted developmental progress for each cell type and used optimal transport to infer the paths cells follow. They also named regulators that steer those paths.

To test the atlas, the team profiled mutants lacking two key regulators, shortroot and scarecrow. The scarecrow mutant showed cells switching identity, backed by live imaging. The authors offer the atlas as a shared resource for studies of plant development.
europmc-pmc9224686:
Park and co-authors discuss how breast cancer spreads to distant organs and what that means for therapy. Metastasis is the leading cause of death in most cancers. Breast cancer often is found only after it has spread. Spread cells gain aggressive traits from the tumor microenvironment.

Two mechanisms get close attention: epithelial-mesenchymal transition and epigenetic regulation. The review explains how cancer cells leave the primary tumor, evade immunity, and settle elsewhere. Common destinations include lymph nodes, brain, bone, lung, and liver. Current therapies for metastatic disease are surveyed with their limits. The authors argue that grasping spread mechanisms can guide targeted drugs. Early detection before spread remains a key goal.
europmc-pmc9302186:
Hastie and co-authors map which parts of the SARS-CoV-2 spike that antibodies attack resist variant change. A global consortium of 56 partners pooled candidate antibodies for side-by-side testing. The panel held 269 monoclonal antibodies from many sources. Binding contests sorted the spike-binding set into groups.

The team sorted 186 antibodies that target the receptor binding domain into seven communities. Structure studies showed how members of each group grip the spike. Fake-virus tests then measured how single and combined mutations weaken each group. Variant mutations cluster in a few hot spots on the spike. Knowing each group's weak points guides treatment mixes. It also helps predict which new antibodies may fail as the virus evolves.
europmc-pmc9985086:
Cascella and co-authors evaluate whether ChatGPT is feasible for use in healthcare. ChatGPT is a large language model trained on a vast text dataset for dialogue. Its skill is clear, yet real medical work needs complex, high-level thought. Use in science writing also raises ethical concerns.

The team tested four areas: clinical practice support, scientific production, misuse risks, and public health reasoning. Results pointed to both promise and clear pitfalls. The authors stress training on proper use of such models in medicine. Knowing limits matters as much as knowing strengths. The study frames feasibility as a question of fit, not hype. It urges care before these tools enter daily care.
flaubert-madame-bovary-marx-aveling-1886:
Gustave Flaubert wrote Madame Bovary in French, and Eleanor Marx Aveling made the first English version in 1886. Many call the novel the founding work of literary realism in the modern sense. Flaubert polished each sentence for sound, and Marx Aveling kept his cool, exact style.

Emma Bovary, a farmer's daughter wed to a dull doctor, dreams of romance and luxury. Affairs with Rodolphe and Léon and debts to a sly draper ruin her by degrees. Flaubert shows her longings with pity and scorn in near equal measure throughout the tale. She poisons herself, and her husband dies of grief, leaving their child to factory work. The book was tried for obscenity in France and cleared, to lasting fame.
flaubert-salambo-chartres-1886:
Gustave Flaubert wrote Salammbô in French, and J. S. Chartres made this English version in 1886. The J. M. Dent edition carried Flaubert's great Carthaginian epic to English readers then. Flaubert spent years on research to rebuild ancient Carthage in lush, strange detail for readers.

After the Punic War, Carthage's unpaid mercenary troops revolt in a savage, sprawling war. Salammbô, daughter of Hamilcar, is priestess of Tanit and prize in the rebels' wild plans. Matho steals the sacred veil of the goddess and dooms himself by love and theft. Sieges, crucifixions, and child sacrifice fill pages of gorgeous and brutal antique color and rite. Flaubert called the book a nightmare of splendor, and few historical novels match it.
fontenelle-plurality-worlds-1686:
Bernard le Bovier de Fontenelle wrote his talks on the worlds in 1686. The book was the first hit work to say the planets may hold life. A man of science speaks with a marquise on fine nights in a garden. Their light tone made hard new thought easy to read.

Talk by talk, they weigh the Moon, Venus, Mars, and the rest. Fontenelle draws on the new star science of his day. He asks what folk on other worlds might be like. The book made the claim of many worlds a smart topic all over Europe.
fraipont-lohest-spy-1886:
Julien Fraipont and Max Lohest, two Belgian scholars, wrote this memoir in French on the Spy finds in 1886. Work men at Spy in Belgium had found two whole frames in a cave that year. The frames lay with stone tools of the Mousterian kind by their sides.

The two men were of the same bent, low browed race as the Neanderthal skull. With tools by them in firm ground, they proved that race was real and old beyond doubt. The Spy memoir shut the long row on Neanderthal as a mere sick modern man.
frus-1861-d186:
On 9 November 1861, William H. Seward wrote to Carl Schurz in the last hours before the Trent news. The letter is document 186 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Seward wrote the day after the Trent was stopped at sea, before the news reached him. His letter to Madrid keeps the plain course of the month. In the file it marks the last hour of the old world before the crisis broke. The old world of routine ended that weekend, though no man in Washington knew it yet. No man in Washington knew it yet, but the telegrams were already on their way.
frus-1861-d286:
One more Washington letter went abroad on 19 August 1861, addressed to Mr. Haldeman. It was printed as Document 286 in the foreign affairs papers sent to the two houses of Congress. By then, in the first summer of the Civil War, the Lincoln government knew foreign backing could change the war's course.

Readers see the home office side of the exchange, where policy was set before talks began. Alone it is a small piece of paper, but in sequence it helps show how the Union held its ground abroad. The State Department's Office of the Historian keeps the series, called Foreign Relations of the United States.
frus-1861-d86:
On 25 September 1861, Secretary of State William H. Seward sent another letter to Charles Francis Adams. It is document 86 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1861.

Paired letters on one day were Seward's way of sorting a crowded agenda. Each Adams file could be read, acted on, and answered on its own. The habit kept a vast correspondence clear, and it keeps the record clear for readers now. Clear files served the cabinet as well, since Lincoln read many of these pages. Lincoln read these pages too, which raised the worth of every clear line.
frus-1862-d186:
The second Seward letter of 10 November 1862 is printed as Document 186 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, was its reader, as he was for the other three sent that day.

Same-day letters often divided news from orders, or public business from copies meant for the file. The split lets a reader see the clerks' logic at work in a busy wartime office. For the story of the war abroad, batches like 10 November matter because they show the brief whole rather than in scraps. Union consuls in British ports fed the legation word of ships fitting out for the South.
frus-1862-d286:
William L. Dayton sent a report to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 12 June 1862, printed as Document 286 in the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It was one of two Dayton reports in two days.

Mid-June 1862 was a waiting season in Paris: France was reinforcing Mexico. Britain was watching Richmond, and no power wished to move first on the American war. Dayton's paired reports from this week capture that pause from inside the French capital. They also show his steady method, reporting talk as talk and fact as fact. French mills wanted Southern cotton, and French yards watched the Union blockade with care.
frus-1862-d386:
Simon Cameron reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 5 August 1862, in a letter printed as Document 386 of the 1862 Foreign Relations volume. It is one of two Cameron reports filed close together that month.

Cameron's term in Russia was brief and largely quiet, which was its value: the channel needed tending, not feats. His August reports reached Washington in the autumn, when the contrast between friendly St. Petersburg and doubtful London and Paris was stark. This letter forms part of the Russian file's steady, cordial run. Prince Gorchakov, Russia's foreign minister, made his government's sympathy for the Union plain.
frus-1862-d486:
On 8 March 1862 Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this instruction to James Shepherd Pike at The Hague. It is Document 486 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

Early March 1862 was a busy week at the State Department, with orders going out to many posts as the Virginia campaign took shape. For The Hague, the standing concerns were Dutch neutrality, the treatment of American shipping, and the colonial ports of the Dutch West Indies. Pike, a plain-spoken editor by trade, carried those points to the Dutch foreign ministry. The dispatch is one of several March orders that kept the smaller European posts in step with the great ones.
frus-1862-d586:
Thomas Corwin reported from Mexico to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 28 April 1862. The dispatch is Document 586 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, laid before Congress.

April brought the allied breakup in Mexico into the open, and Corwin wrote in the weeks before the French defeat at Puebla on 5 May. His reports described a republic bracing for a war with France while its northern neighbor fought for its own life. Washington read his letters with the Monroe Doctrine in mind and no army to spare for it. The April dispatch helps explain the Union's policy of that year: moral support, close watching, and patience until its own war allowed more.
frus-1862-d686:
The President of the United States sent this formal letter to the Viceroy of Egypt on 11 October 1861. It was written in President Abraham Lincoln's name and carried through the American consul general there. The letter is document 686 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862, in the Egypt file.

Letters between heads of state kept up the forms of friendship, and Egypt's ruler held a land that trade could not pass by. With war at home, Washington had cause to keep such ties warm on every sea road. The letter stands out from the desk mail around it: a set piece of courtesy, printed in the record next to a consul's working reports.
frus-1862-d86:
News and judgment from Charles Francis Adams reached Seward's desk in a letter dated 26 June 1862. It was printed as Document 86 in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs for 1862. It was written in the summer of 1862, the war's second year, while the North worked to block foreign aid to the South.

Such reports fed the facts and rumors together into one desk in Washington, week by week. Letters of this kind are the raw record from which the story of wartime diplomacy is built. Foreign Relations of the United States, the official record series, is where the full exchange can be traced.
frus-1863p1-d186:
On 5 May 1863, orders left Washington for London: Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London. The paper is document 186 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public. It was one of 5 letters between the same men dated that day.

For readers today, these instructions reveal the thinking inside the State Department as clearly as any memoir. They show choices being made in real time, with poor information and high stakes. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d286:
One of the Secretary's regular instructions to London, this letter from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, is dated 7 September 1863. It appears as document 286 of the 1863 papers. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

The CSS Alabama, built near Liverpool, had slipped away in 1862 and was raiding Union trade. Washington pressed London to stop such ships and answer for the losses. It belongs to the tense autumn when the fate of two Confederate ironclad rams in British yards hung in the balance. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d386: On 7 February 1863, Secretary of State William H. Seward addressed this note to Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington. It is document 386 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, part of the formal exchange through which the two governments handled Civil War disputes. Notes on this route dealt with neutral rights, stopped ships, and British complaints.
frus-1863p1-d486:
Among the day's business on 29 April 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons to William H. Seward. Lyons was Britain's minister in Washington, and Seward was the American Secretary of State. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863. America was then in the third year of its Civil War, and every letter to or from London carried weight.

Trade ran through the whole exchange. British mills wanted Southern cotton, while Union officials watched every cargo for war goods bound to the South. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. Alone it is one note among hundreds.
frus-1863p1-d586:
Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington directed a letter to Secretary William H. Seward on 15 July 1863. The two men at the ends of this channel, Seward in Washington and Lyons speaking for Britain, wrote to each other almost daily. Behind the formal phrases stood a live question: would Britain stay neutral, or step into the American war?

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The letter also shows the craft of the period: a few stiff phrases could carry a warning, and both sides knew how to read them. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
frus-1863p1-d686:
A dispatch dated 10 November 1863 went from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Lord Lyons in Washington. Lyons spoke for Britain in the United States through most of the Civil War. The text is document 686 in Foreign Relations of the United States for 1863.

Two Seward notes to Lyons share this date, a sign of how much Anglo-American business was live that week. The Union and Britain had to sort out sea rights, trade, and the fate of ships tied to the South. This letter is part of that sort. On its own it is brief. In the full run, it helps map how the two sides kept talking.
frus-1863p1-d86:
Charles Francis Adams sent this dispatch to Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 February 1863. Three Adams letters in the volume share the date. Adams was the American minister in London, and this letter is document 86 in part one of the 1863 volume.

The legation's mid-February mail dealt with the run of its work: British officials, the press, and the South's agents in the city. Adams split the load across three sheets. This one opens the set. Its place in the file, right after a Seward letter of the same date, shows how thick the exchange had grown. By the war's second year it ran near daily.
frus-1886:
Claims open the 1886 message, with Chile in default. Cleveland notes no provision exists for American claims. They arise from Chile's late war with Peru and Bolivia. The country files follow. Ecuador and Mexico take the longest runs. Britain's papers split three ways this year. One block prints letters from parties in molested fishing vessels. Canadian waters supply their grievances.

A mid-volume case gives the pattern. A Gloucester vessel entered Shelburne, Nova Scotia, for water and shelter. The Canadian cutter Terror seized her papers. Her captain had reported on every visit but one storm stop. The collector saw no liability; the cutter's captain held her. Such seizures fill the selection. The volume is a fisheries dossier in part. Diplomacy here smells of salt and tar.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d186:
Writing from Moscow on 2 November 1943, Secretary of State Cordell Hull told President Roosevelt how he had handled the Soviet request for Italian naval and merchant ships. Italy had surrendered, and Moscow wanted a share of its fleet. Hull said he had promised Molotov a fair hearing in Washington.

Hull reports that Britain's Eden, backed by Churchill, favored saying yes in principle but worried about details, such as holding back the two Littorio-class battleships. Hull urges joint British-American instructions to both ambassadors, a meeting of the three naval staffs, perhaps at Algiers, and no talk yet of giving the Soviets a full one-third share. He adds that Soviet crews could not man many more ships in any case.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d286:
Ambassador Averell Harriman wrote to Soviet foreign minister Molotov from Cairo on 22 November 1943, in a secret telegram sent through Moscow for delivery. Its business is practical: getting the Tehran conference site ready before the leaders arrive.

British and American representatives, Harriman says, leave Cairo for Tehran the next day, 23 November, to arrange the physical side of the conference, including living quarters and security in all details. He asks Molotov to tell General Connolly, the American commander in Tehran, which Soviet official he should work with. Connolly needs the name to coordinate the planning. Molotov is asked to cable word back to Cairo once that is set. Harriman closes with thanks for a hospitable, unexpected stop at Stalingrad, where engine trouble had forced his plane down.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d386:
President Roosevelt telegraphed James Byrnes from Tehran on 28 November 1943 about the proposed increase in landing craft building. The short message, sent by military channels, turns down the change Byrnes had urged in his telegram of 24 November.

The increase in critical types proposed, Roosevelt writes, coupled with its unstated effect on other critical programs, does not become effective soon enough to justify changing the present construction programs. The editors add an irony. Despite the negative tenor of this answer, the exchange of telegrams between the two men had a surprising result. Washington in fact adopted the very program Byrnes had described on 24 November. Later official histories of war production record this.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d486:
Admiral William D. Leahy, chief of staff to the President, addressed a message to President Roosevelt on December 5, 1943, during the Second Cairo Conference. Leahy was the senior American military officer and rarely left Roosevelt's side on these journeys. The State Department printed the message in its Cairo-Tehran volume.

Leahy chaired the American chiefs of staff and spoke to Roosevelt with unusual directness. A note from him at a conference usually meant military business needing the President's own attention. For readers, the message shows the top of the American command chain at work: the soldier closest to Roosevelt putting a matter before him in writing.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d86: Roosevelt wrote to Secretary Hull on November 2, 1943, and the letter is Document 86 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. Hull was back from Moscow, and the two men were aligning the American line for Cairo and Tehran. The record names the parties and the date only. In the Foreign Relations series the letter belongs to the short, intense season between the ministers' meeting and the leaders' meetings.
frus-1944-quebec-d186:
Lord Cherwell's memorandum records the September 14, 1944 discussion of the Treasury's Germany proposals with Roosevelt and Churchill present. Morgenthau asked Cherwell to give his impressions. Cherwell said he was definitely attracted: hamstring Germany's war capacity by removing usable machinery from the Ruhr to the countries she had devastated, and place the region under an international authority.

Without large-scale steel, chemicals, and electrical machinery, Cherwell argued, Germany could not arm for modern war, yet would not starve. Roosevelt said it was no undue hardship to require Germany to revert toward the agricultural status of the late nineteenth century. Churchill, converted to exploring the approach, noted the Russians would in any case insist on taking machinery to restore their ruined factories.
frus-1944-quebec-d286: A short minute of September 15, 1944, records a decision on France. Roosevelt and Churchill agreed the time had not yet come to recognize formally the French Committee of National Liberation. It would not yet be recognized as the Provisional Government of France. The matter, they agreed, should be kept constantly under review. Both leaders' initials appear on the text, and Colville's covering memorandum dates the agreement to September 15.
frus-1944-quebec-d86:
Treasury Secretary Henry Morgenthau Jr. wrote to Secretary Hull on September 6, 1944. The message appears in the State Department's Quebec 1944 volume. It dates from the final week before the Quebec Conference. Morgenthau had long handled war finance and allied aid.

Cabinet colleagues exchanged views as the summit approached. Finance, diplomacy, and military plans all met at Quebec. Germany's economic future stood among the hardest questions there. A letter from Morgenthau to Hull placed Treasury's position on record. For readers, it shows two departments aligning before the leaders met. Their staffs would defend those positions in Canada.
frus-1945-50-intel-d186:
On 15 February 1947, the Secretary of State’s Special Assistant for Research and Intelligence (Eddy) sent a memorandum to Secretary of State Marshall. It is document 186 in the Foreign Relations of the United States volume on intelligence for 1945 to 1950. The war had just ended, and the United States was keeping a central spy service in peace for the first time.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. Its place in the file shows the matter at the moment it passed from one desk to the next. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d286:
The Director of the Policy Planning Staff(Kennan) addressed a memorandum to the Under Secretary of State (Lovett) on 8 June 1948. In the printed Foreign Relations series it is document 286, in the volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. Across Washington, the new security bodies were moving from setup work to the real business of the Cold War.

The value of the form is its speed: a page or two, a clear ask, and a name at the top to answer for it. Kept in sequence, such memos form the true diary of the office that sent them. Kept with its neighbors in the volume, it shows the new system being built one dated paper at a time.
frus-1945-50-intel-d386:
On 7 July 1949, the Executive Secretary of the National Security Council (Souers) sent a memorandum to President Truman. Readers meet it as document 386 of the Foreign Relations series volume on intelligence from 1945 to 1950. With the Dulles Report now public inside the government, agencies were sorting out what to change and what to defend.

The form is plain on purpose: a named sender, a named reader, and a short statement of the matter at hand. The note's brevity hides its weight: men at this level did not write to each other for practice. Pages like this one are the bricks of the story: plain, dated, and load-bearing.
frus-1945-50-intel-d86:
Spruille Braden, assistant secretary for American republic affairs, wrote to Secretary Byrnes on 25 February 1946. Braden's bureau ran policy toward Latin America. Foreign Relations of the United States prints it in the later volume covering American intelligence between 1945 and 1950.

Latin America was the FBI's intelligence field by wartime practice, and the question of who would work there in peace ran hot through the volume. Braden, whose bureau owned the policy, had a direct stake in the answer. His memorandum brings the regional bureaus into a fight often told as one among spy chiefs. Readers gain a wider view: the customers of intelligence, the policy desks, also claimed a voice in who should collect it for them.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d186:
Stettinius wrote to mend fences on 7 December 1944, three days into the row over Italy. His letter to Lord Halifax, printed in the Malta and Yalta volume, encloses the personal message he sent Eden the night before. Regret opens both texts.

It is a source of deep personal regret, he tells Halifax, that any difference should have arisen so soon. The difference had come in his first days in office, between two countries he had worked with closely. His message to Eden says the same. It stresses how much he prizes the closest and most friendly personal ties. As long as the two men can talk things out freely and frankly, he closes, no serious differences can stand between their countries.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d286:
Stettinius kept a daily record of his secretaryship, and this editorial note introduces the excerpts printed in the volume. The editors of the Malta and Yalta volume describe the source: a top secret typewritten ribbon copy, titled “Record of Edward R. Stettinius, Jr., Secretary of State.”

In his own prefatory note, Stettinius calls the record a straight factual account. It rests on his conversations, letters, cables, and press reports, and is set out in weekly sections with topical subsections. The first five sections are written in the third person, the rest in the first. The record covers only his days in Washington. It therefore holds no entries for Malta and Yalta themselves, for which he left the Department on 23 January 1945.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d386:
Petroleum and cargo shipping head the Combined Chiefs' record of February 8, 1945. The chiefs first approved the minutes of their 186th meeting. Then they took up levels of supply of oil products in all theaters. An overall review of cargo shipping followed, built on a joint staff paper.

Admiral Leahy said the American chiefs found the shipping paper acceptable with one change. A date in it should move from April 30 to April 1. Lord Leathers, Britain's transport minister, answered that the change suited him well, if the staffs could match it. The record is dry, but the stakes were real: shipping set the speed of every plan the alliance made.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d486: An air pact with Ireland caused a flap in this short cable from Stettinius to Grew, sent February 7, 1945. The British were disturbed that the United States had made an aviation pact with Ireland without consulting or informing them. Stettinius asked Grew to send a fitting explanation promptly, for the delegation to present to the British. The pact, covering air transport service, had been signed at Washington on February 3, while the conference party was at Malta. Even a side quarrel over air routes reached the Secretary mid-summit.
frus-1945-malta-yalta-d86:
At the White House on 8 January 1945, the voting formula came back to the President's desk. Leo Pasvolsky's record of the meeting is printed in the Malta and Yalta volume. Stettinius, Dunn, Pasvolsky, and Bohlen sat with Roosevelt to plan the coming talks with Churchill and Stalin.

Stettinius warned that without agreement on voting, the United Nations conference might be delayed for a long time. Interest would slacken and opposition could grow. The President said he was determined to press for a decision. Yet he remained puzzled over one case: a dispute between the United States and, say, Mexico, reaching the Council with the United States denied a vote.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d186:
The American chargé in Prague forwarded a Czechoslovak request in a despatch dated July 5, 1945. The short covering letter is document 186 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It transmits the Czechoslovak Foreign Office's note asking that its application be heard by the Big Three.

President Beneš and his government want their request for the transfer of minorities placed on the agenda of the meeting of Truman, Churchill, and Stalin. The minorities in question were chiefly the Sudeten Germans, whose expulsion from Czechoslovakia Prague sought to have the great powers approve. The full note is printed later in the volume. Klieforth's brief letter shows a small state lobbying to get its case onto a table where it had no seat.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d286:
A background paper described Communist gains in Bulgaria, dated July 5, 1945. The paper is document 286 in the Foreign Relations volume on the Potsdam Conference. It is one of the country studies made for the President's briefing book.

Since the Fatherland Front took power, the summary says, the Bulgarian Workers' Party, the Communists, has worked hard to tighten its grip. By maneuver and by threats from the party-run militia, moderates have been pushed out of the Agrarian, Social Democratic, and Zveno parties. The Front now faces the vote set for August 26 with a wholly Communist face. The control body still lacks real U.S. and British voice, no U.S. newsmen have been let in, and Soviet troops in the country are said to number 200,000.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d386:
German ships and the Soviet share of them fill an undated memorandum by George Elsey. On May 23, 1945, Stalin had cabled Truman and Churchill a complaint: not one German naval or merchant vessel had surrendered to Soviet forces. How, he asked, would the Soviet Union obtain the one-third of German ships that rightfully and justly should fall to it?

Stalin also wanted the Red Navy to examine all papers on the surrender and state of the German ships. Churchill replied on May 27 that the matters belonged in the general discussion among the three leaders. Elsey's memo assembles the exchange, including Hopkins's report of his own talk with Stalin, for Truman's use.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d486:
The Polish Commission's agreed statement is cabled by Harriman from Moscow on June 23, 1945. The Commission that night agreed a communiqué, for release twenty-four hours later, on the formation of a Provisional Polish Government of National Unity. Harriman sends the text in full for the Department's record.

The communiqué recalls the Commission's mandate. Molotov spoke for the Soviet Union. The British ambassador, Sir Archibald Kerr, spoke for Britain. Harriman himself spoke for the United States. The three were empowered by the Crimea conference to consult with members of the Provisional Government. They were also to consult with other democratic leaders, from Poland itself and from abroad.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d586:
Ambassador Sato reported from Moscow on July 13, 1945, how he delivered the Emperor's message. His cable, in translation, is document 586 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on the Potsdam Conference. Molotov, it turns out, could not see him that day.

Sato met deputy minister Lozovsky at 5 p.m. instead. He handed over the Emperor's wishes in Russian, addressed to Molotov, with a private note of his own. The note sought Soviet leave for Prince Konoye's visit and help with a plane if leave was granted. Sato stressed that this mission differed from past ones, since it came from the Emperor himself. He asked for an answer in principle before Molotov left for Berlin. Lozovsky doubted an answer could come that fast, as one Soviet party left that very night.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d686:
A second round of Soviet-Turkish talks in Moscow is reported by Ambassador Wilson on June 22, 1945. His secret wire from Ankara is document 686 in volume one of the Foreign Relations papers on Potsdam. The Turkish ambassador had seen Molotov again on June 18.

Under instructions, the ambassador told Molotov Turkey could not accept his three points as a basis for discussion. The long talk stayed civil in tone. Molotov then floated a treaty of collaboration and alliance between the two states. He also raised a new point of his own. Moscow might wish to present to Turkey the views of the Balkan states on questions touching them. Turkey's acting foreign minister noted that no such questions were pending. The Balkan states were beaten belligerents under Allied control commissions, and Turkey would not receive claims voiced for them by Moscow.
frus-1945-potsdam-1-d86:
Ambassador Harriman updated Admiral Leahy from Moscow on June 22, 1945, in a telegram printed as document 86 in the Foreign Relations volume on Potsdam. He had asked Foreign Minister Molotov the night before to get Stalin's reaction to the American Chiefs of Staff coming to Berlin with the President.

Molotov said he would consult Stalin at once, but felt quite sure there would be no objection. Harriman also passes on Vyshinsky's urgent request for the size and shape of the President's party, so the Soviets can plan housing. He asks Leahy for a first estimate: chiefs, officers, political advisers, and clerks. The message captures both sides still counting beds and chairs a month before the leaders met.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1086:
Ambassador Lincoln MacVeagh cabled Washington from Athens on August 1, 1945, about Greece's handling of the Yugoslav protest. He had passed the American reply to the prime minister, who made no comment yet. From the British chargé, he gathers that Athens wants the Macedonian question kept quiet. Greek officials suspect the Yugoslav note grew from inexperience, not menace.

Athens would rather settle with Belgrade directly once a new Yugoslav minister arrives. It will study border incidents, but insists no foreign government may intervene over Greek nationals. MacVeagh adds British findings that shrink the charges: refugee numbers near 5,000, and only three of six alleged incident sites can even be identified.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1186:
Clement Attlee wrote to President Truman on 31 July 1945, five days after becoming prime minister. He was already bargaining at the sharp end of the summit. His message carried the voice of the new Labour government in London.

The change of leaders mid-summit could have wrecked the talks. It did not, in part because notes like this one kept the personal channel warm. Attlee's plain style differed from Churchill's grand manner, and the record shows the shift. This message is the new prime minister at work, two days before the conference closed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1286:
On 21 July 1945 the United States Chiefs of Staff issued this memorandum. Staff papers like this one did the thinking that leaders later turned into choices. The chiefs' run of notes by now covered the summit's first full week.

Each note added the services' judgment on the questions of its day. The file they built gave the American team a military brief that grew with the talks. This memorandum is a mid-series piece. Its worth is in the sequence: read in order, the run shows the staff mind at work across the whole conference.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d1386:
Mikołajczyk, Poland's deputy prime minister, wrote a second memorandum on 25 July 1945, the day after his first in this run. The volume prints his papers as a group near its end. The text comes from the second Potsdam volume of Foreign Relations of the United States, the State Department's official history series.

A run of papers by one man lets readers follow a single mind at work under pressure. Mikołajczyk wrote while the Potsdam leaders fixed Poland's western border and argued over its elections. His memoranda were bids to be heard by the powers deciding his country's future without him in the room. Read in sequence, they show hope narrowing day by day, in step with the summit's own calendar.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d710a-86:
Staff of the United States delegation at Potsdam drew up this memorandum on July 24, 1945. Delegation memoranda were the team's daily work tools. They briefed leaders, summed up talks, and set out facts for the next round. This one was kept with the conference files and printed in the second Potsdam volume of the official record.

Because such papers were written for use, not for the public, they tend to be plain and direct. They show the American team thinking on paper between sessions. Read with the formal minutes, they fill in the staff work behind the heads of government. The memo is one piece of a large, careful paper trail.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d786:
Winant answered Mosely on July 27, 1945, in document 786. The ambassador in London replied the same day he was written to. Their exchange sits in the second Potsdam volume as a neat pair. It shows the London end of the Germany planning web during the conference's last week.

Same-day replies mark an urgent, trusted channel. Winant valued Mosely's counsel on the Commission's work. Readers see two veterans closing a question between them. The document adds a human note to the volume's machinery: old colleagues, writing plainly, at the end of a long shared task. Their letters outlast the summit as a record of how it was staffed.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d886:
Soviet delegates proposed this addition to the Political Principles for Germany on July 30, 1945. It would help set up a central German administration under the Control Council. Department heads would run foreign trade, industry, finance, transport, and communications.

The bracketed part of the text goes further. It would have the new administration coordinate the provincial governments. Its task would be to see that Control Council decisions are carried out across Germany. The bracketed passage also covers problems of an all-German character. A margin note on the paper records that Secretary Byrnes suggested cutting that bracketed passage.
frus-1945-potsdam-2-d986:
Edwin Pauley and William Clayton cabled the Acting Secretary of State from Babelsberg on July 21, 1945. They advise sending Washington's telegram on Rumanian oil shares to Moscow as well, and to Bucharest. Details of Soviet talks over German property in Stockholm should also go to Moscow, in case the Soviets question the embassy's recent note.

The pair report what the American delegation is putting before the conference. A declaration by the United States, Britain, and the USSR, with France if possible, would place German external assets under the occupying powers and the Control Council. Their envoys would act as agents for both. Staff are also drafting a vesting decree for the Control Council.
frus-1964-68v01-d286: An editorial note in the Vietnam, 1964 volume follows the night of August 4, 1964, hour by hour. Admiral Sharp confirmed that the Ticonderoga's planes were off at 10:43 at night, Washington time. Late that night, President Johnson told the nation that air action was under way against North Vietnamese gunboats and their shore bases. His speech joins the high-seas attack to the war on South Vietnam's villages. Full commitment, he pledges, will be redoubled by this outrage. The note rests on the Tonkin chronology files.
gao-gaoreports-b-297686:
CRAssociates protested its cut from a Health cost study contest in GAO decision B-297686, dated March 7, 2006. The study weighed in-house work versus a deal for detainee health care. The firm's bid was ruled not fit on tech grounds. It was cut from the field. The firm said study rules forced talks with it in any case.

GAO denied the protest. The call said talks would be with firms in the field. Not all firms would be in the field. That text was clear. If the firm thought the rule was wrong, it had to protest before the close for bids. It did not. A late attack on a clear call term will fail.
gao-gaoreports-b-297986:
Knowledge Connections protested the terms of a Veterans Affairs travel call in GAO decision B-297986, dated May 18, 2006. The work was a single travel center for the whole agency. Firms could use any web travel tool that links to the state eTravel System. The firm said that choice tilts to the firm that owns one such tool.

GAO denied the protest. The call did not lock firms to that one tool. Any tool that links could be used. An edge that comes from past deals is not an unfair tilt by the agency. Firms gain edges from past work in fair ways. No bar to fair play was shown.
gao-gaoreports-b-298086:
Bristol Group protested the rejection of its lease bid in GAO decision B-298086, dated May 30, 2006. The buyer was the General Services Administration. The tenant was the Surface Transportation Board. Space sought was up to 74,870 square feet in Washington. The call set a walk range for food and shops near the block. The firm's block missed that range.

GAO denied the protest. The cut from the field was sound. The block did not meet the walk rule in the call. Claims of hidden tests and of spite for the zone were not backed. The review tracked the call terms. A block that misses a set place rule can be cut.
gao-gaoreports-b-299086:
Synectic Solutions, Inc. protested a Navy award to Evolving Resources, Inc. The contract covered information technology support services. The work serves the Naval Air Warfare Center at Point Mugu, California. The contest was limited to 8(a) program firms. GAO ruled in B-299086 on February 7, 2007.

The firm attacked the technical and price reviews. It also faulted the agency for holding no talks. The terms had warned that award could come with no talks at all. GAO found the scores sound on the record. It also found a firm base for the pick that followed. The cost-merit trade-off was fair. GAO denied the protest.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-486:
Computer controls at the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation are checked in GAO report GAO-05-486, dated May 19, 2005. GAO tested the controls as part of its audit of the corporation's three funds for calendar year 2004. The review asked how many old weaknesses had been fixed. It also tested whether general controls over financial systems work as they should.

The corporation had fixed 19 of the 22 weaknesses from the 2003 audit. It had closed the last open item from 2002. New weaknesses showed up, though. GAO found gaps in access controls, network security, and the separation of computer duties. Physical security and control over program changes also needed work. The flaws did not pose a deep risk to the funds, GAO said. Their root cause was a test process that skipped some key areas. The report urges the corporation to hold its gains and finish the job.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-686:
Foreign takeovers of U.S. firms and national security meet in GAO-05-686, dated September 28, 2005. A 1988 law lets the President block such deals; the power has been used once. An interagency committee chaired by the Treasury reviews cases first. GAO finds the chair and several members read security threats narrowly and shun formal probes, partly to keep investment welcome. Firms are often urged to pull a filing and resubmit later, which buys time but leaves some done deals unexamined for good.

Watch over firms after clearance has improved since 2002. GAO offers fixes and points Congress to choices about how wide the security lens should be.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-886:
Apprenticeship oversight by the Labor Department is graded in GAO-05-886, dated August 29, 2005. Nearly 850,000 construction jobs will open from 2002 to 2012. Skilled workers may be too few to fill them. That puts program quality in the spotlight. GAO checked how the department monitors programs in states it oversees directly. It checked its review of states that monitor their own. It also compared outcomes by sponsor type.

GAO found direct monitoring is thin. In 2004, the department reviewed only 4 percent of programs in the 23 states it oversees. Staff limits were the stated cause. The department gathers much data but does not mine it for performance clues like completion rates. Reviews of the 27 self-monitoring states and the District of Columbia are rare, and only summary data flows back. GAO urged better use of data to target oversight.
gao-gaoreports-gao-05-986:
Top tech officers at big firms are profiled in GAO-05-986, issued September 9, 2005. A 1996 law made each federal agency name a chief information officer. Congress asked how the private role compares. GAO met with officers at 20 leading firms. It mapped their duties against 12 key areas. It asked their top challenges. And it studied how their firms govern tech assets as a whole.

Most of the 20 officers held or shared duty in 9 of the 12 areas. Nearly all cover system buying, tech investment planning, security, tech staff, and e-commerce. Three areas, like public information duties, sit with half or fewer. Eleven officers named aligning tech with business goals as their greatest challenge. Cost control and data security also rank high. Governance runs through executive committees and cross-company teams, GAO found.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-386:
Banks must report suspect money moves, and many examiners check that duty. Report GAO-06-386, issued April 28, 2006, reviews oversight under the Bank Secrecy Act. The Financial Crimes Enforcement Network and the banking regulators share the work. GAO wrote the report for a Senate banking panel. Its focus is how steady that oversight is across regulators.

GAO found regulators used similar exam steps before 2005, but applied them in widely varied ways. Joint procedures and more training have since helped. Word choices in data systems still risk uneven results. GAO saw chances to strengthen the framework further. Readers get the exam process and its weak joints.
gao-gaoreports-gao-06-86:
