Workforce management at the stock market regulator is assessed in GAO-06-86. The report is dated January 10, 2006. Corporate failures and accounting scandals had expanded the duties of the Securities and Exchange Commission. Congress answered with large budget increases so the agency could hire. GAO reviewed how the agency plans for the staff it needs. Strategic human capital management was the test: matching people, skills, and workload over time.

GAO found that the agency had made progress on several workforce efforts. It was building a strategic human capital plan. In 2003, it finished a full review of its workforce and workflow. It then split its personnel office into two units, one for administrative services and one for human resources. That split raised focus on each task. GAO said more work remained to finish the plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-1186:
U.S. aid to help other lands spot disease outbreaks is described in GAO report GAO-07-1186, dated September 28, 2007. The fast spread of SARS in 2003 showed that outbreaks cross borders. For a decade the United States has helped lands build the skill to spot a health emergency of world concern.

Three agencies run that aid: the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, the aid agency USAID, and the Defense Department. GAO set out their programs' costs, aims, and acts. It told how the agencies track headway. The study skips disease-specific work, such as polio or malaria. GAO made no recommendations, and the agencies largely agreed with its findings.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-486:
Child and maternal health aid reaches wide but reports thin, and GAO-07-486, a GAO report from April 20, 2007, makes that case. Each year, disease and other causes kill about 10 million children under age 5. More than 500,000 women die from pregnancy and childbirth causes. Congress funds the U.S. Agency for International Development (USAID) to fight those tolls. A 2006 law told GAO to review the fund's use for fiscal years 2004 and 2005.

GAO surveyed 40 health officers and visited missions in four countries. It traced where the money went and what work it bought. Missions ran many local efforts, from clinics to training. But head office did not require full spending reports, so it could not fully account for the funds. Nor had the agency proven which ways of sharing good practice work best. GAO urged tighter data and tested sharing.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-786:
The Congressional Award Foundation's books are audited in GAO-07-786, dated May 15, 2007. The foundation runs a youth awards program set up by Congress. Law at 2 U.S.C. 807 tells GAO to audit its accounts. This report gives GAO's opinion on the statements for fiscal years 2006 and 2005. It also judges the foundation's internal controls as of September 30, 2006. A check on compliance with key laws and rules rounds out the audit.

GAO found a material weakness in controls over financial reporting. The flaw had carried over from past audits. The foundation lacked written steps for closing entries in its books. It also lacked steps to ensure its statements were complete and accurate. Such gaps raise the risk of errors in the public accounts. The report lays out the audit work and findings in full. It gives Congress a base for pressing the foundation on fixes.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-86:
Surgery center payments under Medicare are studied in GAO-07-86, dated November 30, 2006. Medicare pays ambulatory surgical centers and hospital outpatient units under distinct systems. Both settings perform many of the same procedures. No one had compared their per-procedure costs. The 2003 Medicare law told GAO to make that comparison. GAO surveyed surgery centers for cost data.

Hospital payment groups track surgery center costs well, GAO found. The cost ratios for center procedures clustered more tightly than those for hospital work. Extra services billed with the top 20 procedures were much the same in both settings. Hospitals got paid for some extras, such as X-rays, inside their system. Outside providers billed those extras for center cases. GAO urged one payment system for centers based on the hospital model. It should reflect the lower costs of center care. The agency said the call matches its own plan.
gao-gaoreports-gao-07-986:
Spending of drug benefit start-up funds is audited in GAO-07-986, dated August 31, 2007. The 2003 Medicare drug law gave the Social Security Administration up to $500 million. The money covered the agency's new duties under the law. It was spent from December 2003 through January 2006. Staff time took more than half of the total. Contractors and indirect costs took much of the rest. Systems tracked the spending by task. Sixteen of 22 planned tasks were done by February 2007.

Rules for the money existed but did not always bind, GAO found. Special cost guidance never reached all staff who needed it. At least $4.6 million in costs landed on the wrong account first. The agency caught and fixed those charges itself. Some vendor payment steps skipped required checks. Overall controls earned a passing picture with flagged lapses. The report names where compliance broke down. Congress asked for the review of this discretionary fund.
gao-gaoreports-gao-08-486:
Workforce training grants from the Department of Labor are evaluated in GAO report GAO-08-486, dated May 7, 2008. Since 2001, the department has spent nearly $900 million on three grant drives: High Growth, Community Based, and WIRED. The drives aim to aim the public workforce system at fast-growing industries.

The department awarded 349 grants worth almost $900 million. But the drives sit outside its strategic plan and research agenda, and it lacks data to compare their results with other training services. Over 80 percent of High Growth grants were given without competition, and the department could not document how those picks met the law. Most local workforce boards were shut out of talks on industry needs. GAO urged impact checks, better records, and risk-based monitoring. The department said steps were begun or planned.
gesner-historia-animalium-lib2-1586:
Gesner's second volume of the Historiae animalium treats the oviparous quadrupeds, the egg-laying four-footed beasts. It first appeared in 1554, and this text is the second edition of 1586. Tortoises, lizards, frogs, and crocodiles fill a class that modern science has long since rearranged.

Gesner works through each creature with names, pictures, habits, and reports from old authors. His patience looks endless, and his woodcuts carry much of the charm. The volume marches steadily on with the same plan as the first. Readers watch the Renaissance survey the created world beast by beast. Few books of its age match its order and scope.
goad-astro-meteorologica-1686:
John Goad was a London schoolmaster and astrologer whose Astro-Meteorologica appeared in 1686. The book matches thirty years of weather observations against the positions of the planets. Goad kept daily records of wind, rain, frost, and storm for the whole span.

He argues that aspects between planets, and their places in the signs, foretell heat, cold, and tempest in usable patterns. His tables let the reader test the claim year by year against his logged weather. The work is a serious early try at weather forecasting by rule, whatever a modern reader makes of its stars.
gospel-james-walker-1886:
The Protevangelium of James, Englished here by Alexander Walker, is an early Christian writing that tells what the four Gospels leave out: the birth and childhood of Mary. It opens with Joachim, a rich man of the twelve tribes, shamed because he has no child. He checks the registers of the tribes and finds he alone is childless among the righteous.

The tale goes on to Mary's birth, her upbringing in the Temple, her betrothal to the widower Joseph, and the birth of Jesus, with the midwife and Salome as witnesses. The Church never took the book into its canon, yet its tales shaped art and feast days for centuries. Walker prints it among the other early writings of the Ante-Nicene Fathers set. It is short, strange, and full of wonder.
gould-mythical-monsters-1886:
Charles Gould asked a plain question in 1886: what real beasts stand behind the monster tales? Mythical Monsters surveys dragons, sea serpents, and other famed creatures of lore. Gould was a geologist who had worked in China and read its dragon lore at first hand.

He weighs old reports with a cool head and finds big real animals behind many of them. The dragon, the kraken, and the serpent each get a fair hearing and a strict test. His book treats old tales as clues for science, not jokes. It founded a line of study now called cryptozoology.
granada-sinners-guide-1886:
Luis de Granada was a Spanish Dominican whose Sinner's Guide, first published in 1555, guided Catholic devotion for centuries. McKenna's 1886 English translation carries the ascetical masterpiece to a new audience. Granada wrote for ordinary Christians, not only for monks and nuns.

The guide weighs the reasons for a good life, then gives rules for prayer, fasting, speech, and the care of the poor. Its tone is warm and urgent rather than severe, pressing readers toward virtue as gain, not loss. The book is said to have converted millions, and it still anchors Spanish Catholic devotion. Its counsel assumes a reader who wants heaven and fears the cost.
gurney-myers-podmore-phantasms-vol1-1886:
Edmund Gurney, Frederic Myers, and Frank Podmore published Volume 1 of Phantasms of the Living in 1886 for the Society for Psychical Research. They gathered reports of people who seemed to appear to friends or kin at a moment of crisis or death. Their name for such cases was crisis apparitions.

Hundreds of cases fill the volume, drawn from letters and sworn statements, with names, dates, and checks where the authors could make them. The writers argued that chance alone could not explain so many close matches. Their claim, called telepathy, held that one mind could affect another at a distance, and the cases were their proof.
gurney-myers-podmore-phantasms-vol2-1886:
Volume 2 of Phantasms of the Living, published in 1886 by Edmund Gurney, Frederic Myers, and Frank Podmore, completed their large study of crisis apparitions. The first volume had laid out hundreds of cases. Here the authors pressed further into the theory behind them.

More cases appear, sorted by type, along with long discussion of dreams, waking visions, and shared sights. The authors tried to answer critics who blamed lies, poor memory, or chance. They defended telepathy as the best account of their facts. By that they meant a dying or endangered person could impress his image on a distant mind.
gurney-phantasms-of-the-living-1886:
Three keen men counted ghosts with care in Phantasms of the Living, the vast study of 1886. Edmund Gurney, Frederic Myers, and Frank Podmore were chiefs of a new band for the study of such things. Folk oft claim to see a far kin at the hour of that kin's death. The three sought such tales, checked them, and weighed the odds.

Scores of cases fill two fat tomes, each sifted for fraud and flaw. Their claim is that thought can leap from mind to mind. The work founds a whole field of study. Its care still stuns.
hardy-mayor-casterbridge-1886:
Thomas Hardy published The Mayor of Casterbridge in 1886, a novel that opens with a shocking act. Michael Henchard, a drunken hay worker, sells his wife and child at a fair. Sober, he swears off drink for twenty-one years. He rises by hard work to become mayor of Casterbridge.

Henchard's past returns when his wife reappears in town. His pride, temper, and rivalry with a young Scots manager undo him step by step. Hardy builds the fall with the force of Greek tragedy. The town and its corn trade are drawn in rich detail. Many readers rank the novel as Hardy's supreme tragedy of character.
hunter-animal-oeconomy-1786:
Observations on Certain Parts of the Animal Oeconomy gathers John Hunter's comparative anatomy papers of 1786. Animal oeconomy was the era's term for how living bodies run themselves. Hunter compares organs and functions across species to find shared plans. Digestion and the lymphatic system both receive his sharp attention.

One paper treats the electric organs of the torpedo, a fish that stuns its prey. Such studies built the research program behind his fame in surgery. The first edition joins papers that journals had scattered. Readers see Hunter the naturalist behind Hunter the surgeon. His curiosity ranged over all life. The volume explains his standing among scientists.
hunter-venereal-disease-1786:
John Hunter treated venereal disease in a full treatise in 1786, the first study of its kind. He examined syphilis and gonorrhoea with clinical and experimental methods. Cases from his London practice fill the pages with close detail. Hunter sought the laws by which these diseases spread and changed.

The book includes his famous self inoculation trial, which misled him badly. Working before germ theory, he took the two diseases for one poison. That error, and the careful work around it, both shaped later research. The first edition preserves his reasoning in full. Readers see a great surgeon reasoning at the edge of his era's knowledge. History of medicine courses still assign it.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-aaron-sabaoni-8: Aaron Sabaoni edited the cabalistic ritual "Hekal ha-Ḳodesh" by Moses Albaz, and added notes to it. The book was printed in Amsterdam in 1653. His name may come from the city of Sabbionetta, though the entry calls that only a guess. In the seventeenth century he lived in Sale. There, with Jacob Sasportas, he joined in condemning the followers of Shabbethai Ẓebi. Those followers had dropped the four chief fast-days, claiming the Messiah had come.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abd-al-daim-186: Abd-al-Daim was the son of Abd-al-Aziz, son of Muhasan ha-Israeli. He came of a line of Jewish physicians and was a physician himself. He flourished about 1300. On August 30, 1316, he finished an Arabic work called "The Two Sciences." It has two parts, one on physics and one on metaphysics. The work is set out as a chain of questions and answers. The manuscript is kept in the Bodleian Library in Oxford.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-abigdor-ben-isa: Abigdor ben Isaac was a French rabbinic scholar of the second half of the thirteenth century. He is most likely the man old manuscripts call Abigdor the Frenchman. That man wrote a commentary on the Maḥzor, the festival prayer-book. A note in a Munich manuscript shows the Frenchman as a follower of the Cabala. It is also possible that he and his father Isaac are the two rabbis of Béziers named by Naḥmanides. The entry rules out a match with a later Abigdor in the Mordecai.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-addan-786: Addan was a city of Babylonia. Some of its folk came back with the Jews under Zerubbabel. They could not prove that they were of Israel stock. Ezra ii. 59 tells the tale. The like list in Nehemiah vii. 61 calls the place Addon. I Esdras v. 36 has a merged form of the name. The hosted text gives that return, that lack of proof, and the name forms. It gives no site for the city and no later past.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-agag-886: Agag was king of the Amalekites, taken by King Saul in war. Saul spared his life, as I Samuel xv. tells. The prophet Samuel saw that mercy as defiance of God's will. He put Agag to death at Gilgal. Balaam's words in Numbers xxiv. 7 hint that Agag was a standing title of Amalek kings. Rabbinic lore says the death came one day too late. Had Agag died on his capture day, no Haman would have sprung from him to vex the Jews.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ahimaaz-ben-pal:
Ahimaaz ben Paltiel was a liturgical poet and the author of a family chronicle. He was born in Capua, Italy, in 1017 and died about 1060 in Oria. Little is known of his life. He came from a family of scholars and poets, and had two sons, Paltiel and Samuel.

His Chronicle was meant to glorify his own ancestors. In doing so, it preserves early facts about Jewish life in southern Italy. It covers towns such as Oria, Bari, Otranto, Capua, and Amalfi, across the years 850 to 1054. Only one manuscript of it survives, kept at Toledo in Spain. The entry also tells of the marvels the Chronicle records, from wonder-working Aaron to the book Sefer ha-Merkabah.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alcala-de-guada: Alcala de Guadaira is a town seven miles east of Seville, in Spain. At one time it held a small Jewish community. Its synagogue was torn down by order of Archdeacon Ferrand Martinez. That was in December 1390. Soon after, the members of the community were put to the sword. The entry is only these few lines, but they record the whole fate of the place: a congregation, a razed synagogue, and a massacre.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-alfaquin-joseph: Joseph Alfaquin was a physician to Don Sancho of Navarre. He served in the twelfth century. His colleague was Don Moses ben Samuel. The king was grateful for his services. In thanks he gave Joseph a share of the revenues drawn from the Jews of Tudela. The entry is very short. It gives no dates for Joseph's birth or death, and it names no cure or writing of his.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-almodad-septuag: Almodad is named in the Bible as a son of Joktan. The entry calls him the eldest son. It cites Genesis chapter ten and First Chronicles chapter one. Two old versions read his name as El-modad. The entry says the sense of the name is not sure. Its first part may be the Arabic article. Its second part may be a worn form of Maudad. The hosted entry is brief and gives no life story for him. It points readers to the entry on Joktan for more.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-america-judaism:
Judaism in America is the faith in its newest sphere. The entry holds that it will react on all older forms. It grew from the new world round it. Three threads run through its weave. One is the old faith brought by the first settlers. One is the Spanish strain of the middle ages. One is the German Reform strain of late years.

First settlers were strict Jews of Sephardic type. A burial lot was granted at New York in 1656. The first synagogue rose there in 1695. Newport set out a burial ground in 1677. The long entry tracks all three threads on. Platforms of Reform take up much of its length.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-anaw-zedekiah-b:
Zedekiah ben Abraham Anaw, younger brother of Benjamin, was a writer on ritual who lived at Rome in the thirteenth century. He trained in Rome and in Germany, where Jacob of Würzburg taught him. His fame rests on one big compilation rather than on new research.

That work, Shibbole ha-Leket, holds 372 paragraphs in twelve sections. It covers prayer, Sabbath, blessings, fasts, and the yearly feasts, plus added treatises on topics like mourning and inheritance. Zedekiah drew the material from many older authorities and shaped it into a clear, popular form. The entry credits that skillful shaping, not fresh findings, for the book's wide vogue.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-antioch-1586:
Antioch was the old capital of Syria, fifty-seven miles west of Aleppo, on the left bank of the river Orontes. Seleucus Nicator founded it in 300 B.C. and named it for his father or his son. As Syria's chief city, it housed the Roman governor who also ruled Palestine.

Many Jews lived in Antioch from its founding, the entry says. Seleucus gave them full citizen rights, set down on brass tablets and kept with care. Their communal head bore the title of archon. Later Syrian kings gave rich gifts to its synagogue. The entry follows the city's Jews through wars and revolts, including the day Maccabean troops saved a Syrian king in his palace there.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-arabic-language:
Arabic language among Jews begins with an unknown, the entry admits. When Jews first settled in Arabia cannot be fixed, so neither can the first Jewish use of Arabic. Firm facts reach back only to the first century of the common era.

By then Jews held weighty posts in parts of Arabia and bore pure Arabic names, signs they had lived there for centuries. Some pre-Islamic poets were Jews. Sarah, a Jewess, poured out grief in Arabic verse for her slain tribe of Kuraiza. Al-Samau'al won fame for loyalty and for poetry alike, and Arabs still praise a man as loyal as Al-Samau'al. The entry then shows how Jews fed Hebrew words into Arabic where they lived in strength.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-armavir-1786:
Armavir, the old capital of Armenia, stood on the southeastern slope of Mount Ahaghoz. Tradition in Moses of Chorene credits its founding to King Armais in 1980 B.C. When King Vaharshak settled there in 149 B.C., he built a temple and pressed his favorite, the Jew Shambu Bagarat, to worship idols. Shambu refused.

Jewish captives shape the rest of the account. Tigranes II, who reigned from 90 to 36 B.C., carried many Jews from Palestine and settled them at Armavir. Later kings moved them to new capitals. When Sapor II of Persia invaded in 360 to 370, he led away 9,000 Jewish families among 30,000 Armenian ones and destroyed the city.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-abrah:
Abraham Ashkenazi, chief rabbi of Palestine, was born at Janishar near Salonica in 1813. At fifteen his father took him to Jerusalem, where he studied in the colleges there. By the age of thirty-five, Turkish rabbis who consulted him on points of law addressed him as Gaon. In 1850 he became a dayyan, a judge, of the Jerusalem community.

In 1869 the rabbis of Jerusalem chose him as their chief after the death of David Hazan. The sultan confirmed the choice and gave him the title Hakam Bashi, making him chief rabbi of Palestine for about twelve years. The sultan also gave him the medal of the Medjidie, and Emperor Franz Josef decorated him in person at Jerusalem. He died there on January 22, 1880, mourned by Jews, Christians, and Muslims alike.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ashkenazi-nissi:
Nissim Abraham Ashkenazi was a Talmudic author who lived in the first half of the nineteenth century. He officiated at Smyrna. His book Nehmad le-Mareh, Graceful of Appearance, sets out methodical rules for studying two parts of the Jerusalem Talmud: the treatise Berakot and the order Seder Zeraim.

Alongside the rules, the book gives decisions of older and later authorities on the laws those treatises cover. It was printed at Salonica over a long span, from 1832 to 1846. The entry rests on Benjacob's catalogue of Hebrew books. It gives the author's city, his period, and his single work, and records nothing of his birth, family, or death.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-athletes-athlet:
Athletes are men who perform feats of strength or play games that rest on strength. The entry begins with the Bible's mighty men. Nimrod and Esau were famed hunters. Jacob rolled a great stone from a well and wrestled till dawn. Samson tore a lion apart in the vineyards of Timnath, and the book of Judges credits his strength to the spirit of the Lord.

David and Jonathan get long treatment as fighters and archers. Later parts ask how Jews in Greek and Roman times viewed Greek games, which their law and custom often resisted. Training with stones, archery practice, and Herod's skill with javelin and bow all appear. The entry weighs a mixed record: pride in strong heroes of old, set against deep doubt about the games of the gymnasium.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-axenfeld-august:
Auguste Axenfeld was a French physician. He was born at Odessa on Oct. 25, 1825, and died at Paris on Aug. 25, 1876. He was a son of Israel Aksenfeld. He studied medicine in Paris and took his degree from the Sorbonne. For his work in the cholera outbreaks of 1849 and 1854 he won two medals.

In 1853 Axenfeld began lecturing at the Sorbonne, and in 1857 he was elected a fellow. He became physician-in-chief at the Beaujin hospital and stood in for famed professors at two Paris schools. He kept those posts until 1871, when a grave disease of the brain struck him. The entry lists his books: works on hospital-caused disease, on wasting of the spinal cord, and a treatise on nervous disorders. He also wrote on Jean de Wier and the witch trials.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baking-2386:
Baking, for the ancient Hebrews, meant thin cakes rather than thick loaves. The entry starts with the oldest way: heat sand or small stones, brush off the fire, lay the dough on the hot ground, and cover it with glowing ashes. A few minutes did the work. Other ways used a heated iron plate, still common among Bedouins, or the house oven called "tannur."

A second half draws on rabbinic writing, which treats baking more fully than any other craft. Temple ritual held twelve meal-offerings, so flour, kneading, and leaven all mattered. Nearly all offerings were unleavened, and priests used lukewarm water to keep dough from rising. The showbread was so hard to make well that one family, the Garmu, alone was judged expert enough. The entry closes with women as bakers and the trade in Talmudic times.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baraita-of-the-:
Baraita of the Thirty-two Rules gives the thirty-two rules by which the Bible is read. Rashi uses it often and ascribes it to R. Eliezer b. Jose ha-Gelili. The Karaite Judah Hadassi took it into his "Eshkol ha-Kofer" and agreed on the author. It does not survive on its own. Knowledge of it comes from the recension in Samson of Chinon's "Keritot."

The entry divides the work in two. The list of rules is the real Baraita, from Eliezer's hand. The sections that explain each rule form a kind of Gemara on it, with sayings of tannaim and amoraim mixed in. Its method is chiefly haggadic, dealing with the syntax, style, and matter of the Bible. Written about 150, it may be the earliest work on Biblical hermeneutics. Two worked examples, on ellipsis and on a clause out of place, show its method.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-baruch-simon-25:
Simon Baruch was an American physician born at Schwersenz, Prussia, on July 29, 1840. He studied in Posen, then came to America and earned his medical diploma in 1862. He served three years in the Confederate army and was captured twice.

After the war Baruch led a hospital in North Carolina and later moved to New York. He wrote on malaria, childhood disease, and the uses of water in medicine. The entry credits him as a pioneer in the surgery of appendicitis. It also describes his work for free public baths in New York.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-beit-alfred-278:
Alfred Beit was a South African financier born in 1853 to a well known Hamburg Jewish family. He reached Kimberley in 1875, in the early days of the diamond rush. With partners such as Barnato and Rhodes he gained control of claims in the great mines there.

Beit supplied the money behind the De Beers venture and became a life governor of the mines. When gold was found on the Rand, his group staked claims fast and floated company after company. Shrewd selling by 1889 made him very rich. The entry also notes his part in the Jameson raid inquiry.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ben-oni-child-o: Ben-Oni, glossed as child of my affliction, is explained as a play on the name Benjamin. According to Genesis xxxv. 18, the dying Rachel gave that name to her son Benjamin. The entry gives no separate person or story under this heading. It offers the wordplay, the Genesis citation, and a pointer to the Benjamin entry for the fuller account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-benjamin-simeon: Simeon Benjamin, also known as Benjamin Levi, was an English Hebrew grammarian. At London in 1773 he published Da'at Ḳedoshim, or Knowledge of the Holy, a short Hebrew grammar. The entry singles the book out for one reason in particular. It counts among the earliest works written by an Ashkenazi Jew in England. No facts of his life, teaching post, or later years are given in this brief record.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-berlin-aryeh-lo:
Aryeh Löb Berlin, a German rabbi, was born in 1738 at Fürth, in Bavaria. He died at Cassel on May 21, 1814. Young, he served as a judge at Fürth and rabbi of Baiersdorf. In 1789 he became chief rabbi of Bamberg.

At Bamberg a lawsuit over the split of a large estate charged him with taking unlawful fees. He was cleared of dishonesty and paid only a fine on a tangled account. At Cassel he rose to chief rabbi of the Westphalian consistory in 1808 and to a council post the year after.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bessels-emil-31:
Emil Bessels was a German-American Arctic explorer and naturalist. He was born at Heidelberg on June 2, 1847. He died at Stuttgart on March 30, 1888. He studied medicine and zoology at Heidelberg. In 1869 he sailed to the Arctic Ocean. There he traced the Gulf Stream east of Spitzbergen.

In 1871 he joined the Hall expedition as surgeon. The ship "Polaris" reached far northern waters. Captain Hall fell ill and died that November. A charge of murder was later brought against Bessels. An official inquiry cleared him fully. It ruled that Hall died of apoplexy. Bessels later worked at the Smithsonian Institution. His tidal work proved the insularity of Greenland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bien-julius-328: Julius Bien was an American lithographer. He was born at Naumburg on September 27, 1826. His father was a ḥazan, lecturer, and lithographer. Bien studied art at Cassel and Frankfort. Moritz Oppenheim was among his teachers. He came to New York and set up business in 1850. His firm excelled at scientific work. It issued atlases and geological charts. It also made hydrographic charts. Exhibitions brought him medals and diplomas. They came at Philadelphia, Paris, and Chicago. The last Paris honor fell in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bloch-hermann-h:
Hermann Ḥayyim Bloch was a German author. He was born at Breslau on April 26, 1826. He died on November 19, 1896. His grandfather was chief rabbi Abraham Tiktin. At twenty-seven he issued his "Mebo ha-Talmud." It proposed a new theory of Halakah's growth. He never completed that vast theory.

Samples of his system appeared as "Hirhure Torah." Four parts came out from 1887 to 1893. They filled 519 quarto pages. He also modeled Herod's Temple plan in 1883. Private misfortunes drove him to Wisdom literature. His "Omri Inshi" versified 107 Oriental proverbs. He left much material unpublished.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-boleslaw-v-wsty: Boleslaw V Wstydliwy, the Bashful, was king of Poland from 1228 to 1279. In 1240 the Mongols under Batu-Khan invaded Poland in his reign. The entry says they carried many thousand Jews away as slaves to Asia. He also welcomed German artisans and brought in Magdeburg law. That influx stirred anti-Jewish hatred, and the entry marks his reign as the start of persecution in Poland.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-bosheth-shame-d:
Bosheth is a Hebrew word meaning shame or disgrace. The Prophets used it as a name for the shameful thing, the Baalim and their images. Hosea and Jeremiah both use it beside the name Baal itself.

Later use made Bosheth a stand-in for Baal in personal names. Ish-bosheth appears as Esh-baal in Chronicles, the entry notes. Mephibosheth likewise appears as Meri-baal in that book. One view ties the vowels of Molech to this word. The entry reports that view but does not fully accept it. Another view derives Bosheth from a deity named Basht or Bashta.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-breslau-marcus-: Marcus Heymann Breslau was an author and journalist who died in London on May 14, 1864. He came to London as a youth and taught Hebrew there. For a time he was attached to a synagogue. He worked on the Hebrew Review under Raphall. When the Jewish Chronicle started, he ran it for years and briefly owned it. He wrote a Hebrew grammar and dictionary as well. He also copied Hebrew manuscripts at Oxford for other scholars. A public testimonial honored his thirty years of literary work.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-buchholz-p-3786: P. Buchholz was a German rabbi born Oct. 2, 1837, and trained as a Talmud scholar with a taste for modern philosophy. He served at Märkisch-Friedland from 1863 to 1867, then at Stargard in Pomerania. In 1875 he became chief rabbi of Friesland and held the post until his death at Emden on Sept. 20, 1892. His small book of 1867 treated family relations in law and morals under Jewish teaching. Some of his speeches were printed. His journal pieces dealt with the codification of Jewish law and with Azaria Figo's sermons.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cantillation-39:
Cantillation is the mode of chant used in the public reading of prayers and Scripture. The entry begins with speech itself: tone shades show how words hang together. In a large space, a sing song delivery makes those links clear to every listener. Jews, it says, have used such musical declamation for Scripture from time beyond memory, aiming at the clear reading told in Nehemiah.

The long article then separates the chant of prayer from the chant of Bible reading. It follows signs, accents, and melody lines across rites and lands. Much space goes to how the accents mark both music and sentence sense. Closing notes point to studies of synagogue song from Talmudic times onward and to collections of the varied traditions.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cerfberr-freder: Frédéric Cerfberr, a French consul born at Strasburg on Oct. 27, 1786, died at sea on Sept. 18, 1842, while sailing from New York to France. Fond of travel and languages, he served France at New York, at New Orleans, and in Haiti. In 1826 he volunteered for Santo Domingo when no other envoy would go, owing to yellow fever there. Learning of misery at Cayes after an earthquake, he sent a ship of food at his own cost. A later Haiti earthquake, on May 7, 1842, killed his only daughter and wounded him fatally.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-chellus-codex-s: Chellus is a place named in Judith i. 9 as lying before Kadesh and the River of Egypt. Reland identified it with Elusa, south of Beersheba, a town noted for a special cult. That view is probably right, the entry says. A rival view takes Chellus as the biblical Halhul, named in Joshua xv. 58, but that is less likely. The name appears as Alusa in Josephus. The modern name is Chalasa, and the site holds only ruins.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cid-campeador-r:
Ruy Diaz de Vivar, known as El Cid Campeador, conquered Valencia in 1094 and stands as Spain's popular hero. The entry looks only at his dealings with Jews. Short of cash to pay his knights, he borrowed 600 marks from two rich Jews of Burgos, Don Rachel and Don Vidas, working through his nephew Martin Antolinez. Despite their care, he cheated them, the entry says plainly.

It also names a Jewish page, Gil, praised for rare loyalty, who later took his master's name, Diaz. The Cronica del Cid is judged a careless later mix of older chronicles. The first full translation of the Poema del Cid, by a Jewish convert, O. L. B. Wolff, appeared at Jena in 1850.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-cohen-jules-emi:
Jules Emile David Cohen, a French composer, was born at Marseilles on Nov. 2, 1830, and died in Paris in January, 1901. At the Paris Conservatoire, from 1847 to 1854, he won first prizes in piano, organ, harmony, counterpoint, and fugue. In 1870 he took charge of its choral class, and in 1877 he became chorus master at the Grand Opera.

His output was large: songs without words, harmonium studies and preludes, ballads, chamber music, and orchestral suites. Music for his sister's wedding at a Paris Jewish temple and a mass for men's voices were often played. For the stage he wrote operas from Vive l'Empereur in 1860 to Dea in 1870, plus fresh chorus music for Athalie and Esther.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-conditions-4586:
Conditions are the qualifications tied to an agreement that can start it, change it, or void it, based on whether something happens or not. A condition that must be met before the deal works is precedent; one that can end it later is subsequent. Roman and common law sort them seven ways, from positive and negative to mutual and mixed.

Jewish law knew all these classes, the entry says, but sorts them by its own logic. Three spoken formulas build an express condition: if, from now on if, and on condition that. The first carries four strict rules. A betrothal example shows the stakes. Say from now on, and a later gift of two hundred zuzim seals the match from the first rite, voiding any second man's claim in between.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-costa-da-pedigr: Da Costa Pedigree argues that the Da Costa family is probably one with the Mendez da Costa family. Their arms in England and Holland are nearly the same. The entry lists wide Marano kin ties, from Bravo and Bueno to Ricardo, Belmonte, and Aguilar. Those links make this pedigree a key to Sephardic family history. Four charts follow: two Dutch lines and two English lines. Emanuel Mendez da Costa, secretary of the Royal Society, compiled the early English stages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-crypto-jews-478: Crypto-Jews are Jews who profess another faith but practise Jewish rites in secret at home. Traces appear early, the entry says. The first wide spread came after the Almohade persecutions in Spain in 1146. The father of Maimonides is said to have taken Islam in name at that time. After 1391 a whole body of Spanish Jews took Christianity in form. They were called Maranos, or New Christians. The Inquisition aimed its chief work at them. Maranos could still be found in Portugal when the entry was written.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-csar-caius-juli:
Caius Julius Cæsar was a Roman dictator, consul, and conqueror. He was born on July 12, 100 B.C. He was assassinated on March 15, 44 B.C. His stance toward the Jews shows in the many decrees issued for them by him and the senate. An early decree, probably from July, 47 B.C., honors Hyrcanus, high priest and ethnarch of the Jews. It thanks him for aid in war, including 1,500 soldiers in the Alexandrian war.

More decrees follow. The Jews are to hold Jerusalem and wall it as they wish. Tribute terms are eased in the Sabbatical year. One quoted judgment praises Cæsar's keenness as a statesman. He saw the Jews, spread across the empire yet acting as one, as useful partners in a great Roman order. Josephus is the main source throughout.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-d-israeli-benja: Benjamin D'Israeli heads an entry that covers two men of the name. The first was an English merchant and financier. Born in Venice on Sept. 22, 1730, he came to England in 1748. He took out papers of denization only in 1801. A conforming Jew who gave to the synagogue, he held one minor post, inspector of charity schools in 1782. He died at Stoke Newington in 1816. The second was a Dublin notary from 1788 to 1796. He died in county Carlow in 1814.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-daniels-d-polak: D. Polak Daniels was a Dutch communal worker at The Hague. He died in 1899. The entry is short and gives only his service. He was active in Jewish communal affairs for many years. For more than forty years he presided over the Jewish community. He sat on the municipal council for the same long span. His funeral drew the highest dignitaries of Holland. No birth date, family, or writing is named. The single source cited is the Jewish Chronicle of May 12, 1899.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-davidovich-juda: Judah Löb Davidovich was a Russian Hebraist born at Wilna in 1855 who died at Odessa on January 1, 1898. His early life wandered: army service, study of surgery, work as an assistant surgeon, and a failed try at a singing career. About 1885 he settled in Odessa as a private teacher. There Asher Ginzberg turned him toward Hebrew literature. His chief work was a Hebrew translation of Herbert Spencer's essay on education, printed at Warsaw in 1894 with his own preface and notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-demophon-5086: Demophon appears in this slice as a name with a single short notice attached. The entry says he was apparently an officer under the command of Lysias. He served as a Syrian general in Palestine about 164 B.C. In that role he harried the Jewish population, who were already worn out by their many wars and were then busy with farming. The entry is only two lines long. It gives no dates for him and no source beyond the second book of Maccabees, chapter 12, verse 2.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-devotional-lite:
Devotional literature covers the private prayers Jews composed for special occasions, apart from the fixed liturgy. The Talmud strongly recommends such prayers and preserves many of them. Rabbi Eliezer warned that a prayer kept as a fixed form has no true devotion, since the worshiper adds nothing of his own.

The article sorts Talmudic devotions into kinds: general prayers, prayers for forgiveness, prayers said when studying the Torah, and prayers for the Temple's rebuilding. It prints examples of each. One asks that no envy enter the speaker's heart. Another blames sin on the leaven in the dough, meaning bad impulses, and on foreign rule. Later sections trace private devotion through later Jewish ages.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-diego-de-valenc: Diego de Valencia was a Spanish troubadour of the fifteenth century, born of Jewish parents at Valencia de Don Juan, in Leon. After converting to Christianity he became a Franciscan monk and a doctor of theology. Contemporaries called him a very learned physician, astrologer, and master of sciences. He was one of the leading poets of Valencia, and most of his poems stand in the "Cancionero de Baena." In satirical songs he mocked Jews and Maranos, using Hebrew terms and thereby mocking himself, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dorotheus-5286: Dorotheus, son of Nathanael, was one of the envoys the Jews sent to Rome in 45 C.E. The entry is very short and gives him no life story of his own. It records only the embassy's errand and its success. The envoys persuaded the emperor Claudius to agree that the high priest's garment should stay in Jewish hands. The entry cites Josephus, Antiquities xx, for the mission and its outcome.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-dyes-and-dyeing:
Dyeing is never named as a special art in the Bible, yet dyed cloth fills its pages. High priest vestments and Tabernacle gear used colored stuffs. Red seems the only color made at home. The Hebrew word for red often stands in for dye itself.

Talmudic pages name dyers and dyeing often. Phoenician purple was the famed trade, and the tribe of Zebulon was said to learn it from them. Jews near Tyre made purple for market, Benjamin of Tudela reports. A Jewish guild of purple dyers is cut on a tombstone at Hierapolis. For long stretches, the entry says, Jews held a near monopoly of the trade.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eberlen-abraham: Abraham ben Judah Eberlen was a German mathematician who lived at Frankfort-on-the-Main in the first half of the sixteenth century. The entry is only a few lines. It names a single work of his, the Sefer ha-Zifar. That book sets out mathematical problems together with their solutions. The entry even gives the day the book was finished: Tuesday, Feb. 27, 1537. No birth date, teacher, or other writing is recorded for him in these lines.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-einstein-edwin-: Edwin Einstein was born at Cincinnati on Nov. 18, 1842. He was schooled in New York city. Union College, at Schenectady, gave him a master of arts degree. He sat for New York in the Forty-sixth Congress. In 1892 he ran as the Republican candidate for mayor of New York. He polled more votes than any mayoral nominee of his party before him, yet the entry does not call him mayor. From 1895 to 1898 he served as docks commissioner and treasurer.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eliam-5586: Eliam is a name given to two men in the Bible. The entry keeps the record very short. One Eliam ranks among the heroes of David. He was a son of Ahithophel the Gilonite. The other Eliam was the father of Bath-sheba. First Chronicles gives his name in a swapped form, as Ammiel. The entry adds one point from stone records. The name is found in a Phoenician inscription as well. No deeds or words are told for either man.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-elishah-5686: Elishah is a name in the Bible's table of nations. Genesis counts Elishah among the four sons of Javan. That makes it a land kin to the Ionian Greeks. Ezekiel names it as a source of purple dye for Tyre. It lay somewhere on the Mediterranean Sea. Scholars have placed it in many spots since then. Some name the Peloponnesus, famed for its purple shellfish. Some name Aeolis, on an old tradition in Josephus. Others point to Sicily or the south of Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-eotvos-baron-jo: Baron Joseph Eotvos was a Hungarian statesman of note. He worked to free the Jews of Hungary from bars. He was born at Ofen on Sept. 13, 1813. He died at Budapest on Feb. 2, 1871. Years of travel in France shaped his liberal views. In 1840 he spoke in the Diet for Jewish freedom. A year later his pamphlet on the theme spread wide. It was turned into German and Italian for readers. His novel the Village Notary drew fine Jewish figures. In 1867 he won full freedom for Hungary's Jews at last.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ether-5886: Ether was one of the cities in the lowland of Judah allotted to Simeon. That single sentence is nearly the whole of the entry. It cites Joshua, chapter fifteen, verse forty-two, and chapter nineteen, verse seven. No history, size, site, or later fate is given for the town. The entry does not say who lived there or what happened there. A reader learns only where Ether stood in the tribal lists: a lowland town of Judah that passed to Simeon's share.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-fernandez-manue:
Manuel da Villareal Fernandez was a political economist and dramatist born in Lisbon of Marrano parents. He studied at Madrid and served years in the army, reaching captain. He then went to Paris as Portuguese consul-general. Back in Lisbon about 1650, he was seized by the Inquisition and garroted there on December 1, 1652.

His works praise Richelieu's statecraft in a life of the duke, defend Portugal's king against a critic, and mourn a sold prince. A five-book twelfth decade of the history of India also came from his pen in Paris. His son Jose taught Greek at Marseilles in 1682. The entry lists Spanish and Portuguese titles with their years, from 1637 to 1643.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-flesch-abraham-: Abraham Flesch was a rabbi in Vienna at the start of the seventeenth century. The brief entry gives no dates for his birth or death. It reports G. Wolf's view that he is the same man as Abraham Austerlitz. Its one named work is a eulogy by Flesch. The piece begins with set Hebrew words. It was printed at the end of a work by Isaac ben Judah Löb Mentz of Nikolsburg. That book came out at Amsterdam in 1688. Four short source lines close the notice.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-frankel-alexand:
Alexander Fränkel was an Austrian physician born at Vienna on November 9, 1857. He took his medical degree in 1880 and joined the sanitary corps of the Austrian army. As surgeon of the Teutonic Knights he took part in the Servian-Bulgarian war of 1885-86. He left the army in 1890 and became a lecturer on surgery at Vienna.

Since 1893 he has been chief surgeon at a Vienna children's hospital. Since 1895 he has also been assistant chief surgeon of the general dispensary there. In 1896 he became editor-in-chief of a Vienna clinical weekly. He has written many essays for medical journals. The entry adds that Fränkel has embraced Christianity.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-friedmann-berna:
Bernát Friedmann was a Hungarian jurist and criminal lawyer born in Grosswardein on October 10, 1843. He studied law at the law academy of his home town and at the University of Budapest. He won wide sympathy by his brave bearing in the noted Tisza-Eszlár trial. His first book treats Hungarian mining in trade and number terms, printed at Budapest in 1866.

A book on people's judges and juries followed in 1876. It won the grand prize of the academy. A work of 1878 treats appeals in criminal cases, with stress on open spoken trial. His last named book, of 1889, notes flaws in a plan for Hungarian criminal process.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gallows-6486: Gallows in the Hebrew Bible is named by the word for tree. It appears in Genesis, Deuteronomy, Joshua, and Esther. The frame Haman raised, and on which he himself died, is said to stand fifty cubits high. It was likely a stake for impaling, not a beam for hanging. The Mishnah form has an upright post and a cross beam. The condemned hung from it by the hands. It was not used to kill by choking.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gentili-6586:
Gentili is an Italian family of Gorizia whose members ranked as rabbis and Talmudic scholars. Azriel Gentili, a cabalist of the seventeenth century, is quoted on a verse of Exodus. Gershon ben Moses Gentili, born at Gorizia in 1683, died there in 1700 at age seventeen. He had already won fame as a scholar. His rhyming word book came out after his death.

Moses ben Gershon Gentili, born at Triest in 1663, taught Talmud and Midrash at Venice for many years. He wrote a comment on the Pentateuch, printed in 1710, and a tract on the Second Temple with a map. Manasseh ben Jacob Gentili headed the Verona rabbinical school. Jacob Hai Gentili won note as preacher, poet, and Talmudist at Gorizia.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gomel-benshen-g:
Gomel benshen is the saying of a thanksgiving blessing after escape from danger. Four escapes call for it. They are a desert crossing, release from prison, recovery from grave illness, and a safe sea voyage. The Talmud drew the duty from Psalm cvii. It must be done in public, before ten or more men at worship.

The Talmud's own wording blesses God "who bestoweth goodly mercies." Modern practice adds a Torah reading first. The saved person is called to the desk for a Pentateuch section. After the usual blessings he speaks the gomel formula. The bystanders answer with a wish for more of God's goodness. Maimonides and the Shulḥan 'Aruk are cited for the rules.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-gross-heinrich-:
Heinrich Gross was a German rabbi and scholar. He was born at Szenicz, Hungary, on Nov. 6, 1835. He finished the Breslau seminary and Halle University. His Halle thesis on Leibnitz won a prize in 1866. Baron Horace Günzburg then hired him as a private teacher in Paris. Two years there fed his great work.

That work is "Gallia Judaica" (Paris, 1897). It maps the towns and letters of medieval French Jewry. The entry calls it a standard work. Gross gathered its matter in the Bibliothèque Nationale. From 1875 he held the Augsburg rabbinate. His journal studies treat figures such as Abraham ben David of Posquières. He also wrote a textbook of Israelite religion for schools.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-habib-levi-ben-:
Levi ben Jacob ibn Ḥabib, born at Zamora, Spain, about 1480, became chief rabbi of Jerusalem and died there about 1545. As a youth of about seventeen in Portugal he was forced to accept baptism. He fled at the first chance to Salonica, where he could live openly as a Jew.

He reached Jerusalem in 1523, left, then settled there for good in 1525. His learning won him the chief rabbinate. There he fought a bitter feud with Jacob Berab of Safed over Berab's revival of rabbi ordination. Berab threw the forced baptism at him; Ibn Ḥabib owned it plainly. The feud helped end the ordination practice. He also edited his father's "'En Ya'aḳob" and left 147 responsa.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-halberstadt-jud: Judah ben Benjamin Halberstadt, also called Stadthagen, was a rabbinical author of the eighteenth century. He wrote "Minḥat Yehudah," which explains every passage in Rashi on Berakot where the word "ke-lomar" occurs. A like work of his, on Shabbat, 'Erubin, and Berakot, came later, at Altona in 1768. He also wrote a discourse on a passage at Berakot 36a: the blessing to say when eating radishes and olives. That piece came out at Altona in 1765.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hananiah-hanina:
Hananiah (Hanina) b. Hakinai was a tanna of the second century. He was a contemporary of Ben 'Azzai and Simon the Temanite. His regular teacher was Akiba. He left his wife and stayed with Akiba for twelve or thirteen years. In all that time he sent his family no word. Then he recovered them in a remarkable way. Though not regularly ordained, he was one of the few allowed to argue cases before the sages.

Several halakot and halakic midrashim survive in his name. Eleazar ben Jacob II preserved most of them. He also studied the mysteries of the Creation. He left homiletic remarks too. One says no man acts dishonestly toward his fellow without first becoming faithless to God. A late statement counts him among the ten martyrs.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hartmann-anton-:
Anton Theodor Hartmann, born at Dusseldorf on June 25, 1774, was a German author and Bible scholar. At Gottingen, Eichhorn drew him toward the Old Testament and Oriental tongues. After fifteen years of teaching, he took a chair of Old Testament theology at Rostock in 1811.

His books range from a study of Hebrew women's dress and bridal custom to a large work on the five books of Moses. That later work set out the fragment theory in a steady form. Near the end of his life he wrote pamphlets against Jewish emancipation, which drew a reply from Gotthold Salomon. He died on April 20, 1838.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hasdai-abu-yusu:
Hasdai ibn Shaprut, born about 915 at Jaen, was a Spanish doctor, diplomat, and patron of Jewish learning. He knew Hebrew, Arabic, and Latin, and he studied medicine. As court doctor to the calif Abd al-Rahman, he won deep trust. Without the title of vizier, he in fact ran foreign affairs and port dues at Cordova.

Hasdai received foreign envoys and helped turn a Greek book on plants into Arabic. He guided talks with envoys from Otto, the German ruler, and he settled a hard dispute between Leon and Navarre. The entry also tells of his work for fellow Jews. He sought word of the far-off Jewish realm of the Chazars.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hayyim-ben-mena: Hayyim ben Menahem of Glogau was a German scholar of the seventeenth and eighteenth centuries. He wrote a handbook on reading and writing Judeo-German. It was printed at Berlin about 1717 and aimed chiefly at women readers. The book gives rules for vowel points and short forms. It also gives correct spellings for personal names and for Polish and German towns. A Judeo-German word list closes it. Another writer later lifted a shortened form of the book, the entry notes.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-heilbronn-7486:
Heilbronn was a town in Wurttemberg on the Neckar with a long, harsh Jewish history. In 1298 Rindfleisch and his bands killed nearly 200 Jews there. In 1349 attackers burned the synagogue and looted Jewish homes. Kings and councils squeezed the community with taxes and decrees. At the end of the fifteenth century the Jews were ordered out for good.

No Jews lived there through the next century. A law of 1828 let them return. In 1861 twenty-one families dedicated a new synagogue. By 1903 the town held 920 Jews in a population of 37,889. It had become the seat of a district rabbinate covering many small towns.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-herder-johann-g:
Johann Gottfried von Herder, born at Mohrungen, East Prussia, on Aug. 25, 1744, was a German Protestant theologian, poet, and writer. He studied at Königsberg. He taught and preached at Riga, then served as court preacher at Bückeburg and Weimar.

Herder's work on Hebrew Bible literature had wide influence. He treated the oldest Bible poems as Oriental national songs, not simple revelation accounts. He read Canticles as natural love songs. His famous 1782-83 work praised Hebrew poetry as the world's oldest and most soulful. Grätz notes his admiration for Jewish antiquity, yet also an early dislike of Jews that softened toward Mendelssohn later. Herder died at Weimar on Dec. 21, 1803.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hierei-7686: Hierei is a term used for the priests in the Jewish community of Rome, the entry explains. Even as late as the fourth century they held a distinct place in the community's religious life. They ranked higher than the archisynagogi. That ranking is drawn from a novel of Justinian in the Theodosian Code, as cited here. The entry is only three lines long. It names one history of the Jews in Rome as its source and gives no names of individual priests.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-hiyya-b-meria-o: Ḥiyya, son of Meria, was a Palestinian amora of the fourth generation, in the third and fourth centuries. He appears only in the Jerusalem Talmud, the entry says. He was a pupil of Jonah and of Jose. One teaching he passed on, in the name of Levi, holds that a man's wife is chosen for him before birth. It is proved from a psalm verse. The entry notes that the same teaching appears elsewhere under another Ḥiyya's name, likely by a copyist's error.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-ibn-ezra-isaac-:
Isaac ibn Ezra, called Abu Sa'd, was a Spanish poet of the twelfth century and son of Abraham ibn Ezra. He won fame as a poet while still young in Spain. Al-Harizi says the father's brilliance flashes in the son's songs. He probably left Spain with his father before 1140.

By 1143 Isaac was at Bagdad under the patronage of the Arab Hibat Allah. He praised that patron in verse and wrote on Ecclesiastes. When Hibat Allah turned to Islam, Isaac followed him. Al-Harizi laments that the glory of God no longer shone over him in eastern lands. Abraham mourned the loss in two elegies. He seems to have heard the news only years after it happened.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaac-ben-judah: Isaac ben Judah Löb was a rabbi at Offenbach in the first half of the eighteenth century. He wrote "Be'er Yitzhak," a commentary on the Haftarot, printed with the text in 1729. He also wrote "Me'irat Enayim," on the 613 Biblical precepts as Maimonides ordered them, printed at Fürth in 1730. In the preface to that second work he mentions the first one. Apart from that preface, the entry notes, the "Be'er Yitzhak" is otherwise unknown.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-isaiah-ascensio:
The Ascension of Isaiah is an apocryphal book built from three parts that once stood alone. One part is Jewish in origin and two are Christian. The name itself fits only chapters vi to xi, where Isaiah journeys through the seven heavens. The earlier chapters hold the Martyrdom of Isaiah, a Jewish piece, and a Christian apocalypse linked with the Testament of Hezekiah. In the Ethiopic version the whole work carries the one title.

The entry lays out the contents section by section, then weighs the studies of Dillmann and Charles on how the parts were joined. From internal signs and from quotes in later writers, it dates all three parts to the first century. It also traces three threads in Jewish writing behind the book: the legend of Isaiah's death, the Beliar myth, and the seven heavens. Editions by Laurence, Dillmann, and Charles close the account.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-israel-b-moses-: Israel b. Moses was a Polish cabalist of the end of the sixteenth century. The entry knows him only through one book, "Tamim Yahdaw." In it he gathered every verse of Psalms and Proverbs that the Zohar quotes, together with the Zohar's own explanations of them. A cabalistic treatise on the soul opens the collection. A prayer poem by the compiler also stands at its head. No town, teacher, or date from his life is given here.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jacobsthal-joha: Johann Eduard Jacobsthal, a German architect, was born at Stargard, Pomerania, on Sept. 17, 1839. He studied at the architectural academy in Berlin and traveled long in Greece and Asia Minor. In 1874 he became a professor at that academy. His best-known work was on railroad stations in Alsace-Lorraine, at Metz from 1874 to 1878 and Strasburg from 1877 to 1884. He also built the Alexanderplatz station in Berlin and gates for railway bridges at Dirschau and Marienburg. His books cover ornament grammar and tile designs from southern Italy.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jeremiah-8586:
Jeremiah, son of Hilkiah, was a prophet in the days of Josiah and his sons. Born in 650 B.C. at Anathoth, a small town three miles north of Jerusalem, he came from a priestly family with land there. Called while still young in 626 B.C., he spoke for more than forty years, until after Jerusalem fell to Nebuchadnezzar in 586 B.C.

Of a gentle nature, he longed for his people's peace yet had to announce its ruin and watch it come. The entry gives the fullest life known for any Israelite prophet, drawn from his book's history parts and his own words. It traces his fights with false prophets, priests, and princes across a whole age of crisis.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joab-ben-jehiel: Joab ben Jehiel was a writer of sacred poems who lived at Rome in the fourteenth century. He belonged to the Beth-El family. He wrote five poems for Passover on themes from the Song of Songs, printed in the Roman prayer book. He also wrote poems for the Festival of Weeks, the New Year, and the Day of Atonement. A dawn prayer and a penitential poem carry his name as well. He is thought to be the young poet whom Immanuel of Rome mocked in verse.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-jose-b-abin-cal: Jose ben Abin, also called Jose ben Abun, was a Palestinian teacher of the fourth century. A son of Abin the First, he first studied under a master whose coldness to his own family drove the pupil away. He then followed Assi, or Jose the Second. He became the weightiest of the last law men of his age in Palestine. He knew Babylonian teaching as well as local custom, likely through his father's travels. His chief work was setting out the Mishnah and the masters' rulings clearly.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-joseph-ben-samu: Joseph ben Samuel ibn Rey was an Italian rabbi who died young at Venice on April 2, 1608. His gravestone hints that his surname meant son of a king, though Wolf read it in another way. He wrote Sefer Massoret, a study of the Masorah, the notes guarding the Bible text. In it he tried to show that no repeat in the Bible lacks a reason. Samuel Aboab names him in his responsa called Debar Shemuel. The entry is short and gives no birth date or place.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judah-ben-elija: Judah ben Elijah Tishbi was a Karaite scholar and liturgical poet who flourished at Belgrade in the first half of the sixteenth century. He was a grandson of Abraham ben Judah. Judah copied and finished his grandfather's work on the Bible, called Yesod Mikra. His own liturgical poems entered the Karaite prayer book. He also copied the Yehi Me'orot, a work on the commandments credited to Tobiah ben Moses. The entry rests on Pinsker and on Fuerst's history of the Karaites.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-judgment-12686:
Judgment, in law, is the final order of a court in a civil or criminal case. Under Talmudic law the chief of the court spoke the judgment in the accused's presence. An acquittal could not be reversed, while a conviction could, on a sound plea or on new witnesses for the defense.

In civil cases the form was bare: A, thou art guilty; B, thou art innocent. Judgment could be given even with the parties away. A written copy could be had only before the parties left the room, and it left out the judges' names. Reasons were added only in set cases. Judges might not later reveal their private views, and new facts could ground a fresh trial.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kamnial-kambil-:
Abraham b. Meïr ibn Kamnial lived at Saragossa about the year 1100. In Arabic he was known as Abu al-Ḥasan. He was a Spanish physician. He was also a patron of poetry and letters. He used his place to guard Jewish communities in Spain, Babylonia, and Egypt. In Hebrew grammar he is known for a memory line. It joins the eleven servile letters of the Hebrew alphabet.

Great poets praised Kamnial in his own day. Moses ibn Ezra lauds him at length in his "Tarshish." That book is dedicated to Kamnial. Judah ha-Levi praised him in verse as well. Judah also composed his epitaph. The entry names a kinsman, Joseph ben Kamnial, likewise a physician.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-kermanshah-pers:
Kermanshah is the capital of the Persian province of Ardilan. It stands on the road between Bagdad and Hamadan. Benjamin II. found forty Jewish families there. About 1894 the governor's attacks sacked the Jewish quarter. Twenty families of Jewish physicians turned Moslem under that pressure. In Oct. 1902 two Jews of the town were killed nearby.

In 1903 the community counted 1,406 souls. Its quarter sits by the eastern wall, cut off by a stream. Jews may not buy land past that stream. The quarter holds 135 houses and three synagogues. Most Jews work at spinning; about thirty trade. The entry notes the town's Jewish doctors. It also lists nearby hamlets with Jewish families, some with as few as twelve.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-klemperer-georg: Georg Klemperer was a German physician. He was born at Landsberg-on-the-Warthe on May 10, 1865. He was a son of Wilhelm Klemperer. He studied at Breslau, Halle, and Berlin, taking his M.D. in 1885. From 1887 to 1896 he was assistant to Professor von Leyden. In 1895 he became professor at the University of Berlin. Since 1899 he has edited the "Therapie der Gegenwart." His works include a manual of clinical diagnosis. It reached its eighth edition in 1900.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lazarus-josephi: Josephine Lazarus, an American essayist born in New York city on March 23, 1846, has lived there all her life. Her first noted work was the life sketch of her sister Emma, printed in The Century in Oct. 1888 and set before Emma's poems in 1889. Essays on Bashkirtseff, Alcott, and Fuller followed by 1893. Six essays on Jewish themes became The Spirit of Judaism in 1895. She urges Jews to leave spiritual isolation and Christians to judge Jews with more fairness. Four Zionist pieces ran from 1897 to 1902.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lesser-ludwig-9:
Ludwig Lesser, a German poet, editor, and publicist, was born at Rathenow on Dec. 7, 1802, and died at Berlin on Dec. 2, 1867. He went to Berlin young and wrote for most of its literary journals, often as Ludwig Liber. The humorist Saphir drew him onto his staff, and the two stayed firm friends.

In 1827 Lesser and Saphir founded the Literarische Sonntags-Verein. He wrote a chronicle of the Gesellschaft der Freunde in 1842. A choice of his poems came out after his death in 1870. For Jewish life he helped found the Jüdischer Kulturverein, a fund for Jewish teachers, and the Berlin Reform congregation.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-levy-hayman-988:
Hayman Levy, a colonial merchant of New York, was born in 1721 and died in New York in 1789. He went into business young. By 1760 he owned a privateer and traded in furs. In 1770 he signed strong non-importation resolutions in New York. He had failed in business in 1768 but soon won back his losses.

When the British took New York, Levy moved to Philadelphia. He helped found Congregation Mickvé Israel in 1782 and sat on its first board. In 1784 he came back to New York and helped rebuild the congregation there. The entry calls him one of the city's best known merchants. He was probably the first employer of John Jacob Astor.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-lilith-lxx-symm:
Lilith is a female demon. Of three Assyrian demons named in the entry, the second, Lilit, is the one tied to Isaiah chapter thirty-four. Scholars split on her name. Some take her as a goddess of the night. Others, backed by cuneiform texts, make her a storm demon with no tie to the Hebrew word for night.

In Talmud and Midrash, Lilith takes fuller shape as a demon of the night. The entry classes demons in three kinds: spirits with no body, devils in full human shape, and lilin in human shape with wings. Lilith appears as a tempting woman with long hair. Traditions link her to Adam and to Eve and to the births of spirits over long years.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-loewenthal-edua: Eduard Loewenthal was a German writer and editor born on March 12, 1836, at Ernsbach. He studied law and philosophy at Tübingen and took his doctorate in 1859. He founded and edited several papers in Frankfort, Leipsic, and Berlin. In 1874 he founded a German group to spread peace ideas. After two prison terms from press cases, he lived in Brussels, London, and Paris, then returned to Berlin in 1888 under an amnesty. His books cover philosophy, law, and peace.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-luncz-abraham-m:
Abraham Moses Luncz, a Russian scholar who made Jerusalem his life's work, is profiled in the 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia. Born at Kovno on December 9, 1854, he moved to Jerusalem while still very young. Blind for many years, he helped found an institution for the blind there with Dr. Koisewski. He was still living in Jerusalem in 1904.

The article praises his service to the study of the Holy Land. He wrote guidebooks, Palestine annuals, and a Jerusalem almanac covering history, geography, and the land itself. His six-volume Jerusalem yearbook appeared in Hebrew and German between 1881 and 1903. He also ran a Hebrew printing press and began a Palestinian library. A new edition of the Jerusalem Talmud, with his commentary, was in press. The entry honors a blind scholar who mapped his city for others.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mahanaim-10286:
Mahanaim, a city east of the Jordan, is located and traced in a Jewish Encyclopedia article from 1906. It first appears where Jacob, returning from Aram, saw a vision of angels. That implies the place was a sanctuary from a very early period. In Joshua's allotments it belonged to Gad and was assigned as a Levitical city. It stood near the river Jabbok.

The article follows the city's brief hour in Israel's history. Abner brought Saul's son Ish-bosheth there and made it his capital. David later fled to Mahanaim during Absalom's rebellion and stayed until recalled. Solomon placed one of his supply officers there. After Shishak's invasion the city vanishes from the record, perhaps destroyed in resisting him. Its name seems dual in form, read as two camps. Scholars still argue over its exact site, most placing it near the wadi Ajlun.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mar-10386:
Mar, an Aramaic word for lord, is traced through Jewish usage in a 1906 Jewish Encyclopedia article. Daniel addresses the king as Mari, my lord, in the Bible. In Palestinian schools Mari and Rabbi were the polite address for sages. King Jehoshaphat, the Talmud says, rose to greet a scholar with both titles.

The article shows how address became a fixed title in Babylonia. There Mar stood before a scholar's name, as with Mar Samuel and Mar Ukba. Abaye called his uncle and teacher simply Mar, with no name added. A scholar's son citing his father said Abba Mari, my father, my lord. In the geonic period Mar and Rab combined into the double title Mar Rab. The prayer Yekum Purkan still calls scholars our lords and masters. The entry follows one small word from courtesy into the official style of the Babylonian academies.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-michael-moses-g:
Moses Gerson Michael, born on August 15, 1862, at Jefferson, Georgia, was an American merchant who built a dry-goods fortune at Athens. Cyrus Adler and Herbert E. Choate wrote his Jewish Encyclopedia entry in 1906. He graduated from the University of Georgia with highest honors and went straight into business with his brother Simon.

Michael's money and energy fed the growth of northeastern Georgia, where he backed several large industrial ventures. He held the rank of lieutenant-colonel in the state militia and served as aide-de-camp to Governor Candler, with a seat on the Democratic committee of his congressional district. At home in Athens he ran the Jewish Sabbath-school for years as his own special charge.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-mordecai-dato-b:
Mordecai Dato — Dato being the Italian of Nathan — was a Ferrara poet of the sixteenth century, recorded by Wilhelm Bacher and S. J. Levinson in the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He annotated Samuel Gallico's cabalistic 'Asis Rimmonim with notes he called Hagahot, glosses, when it was printed at Venice in 1601.

Azariah dei Rossi credits him with a book on the coming of the Messiah, Migdal Dawid. His lasting work was verse: many liturgical poems survive in manuscript, and one, for the eve of the Sabbath, entered the Italian ritual itself — still sung when the entry was written. The bibliography is long for so short a notice, running from Steinschneider to Mortara.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-motot-simeon-be:
Simeon ben Moses ben Simeon Motot was a Jewish mathematician of the fifteenth century, probably in Lombardy. The Jewish Encyclopedia entry, by its editorial committee and Max Schloessinger, admits that nothing is known of his life. His date is guessed from the friends to whom he dedicated his algebra. They flourished at Mantua in the middle of the century.

Two small works of his survive. His Sefer ha-Alzibra takes a Christian book of theorems stated without proof and supplies the missing demonstrations, adding theorems of his own. The other work solves the problem of the asymptotes, the two lines that approach but never meet. Later scholars credit him with the pure equations of the third and fourth degrees.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nahmoli-joseph-: Joseph Nahmoli was an eighteenth-century Talmudist and rabbi of Larissa, given a short notice in the Jewish Encyclopedia by its editorial committee and J. S. Raisin. He had studied under Hayyim Abulafia. His son-in-law was Isaac ibn Shangi, author of a commentary on the Pentateuch. Nahmoli himself wrote homilies for Sabbaths and holy days, printed at Smyrna, and another work issued with his teacher's.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-naumbourg-samue:
Samuel Naumbourg was a French composer of synagogue music. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Dennenlohe, Bavaria, on March 15, 1817. He died at Saint-Mandé, near Paris, on May 1, 1880. He first served as hazzan at Besançon.

Naumbourg directed the choir at Strasburg after Besançon. In 1845 Paris called him to the Nazareth synagogue. He also taught liturgical music at the Séminaire Israélite. His Chants Liturgicals appeared in 1847. Zemirot Yisrael, in 1864, held the complete liturgy in music. His last work revived songs by Solomon de Rossi. Baron Edmond de Rothschild had found part of them.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-nevakhovich-lob:
Löb Nevakhovich was a Russian writer who defended his people. Herman Rosenthal and J. G. Lipman wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in Letichev, Volhynia, in the 1700s. He died at St. Petersburg in August 1831. He went there young under Abram Peretz's patronage.

Trade came first, then literature won him over. He was among Russia's first Jews fluent in Russian. He loved Mendelssohn and took pride in Russian patriotism. His Cry of the Daughter of Judah pled for tolerance. It was a Russian Jew's first public defense of Jews. His play Sulioty reached the Imperial Theater in 1809. The emperor himself saw it performed that October. His grandson was the scientist Mechnikov of later fame.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-norden-joshua-d:
Joshua D. Norden was an English soldier and adventurer. Joseph Jacobs and Goodman Lipkind wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He died at Graham's Town in Cape Colony. The date was April 26, in 1846. He held a captain's rank in the yeomanry.

He was field commandant in the Kaffir war then. In 1846 he led mounted men against the Kaffirs. Six men rode with him toward the hills. The enemy lay in ambush along their path. A rifle ball pierced Norden's head in the fight. His men were forced to retire without him. Next day they recovered their commandant's body. It was found in a shockingly mutilated state. The Jewish Chronicle reported his death that July.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-olive-11686:
The olive is a green tree that keeps its leaves all year. Emil G. Hirsch and Immanuel Benzinger wrote on it for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. It is one of the most marked trees of Palestine. The Hebrew word zayit names the grown, tame tree. A wild kind grew in the land as well.

No one can say just where the olive first grew wild. Its use in Egypt and Syria goes far back. In Palestine it was grown long before Israel came. The Canaanites taught the new folk how to raise it. A branch of it comes in the tale of Noah's ark. The tree is grown from wild stocks that are grafted. The soil round it must be plowed more than once a year. Its fruit is picked in the fall months.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-osiris-daniel-1:
Daniel Osiris was a French giver of gifts and patron of art. Isidore Singer and Jacques Kahn wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born at Bordeaux on July 23, 1825. For more than half a century he knew great men. Those men led in art, in rule, in books, and in science.

Daniel gave his life and his wealth to good works. He gave his home town a set of public springs. At Arcachon he built a fine synagogue for the Jews. He set up a statue of Joan of Arc at Nancy. That town gave him its freedom for the gift. He built a Paris synagogue in the Rue Buffault. It was opened on September 3, in 1877. In 1903 he gave the state the famed Malmaison house. That house had been the home of the empress Josephine.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-panzieri-or-pan:
Panzieri was a Portuguese family found in two great towns. Richard Gottheil and Ismar Elbogen wrote its entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. Its men are met at Constantinople and at Rome. They are met there from the sixteen hundreds on. The family still had men in Italy in 1904.

The chief man of the Constantinople branch was Ephraim Panzieri. He was a doctor and a man of the Cabala school. He thrived at Constantinople about the year 1550. He went to Damascus to read with Hayyim Vital there. He lived a strict life of fast and prayer in that town. Men held him in awe and called him a saint. The Rome branch held Moses and Shabbethai Panzieri. Shabbethai was rabbi of Rome in 1652 and 1653.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pedro-de-toledo:
Pedro de Toledo was Spain's viceroy in Naples. Isidore Singer and Meyer Kayserling wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He stood out as a friend and protector of Jews. Few rulers of his age earned that name. His court gave Jews room to serve and teach.

About 1530 he took Don Samuel Abravanel into his service. Samuel, the youngest son of Isaac Abravanel, ran his finances. The viceroy's daughter Leonora also crossed the usual lines. She took lessons from Samuel's wife, the learned Benvenida. Leonora later married Cosimo de Medici of Florence.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pharaoh-lxx-120:
Pharaoh is the Bible's title for the kings of Egypt. Emil G. Hirsch and Louis H. Gray wrote the article for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. The word starts as Egyptian for great house. It first named the palace, not the king.

The meaning shifted slowly from house to ruler. By the eighteenth dynasty it named the monarch outright. The Bible speaks of eleven Egyptian kings in all. The first took Sarai into his harem in error. He freed her when God struck his house. Joseph's Pharaoh gets a close look at names and dates.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-pirogov-nikolai:
Nikolai Pirogov was a Russian surgeon and school reformer. Herman Rosenthal wrote his entry for the Jewish Encyclopedia of 1906. He was born in 1810 and died in 1881. His fame in medicine reached across Russia.

Alexander the Second sought Pirogov's counsel on schools. He made him superintendent at Odessa, then at Kiev. There Pirogov first came to know the Jews. He treated them with rare and open fairness. Class prejudice, he said, had no place in science. His farewell to Berdychev's Jews disclaimed all credit. Fairness, he told them, was simply his nature.
jewish-encyclopedia-1906-porges-nathan-1:
