The built sample kept signal loss low, kept the four ports well isolated, and held the four signals closely matched in strength and timing across its band. Heat-spreading features dump stray energy safely when outputs mismatch. Radar builders get a compact combiner proven at high power.
plos-pone-0354186:
Candace Alagata and colleagues balanced the carbonate books for coral reefs at seven sites around O'ahu, Hawai'i. A reef grows when corals build limestone faster than other organisms and forces wear it away. Their 2026 census-based study used regional growth rates for each coral type and measured cover, diversity, and surface complexity.

Net production ranged from slightly negative at the weakest site to strongly positive at the best. Overall, production across the island's reefs came out net positive. The team also tested which reef traits best predict growth and erosion balances. Alagata and colleagues say such budgets give managers a single health metric that tracks whether a reef is building or crumbling.
plos-pone-0354386:
Mukesh and colleagues, in a 2026 study, forecast disturbances in the ionosphere, the charged upper layer of the air, during volcanic eruptions. Eruptions send waves up that stir this layer, which can bend satellite signals and throw off GPS positions. Their measure is the total count of electrons along a signal's path, drawn mainly from a station in Indonesia.

The team built a hybrid forecaster that averages two learning methods, one based on decision trees and one on memory networks. They compared it against each part alone and against two classic statistical methods. Six eruptions served as test cases, with data from other latitudes used to check that the model travels. Four error measures judged the forecasts. The authors aim to give satellite and navigation services warning time when an eruption is likely to scramble signals, so operators can plan around the worst hours.
plos-pone-0354486: Li and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on social media and false beliefs. The title states its main point directly: using social media has only a limited effect on what people wrongly believe. That cuts against a common fear that feeds are the main driver of misperceptions. The work adds evidence to debates about platform rules, media habits, and how false claims spread.
plos-pone-0354886:
Hasan Öncül and four colleagues published this 2026 study of blood groups and age-related macular degeneration, a leading cause of vision loss in older adults. Records covered nearly five hundred patients at a specialist center, classed as wet or dry degeneration, with major risk factors like smoking excluded. Blood group and Rh status came from medical files.

The overall blood group distribution differed modestly between the two degeneration types, while Rh status showed no link at all. Öncül calls the clinical meaning uncertain and asks for larger studies that adjust for many factors at once.
plos-pone-0355186:
Yanqin Liu, Miao Zhang, and Yuwen Peng survey doctoral students in 2026. They ask what turns drive into fresh academic work. The setting is research shaped by new AI tools. More than five hundred students took part. They rated self driven drive and pressure driven drive. They also rated having no drive at all.

Both kinds of drive linked to more fresh work. Having no drive linked to less of it. Good resources and support made the good links stronger. Belief in one's own creative skill helped too. Skill with AI tools helped as well. These factors also softened the harm of having no drive. Schools should pair drive support with real resources and sound training.
plos-pone-0355286:
Elena Galitsyna and colleagues work in 2026 on coaxing stem cells from human fat tissue to become bone forming cells. Their method silences a gene that holds back bone growth, using short RNA pieces carried into the cells. They compared several carrier products and several RNA designs to find a mix that entered cells well without harming them.

One common carrier worked best and stayed gentle even at high amounts. With it, the chosen RNA cut the target gene's activity and pushed the cells toward bone formation. The team frames the result as groundwork, with animal studies still needed before any clinical use.
plos-pone-0355386:
Bingtong Wang, Shunchao Wang, and Gaili He model in 2026 how drivers decide to merge onto a freeway when a lane change is forced. Their game based model treats the merging driver and the main road driver as two players weighing speed gains against safety loss. Ideas from the study of risky choice shape how losses loom larger than gains.

Real vehicle path data from two United States freeways were used to tune and test the model. It spotted the observed choices in more than nine cases out of ten. Adding the risk based view improved both accuracy and how well the choices made sense in human terms, the authors report.
plos-pone-0355486:
Paul Mellor, Stephanie Kendall, and Deborah Anderson screen drugs in 2026. They test a large set of approved drugs on a lung cancer. The cancer is hard to treat and has few targeted options. Cells were grown flat in dishes and as small balls. Drugs that killed flat cells were checked for strength. Ball models were checked for shrinkage after treatment.

Cells in balls resisted drugs more than flat cells did. Still, dozens of drugs worked in both models. Four stood out for one key reason. They hit a spreading form harder than its less spreading match. One was a hormone related drug. The other three are used against infections. Those four merit further study, the authors say.
plos-pone-0355686:
Selamawit Gebeyehu and colleagues explore in 2026 why young children in Ethiopia rarely get checks for early development during routine care. Their qualitative work in the Gamo Zone drew on interviews with health workers and parents of children under five. Discussion covered both giving the checks and reaching them.

Workers pointed to weak buildings, scarce funds, limited backing, and gaps in their own training. Parents faced low income, stigma, and local beliefs about delay. Trust in routine child health work and a clear referral route helped. Strengthening frontline skill while building on that trust is presented as the most workable path forward.
plos-pone-0355986: Aksen and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on abuse, impulse control, and drug use. They asked whether poor impulse control changes the strength of the link between sexual abuse and how often people use substances. The data spanned many countries and many gender and sexual identities. Knowing where that link is strongest can help target support to survivors at highest risk.
plos-pone-0356186:
Peng Liu and coauthors published a 2026 animal study in PLOS ONE on easing transport stress in piglets with astragalus polysaccharides, plant sugars from a traditional medicinal root. Transport is among the worst days of a young pig's life: crowding, fasting, vibration, and heat swings spike stress hormones, oxidative damage, and inflammation. Piglets were trucked with no supplement, or a low or high dose, and blood was sampled over the following week.

Unsupplemented piglets showed the expected surge: stress hormones up, reactive oxygen up, a key antioxidant enzyme down, inflammatory signals raised. Supplemented piglets blunted every move on day one, the high dose protecting more strongly, and by days three and seven their values drifted back toward unstressed controls. The supplement is proposed as a feed strategy for welfare around transport, when antibiotics are a poor substitute for prevention.
plos-pone-0356286:
Ville Kailankangas and seven colleagues in Finland profile gene activity in the blood of patients with invasive group A streptococcal disease in this 2026 study. Their aim was to learn why some die weeks after surviving the worst. Forty-five patients were recruited, with blood drawn in the first days after admission and again about a week later. Eight patients died within three months, half of them in the first week.

The gene patterns tied to severe disease looked markedly different between the two draws. At the later timepoint, high activity of genes involved in a form of cell death called necroptosis, together with low activity of immune-presentation genes, was associated with death. The authors caution that the group was small, so these signatures are leads about distinct mechanisms for early and late deaths, not ready predictors.
plos-pone-0356386:
Guangjing Wen and five colleagues follow patients through their first six months on maintenance dialysis to map how psychological resilience evolves, in this 2026 multicenter study from China. Nearly seven hundred people starting regular hemodialysis were assessed seven times, and modeling sorted them into groups whose resilience followed distinct paths. Starting dialysis is a profound life change, and the team wanted to know who adapts and who sinks.

Just over half stayed highly resilient throughout. About a third stayed low and flat, while a smaller group started high but fell fast. The falling group was marked at baseline by depression, anxiety, poor sleep, and more illness burden. The low group added older age, being unmarried, lower income, more hospitalizations, and less activity. The authors argue resilience screening belongs in early dialysis care, with support aimed at the groups most likely to struggle.
plos-pone-0356486:
Tuba Şafak and Ahmet Burak Erdem asked whether a quick bedside ultrasound can judge body fluid levels. Their patients were emergency cases whose blood sodium was dangerously high. Their 2026 study enrolled sixty adults at a Turkish hospital. It measured the width of the large vein returning blood to the heart. It also measured that vein's ratio to the aorta. Readings came before fluids and again three hours into treatment.

Patients whose sodium failed to improve early started with a notably higher vein-to-aorta ratio. The ultrasound measures separated early responders from non-responders fairly well. They were also quite sensitive. Pressure readings from catheters, by contrast, did not differ between groups. The authors suggest ultrasound can add fast, harmless information when deciding how much fluid to give.
plos-pone-0356686:
Oliver Ombeva Malande and a large team report a pilot quality project in Kampala, Uganda. It aimed to strengthen HPV vaccination for teenage girls who live with HIV. These girls face higher risk from the virus, yet uptake and course completion in the city were low and the reasons poorly understood. At two urban HIV treatment centers, several hundred girls were enrolled. They joined surveys on knowledge and attitudes. They also joined discussion groups and a vaccination drive. The team documented the drive's lessons.

Baseline coverage, knowledge gaps, and practical barriers were mapped before and during the drive, with a small number of families declining to join. Malande and colleagues use the pilot to show what a clinic-anchored vaccination push requires, from consent to follow-up, before any wider program for this high-risk group.
plos-pone-0356786:
Jutima Rattanakoch and colleagues tested whether a consumer-grade wearable motion sensor system can measure walking in people with below-knee amputations well enough for clinic use. A research-grade reference served as the yardstick. Their 2026 study fitted thirty-two unilateral amputees with both systems at once. It walked them through repeated trials. Hip, knee, and ankle angles were derived from each system. Trial-to-trial consistency and agreement between the workflows were checked.

Repeatability was excellent nearly everywhere. Agreement between systems was strongest in the forward plane of motion. There, knee and ankle readings differed by only a couple of degrees on average. Agreement ran looser for side-to-side and rotational measures, and for the prosthetic ankle. The transparent, low-cost workflow could let ordinary clinics quantify gait without a motion laboratory.
plos-pone-0356886:
Shuyi Tang and colleagues test whether a sugary coating shed by a yogurt bacterium can slow norovirus, the stomach bug behind much foodborne illness. No solid prevention exists for this virus, so food-based defenses draw interest. In lab dishes, mouse immune cells were infected with a mouse form of the virus, then treated with the bacterial coating, and virus levels and immune gene activity were measured.

Treatment after infection cut the amount of virus released by the cells. Gene readings showed the coating steered the cells toward antiviral alarm signals, boosting the very pathways that fight viruses. Tang and colleagues suggest the coating works by waking up innate defenses rather than attacking the virus directly, a route worth testing in animals next.
plos-pone-0357086:
Xiufang Hou, Yanglan Wang, Fangfang Wang, and Qiuping Li interview nursing undergraduates in a geriatric nursing minor about whether they would work in long-term care homes. Demand for elder care staff is climbing, but hospitals still win graduates' hearts. Fourteen students spoke in depth about their hopes and hesitations, and the team distilled their accounts into themes.

Three themes stood out. Interest in elder care is real but young, fed by the visible market need. Students doubt their own readiness, feeling their skills misfit the setting. And they see the wider support web of government, society, and family as underbuilt, alongside worries about status, workload, and thin career ladders. Hou and colleagues say fixing the pipeline means raising the setting's standing, not just recruiting harder.
plos-pone-0357186:
Georgios Bouloukakis and colleagues use artificial intelligence tools to chart and forecast world publication trends in microsurgery, the fine vessel-and-nerve repair specialty. Research fashion shapes funding and training, yet this field's output had never been projected formally. The team pulled metadata from twenty surgical journals across fifteen years, sorted true microsurgery papers with a keyword system checked against human review, and raced several forecasting models against each other.

From ninety thousand records, about eleven and a half thousand verified microsurgery papers remained, and yearly output grew by well over half across the period. A straight-line projection proved most stable for short horizons in their tests, and forecasts run to the decade's end. Bouloukakis and colleagues offer editors and societies a planning lens, with uncertainty stated openly.
plos-pone-0357286:
Kristina W Dreiås and five colleagues examine how often couples trying to conceive have intercourse, and how quickly pregnancy follows, in PLOS ONE in 2026. The analysis draws on Norway's large mother, father and child cohort, covering more than sixty-four thousand women with planned, naturally conceived pregnancies who reported their habits in the four weeks before conception.

Average time to pregnancy shrank as frequency rose, from just under five months for less than weekly to under four months for more than four times a week. The gain concentrated at the top: the most frequent group had about a sixteen percent higher chance of conceiving in any given cycle than the once or twice weekly reference group. Below that top band, frequencies barely differed from each other. The pattern held after accounting for body weight, prior children, cycle regularity, and endometriosis.
plos-pone-0357586:
Afsaneh Omidimorad leads a community-based survey of what Indigenous adults in Canada's Northwest Territories know about a common virus and its vaccine. The virus spreads through sexual contact and can cause several cancers, yet awareness in these communities had never been measured. Local trained assistants surveyed just over two hundred adults across eleven communities and also gathered open comments on why people skip vaccination.

About half had heard of the virus, and fewer than a third knew a vaccine exists. Schooling shaped awareness most: adults with less education knew far less, and women and younger adults knew more about the vaccine. Only about a quarter of the youngest adults had actually received it. Omidimorad and colleagues say outreach must be local, plain, and built with the communities.
plos-pone-0357886:
Jinze Li led a team of eight authors linking vessel aging and heart failure through one gene, published in PLOS ONE in 2026. The gene, HMOX2, may drive shared processes as blood vessels age and hearts fail. The team combined bioinformatics, explainable machine learning, and lab validation to trace that crosstalk.

Li's multimodal approach is notable for testing computer findings in the lab rather than stopping at predictions. A shared driver names a treatment target at the crossing of two major killers. Explainable models also let other scientists judge the reasoning. Aging vessels and failing hearts are usually studied apart; work that joins them can reveal therapies that help both at once, which matters for older patients who have both.
plos-pone-0358986: Heo and one co-author published a 2026 PLOS ONE study on a fast test for pneumonia germs. The BioFire FilmArray panel names viruses and bacteria from one sample in about an hour. The team compared it with standard lab culture in hospital patients with pneumonia. They also judged whether the fast result changed care. Speed matters because the right antibiotic given early saves lives.
plos-pone-0359086: Park and seven co-authors published a 2026 PLOS ONE study using mini gut models grown from pig tissue. They added lipopolysaccharide, a part of bacterial walls that sparks inflammation. Then they watched the gut lining's barrier weaken and its alarm signals change. These organoids let scientists study gut injury without whole-animal tests, and the work may guide care for gut inflammation in pigs and people.
plos-pone-0360186:
Jwel Sharma and Ahmad Abdullah Mahdeen designed a candidate vaccine against Oropouche virus in 2026 using computer based immunology methods. Oropouche virus spreads through biting midges in parts of the Americas and causes feverish illness, with no licensed vaccine available. Their approach, called immunoinformatics, predicts which small pieces of the virus, called epitopes, the immune system is most likely to recognize.

The authors stitch several chosen epitopes into a single multiepitope subunit vaccine design. They then test the design in simulation, docking it against immune receptors and modeling how the body might respond and how stable the construct behaves. Computer first design cannot replace laboratory testing, but it narrows the field of candidates worth building.
pmc-10653486:
Siying Zou and five co-authors checked whether women who consume probiotics have different sex hormone levels, in a study published in 2023. Gut microbes and sex hormones influence each other, and foods that seed the gut might shift the balance. The team used a United States health survey from 2013 to 2016, with 2,699 women. Intake meant yogurt or a probiotic supplement reported in the recall period.

About one in five women consumed probiotics. Among women before menopause, intake tracked with higher estradiol, a key female hormone. Among women after menopause, intake tracked with lower total testosterone. The links held when the team matched women on similar traits to reduce bias. The authors present intake as a low-cost way to guard against hormone-related illness. They note that the cross-sectional design shows links, not causes.
pmc-10655486:
Wei Wei, Dong Wang, Weiting Liu, Hui Du, Zhiye Zhang, Shengying Che, Rui Ding, and YanBiao Yang wrote a 2023 paper on inhaler skills in western China. The patients had asthma or a long-term lung disease and used one of two dry powder inhalers, Turbuhaler or Diskus. Good technique matters, since a wrong step can keep the drug from reaching the lungs.

Pharmacists taught each patient once, and staff scored their next use against a seven-step method. The study covered ninety-six Turbuhaler users and seventy-four Diskus users. About one in five Turbuhaler users could not use it well, and the share was higher, over two in five, for Diskus. The team also checked which traits, such as age and schooling, lined up with poor skill.
pmc-10668586:
Jennifer Eckhoff and Ozanan Meireles ask whether artificial intelligence could one day guide surgeons' hands, in a 2023 editorial. AI already sifts surgical data at inhuman speed and sharpens what surgeons see. The writers concede the promises: smoother operations, risk flagged mid-procedure, navigation help, and relief from repetitive tasks. They also stress the obstacles that keep AI out of daily operating rooms.

After antiseptics, anesthesia, and keyhole surgery, they argue, AI may be surgery's next revolution, through video study, layered displays, practice simulators, and robots. The editorial calls for debate across fields inside surgical societies. It ends with an invitation to join a global challenge on a standard safety view in gallbladder surgery.
pmc-10670286:
Dmitriy Viderman and co-authors compare two ways of guiding back pain injections in this 2023 review and meta-analysis. One way uses ultrasound images, the other uses live X-ray, called fluoroscopy. Both aim the needle, but they differ in cost, gear, and radiation. The team searched three databases for randomized trials published before May 2023.

Eight trials met their rules. Pain relief after the procedure did not differ between the two methods at any checked time point, from one week to three months. Complication rates also matched. Function scores leaned slightly toward the X-ray method, though the gap was borderline. The authors say either guide can serve for back pain care, with function results worth a closer look in future trials.
pmc-10674786: Leszek Tylicki offers a short overview of immunity after vaccination against COVID-19, published in twenty twenty-three. The piece opens by noting that the pandemic at the turn of twenty nineteen and twenty twenty posed a substantial challenge for the world. Its subject is how protection builds after vaccination and what shapes its strength and span. The hosted text is brief, and its body beyond the opening lines is not shown here. The item is best used as a pointer to the subject of post-vaccine immunity.
pmc-10686586: Jun Guo and co-authors published a 2023 letter presenting real-world evidence from Jilin, China, on whether a booster of the same inactivated COVID-19 vaccine works against the Omicron variant. Omicron arrived in late 2021 with more than thirty spike mutations, spreading faster and dodging immunity better than earlier forms. Protection from the first vaccine course also fades with time. Drawing on large studies abroad and their regional experience, the authors argue the case for a same-vaccine booster, weighing its real-world performance against the variant then dominating infections worldwide.
pmc-10691086:
Jesse Ross and co-authors lay out the protocol for the ADAP-TIV trial in this 2023 paper. The trial tests ways to help South African patients stick with treatment for drug-resistant tuberculosis and HIV at once. New short drug courses have transformed care for both diseases, but gains depend on patients completing them. The adaptive trial runs in KwaZulu-Natal with adults starting the new regimens.

Four support arms compete: enhanced standard care, psychosocial support, phone-based dose monitoring, and the two combined. Support levels adjust to each patient's assessed needs. The main outcome at twelve months joins survival, cleared TB tests, staying in care, and an undetectable HIV load. The design lets weak arms drop and strong ones expand as results come in.
pmc-10694386:
Wenrui Yuan and co-authors published a 2023 study on habitat quality around Poyang Lake in China. The lake is the country's largest freshwater lake and a key wetland on the Yangtze River. Its shores support farms, towns, and rich wildlife. Human activity and land change press on that balance, but which pressures matter most, and where, needed mapping.

The team modeled habitat quality for 2022 and tracked land use from 2000 onward. Built-up land held the worst habitat scores and kept expanding fastest. Grassland and mudflats shrank the most. New farmland came mostly from water surface and forest. A geographic analysis tool then weighed which factors drive habitat change, alone and in combination. Population density paired with yearly totals proved especially powerful. The authors argue habitat harm around the lake is driven mainly by interacting social and economic forces, not single causes.
pmc-10696486:
Samantha Keil and co-authors look at sleep patterns tracked over time, and at cognitive impairment in older adults. Their 2023 study draws on the Seattle Longitudinal Study, a cohort from the local area that has run for long.

How long people said they slept was tracked across many years, with tests of cognitive performance at the same time. Cognitive impairment was set by scores below a fixed mark on two standard screening tools. The team grouped people by the median length of their sleep, into short, medium, and long sleep phenotypes. They also gauged how sleep length changed over time, and how much it swung. The point at issue was how shifts in sleep link to a fall in thought at a later date, past what one snapshot can show. The results speak to how dementia risk is tracked in healthy older adults.
pmc-10696686:
Corey Scholes, Tobias Schwagli, and John Ireland report a study from two thousand twenty-three on a handheld guide used during hip replacement surgery. The guide tracks bone markers and reports where the new socket sits, without needing scans during the operation. Surgeons need proof that its readings match reality.

Patients of one surgeon received new hips through a muscle-sparing approach while lying on their backs. CT scans before and after surgery were rebuilt in three dimensions and used as the truth standard. The guide's angle readings differed from the scans by only a few degrees on average, and leg length by a few millimeters. The authors note a small steady bias in some measures, which users should keep in mind.
pmc-10697586:
Ramy El-Ansary and co-authors identify the foot-and-mouth disease virus strain behind a 2022 outbreak in Egypt, in a study from 2023. The disease spreads fast among cattle and other hoofed stock. Three virus types already circle in Egypt. The team took samples from sick cattle in the north of the country during the epidemic.

Lab tests found the virus in skin and blister fluid, but not in blood. Seven of sixteen samples proved to be serotype A. Six of those matched an African lineage known as G-IV. The team grew those samples in lab cells, where the virus showed its classic cell-killing effect. The authors stress steady tracking of the virus as it changes. Watching the strains helps farms pick the right vaccine for control.
pmc-10698886:
Silvia Cruz, Miguel Bencomo-Cruz, María Medina-Mora, Fabiola Vázquez-Quiroz, and Clara Fleiz-Bautista ran Mexico's first drug-checking study at an electronic music festival, in a 2023 paper. Forty attendees, mostly young men, brought 51 samples to a free, confidential testing station. Staff asked about use patterns and what each person believed they held. Color tests, infrared scans, and fentanyl strips then checked the samples.

Most samples held the expected drug plus adulterants. Common extras included amphetamine-like compounds and an antidepressant, venlafaxine. Fentanyl turned up in half of the cocaine samples and in most of the confirmed MDMA ones. The authors warn that such hidden mixes, above all fentanyl, carry grave risks. They present on-site checking as a practical harm-reduction step for festivals.
pmc-10701186:
Jorge Lobo and co-authors turn museum records into a climate change detector in a 2023 study of Iberian dung beetles. Old occurrence records were gathered opportunistically, whenever a collector found a beetle, with no design behind them. Such data is usually dismissed as too messy for trend work. The authors show the mess can be read, when it is set against fine-grained historical temperature data.

Their method compares two trends. One is the overall drift of place and temperature across all collecting events over time. The other is the same drift within the records of a single species. Where a species' trend departs from the background, it is shifting its range or timing in answer to warming. They link which species respond to life history and family traits, naming the factors that make a beetle likely to move.
pmc-10702086:
Wafaa Jameel Tohol and co-authors survey nurses on non-drug pain care in Palestine in a 2023 paper. Intensive care nurses can ease pain with drugs or with methods such as positioning and relaxation. The study measured how often such methods are used and what blocks them.

The team surveyed 215 nurses in six hospitals in late 2022. More than two thirds used non-drug methods, and most showed high levels of use. The top barriers were lack of time, heavy workload, and unstable patients. The authors argue these hurdles, more than knowledge gaps, limit bedside use.
pmc-10709986:
Yinxing Cui and co-authors review a master energy switch inside macrophages in a 2023 paper. The switch, a protein kinase called AMPK, senses when a cell runs low on fuel. Macrophages, the immune system's roving eaters, rewire their metabolism as they switch between attack mode and calm, healing mode. AMPK sits at the crossing point of that rewiring and the inflammation the cells produce.

The review covers the switch's structure and how it steers macrophage metabolism and polarization, the lean toward the anti-inflammatory form. It then sums up what the pathway means for disease, from infection to cancer, and for the drugs that activate it. Because macrophage behavior feeds so many conditions, a single well-placed lever is an attractive target. The paper maps both the biology and the drug prospects.
pmc-10710386:
Mandy Foyster and colleagues published a 2023 study of obsessive healthy eating in athletes and patients. Orthorexia means restricting food by quality, not amount. Risk groups include endurance athletes and people with eating disorders. Nearly two hundred adults completed online measures. Motives for food choices were also assessed.

Patients with eating disorders scored highest for orthorexia symptoms. Athletes scored above healthy controls. Weight control motives tracked symptom severity strongly. Hunger and pleasure motives tracked it weakly downward. Compulsive exercise habits were measured too. Healthy eating messages can twist into harm for some people. Screening in sport and clinics may catch it earlier.
pmc-10710486:
Michael Landi and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-three genome study of an African cassava variety called TMEB117. Cassava feeds hundreds of millions in the tropics. Breeding better varieties needs an accurate genome, which mixed parentage makes hard.

The team assembled both chromosome sets separately at near-complete quality. Accuracy and completeness scores topped earlier cassava genomes. Over half the genome is repetitive sequence. Tens of thousands of gene models were predicted for each set. Because this variety catches a major virus easily, its genome is a prime reference for studying virus resistance.
pmc-10712086:
Arash Ziapour and co-authors report a 2023 study of what older people with heart failure went through during the COVID-19 pandemic in Iran. People with heart failure, above all the elderly, faced extra strain when hospitals filled and daily life shut down. The authors set out to record those hardships in the patients' own terms.

They interviewed twelve elderly patients who attended a heart hospital in Kermanshah, with talks held from August to November 2022. Each talk followed a loose guide, and the team sorted the answers with a standard method for lived-experience research. The accounts cover fear of infection, breaks in routine care, and the weight of isolation. The findings can help health services plan support for frail patients in the next crisis.
pmc-10712786:
News coverage from twenty twenty-three reports a clinical trial that tracked a fetal heart disorder in at-risk pregnancies. The condition is AV block, a fault in the heart's electrical timing. The mothers carried anti-Ro/SSA antibodies, which raise the risk. The trial, named STOP BLOQ, tested whether antibody levels and home monitoring could flag trouble early.

Risk rose with antibody level. Mothers in the top band faced the highest rates, and risk climbed further after a prior affected child. Antibody levels stayed flat over time. Home fetal heart rate checks caught conduction faults reliably. Trial leads say low levels may spare mothers close watch, while high levels merit it. Home checks could cut the need for repeated scans. Other factors besides antibodies still shape the risk.
pmc-10716086:
Anna Hundt Golden and a large team compare three digital tools for gathering health reports from patients. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-three. Such reports matter in trials, but patients often fail to fill them in, which leaves gaps in the data. Friendly, patient-led tools may raise how often people respond.

Adults in the United States test each tool for a week: a phone app, a web chatbot, and a voice tool. They fill two standard health surveys on each. Speed, ease of use, and a tool that can travel with them matter most. The app wins by a wide margin. Users ask for set alerts, tone speed control, and more reminders.
pmc-10719286:
Rita Nagy and a large international team surveyed discharge practice after acute pancreatitis and analyzed a patient cohort. When patients leave hospital too early or without clear criteria, relapse and readmission become likelier. The twenty twenty-three study combined an international survey of clinicians with cohort data. It asked what rules centers actually use to decide that a pancreatitis patient can go home.

Findings from the survey and cohort together show how variable discharge protocols remain across countries and hospitals. The authors use the comparison to argue for clearer, shared criteria. A common protocol could make discharge timing safer and more consistent. The work speaks to gastroenterology teams trying to balance bed pressure against the risk of sending patients home too soon.
pmc-10720086:
Xu and co-authors show how cyclosporine A calms colon inflammation by blocking neutrophil traps in mice and cells. Excess trap formation is tied to ulcerative colitis, a chronic gut disease that flares again and again. The drug is already a rescue therapy for severe cases.

Trap levels were checked in public data and in the team's own patient samples. A chemical colitis model in mice tested the drug's effect in colon tissue. In cells, the team measured energy products, reactive oxygen, and a key enzyme, G6PD. The drug acts through the pentose phosphate pathway, which feeds trap formation.
pmc-10721386:
Ismaila Yakubu and Hyun Gi Kong review how plant pathogenic bacteria choose their sugars, in a paper from two thousand twenty-three. Bacteria that live on plants feed on plant sugars. They siphon off sugars on their way to storage organs. Or they break down structural carbohydrates in the tissue of the plant itself.

Which simple sugars sit where in a plant shapes which bacteria thrive in that place. Preferences for particular sugars and sugar alcohols may steer virulence as the bugs spread. The review maps sugar distribution across plant tissues. It ties that map to infection dynamics in the field. The topic, the team notes, has been oddly neglected in past work. To grasp the sweet teeth of these bacteria could point to new crop protection strategies. To starve a pathogen of its preferred sugar is a unlike tack from poisoning it outright.
pmc-10725686:
Wang and co-authors place guard cells at the hub of nerve-waste ills in a sweep. Waste ills dent life and health and load crowds with care costs. Guard cells, called microglia, sit in brain and nerve webs alike. The sweep tells their paths in waste ills of more than one kind. Hear loss with age, Alzheimer's, and Parkinson's all get care. Waste ills of the far nerve web join the sweep too.

Two drug types get care: block drugs and a wake drug. Block drugs PLX3397 and PLX5622 curb guard cell counts in tests. The wake drug is a germ part that stirs the cells up. Curbs on the cells slowed birth and growth of waste ills. The cells play both flare and calm roles in the webs. That dual role makes them a prime care aim.
pmc-10725786:
Xin Chen and six co-authors assess one gene as a cancer signal in this two thousand twenty-three paper. The gene, named in the title, switches on early in cell responses and has been tied to several tumors. Its role in the most common lung cancer type was unclear. The team pulled expression, mutation, and clinical data from public cancer databases. They checked the gene across many cancers, then zoomed in on lung tumors.

Higher or lower levels tracked with patient outcomes in several settings. The gene's activity also tracked with how many immune cells entered tumors and with immune molecules. Network analyses sketched what controls the gene and what it may control. Such markers could refine prognosis. Cancer bioinformatics readers are the audience.
pmc-10734286:
Ahmed Kamel and Ahmed Alzahabi report, in a 2023 paper, a field pilot of a redesigned gas flare tip in Texas's Permian Basin. Flares burn off excess gas at oil sites. The practice wastes about 5 percent of the world's gas supply and releases over 350 million tons of carbon dioxide a year. Better tips could burn cleaner. Their design puts a bullet-shaped cap on the flare, pierced by four angled openings.

The cap rides on springs, lifting as pressure rises, and its shape exploits the Coanda effect to pull in air for a fuller burn. The team modeled the radiation around the tip with a standard heat model. They also ran real burns at two flow rates, measuring heat, noise, and exhaust gases. This first part of the report covers the design and the evaluation setup for judging whether the tip tames the flame.
pmc-10735786:
Kristine Williams, Yelena Perkhounkova, Carissa Coleman, Maria Hein, Frances Yang, and Clarissa Shaw check whether one dementia training fits a diverse nursing home workforce, in a 2023 study. The program, CHATO, teaches communication for dementia care. Year one results compared white non-Hispanic staff with staff of other backgrounds. Six hundred three staff finished the course. The diverse group started with lower knowledge scores.

Both groups improved on knowledge after training. The diverse group gained even more ground. Communication ratings also rose in both groups. Confidence in giving dementia care, though, rose only for the white group. The diverse group intended more strongly to use the skills. Yet they rated their satisfaction lower. The authors read this as a tailoring gap. The content worked, but it was not shaped for all learners. Making training more inclusive could lift outcomes. It could also narrow care gaps in diverse homes.
pmc-10735886:
Nicholas Bishop, Steven Haas, and Ana Quinones track a 2023 trend in US health: younger generations reach old age carrying more chronic diseases at once. Having several long-term illnesses together is called multimorbidity, and it raises care costs and strain. Past work showed later-born groups fall ill earlier, but it was unclear whether that pattern reaches people just turning fifty.

The team used a long-running national panel study with data from 1999 to 2019. They counted nine chronic conditions, from stroke and diabetes to arthritis and memory loss, in adults aged fifty and over. Their models trace how the count changes with age for each birth group. The results test whether gaps between generations are still growing as new groups enter early old age.
pmc-10735986:
Seven researchers track how spousal bereavement affects life satisfaction across decades in Germany in a paper from 2023. Losing a spouse is among the most stressful events of older age. The team used a long-running national panel with yearly surveys since 1984. More than two thousand widowed people were followed from five years before to five years after the loss.

People widowed in the 2000s and 2010s declined less overall than those widowed in the 1980s and 1990s. Smaller dips before the loss and faster recovery afterward drove the improvement. The immediate reaction phase may even have grown slightly sharper. The authors discuss social and societal changes that could explain the shift.
pmc-10736986:
Stephanie Giordano and Rosa Plasencia report findings from two thousand twenty-three on person-centered services for older adults and people with physical disabilities. Such services are treated as a gold standard, yet the views of the people receiving them are less often heard. The pandemic also shifted how many people judged their care.

The report draws on a national survey program that interviews service users directly. In data from two thousand twenty-one and twenty-two, adults who felt providers responded well also reported better access to community life. They kept relationships more easily and had fewer unmet service needs. The authors discuss what this link between responsive care and quality of life means for policy and daily practice.
pmc-10737086:
Proulx, Skoblow, and Rauer examine how sleep relates to the sex lives of older caregivers and their partners. Poor sleep is common in caregivers and is linked to less frequent sex. The study used a national survey wave with 146 couples where one spouse cared for the other, plus 211 couples caring for someone else.

Sharing a bed more often was the one sleep habit tied to more frequent sexual activity in both groups. Sleep length itself showed no links. In spouse-caregiver couples, more napping by the caregiver went with less pleasure reported by the partner. Feeling rested went with more pleasure for caregivers themselves. The authors stress that caregiving context shapes these links.
pmc-10737286:
Jee studies whether long-term air pollution links to urinary symptoms in older Korean men. Such symptoms are common at older ages and drag down quality of life. Participants came from a Seoul National University Hospital checkup center from 2015 to 2019.

In total, 7,979 men over sixty-five took a prostate symptom survey during screening. Exposure came from hourly readings at air monitors across the nation. In raw models, most pollutants, including PM10, nitrogen dioxide, and carbon monoxide, tied to symptoms. After adjustment, only fine particles, PM2.5, kept a clear link. It tied to voiding symptoms with an odds ratio of 1.07.
pmc-10737586:
Aung Zaw Zaw Phyo and co-authors asked whether blood-based measures of biological aging link to health in the same way for older men and women, in a study published in 2023. Women live longer than men on average, yet aging measures do not always agree. The team used data from five hundred sixty healthy Australians aged seventy and over.

They compared five DNA-based age scores with a frailty score built from sixty-seven health items and with a brain-age estimate from scans. Two DNA scores tracked frailty best in both sexes, while brain age matched none of them. Links with strength, walking speed, and rated health were more common in women. Disease links also split by sex. The authors urge care in treating aging scores as one-size-fits-all.
pmc-10737986:
Steffi Kim and Jordan Lewis outline a symposium on dementia care in Indigenous communities. The talks cover American Indian, Alaska Native, Native Hawaiian, and Pacific Islander caregivers. Dementia ranks among the top causes of death in these groups. One in three older Native adults is set to face a diagnosis in the next twenty-five years, yet caregiver life there is barely studied.

Talks show how cultural values shape what caregivers face and choose. One talk urges dementia resources that are safe in a cultural sense, drawn from Alaska Native advice. Another studies how caregivers in the Oneida Nation decide to use state and tribal services. The aim is better use of the help that already exists.
pmc-10738086:
Blakelee Kemp, Carli Rush, and Patricia Morton wrote a study in two thousand twenty-three on schooling across generations and heart disease in later life. They ask whether the mix of a parent's schooling and a person's own schooling shapes heart health after age fifty. They also check whether the pattern differs for men and women or across age cohorts.

Using a large national panel survey, the team tracked heart disease over twenty years in more than thirty-one thousand adults. People with high schooling in both generations had the least heart disease. Those with low schooling of their own had the highest risk, whatever their parents had. The gaps were sharpest for women and for the youngest cohort in the study.
pmc-10738886:
Joanne Yee and co-authors present a 2023 clinic study of swallowing trouble in veterans living with dementia. A specialty clinic checks veterans for dementia and folds speech and swallow experts into the team. Early spotting of swallow trouble can head off choking and lung harm.

Most patients in the group had Alzheimer disease, and most sat at a mild stage. On bedside tests, over a third failed a water swallow screen and near half failed a solid food test. A quarter scored at risk on a self report scale. Of those who got a video swallow study, over half showed unsafe swallows. Self report scores did not split safe from unsafe cases. The authors back a fixed place for swallow experts in dementia teams.
pmc-10739486:
Mariana Mateus and Alexandre Castro Caldas report physio care in three palsy cases. Their report from twenty twenty-three deals with progressive supranuclear palsy. It is a brain disease that cuts function and life quality.

Physio should start at diagnosis to slow loss of ability. Three cases are told with motor and non motor signs. Their course with physio care is tracked over years. In the first years, falls dropped for these patients. Walking and balance also got better with the care. Fall control is named the top goal.  Quality of life is the wider aim.
pmc-10743586:
Athanasia Pataka and seven colleagues review quit-smoking medicines in patients who also stop breathing in their sleep, in a paper published in two thousand twenty-three. Smoking and obstructive sleep apnea each raise cardiovascular risk independently. Their combination is common and deadly. Whether cessation drugs worsen or improve apnea was unclear.

The review gathered the sparse evidence on nicotine replacement, bupropion, and varenicline in apnea patients, emphasizing cardiovascular effects. Only small studies addressed nicotine replacement in apnea. Nicotine gum improved respiratory events temporarily in one line of evidence. No specific studies were found for some drugs. The authors map an evidence desert: clinicians must prescribe into it anyway, so the review's value is charting exactly what is unknown.
pmc-10743686: Nadia Lampiasi introduced a special journal issue in 2023 on macrophage polarization. Macrophages are immune cells that reshape themselves for many tasks. They clear dead cells and debris to keep tissues stable. Special forms live in the brain, liver, lungs, and bones. When balance breaks, plain macrophages switch into set states. Some states drive inflammation, while others calm it. The issue gathers work on that switching process. Studies cover diseases, infections, and immune-shaping molecules. The aim is learning to manage cell states for therapy.
pmc-10744586:
Italo Cavallone and co-authors examine skin from patients with a chronic fungal infection to see why the fungus persists despite immune attack, in work from twenty twenty-three. The disease, chromoblastomycosis, scars the skin and resists treatment. Resistance tracks with one immune style, yet the fungus survives even when helpful signals are present.

Patient skin held a moderate mix of immune cells, rich in several signal types at once. That mix did not track how much fungus was present. Cells bearing two exhaustion markers, PD-1 and PD-L1, were sharply more common in patient skin. The authors suggest these markers help the fungus stay put and drive the disease onward.
pmc-10745686:
Hyzy, Jaworski, Cieslak, Gotlib-Malkowska, and Panczyk review programs that aim to improve eating at work in twenty twenty-three. Better food habits at the office may help health and work output. Many types of programs exist, and their success is unclear. The authors gather prior reviews into one umbrella review.

They sort programs into those aimed at the person and those that change the work setting. No single type of program worked well in all cases. Programs based on behaviour change, and mixed programs, did better than those based on knowledge alone. Design, setting, and the group targeted all shaped success. The authors call for more evidence based work to guide workplace food programs.
pmc-10745786:
Shujing Sha and eight co-authors improve the path a polishing tool follows so that the edges of a workpiece keep their shape. Their study came out in 2023. In bonnet polishing, a soft inflated tool smooths precision parts, but edges tend to collapse because the tool cannot converge there properly.

Their method lifts the bonnet gradually near the edge and offsets each pass by a computed amount. Correction factors, fitted from the edge profile with smooth curves, adjust the offsets further. In experiments, the new path left an edge collapse of barely over one micrometer. The traditional raster path collapsed the edge by nearly a hundred micrometers, about seventy-six times worse. The authors show the method both preserves the original edge and tames the edge effect.
pmc-10747386:
André Montanholi Fornaziero and co-authors track what a single football match does to the blood of elite youth players, in a study from 2023. Sixteen under-18 players were split into a group that played a friendly match and a group that rested. Blood was drawn before, at half time, and after the match.

The first half proved more demanding than the second. White cell counts and the stress hormone cortisol roughly doubled from pre-match to post-match in the players. Muscle damage markers rose as well, as did lactate and glucose. The resting group stayed flat on the stress measures. The authors use the panel of markers to show how one match loads the immune, muscle, and energy systems of young athletes.
pmc-10766386:
Ali, Wu, and KC report a blood infection with Serratia marcescens in a 69-year-old woman in Chicago. This bacterium mainly strikes people with weak immune defenses. She arrived at Mount Sinai Hospital on February 11, 2022, after a mechanical fall.

Her history included lung cancer spread through the body, chemotherapy, high blood pressure, and lung disease. She met criteria for a body-wide inflammatory response on arrival. Broad antibiotics began at once, and blood tests soon grew Serratia. Drug advice shifted to ceftriaxone, then levofloxacin. Repeat cultures cleared within two days, and she stayed under watch until discharge.
pmc-10768386:
Chuang Wang and co-authors probe why fatty livers carry less hepatitis B virus in a 2023 study. Patients with hepatitis B plus fatty liver often show lower virus levels, a puzzle with treatment stakes. The team studied over sixteen hundred virus-positive patients, then built a cell model fed with fatty acids. A fat-droplet protein called perilipin2 sat at the center of their tests.

In patients, fatty liver and blood fat levels ran lower where virus load was high, a negative link that held across subgroups. In cells, fatty acids piled up fat droplets and cut virus markers and DNA load. The treatment raised perilipin2 and quieted autophagy, the cell's self-eating cleanup. Blocking perilipin2 reversed the virus drop. The authors argue this protein restrains viral copying by tuning autophagy under high-fat conditions.
pmc-10782186:
Aditya Pedaprolu and four co-authors tell the cases of two HIV patients with cysts in the parotid glands, the large spit glands by the ears. The cysts link to a rare syndrome where immune cells spread through body tissues. The report came out in twenty twenty-three.

The syndrome shows as swelling of both parotid glands, swollen neck glands, and high counts of one immune cell type. It is thought to stem from the immune system itself and strikes a small share of people with HIV. Both patients came to a rural top level hospital with swelling on both sides. One was treated with drugs alone, while the other had surgery to cut out the cysts.
pmc-10790886:
Marketers would love to know what shoppers quietly want, not just what they say they want. Kenta Nakazawa and co-authors test a way to measure that hidden pull with a game they call the product-rewarded traffic light task. Thirty students took risks under time pressure to win chocolate products, while a light-based brain scanner watched blood flow in the front of the brain.

One chocolate was clearly worth more than the other, and players tended to score higher when the prize was the pricey one. Brain signals differed between the two prize conditions in the frontopolar cortex and the left part of a nearby control region. The authors take this as evidence that the game, backed by brain data, can reveal differences in quiet demand for products that shoppers might not state out loud.
pmc-10811786:
Fábio Santos Lira, José Cesar Rosa-Neto, and James Edward Turner wrote this editorial in twenty twenty-four. It introduces a research topic on immunometabolism applied to exercise, nutrition, and drug treatment. Immunometabolism studies how immune cells produce and use energy. The field has expanded quickly over the past decade.

Nutrients and energy substrates shape how immune cells behave, especially amid metabolic disruption and inflammation. Ageing, obesity, type two diabetes, and autoimmune diseases all raise questions the field tries to answer. Exercise and nutrition are widely used to improve metabolic and inflammatory health. Their interaction with immunometabolism, the editors note, remains understudied. The editorial previews studies in the collection, including work on dietary fats, infection, and bone health in mice.
pmc-10822686:
Juan Huaroto, Etsel Suarez, Wangdo Kim, and Emir Vela build a soft air-driven beam that folds and bends in work dated two thousand twenty-three. Air-filled fabric beams with pleat folds can move in complex ways, but they spring back poorly once opened. The hosted text dates the work to two thousand twenty-three.

Soft elastic pads, set onto the pleats in a planned pattern, fix the return. At low pressure the beam lifts out of plane; past that point, more pressure steers its bend angle. A matrix model maps the motion. Tests varied pad shape, fold size, and pad spacing. Two pads on one fold let the beam refold fully when air is released. Stiff pads and fold sizes tune the stroke.
pmc-10823886:
Barua and co-authors draw lessons from a teen health initiative in India in a paper on work from two thousand nineteen to two thousand twenty-three. The effort aimed to strengthen a national adolescent health program in six districts. Local groups helped district health teams plan, run, and monitor activities, with expert oversight.

By two thousand twenty-two, teen health sat on district agendas, staff skills had grown, and clinic and community work ran in a structured way. Officials found the approach workable and acceptable. Gaps remained, such as unfilled posts, supply problems, and weak links across sectors. Teen involvement in running the program also stayed low. The authors say the gains need independent checks.
pmc-11046586:
Subashini Chandrapalan and colleagues reported a United Kingdom physician census analysis. The census covered research activity among physicians. It asked who does research alongside care. Barriers to research were also surveyed. The Royal Colleges ran the census. Responses came from across the country.

Four in ten physicians reported research activity. Men reported research more often than women. Time shortage topped the barrier list. Organisational factors blocked many doctors too. Low confidence held others back. The authors discuss fixes for each barrier. Protected time is one clear need. Fairer access matters for women especially.
pmc-11065186:
Nwaze, Eghwrudjakpor, and Chinedu-Anunaso present a 2023 review and case report of neuromyelitis optica tied to a water-channel antibody. The disease attacks the optic nerves and spinal cord in flares. A 25-year-old Nigerian woman came in with rounds of weakness, pain, and numbness in all limbs, painful spasms on one side, and bladder leaks. Her past held rounds of vision loss in each eye with eye pain.

Scans of brain and spine read normal, a trap for the unwary. The blood antibody test came back positive and sealed the call. High-dose steroids brought slow gains. Few cases reach print from sub-Saharan Africa. The report argues the antibody test, not the scan, is the hinge.
pmc-11331986:
Nadav Klein and Olga Stavrova test whether people with extreme views really change their minds less than moderates, in a 2023 study. The common belief is that extremists dig in, which would lock in social conflict over time. The team used panel surveys from the United States and the Netherlands that tracked the same people for up to thirteen years. The joint data cover more than sixteen thousand people and many policy topics.

Extreme holders in fact changed their views more than moderates did. Over the years, their views also tended to soften toward the middle. A final test showed that lay people expect the reverse, and so misread how views move. The authors say the myth of the stubborn extremist skews how groups see each other. Correcting it could ease false views of polarization.
pmc-11538186:
Julius Pochhammer and three co-authors ran a trial on drains after hernia repair with mesh. Their trial, from twenty twenty-four, set forty-two patients with open repair of midline hernias. Half got a drain behind the muscle near the mesh; half did not. All got skin level drains so surface fluid would not skew the read. The team scanned and checked patients at two and four weeks after surgery.

Drains cut fluid pools behind the muscle. But the drain group stayed in hospital longer and used more pain drugs. The effect on true clinical gains stayed unclear. Readers who fix hernias get a trade off, not a plain win, for this drain step.
pmc-11574986:
Sharkawi, Farid, Hassan, and Hassan built two lab ways in twenty twenty-four to read three allergy and breath drugs in one mix at once. Costly flow tools are the norm for such checks, which labs may lack. Their ways use light reads plus smart math to split the three signals.

A gene search picked the best light bands to feed each math way. Test mixes were built at five levels for each drug to train the tools. Both ways read the drugs in real pills and tabs with good truth. One drug's break-down part is the third drug, so the ways can flag stale stock too.
pmc-11576686:
Manraj Kaur leads a large team building a survey tool for gender-affirming care, reported in twenty twenty-four. To judge whether such care works, doctors need to hear outcomes from patients in their own words. No full tool built on what patients say matters existed.

The team followed set rules for building patient surveys. They held deep interviews, from late twenty eighteen into early twenty twenty, with teens and adults who sought or had this care at clinics in several countries. The draft tool, called GENDER-Q, covers the outcomes patients raised. It is meant for clinics, research, and quality checks once field testing is done.
pmc-11580586:
Jiang Liu and colleagues published a kidney research study in 2024 on diabetic nephropathy. Diabetes can damage the small vessels in the kidney's filters. Injury to the cells lining those vessels marks the disease's early stage. The team studied a signaling protein that was raised in patients and diabetic mice.

In high-sugar conditions, the protein increased stress inside the cells. It switched on a stress factor that pushed cells toward death. Silencing the protein reduced cell death in lab tests. Turning the stress factor back up canceled that protection. In diabetic mice, a virus-delivered silencer eased kidney cell injury. The authors name the protein chain as a possible treatment target.
pmc-11581186:
Rukaiah Fatma Begum, Chitra Vellapandian, and Sumithra Mohan survey symptoms and quality of life in women with polycystic ovary syndrome, in a 2024 study. The syndrome is a common hormone disorder. Its cause, genetic or environmental, is still unclear. The team ran a web survey of one hundred eight women with the condition. A standard twelve-item form measured physical and mental quality of life.

Irregular periods were the commonest symptom. Excess hair growth and acne followed. About a fifth reported obesity. Complications included diabetes in about thirteen percent. Miscarriage history appeared in nearly a third. Women with infertility scored lowest on physical quality of life. Night shift workers scored lowest on the mental side. The authors call for care that joins body and mind. Young working women need special attention, they say. Support should match the burdens each subgroup carries.
pmc-11587586:
Haolin Zhang and co-authors present a 2024 study on obesity in women with polycystic ovary syndrome who also have insulin resistance. The syndrome upsets hormones and metabolism, and obesity often comes with it. The team asked whether weight tracks more closely with hormone levels or with blood fats in this group.

The study covered 206 Chinese women seen between 2016 and 2021. Body measures and fasting blood samples were collected for sugar, insulin, fats, and sex hormones. Obesity linked clearly to lower levels of a hormone-carrying protein and to higher free androgen and insulin scores. No clear link appeared between obesity and blood fat profiles. The authors read this as a hormone story more than a lipid story.
pmc-11590486:
Anas Odeh and co-authors survey hospital patients in 2024 in northern Palestine about their rights. Patients have rights to respectful care, clear information, and a say in treatment. How well patients know these rights, and how well staff honor them, varies widely by place.

Four hundred patients took part through in-person interviews. Just under half showed good awareness of their rights. Awareness ran highest for respectful care and lowest for the simple act of staff introducing themselves. Private and charity hospitals explained procedures, options, and costs better than public ones. The authors call for joint reforms, since over half of patients lacked basic knowledge of their rights.
pmc-11600386:
Irina Zaidman and co-authors study a grave liver complication in children after stem cell transplant, in work from two thousand twenty-four. The complication blocks small liver veins and can cascade into organ failure. Records covered over twelve hundred children treated at two large centers over twenty years.

About eight percent developed the complication, most after donor transplants. Survival a hundred days after transplant sat near seventy percent for those cases. Overall survival rose across the study years. Prior infection, liver test issues, fluid in the belly, and organ failure each tracked with worse odds. Adding steroids to the standard drug did not help.
pmc-11604986:
Qiuhong Ke and co-authors use genetics to test whether type 2 diabetes itself raises the risk of colorectal cancer, in a study from 2024. Past observational work linked the two diseases, but shared habits and reverse effects cloud that link. The team applied Mendelian randomization, which uses gene variants as natural instruments.

The analysis ran in both directions, with pooled results across gene data sets. Genes that raise diabetes risk also raised colorectal cancer risk by a modest amount. Genes for colorectal cancer, by contrast, showed no clear effect on diabetes risk. Checks for bias and mixed effects supported the main result. The authors say diabetes care should count as part of colorectal cancer prevention.
pmc-11605886:
Huanhuan Luo and four co-authors published a 2024 meta-analysis of multicomponent exercise for older adults with cognitive frailty, a reversible mix of body weakness and mental decline. Searching nine databases, the team pooled 11 trials with 2,222 participants. Exercise programs combining strength, aerobic, and balance work improved thinking scores, grip strength, and leg strength.

Frailty scores fell and depression eased as well. Daily-living ability and quality of life, though, showed no clear gain. Subgroup checks favored aerobic mixes, more than 120 minutes a week, and group formats. The authors endorse multicomponent exercise as a potent lever against cognitive frailty. They flag the missing proof on daily function as the next question for trials.
pmc-11607386:
Yiqing Liu and five co-authors report a cleaner way to break down a common drug pollutant in water, in this 2024 paper. The drug is sulfamethoxazole, and the base method pairs a manganese salt with peracetic acid to attack it. The team added a compound called NTA and found the cleanup sped up sharply.

Tests with light spectra, scavenger trials, and probe chemicals showed what does the work. The additive first binds the manganese, which then activates the acid and forms a high-energy manganese state plus organic radicals. That state proved to be the main attacker. The group traced six breakdown products and mapped four routes the drug can take apart, noting the process works in acidic and neutral water.
pmc-11607686:
Roger Colominas-Ciuró and co-authors report a bird study from two thousand twenty-four on long-term stress in zebra finches. Animals respond to hard conditions with body changes that restore balance. The team asked how heat and limited water each affect blood markers of lasting stress and body condition.

Male finches lived for eighteen weeks in hot or cool air, with water always present or limited to half the active day. Cool air raised stress markers more than limited water did. Water limits lowered one type of white blood cell. Birds in better body condition handled stress better, based on linked blood measures. The authors conclude that long cool spells may strain these birds, above all when condition is poor.
pmc-11608386:
Jun Jie Lim and co-authors link diet to allergy in 2024, studying 13,561 young Chinese adults in Singapore and Malaysia. Their focus is eczema, or atopic dermatitis, and allergy to house dust mites. Diet surveys measured how much fiber and how many probiotic drinks each person took in.

People with high fiber intake had lower odds of both mite allergy and eczema. Probiotic drinks alone showed no direct link to eczema, but among frequent probiotic users even moderate fiber cut the risk more. A fiber-rich diet also blunted risks tied to high fat and protein intake. The authors suggest fiber, especially with probiotics, as a simple protective habit.
pmc-11610086:
Beijia Liu and co-authors scope how studies define and measure adherence to oral nutritional supplements in cancer care. Cancer and its treatment often bring malnutrition, which erodes quality of life and treatment success. Supplement drinks can help, but only if patients keep taking them. The catch: past studies did not agree on what adherence even means, or how to count it.

The team searched six databases to August 2024 and kept 37 studies from 2005 to 2024. Definitions and tools varied widely. The most common definition was simply the share of the prescribed amount that the patient in fact drank. Tools ranged from patient diaries to a standard medication adherence score. Rates varied a lot too, and some studies saw adherence fade over time. Without a shared yardstick, clinics cannot tell a failing supplement plan from a failing measure. The review lays the ground for a standard.
pmc-11612286:
Samaneh Nakhaee and colleagues examine blood factors linked to thinking problems in older adults. Their case-control study from twenty twenty-four draws on an aging study in Birjand. Nitric oxide, insulin resistance, and low vitamin D all change with age. Each factor may affect memory and mental function.

The study compared forty adults without impairment against sixty-four with impairment. Cases split into mild and moderate groups by a standard test. Blood tests measured nitric oxide products, vitamin D, insulin, and glucose. Insulin resistance scores were calculated from those measures. Nitric oxide products were clearly lower in the impaired group. The paper gives readers one local picture of how these factors travel together.
pmc-11612486:
Vahid Shahabadi and co-authors published this study in 2024. It measures the surface tension of single aerosol droplets without touching them. Surface tension steers how air particles form, grow, and change phase. Air droplets often sit in unstable states, supercooled or supersaturated, which bench tools cannot reach. The new instrument traps one droplet in light beams between two electrodes. A strong electric field then stretches it by mere tens of nanometers.

Laser light scattered off the droplet sings at sharp tones that split as the shape changes. Reading the split gives the tension precisely. The team measured across supersaturated conditions where data were scarce. Results matched older data where the ranges overlap. Unlike past levitation methods, this one handles thick, syrupy droplets too. The tool opens a window on the hidden states air particles actually live in.
pmc-11614186:
Rajat Gupta, Armaan Khosa, Priya Bansal, and Gautam Chaudhury reviewed outcomes of eyelid surgery done from inside the lid, in a study published in 2024. The approach reaches the fat pads of the lower lid without a skin cut, lowering risks such as the lid pulling down or turning. Their series covers eighty-eight patients at a private hospital in northern India.

Patients ranged from twenty to seventy-six years old, and many combined the operation with skin trimming, lid-tightening, or fat transfer. Swelling, bruising, and eye watering were common but faded within two weeks. A gritty feeling in the eye, reported by fourteen patients, cleared within three days. Most people resumed social life at about two weeks. The authors back the inside route as versatile and quick to heal.
pmc-11614486:
Min-Jeong Kim and a team of co-authors studied a small amoeba that can cause eye, brain, and skin disease, in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. The amoeba lives as an active cell, then forms a hard cyst when conditions turn bad. When conditions improve, it leaves the cyst and grows again.

The team compared gene use as cells formed cysts and as they left them. They found five genes that rose sharply early in the exit stage. When four of those genes were silenced, the amoebas could not leave their cysts well. Those genes may help stop the amoeba from coming back after treatment.
pmc-11616886:
Chang and a large team built a deep learning model in twenty twenty-four to map how brain zones drive each other at many scales. Brain talk spans fast and slow waves of group acts, and no broad model yet fits that spread. Their model is built from brain facts and learns curves that link zones and scales.

On fake data and on live brain reads the model caught multi-scale acts well. The drive links it found fit the known tiered build of the mammal brain. Those links also shifted with what the host was doing. The team sees a new route to probe brain work in a firm way.
pmc-11618086:
Alban Joseph and colleagues reported a physics study in 2024 on cavity magnonics. The field studies how magnetic waves interact with microwaves in a resonator. Such control could serve quantum and spin-based devices. The team introduced excitation fields with tunable direction and shape. A two-port cavity setup made those fields easy to adjust. The fields act like a dial for probing coupled magnetic and light waves.

The team also built theory models for the system. The models matched the experiments for any field direction or shape. Real-time control of the field state gives a direct handle on the coupling. That handle can steer how information passes between the two parts. The authors present the platform as a flexible tool for spin-photon work. It may help design future hybrid quantum systems, they argue.
pmc-11619086:
Jumanah Essa-Hadad leads a team on high vaccine uptake in Israel's Arab population. Their study from twenty twenty-four deals with a disadvantaged minority group. Despite health gaps, their HPV and MMR rates top the majority.

Interviews were held with providers, mothers, and teenagers. All talks ran in Arabic with an Arab researcher. Themes were mapped to a WHO systems framework. Easy access and school based delivery stood out. Mother and child clinics also carried vaccines. Staff warmth and trust played their part. Framing vaccination as the norm helped uptake.  Clinics for mothers and children helped too.
pmc-11625786:
Wu and seven colleagues build a risk model for osteosarcoma based on its tumor microenvironment in twenty twenty-four. Osteosarcoma is a bone cancer that spreads early and resists drugs. Immune traits of the tumor surroundings may predict outcomes. The team analysed eighty-four tumor samples from a public database.

Samples were split into two groups by their immune properties. Genes that differed between groups were mostly immune related. Intersecting those with known immune genes gave a focused gene set. Regression methods selected ideal genes for a risk score model. Survival differed clearly between high and low risk groups under the model. Immune checkpoint patterns also fit the model's predictions. The authors call the model precise and dependable for prognosis.
pmc-11625886:
Yujiao Wang and five colleagues feed rabbits, published in 2024, a rich diet to model the early stages of age-related macular degeneration. That disease blinds older people, and diet and blood fats are known risk factors. Male Chinchilla rabbits ate one of four diets for six months: normal, high fat, high sugar, or both together. The team tracked blood lipids, scanned the eyes, tested retinal response, and read gene activity in the retina. Neither rich diet alone did much to blood fats. Together, they clashed into severe lipid disorder without making the rabbits obese.

Only the combined diet scarred the retina. It produced deposits like the reticular pseudodrusen seen in patients, mostly fat droplets around the pigment layer. Eye fluid carried more of an immune protein, and retinal vessel density thinned. The authors present these rabbits as a good model of early disease in a normal-weight animal.
pmc-11626486:
Wang, Shangguan, Li, and Zhang show that naming negative feelings precisely helps people rethink them in this 2024 brain study. Cognitive reappraisal means reframing a bad event to soften its emotional hit. People differ in how finely they sort negative emotions.

The team recorded brain waves while participants reappraised negative material. Those with high emotion differentiation showed smaller late positive brain responses, a sign of easier regulation. They also showed stronger gamma synchrony and stronger coupling between rhythm pairs in parietal and frontal areas. Machine learning using all signal types classified differentiation level better than any single type. The authors see support for training emotion vocabulary as a route to better regulation.
pmc-11626786:
Jin, Pan, Zhao, Ouyang, Qin, and Tian study a birth defect of the aorta in forty-six children in twenty twenty-four. In this defect, the main artery from the heart is narrowed. The team compared genes and proteins in aorta tissue from several patient groups. Samples came from hospitals in southwest China over three years.

Several genes were turned down in the narrowed tissue, including one called STRA6. That gene starts a pathway linked to retinoic acid, a form of vitamin A. Protein tests confirmed the drop for STRA6 and for some related genes. The team then knocked out STRA6 in mice with gene editing. Many offspring mice showed a narrower aorta on ultrasound. The authors suggest STRA6 loss may help cause the defect.
pmc-11628986:
Wilson Leung and four co-authors lay out their plan to sum trials of chat bots for mind health in Asia. Their plan appeared in twenty twenty-four. Shame gainst mind ills and short hands block care in Asian lands, and chat bots may step past both. Four bases will be swept to December twenty twenty-four for chance trials in English or Chinese full text.

Trials will be pooled with chance-mix math. Bias risk and proof trust will be graded with set tools. No ethics pass is need, since no new folk data is drawn. Finds will go out through trade texts.
pmc-11632086:
Atsuki Nakagami, Qiyue Mao, Masaki Horitani, Masahito Kodera, and Hiroaki Kitagishi build synthetic antidotes for hydrogen sulfide poisoning in a paper from 2024. The gas blocks cellular respiration and has no approved antidote. Their compounds wrap an iron porphyrin inside a sugar cage, mimicking blood proteins. Two versions differ in the ligand attached to the iron. Both bound sulfide firmly under body-like conditions.

One version bound ten times tighter than natural met-hemoglobin. After binding, the sulfide was oxidized into harmless sulfite and sulfate. Poisoned mice injected with the compound survived at much higher rates. Their brain and heart mitochondria recovered, and the drug left in urine intact. The authors propose it as a treatment candidate.
pmc-11633386:
Adrian Campey and co-authors report evolution research from two thousand twenty-four on how bacteria survive an antibiotic by growing oddly. Antibiotics spill into farms and wild waters, where germs meet low doses. Most lab evolution studies stir bacteria in uniform liquid, which hides how single cells respond.

The team evolved Escherichia coli against the drug ciprofloxacin in mixed and in structured settings, watching single cells under microscopes. Resistance grew stronger in mixed settings through target mutations, while structured settings bred pump-based mutants with dormant survivors. Both kinds kept dividing under drug doses that should stop them, yet shrank as they did so. They regained normal size once the drug was gone, a response not reported before.
pmc-11639686:
Nur Betül Karatoprak and five co-authors test whether a faster MRI technique can replace the standard protocol for spotting sacroiliitis, the spinal joint inflammation behind inflammatory back pain. Dixon sequences separate fat and water signals in one acquisition, potentially substituting for several conventional scans. One hundred seven patients aged eighteen to fifty with inflammatory back pain underwent three-tesla MRI with both protocols.

Signs of active inflammation seen on standard fat-suppressed images were re-read on Dixon water-only images; chronic damage signs from standard images were compared against Dixon fat-only and phase images. Signal and contrast measurements for bone marrow edema and fat deposition were quantified, and readers' agreement was tested. The study is a head-to-head diagnostic performance comparison.
pmc-11639886:
