Cima and co-authors report a boy with persistent Müllerian duct syndrome plus an extra testicle, tied to a new gene variant. This rare condition leaves womb structures in boys who otherwise develop as male. It stems from faults in a hormone or its receptor gene, AMHR2.

Their patient was a 13-year-old boy with both testicles undescended from birth. Two past surgeries had tried to fix the right side, at ages four and five. Gene tests found a new two-copy variant in AMHR2 behind the case. Extra testicles had been reported only twice before, without gene tests. A literature search maps related birth defects.
pmc-11640086:
Alessia Facchin and colleagues published a 2024 study of drug-resistant gut bacteria in Italian dogs. Resistant bacteria threaten human and animal health alike. Dogs may carry and spread them silently. The team tested feces from one hundred dogs. Samples came from clinics and kennels in northern Italy.

Fourteen dogs carried resistant E. coli strains. The bacteria resisted several important antibiotic classes. Gene tests confirmed the resistance mechanisms involved. One dog carried a strain resisting last-resort drugs. Risk factor analysis looked for patterns in the dogs' histories. Monitoring pets matters for the wider resistance problem.
pmc-11640786:
Lili Li and co-authors report a study from two thousand twenty-four on how apples change during combined freeze drying and hot air drying. Drying extends shelf life but can warp fruit and weaken structure. Understanding cell-level changes helps explain the visible shrinkage and softening.

The team tracked pectin, the glue-like cell wall material, and stiffness traits through the process. During hot air drying, samples softened while warm above a key transition temperature, then stiffened as they cooled toward it. Hot air also sped the loss of water-soluble pectin at the moisture transition point. The degree of esterification of another pectin fraction rose, cutting support for cell walls. The findings link chemistry to the dried apple's final texture.
pmc-11643586:
Jiaxing Liu and co-authors build a jelly-like film for solid-state energy storage in a 2024 paper. The film is a gel polymer soaked with a protic ionic liquid, a salt that stays liquid and carries charge. Cast from a common polymer, the film comes out clear and bendable.

Tests show the film survives heat above three hundred degrees and stays stable across a wide voltage range. It conducts ions well at room temperature. Built into a symmetric carbon capacitor, it delivered strong charge storage and kept over ninety percent of its capacity after 4,500 cycles. The authors hope the design serves future solid-state devices that must be safe, flexible, and long-lived.
pmc-11643786:
Nuria Trujillo-Garrido and co-authors survey Spanish primary care doctors and nurses on their attitudes toward vegan diets, in a study from 2024. As eating habits shift for health and climate reasons, frontline clinicians are asked about plant-only diets more often. What those clinicians believe shapes the advice patients get.

Just over two hundred professionals answered. Most ate an omnivorous diet; only a small share were vegetarian or vegan. Women were more likely than men to link livestock farming with global warming and to accept vegan diets for pregnant women and children when supplemented. Clinicians who themselves ate vegetarian or vegan diets most strongly rejected the claim that such diets lack needed nutrients. The authors suggest nutrition training has not kept pace.
pmc-11644386:
Li and colleagues tune in twenty twenty-four the pressing process for bamboo fibre plastic panels and weigh their lifetime carbon cost. Bamboo fibre panels suit car parts: they regrow fast, weigh little, and store carbon. But pressing settings affect both strength and emissions, which has slowed wider use.

Testing mixes of preheat temperature, preheat time, and hold time, they found a sweet spot that gave strong panels with lower water uptake. A lifetime review flagged energy use, the pressing step, and material mix as the main carbon drivers. The authors offer their settings as a base for low-carbon car parts. They plan further work on fibre share to cut impact more.
pmc-11644786:
Chad Kerksick tests if a choline supplement sharpens thinking within an hour, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. Choline feeds production of acetylcholine, a neurotransmitter at the heart of cognition and muscle control. Alpha-GPC supplements raise how much choline is on hand, and they do so efficiently.

Twenty resistance-trained men took part in a randomized, double-blind crossover trial. Each took a placebo, a low dose, or a high dose of alpha-GPC, on separate visits to the lab. Cognitive tests, Stroop, N-back, and Flanker tasks, ran sixty minutes after ingestion. Mood scales and blood pressure measures went with them. The title reports enhancement of cognitive performance from the supplement.
pmc-11645086:
Ruikang Luo, Yaofeng Song, Longfei Ye, and Rong Su build a lean neural network that names vehicle types in satellite images. Their study was published in twenty twenty-four. Knowing what vehicles are on the road helps traffic systems react and ease congestion.

Pure convolutional networks miss wide scene context, and bad weather blurs their reads. The team's design stacks dense connections inside a transformer-in-transformer frame, joining local detail with global structure. Satellite and aerial views supply richer input than roadside cameras. The network aims to stay accurate in the messy settings where simpler models falter. The authors offer it as an efficient tool for smart traffic monitoring from above.
pmc-11646686:
Yaser Ata and co-authors present a case report and literature review from two thousand twenty-four on pelvic lipomatosis. In this rare condition, harmless fat grows in excess around the rectum and bladder. Left untreated, it can squeeze the urinary system, harm the kidneys, and cause wider complications.

The report follows a forty-two-year-old man with lasting urinary symptoms whose workup ended in this diagnosis. The authors trace how imaging confirmed the excess fat and how care was planned. Surgery is often needed to relieve pressure and protect kidney function. Alongside the case, the review gathers what is known about causes, signs, and treatment of the condition. The authors stress early recognition to improve quality of life.
pmc-11647386:
Beong Ki Kim, Hangseok Choi, and Chi Young Kim pooled twelve studies to ask when a tracheostomy should be done in COVID-19 patients on ventilators. Cutting the windpipe helps long ventilation, but timing may trade survival against time in intensive care. Across 3,465 patients they compared cutting at seven, ten, and fourteen days. At the ten-day split, patients cut later had lower short-term mortality. At seven and fourteen days, the timing showed no mortality difference.

Earlier cutting bought shorter ventilation and shorter intensive care stays. Later cutting trended toward longer hospital stays. The authors read the pattern as a dilemma rather than a rule: a few days' difference at the ten-day mark seems to matter, yet waiting costs ICU days. They call for research that finds the timing balancing survival and resources. The analysis cannot set one date, but it narrows the argument.
pmc-11647486:
Sahana Kumar and Gregg Duncan work on inhaled gene delivery to the lung in a 2024 paper. Cystic fibrosis is caused by a faulty gene for a channel that moves salt and water across airway cells. Thick, dry mucus builds up, breeds infection, and drives the lung damage that kills most patients. Gene therapy could in principle fix the root cause.

Virus carriers have limits, so the field wants non-viral carriers that match them. Stealth coatings help particles cross mucus but can block entry into airway cells. Their paper, per its title, uses a peptide that does both jobs: crossing mucus and entering cells, boosting delivery of messenger RNA particles to the lung.
pmc-11647786:
Makoto Kobayashi and colleagues report a perforated throat injury caused by surprisingly minor blunt trauma to the neck. Their 2024 case involves an eighteen-year-old woman whose bicycle handlebar struck her neck in a collision with a vehicle.

Pharyngeal perforation usually follows substantial force with other organ damage or fractures, none of which appeared here. The patient had only a minor neck bruise, no bleeding, and no throat complaints. Breathing sounds and airway shape were normal. Computed tomography nevertheless showed free air tracking toward the back wall of the pharynx. While the wound was washed, she felt water entering her mouth, confirming the perforation. Hospital follow-up followed the diagnosis.
pmc-11648886:
Vijaya Anil Pandit and co-authors tested the safety of a traditional Ayurvedic mineral preparation in rats in a 2024 study. The preparation, Krishna Vajra Abhraka bhasma, is made from biotite mica by repeated processing. Such herbo-mineral products are used clinically but have raised toxicity concerns.

Sixty-six rats took part under standard guidelines. A single large dose in the acute test caused no deaths or organ damage. In the 28-day study, groups received low, medium, or high daily doses. Body and organ weights, blood counts, and kidney function stayed normal. The results support the preparation's safety at tested doses, within the limits of animal testing.
pmc-11651386:
Mahnaz Etehadtavakol, Parvaneh Shokrani, and Ahmad Shanei wrote a 2024 review on software used to plan proton therapy for cancer. Proton beams can hit a tumor hard while sparing nearby healthy tissue better than standard radiation. Planning that precision requires simulating how the beam travels through the body. A widely used simulation toolkit, Geant4, models those physics in fine detail.

The authors searched major databases for studies from 2002 to 2023 that used the toolkit in proton therapy. Across the literature, the simulations proved reliable and matched real-world behavior closely. Researchers used them to tune treatment plans and check how therapy machines perform. The review notes that comparing simulations with real experiments is what makes the numbers trustworthy. The authors conclude the toolkit is a sound base for improving proton therapy planning. Hospitals weighing this treatment can use the review to judge the planning tools behind it.
pmc-11651686:
Marco Calvigioni and co-authors present a 2024 pilot study of the urine microbe mix in type 2 diabetes. Bladder complaints are common in the disease and may trace to that mix, yet the ground was barely mapped. Fifty patients without bladder complaints and 25 healthy peers gave urine samples. Germ DNA was counted by targeted tests and read by gene sequencing, with a second counter for proof.

Patients carried a heavier total germ load and more of one big germ phylum. Split by sex, the gaps showed in women alone. Kind-level counts tied out, and variety scores matched across groups. Fine species reads shifted in sex-tied ways. The pilot frames bigger hunts for a diabetes-bladder link.
pmc-11651786:
Yunqi Hua and eleven co-authors hunt for blood markers that predict which stomach cancer patients will benefit from immunotherapy plus chemotherapy, in a two thousand twenty-four oncology paper. Responses to PD-1 blockade combined with the SOX regimen vary widely for unknown reasons.

Serum exosomes, tiny vesicles shed by cells, carry stable microRNAs that reflect tumor biology. Sequencing exosomes from eleven patients found seventy-four microRNAs differing between responders and non-responders. Validation in an independent cohort confirmed two, miR-451a and miR-142-5p, as significantly different. Their target genes cluster in major cancer signaling pathways. The authors propose exosomal microRNA testing as a step toward personalized gastric cancer treatment.
pmc-11652786:
Homa Vahidi and a large team map brain network patterns in newborns using light-based imaging. Their study from twenty twenty-four uses near-infrared spectroscopy at rest. Brain networks for movement form before birth and mature fast. Their health predicts later neurological outcomes in babies.

Forty-one healthy newborns were scanned in their first week. Babies stayed awake during the resting measurements. Both single channels and whole-hemisphere patterns were analysed. Strong two-sided connectivity marks healthy sensorimotor networks. Light imaging suits fragile newborns better than big scanners. Norms from healthy babies anchor later comparisons. Early brain development gains a bedside-friendly window.
pmc-11653586:
Chunyan Dai and co-authors present a 2024 lab study on Tianma, a dried plant tuber used as both food and medicine in China. Growers often treat the tuber with sulfur smoke while drying it. The team asked how that step changes the plant sugars tied to its health effects, and how well those sugars fight cell damage.

The group first found the best hot-water method for drawing the sugars out of treated and untreated samples. Sugars from the sulfur-treated tuber scored lower on three lab tests of antioxidant strength and held less iron in a fourth test. Still, both kinds of sugar shielded mouse cells from damage by a harsh chemical. The results give growers and buyers a science base for weighing a common drying step.
pmc-11654386:
Zeitouni and a large team review six years of ultrasound training for medical students in Texas in twenty twenty-four. Handheld ultrasound at the bedside is now a core skill for new doctors. Their school wove scanning into the first year anatomy course. Students scanned live bodies to firm up what they learned from donor dissections.

Quiz scores jumped after each of three scanning sessions. Most students rated the training as valuable for grasping anatomy. By the block's end, nearly all felt at ease capturing images. The authors say early scanning builds a base for later clinic skills. Their review can guide other schools adding like training.
pmc-11654686:
Carolyn Shembrey and co-authors teach a gene-editing tool to silence cancer RNA that differs from healthy RNA by a single letter. The tool, CRISPR-Cas13, cuts chosen RNA strands, but it normally tolerates small mismatches, so mutant and healthy copies both fall. The team found that placing deliberate mismatches at exact spots in the guide strand flips that behavior.

Guides built on these rules strongly silenced three famous cancer targets, in the KRAS, NRAS, and BRAF genes, while leaving the healthy copies mostly alone. The tuned guides also cut the stray, off-target cutting that this enzyme version is known for. The authors present the rules as a general design kit for editing the RNA of single-letter mutations, a step toward treatments matched to each patient's tumor.
pmc-11654786:
Sachie Oda and co-authors present a 2024 surgical case study on rebuilding an elbow muscle. The triceps extends the elbow, and the hand is useless without that motion. A fifty-year-old patient lost the lower third of the triceps to wide cancer removal. The surgery had taken a leiomyosarcoma at the left elbow, leaving the elbow bone exposed. The team rebuilt with a flap of back muscle and skin, still attached to its own blood supply. The flap tunneled under the skin to reach the elbow.

Its nerve was cut on purpose to stop mixed signals. Ten months later, elbow function had improved. Reconstructive surgeons get a worked plan for distal triceps loss. The case also clarifies when a transfer is not needed: a working upper triceps remnant can suffice. Sarcoma resections trade tissue for cure margins, so reconstruction planning belongs in the first operation's design.
pmc-11655286:
Chiara Tarracchini and co-authors present a tool for picking reference strains of bacteria in a 2024 paper. Labs often use old standard strains, but one strain may not reflect a species' full range. Their tool judges how well a strain stands for its whole species.

The Optimal Representative Strain selector scores strains on genes, traits, and where they live in nature, using public genomes. A companion program helps labs pick the best strain from their own shelves. The team tested the approach on five named species of bacteria. The work aims to make lab results more true to the species as a whole.
pmc-11663586:
Gibbs, Theodoulou, and Bailey-Serres review how plants regulate their response to low oxygen in twenty twenty-four. Flooding and normal growth both expose plant cells to hypoxia. Plants must retune gene activity fast to survive. Control operates at many layers, from DNA packaging to protein stability.

Signals from mitochondria and the endoplasmic reticulum feed into transcription factor control. Chemical marks on chromatin and DNA methylation shape which genes can answer. Translation of messenger RNA is tightly managed during oxygen shortage. Protein modifications, including phosphorylation, adjust the response minute by minute. The authors list open questions for the field. Answers could guide breeding of flood resilient crops.
pmc-11667686:
Arulmukavarathan and colleagues report in twenty twenty-four that dengue cases in France hit record highs that year. Dengue is a virus spread by mosquito bites. It is most often brought in by travellers, but it can also spread locally once the right mosquitoes are present.

The report explains how the tiger mosquito has spread across much of France. Warm weather, travel, trade, and city water pots all help it breed. Most dengue cases are mild or cause no symptoms, but a second infection can turn severe and can kill. The authors set out case counts and the steps used to spot and track the disease. Their account helps health teams plan for more local spread.
pmc-11672386:
Jie Zhang and co-authors report a stroke case that began with sudden deafness in a paper from two thousand twenty-four. A man aged fifty-nine lost hearing in both ears at once, a rare first sign. He had high blood pressure and a long history of smoking and drinking.

Treatment for sudden deafness did not stop his decline. Scans then showed a blocked and narrowed basilar artery, the vessel feeding the brainstem. Surgeons reopened the artery with a mechanical procedure, but he died five days later. The authors warn that sudden deafness in both ears can precede a brainstem stroke. They stress early scanning and fast treatment to cut death and disability.
pmc-11672686:
Qinyu Zhu and co-authors use data methods and lab theory to speed the search for better battery plastics, in a study from two thousand twenty-four. The plastics carry lithium ions along one fixed charge type, but flow is still too slow at room heat for wide use. Old fits to heat data gave odd values, so the team tried a fixed-start fit instead.

The new fit showed hurdles that shift with heat and flagged three charge groups with low hurdles. Lab math then linked how tightly lithium sticks to a charge group with the size of the hurdle. That link points to fresh boron-based groups that could pass the target flow. Readers get a design rule for the next round of materials.
pmc-11673086:
Xue Zhang and co-authors test a skin-based gel as a lab home for fat tissue extract in a 2024 study. The extract, drawn from fat by a mechanical process, is being explored to speed skin wound healing and limit scars. The team mixed it into a hydrogel made from skin matrix and watched the pair over ten days.

The extract stayed alive for the full ten days and stayed inside its own matrix. The gel's collagen fibers kept their alignment and layout. No new capillaries grew out, by stain checks. Healing signals stayed switched on, two inflammatory genes quieted, and one remodeling gene rose from day three. The authors call the gel a versatile test platform, while noting the extract needs extra triggers to grow vessels.
pmc-11674686:
Yao Yin, Xueke Wang, and Tingyong Feng present a 2024 review of noninvasive brain stimulation for attention-deficit/hyperactivity disorder, known as ADHD. The methods pass mild currents or magnetic pulses through the skull to nudge brain activity. Results vary with who is treated and how. The authors pooled randomized trials that measured thinking skills and symptoms in people meeting standard ADHD criteria.

One current-based method improved control of impulses, working memory, and attention compared with sham treatment. A magnetic pulse method showed no clear benefit for symptoms. Two newer current methods showed early promise for executive skills and symptom relief, though each rested on few studies. The authors judge stimulation a promising add-on to standard ADHD care. They note that stronger trials are still needed to settle dose, site, and patient fit.
pmc-11675486:
Ramashia and colleagues review what blocks radiotherapy access for cancer patients in sub Saharan Africa in twenty twenty-four. Cancer cases there rose steeply over the past decade, and radiotherapy anchors cure for many types. The team searched a decade of studies and sorted barriers into four groups. Health system, patient traits, patient factors, and provider factors framed the sorting.

Distance, cost, thin infrastructure, and uneven spread of machines led the list. Policy gaps and weak governance deepened the skew. Culture and logistics added further drag. The review feeds a framework to widen access in one South African province. Targeted fixes are urgent, the authors stress.
pmc-11675686:
Anja Osswald and co-authors train an artificial intelligence system to spot clotting in the false channel of a torn aorta after repair. Their study appeared in 2024. The operation studied, the frozen elephant trunk, leaves some patients with a residual split in the aorta. Whether the false channel clots shut matters for their future. The team fed cross-section images from eight patients into an autoencoder network that learns patterns without labels.

The network's inner map separated images with an open channel, a clotted channel, and no channel at all. Each image earned a clot score, averaged per patient. Reconstructions matched the originals well, including clot texture. The authors present this as a step toward automatic, consistent reading of follow-up scans, though the patient count is small.
pmc-11676386:
Cuesta, Valero, and Patarca test gene shuttles in fish brain cell lines. Work on fish virus vaccines needs new lab tools. The team used two adenovirus vectors, Ad5 and a chimera Ad5/40. Both carried a green glow gene as a marker. Lines came from sea bass and gilthead seabream brain cells.

Both vectors entered both cell lines and lit the marker gene. Uptake was low but clear by microscope and flow tests. Infection also shifted two immune gene markers, irf3 and mx. The chimera gave steadier spread through the cells. The authors say such vectors may deliver genes and stir local immune replies in fish.
pmc-11676586:
Yan Wang and six colleagues examine how filler content and heat change the microwave performance of carbon-titanium carbide mixes, in a study from twenty twenty-four. Titanium carbide suits absorbers used at high heat thanks to thermal stability, its charge flow, and its strength of form. The mixes were made by simple blending and cold pressing. Silica formed the supporting matrix.

Raising the filler share increased dielectric constant and loss, plus stability at high heat. One mix absorbed strongly from room temperature up to one hundred degrees. A richer mix kept absorbing well at two and three hundred degrees. Bounce losses stayed deep across these conditions. The study presents titanium carbide absorbers as a fresh option for extreme settings. Stability, wide use, and flex are the selling points for harsh work sites.
pmc-11678286:
Karim Saadé and co-authors build a low-cost device that watches the placenta barrier form in a dish, in a paper from 2024. The placenta guards what passes from mother to fetus, yet drug effects on it are poorly known. Their setup measures electric flow across a layer of placenta-like cells. Shifts in that flow reveal how tight the barrier is.

The cells were grown on a porous sheet and dosed with a drug that makes them fuse, as they do in real tissue. By day four the layer sealed shut, and its electric resistance tripled in treated wells. Computer models then showed why probe placement skews such readings between labs. Values shifted a lot with depth and spacing of the probes. The team urges standard setups so results can be compared. Their cheap system can screen drug effects on the barrier.
pmc-11678486:
Cindy Crawford and five co-authors checked the labels of weight-loss supplements sold on or near US military bases in a 2024 study. Many service members try such products on their own, without asking a clinician first. The team bought 44 products at shops across twelve military sites between March 2023 and January 2024.

Lab tests showed that 82 percent of the products had inaccurate labels. Many listed ingredients that tests could not find, and over a third held hidden ones. Forty products scored "no-go" on a safety scorecard used by the military, and none carried a third-party seal. Several products mixed stimulants in ways whose safety is unknown.
pmc-11678886:
Shimon Reif and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-four, whether tiny vesicles from milk can help heal the gut lining. Inflammatory bowel disease is a chronic, relapsing gut disorder that breaks the gut barrier. Even with modern biologic drugs, lasting remission is hard for many patients. Milk-derived vesicles are small packets shed by cells, now eyed as a therapy. The team isolated them and tested their effects on gut lining cells. In a mouse colitis model, the vesicles eased disease signs.

In colon tissue, a key Wnt pathway protein, beta-catenin, rose, which hints at lining repair. In patient-derived colon organoids, lab-grown mini guts, the vesicles entered cells and raised growth markers. In colon cancer cells, they did the reverse, lowering those proteins and slowing growth.
pmc-11678986:
Naiwei Lu and colleagues present a two thousand twenty-four method for spotting damage in large structures from sensor data. Bridges produce acceleration signals that are hard to read directly. Machine learning can classify damage, but weak feature extraction limits older methods.

Their approach turns time signals into two-dimensional images using a time-frequency transform. A convolutional neural network then learns damage patterns from the images. Tests used a scale model of a cable-stayed bridge. Engineers get a data-driven route that skips hand-built features and may suit complex structures where damage hides in vibration records.
pmc-11679386:
Mingrui Hao and a team of co-authors present a driverless transport robot for underground coal mines, in two thousand twenty-four. Mine haul roads are long, tight, and must be explosion-proof, and current haulage relies on heavy human labor with high accident rates. Their robot is built to carry materials without a driver in that setting.

A method joining wheel counts with motion sensing improves position estimates where satellite signals cannot reach. It also steadies large-scale mapping of roadways that look alike. A control strategy based on the robot's motion model tracks a planned path on its own. Tests in a virtual roadway and a working mine beat rival mapping methods on accuracy.
pmc-11679986:
Zhengying Cai and co-authors design a scheduling method for factory vehicles that saves energy and avoids crashes. Driverless carts, called AGVs, move goods in plants, but their paths can clash. Output, safety, and energy use pull in opposed ways. The team built a system where each cart computes at the edge, close to the machine. State diagrams guide safe moves, and the problem is framed with a battery limit in mind.

A search method based on plant colony growth steers the fleet. It uses swarm cues from many carts to find good plans. The method runs on small embedded boards, suiting live plant use. Tests on a bench data set show the plans keep carts apart with high energy savings. Plants could use the method to run fleets with less waste.
pmc-11680186:
Yue Zhang and a team of co-authors built a gene mark from neutrophil traps to call ovarian cancer outcomes. Their study, from twenty twenty-four, deals with the most lethal cancer of the female tract. Neutrophils can cast net like traps of DNA and protein, which play a role in tumors. That role in this cancer was not full mapped. Gene data came from a large cancer bank as the train set, with two more banks as check and control.

A shrink Cox screen cut eighty-seven trap genes to an eight gene mark. The mark tied in a firm way to poor outlook in both cohorts. A chart that joins the mark with clinic traits was built and checked. Readers get a trap based score for risk calls.
pmc-11681286:
Alyssa Bernanke and a large team lay out a trial plan in 2024 for veterans with mild brain injury. Suicide is a leading cause of death among veterans, and a mild traumatic brain injury raises the risk of suicidal thoughts. Such injuries also worsen impulsivity, which adds to the danger.

The trial tests a magnetic brain treatment aimed at the front pole of the brain, given in quick bursts. Fifty-six veterans will get the real treatment or a sham version, daily for two weeks. The team will track suicidal thoughts, impulsivity, mood, and daily function, and will interview participants about the experience. This pilot checks safety and acceptability first, to guide a larger trial.
pmc-11685086:
Fuqing Feng and six co-authors review a hormone pathway as a target in ovarian cancer. Their 2024 review centers on follicle-stimulating hormone and its receptor. Ovarian cancer has the poorest outlook among women's cancers, and it often returns after surgery and chemotherapy. Blood levels of the hormone track with worse outcomes, and cancer cells carry its receptor.

The review first covers the hormone's normal roles in reproduction, bone, heart, and fat. It then maps how the pathway drives cancer growth, survival, and spread. New attack routes include tiny carriers built with nanotechnology and immune-based treatments. The authors weigh what targeted receptor therapy could add to standard care. They close with open questions and next steps for the field.
pmc-11688086:
Kang Liu, Zhi Yang, Weipeng Xie, Sicheng Wang, and Shouye Hu report a stubborn knee implant infection caused by an unlikely germ, in a 2024 case report with a literature review. Two years after both knees were replaced, a 68-year-old man developed swelling, pain, and a mass. Standard cultures often miss Mycoplasma hominis, a germ that usually lives in the urinary tract. Gene sequencing of joint fluid found it, and tissue study confirmed chronic infection.

Each knee got a one-stage revision, swapping the implant in a single operation. Targeted antibiotics followed, first by vein and joint injection, then by mouth for six weeks. Pain eased markedly and no infection returned. The authors urge doctors to suspect this germ when implant infections resist standard antibiotics and cultures stay silent.
pmc-11690486:
Ryan Mace and seven co-authors published a 2024 study on fair access to dementia trials. Behaviour programs can slow decline, but trials often miss the older adults who need them most. Cost, language, tech gaps, and bias can all shut people out.

The team ran five group talks with 26 care staff from a large medical centre and local clinics. Staff named blocks at each level, from a patient’s own means to clinic rules and wide social bias. The authors then matched each block with known fixes: simpler sign-up, staff training, clinic-level support, and work with local groups. They frame the paper around a brain-health program called My Healthy Brain. The goal is trials that reach the full range of patients.
pmc-11690886:
Aleksiina Martikainen and three co-authors published a study in 2024 on people in Sweden who kept working after the age of sixty-five. As retirement ages rise across Europe, more people extend their working lives. The researchers asked how earlier sickness absence related to mental health affects whether people stay in paid work.

The study followed all Swedes aged sixty-five to sixty-nine, and those aged seventy or older, who had some income from work in 2014. Sickness absence or disability pension related to physical illness was far more common than the same for mental health. Among women in the younger group, earlier mental health related absence made it slightly more likely that they would leave work. No such link appeared for men or for the older group. The authors conclude that prior mental health and gender both matter when studying working life at older ages.
pmc-11691386:
Rachel Missell-Gray, Alexander Eustice-Corwin, and Silvia Sörensen wrote a theoretical paper in 2024 on adverse childhood experiences and cognition in later life. Earlier studies disagree on whether such early hardship is associated with poorer cognitive performance with age. Some find a clear decline, while others find no association at all.

The paper argues that one component has been missing: moral development. The authors set out a framework that places practical wisdom at its center, in the classical Greek sense of sound judgment in everyday life. They suggest that early hardship may actually help build that kind of wisdom, which standard cognitive tests do not capture. The paper first summarizes what the empirical literature shows, then examines its limitations. It ends with a call for new research testing whether early adversity shapes moral identity and wise decision-making in old age.
pmc-11691786:
Mary Milnamow, Lillian Agyemang, Louanne Bakk, and Jason Dauenhauer published a study in 2024 on virtual reality used in a respite program for people living with dementia. Respite programs give caregivers a break while providing social connection for participants. Virtual reality is usually used in nursing homes and residential care, and few studies have examined it in community and home-based respite.

The researchers trained respite staff and volunteers, then surveyed them before training and after one virtual reality session. The surveys tracked skills, confidence, comfort, and support for adopting the technology. Scores rose in all areas, with skill gains the largest. Strong support from leadership, in both funding and hands-on help, was the leading facilitator of adoption. Cost was the leading barrier. Steps that helped included training lead users as champions and providing a short guide that took past trauma into account.
pmc-11696386:
Guoju Lu and four co-authors strip coal with sound waves to find the parts that drive self burn. Their study appeared in twenty twenty-four. Coal can catch fire on its own as its small parts meet air and give off heat. Four bath fluids drew out split part kinds, from ring and chain fats to air-hold groups, and light and heat tests read raw and drawn coal.

Drawn coal gave off less heat and bore low burn risk marks. Bath kinds that drew air-hold groups cut risk most. Two parts tied most tight to the risk marks, with the chain part in front. A guess frame was built on them.
pmc-11699586:
Young-Jae Cho and four co-authors study a fermented flower extract against fat cell growth, in this twenty twenty-four paper. The flower, a type of chrysanthemum, was already known to slow the making of fat cells. Fermenting it with lactic bacteria seemed to boost that effect.

The team tuned the ferment: which bacteria strain, how much flower, and how long to brew. They then tested the broth for antioxidant power and for signals that guide fat cell growth, in mouse cells used as a fat model. Fermentation raised a gene signal that holds back fat formation. The work explores a plant route to anti-obesity products.
pmc-11709886:
Mario A Parra-Rodriguez and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on two memory tests in southern Colombia. Standard tests often miss the earliest stage of Alzheimer's disease, above all in poorer communities. The team tried two newer tests, one on binding features in memory and one on cued recall, in local older adults.

The study enrolled 390 volunteers, of whom 248 had mild cognitive impairment and 142 were healthy. Both tests separated the groups. The binding test showed that impaired patients lost far more when features had to be held together than when held apart. The work supports using both tests for early screening in such settings.
pmc-11709986:
Bo-Xiang Lin and co-authors report a 2025 conference abstract on long pauses in speech as a sign of early Alzheimer's disease. Speech tests are cheap and gentle, and silent pauses grow more common in the disease. The team measured the share of long pauses while people described pictures, then compared it with standard markers.

The study enrolled 104 memory clinic patients in Taipei, Taiwan, from 2021 to 2023. The pause share ran highest in Alzheimer's disease, lower in mild impairment, and near zero in healthy controls. It also rose with dementia severity and rose as hippocampus volume shrank. No link appeared with amyloid burden.
pmc-11710486:
Byron Creese and co-authors present a 2025 study of shared gene risk for late life psychosis like signs. Such signs, when seen as part of mild behavior change, track with later decline. The team asked if gene risk for these signs is shared with other traits.

They studied thousands of older adults with no dementia. Each person got gene risk scores for traits such as schooling, mood, and memory. Higher scores for low mood disorder, schizophrenia, and a tense trait tracked with higher odds of the signs. Higher scores for schooling and smarts tracked with lower odds. One link held only for self reports, not partner reports. The authors note the split needs more study.
pmc-11710686:
Kristin Basche and co-authors report a 2025 study of practice gains in home based memory tests. Taking the same kind of test again and again can lift scores, even when the items change. That lift can hide real decline, so the team measured how strong it was.

Adults from aging studies used a phone or tablet app at home for a year. Each person did four memory tasks six times, with weeks between repeats. Two plans spread the tasks in distinct ways. Scores rose with practice on most tasks in both plans. Burst plan users started lower on one task but gained faster. Brain amyloid status did not change the pattern in this sample.
pmc-11711886:
Annikka Immonen explores how care staff see agency in people with dementia in a 2025 study drawn from dissertation work. Agency means a person's power to act with purpose. Immonen surveyed 191 care staff who also cared for a relative, and read Finnish care textbooks printed between 1985 and 2019.

Staff recalled their loved ones before illness as social, cheerful, and full of plans. As illness advanced, they saw agency fade, mostly through lost memory and speech. Both the survey and the textbooks said little about body language and other non-verbal signs. Immonen urges staff to watch the body for wishes and needs. A remote course is being built to teach that skill.
pmc-11711986:
Lenora W Smith and Charles O'Brien describe a 2025 project to catch memory decline early with a phone app. The app, called Neurospective, uses short games based on standard screening tests. No cure exists for Alzheimer's disease, so finding decline early gives people more time to plan and seek care.

Along with game scores, the app records play time, success rates, and reaction times, plus survey answers about health and background. Machine learning models learn from this mix and sharpen as more people join. The goal is a data set of more than twenty-five thousand users, shared openly for research. Use is voluntary, and data stay anonymous.
pmc-11712186:
Marissa Ciesla and colleagues evaluated a brief digital test of memory and drawing as a way to spot problems with daily life skills. Their paper, published in twenty twenty-five, draws on a large multi-site study of older adults. Some participants were cognitively healthy, some had mild impairment, and some had probable Alzheimer dementia. The test scores itself and records many details from speech and drawing. The team trained a model to predict who struggled with everyday and complex daily tasks.

The digital test predicted functional problems well enough to sort patients by need. People flagged by the test could be sent on for a full functional assessment, while others could skip that step for now. The authors present the test as a triage tool that can save clinic time and reduce burden on families who often must answer long questionnaires.
pmc-11717486:
Yo Iwata and Yuki Kusayanagi treat three children's lazy eye that patching made worse, in this case series from twenty twenty-four. Their patients had amblyopia with fusion maldevelopment nystagmus, an involuntary eye wobble born of failed binocular development. Covering the good eye, the standard therapy, consistently aggravated the wobble.

The team switched to dichoptic treatment with the Occlu-pad, which shows each eye different content so both must cooperate, no patch needed. The nystagmus stayed calm under this regime. Vision in the weak eye climbed to normal, zero on the logMAR scale, in all three cases. The authors present dichoptic therapy as the sensible first route when amblyopia and this nystagmus travel together: treat the binocular failure, and the acuity follows.
pmc-11726886:
Maiara Fava de Souza and co-authors published a 2024 study of a Brazilian plant's effects on the brain, tested in mice. Duguetia furfuracea, called araticum-seco, carries compounds that fight oxidation and slow an enzyme whose overactivity is tied to memory loss. Traditional use and chemistry alike suggested it might protect memory and calm anxiety. The team ran preclinical tests of both promise and safety.

Mice received the plant preparation before a chemical that induces amnesia, letting researchers measure whether memory survived. Anxiety-related behavior was tested in standard mazes. Safety was screened for early toxic effects. A plant can only move toward human study if all three ledgers, memory, calm, and safety, look acceptable. The authors frame the work as a first gate: folk knowledge turned into controlled evidence. The study adds a candidate to the search for gentle, plant-based aids for the aging brain.
pmc-11727586:
Si-Wook Lee and a team of co-authors compare printed ceramic and titanium ankle parts in minipigs, in a paper dated twenty twenty-four. Bad ankle arthritis can call for replacing the talus bone, at times only in part. The team printed partial talus parts from scans of each animal.

Six minipigs got implants, three ceramic and three titanium, in a hind ankle. Blood tests and scans ran monthly for three months after surgery. The checks gauged swelling, safety, and how firm the parts sat. The study asks whether printed metal can match ceramic for body friendliness and stability.
pmc-11728086:
Rosa and co-authors check voice change after thyroid removal for cancer. Voice harm is a known risk of thyroid surgery. The team used the Acoustic Voice Quality Index to score voices. They enrolled 74 cancer patients from 224 thyroid cases. Voices were scored before surgery and at set points after.

Vocal fold weakness showed in 6.76 percent of patients right after surgery. All of those cases healed within three months. Many patients scored as hoarse before surgery despite normal cord motion. Mean voice scores did not shift much with sex, age, or neck node removal. The authors say skilled surgery left voice quality largely intact.
pmc-11728586:
Hui Gao and Xiaoquan Luo pooled studies of knee strength in young athletes in a 2024 review. They asked how bending and straightening strength changes from childhood through puberty, and whether boys and girls diverge. Thirteen studies from 2003 to 2021 met their criteria.

Before puberty, boys and girls matched on both knee actions. During puberty, boys pulled clearly ahead relative to body weight, and their strength jumped sharply across the transition. Girls showed no significant gain relative to weight. The ratio between back- and front-thigh strength showed no sex or age pattern at all. The authors question that ratio's use for injury prediction and argue girls need strength work targeted at the pubertal years.
pmc-11728786:
The authors (2024) tested how biodegradable bone scaffolds lose strength as they break down in the body. Such printed polymer scaffolds support regrowing bone, then dissolve. Dissolving changes their strength, and designers must know by how much. The team soaked solid samples and lattice scaffolds in salt solution at body temperature and at a hotter setting that speeds decay. They squeezed the samples and scanned their structure over time.

At body temperature, solid pieces lost at most sixteen percent of stiffness, and the lattices only four percent. At the hotter setting, the losses grew to 47 and sixteen percent. Strength fell less than stiffness, and the lattices again held up better. Shape analysis tracked how surface erosion drove the changes. The authors say graded lattice designs resist decay better than solid blocks. Their numbers can guide designs that stay strong long enough for bone to take over.
pmc-11740786: Marlene Winfield writes a 2024 personal view on the future of pharmacy in Britain's National Health Service. Living with three long-term conditions, she argues that pharmacies could take on routine care for minor ailments and help manage ongoing conditions. She describes a gap in her own care: no one sees her and her full set of medicines as a whole. She calls for a funded national program to expand what pharmacies do, framing community pharmacy as central to the health service's survival.
pmc-11745186: Nadim Ojaimi, Sofia Zhang, Marcos Wolff, and Christopher Haas report an odd case of herpes simplex type one meningitis from twenty twenty-four. Type one more often causes grave brain infection, while type two is the usual cause of viral meningitis. Their patient had just mild signs, which cleared with plain supportive care alone. The case gives a frame for such vague first shows.
pmc-11782286:

The authors then weigh medical uses: vesicles in blood could serve as painless markers for tracking the disease. Vesicles might also deliver drugs. They caution that better isolation methods and well-designed clinical trials are needed before such uses reach patients.
pmc-12765286:
Santiago Dans-Caballero and colleagues report results on systemic sclerosis from a European study in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Systemic sclerosis is an autoimmune disease that scars skin and organs. Sorting patients by skin spread or antibodies misses much of its variety. The team used clustering on clinical and blood data from over four hundred patients. The groups that emerged were checked in a second cohort of about two hundred patients.

A subset also had their blood proteins profiled for organ damage markers. Patient serum was applied to skin cells in the lab to watch gene responses. The clusters revealed molecular differences behind the clinical picture. Better grouping could guide trials and personal care. The study bridges bedside traits and molecular signals.
pmc-12766386:
Metin Kement leads a nationwide team reporting early results on hemorrhoid surgery in Turkey, in this twenty twenty-five study. Many surgical methods exist for painful hemorrhoids, but real-world proof of which suits patients best is scarce. This study tracks patients across the country as they are treated.

Patients rate their own outcomes, such as pain and daily comfort, after different kinds of surgery. The early results give a first look at how the methods compare in daily practice rather than in tight trials. Findings from patients' own reports can help surgeons and patients pick a method with clearer eyes.
pmc-12780686:
Sijia Ren and co-authors pool trials to test whether adding immune therapy to chemotherapy helps advanced cancer of the food pipe and stomach junction, in work published in 2025. The cancers are glandular types that have spread or cannot be removed. Drugs that release immune brakes have become first-line care in this setting.

The team searched major databases and conference records up to August 2025 for randomised trials. Seven trials with over seven thousand patients met the rules. The pooled analysis compares survival, time without growth, response rates, and side effects between the combined treatment and chemotherapy alone. It also looks for a biomarker that predicts who gains most. The review aims to firm up the evidence base for a fast-changing standard of care.
pmc-12784686:
Yi-Yuan Liang, Shao-Yang Hu, and Chun-Hung Liu compare, in a 2025 study, gut bacteria in fast- and slow-growing eels, then test a helpful strain as a feed additive. The eel type studied is a farmed short-finned species. Gene reading showed both growth groups shared the same dominant gut bacteria.

Slow growers, though, carried more bacteria that can cause disease. Fast growers held more of a strain close to a known helpful species. That strain made many digestive enzymes and passed safety checks as non-harmful. The authors present it as a candidate probiotic to lift eel growth, with feeding trials as the natural next step for farms.
pmc-12784986:
Nora Elfeky, Yongheng Yang, Guoping Zhu, and Yongming Bao map gene activity in an oil making yeast under different feeding regimes in a 2025 study. The yeast can produce fats and orange pigments at once, valuable for industry, but the control of carbon flow between them was murky. The authors stress the runs were single, carefully controlled batches meant as a foundation map for future validation work.
pmc-12790986:
Huilu Zhang and five co-authors present a pilot trial from twenty twenty-five on stool transplants for constipation in Parkinson's disease. Gut flora skew is long tied to the disease. Chemical maps of stool shifted in fat and amino acid paths. The team says the route may ease both bowel and nerve signs, but the group is tiny.
pmc-12799886:

Treated cells lived better and leaked less across the barrier. Harmful immune cell ratios fell after treatment.

pmc-12801886:
Cai-yun Yang and five colleagues present a cheap, one-tube method to pull DNA from plant tissue, in a twenty twenty-five paper. Standard methods are slow, pricey, and wasteful of plastic. Their method skips tube transfers, cutting handling errors and time. It yielded DNA pure enough for standard gene tests in wheat and its wild crosses.

Tests in maize, a model weed, and tomato confirmed wide use. Dried or frozen tissue gave more DNA than fresh. Two simple salt buffers both worked. The authors pitch the method for breeding programs that screen many plants, while noting it is not for jobs needing ultra-pure DNA.
pmc-12802086:
Ibrahima Lyra Sarr and four co-authors studied heart rhythm control in Senegalese dialysis patients whose blood pressure drops during treatment, in a study from twenty twenty-five. Such drops raise heart risk and death in kidney patients. Faulty autonomic control of the heart is a suspect cause.

Fifty-two patients at a military hospital had heart rate variability measured before, during, and after one session. They were grouped by how their pressure moved. The group with the steepest drops oddly showed stronger variability before dialysis and milder autonomic damage. After dialysis, no group differences remained. The authors conclude variability alone does not explain the drops, and other risk factors need hunting.
pmc-12805786:
Prawez Alam and co-authors build a greener lab test for two heart drugs sold in one capsule in a 2025 study. The capsule pairs clopidogrel, a clot preventer, with rosuvastatin, a cholesterol drug. Quality labs must measure both in each batch. Their method uses high-performance thin-layer chromatography, a plate-based technique that sips solvent compared with liquid columns.

The tools judge solvent toxicity, energy, waste, and practicality, giving greenness and whiteness scores. Analytical chemistry rarely audits its own footprint; this paper makes the audit part of the result. A method that is accurate, fast, and light on the planet is the goal.
pmc-12811386:
Shang and a large team trace in twenty twenty-five a chain of cell events that drives long-lasting mouth inflammation in oral lichen planus. The chronic disease varies in look and can turn cancerous, and its drivers were unclear. Using single-cell and spatial gene maps, a big patient cohort, lab tests, and tissue staining, the team followed signals from surface cells to immune cells.

They found surface cells dying by a fiery route switch on a class of macrophages. Those cells release a signal that activates a helper T cell type, speeding tissue inflammation. The team also built a public atlas linking mouth and gut inflammation data. They offer the chain as a drug target and the atlas as a shared tool.
pmc-12815286:
Romé Charrière and eight co-authors study patients who develop both sarcoidosis and lymphoma in this two thousand twenty-five paper. Sarcoidosis inflames organs with small cell clusters; its link to blood cancer is suspected but fuzzy. The team gathered cases from three French hospitals over more than two decades. Forty-six patients had both diseases. They were compared with ninety-two who had sarcoidosis alone.

The combined cases were sorted by which disease came first. Records covered symptoms, labs, scans, and treatments. Contrasts with the sarcoidosis-only group hunted for signs that warn of coming lymphoma. Such warnings would change follow-up for a large patient pool. The rarity of the pairing makes pooled cases precious. Internal medicine specialists are the readers.
pmc-12815886: A list from twenty twenty-five thanks the peer reviewers of the Annals of the Entomological Society of America. It covers the year from November twenty twenty-four to October twenty twenty-five. The editor-in-chief and the subject editors thank these scientists for giving their time and skill for free. They say the quality of the journal rests on that careful work. What follows is a long list of names, given in alphabetical order, with no research findings of its own.
pmc-12816686:
Yuxuan Zeng and a team of co-authors built a computer model to estimate pressure in the lung arteries, in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. High pressure there is a sign of a serious lung and heart condition. The usual way to measure it is invasive, so a safer estimate would help doctors.

The model learns from past patient records and uses signs that can be gathered without surgery. It also adds features from heart scans, which older methods often left out. The authors add a measure of doubt to each estimate, so doctors can see how firm a result is. They present the model as an aid to diagnosis, not a full replacement.
pmc-12817786:
Bo Yi and co-authors study, in twenty twenty-five, how outdoor temperature links to death in people with severe mental illness in western China. Past work ties heat to excess deaths in people with mental disorders. Less was known about cold, heat waves, and cold spells in severe cases who live at home. The team used death records for more than twenty-two thousand such patients, from twenty oh six to twenty eighteen. Each death was matched to its own control days.

Heat in hot seasons raised death risk by close to a quarter. Cold in cold seasons raised risk too, with a lag of days. Heat waves raised risk, more so when long or hot. Cold spells showed no clear link.
pmc-12818186:
Takakazu Miyake, Hiroshi Nakase, and seven co-authors review outcomes of a scope surgery for throat cancer. Their study, from twenty twenty-five, covers cancers of the esophagus cut out through a scope. Whole-ring removal is used for shallow tumors, here split by length above or below fifty millimeters. Sixty-seven patients at one Japanese center were treated over a decade.

The feared side effect is narrowing of the throat after healing. Rates of narrowing were near equal in long and short tumor groups. Strong prevention with stretching and steroids likely helped. Counts of stretching sessions and long-term survival were also tracked. The results support the method even for long tumors.
pmc-12821786:
Renata Kelemenic-Drazin and co-authors survey cancer doctors in Croatia about gender and careers in a 2025 study. Global surveys by a European oncology society in 2016 and 2021 found stubborn gender gaps in the field. The Croatian team adapted the later questionnaire to their setting to see how local careers compare with the world pattern.

Two hundred six professionals answered the anonymous online survey, three quarters of them women. Most were medical or radiation oncologists, with pathologists next. The questions probed whether gender, politics, religion, or sexual orientation had shaped their careers, and answers were split by sex and age. Set beside the global data, the results show where Croatia shares the common gaps and where it stands apart. Such mirrors help a profession target its fixes.
pmc-12827186:
Dina Eskander and five co-authors search a common reed for fungi that live inside it and make useful compounds. Such inner fungi are a little-charted source of drugs. The team grew one fungus from the reed, farmed it at scale, and purified three compounds from it. One compound is reported from this reed's inner fungi for the first time.

All three compounds fought free radicals, bacteria, and inflammation in lab tests. The new one worked best on most tests, though it did not touch one brain-linked enzyme. Computer models showed it binds well to targets for those effects and looks safe and stable as a drug lead. The paper adds the reed to the map of sources worth mining.
pmc-12828586:
Mariacarolina Salerno and co-authors present a review, published in 2025, on acquired hypothyroidism in children. An underactive thyroid is the most common thyroid disorder of childhood, and Hashimoto thyroiditis is its leading cause where iodine is plentiful. Signs range widely, and odd presentations can delay diagnosis, harming growth and development.

The review walks through four real cases from the authors' clinics, showing both typical and unusual faces of the disease. Around the cases it lays out causes, symptoms, testing strategies, and treatment. The aim is practical: help pediatricians spot the condition earlier, including when it hides behind unexpected complaints, and manage it well once found.
pmc-12829086:
Delphine Bosson-Rieutort, Jean-Frédéric Boulianne, Juliette Duc, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2025. It tallies what healthcare people use, and what it costs, in the last year of life in Quebec, split by what they died of.

Everyone studied died at sixty-six or older between 2014 and 2018. The team sorted deaths into cancer, organ failure, frailty, and other causes. Records covered doctor visits, emergency trips, hospital stays, home care, and long-term care. Costs came from administrative databases and public financial reports. Statistical models compared the groups' patterns of use and spending. The authors say end-of-life care is heavy and complex for aging patients with many conditions. Knowing which dying trajectories consume what care, they argue, helps planners fund the final year fairly.
pmc-12829186:
CangMei Fu and co-authors review how user profiling is being used to manage mental health care, in this 2025 scoping review. Profiling blends artificial intelligence with data from many sources to personalize support. The team searched seven databases across six decades and screened the haul by set rules. Eighteen studies made the cut.

Profiling work fell into three phases: gathering wide-ranging data, extracting features, and presenting profiles visually. Uses spanned teens, young adults, and psychiatric patients, aiding personal plans, resource allocation, and crisis response. Reported gains included easier access, sharper targeting, and better remote care. The authors flag open problems: long-term proof of benefit is scarce, and tools do not transfer everywhere. They call profiling promising but unfinished for digital mental health.
pmc-12830686:
Songwei Zhang and co-authors improve drone landing on polar ice, in work from 2025. On drifting floes, satellite signals drift too much for safe return and landing. The model adds a global feature block, a fog-aware feature stack, and a leaner detection head. On the team's own polar data sets, it beat the base model on hit rate, recall, and balance scores. It kept its frame rate high too. That mix suits the real-time sign spotting that polar landings demand.
pmc-12831586:
Jesse Handler, Zijie Li, and Rachel Dveirin lead a team uncovering a cell-state axis that predicts whether carcinoma cells can colonize the liver. Their paper appeared in two thousand twenty-five. pmc-12836986:
Madelein Dippenaar, Hans Jacob Maree, and Rachelle Bester weigh how RNA extraction method sways the spotting of citrus viruses and viroids. Certification and disease control rest on exact pathogen tests, and extraction is their base step. The study came out in twenty twenty-five.

A second round resampled leaves and added a fifth protocol and a tweaked one. Protocols were judged by pathogen counts and data checks, with housekeeping genes as anchors.
pmc-12842686:
Sourabh Khatri and eight colleagues published a 2025 literature review on endocan, a possible blood marker for heart attack outcomes. A STEMI is a severe heart attack caused by a blocked coronary artery. Damage also occurs in the small vessels and in the endothelium, the lining of the blood vessels, and this damage shapes recovery.

The review gathers this evidence and weighs how endocan might be used alongside existing risk scores in the clinic.
pmc-12845186:
Zhifeng Liao and six co-authors test, in two thousand twenty-five, a soft acid gel as a carrier for skin cells in early burn care. Burns heal poorly, and cell therapy could help if the cells reach the wound and stay there. The gel is a non-crosslinked hyaluronic acid product sold as Redensity 1.

The authors see a simple path toward use in burn care.
pmc-12849186:
Dongfei Ma and co-authors study home care for people with dementia who also have other illnesses in a paper from two thousand twenty-five. They spoke with eighteen family caregivers and eight people with dementia at a memory clinic in northeast China. The authors warn that badly timed takeovers can harm identity, and they suggest support that keeps the person involved as long as safety allows.
pmc-12857586:

pmc-12859886:
Yiliya Yilihamu, Jun Mo, and Zhanjun Ma lead a team comparing two fusion operations for severe narrowing of the lower spinal canal. Their study appeared in two thousand twenty-five. pmc-12860286:
Shio Kinami, Yasuo Sasagawa, Takuya Nakamura, Daiki Kakita, and Mitsutoshi Nakada report a gentle surgical fix for a rare chest problem, in a 2025 case report. pmc-12872786:

pmc-12885186:

pmc-13084786:

pmc-13094586:

pmc-13126586:
Milton Anguyo and co-authors describe a hard diagnostic case mixing bipolar disorder with recent drinking in a 2025 paper. Bipolar disorder often travels with alcohol use disorder. pmc-13150886:
Lei Tao, Dan Luo, Limin Tan, Cangyun Zhang, and Yuci Li tested a transitional care program after heart stent treatment in two thousand twenty-six. No gap in self-management showed at one month, but the program group pulled ahead at three, six, and twelve months. Their physical and mental quality of life scores were also better at one year. Analysis showed better self-management explained part of the quality gain.
pmc-13156886:
Abdul Walusansa and co-authors survey herbalists in eastern Uganda on plants used for gut illness and their risks. Herbal care is the first resort for stomach disease in the Sironko District. pmc-13157486:

Eligibility rules, they argue, deserve the same scrutiny as results.
pmc-13174186:
Jia He and colleagues measured vitamin D and metabolic syndrome in a large health-screening group in 2026. Whether blood vitamin D levels relate to metabolic syndrome has stayed controversial. pmc-13180586:
Yu Chen, Guohong Jiang, Xiaohe Zhang, Zhiwei Zhou, and Ping Xu review what is known about links between nose and sinus disease and trouble with thinking, in this 2026 paper. Poor sleep, facial symptoms, and nose-to-brain signaling may all play a part. The authors say firm proof still lags and more work is needed.
pmc-13180786: Yu, Liu, Han, Liu, and Bi reported in twenty twenty-six a rare case of nodular fasciitis in the breast of an older woman. Nodular fasciitis is a harmless soft tissue growth that can enlarge fast. It mostly grows from fiber-making cells and usually settles on its own. In the breast it is seldom seen. Their patient was sixty-one years old with a fast-growing mass in the middle of her right breast.
pmc-13180886:
Afif Nakhleh and five co-authors report a gene-guided triple therapy for a rare adrenal cancer. Their paper is from two thousand twenty-six. The cancer had spread and made excess cortisol, the stress hormone. It grew past surgery, radiation, and the standard drug. Few options stay at that point.

The patient's Cushing signs clear, and scans show a deep, lasting shrink of the spread. The case shows how a full gene read can back a bold mix.
pmc-13182886:

Four children were found to have drug-resistant TB using newer sampling approaches at the hospital. All received fully oral drug plans suited to their condition. Every child completed treatment in the end. The small series shows these testing advances working in a real district hospital, where resistant TB in children is usually missed until far too late.
pmc-13189786:
Mei-Lian Zhang and six colleagues use latent class analysis of ultrasound features to predict non-response to chemotherapy in breast cancer, in a study from twenty twenty-six. pmc-13194186:

pmc-13194386:

pmc-13194486:
Training people to stop themselves reaching for rich food can shift cravings, and virtual reality offers a controlled place to practice. pmc-13194686:
Mohamed ELGabry is first author on a 2026 study of earthquake resilience in Egypt's Great Pyramid of Khufu, built in the Old Kingdom over four thousand years ago. That frequency band differed clearly from the surrounding soil's, preventing resonance build-up between ground and building. Shaking grew with height but eased inside the pressure-relieving chambers. pmc-13195186:
