It shows strong biological effects, even against cancer cells in lab reports. Safety data, though, were missing. The team tests a fruit extract in Wistar rats of both sexes. A single large dose of 2,000 milligrams per kilogram covers the acute fourteen-day test. Three lower daily doses cover the ninety-day test.

Behavior, body and organ weights, blood chemistry, blood counts, and tissue slides are tracked throughout. Standard guideline protocols frame both phases. Food safety readers get the missing base record for a spice eaten by millions. Potent plants deserve the same scrutiny as drugs when extracts concentrate them. Sex-balanced testing matters because spice exposure is universal in the cuisines that use it.
pmc-13196986:
Qing Ma and colleagues present a 2026 model of a closed-loop supply chain for new products. In such a chain, used goods return for recycling or remaking. The team added two kinds of buyer regret: regret after buying, and regret after swapping an old item for a new one.

Their game model covers makers, sellers, and third-party recyclers over time. It solves for best prices and return effort at each stage. Regret after buying cut sales and long-term profit for makers and sellers. Regret after swapping did the reverse, drawing more buyers in. Both kinds of regret kept products on the market longer. Recyclers' profits were not swayed by either kind of regret.
pmc-13197886:
Pei Pei Heng and colleagues studied how soon smokers light up after waking in Malaysia in 2026. Time to first cigarette is a strong sign of nicotine dependence. A quick first cigarette means deeper dependence and harder quitting, so the team sought its drivers in a national survey.

Data came from a 2023 tobacco survey of more than four thousand adults. About twenty-nine percent of current smokers lit up within thirty minutes of waking. Starting smoking before age eighteen raised the odds of a quick first cigarette. So did never having tried to quit and feeling quitting would be hard. Smokers not worried about health harms had about double the odds. Targeted help may suit these groups.
pmc-13198786:
Abhishek Man Shrestha and colleagues present a 2026 case report on Collet-Sicard syndrome from a skull base tumor. The syndrome knocks out four lower cranial nerves where they exit the skull, harming swallowing, voice, shoulder lift, and tongue motion. Tumors are the usual cause, but benign paragangliomas, nerve-cell tumors, rarely are.

Their patient was a 58-year-old woman with worsening trouble swallowing. Exam showed weakness of all four nerves on the right side. Scans revealed a lobed, strongly enhancing mass centered in the canal for the tongue nerve, reaching into the vein opening and neck artery space. The picture fit a skull base paraganglioma. The authors stress full nerve exams and early scans for such signs.
pmc-13198886:
Dimitrios Karamanidis and colleagues present a 2026 case report on bloody nipple discharge in pregnancy. Bloody discharge often raises fears of cancer or duct growths. In pregnancy it can instead be a benign quirk from richer blood flow and fast duct growth, nicknamed rusty pipe syndrome.

Their patient was a 31-year-old woman in her first pregnancy, at sixteen weeks. Both breasts leaked blood from several ducts, with no lump or pain. Ultrasound showed only normal pregnancy changes, and cell tests were benign. Care stayed watchful, with no invasive steps. Symptoms held steady through pregnancy and cleared ten days after birth. The authors back a stepwise, non-invasive workup that keeps mother and baby safe.
pmc-13202686:
Bacteria in the mouth may mirror lung cancer severity, and a 2026 prospective study headed by Vanessa DeClercq tests that link in surgical patients. The research article profiles saliva microbes from patients undergoing curative surgery for non-small cell lung cancer, using full-length gene sequencing.

Samples from sixty-four patients were compared across cancer stage, tumor subtype, and survival outcomes. Most diversity measures were lower in stage III disease than in stage I, suggesting the oral community thins as cancer advances. Two genera, Haemophilus and Solobacterium, differed reliably in abundance at the later stage. The authors caution that the sample is small and call for confirmation in larger cohorts.
pmc-13204786:
Stephanie Glover and Josh Tiller-Ormord lead a team describing a psychology service run by trainees inside a childhood cancer survivorship clinic. Their process paper appeared in two thousand twenty-six. Survivors face thinking and mood difficulties long after treatment ends. Most clinics screen for these and refer out, leaving help slow to arrive.

A psychology intern instead met families during the clinic visit itself. Twenty-minute sessions targeted one concern picked from prior assessments. Anxiety management was the most common topic, ahead of sleep and mood. Nine in ten families found the visit helpful. The same share judged twenty minutes enough. The model costs little, since trainees staff it as part of training. It also reaches families who might never book separate therapy. The authors detail the setup so other clinics can copy it.
pmc-13206286:
More schooling may genuinely lower some cancer risks, and a 2026 genetic study by Mengdan Miao tests that claim with Mendelian randomization. Using inherited variants as instruments, the analysis probes whether educational attainment causally affects endometrial, ovarian, cervical, and vulvar cancers, and which traits carry the effect.

Higher education was linked to lower risk of endometrial, ovarian, and cervical cancers in the genetic analysis. For endometrial cancer, much of the protection ran through body weight, body fat, insulin, and hormone-related traits that education also influences. Body mass index and age at menopause partly mediated the ovarian finding too, suggesting prevention targets for women with less schooling.
pmc-13207586:
Brett Cohen comments on a new open dataset of private equity deals for hospitals. The dataset, built by Kim and colleagues, joins six deal databases into one checked catalog. It lists one hundred forty-one deals across five hundred fifty-five hospitals. Its open release should make studies easier to compare.

Cohen raises three points as the dataset moves into use. First, deal types differ a lot: buyouts bring control and debt, while other deals only add minority cash. Pooling them by default can hide real differences. Second, the dataset is not a live feed and will need manual updates under a named steward. Third, research data alone does not create accountability. He urges builders to plan for upkeep and oversight, not just release.
pmc-13208086:
Asmae Guennouni and nine co-authors report a rare liver tumor case in two thousand twenty-six, with a review of past literature. Neuroendocrine tumors that start in the liver are extremely rare, making up a tiny share of all such tumors. They can grow silently and are hard to confirm.

The patient was a thirty-year-old woman with painless swelling of the abdomen. Scans showed many liver masses, the largest over twenty centimeters across. Lab tests were normal, but tissue tests confirmed a slow-growing neuroendocrine tumor, and a full workup found no primary tumor elsewhere. She was treated with a long-acting drug, lanreotide, and follow-up scans showed stable lesions. The authors stress team review and tissue proof in such cases.
pmc-13210686:
Moretti and seven co-authors test a new biostimulant sprayed on soybean leaves, in work from twenty twenty-six. Soybean is a top world crop, yet drought and heat often cut its yield. Such stresses impair photosynthesis and metabolism.

Biostimulants are products meant to help plants perform under adverse conditions. The new product, applied to leaves at key growth stages, was evaluated for effects on photosynthesis, antioxidant metabolism, growth traits, and grain yield. The title reports improved performance. Stage timed spraying matters: the same product can help at one growth phase and waste money at another.
pmc-13211286:
Le Chung Tran and colleagues build an artificial intelligence vision alarming system helping blind and vision-impaired people navigate safely. Their 2026 paper describes a low-cost wearable aid addressing devices that are expensive or overload users with information.

The system combines a small computer, a laser distance sensor, and an artificial intelligence depth camera in modular software containers. It detects obstacles and reports both their positions and nature to the user. Spoken warnings arrive by Bluetooth using a neural speech synthesiser. The proof-of-concept device is standalone, open-source, very cheap, and low in power use. The authors aim to cut collisions and accidents while boosting users' independence and confidence in traffic.
pmc-13212686:
Gianpaolo Demarchi and co-authors reply in 2026 to critics of their past claim that the brain readies itself for a sound it expects. The critics reworked the team's open data and said the key pattern could arise with no true prediction at all.

Their trick was to shuffle tones from random sets so the sets looked ordered, then decode them the same way. Scores rose just as in the real data, which they blamed on mix-ups between tones close in pitch. Demarchi's team says the fake data differ from real brain data once sounds start. They also warn that the shuffle may reuse test items in training, which inflates scores. They grant the critique makes fair points about method, but reject its broad claim.
pmc-13212986:
Marvin M. Urban and colleagues report in 2026 the first genome-wide look at chemical DNA marks changed by psilocybin in people treated for alcohol use disorder. Such marks may help explain why one dose of the psychedelic can have lasting effects.

Thirty-seven detoxified patients gave blood before treatment, a day after receiving psilocybin or placebo, and one month later. One DNA site in a gene called TLE4 changed with treatment, and a region in another gene shifted as well. Networks of related marks tied to mood improvement and drinking behaviour, pointing toward brain plasticity and immune roles. The pilot is small, so the authors present the signals as starting points.
pmc-13214086:
Xuling Chang leads a large team reporting in 2026 a fresh genetic clue to who catches pulmonary tuberculosis. Earlier genome scans rarely replicated across populations, and much of the inherited risk stayed unexplained.

Genome-wide studies in Singapore Chinese and Vietnamese groups fed into a meta-analysis of East Asian data covering nearly twelve thousand cases. One DNA variant on chromosome 22 nudged risk upward, and the signal replicated in Europeans too. Gene-level tests highlighted a signalling molecule, and the lead variant influences two nearby genes in immune cells. Zebrafish embryos edited to lose that molecule handled a related infection worse, supporting a real biological role.
pmc-13214186:
Malin Stenborg and co-authors interview in 2026 eight Swedish school nurses about supporting students who experience gender dysphoria. These students face more harassment and violence at school than peers, and nurses are frontline adults for their health.

Nurses described students struggling with anxiety, depression, and self-harm, while school climates ranged from open to hostile. Building trust, staying accessible, listening, and signalling openness were their core strategies, with health dialogues and forms as conversation starters. They asked for shared staff training and clearer direction from school leadership, admitting their own preparation felt thin. Openness itself, they suggested, can partly offset missing formal competence.
pmc-13215486:
Richa Giri and co-authors report a 2026 survey of citrus greening disease across Nepal, using DNA testing to find the bacterium behind it. The disease, also called huanglongbing, is one of the most damaging threats to citrus crops worldwide.

The team tested 1,026 leaf samples from thirteen districts in six provinces with a PCR test aimed at the pathogen's 16S gene, and 255 samples came back positive. Sequencing of five samples showed the Nepali bacteria were over 99 percent similar to reference strains and closest to ones from India. The authors call for certified clean planting material and control of the psyllid insects that spread the disease.
pmc-13216086:
Myung-Sub Lee and co-authors present a 2026 retrospective study of shoulder injuries that hide alongside fractures of the coracoid process, a small bone in the shoulder blade complex. Damage to the acromioclavicular joint is easily missed in the acute phase.

The team reviewed 60 patients treated between 2016 and 2023, classifying fractures by position on three-dimensional scans. Joint injury appeared in 15 patients, and every one of them had a fracture at the coracoid base. A sideways displacement gap of about 5.82 millimetres or more on imaging predicted the hidden injury. The authors advise targeted checks whenever a base fracture shows that degree of displacement.
pmc-13216286:
Mehdi Behroozi and co-authors present a 2026 neuroscience study that scanned pigeons' brains while the birds actively unlearned a rewarded behaviour. Extinction learning, where a learned response fades when reward stops, had never been mapped with brain imaging in a non-human animal.

Awake pigeons worked a Go/NoGo task for water rewards inside the scanner. Imaging revealed a wide, mostly left-sided network spanning sensory, limbic, executive, and motor areas of the forebrain. Activity across that network ebbed slowly as extinction proceeded. The authors propose that extinction begins by updating the expected consequences of the bird's own actions across this whole network until a competing new association takes hold.
pmc-13217486:
Fan Tong and co-authors present a 2026 review of nanozymes, engineered nanoparticles that imitate natural enzymes, as a platform for precision dentistry. Conventional dental treatment struggles with targeting, stability, and genuine tissue regeneration, and the mouth's shifting chemistry defeats many materials.

Drawing on cell, animal, and early clinical literature, the review maps nanozymes onto three jobs in the mouth. They kill biofilm bacteria behind decay and gum disease, tune the reactive oxygen balance that drives inflammation, and help tissues repair and remineralize. Delivery platforms that carry the particles are surveyed as well. The authors recommend multi-enzyme designs and better biocompatibility work, arguing nanozymes could cut antibiotic dependence across uses from mucositis to oral cancer support.
pmc-13218186:
Michele Orsi and co-authors set out a 2026 protocol for testing an assisted vaginal birth device, OdonAssist, in Ethiopia. Assisted vaginal birth accounts for only about one percent of births in sub-Saharan Africa, versus sixteen percent in Western Europe. Women in prolonged labour thus often face complications or a caesarean that might have been avoided. OdonAssist was designed to be safer, simpler, and more acceptable than forceps or vacuum devices.

The feasibility study will run at Saint Luke Catholic Hospital in Wolisso, where midwives and health officers perform assisted births under specialist supervision. Sixty women in the second stage of labour will form three groups of twenty: OdonAssist, vacuum extraction, and caesarean without an attempt at assisted birth. The team will collect data on safety, acceptability, and effectiveness against current care, plus an exploratory costing of direct expenses. Findings will shape a future larger evaluation of the device.
pmc-13222086:
Tolay Almahdi Altounsi, Mohammad Luai Morad, and Mohammad Y Hajeer test a digital intraoral scanner against articulating paper for finding bite contact points, in a 2026 in-vivo study. Thirty-five patients with natural teeth had contacts marked with eight-micron paper, then scanned in the same visit. The comparison covered 412 contacts on 140 back teeth.

The scanner caught about ninety percent of paper-marked contacts, showing high sensitivity. Specificity was poor, near fourteen percent, and overall agreement was negligible. Premolars performed better than molars, though still weakly. The authors conclude the scanner under-records contacts compared with paper, so it cannot yet replace the cheap standard for checking occlusion.
pmc-13222586:
Doris K Hansen and co-authors track unusual neurologic events after cilta-cel CAR-T therapy for multiple myeloma in real-world records, in a 2026 study. The events of interest sit outside the standard neurotoxicity syndrome: cranial nerve palsy, parkinsonism, and Guillain-Barré syndrome. Records covered 171 patients treated between 2022 and 2025, grouped by how many prior therapy lines they had received.

Cranial nerve palsy appeared in seven patients across both groups, and nearly all improved. Parkinsonism and Guillain-Barré each occurred once, in the heavily pretreated group. Patients with events showed higher peak lymphocyte counts after infusion, a possible warning marker. Every affected patient responded at least partly to the therapy and survived the follow-up period.
pmc-13223986:
Minghui Hang and a large multi-centre team report a 2026 randomised trial of electroacupuncture for knee osteoarthritis in Shanghai. Earlier evidence suggested the treatment eases pain, but large rigorous trials were scarce and effects on joint structure were unknown. Across six hospitals, 480 participants received either real electroacupuncture or a sham version three times weekly for six weeks.

Outcomes centred on the WOMAC score, a standard measure of pain, stiffness, and function, with follow-up lasting thirty weeks. At six weeks the treated group improved more on the global score than the sham group. Secondary measures covered pain scales, walking capacity, and imaging-based assessments of cartilage and joint inflammation.
pmc-13224686:
Hui Gao, Xuemei Yu, and Zhiyong Guo run a 2026 training trial in trained male swimmers, testing upper-body plyometric exercise, beta-alanine supplements, or both. Plyometrics use explosive movements to build power, but their value in swimming was little studied. Thirty swimmers were split into three groups for eight weeks of twice-weekly sessions, with supplements or placebos given daily.

Both training groups improved across every performance test, from medicine-ball throws and push-up endurance to bench press strength and swim-ergometer power. Some measures, including throw distance and peak power, favoured the combined approach in group-by-time comparisons. Blood tests tracked testosterone, cortisol, and an immune antibody to capture hormonal and immune responses to the programme.
pmc-13225486:
Huan Yao, Yujie Qian, and Zhi Xu chart tuberculosis burden in three East Asian countries in a paper from 2026. Tuberculosis still kills more people than most other single infections. The team used a global disease database to track new cases, deaths, and lost healthy years. Their window runs from 1990 to 2023, with forecasts to 2035.

Rates fell steadily in China, Japan, and South Korea, faster than the world average. China kept the highest case rate, while Japan had the lowest. Men and older people carried more of the burden in all three lands. Smoking stayed a top driver, but high blood sugar rose fast. Forecasts point to further decline if current trends hold.
pmc-13226886:
Furong Hou and co-authors examine a 2026 food-science question: how an ultrasound-assisted enzyme extraction changes the prized polysaccharide of Tremella fuciformis, a jelly fungus eaten widely in Asia. That polysaccharide makes up most of the fungus's dry weight and brings antioxidant, anti-inflammatory, and texture-giving properties prized in foods and skincare. Extraction method strongly shapes its molecular size, composition, and behaviour.

Earlier work mostly tested single conventional methods such as hot water, leaving combined techniques underexplored. The study therefore set out to characterise what the ultrasound-enzyme route does to the polymer's structure and functional performance, then to trial the extract in almond-based milk. Such plant milks need natural thickeners and stabilisers, a role this fungus polymer is well shaped to fill.
pmc-13226986:
Nalia Gurgel-Juarez and colleagues study a 2026 mixed-methods look at mouth care after stroke, when weakness and thinking problems make brushing teeth or cleaning dentures hard. The team surveyed hospital professionals, reviewed a year of patient charts, and followed individual survivors through observation, mouth examinations, and interviews in rehabilitation.

Every professional surveyed agreed mouth care belongs to self-care, and most said brushing comforts patients. Yet nearly sixty percent felt undertrained for oral assessments, and charts showed mouth care happening less than once a day in acute care. Survivors valued their oral health and regained confidence in rehabilitation, but support stayed inconsistent and documentation patchy, leaving heavy reliance on family caregivers.
pmc-13228186:
Tao Sheng and colleagues test a 2026 plant compound, polydatin, in mice with kidney damage induced by adenine, a standard model of uric-acid-related kidney injury. The model produces blocked tubules, inflammation, cell death, and progressive scarring. Fifty male mice were divided among a healthy group, an untreated injury group, and three treatment groups receiving polydatin or one of two standard uric-acid drugs.

Injured kidneys showed clearly abnormal function and tissue structure under the microscope. Polydatin treatment significantly improved those measures, protecting both the tissue architecture and kidney performance. The authors link the benefit to calming immune inflammation, cell death, and scarring processes, and they present the work as groundwork for possible clinical use.
pmc-13231186:
Oleksiy V Voytsekhivskyy develops in 2026 a new formula for choosing artificial lens power during cataract surgery. Accurate power choice decides whether patients see clearly without glasses after the cloudy lens is replaced. Records covered more than one thousand eyes operated by one surgeon with a single lens model.

Half the eyes served to build the formula, which traces light rays under a thin lens shortcut with two tuning constants. The other half tested it against thirteen rival formulas used worldwide. The new method posted the lowest spread of prediction errors and beat all older formulas clearly. It matched the best modern methods, though testing used one lens type and one patient population only.
pmc-13231886:
Laura Hesters and colleagues examine in 2026 how the way therapists talk shapes whether rehab patients stick with treatment. Three hundred forty-six people in physical or occupational therapy rated how supporting or controlling their clinician felt. Questionnaires also covered basic mental needs, reasons for doing therapy, and how closely they followed the plan.

Patients who felt supported in their choices reported fuller need satisfaction and less frustration. Feeling controlled fed frustration instead, which dulled inner motivation and raised giving-up attitudes. People whose motivation came from valuing the goal itself followed treatment best. Training clinicians to support choice rather than apply pressure is the practical takeaway for rehab services.
pmc-13234186:
Ha Nui Kim and colleagues published a 2026 correction to their Scientific Reports assessment of the BMIA-12 system. The machine counts bone marrow cells in healthy samples and in blood cancers. The original article contained two kinds of error. One author's name was printed reversed, reading Yoon Jung instead of Jung Yoon.

A discussion sentence also misstated the system's throughput. The paper had claimed the machine counted roughly thirty-five to forty thousand cells per sample. That dwarfed the five hundred cells of a hand count. Those totals were actually the counts summed across each disease cohort. The corrected sentence puts the per-sample figure at about 755 to 890 cells, still a more detailed sample than manual counting. The notice states the article has been corrected.
pmc-13234486:
Chenxi Zhang and co-authors benchmarked in 2026 short genetic elements that end gene transcription in a fungus used for production. The fungus, Aspergillus oryzae, is widely used in food fermentation and enzyme making. Terminators set where a message ends, which affects stability and protein output. Fifteen terminators borrowed from other organisms were tested in a uniform setup.

Protein output varied more than fivefold across the set, while readthrough past the intended end varied far more widely. Output strength and stopping efficiency were only weakly related, so each trait can be tuned separately. Several terminators combined strong output with very low readthrough in the tests. Short synthetic sequences performed poorly, and two popular toolkit elements also disappointed in this host. Rankings held across different food sources and a second reporter, guiding future strain design.
pmc-13234986:
Damiana Scuteri and a team of co-authors review why some migraines resist every drug in a 2026 paper. Migraine ranks among the top causes of disability worldwide. New drugs that target CGRP, a molecule tied to migraine pain, changed care, yet about forty percent of patients still do not respond.

The review gathers what is known about the nerve and blood vessel changes behind stubborn migraine. Genes and gene switches can alter how a body handles drugs, which helps explain uneven responses. CGRP is not the only messenger at fault; other peptides share the stage. The authors searched five major databases for work up to July 2025 and map routes beyond CGRP for future treatment.
pmc-13235486:
Marion Ravelojaona and co-authors tested in 2026 two related immune signals as treatments for sudden womb inflammation in animals. Bacterial toxin from Gram-negative germs triggers the condition and can threaten fertility and pregnancy. Both signals belong to a family that includes interleukin-6 and act through shared cell machinery. Peritoneal immune cells called macrophages were central to the effects measured in living animals.

Both treatments preserved the womb lining's structure and limited invading inflammatory cells in the experiments. A damaging enzyme linked to inflammation fell under both treatments, while repair-oriented macrophage behaviour rose. One signal gave stronger whole-body and liver protection than the other in the comparisons. The two signals pushed macrophages toward healing states through partly different internal pathways. The authors propose both as candidates for protecting uterine immune balance.
pmc-13236186:
Krishna Prasad Acharya and others argued in two thousand twenty-six that ending rabies by the global target year requires a joined-up One Health strategy grounded in evidence. Rabies spreads mainly through bites from infected animals and is almost always fatal once symptoms begin, yet it is preventable with timely care.

 Their piece addresses health workers and policymakers, especially in lower-income countries where the burden falls hardest, and aligns with the international Zero by Thirty goal. Coordinating human medicine, animal vaccination, and surveillance is presented as the realistic route to elimination.
pmc-13238886:
Maurine Vilcot and a large international team compared reef fish diversity patterns in 2026 across the Caribbean Sea and the Western Indian Ocean, two regions with very different reef spacing. Occurrence records for five fish families supplied the species picture, and DNA markers from nineteen species supplied the genetic picture. The question was whether the two levels of diversity rise and fall together across space.

In the Western Indian Ocean, both genetic and species differences grew with distance, and the two measures correlated across species. In the Caribbean only the species level showed distance effects, and the two levels decoupled. The authors credit the Caribbean's shorter gaps between reefs, which keep populations connected. Seascape layout, they conclude, governs whether genes and species tell the same story.
pmc-13239086:
S. Leena Sankari and colleagues presented six cases in 2026 of the orthokeratinized odontogenic cyst, a rare jaw cyst long mistaken for a variant of the better-known odontogenic keratocyst. The two look similar at a glance, yet under the microscope this cyst's lining is thin and even, topped by orthokeratin with a clear granular layer, unlike its cousin's wavy parakeratin surface. The distinction is more than academic.

The preferred treatment is simple enucleation with an excellent outlook. The series walks through the clinical, imaging, and tissue features of the six cases. Correctly naming the cyst, the authors argue, prevents overtreatment planned for the more aggressive look-alike.
pmc-13239186:
Kuruveetil Manikandan Ashitha and colleagues dissected two food fish species from Udupi, Karnataka, in 2026 to map microplastic contamination organ by organ. Rohu and pangasius were checked across gut, gills, liver, gonads, and muscle. Every single specimen carried microplastics, which the team counted and identified chemically.

Rohu averaged about fifty-eight particles per fish and pangasius about forty-two. Rohu concentrated particles in gills and gut, while pangasius spread them more evenly. Fibers made up nearly ninety-eight percent of the haul, mainly polypropylene and polyester. Finding plastic in edible muscle and in reproductive tissue worries the authors most, since it opens a direct route to human plates and a possible fertility risk. The study sets a baseline for the region's fisheries.
pmc-13239286:
Anaïs Astier and a large team built a panel of cell lines in 2026 carrying the ribosomal protein mutations that recur in blood and solid cancers. Ribosomes are the cell's protein factories, and their faults show up in leukemias and anemia syndromes, yet the translation defects were poorly understood. The panel received full multi-omics profiling of what its ribosomes actually translate.

The chronic lymphocytic leukemia mutation in Rps15 caused the deepest changes, altering translation of up to a tenth of expressed genes. Microscopy showed the mutation loosens the protein's tail and jams the step where transfer RNAs settle into the ribosome, for eleven specific codons. Genes heavy in those codons, including immune regulators, were dialed down. The authors call the panel a resource for ribosome-driven cancer biology.
pmc-13239486:
Tiancheng Xu and Songpeng Su pool trial evidence on sprint interval training for teenagers in a 2026 systematic review and meta-analysis. Short, intense bursts of sprinting promise fitness gains in little time, yet adult programmes may not suit growing bodies, so youth-specific evidence matters.

Eighteen randomised trials with 565 adolescents met the criteria after searches of four databases up to June 2025. Training raised aerobic capacity, sprint speed, jumping power, and change-of-direction ability compared with controls. Body mass index and body fat percentage also fell modestly. Quality checks used standard bias and evidence grading tools. The authors endorse sprint intervals as an efficient option for school and sport settings.
pmc-13239686:
Keiichiro Yasuda and co-authors report a rare adult tumour of the adrenal gland in a 2026 case paper. Ganglioneuroblastoma grows from early nerve cells and almost always appears in young children, with only about twenty-five adult adrenal cases described before this one.

A 20-year-old woman with stomach pain was found to have a large thirteen centimetre mass on her left adrenal gland. Hormone tests were mostly normal, and surgeons removed the gland in an open operation. Tissue study confirmed the mixed tumour type with very slow growth activity. No extra treatment was given, and she stayed free of recurrence for thirty-nine months afterwards.
pmc-13239886:
Marc Rudolph and eleven co-authors test a brain-scan marker of small-vessel disease against memory, imaging, and blood markers in a community cohort, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The marker, ARTS, aims to detect arteriolosclerosis while patients are alive. Two hundred thirty-eight participants had amyloid and tau scans within a year of their MRI.

As expected, ARTS tracked most strongly with age, white-matter damage, and diffusion signs of microstructural breakdown. It ran highest in participants positive for amyloid, tau, and neurodegeneration markers. It also tracked higher plasma levels of a glial injury protein in particular. The authors conclude ARTS ties vascular injury to neurodegeneration, amyloid and tau burden, and inflammation.
pmc-13239986:
Abolfazl Zendehdel and co-authors compare two antibiotics for Gram-positive infections in burn patients in a 2026 retrospective study. Burn wounds invite resistant bacteria, and the team reviewed seventy-seven patients treated at Shahid Motahari Hospital between 2020 and 2022 with linezolid, teicoplanin, or both.

Linezolid patients finished treatment in roughly half the time of teicoplanin patients and improved clinically about twice as fast. Death rates also differed sharply, at five percent against roughly forty percent, though the study was not randomised, so sicker patients may have clustered in one group. Low platelet counts and other safety measures were similar between the drugs.
pmc-13240286:

Postpartum depression is well recognised in mothers, yet fathers in the region are seldom screened, and cultural expectations that men stay strong can hide their distress from services and researchers alike.

Thirteen studies from five countries published between 2015 and 2025 met the criteria, with samples from fifteen to more than eight hundred men. Reported rates ranged enormously, from three percent to sixty percent, and the Edinburgh scale was the tool used most. Risk and protective factors varied between studies. The authors urge routine screening of fathers inside mother and child health programmes.
pmc-13240586:
Bahareh Damankeshan and co-authors report a 2026 orchard trial on feeding Mazafati date palms through trunk and root injections. The palms grew in Kerman Province, Iran. Nutrient uptake from the local chalky soils is often poor, so direct injection was tested as an alternative.

Nine treatments compared iron, zinc, and calcium products at several doses against untreated palms. One iron dose gave the heaviest fruit flesh, while one zinc dose gave the heaviest whole fruit. Injections also shifted leaf mineral levels, sometimes helping one nutrient while lowering another. The authors advise balanced dosing and longer trials before wide use. Growers gain a promising option for orchards where soil feeding falls short.
pmc-13240786:
Xianqi Wang and a large team report a 2026 study of a medicated hydrogel for diabetic wounds. Such wounds heal slowly and often lead to serious complications. The team traced part of the problem to aging blood vessel cells inside the wound.

A protein called BAI1 reduced that leakage and calmed the pathway. The protein was packed into tiny silica particles inside a soft gel for skin application. In diabetic mice, the gel sped wound closure and improved healing quality. The work points toward dressings that treat a root cause.
pmc-13240986:
Lange and colleagues at the University of Southern Denmark protocol a school trial trading screen time for face-to-face play. Eighteen Danish schools joined the cluster-randomized Screen-Free Time With Friends study. Children aged nine to eleven and their parents take part. Five components mix classroom activities, family meetings, and community workshops.

Six hundred eighty-five children enrolled at baseline, about half with a parent answering surveys. Parents report peer interaction time through short text-message questionnaires. Follow-ups run past the first year, with a process evaluation tracking how delivery unfolds. Results are expected by the end of 2026.
pmc-13241486:

pmc-13257486:

Xiaoyu Yang and colleagues show how a short form of a host protein restricts Zika virus, published in 2026. Related proteins are known antiviral defenders. The shorter RNF213 isoform was unexplored. Cell experiments tested its effects on viral sensing pathways and viral proteins.

A twenty-three-amino-acid fragment taken from it reproduced the antiviral effect in cells. Viral replication fell under the fragment. The authors define a minimal active piece that could inspire antiviral design.
pmc-13266386:
Latifa Oumaiouf and colleagues describe two young mothers whose retinas detached under the strain of severe preeclampsia, in this case report from twenty twenty-six. Serous retinal detachment is a rare, sight-threatening complication of pregnancy hypertension. Both women were first-time mothers, and both had the HELLP syndrome, where blood cells break down, liver enzymes climb, and platelets fall.

Each arrived with sudden vision loss in both eyes. Scans that image the retina in cross-section confirmed fluid lifting it from its bed. No eye procedure was needed. Blood pressure treatment, magnesium sulfate, and delivery, the definitive cure for preeclampsia, resolved both cases. Vision returned fully within two weeks in each woman. The authors stress prompt recognition: the eyes recover when the obstetric emergency is treated, but only if the team connects the two in time.
pmc-13266586:
Mehmet Okçu and colleagues wrote a 2026 study on safe needle depth for injections near the shoulder blade. Such shots treat trigger points, tight painful spots in muscle. A needle placed too deep could pierce the lining around the lung and collapse the lung.

The team read chest CT scans from 1,015 patients treated between 2017 and 2019. They measured skin-to-muscle and skin-to-lung-lining depths at four points near the shoulder blade. Depths differed by age, sex, and body size. In women the lung lining was closer to the skin at most points. The authors give tables to guide safe shot depth for each patient group.
pmc-13267486:
Anatolie S Sidorenko and Gerhard Wilde survey in 2026 the push to build artificial neural networks from superconducting quantum circuits. Software networks are powerful, but hardware versions promise far lower energy use and higher speed. Superconducting elements based on Josephson junctions switch with about a million times less energy than semiconductor parts, a gap that matters for large computing tasks.

Working networks of tunable superconducting neurons have already been demonstrated. Open problems include reading ultra-weak signals from sensitive cold detectors for space communication and astronomy, plus wideband sensing for cognitive radio. The authors weigh what stands between laboratory devices and practical machines, arguing that the energy advantage justifies solving the remaining physics and engineering hurdles.
pmc-13267786:
Esther Ebstein and a large team describe in 2026 a French clinic built to assess suspected arthritis within two days of referral, following national guidance. Over one year from October 2023, the clinic saw 900 patients at a median of just one day after referral. Every patient received a standard package of examination, blood tests, and ultrasound.

Inflammatory arthritis was confirmed in about two thirds of cases. Diagnoses included flares of immune-mediated disease, crystal arthritis such as gout, and infections of joints or nearby tissue. Nearly half had fluid drawn from a joint, a third received steroid injections, and one in ten needed hospital care. The authors argue that a dedicated pathway makes rapid arthritis assessment achievable despite workforce shortages.
pmc-13269286:
Sean W Boland and co-authors examine in 2026 aging dogs with canine cognitive dysfunction, a natural mirror of human Alzheimer's disease, for signs of toxic glial activation and a leaking brain barrier. Unlike engineered mouse models, these dogs develop dementia spontaneously with age. The team compared brain tissue from affected and unaffected dogs using staining, fluorescence, and shape analysis of immune and support cells.

Affected dogs showed glial shapes typical of the neurotoxic state seen in human neurodegeneration, plus stronger activation markers in astrocytes. A key sealing protein of the blood-brain barrier, claudin-5, was reduced, and a water channel protein around vessels shifted in a region-dependent way. The findings strengthen the case for studying dementia in aging dogs and spotlight barrier failure as part of the disease.
pmc-13270586:
Simon Ueberschaar led a 2026 journal article on patients with allergy to wasp or bee venom who turn down venom immunotherapy. That therapy is a long course of shots. It lowers the risk of a severe sting reaction. The patients had tested positive and been advised to take the treatment.

Of 1,163 treatment candidates, 271, or 23.3 percent, declined or delayed for at least a year, and full records were reviewed for 166 of them. Those declining were more often female and had milder first sting reactions. Most cited time cost or feeling treatment was not needed. Over a median five years, 39.2 percent were stung again, and 13 of 65 re-stung patients had a severe allergic reaction.
pmc-13271486:
Saul Martin-Rodriguez is lead author of a 2026 Policy Forum article on what it calls a data transparency crisis in research. Systematic reviews and meta-analyses, studies that pool other studies, underpin clinical guidelines and health policy, yet reviewers often cannot access the underlying data sets or analysis code behind them.

Forced to rely on patchy summary numbers, reviewers use guesses and uncheckable assumptions that can distort results and mislead care decisions, the authors argue, citing past cases such as hormone replacement therapy. Despite widespread data-sharing policies, compliance stays low and enforcement weak. The article calls for enforceable sharing rules, with clearer checks built into journal editorial workflows.
pmc-13271586:
Kun He is lead author of a 2026 cross-sectional comparative study on using large language models, boosted with authoritative textbooks, for public health medical education in Tibet. The region, formally the Xizang Autonomous Region, is high-altitude and low-resource. Old textbooks lack accessibility and interaction, while general AI models can invent facts in specialised medicine.

In the first stage, four public models, from OpenAI, Google, DeepSeek, and Tencent, answered an 80-question benchmark on high-altitude public health, written by specialists. Each question was asked three times, giving 960 outputs, and two blinded panels of eight physicians scored the first replies for completeness, accuracy, clarity, and relevance. A second stage tested adding textbook retrieval to the models.
pmc-13271986:
Anne Song and coauthors review in 2026 how palliative care is used for patients after cardiac arrest and during cardiogenic shock. These emergencies leave heavy physical and emotional burdens on patients and families, with hard choices about life support. Comfort-focused care is increasingly seen as part of good cardiovascular treatment.

Use of palliative care in United States hospitals for these conditions has grown over two decades. Consultation is linked with more do-not-resuscitate orders, less life-sustaining treatment, and lower use and cost of hospital care. Outcomes that matter most to patients and caregivers, though, remain unstudied, and the authors set research priorities to close that gap.
pmc-13272086:
Yuchen Wen and coauthors combine in 2026 several omics layers to find gene changes behind immune and metabolic disorder in childhood asthma. Two related genes that present antigens to immune cells, HLA-DPA1 and HLA-DPB1, emerged as reduced in patients. Macrophages, a versatile immune cell type, seem central to the disturbance.

The team screened airway gene data with four machine learning methods, then checked the candidates in an independent dataset. Lab tests with patient blood cells and airway cells supported the finding. Single-cell analysis traced how macrophage subgroups change over the disease course and talk with other cells, building a diagnostic model around the two genes.
pmc-13272486:
Delphin B. Kyubwa wrote a 2026 analysis of how young people adopt artificial intelligence in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Much work in the country is informal, and formal training routes are weak. Kyubwa asks how young users still gain skills that look professional.

The study draws on 125 interviews in Kinshasa, Lubumbashi, and Goma, read through ideas about technology, society, and human capability. Young people used AI tools for translation, content work, customer contact, and small business tasks. Kyubwa calls this fast skill gain outside formal routes compressed professionalization. Gains were uneven, since access, skills, and power supply differ widely. A proposed action framework aims to make these systems fairer and more local.
pmc-13272586:
Z. L. Abo-Shanab leads a 2026 study that changes waste polystyrene so it can improve bitumen, the sticky binder in asphalt. Plain polystyrene is stiff and low in polarity, so it mixes poorly and stores badly. The team grafted acrylic acid onto it, then reacted it with an amine to make a new form.

Tests confirmed the new groups were added, and the changed polymer bonded well with bitumen through hydrogen bonds. At 7 percent by weight, storage stability was much better than with plain polystyrene, and elastic recovery rose from 25 percent to 55 percent. Resistance to rutting also improved, raising the grade from 70 to 76.
pmc-13273286:
Joel Pires leads a 2026 study identifying a brain enzyme called STEP as a developmental brake on synapse formation. Synapses are the junctions where nerve cells pass signals. Balance between adding and removing phosphate groups on proteins controls how synapses form and mature, and STEP removes such groups.

Suppressing STEP, by genes or by drugs, promoted synapse formation through a mechanism on the sending side of the junction. That reveals a previously unrecognized role for STEP in early circuit assembly, beyond its known role in weakening mature synapses. The authors suggest STEP as a possible target for correcting synapse problems in Fragile X syndrome.
pmc-13273686:
Mohammed Yassine Cherqaoui and co-authors reported a neglected elbow fracture in a child in a 2026 case report. Fractures of the capitellum, the rounded end of the upper arm bone, make up only about one percent of children's elbow fractures. A missed case is rarer still.

Their patient was a twelve year old girl whose fracture went untreated for seven months after a fall, having first been misread and splinted. Her elbow was stiff, and imaging showed a chronic type IV fracture with callus. Surgeons opened the elbow, removed scarred capsule, and fixed the fragment with two screws. Rehab began after one week. A year later her movement and function scores had improved greatly, with no sign of bone death or joint wear. The authors urge fixing, not removing, the fragment.
pmc-13274186:
Mariano Paracuellos wrote a 2026 journal article measuring dialect change across Almería in southeastern Spain through local bird names. The province sits where eastern Andalusian and Murcian speech meet, but that claim had rarely been tested with numbers. He analyzed folk bird names recorded across the province's seven districts.

Name patterns split the districts into southwestern and northeastern groups, matching the pull of neighboring Granada and Murcia. The Filabres Mountains may have limited mixing between the two sides. A second split ran coastal versus inland: coastal districts named more species, while inland districts kept more varied names per species. He links both patterns to landscape, habitat variety, and how people historically moved and talked.
pmc-13274586:
Koomok Lee and colleagues present a 2026 journal article demonstrating voltage-controlled magnetism in tiny dots of a special ceramic. The material, bismuth ferrite with cobalt substituted in, is both ferroelectric and weakly magnetic at room temperature, and its magnetism is yoked to its electric polarization. Flipping one should flip the other, promising memory chips written with voltage instead of current.

Working on a structure just 190 nanometers wide, the team scanned it with a biased probe tip and watched both orders with two microscope methods. The polarization flipped from net-down to net-up, and both sideways and vertical components of the magnetization reversed with it. They call this direct proof of full electric-field magnetization reversal at device scale.
pmc-13274786:
Qingtao Yang and a large team present a 2026 journal article on melatonin protecting rats from erectile problems caused by a scrambled body clock. The team disrupted rats' light cycles with rapid two-hour light and dark alternation for four weeks. Some rats also received daily melatonin, the hormone that normally rises at night, at low or high doses.

Clock disruption measurably weakened erectile function and damaged the spongy penile tissue, while melatonin preserved both. The harm ran through oxidative stress, which switched on a fiery form of cell death called pyroptosis. Melatonin revived a protective pathway, Nrf2 and HO-1, cutting the stress and the cell death. A separate antioxidant reproduced the benefit in human vessel cells.
pmc-13274886:
Siti Watiqah Samsuddin and colleagues report a 2026 journal article charting how four mood-stabilizing drugs were prescribed in British primary care from 1995 to 2018. The drugs, carbamazepine, lamotrigine, lithium, and valproate, treat epilepsy and psychiatric illness. Using anonymized records from a national primary care database, the team tracked new starts and overall use by age and sex.

Carbamazepine prescribing fell sharply from the early 2000s, while lamotrigine starts climbed from 2005 and led among adults under forty by 2018. Valproate starts dropped steeply, though its ongoing use in younger men stayed comparatively high. Lithium remained the least prescribed throughout. Prescribing of all four ran higher in more deprived areas, for both new starts and ongoing use.
pmc-13275786:
José Ángel Martínez-Huertas and Emilio Ferrer present a 2026 methods article on tracking how several traits change over time. Studies of growth often follow different age groups for short spans, then stitch the results together. That design leaves much data missing by plan, which makes full growth curves hard to estimate.

The authors test a mixed-effects model, a method that separates shared patterns from person-level and trait-level differences. Computer simulations varied group sizes and curve shapes. The model recovered the shared growth curve and trait-specific curves well. Its error ranges for trait differences were wide, yet still useful for decisions. With only a few readings per person, it forecast full curves for each person and trait. A real example used data on children's thinking skills.
pmc-13275986:
Qiong Li and co-authors report a 2026 study comparing two MRI methods for stomach cancer. Both methods use diffusion-weighted imaging, which tracks how water moves in tissue to reveal tumors. Judging how deeply a tumor has grown, called T staging, guides surgery, so image quality matters.

The newer method, with a long technical name shortened to FOCUS-MUSE, was tested against the standard method in patients with proven stomach cancer. Two radiologists scored the images, and the team measured clarity with several ratios. The new method produced sharper images and clearer tumor outlines across one hundred seventy-seven patients. Among patients with confirmed stages, it staged tumors correctly far more often than the standard method. Readers also agreed with each other well, the authors report.
pmc-13276186:
Shahenda Khalaf and co-authors report a 2026 journal article on whether a rock layer in Egypt's Western Desert could be a source of oil and gas. The Khatatba Formation, from the Jurassic period, holds dark shale in its Upper Safa Member. Source rocks cook organic matter into hydrocarbons over geologic time.

The team examined one hundred rock samples from four wells in the Obaiyed Field. Lab tests measured minerals and total organic carbon, the fuel content of the rock. Carbon levels averaged near two percent, a moderate to very good richness. Heating tests showed the organic matter is mature and mostly gas-prone. A method that estimates carbon from well logs matched lab values closely. The authors call the layer a fair to good source rock tied neatly to nearby reservoir sands.
pmc-13276586:
Wei Wang and colleagues link knee bone shape before surgery with recovery after joint replacement, in a 2026 study. Total knee arthroplasty relieves advanced arthritis, yet some patients gain little function. The team asked whether three-dimensional bone shape from CT scans predicts who misses a meaningful improvement.

The study covered 151 operated knees with complete one-year function scores. About one in six knees failed to reach the set improvement threshold. Five shape patterns matched that failure, involving the kneecap joint surface and the top of the shin bone. Adding shape data to basic clinical factors improved prediction modestly, though the gain was not statistically secure.
pmc-13277386:
Amine Aiddi leads a 2026 study of dangerous Escherichia coli bacteria in Moroccan waters. Some E. coli strains resist many antibiotics and cause severe infections worldwide. The team collected water from seven rivers and three wastewater plants in eight cities between February and June 2024 and sequenced the full genomes of recovered bacteria.

Twenty-two isolates yielded thirteen strain types, led by three globally known high-risk clones. Most carried a gene that breaks down key antibiotics, and five carried genes that defeat last-resort drugs. The study is the first genomic proof that such clones circulate in Moroccan waters. Stronger joint human, animal, and environment monitoring is urgent, the authors warn.
pmc-13278586:
Sanjoy Kumar Mukharjee leads a 2026 genome study of a salt-tolerant bacterium that helps rice grow, tested as a candidate for climate-resilient farming. From 283 bacteria collected around rice roots, the team selected strain OSNO4 for deep profiling. Lab tests showed it frees phosphate and potassium, makes a plant growth hormone, fixes nitrogen, and forms protective biofilms.

The strain tolerated high salt, drought-like conditions, heat, and a wide acidity range, and it suppressed a rice fungus in dishes. Its genome held about four thousand five hundred predicted genes, including clusters for helpful compounds. Under salt stress, treated rice seeds germinated far better and grew stronger roots and shoots. Safety tests suggested a low-risk profile.
pmc-13279386:
Anne Neubert and colleagues present a 2026 systematic review, part two, of blast injury patterns. Part two covers landmines, unexploded ordnance, meaning old shells and bombs that still can burst, and terror attacks with suicide bombings. The team searched two databases in March 2025 for studies of blast harm in troops and civilians of all ages.

The full review held one hundred twenty six studies. This part weighs forty five terror studies and twelve mine studies. Mine studies from 1980 to 2006 held more than thirteen thousand people, mostly men in poor, post war lands. Leg harm and loss were most common, then eye harm. Terror studies held more than twelve thousand victims, mostly civilians. Limb harm led there as well. Clear patterns help medics plan triage and gear.
pmc-13279486:
Jeffrey Li and colleagues report a 2026 pilot study of cocoa extract in a zebrafish model of autism. Autism is a brain development condition with few drug options. Plant phenols, health linked plant compounds, may guard nerve cells. The team used valproic acid, a drug known to cause autism like traits in fish, to build the model. Cocoa extract rich in a phenol called epicatechin was the test treatment.

Fish got the drug, cocoa, both, or no treatment in four groups. The drug alone caused hyperactive acts and grave gut shape harm. Cocoa given with the drug eased both the acts and the gut harm. Broad chemical and protein scans showed drug linked breaks in nerve signals, cell power and cell defence. Cocoa moved many of those marks back toward normal. Early fish proof backs wider tests of food based nerve guards.
pmc-13280586:
Tarek Zieneldien offers a 2026 poem, The dose divided, on fractionated radiation therapy. Radiation comes in weekdays, hope measured out in calibrated light. Every morning, the body returns in nervous posture to the same unadorned white room and the same mask cooled against the face. The machine knows how to divide harm from healing so finely they nearly share a name. She lies while the beam is delivered, trespassing in exactness, as if the body could be persuaded one small portion at a time.

In the hall, an old woman folds her appointment card in something like a prayer. Outside, deadly nightshade petals gather in the gutter, purple as a bruise. She thinks of Avicenna crossing sandstorms by memory and vow, his companion lost on the road. By Friday, the chart calls it a fraction and the body calls it return. Fractals and an elsewhere of health close the poem.
pmc-13280686:
Stefanie Linnhoff and colleagues wrote a 2026 letter replying to a comment on their work on mental fatigue. Their study had pointed to a brain wave measure as a sign of fatigue. The sign appeared in both multiple sclerosis and long COVID, two very unlike illnesses. A fellow scholar praised the work but raised doubts about who was studied and what the sign means.

The authors agree that their group was small and alike in background, all from one center. They stress that the sign is an early clue, not a firm test. They also agree that fatigue can arise by unlike paths in unlike people. Wider and more mixed groups, they say, must test the sign next.
pmc-13280786:
Ayça Muhterem and colleagues tested an extra toothbrush in a 2026 study with dental students. A plain hand brush can miss plaque, the sticky film on teeth, in tight spots. Forty healthy students took part in a split-mouth test. For two weeks they brushed one side with a plain brush only. On the other side they added a small brush with one tuft of bristles. A blinded checker scored plaque and gum health.

Both sides got cleaner and gums got healthier in two weeks. Plaque fell by about the same amount on both sides. Gum health, though, improved more on the side with the extra brush. More than four in five students said they would keep using it. The authors say the small brush is a cheap add-on for hard-to-reach spots.
pmc-13280986:
Kefiyalew Jote and colleagues mapped gene variety in malaria parasites in a 2026 study from southern Ethiopia. Malaria still burdens health and income where it spreads fast. The parasite's variety helps it dodge the immune system and adapt to drugs. The team took blood from two hundred patients at clinics in two towns. Gene tests sorted the parasites by two surface protein genes, which come in many forms.

About seven in ten patients carried a single parasite strain. Tests found more than one hundred distinct forms of the first gene and even more of the second. Two form families turned up most often. The wide mix shows the parasite pool there is rich and shifting. The authors say such maps help track how malaria changes and how well control plans work.
pmc-13281586:
Schee Li Kwa and co-authors report a registry study from two thousand twenty-six on guideline drug therapy for older heart failure patients in Sarawak. Older adults are underrepresented in the trials behind the guidelines, leaving their real treatment patterns unclear. The study split patients aged sixty-five and up into three age bands.

One hundred seventy-six patients were tracked at entry, three months, and six months. Illness burden rose with age, while coronary disease was commoner in the youngest band. Use of the four guideline drug pillars fell with age, mainly for two classes, while beta-blockers stayed high across bands. Half of the oldest group reached three pillars by six months, though fewer reached four. Heart pumping strength improved in all age groups. The authors probe what drives optimization gaps.
pmc-13281886:
Qi Xu and colleagues reviewed tiny cell sacs in psoriasis in a 2026 paper. Psoriasis is a lasting skin disease of red, scaly patches driven by immune crosstalk. Cells trade messages in small sacs called exosomes. In sore skin, those sacs carry code scraps and proteins that skew immune cells. They fan skin cell swelling and keep a key immune loop running. The review follows the sacs from villains to tools.

Blood sac patterns may flag disease activity without a biopsy. They may also split plain psoriasis from its joint form. Sacs from stem cells, plants, and germs are being tested as cell-free care. Loading cargo, dressing their skins, and smart needle patches aim to sharpen them. Blocks remain: no standard making, unclear active parts, and thin trial proof. The authors urge shared rules and strict trials.
pmc-13281986:
Giovanna Pestana Silva and colleagues checked hearts in dogs of three body weights in a 2026 study. Dog obesity is rising and strains the whole body, yet its heart effects are murky. Thirty owned dogs were split into lean, overweight, and obese groups of ten. Each dog had a physical exam, a heart tracing, and a heart scan. Body scores and belly measures were logged. The team compared the groups on every measure.

Obese dogs panted and tired far more than lean ones. Their heart tracings showed longer signal times, a sign of slower conduction. The left upper chamber ran wider in obese dogs, and valve flaws were more common. Belly fat share rose as the waist-to-chest pattern shifted. Pump strength scores, though, did not differ between groups. The authors say fat reshapes the dog heart early, before frank failure. Routine heart checks for heavy dogs are their advice.
pmc-13282286:
Karla Susanna Tavares Grangeiro Belém and co-authors report a 2026 lab study on a new compound that may help antibiotics beat resistant Staphylococcus aureus. That bacterium pumps many drugs back out of its cells using efflux pumps, a key resistance trick. The team made a hydrazone compound, a type of chemical built here from the drug hydralazine, and tested it against pump-carrying strains.

Alone, the compound did not kill the bacteria at the doses tried. It also lowered the survival of immune cells as dose rose, a safety flag. Paired with antibiotics, though, it cut the dose needed in one strain and sharply lowered the dose of a pump test dye in another. Computer docking suggested it sits in the pumps' binding sites, blocking their action. The authors see promise as a resistance breaker to restore old antibiotics.
pmc-13282386:
Rehab Alharbi and co-authors report a 2026 study identifying a gene switch that marks a harmful blood vessel pattern in pulmonary arterial hypertension. That disease narrows lung arteries and is currently incurable. Vessel lining cells get injured, then repair excessively, worsening the narrowing. The switch, called KLF6, was higher in human disease tissue and in lab models than in healthy controls.

Switching KLF6 on reshaped gene activity in vessel lining cells, driving repair and new vessel growth. Its effects differed from two related switches. It also pushed neighbouring muscle cells in vessel walls to multiply, an effect blunted by two existing drugs. Data set and tissue mapping analyses found high KLF6 in lining cells, their precursor cells, and in a related lung condition of infants. The authors describe KLF6 as an orchestrator of the overgrown vessel pattern. They suggest it could become a target for slowing the disease.
pmc-13282486:
Seong Dae Yun and co-authors describe a 2026 imaging methods study on a new brain scan sequence that fixes a mismatch between functional and anatomical MRI images. Functional MRI, which maps brain activity, uses a fast method that warps images through magnetic field unevenness. Anatomical scans warp differently, so aligning the two is error-prone. An earlier sequence copied the functional warp into the anatomical scan, easing alignment but bending the reference image.

Correcting that bend needed extra data in the reverse direction, which lengthened scans. The new sequence captures the reversed data inside the same single acquisition, adding no scan time. The work focuses on technical build and validation for very fine, submillimetre functional imaging at high field strength. The authors say distortion-matched anatomy with built-in correction should sharpen where activity is localised in the cortex.
pmc-13282686:
Xun Wu and co-authors present a 2026 study on deaths and disability from fatty liver disease driven by high fasting blood sugar, in China and worldwide, from 1990 to 2021. The liver condition, shortened to MASLD, is now the commonest chronic liver disease. Using Global Burden of Disease data, the team tracked deaths and healthy years lost, then projected trends to 2046 with an age-period model.

In 2021 this cause accounted for about ten thousand deaths and over two hundred thousand lost healthy years worldwide. Age-adjusted rates rose significantly over the three decades, faster globally than in China. Burden was higher in men and climbed with age, peaking past eighty. Forecasts show absolute deaths and disability still rising by 2046 in both China and the world, driven by population ageing, even as age-adjusted rates are expected to fall, especially in women.
pmc-13282886:
Severe infections tied to modern myeloma immune therapies are pooled and weighed in a 2026 meta-analysis from Federico Spataro's team. The therapies include bispecific T-cell engagers and CAR-T cells for relapsed myeloma. Severe infection is a major safety concern in routine care.

The review pooled 16 real-world studies with 2,097 patients in total. About one in four patients had a severe infection classed as grade 3 or 4 in severity. Rates were higher with bispecific drugs than with CAR-T therapy in pooled results. Rates also varied by drug target. The authors stress careful infection control when these treatments are used outside trials.
pmc-13283986:
Xiao Chen and co-authors unveiled a feeder-free culture recipe in 2026 that shifts rabbit embryonic stem cells toward a more flexible state. Most rabbit stem cell lines sit in a primed state, which blocks their path into germ cells and limits breeding uses. Their 3C system adds three small compounds to a base medium with growth factors, removing the need for feeder cells.

Cells kept in the system held steady expression of core pluripotency genes, switched on some early-state markers, and showed formative-state markers, a middle stage with wide potential. When guided with three signalling factors, the cells turned into primordial germ cell-like cells, the precursors of eggs and sperm. The authors offer the platform for genetic modification and livestock breeding research.
pmc-13284086:
Fear of new foods ties to narrower diets in type 2 diabetes in a 2026 pilot study from Turkiye by Merve Sena Topkaya and colleagues. Food neophobia means avoiding unfamiliar foods and resisting new tastes. That reluctance may undercut varied eating and treatment follow-through.

Face-to-face surveys covered 35 patients and 35 healthy people at one hospital clinic. Scores captured food fear, diet variety, and treatment adherence in both groups. Higher fear scores linked to lower diet variety among patients with diabetes. Poorer treatment adherence also tracked with higher fear scores in patients. Fear levels alone did not split patients from healthy peers. Tackling food fear may widen diets.
pmc-13284486:
Yun Ouyang and colleagues map research trends on mitochondrial DNA and atherosclerosis in a 2026 bibliometric analysis. Papers from 2004 to 2025 were drawn from the Web of Science Core Collection and charts were built with CiteSpace software. The team tracked authors, institutions, and keywords to see how the field has grown and shifted.

A total of 341 papers were included, with yearly output rising over time in the authors summary. Ten keyword clusters emerged, led by oxidative stress, mitochondrial DNA copy number, and vascular disease themes. Work has moved from basic mechanisms toward clinical use. The authors call for stronger team links and deeper pathway work to support translation into care.
pmc-13284686:
Sang Eun Ha and co-authors test a plant extract on human skin cells in a 2026 laboratory study. Extract from Belamcanda chinensis rhizomes is rich in polyphenols, compounds linked to antioxidant action. The team named five main polyphenols by liquid methods and tested how the extract calmed inflamed keratinocyte cells.

In cells stirred by bacterial toxin, the extract lowered key inflammation drivers such as COX-2 and iNOS and shifted STAT3 and NF-kappaB signaling. Docking work showed the five compounds bound strongly to NF-kappaB targets. The authors conclude the extract shows antioxidant and anti-inflammatory effects in cells, giving a base for drug work, though human testing has not been done.
pmc-13284886:
Yashendra Sethi and co-authors review, in a 2026 article, links between geomagnetic activity during auroras and human health, with a focus on the brain. Shifts in Earth magnetic fields have been tied to varied body and mind outcomes. The team searched peer-reviewed work in PubMed and Google Scholar on surgery, nerve, and mental health settings.

Reported links included more seizures in epilepsy, poor sleep that slows recovery, and thinking problems that could affect consent. Stress and anxiety may also rise during magnetic storms, adding risk after surgery, notably in older patients. The authors call for deeper work on mechanisms and for care guidance that accounts for geomagnetic conditions.
pmc-13285186:
Yunfei Wang and co-authors map gene splicing faults in esophageal cancer in a 2026 data study. Faulty splicing makes many protein forms from one gene and can drive tumor growth, yet its full pattern in this cancer was unclear. The team pooled gene data from five public sets and used network and motif tools to link splicing events to cell processes and drug response.

Thousands of changed splicing events were found, mostly in protein-coding and long non-coding RNAs in the pooled analysis. Events tied to cell cycle, immune response, fuel use, spread, and cell death. Eighty-five binding proteins stood out as hub factors. Two drugs, bortezomib and BI-2536, tracked strongly with the fault pattern and curbed cell growth in checks.
pmc-13285586:
A back pelvic joint slipped out while the front ring stayed whole in a 2026 case report by Leonardo Comerlatto and co-authors. Such back-only damage is vanishingly rare, since hard pelvic crashes usually break the weaker front first. A 15-year-old boy was hit in the back by a heavy metal frame and arrived with one-sided back joint dislocation.

Doctors eased the joint back shut and pinned it with a single thick screw through skin. Current grading schemes do not quite hold this pattern, the authors note. They urge careful checks of front ring soundness in high-energy back pelvic trauma, since missing a hidden break can doom fixation. The case adds a new pattern to the record.
pmc-13285986:
Nozomu Motono and colleagues report surgery for a chest infection in a man with advanced lung cancer in their 2026 case report. The 75-year-old had just learned that a squamous tumor filled his left lower lung lobe and nearby nodes. Three weeks after the biopsy that proved the cancer, fever signaled pus gathering in the space around the lung.

Surgeons used keyhole chest surgery to strip the infected peel from the lung, a step called decortication. pmc-13286486:

pmc-13286786:
Fang Zhang, Zhide Wu, and Xi Zhou study where visitors linger to take photographs in Yipu, a classical Chinese garden in Jiangnan. Social media sharing has changed garden tourism: visitors now record, post, and spread their experience, creating feedback that designers can use.

The team modeled how spatial experience connects with these dwell-photo stops, aiming to extract what makes spots culturally and visually attractive. The authors also suggest the approach could inform street design in cities, keeping humanistic qualities inside technical planning.
pmc-13287186:
Luise Geithner and Michael Wagner used survey data in 2026 from very old adults in Germany to ask whether feeling disoriented by social change helps explain who stays socially active. Their model linked money, schooling, health, values, and relationships to participation, with that sense of disorientation placed in between.

pmc-13287786:
Daniel Auguin and co-authors study how heart muscle myosin switches itself off, in work published in 2026. Myosin is the motor protein that powers each heartbeat. When the heart rests, pairs of myosin heads fold together into an off state called the interacting-heads motif. pmc-13288386:
Vanessa Miß and colleagues describe a test station for battery powders under pressure, in a 2026 methods paper. All-solid-state batteries pack cathode particles together with solid electrolyte particles. Both kinds must carry charge while squeezed, since these batteries run under stack pressure. How well they conduct depends on pressure and on how much empty space remains. The new station measures conductivity and porosity at the same time during compression.

Knowing which regime a material sits in helps engineers set pressing conditions. The station gives battery makers a direct way to link factory pressure with performance.
pmc-13288886:

Specialist teams and ultrasound formed the response kit.
pmc-13289186:

pmc-13289786:

pmc-13290086:

Moriyama and colleagues also weigh the problems: hard trial design, gaps between animal results and patient benefit, real-world burdens, and narrow eligibility. pmc-13290386:
Three robotic prostate surgery techniques end at nearly the same place for continence, but one gets patients dry faster, Shih-Hsuan Lin and colleagues show this in a 2026 comparison. Their retrospective study compares Retzius-sparing surgery with conventional two-layer and three-layer reconstruction after radical prostatectomy.

pmc-13290786:

pmc-13290986:

The online version has been updated to match.
pmc-13291786:

pmc-13292386:

pmc-13292686:

pmc-13292786:

The report urges rental owners and guests to take hot tub hygiene seriously.
pmc-13293286:

Blocking fat making may explain the benefit.
pmc-13293386:

pmc-13293586:
Marc A. pmc-13293786:

pmc-13293986:

pmc-13294286:

pmc-13294386:

pmc-13294686:

pmc-13295186:

pmc-13295386:

pmc-13295786:

pmc-13295986:

pmc-13296486:

pmc-13297286:

pmc-13297486:

pmc-13297586:

pmc-13297786:

pmc-13297986:

pmc-13298086:

pmc-13298286:

pmc-13298486:

pmc-13299086:

pmc-13299586:

pmc-13299686:

pmc-13300086:

pmc-13300286:

pmc-13300386:

pmc-13300686:

pmc-13300886:

pmc-13300986:

pmc-13301486:
