The target paper used T-Scan digital analysis to show that selective occlusal adjustment shortened disclusion time and balanced contacts in patients with temporomandibular disorders.

Kerstein argues the team never set per-patient sensor sensitivity before recording, so maximum bites oversaturated the sensors. Their figures show clusters of pink, saturated cells, which inflate force percentages and fake balanced distributions, he writes. Proper calibration keeps only one to three pink cells at full bite. The comment urges readers to discount the reported gains until recording technique is fixed.
pmc-13301986:
Isabella Burger and a large team identify, in a 2026 fungal genetics study, the gene cluster that makes a compound called diaporthinic acid. The molecule had been isolated from several fungi, but no gene cluster had been firmly assigned to it. The researchers switched the cluster on inside Trichoderma reesei by boosting its internal regulator.

Once activated, the fungus produced mainly diaporthinic acid plus several related compounds, confirmed by mass spectrometry and magnetic resonance analysis. Deleting single genes showed that three cluster members are essential for making the compound, including an enzyme that adds chlorine atoms. Two other genes proved dispensable, overturning roles proposed from test-tube work in a different fungus. The compound showed no antibacterial or antifungal action under their test conditions.
pmc-13302286:
A past cytomegalovirus infection leaves faint fingerprints on the brain waves of people with schizophrenia, Mădălina Georgeta Sighencea and colleagues explore in a 2026 study. One hundred twenty-three patients with schizophrenia spectrum disorders received clinical, cognitive, and lab assessments plus visual EEG reading. Blood tests sorted them by CMV antibody status for comparison.

Overall EEG organization did not split by virus status. Sharp-wave discharges appeared somewhat more often in patients without CMV exposure, independent of background rhythms, while virus-positive patients carried higher white cell counts. Patients showing sharp waves scored better on cognition and memory items. The authors frame these exploratory patterns as non-causal hints for longitudinal work.
pmc-13302586:
T Kamakura and co-authors evaluate, in a 2026 study, frequency mapping as a way to find the nerve clusters targeted in ablation for slow-heart conditions. These ganglionated plexi clusters influence the heart's natural pacemakers, yet no standard method locates them. Sites with scrambled signals may show characteristically high peak frequencies.

Five patients treated for fainting, sinus node disease, or heart block had their cluster sites checked against frequency maps. Cluster sites consistently showed higher peak frequencies than surrounding negative tissue across all named locations. Overlap with the highest-frequency zones was good on the right side but weaker on the left, where the fixed threshold missed some clusters. The authors conclude mapping helps but lacks the precision to work alone.
pmc-13302986:
Choosing the solvent steers which crystal phase grows on a catalyst sheet, Yuntao Huang and colleagues demonstrate in a 2026 photocatalysis study. Titanium dioxide was grown directly on MXene nanosheets in a heated water-acetonitrile mixture. Adjusting the ratio between the two liquids selected either the anatase or the rutile form of the oxide, a long-standing control problem in heterostructure design.

Acetonitrile appears to coat the growing crystals and lock in the anatase phase. The tuned pairing separates light-generated charges more effectively and produces more singlet oxygen, the reactive species that chews through pollutants. The authors present solvent regulation as a simple dial for phase engineering in environmental catalysts.
pmc-13303086:
Sugar substitutes look broadly safe yet leave open questions, Stanislava Ivanova and colleagues survey in a 2026 overview. Searching four databases, the review covers how these sweeteners are ruled on and what studies say about hormones, gut germs, the brain, and behavior. Groups seen as more at risk, children and people with diabetes among them, get their own sections.

Some studies link sweeteners to changed insulin response and shifted gut germs, but results clash and proof for at-risk groups stays thin. Effects on nerves and hormone systems also remain unsettled. The authors call for ongoing human trials, market watch, and fresh safety reviews rather than a final verdict.
pmc-13303586:
Saveria Batti leads a 2026 laboratory study of fabrics containing germanium and their effects on inflamed blood vessel cells. Such fabrics are said to emit infrared radiation and negative air ions that may calm swelling and oxidative stress.

Human vein cells and immune cells were inflamed with standard triggers, then exposed to the fabric in single cultures, shared cultures, and a flowing 3D system. Cell survival stayed intact, harmful reactive oxygen fell in vessel cells, and several signaling proteins shifted in calmer directions. The layered models show how vessel and immune cells influence each other under fabric exposure.
pmc-13304386:
David Mendonça-Soares and co-authors systematically review, in a 2026 paper, the NLRP3 inflammasome as a marker of dangerous neck-artery plaques. This molecular alarm triggers interleukin-1 release, and unstable plaques cause strokes when they rupture. Studies of tissue removed during carotid surgery offered the most direct evidence.

Sixteen studies with 1,677 participants were pooled narratively because methods differed too much for statistics. Alarm components and interleukin family members ran consistently higher in unstable plaques and in patients with symptoms. The markers tracked with bleeding inside plaques, big fatty cores, and heavy immune cell invasion. Links to later heart events were hinted but weakly proven, since few studies adjusted properly for other risks.
pmc-13305486:
Zixiao Li and colleagues present a 2026 case of a blood vessel growth in the sacral spine canal that masqueraded as a nerve sheath tumor. Such cavernous hemangiomas in that spot are exceptionally rare and fool scans regularly.

A woman in her mid-fifties had one month of night pain and mild weakness in the left leg. Scans showed a brightly enhancing lump near a lower spine nerve opening, read as schwannoma. Surgery found a dark red, soft, vessel-rich mass instead, and quick tissue checks confirmed hemangioma. Pain eased greatly after removal, with full relief and clean follow-up scans.
pmc-13306786:
Vasilis Vasileiadis added scent delivery to a room-scale virtual reality cave in a 2026 study. Smell feedback lags behind sight and sound in immersive systems, especially in large CAVE rooms where almost no prior work exists.

The Scentree device releases scents in real time as users act, inside a themed experience called Smelling Ancient Greece. Feedback is framed as part of the story action, not background perfume. A user study with 51 people rated immersion, presence, realism and ease of use, supporting live scent as a workable design layer. Users in the trial gave the scent loop strong marks for feel and ease of use.
pmc-13307186: A 2026 retraction notice withdraws a 2022 article on facial emotion reading for crime investigation that fused two image methods. Publisher John Wiley & Sons acted after an inquiry found signs of systematic manipulation of the publishing process. Listed concerns cover scope mismatch, unclear research description, data availability gaps, poor citations, incoherent content and compromised peer review. The notice is brief and gives no replacement findings, so the original claims should no longer be trusted.
pmc-13307286:
Hui Yang catalogued ABI4 hormone-response genes in oilseed rape and tested their drought role in a 2026 study. Four copies were found in the elite ZS11 cultivar, each holding one conserved AP2 domain and promoters rich in stress switches.

Plants with extra BnaABI4-4 copies lost less water, held lower pore conductance and grew fewer stomata, surviving drought better in reported trials. Knockout plants showed the exact reverse pattern across the same measures. The gene acts through the abscisic acid pathway, making it a breeding target for water saving. Such pore control could cut water loss in dry fields while still letting the crop breathe well.
pmc-13307386:
Lingling Wang and co-authors survey in 2026 whether parents of children with special health care needs in Wuxi, China, will accept routine vaccines for their children. Their stratified survey gathered 904 parents or guardians and used group comparisons plus regression to weigh what drove the choice.

Most parents, 864 of those who took part, said they were willing to vaccinate their child. Willingness rose with parent schooling and with knowing about clinics that assess vaccine fitness for such children. Parent knowledge about vaccines also mattered in simple comparisons. Better outreach about those clinics could help close gaps in cover for a group at higher risk of infection.
pmc-13307586:
Clara Guarneri and Léticia Al-Kai describe in 2026 a forty-four-year-old woman whose severe potassium loss traced back to drinking about two litres of licorice tea daily for a year. She arrived with nausea, vomiting, chills, tingling, and high blood pressure. Heart tracings showed U waves and a markedly stretched QT interval, raising arrhythmia risk.

Blood tests showed very low potassium, low phosphate, and alkalosis, with kidneys wasting potassium despite suppressed hormone levels. That pattern fits licorice blocking an enzyme that normally shields hormone receptors from cortisol. Intensive care brought aggressive potassium replacement and pressure control. After she stopped the tea, chemistry and blood pressure normalised gradually. The authors stress dietary history taking in unexplained potassium loss, since the cause is reversible once spotted.
pmc-13308186:
Sarah Samuelson and co-authors map in 2026 new ideas at work in Swedish primary care, as seen by centre managers across the country. Their mixed survey drew 392 replies from 1028 invited managers, with counts for scale and text study for free replies.

About 80 percent of managers told of a new product, process, or way of organising care at their centre. Most ideas were born inside the centre, and joint work stayed mostly internal, with outside partners in only a small share of cases. Leaders gave time and room for skill growth, yet tight budgets and output demands capped staff input. Broader links across sectors need system level plans, the authors argue, to spread gains.
pmc-13308386:
Dires Delessa Alemu and co-authors study in 2026 weight gain in adult tuberculosis patients during the first two months of care in East Gojjam Zone, Ethiopia. Their survey covered 619 adults at 31 public sites from June to August 2025, with talks and chart checks for each patient.

Weight rose for 428 patients, which is 69.1 percent of the group in the first phase of care. Full drug adherence, early start of care, extra food, three or more meals a day, good knowledge, and a hopeful stance all raised the odds of gain. Food aid and teaching thus stand beside drugs as core parts of strong tuberculosis care.
pmc-13309386:
Ridzky Firmansyah Hardian and colleagues present a 2026 study in rats on what makes brief electrical pulses injure the brain surface. Such pulses are used during brain surgery to check movement pathways. Old safety rules stress total charge, but high pulse rates may change what matters most.

Thirty-two rats received pulse trains that varied in current, pulse length, repeat count, and rest gap. Slices of brain tissue were then checked for lesion depth. Higher current and more repeats deepened injury, while total energy predicted depth better than total charge did. The authors argue that energy, not charge alone, should guide safe limits for this kind of monitoring.
pmc-13310686:
Tianyu Gao and co-authors chart a rare autoimmune brain disease in Chinese patients in a 2026 study. Anti-mGluR5 encephalitis attacks a brain receptor and most often travels with Hodgkin lymphoma, yet it makes up under 1 percent of reported autoimmune encephalitis cases worldwide. Asian data were especially thin.

Eight patients at one referral center between 2019 and 2025 were joined with 31 published Chinese cases, giving 39 in the combined summary. Mean onset age was 42.5 years across the group, with thinking problems the top first feature at 61.5 percent, ahead of behavior change and seizures. Tumors were found in a share of cases, and antibody testing patterns in fluid and blood were compared. The authors set regional benchmarks for recognition.
pmc-13310786:
Wenni Dai and co-authors review ketone bodies and kidney disease in a 2026 paper. Ketones serve as backup fuel and also shape cell signals, swelling, and organ cross talk. Kidney disease is common and deadly, and faulty energy use sits at its core, so ketone paths draw growing interest.

Care paths under review include low carb ketogenic diets, diabetes drugs that raise ketones, and direct ketone drinks. Each path may help or harm the kidney based on dose, timing, and illness type. Past work links ketones to slower harm in some settings. Clear rules for safe use are still lacking, and trials must sort benefit from risk.
pmc-13310886:
Hajed M. Al-Otaibi and Malik A. Althobiani survey nicotine pouch use among adults who once smoked cigarettes in a 2026 study. Pouches are sold as a cleaner option than smoking, yet use habits in former smokers are little known. The team asked about daily amount, timing, craving, and views on quitting help.

Answers covered 693 adults in the final count, with 560 current pouch users who had quit smoking and 133 current smokers. Over two fifths of users took at least ten pouches a day, and most took the first within half an hour of waking. Heavier past smoking linked to heavier pouch use. Many users rated pouches as highly effective for quitting.
pmc-13310986:
Shujie Fu and colleagues test dragon fruit flower extract against acute lung injury in mice in a 2026 study. The dried flower has a long folk use for lung ills, yet proof for sudden lung injury was lacking. A bacterial toxin model was used to probe gut and lung links.

Dosed mice showed less lung swelling, less tissue harm, and calmer swelling signals. Gut barrier protein rose, gut germ mix shifted, and helpful short acids grew. Moving gut germs from dosed mice to fresh mice carried much of the lung gain, which backs a gut lung path. Gene and network maps pointed to key targets for checks.
pmc-13311086:
Iftikhar Ahmed and co-editors open a 2026 collection on germ based cleanup of heavy metal pollution. Metals such as cadmium, lead, and mercury persist in soil and water for decades and climb food chains. Standard fixes cost much, burn energy, and can spawn fresh pollution, which drives interest in living methods.

Germs can bind, store, transform, or free metals through distinct chemical tricks. Gene tools and synthetic biology now let teams design strains with stronger cleanup powers. Studies in the set test those paths in soil and water settings. Safe field use needs checks on strain spread and metal fate after capture.
pmc-13311186:
Brendan Layton and co-authors compare 90 day complications by sex in anemic hip replacement patients in a 2026 study. Low blood counts raise risk after hip surgery and hit women more often, yet sex splits inside anemic groups were rarely tested. Matched records were used to compare matched men and women.

The matched group held 45,788 anemic adults who had first time hip replacement. Women faced higher rates of readmission, wound opening, urine infection, and transfusion. Men faced higher rates of vein clots and acute kidney harm. Death, sepsis, lung infection, and joint infection showed no clear sex split. Sex aware risk plans are backed.
pmc-13311786:
Mohammad Asghari-Jafarabadi and co-authors re-analyze the ENIGMA-II trial in a 2026 study of lasting pain after surgery and quality of life. Lasting post-surgical pain is common and has many drivers.

The analysis covered 2999 trial patients with twelve-month follow-up. A grouped lasso method picked predictor sets, and a structural model then explored paths among pain history, lifestyle, surgical factors, and outcomes. Pain before surgery showed the strongest tie to lasting pain in the model. Accuracy stayed moderate, and the authors stress the work is exploratory, not proof of cause. Better sorting of high-risk patients remains the goal.
pmc-13312586:
Emmanuelle Baillet and colleagues test, in a 2026 daily-life study, whether craving carries the effect of mood onto substance use in people with substance use disorders. Thirty-six adults in outpatient addiction treatment answered phone surveys three times a day for fourteen days, reporting positive and negative feelings, craving, and any use, just before entering a clinical trial. Multilevel mediation models then traced within-person chains from one survey to the next.

Craving did the carrying in both directions. Feeling better than usual came with lower craving at the same moment, which in turn meant less use at the next check-in. Feeling worse raised craving and then the likelihood of use. The authors suggest that treatments delivered in the moment, through phones, could interrupt this chain by targeting mood and craving as they flare in ordinary life rather than in weekly sessions.
pmc-13312686:
Julie Vendrell, Inès Dalmon, Simon Cabello-Aguilar, Jacques Colinge, Eric Assenat, and Jérôme Solassol combine DNA and RNA profiling to sort bile duct cancer patients by outlook, in a 2026 study. The cancer varies widely between patients. Gene tests already find some drug targets. RNA patterns add immune and growth profiles. The team profiled sixty-two patients at one specialist center. Both tumor DNA and RNA were read in depth.

Two gene faults together marked the worst outlook. Patients carrying both lived far shorter than others. Tumors with drug targets lived longer, likely from matched therapy. RNA reading found five subtypes. The commonest had a connective-tissue character. That subtype progressed faster under standard treatment. The authors say combined profiling sharpens prognosis. It does so beyond simply finding drug targets. Treatment planning could use both layers at once.
pmc-13312786:
Guang Du and co-authors introduce, in a 2026 study, a model that reads online course reviews across languages while respecting cultural context and the skills learners believe they gained. Reviews of massive open online courses carry emotional verdicts on quality and job value, but standard sentiment tools flatten how different groups express opinions and never tie feelings to named skills.

Their model, CA-MuSiC, treats language, platform, and subject field as stand-ins for cultural context, a limit the authors state openly. It grounds opinions in outside skill references, blends extraction with generation, and bootstraps extra labels from a teacher ensemble. Across three benchmarks, including an English-Chinese set, it beat rival methods on structured sentiment and skill-linked scoring tasks. The authors frame reviews as evidence about perceived skill growth, useful to learning analytics.
pmc-13313186:
Fei Lu and fellow authors review Z-nucleic acids, rare forms of DNA and RNA that twist to the left instead of the right, in their 2026 paper. Two proteins with Z-binding parts, ZBP1 and ADAR1, sense these odd shapes, and their roles in health and disease have long been a puzzle.

The review draws on mouse genetics, using knockout mice and mice with changed Z-binding sites, to show what these sensors do. The evidence casts Z-nucleic acids as key triggers of planned cell death, swelling, defense against viruses, and attacks on tumors. That same sensing can also drive diseases of excess inflammation. By weighing both sides, the review helps readers see when blocking or boosting this system might help patients.
pmc-13313386:
Evangelia Florou and colleagues recount, in a 2026 case report, a pancreatic head mass that turned out not to be pancreatic cancer at all. Their patient, a 47-year-old man with PMS2-related Lynch syndrome, had curative surgery in 2021 for duodenal adenocarcinoma. That rare gut cancer is one Lynch syndrome makes more likely. Four years later, scans showed a pancreatic head tumor. Its features matched locally advanced primary pancreatic cancer closely enough to settle the working diagnosis.

He received six months of chemotherapy before surgery. The mass shrank substantially, and surgeons removed it with a pancreaticoduodenectomy. Only the final pathology overturned the assumption: the tissue was recurrent duodenal cancer, not a new pancreatic primary. The authors use the surprise to argue that tumor biology can override anatomical expectations in hereditary syndromes. Vigilance must survive convincing imaging. Aggressive treatment across specialties, including chemotherapy before surgery, can still be the right call.
pmc-13314286:
Xueqiang He and colleagues report a 2026 case of a homemade magnet tool used to pull swallowed blades from a child throat and chest. A 13-year-old girl with an emotional disorder came in with chest pain after swallowing blades for 7 hours, by the times given in the report.

Scans showed a metal body low in the neck beside the food pipe, plus air leaks in both lungs coverings, the chest center, and under the skin. The team drained both sides of the chest, eased the skin air, and gave anti-infection care first. Through a scope they then removed the blades from a complex hole joining the food pipe to the chest center, found 15 cm from the teeth as stated in the report. The case shows a low-cost magnet trick for a rare and risky removal.
pmc-13314486:
Yanling Yao and co-workers track soy isoflavones in the diet and later diabetes in Chinese adults in their 2026 study. Whether these plant compounds guard against type 2 diabetes over years was still open.

The team drew on the China Health and Nutrition Survey from 1997 to 2015 and enrolled 14,652 adults, as counted in the report. Diet was gauged by three days of recalls plus food weighing. Over a mean follow-up of 10 years, a total of 1051 new diabetes cases arose, as stated in the report. Higher intake of total isoflavones and of subtypes such as daidzein and glycitein tied to lower risk in fully adjusted models, with trend values kept in the report. The long view from a big national cohort strengthens the case for soy foods in prevention.
pmc-13315186:
Fei Chen and a large team report a lab study from 2026 comparing guided and freehand ways to find root canals in pulled human molars. Three dynamic navigation systems, using infrared or visible light tracking, were tested against freehand work done with a microscope and scan images.

Ninety-six molars were split evenly into four groups. Navigation cut angle error to about 0.6 degrees, compared with about 11 degrees freehand, and entry and target errors were also much smaller. Guided work removed less tooth structure as well. The results support navigation for hard canal cases, where saving tooth tissue and hitting the canal matter.
pmc-13315686:
Michiel L.A.J. Wieërs and colleagues run, in a 2026 randomized cross-over trial, a direct comparison of salt supplements in chronic kidney disease. Raising potassium lowers blood pressure in healthy kidneys, but in kidney disease the accompanying anion matters and hyperkalemia looms. Their earlier work showed potassium chloride raised plasma potassium and caused mild acidosis. The trial enrolled 31 patients, mean age 69, with an estimated filtration rate of 29, each cycling through six treatment periods.

Compared with placebo, potassium chloride slightly lowered plasma bicarbonate, by 0.4 millimoles per liter. Potassium bicarbonate, sodium bicarbonate, and potassium gluconate raised it instead, to 27 to 28 versus 25 millimoles per liter, with higher urinary bicarbonate and pH. The alkalizing salts thus avoided the acidifying drawback of the chloride form. The authors offer the comparison as a guide to choosing potassium supplements that protect both blood pressure and acid-base balance in kidney disease.
pmc-13316086:
Han Wang and co-authors tested in 2026 whether glowing dye imaging can reveal leftover giant cell tumor of bone during scraping surgery. Finding hidden residual tumor inside the cavity is crucial, since missed tissue can regrow, so indocyanine green near-infrared imaging was used after standard curettage under white light.

Data from 20 patients with at least two years of follow-up were reviewed. All tumors took up the dye, and only one patient, or 5 percent, had a local recurrence. Overall accuracy for spotting residual tumor was 68 percent, with both false positive and false negative results reported against biopsy checks.
pmc-13316186:
Chrysoula Kourtidou-Papadeli and co-authors report EEG evidence in 2026 that graded extra gravity reshapes resting brain networks in people with a nerve inactivity profile, mostly multiple sclerosis. Long inactivity and low sensory input alter large-scale brain wiring, and spinning in a short-arm centrifuge can deliver controlled gravity without voluntary movement.

Brain waves were recorded before and after repeated centrifuge sessions. They were rebuilt at cortex level with a standard imaging method. The pilot study tests whether balance and body sense input from extra gravity can nudge brain change linked to inactivity. That would offer a passive route to network change.
pmc-13316286:
Abigail Low led a small 2026 pilot trial testing whether online group talk therapy for poor sleep can work for women treated for cancers of the reproductive organs. Sessions ran weekly over video in a small group format.

Five patients joined and four finished the program, with three of them attending at least four sessions. Connection quality, joining in, and patient ratings all met the preset goals for a workable program. Sleep severity scores fell by more than six points by week six and stayed lower through 24 weeks of checks, while night waking also dropped. Other sleep and life quality scores barely moved. The team reads the early signs as support for a larger trial and wider access.
pmc-13316786:
Yanliang Ji and co-authors built a 2026 prediction model that fuses brain scan signals with routine clinical data to forecast recovery after ischemic stroke. The target was poor function at ninety days, defined on a standard disability scale.

The single-center study covered 562 patients scanned one to seven days after symptoms began, split into training, tuning, and test groups. In the held-out test set, the fused model scored the highest discrimination figure, 0.951 in the reported analysis, beating the scan-only model clearly. Against strong clinical models, though, its extra gain looked limited on calibration and benefit curves. The authors ask for outside testing and recalibration before any bedside use.
pmc-13316986:
Bastien Petit and colleagues report a 2026 discovery from a Chilean fungus, Anthracophyllum discolor, a little-studied mushroom relative from Patagonia. Fungi hide vast chemical wealth, and this genus had never been mined, so the team grew it and screened its products.

They found anthracaurisin A, the first known fungal nor-sesquiterpene dimer, with strong cell-killing power in dishes and in living tests. Alongside it came one new and several known illudin compounds, whose exact 3D shapes the team pinned down. The work shows that even obscure mushroom genera can yield drug-like molecules, strengthening the case for wider fungal collecting and screening.
pmc-13317386:
Muhammad Daud and co-authors rank, in a 2026 study, eight alfalfa varieties for salt tolerance, a growing threat to forage farming as soils turn saltier. They grew each variety at four salt levels and read shape, water, and chemistry traits together.

Strong salt slashed plant height, weights, and leaf counts by roughly half or more across the board, while cell damage markers climbed steeply and defense enzymes surged. Combined scoring named variety V5, A'erjienong, the most tolerant and V4, Fudina, the most sensitive, with a few enzyme and pigment traits carrying most of the signal. Breeders gain both parent picks and a screening recipe for future salt-hardy forage lines.
pmc-13317586:
Dong Fan and co-authors show, in a 2026 study, that plumbagin, a plant compound from Plumbago roots, kills nonfunctioning pituitary tumor cells by forcing ferroptosis, an iron-driven death. These tumors, among the most common in the skull, rely on surgery today, so drug options are prized.

In cell and ball-of-cells models, plumbagin beat the standard drug temozolomide at stopping growth. It turned down a protective pathway, Nrf2 and FTH1, while raising NCOA4, the ferritin eater, so free iron piled up and fats burned in the pattern of ferroptosis. Computer docking and dynamics helped pick the targets before bench checks confirmed them. The plant compound earns a place on the candidate list for these stubborn tumors.
pmc-13318386:
Sneha Ann Johnson and co-authors ask, in a 2026 narrative review, whether nerve blocks around surgery really cut opioid use as much as often claimed. Regional anaesthesia is a pillar of multi-drug pain control in an era of opioid harm. The team searched major databases for studies on spinal, epidural and peripheral blocks.

Evidence shows clear reductions in opioid needs and better pain control during the first day or two after surgery, with less nausea, sedation and breathing suppression. Evidence for lasting reductions in long-term opioid use or chronic pain is thin. Study designs vary widely, and other pain drugs given alongside make the block's own effect hard to isolate. Rebound pain and short block duration also limit benefit, the authors argue.
pmc-13318686:
Vanitha Innocent Rani leads a 2026 randomised study of knee pain treatment. The trial pairs cold therapy with the Graston Technique, a tool-based soft tissue method. Participants had non-traumatic knee pain. The question was whether adding cold improves pain and daily function.

One hundred adults aged 31 to 50 joined the trial. Half received Graston work alone, and half received cold packs afterwards. Everyone had ten daily sessions over two weeks. Both groups improved clearly by the end. The combined group gained more, with a pain drop of 2.18 points against 0.56 in controls on the scales used. Daily task scores also rose more, and pain relief tracked closely with better function.
pmc-13318786:
Yilian Zhang and colleagues present a 2026 study building a screening chart for carotid plaque from routine health check data. Finding plaque early supports prevention of cardiovascular disease. Their model adds a combined index of triglycerides, glucose, and waist-to-hip ratio. That index aims to capture insulin resistance plus central obesity.

The development group held 4,992 people from a health examination cohort. A further 3,812 people formed a later-time validation set. The combined index alone reached an AUC of 0.689 for spotting plaque, beating the standard index. A chart using eight routine measures reached 0.85 in the later validation set, with good calibration. The authors stress it flags current plaque, not future events, and needs outside testing.
pmc-13319086:
Bofei Liu and colleagues present a 2026 retrospective study of Brucella infection spreading to the testis and epididymis in men in Northwest China. Records came from the regional infectious disease hospital in Ningxia. The window ran from January 2021 to December 2023. Among 1,188 male brucellosis inpatients, cases with confirmed genital involvement were compared with the rest.

Seventy-two men, 6.06 percent of the cohort, had the genital complication. After adjustment, four factors stayed associated with it. Fatigue and back pain were reported less often in affected men. Higher white cell counts and positive blood cultures were more common. Platelet counts and symptom duration lost significance after adjustment. The authors read the pattern as a distinct local form of the disease, needing prospective study.
pmc-13319186:
Timur I Bikulov and colleagues present a 2026 method for telling magnetic nanoparticles apart by their magnetic moments, aimed at multiplex medical assays. The standard rebuild from a static magnetisation curve has limited resolving power. Their approach probes higher-order responses head-on using two excitation tones at once. A purpose-built setup reads the mixed signals in sync.

Spectral patterns separate amplitude effects from rate effects, clarifying where each nonlinearity comes from. Tests on shop-bought particles compared the method with standard techniques. A two-particle mixture was measured with only 8.9 percent deviation from the true ratio. The particles' average moments differed threefold, with no prior knowledge supplied. The authors see room for three independent contrast channels. The method may also reveal how particles interact inside mixtures.
pmc-13319486:
Fangqing Liu and Yixuan Li pool trial proof on gentle ear nerve pulses and thinking skills in a 2026 review. The method sends mild pulses through the skin of the ear to reach a major nerve linked to alertness. Past small trials gave mixed scores by skill type, so a pooled count was used to weigh the overall gain.

Fifty three studies were found across seven databases, and 30 gave data from more than 1500 people for the pooled count. Scores rose overall, with clear gains for planning and flexible learning and smaller gains for memory and focus. Stronger pulse levels gave larger gains. Brain scans in future trials could show how the pulses work.
pmc-13319786:
Valerie J Parker, Lauren J Reynolds and Jessica M Quimby compare, in 2026, vitamin D profiles between cats with chronic kidney disease and cats without it. Vitamin D governs calcium balance, immunity and blood formation, and kidney disease might be expected to disturb it. Supplement advice in cats rests on thin evidence.

Ninety-nine cats were enrolled prospectively, two thirds with kidney disease across all severity stages. Four vitamin D metabolites were measured with a precise laboratory method. None differed significantly between sick and healthy cats, and values overlapped widely. No metabolite tracked with age, kidney function marker, blood pressure or urine protein. The authors suggest their findings should temper assumptions behind calcitriol supplementation in feline kidney disease, though clinical decisions still need broader evidence.
pmc-13319886:
Zeffry Alkatiri and co-authors study how market led growth has split urban space in Batam, Indonesia in a 2026 article. The island city was set up in 1973 as a state planned factory zone meant to rival Singapore and has since become a showcase of market led city growth in the region. How state power, foreign cash, and daily life jointly shape its streets was the core focus.

Four weeks of field work and eighteen deep talks were paired with policy and plan records. Factory zones, road corridors, and gated housing sit apart from informal worker housing that lacks formal status. Even so, those informal areas push back by building their own ways of living and shared life. The case shows how growth can split a city while local life resists.
pmc-13320286:
Weipeng Zhang and co-authors test needle pulses at a leg point for nerve linked erection failure in a 2026 rat study. Pelvic surgery often severs the fine nerves that drive erection, and drug care helps such cases poorly. Rats with both nerves crushed showed lasting overdrive of one nerve branch and shutdown of its partner branch in the organ, a skew that tracked with scar buildup.

Gentle electric needle care at the leg point rebalanced the two branches, restored function, and eased organ scarring. Tissue scans showed a rise in a building block for the key erection gas signal, made by an enzyme rich in vessel lining cells. Blocking that build path wiped out the gain, while topping up the block restored it.
pmc-13320386:
Elizaveta Klockenbring and co-authors present a soil germ data set from a French farm test site in a 2026 data article. The site trials green farming with no pest sprays across four cropping plans that vary tillage and nitrogen use. Soil germs steer nutrient flow and crop health, so their makeup was read by gene scans across many plots and years.

Samples came from 42 plots split into subplots, gathered from 2018 to 2021, and 640 samples yielded usable gene reads before quality checks trimmed the set. Cleaned data hold more than ten thousand germ groups with names, counts, and rich plot facts in shared formats, plus ready made objects for a common stats tool. The set aids method tests and fair contrasts with other soil studies.
pmc-13320586:
Christopher J Phillips writes, in 2026, a history of how statistics entered United States food and drug regulation between 1950 and 1980. Regulators needed to turn animal experiments into a safe human dose for pesticides and medicines. Statistical stretch methods, built largely at the National Institutes of Health, offered a bridge from high test doses to low real-world exposures.

Different methods gave different safety estimates, with little basis for choosing the truest. Phillips argues that statisticians were not really selling machine-like decision making. Instead they built procedures that made assumptions and judgements visible to regulators. Debate about low-dose toxicity went on, yet the new ethos let agencies act under unavoidable uncertainty. The case shows statistics shaping regulatory culture as much as supplying numbers.
pmc-13321486:
Yumei Ma and co-authors test whether adding the amino acid L-citrulline to the diet of nursing mares improves their milk and their foals' growth, in a 2026 paper. Citrulline helps make arginine in the body, boosts blood flow to the udder, and has aided milk output in other farm animals. Its effects in horses, though, were barely studied, leaving a gap this trial set out to fill.

Thirty-two grazing mares were split into four groups: one unsupplemented group and three given 15, 30, or 45 grams of citrulline a day. The middle dose raised milk output the most. All supplemented groups gave richer milk in fat, and their foals grew heavier and bigger than the control group's. Blood markers of muscle strain fell sharply in the supplemented mares. The team also tracked gut microbes and waste chemistry to see how the diet reshaped them.
pmc-13321586:
Pedro Faria Makabe and nine co-authors pool studies on whether a clot-supporting drug cuts transfusion need in bladder removal surgery. Their systematic review and meta-analysis was published in twenty twenty-six. The drug, tranexamic acid, helps in many operations, but its value in this major cancer surgery was unsettled.

Past pooling mixed this surgery with very different ones, and two recent reviews disagreed. The team registered their plan and followed standard review rules. They gathered randomized and observational studies that compared the drug with none. Main outcomes were transfusions around surgery and vein clots, the drug's feared side effect. Their pooled answer gives urologists a firmer basis for a common decision.
pmc-13322486:
Christine Grellmann Schumacher and co-authors test musical auditory training for tinnitus in a 2026 randomised trial. Tinnitus, ringing with no outside source, can burden daily life, and training that engages hearing may reshape brain responses. Twenty adults with tinnitus for at least six months and normal hearing were split into two groups of ten.

Over eight sessions in four weeks, one group did active musical training while the other watched audiovisual material passively. Both groups felt some gain, but only the training group showed wide brain response change plus steady drops in tinnitus loudness, discomfort, and handicap scores. Passive exposure gave a narrower brain change alone.
pmc-13323186:
Stephan Wassong wrote a history article in 2026, published in German. It traces anti-doping policy at the Olympic level. The International Olympic Committee was founded in the late nineteenth century. Its first doping guidelines came decades later. Those early rules condemned doping clearly. They proposed excluding athletes who used banned substances. Stronger institutions followed from the nineteen sixties onward. Drug testing began at the Grenoble Winter Games.

Wassong follows the bodies that run anti-doping today. They include Olympic medical groups and the World Anti-Doping Agency. National agencies and an independent testing agency also feature. Rules grew sharper as the network grew wider. A current challenge closes the article. Privately run Enhanced Games openly allow doping. That model tests the whole system built over decades.
pmc-13324386:
Jian-Jun Shen and team mapped a chain linking the anesthetic sevoflurane to learning problems in newborn mice. Their 2026 study combined RNA methylation sequencing, gene profiling, learning tests, and lab assays, motivated by concern that early exposure to the drug may carry lasting effects on the growing brain. The focus was m6A RNA change and ubiquitin-dependent protein control involving Mid1 and Syngap1.

Analysis found 2,091 changed m6A sites. Mechanistically, Mid1 drove degradation of Syngap1 through the cell's waste pathway, and suppressing Mid1 eased learning and memory deficits while improving neuronal survival and dampening apoptotic signals. The m6A eraser ALKBH5 and reader YTHDF2 jointly tuned Mid1 messenger RNA stability, and pathway analysis tied the Mid1-Syngap1 axis to MAPK signaling disruption. The authors propose this circuit as a target for brain-protecting plans against anesthesia-related harm in children.
pmc-13324486:
Hwa-Young Lee and colleagues test a curcumin nano-liposome product in mice with drug-induced memory loss, in a 2026 animal study. Scopolamine blocks acetylcholine signals and mimics early features of Alzheimer disease.

Male mice took the oral product for 30 days at 250, 500, or 1000 mg per kilogram, then received one scopolamine injection. Maze and open field tests showed better learning and memory after treatment. The product also steadied acetylcholine levels and enzyme activity, cut oxidative stress, and calmed inflammation in the hippocampus. Gene shifts included lower App and Bace1 and higher Adam10 and Bdnf. The authors note blood and brain curcumin levels went unmeasured, so claims stay limited to the tested product.
pmc-13324786:
Olivia Briceño, Iris P. Guzmán-Guzmán, and Malén Massot-Cladera open a 2026 editorial on immune aging and chronic inflammation. Aging weakens immune defense, a change called immunosenescence, and stirs steady low-grade inflammation, termed inflammaging, raising risks of cancer, autoimmunity, and infection.

The editorial introduces a research collection on diet, lifestyle, and treatments that might steady the aging immune system. Highlighted work covers a broad review of the mechanisms, treadmill training that eased muscle inflammation and restored insulin sensitivity, and activity effects in cancer patients. Other pieces address master athletes, gut health, and mind-body care. The editors argue joined-up habits may keep immune resilience longer.
pmc-13325386:
Ni Deng and colleagues probe how cannabidiol acts on melanoma cells grown with T cells in a 2026 multi-omics study. CBD spares the high of cannabis yet shows cancer and immune effects whose full wiring is unclear.

At 10 micromolar, a dose below blanket toxicity, CBD pushed melanoma cells toward death while T cells stayed alive and released more IL-2. Gene and protein readouts lit up the integrated stress response, centered on EIF2 signaling. Both data layers converged on immune cell trafficking, with adhesion proteins such as ICAM1 and ITGB1 rising. The pattern frames CBD as a possible helper beside standard melanoma immunotherapy.
pmc-13325786:
Ovarian cancer is the second deadliest gynecological malignancy, and it feeds on new blood vessels. The nine authors study focal adhesion kinase, a signaling enzyme overactive in many tumors. They ask what blocking it does to ovarian cancer. Expression data and patient samples showed more FAK in platinum-resistant cancers than in sensitive ones. More of its activated form appeared too, and high levels tracked poor prognosis.

In animals, imaging and vessel staining showed FAK inhibitors choking tumor angiogenesis. Both drug blockade and gene knockdown pointed to the same mechanism: FAK steers endothelial sprouting, the first step of new vessel growth. The inhibitors disrupted sprouting across models, including stem-cell-derived endothelial cells. The authors present FAK blockade as a targeted strategy whose anti-tumor punch comes mainly from starving the tumor's blood supply.
pmc-13326486:
Xibing Rao and co-authors move a stress gene from a wild sugarcane relative into Arabidopsis to test its protective power in a 2026 study. Erianthus fulvus shrugs off cold and drought that hurt farmed sugarcane.

The gene EfMYB124 switches on under cold and dry stress. Plants carrying it showed milder visible damage under both stresses than plain plants. Their antioxidant enzymes and proline shot up faster, while the damage marker MDA fell. The gene also tuned known cold and drought response genes, including CBF1 and RD29A, and quieted several ABA signal genes at rest. The results nominate EfMYB124 for sugarcane breeding programs.
pmc-13326986:
Carlyn Patterson Gentile, a child head pain doctor and mother of two school-age kids, takes on a choice from work and home. Should a child play contact sports? Her 2026 essay says there is no one rule for all. The choice should be shaped for each child, made jointly by carers and child, with health staff to weigh gains, harms, and unknowns.

Team sports give real gains for growth. Play lifts fitness, sleep, and social gains, and contact sports may give an outlet that no-contact sports do not. Set against that are concussion risks and doubts on repeat head blows, with no set force level tied to poor brain results. She urges families to weigh the child's own wants and the unknowns side by side. Joint expert notes on concussion show wide views and no clear line on repeat blow risk.
pmc-13327786:
Some babies are born with kidney and urinary tract defects that hide inside wider syndromes. Deepa Singh, Pramit Kumar, and Suruchi Jain checked how nuclear medicine scans perform in such children at one center. They screened nearly a thousand kidney scans done over three years and found thirty-eight patients whose defects came with a complex syndrome.

The commonest syndrome involved malformed lower bowel passages, and the commonest defect was a kidney that did not work at all. Scans were abnormal in thirty-one of the thirty-eight patients, about eighty-two percent. Blood tests for kidney strain also ran higher in the abnormal-scan group. The team urges early scanning in these syndromes, since a silent defect can turn complicated later.
pmc-13327886:
Adolfo Renzi sets out a new staging and decision plan for obstructed defecation in a 2026 article. The syndrome, trouble emptying the rectum, underlies up to half of functional constipation cases and falls mostly on middle-aged women. Care once treated it as a simple mechanical blockage, fixing any bulge or prolapse found.

Many patients stayed symptomatic after sound repairs, pushing the field toward a wider idea Renzi calls ineffective defecation syndrome, where a descended pelvic floor wastes the force of straining. The proposed algorithm stages how damage spreads across sites as the condition evolves, then matches surgery to the exact topographical damage found. One operation for all is rejected in favor of site-specific choices.
pmc-13327986:
Kun Zhang and co-authors single out a monocyte type driving inflammation after traumatic lung injury in a 2026 study. Chest trauma often deepens into acute respiratory distress syndrome, which kills many patients and lacks targeted drugs. Single-cell data from trauma patients' blood, lung macrophage data, and a mouse injury model were combined.

One monocyte subgroup marked by ISG15 and STAT1 grew after trauma and pushed a storm of inflammation, and the gene PIM1 stood out as shared across blood and lung data. Genetic analysis backed PIM1 as a causal risk factor for the distress syndrome, acting through the JAK2, STAT3, and PIM1 chain. The approved JAK2 blocker fedratinib reversed the harmful gene pattern in their drug screen.
pmc-13328186:
Lingyi Chi and co-authors compare irrigation fluids for keeping neurons alive in a 2026 cell study. Artificial cerebrospinal fluid is used in brain surgery, but whether it beats plain saline or phosphate buffer was unproven. Mouse hippocampal HT22 cells were kept in each fluid, with standard medium as control, and survival, death markers, and mitochondria were checked.

The artificial fluid preserved viability best and cut cell death, holding mitochondrial shape and voltage steady, lowering the Bax to Bcl-2 death ratio, and taming reactive oxygen and calcium swings. It also blocked the p38 MAPK and JNK stress pathways while leaving NF-κB alone. The authors back its preferred use in neurosurgery, pending animal proof.
pmc-13329986:
Melanie Odenkirk and team issued a correction to a multi-lab mass-spec paper. The 2026 notice asks for a fix to wrong author affiliations in the paper on variable ion species profiles in electrospray ionization mass spectrometry. It states plainly what was wrong and what the correct record should show, without changing any science claim.

In particular, the correct affiliation for Juliana Chaura, Gabriel Esteban Velez, and Andres Jaramillo-Botero should be the iÓMICAS Research Institute at Pontificia Universidad Javeriana in Cali, Colombia. The correct author list and affiliations appear in the Author Information with the correction. Readers should thus treat the paper's science content as unchanged, with only the record for those three authors fixed.
pmc-13330286:
Mengjia Li and a large team study how steroid drugs boost red blood cell making in a 2026 report. Steroids help anaemia that resists standard hormone care, yet the path was vague. The team used single-cell and gene tools in human, rat, and mouse models, plus lab-grown red cell islands.

A macrophage type marked by CD163 proved central. Those cells handled iron keenly and held island structure together. Without CD163, steroid-driven cell making fell sharply in mice, with islands disrupted and iron handling impaired. In patients with autoimmune haemolytic anaemia, steroid care restored iron handling in those cells and calmed swelling. Targeting island macrophages could open new anaemia care, the authors suggest.
pmc-13330486:
Sogand Sarmadi and co-authors survey crisis prep and mental strength among EMS staff in Tehran Province, Iran, in a 2026 study. Staff filled online forms in 2025 that covered background, prep, and strength scales. In total, 467 pre-hospital staff took part.

Mean prep scored 95.88 in the results, while mean strength scored lower at 44.81 in those same results. Only 3.85 percent counted as highly strong in spirit. Strength rose with prep, years of work, more schooling, and past workshop training. The final model kept prep, degree level, and workshop history as key linked factors. Skill prep alone is not enough, the authors argue: training should also build the mind and add support.
pmc-13330686:
Hongjuan Weng and colleagues build layered scaffolds that guide stem cells into ordered tissue-like networks in a 2026 study. Many body tissues hold cells in aligned, reinforced sheets, yet lab models of that order are scarce. The team joined printed elastic frames with collagen-based gels carrying human mesenchymal stem cells.

The stiff frame gave large-scale direction and spring, while the gel set fast under light to lock cells in place. Adding magnetic particles let fields add fine-scale alignment too. Cells spread, lined up, and matured best in the dual-aligned builds, the authors report, thanks to joined chemical and physical cues. The hybrid route may serve tendon, muscle, and ligament modelling.
pmc-13331186:
Evgenii Belykh and colleagues break microsurgery stitching into measurable steps in a 2026 training study. Four trainees each built vessel joins in a dry lab, swapping between interrupted and continuous stitch styles. In total, 16 joins on standard fake vessels were filmed and coded into 24 stitch moves and 42 flaw types.

Speed rose when trainees bit both walls in one move, used the dominant hand, and stitched toward themselves in the reported analysis. Total time fell as attempts grew and rose as flaws grew. Continuous stitching ran 19 percent faster and drew fewer flaws per join in the mean values given. Flaw types split by style: thread control for one, knot tying for the other.
pmc-13331286:
Wenshuo Zhao and a large team design a braided metal stent for blocked urinary tubes in a 2026 study. Standard stents trade wall strength against open flow. The new stent locks two nitinol braid layers together with a thicker inner wire, boosting layer bonding while keeping walls ultra-thin at about 0.31 mm in the reported build.

The open channel ran about 29 percent wider than a shop plastic stent, while crush strength more than doubled in the bench values given. Bending stayed supple. Under a set squeeze that mimics blockage, the new stent kept a third of its starting flow while the plastic stent lost nearly all flow. Anchor force matched clinical norms.
pmc-13331986:
Haiyan Yin and colleagues review light-assisted 3D bioprinting of tough hydrogels in a 2026 survey of the field. Printing living tissue with light gives fine control over shape and timing. But printed gels are often too weak for organs that bear load, and strength must be balanced against printability and friendliness to cells.

The review compares natural and synthetic gels by their linking chemistry, bond energy, and resulting strength, then sets the main printing methods side by side. A central theme is how mixing permanent bonds, reversible bonds, and weaker physical links can toughen a gel without ruining it for cells. Uses covered include cartilage, bone, tendon, skull, muscle, and dental repair. The authors close with open problems and directions for making printed tissue that survives real mechanical demands.
pmc-13332386:
Pannawat Supapannachart and colleagues carried out a 2026 genome-wide survey of Fea's muntjac, a little-known deer of the Thai-Myanmar border forests, held in Thai captive collections. Numbers there have fallen to critical lows, and patchy pedigrees raised fears of inbreeding and lost diversity.

Using reduced-representation sequencing, the team generated genome-wide SNP data for the remaining animals, including one suspected hybrid, and ran family-tree, clustering, and shared-descent analyses. The animals grouped clearly by holding institution, the suspected hybrid formed its own line, and both close and second-degree kinships appeared, mostly matching pedigrees but adding links the records had missed. One animal was unrelated to all others and carries unique variation worth protecting. The authors present the survey as a baseline for breeding choices in this threatened deer.
pmc-13333286:
Shota Shibuki and colleagues report a 2026 letter on the loss of a key kidney lesion after ibrutinib therapy. The patient was a 61-year-old man referred for nephrotic syndrome with a urine protein-to-creatinine ratio near six grams per gram, low serum albumin, and near-normal serum kidney marker. Early monoclonal studies were nondiagnostic. Kidney biopsy showed mild matrix expansion in the kidney filter and basement membrane thickening with focal spikes and bubbling.

Antibody staining showed a patchy IgG1-kappa pattern, and electron imaging revealed organized thread-to-tube deposits about 22 nanometres wide with focal parallel alignment. Laser-guided mass spectrometry found more kappa than lambda light chain peptides, matching the kappa-led pattern. The letter, on leukemia-linked single-clone immune-pattern kidney disease, tracks how the defining organized lesion vanished after ibrutinib, a finding with implications for disease monitoring.
pmc-13333686:
Guoyong Zhang and co-authors synthesized qualitative studies in 2026 on nursing students learning through virtual simulation. The synthesis gathers what students say they feel, gain, struggle with, and need in this form of teaching.

Nine databases were searched through February 2025, and 17 studies from eight countries passed quality checks with a Joanna Briggs Institute tool. From 65 main themes the authors built four broad themes covering emotional experiences, advantages, challenges, and student needs. Virtual simulation strengthened clinical practice skills, yet students found some controls hard to use and virtual patients not fully convincing. The authors advise simpler interaction designs, richer feedback, and varied case libraries with multilingual support.
pmc-13335986:
Yuqing Zeng and co-authors describe a new cell-free treatment for multiple myeloma, a blood cancer, in a paper from 2026. The cancer grows in bone marrow, where signals help it survive and hide from the immune system. Drugs that target a marker called BCMA can fail when the cancer sheds that marker.

The team built tiny parcels shed by immune cells and fitted them with BCMA on their surface. The parcels soak up a signal that helps the cancer grow, which weakens its survival signals. They also carry parts that wake up killer T cells. In mice, the treatment cut tumor weight and load by a large share and drew more killer cells into the marrow. The work is still at the mouse stage.
pmc-13336486:
Xiaoyan Wang and colleagues study 2026 m6A-run sugar burning by IL-37 driving T cell energy rewiring to regulate colitis. m6A tagging and T-cell energy rewiring are key drivers of bowel disease (IBD). However, how anti-swelling signal interleukin-37 meets m6A-run control remains unclear.

IL-37 eases colitis by cutting m6A levels and rewiring CD4+ T cells. In detail, IL-37 works through SIGIRR to inhibit IRAK4 and JNK tagging, suppress NF-κB p65 switching on, and lower METTL14, cutting m6A buildup. The IL-37/METTL14 axis cuts m6A presence at the A2445 site in the 3′UTR of SLC2A1, weakening its mRNA, blocking sugar burning. In vitro T-cell leaning and transfer of METTL14-heavy CD4+ T cells showed this energy shift holds back Th1/Th17 splitting while boosting Th2 growth. All told, findings reveal the IL-37/SIGIRR-METTL14-m6A axis.
pmc-13336886:
Liquan Zhang and colleagues watch a hydrogen catalyst rebuild its own surface while working in a 2026 study. Ruthenium oxide splits water well, but its true working form and mechanism stayed unclear. The team grew it on a needle-shaped copper base and tracked the surface with Raman signals during the reaction.

The signals flipped back and forth, proving reversible surface reconstruction. Calculations named Ru(II)O as the real active species and detailed the first hydrogen step on its surface. The needle base cut the voltage waste sharply. At 10 mA per square centimeter the overpotential was 68% lower than the flat version in the reported tests, and below a commercial platinum benchmark too. Knowing the true actor guides better catalyst design.
pmc-13337386:
Fulufhelo Nemavhola and Thanyani Pandelani argue in a 2026 perspective that heart digital twins need tissue-level mechanics, not just chamber data. Many models tune passive heart muscle behavior from pressure-volume or imaging traces, which can fit global readings while leaving tissue parameters shaky. Their morphomechanics agenda ties structure, tissue behavior, and organ function together.

Planar two-direction stretch tests on pig, rat, and sheep heart tissue reveal nonlinear stretch, direction dependence, and regional differences. The roadmap feeds such data into law selection and probability-based starting values, uses imaging and histology to set local fiber directions, and constrains organ-level fitting with tissue evidence. Better-grounded twins could predict filling and cell environments more faithfully.
pmc-13338386:
Jannati, Mahmoodi, and Azadbakht ask if plant-rich diets link to weight in girls. Child weight gain is a rising health concern worldwide. Plant compounds in food may help hold weight in check. The team studied young school girls in southeast Iran.

The set held 330 girls aged 6 to 12 in Kerman City. Height and weight gave a weight score for each girl. Food forms gave a plant compound score for each diet. Girls with high scores ate more food in total. The team weighed plant score against excess weight risk. Home facts and play time were taken into account too.
pmc-13338686:
Jihye Park and colleagues studied recurrence in 2026 after clearance of carbapenemase producing gut bacteria in a Korean referral hospital. These resistant organisms threaten patients with few drug options, and whether they return after apparent clearance, and by carbapenemase type, was unclear. The team ran a retrospective case control study covering January 2022 to December 2023.

Of 1,503 patients with NDM or KPC type organisms whose clearance could be judged, 569 achieved clearance. Recurrence meant a matching genotype on culture or PCR within a year of clearance. The findings help hospitals set follow up testing and isolation rules for patients once thought clear of resistant bacteria.
pmc-13340686:
Dong-Ju Lim and Ju-Young Jung reported a ten year follow up in 2026 after repair of a dural tear during spinal cyst surgery. Spinal arachnoid cysts are rare fluid filled lesions, and their removal can tear the dura in 1 to 17 percent of spinal operations. Watertight closure matters to prevent fluid leak, infection, and recurrence, yet long term data beyond five years are scarce.

A 50 year old woman with severe back and leg pain had an intradural cyst at L2 to L3 compressing the cauda equina. During microscopic removal, a large dural tear occurred and was closed with a suturable artificial dural patch. Ten years later she remains symptom free with stable MRI and no cyst return or fluid collection.
pmc-13342486:
Melody A Owen and colleagues compare, in a 2026 methods study, five ways to size hybrid type 2 cluster-randomized trials. Such trials judge a health outcome and an implementation outcome together, and picking the wrong design method can leave a study underpowered.

The team compared p-value adjustment, combined outcomes, a single weighted test, a disjunctive test, and a conjunctive test, both on paper and across 45,000 numeric scenarios using their crt2power R package. Adjustment methods always trailed the combined and single-test options. When treatment effects differed, the disjunctive test usually won; when effects matched, the single test led. Trial planners now have clear rules for choosing.
pmc-13342986:
Yao Qin and co-authors trace how oat flavor forms as grain develops, in a 2026 study joining chemical profiling with gene activity data. Volatile compounds give oats their aroma, yet which ones build up during growth, and which genes drive them, had not been mapped in detail.

Gas chromatography profiling of the cultivar Neiyou 6 found 168 volatile compounds, led by terpenoids and esters that gathered mostly at the filling stage. Pathway checks pointed to monoterpenoid making, with α-pinene oxide as a marker compound. Four candidate cytochrome P450 genes emerged from the combined data, with two flagged most strongly. The map gives breeders targets for improving oat flavor.
pmc-13343086:
Ahmed Abdelwahed and colleagues evaluated an electronic stent register in 2026 at a busy NHS district general hospital, where delayed removal of biliary stents can cause serious, life threatening complications. A robust tracking system is needed to ensure timely removal. The new register was introduced in endoscopy to track patients with biliary stents and ensure removal on time, with data extracted after twenty months.

Endoscopic retrograde cholangiopancreatography was done in 414 patients over the study period, and 89 received stents. After clinical review, management was appropriate in 82 cases, while seven stents were overdue: one by patient preference, two by relocation out of area, and four by inadequate follow up. The register also flagged oesophageal and lumen apposing metal stents with proper follow up plans.
pmc-13345786:
Linhua Feng and four co-authors linked a belly fat score to heart disease risk in China, in a study from twenty twenty-six. The score blends body and blood measures to estimate deep abdominal fat, which is tied to metabolic trouble. Whether it predicts heart disease and stroke over years was not yet clear.

The team followed thousands of adults aged forty-five and older from a national survey. Higher scores went with higher risk of heart and vessel disease as a whole. The link was strongest for stroke. People in the top quarter of scores faced much higher risk than those in the bottom quarter. The pattern held by age and sex, and under extra checks the authors ran.
pmc-13346086:
Metin Çınaroğlu and Eda Yılmazer study cannabis trouble and mental distress among Turkish university students in a 2026 mixed-methods project. Cannabis is illegal and stigmatized in Türkiye, so 512 students from Istanbul, Ankara, and Izmir completed distress and tolerance scales, and 43 high-scoring students sat for interviews about their lived experience.

Heavier cannabis problems tracked moderately with more depression and anxiety and with weaker ability to sit with bad feelings. Interviews exposed a loop: distress drives use for quick relief, relief erodes tolerance, and lower tolerance invites more distress plus academic and social fallout. Building emotion skills, the authors argue, should anchor campus help more than warnings alone.
pmc-13346686:
Sana Khurram and co-authors hunted in 2026 for treatable gene variants in Pakistani adults with acute myeloid leukaemia. This blood cancer varies a lot by gene. Personal care is rare there, since gene testing is seldom on hand. Finding a treatable variant can change drug choice and outlook. Yet many patients never get that news.

Using a focused gene panel, the team tested nine patients with a median age of 42. They found gene changes in six. Thirteen changes across eleven genes emerged, most often missense changes. Adverse variants in WT1 and DNMT3A were among them. The small study shows what wider testing could offer in Pakistan. Broader access might bring standard targeted care within reach.
pmc-13347886:
Lingyu Zhang and Lin Yuan published a 2026 study on cleaning wearable heart signals. Wrist sensors can screen for atrial fibrillation. Motion and noise often distort the readings. Their model tackles two jobs at once. It cleans the signal and flags the rhythm disorder. A transformer network forms the core.

Training used large public signal collections. One dataset held tens of thousands of segments. The model beat standard convolutional approaches. Accuracy held up under added noise. Repeated split testing checked result stability. Better cleaning could make home screening more trustworthy. Fewer false alarms would ease clinic workloads.
pmc-13349886:
Thanushanthahi Loganathan and Helene Volkoff reviewed in 2026 how plastics disrupt feeding and growth in fish and other cold-blooded water animals. Microplastics and nanoplastics now spread widely through aquatic habitats.

Swallowed particles can fake fullness, block the gut, and change behaviour, cutting food intake, while also harming digestion and nutrient uptake. The review links plastic exposure to disturbed appetite hormones, thyroid signals, and growth pathways, plus oxidative stress and liver and gut damage. Fish show the clearest effects, amphibians similar but less studied ones, and reptile evidence stays thin. The authors frame plastic pollution as a direct threat to animal energy balance and fitness.
pmc-13350586:
Shang Gao and co-authors studied prospectively in 2026 sequential surgery after conversion therapy for advanced liver cancer with portal vein tumour thrombus, a group facing very poor outlook. Immune therapy plus targeted therapy can at times shrink tumours enough to make surgery possible. Yet whether this sequence yields lasting survival gain was unclear.

Seventy-six patients with hepatocellular carcinoma and portal vein thrombus got programmed death-1 blockers plus tyrosine kinase blockers, followed by surgery when conversion worked. Long-term efficacy and safety were tracked. The prospective design tests a plan that turns an inoperable diagnosis into a possibly curative path, giving hope for patients whose tumours invade the main portal vein.
pmc-13352186:
Thanna Elsayed Helal and co-authors study unusual dysplasia patterns in ulcerative colitis in a 2026 clinicopathological review. Long-standing gut inflammation raises bowel cancer risk through a stepwise path from dysplasia. Some dysplasia forms lack classic features and are easy to miss. Stored biopsy samples from Ain Shams University Hospitals covering 2020 to 2024 were re-examined.

Of 694 patients, 203, or 29.3 percent, had dysplasia in the chosen biopsy. Standard forms made up 88 cases, while 115 cases, or 56.7 percent, were nonconventional. The most common unusual form showed increased Paneth cell change at 48.7 percent. Over 87 percent of unusual lesions looked flat or invisible during scope exams, which explains late detection.
pmc-13352586: Ali B. Lubis leads a 2026 correction notice for an article on the monooxygenase activity of indoleamine 2,3-dioxygenase. The notice fixes author affiliations: Allen Orville and Anna Bailey gain a Diamond Light Source address, and Lola González-Sánchez keeps a single Salamanca affiliation. One methods sentence in the supporting information is also corrected to a 500 mL reaction volume with overnight dark incubation. The item itself is only a correction notice, and it states that the changes do not affect the conclusions.
pmc-13352986: Shigekazu Ukawa leads a 2026 correction notice for an article on daily sitting time and past-year falls in Japanese adults. The authors used Gemini from Google to reformat the reference list and missed several errors before publication. The notice restores correct author lists for references including the Jiang systematic review and the Tremblay consensus paper, with further reference fixes following the same pattern. The item itself is only a correction notice about reference errors introduced during formatting, with corrected citations as its full content.
pmc-13353186:
Abraham E Libman leads a 2026 case report on lasting dizziness treated with osteopathic cranial manipulation alongside anxiety care. Persistent postural-perceptual dizziness brings chronic dizziness, imbalance, and motion sensitivity with heavy distress. A 30-year-old woman with long anxiety, depression, and trauma history had over two years of dizziness, falls, and imbalance after a car accident.

Talk therapy and drugs had failed her mental symptoms, while therapy and nerve checks failed her balance. Scans showed a pituitary lesion above the sella. Cranial manipulation is rarely used for the condition despite osteopathic ideas linking skull structure, autonomic control, and balance. The report argues body and mind care should proceed together, not in rival camps.
pmc-13354386:
Harshika Khaim Chandani leads a 2026 case of sudden four-limb weakness revealing Gitelman syndrome. The rare inherited kidney tubule disorder, from SLC12A3 gene faults, wastes potassium and magnesium and affects 1 to 10 per 40,000 people. A 30-year-old woman arrived with fever, vomiting, and worsening weakness in all four limbs.

pmc-13354486:

pmc-13356686:

pmc-13357086:
Ya Zhou and co-authors studied in 2026 how a long non-coding RNA called LINC00665 helps breast cancer cells dodge death. Such RNAs steer cancer growth but make no protein. pmc-13358586:
Do-Hyun Kim and co-authors compare workout plans for women after menopause in a 2026 study from South Korea. Seventy-four women who were overweight or obese trained for 12 weeks. pmc-13358786:
Bruno Valle Pinheiro and co-authors wrote a 2026 commentary on freeing patients from breathing machines. That weakness then makes it harder to stop the machine, a trap the authors call a self-feeding cycle.

pmc-13360786:

pmc-13361086:
Diana Tatarciuc and co-authors review heat-proof antioxidant enzymes as future drugs in a 2026 paper. Enzyme drugs often fail because they fall apart at body conditions. The authors judge what stands between these results and real patient care, such as dosing, safety, and delivery. Their map aims to help drug developers pick the candidates most worth pushing forward.
pmc-13362186:
Haochen Ni and co-authors review plant nanocrystals as stabilizers for advanced emulsions in a 2026 paper. Cellulose nanocrystals are tiny rods spun from plant fiber. They can hold oil and water together in Pickering emulsions, where solid particles, not soaps, keep drops apart. In pure form they cling poorly to oil, so the emulsions break under stress.

The authors map design choices for makers of greener delivery systems.
pmc-13362486:
Su-Jin Kim and colleagues report a 2026 trial of electric muscle stimulation for adults with night leg cramps. Twenty adults took part: half used a device that sends mild pulses to both calves, and half did static stretching instead. Both groups trained three times a week for four weeks, and the team measured how much stimulation it took to trigger a cramp, plus pain scores.

Both groups improved, but the device group improved much more. Their cramps took far stronger stimulation to trigger, and their pain scores dropped further than the stretching group's. pmc-13362586:
Sandra Yi Cheng Chee and colleagues report a 2026 study of airway shape and throat tissue size in 404 Singapore children aged 7 to 11. They visited a national dental center for braces care. Narrow airways and swollen tonsils or adenoids raise the risk of disordered breathing in sleep. The team read head X-rays taken from the side and set fresh local norms for airway and face measures.

The local norms give dentists and sleep doctors a fair yardstick for judging Asian children's scans, and the high rates argue for routine airway checks.
pmc-13362986:
Jean-Claude Lavoie and Ibrahim Mohamed wrote a 2026 review on adding glutathione to the IV feeding of preterm babies. Babies born early face heavy oxidative stress from oxygen therapy and IV nutrition, and their stores of glutathione, a key protective molecule, run low. That stress is tied to lung, eye, and gut damage. The review weighs the proof for topping up glutathione through the feeding line itself.

The authors argue for the oxidized form of the molecule, which suits IV use, and they review lab proof that it lowers oxidative stress plus the safety record so far. Shielding the feeding bags from light helps some, they note, but not enough. They conclude the time has come to adopt the supplement.
pmc-13364486:
Yerzhan Imanbayev and co-workers test 2026 waste plastic as a cheap add in for road tar in Kazakhstan. Roads there crack in cold and rut in heat, while trade polymers cost too much. The team blends two common waste plastics into hot tar and checks strength and heat life.

A dose near one to one and a half parts in a hundred gave the best gains in rut defense and stiffness. One plastic mixed more smooth, the other gave more heat strength. Blends with a trade stretch polymer beat state norms by wide gaps. The route recycles waste into longer lived roads.
pmc-13366386:
Petra Czarniak and co-authors systematically review which medications switch the pregnane X receptor on or off. This receptor controls genes that break down and excrete drugs and toxins, and it also influences fat and sugar metabolism. Their 2026 review searches five databases and follows standard systematic review guidance.

Forty-two studies covered prescription drugs and forty covered non-prescription products that regulate the receptor. Forty-seven studies reported effects of this regulation on diseases including cancers, metabolic conditions, and inflammatory disorders, in both beneficial and harmful directions. The authors conclude that many common drugs alter the receptor with clinically relevant consequences, such as changed drug efficacy, but that the potency of most regulators is still poorly quantified.
pmc-13366486:
Yifan Cui and co-workers grow in 2026 a live build stuff from the slime of a soil germ, a stuff that can grow itself. Most live stuffs trap live cells in dead frames, which caps growth. This slime flows for print, firms on cure, and feeds cell growth.

Cross links and clay or gum adds tune its stiff rank by more than ten fold. Print forms hold sun germ cells that live and grow for a month, and the frame spreads to fill its shape. The stuff could yield self grow coats and green build parts.
pmc-13367086:
Zhiwei Chen and others provided a plain language summary comparing ivonescimab plus chemotherapy with tislelizumab plus chemotherapy in advanced squamous non-small cell lung cancer, ran the HARMONi-6 summary in 2026. The trial tested a new care for people with advanced squamous lung cancer in China, and plain language summaries translate trial results for patients and families who need understandable results.

The summary explains what the study tested, who participated, and what it found about the two combination care, in easy language. It helps people understand options without wading through tech trial reports. Readers gain a clear, patient-facing account of a major lung cancer trial's match.
pmc-13369186:
Ahmad Ramazani and co-workers test in 2026 concrete slabs built to block rays still well after a hard air blast near a nuke site. Blasts crack slabs, and cracks leak rays. The team first reads ray pass through whole slabs, blasts them, then reads the pass a new.

A tuned mix of stone dust, fibers, and heavy sand lifts strength and cuts ray pass in whole slabs. A spiral core wrap adds more: slabs with both tricks take blast with near no harm and keep most of their ray block. Mix lone slabs leak far more post blast.
pmc-13370786:
Axioti and colleagues build drug-delivery polymers that use far less polyethylene glycol, or PEG, than usual, in 2026 materials research. PEG coatings help nanoparticles evade the immune system, but heavy PEG use can itself trigger immune recognition and blunt efficacy.
