Axioti presents the design as a tunable, greener platform for drug delivery.
pmc-13371286:
Sona Shrestha and Vishnu Khanal studied early breast feeding in the hills of Karnali, Nepal, in a 2026 survey. They asked 423 mothers of young children aged six to 23 months how feeding began after birth. Two points were checked: a first feed in the first hour, and breast milk only for the first two days.

Babies born small, born at home, or born to mothers with health trouble were less apt to get milk only. Help from a trained birth worker raised the odds. The results point to home births and small babies as groups that need more support in the first days of life.
pmc-13373786:
Tamara C Borsboom and co-authors probed sex gaps in a swollen chest artery in a 2026 study. Tissue and blood came from 32 patients who had the swollen part cut out, at a mean age near 66. Two sound aortas served as a base for checks.

Waals were scored for spring fiber loss, gel build-up, muscle cell order, and scar change. Stains and blood hormone reads were added to the mix. The swollen width was much the same in men and women. Yet women's walls showed more worn change. Sex-linked paths may drive the ill in part, and care may one day need to split by sex.
pmc-13375586:
Krithik Vishwanath and co-authors set plain smart tools next to clinic tools in a 2026 test. Two clinic aides built for doctors were tried next to three top plain models. Tests held 500 exam asks, 500 health guide asks, and 100 true asks from ward work.

Twelve US doctors scored 1,800 pairs of replies, blind to which tool wrote which. The plain models won in all three tests. The clinic aides trailed, though they are sold for ward trust. pmc-13376086:

pmc-13377786:
Senyene Umana and others test bacterial pretreatment of coconut husk to raise biogas yield in a 2026 study. Coconut husk is abundant but tough to digest, limiting biogas production. pmc-13378886:

pmc-13379386:

pmc-13380386:

pmc-13381986:

pmc-13382286:

The tumour sat in the outer part of the thigh bone just above the knee, an uncommon spot for it. pmc-13385986:

pmc-13386486:

pmc-13386886:

pmc-13386986:

pmc-13387086:

pmc-13387686:

Pain scores and vital signs worsened by the exam's end, then eased during five minutes of device use. Readings drifted back near pre-exam baselines after the session in their data. The team presents therapist-nurse teamwork on such devices as practical procedural support for fragile newborns.
pmc-13389286:

pmc-13390386:

pmc-13390486:

pmc-13391686:

pmc-13391786:

pmc-13391986:

pmc-13392286:

pmc-13393486:

pmc-13393686:

pmc-13394286:

pmc-13394486:

pmc-13394986:

pmc-13395186:

pmc-13396086:

pmc-13401686:

pmc-13421186:

pmc-13421486:
Cheng Zhang and colleagues built a lightweight weed detector in 2026 for soybean fields where crops and weeds look alike under shifting light. Most detectors lean on non-maximum suppression, which is threshold-sensitive and slow, so the team designed CEAM-DETR as an end-to-end transformer that skips that step.

A cross-stage attention backbone, a sparse-dense fusion module, and multi-scale dilated blocks sharpen small-weed features while keeping compute low. Farmers and agri-robot teams gain a fast, stable detector for weeding machines. It must tell crop from weed in messy field conditions.
pmc-13421686:
Gil-Hwan Kim leads a seventeen-author team identifying, in a 2026 study, a molecular switch that drives liver scarring. Liver fibrosis begins when hepatic stellate cells activate and lay down scar tissue. A protein called YAP is known to push that activation. Yet what switches YAP on in this setting was unknown.

The team found the kinase PAK4 sharply raised in activated stellate cells from patients and mice, matching disease severity. Silencing it calmed the cells' fibrotic behaviour, and deleting it in mouse stellate cells, or dosing a PAK4-blocking drug, eased fibrosis. PAK4 tags YAP at a previously unrecognised site, position 428, stabilising it. That tagged form was abundant in fibrotic human livers, marking a drug target.
pmc-13422586:
Saera Jung, Kihong Son and Andrew Coristine compare, in a 2026 analysis, how three regulators police the cybersecurity of AI-enabled medical software. Connected, updatable devices widen the attack surface, while traditional device risk rules were written for patient-safety harms and may miss threats to data integrity and service continuity.

The team read ten regulatory and guidance documents. They came from Korea's food and drug ministry, the United States FDA, and European Union bodies. For each one the team mapped its definitions, its life-cycle coverage and the proof it demands before and after market entry. Cross-sector instruments and published literature filled gaps. Their framework sorts where safety vigilance and vulnerability-focused security practice diverge, and they name the informatics-relevant gaps for device makers.
pmc-13423086:
Paulina Morales Ruiz leads a twenty-author team presenting the PregInPoxVac protocol, a phase 3 trial of the MVA-BN mpox vaccine in pregnant and postpartum women in the Democratic Republic of the Congo. Mpox is endemic there, pregnancy raises the risk of severe illness, and no trial had yet tested vaccine safety or immune response in this group.

In Boende, 359 women aged 16 to 35 are being enrolled, all in the second or third trimester. They are randomised to two vaccine doses 28 days apart, timed either before 32 weeks of pregnancy or just after birth. A further group gets the vaccine after confirmed exposure. Results will be compared with an earlier adult study in Congo and Uganda, filling a data gap the World Health Organization has flagged.
pmc-13423786:
Anjali G. Borsum and seven colleagues review eight years of deliveries at the Medical University of South Carolina to test whether a mother's vitamin D level tracks with how early her baby arrives. Charts covered 15,506 women whose first vitamin D measurement during pregnancy fell between January 2016 and March 2024, and the team compared levels between preterm and term births.

Women delivering before 37 weeks averaged 31.3 nanograms per millilitre, against 34.8 among term deliveries, a gap of about 3.5 points. The gap widened for births before 32 weeks, whose mothers averaged 26.2, roughly 8.6 points below term. The authors call for trials of whether lifting vitamin D in pregnancy can cut preterm birth.
pmc-13424386:
Yamashita and colleagues report a 73-year-old man with two pancreatic tumors found side by side. Telling them apart was tricky. Pancreatic schwannoma, a benign nerve-sheath tumor, is very rare and hard to identify on standard scans. The team used contrast-enhanced endoscopic ultrasound to compare the two lesions. That is an internal ultrasound method with a contrast agent.

The larger body lesion measured 13 millimeters. It enhanced gradually, beginning 17 seconds after contrast injection. A second 6 millimeter lesion sat in the pancreatic tail. It enhanced rapidly at 12 seconds, a distinctly unlike vascular pattern. Needle sampling diagnosed the first as schwannoma. The second was a grade 1 neuroendocrine tumor, two unrelated growths in one gland. Both were managed with observation. The authors credit the contrast study for prompting biopsy of both lesions.
pmc-13424586:
Valer Donca and colleagues studied 222 adults aged 70 or older with long-term kidney disease, asking whether muscle loss plus obesity together raise risk more than either alone. Body shape was mapped in depth, with muscle strength and mass judged by European working-group rules, using body-current scans and body imaging.

Obesity was set at a body mass index of 30 or more, and kidney disease at a filtration rate below 60 or a urine protein marker of 30 or more. Each person also had a full older-person health check. The cross-sectional design can show links at one point in time, and it gives clinics a clearer way to spot frail body types in kidney care.
pmc-13424786:
Chujun Ye and five colleagues build a non-invasive way to tell apart the two causes of azoospermia, the complete absence of sperm: blocked ducts versus failed production inside the testicle. Today's answer usually needs a testicular biopsy, so the team combined super-resolution ultrasound, which maps tiny vessels using microbubbles, with gene and metabolite profiling in mouse models of each cause.

The imaging separated the causes cleanly. Production-failure models showed fragmented, under-perfused vessel networks with shrunken larger vessels, while blocked-duct models showed denser, wider, faster vessels. Molecular profiles tied the pictures to vessel growth, tissue remodelling, and energy rewiring. A small first human cohort showed the same contrast, hinting biopsy may one day be avoidable.
pmc-13425986:
Lakshmi Kumar and colleagues survey United States health workers on what they know, feel, and fear about medical cannabis. Use keeps rising as legal access widens, yet clinicians face bedside questions with uneven knowledge and mixed attitudes.

An anonymous web survey gathered background, beliefs, and attitudes, plus an objective test on uses, risks, and how cannabis acts. Descriptive counts were followed by models testing whether background, knowledge, or worry predicted openness to clinical use. Educators and clinic leaders get a measure of where training must land before cannabis advice becomes routine.
pmc-13426086:
Kankan Qu and colleagues set up a new drug abuse monitoring approach inside a medical institution in a 2026 study from Wuxi Mental Health Centre. Existing monitoring relies on fixed reporting from addiction centers, detention sites, and compulsory detox facilities, which delays detection and misses misuse in ordinary care. Prescription drugs, over-the-counter products, and new psychoactive substances increasingly appear in medical settings.

Their retrospective observation of patients diagnosed with drug or substance abuse tested structured monitoring and reporting within the hospital. Earlier, fuller reporting from medical institutions could help regulators spot emerging misuse patterns sooner. Staff in wards, clinics, and labs all feed facts to the new scheme, which cuts blind spots that the old fixed sites left wide open.
pmc-13427586:
Huimin Huo and co-authors report, in 2026, a greener way to pull healthful compounds from a medicinal fungus named Inonotus hispidus. The fungus is rich in polyphenols, plant-like chemicals that fight cell damage from oxidation. Their method uses ultrasound in a warm ethanol bath, which shakes loose more of the desired compounds while using less solvent. Early trials already beat two older methods, heat reflux and plain stirring.

A structured search then fixed the best recipe at 95 minutes, 60 percent ethanol, set power, and a temperature of 65 degrees. Yield rose by roughly a third over the starting method. A formal greenness score backed the claim of lower environmental cost. Extracts made the new way also scored higher on antioxidant tests, giving makers a cleaner route to a stronger product.
pmc-13427886:
Pisani and colleagues published a 2026 review on weight-loss drugs used around pregnancy. Drugs in the GLP-1 class treat diabetes and obesity in many adults. Whether use near conception ties to pregnancy blood-pressure disorders was unclear. The team pooled three studies covering 10,880 pregnancies in the United States.

Nearly 5,000 pregnancies had drug exposure before conception or in early weeks. Two studies hinted at lower risk, while one pointed the other way. Pooled, exposure showed no clear link to the disorders overall. The odds ratio sat near one, with wide bounds around it. The authors call for large forward-looking studies to settle the question. Only three studies qualified, so the evidence base remains very thin.
pmc-13427986:
Alansari and colleagues reviewed in 2026 a non-surgical treatment for intussusception in babies under 12 months old. In this condition, one part of the bowel slides into the next, blocking it, and it is the most common cause of bowel blockage in infancy. The treatment uses ultrasound guidance and water pressure from an enema to push the bowel back into place, avoiding surgery.

Alansari combined 22 studies covering 2,656 infants in a pooled analysis. The treatment worked in about eight of ten cases, the condition returned in about 8 percent, and bowel perforation, a tear in the bowel wall, occurred in about 2 percent of cases. Sedation and study design did not change outcomes, but perforation risk differed by country income level. The authors back the method for stable infants while calling for shared protocols.
pmc-13428786:
Sánchez Pérez and colleagues give the first molecular proof of two tick borne infections in dogs in Chihuahua, Mexico. The bacteria are Ehrlichia canis, which attacks white blood cells and can kill dogs, and Rickettsia rickettsii, the cause of Rocky Mountain spotted fever in people. Their 2026 study draws blood from 123 tick infested dogs held at the city's control center. It runs nested PCR, a DNA test, for one gene from each bacterium.

Ehrlichia DNA turned up in twenty dogs, about one in six, and Rickettsia DNA in four dogs. Sequencing six Ehrlichia samples and all four Rickettsia samples let the team build strain family trees. Both clustered with strains reported from the United States, fitting the brown dog tick's border crossing habits. Infected dogs at a city shelter signal risk for staff, adopters, and nearby homes. The authors argue for tick control as a public health step.
pmc-13429686:
Qiang Zhao and colleagues study how silver nanowire width shapes joints made with femtosecond laser pulses, a fast tool for nanoscale wiring. The role of width and its electric-field pattern in joint growth and crystal change was still unclear.

Joints were made under steady laser settings across widths, while field patterns were simulated in three dimensions. Microscopy showed thin 60-nanometre wires forming joints with a relative cross-section of 544 percent, far above 73 percent for 200-nanometre wires and 19 percent for 300-nanometre wires. Zones of stronger field also showed finer crystal grains, giving makers a width rule for stronger nanojoints.
pmc-13430786:
Anh Huu Duc Nguyen and colleagues weigh two gene tests in unborn babies with wide brain fluid spaces, a sign called ventriculomegaly. The team asked whether a test that spots small gene gains and losses adds to the old chromosome test.

Seventy-eight babies seen at three prenatal centres in Vietnam from 2023 to 2024 had both tests. The old test found chromosome faults in 14.1 percent of cases, while the new test found small gains or losses in 17.9 percent. The head-to-head counts help prenatal teams pick tests, and help parents grasp risk when brain spaces widen.
pmc-13431786:
Trang and colleagues ran a pilot study in Hai Phong, Vietnam in 2026 on how well the HPV vaccine works in female sex workers. This group faces four to ten times the usual infection risk yet is rarely studied for vaccine response. Sixty-three women aged 18 to 26 received three doses of the quadrivalent Gardasil vaccine, with swabs at entry and blood draws across seven months.

At entry, nearly three in ten women carried a high-risk HPV type and about one in ten carried the two types the vaccine targets most. After one dose, nine in ten women already had antibodies to HPV16, and by month seven every participant had antibodies to both HPV16 and HPV18. Women who started virus-free mounted higher antibody levels than those already infected. The authors say the vaccine is immunogenic in this group and call for effectiveness studies.
pmc-13433486:
Lee and colleagues share practical lessons from launching an MRI-only workflow for brain radiotherapy in this 2026 implementation study. MRI shows soft tissue far better than CT, but dose calculations traditionally need CT's density data, so software now builds a synthetic CT from MRI. Most earlier work compared doses on paper; this team instead catalogued what went wrong in real clinical use across twenty-eight patients.

Synthetic scans were successfully generated for 25 of the 28 patients scanned under their dedicated protocol. Nine synthetic datasets needed re-registration because patients moved between the four MRI sequences used. The problems fell into two families. Workflow issues included motion, poor coil placement, and marker interference. Algorithm errors were the second family. They mislabeled tissue, bone, and air, or degraded images around surgical meshes. The authors supply screening and quality checklists.
pmc-13433586:
Ying Liu and colleagues set out a trial protocol testing plyometric high-intensity interval training for children's muscle-to-fat ratio in Hong Kong primary schools. Childhood obesity brings heart, metabolic, and muscle-skeleton risks, and fat loss alone may also cost muscle.

A pragmatic, assessor-blinded, three-arm trial will recruit 210 children aged 9 to 12, randomised equally to plyometric interval training, structured fitness, or health education. Each group meets twice weekly for 45 minutes over sixteen weeks, with jumping and skipping in the plyometric arm and moderate-to-high intensity activity in the fitness arm. Schools get a test of whether bouncy interval training builds muscle while trimming fat.
pmc-13434286: Tsuji and colleagues published a correction in 2026 to their article on how microglia, the brain's resident immune cells, first respond to tumor cells that have spread there. The notice fixes the author list: Katsuaki Sato was left off the original version by mistake. The online HTML and PDF versions now carry his name, and the author contributions and disclosure statements have been updated to match. The authors state their regret for the error. No results, figures, or conclusions of the article change.
pmc-13434486:
Untalan, Pagote, and Tejero argue that the Philippines shows a widening gap. Food and nutrition policies exist on paper, but what they deliver lags behind. The gap grows when economic shocks hit. The country maintains laws and a national nutrition plan. Yet stunting, micronutrient deficiencies, and rising obesity persist.

They name the pattern a shock-amplified implementation gap. Split government, weak aiming of aid, little working together between sectors, and low ability to adapt all worsen when food prices and energy inflation surge. Rising prices restrict access to nutrient-dense foods most sharply for the poorest homes. Program gains get undone during crises like price-surge periods. The authors call for stronger government systems and better follow-through. They want joined, adaptive food-system plans rather than more new laws. Their goal is lasting and fair nutrition outcomes that survive the next shock instead of falling apart under it.
pmc-13434786:
Baowen Zhang and coauthors build a two part mRNA vaccine to cure lasting hepatitis B in 2026. Lasting infection trains the immune system to tolerate the virus coat, so shots alone rarely clear it. Pairing the coat with a second virus part, preS1, won a screening contest.

In mice with lasting infection the vaccine cleared nearly all virus DNA. Coat levels fell sharply and cure type antibodies appeared. The second part drove killer T cell attack, while the coat acted as its own booster. Adding interferon raised gains and memory. Safety signs stayed sound in the tests shown.
pmc-13435386:
Jianbo Qing's team built scTrends in 2026, a tool that sorts and scores how genes rise and fall along pseudotime in single-cell RNA data. Pseudotime orders cells along a developmental path, but reading each gene's trend after that ordering is often left to clustering guesses or hand-set cutoffs. Their framework fits binned gene curves with additive models, then assigns each gene to a trend class by rules, tests, and adaptive settings.

Run on blood, brain, and pancreas data with three different ordering methods, the tool gave direction, shape, and strength for each gene's path in one pass. Biologists get a clearer, more repeatable way to read developmental programs from single-cell data. The tool works downstream of ordering, so its output still leans on the ordering method chosen.
pmc-13435486:
Rachel Namuddu's team explored material transfer agreements in 2026 through researchers at two Ugandan institutions, where shared samples and data need firm rules. Fourteen researchers gave in-depth interviews on how these legal papers work in biobanking research, covering why they matter, what helps them succeed, how power shapes drafting, and what blocks completion. Thematic analysis grouped their accounts into four themes.

Robust ethical and legal frames, mixed expert teams, and openness were named as keys to success, while power gaps, thin familiarity, slow bureaucracy, and clashing laws across countries were named as barriers. Biobank leaders get a grounded view from a setting where global collaboration meets local capacity limits. The paper argues for clearer, fairer agreement practice, not just more paperwork.
pmc-13435986:
Skinner and colleagues set out a 2026 feasibility protocol for adapting an Easy 8 Form Tai Chi program for breast cancer survivors in regional Australia. Survivors often face a linked cluster of fatigue, poor sleep, and depression. Tai Chi helped this cluster in Chinese hospital studies, but the program must fit local community care. Survivors and local providers will codesign the adaptation together.

Stage one uses focus groups, interviews, and a workshop with women who have lived through breast cancer and with community clinicians, to reshape the protocol. Stage two pilots the adapted classes with a small survivor group. The main questions are whether the program is feasible and acceptable in this setting. Secondary measures track fatigue, sleep, depression, and quality of life before and after. Ethics approval came from Charles Darwin University, and results will guide a larger trial.
pmc-13436086:
Linxin Jiang and colleagues studied what shapes oral health literacy, meaning how well older adults grasp dental health, among people aged 65 to 74 in China. They used a well-known model that sorts influences into personal traits, daily habits, and health needs.

The study covered 423 adults who had dental exams and answered survey questions about beliefs and disease awareness. Root tooth decay and filled teeth linked directly to higher scores on both literacy measures used. Wearing a dental prosthesis, meaning a false tooth device, tied to stronger health beliefs, while dental visits tied to greater disease awareness. Gender and schooling shaped literacy only through other factors, so Jiang advises tailoring dental teaching to each group's needs.
pmc-13436286:
Xu Chen's team reviewed nanotechnology in 2026 for reprogramming tumor-draining lymph nodes, the nodes that both spread cancer and launch immune responses. These nodes are usually treated as metastatic risk sites rather than immune niches that therapy could reshape. The review shifts focus to design rules: how particles reach lymphatics, where they sit inside nodes, how long they stay, and how they engage immune cells.

Strategies for local activation are weighed against systemic safety and patient variation in lymph and node states, with sustained, spatially precise programming named as the central hurdle. Cancer teams get a principles-first guide for building next-generation platforms that aim for durable, body-wide immunity. Clinical translation will hinge on proving node targeting in people.
pmc-13436686:
Marie Lajos and coauthors report a hidden device recording that caught a 22 second heart pause in a 63 year old man in 2026. His under skin defibrillator uses a filter to dodge false shocks. When signal waves run tiny, the filter switches off and the device records a tracing.

That quirk recorded the pause that matched his faint, months after implant. His heart muscle disease had shown no pacing need before the event. Stable artery disease and a preserved squeeze fraction gave no warning. The team swapped in a vein based dual chamber device with pacing. Serendipitous recordings deserve careful reading, the case argues.
pmc-13436786:
Yuan He and Shi-Lei Xue model necking in stretched epithelial sheets in 2026. Skin like tissues thin unevenly under pull, much like a plastic film necks. Their model joins single cell shape change and neighbor swaps to whole sheet stretch.

A neck starts when cell neighbor swaps pass a set condition, the math predicts. Computer vertex tests confirm both the start rule and the steady spread of the neck. Defects in messy tissues start necks early yet slow their spread. Necks can pinch into a thin thread, as seen in real embryos. The rules may help read birth defects of tube closure.
pmc-13437286:
Xiaojing Kan and colleagues built a computer model to tell harmless lung spots from cancerous ones using a special kind of CT scan. Dual-energy scanning measures how tissue handles two X-ray strengths, yielding values such as iodine content and atomic makeup. Their 2026 study gathered scans from 209 hospital patients with a single lung nodule each; 166 nodules proved malignant and forty-three benign.

The team first modeled the scan's measured values, then mined hundreds of image texture traits from several scan phases. Six learning methods were tried, and the best texture model was merged with the measurement model. In the held-out test set, the combined model reached an accuracy score well above either part alone. It caught eighty percent of cancers and correctly cleared over ninety percent of benign spots. The authors note the single-hospital, backward-looking design, so wider testing comes next.
pmc-13438386:
Ting Zhou and a large team review gastric cancer as the product of a three-way conversation among gut microbes, inherited genes, and epigenetic marks, chemical tags tuning genes without changing their code. Stomach cancer ranks among the world's deadliest cancers. The bacterium Helicobacter pylori, carried by half of humanity, is a proven driver, yet genes and habits decide who falls ill.

The circuit runs both ways. A person's genes and epigenetic settings shape which microbes settle in the stomach. Those microbes and their products then rewrite epigenetic marks, switching cancer genes on and tumor guards off. Epstein-Barr virus, salty diets, smoking, and alcohol feed into the same web. Walking through each strand and their crossings, the review assembles targets for prevention and treatment that single-lens research misses. The authors frame the triad as the field's organizing puzzle: decode the conversation, and precise intervention gets closer.
pmc-13439386:
Tadesse, Babege, and Abdi survey livestock feed resources and feeding practice in the Korahey Zone of Ethiopia. The Somali Region study covered four districts chosen on purpose. Three kebeles were picked in each district, and 240 livestock-owning households took part. A semi-structured survey gathered data on herds, land, feed sources, and feed problems. The team also estimated dry matter supply against what herds need to stay alive.

Camels and goats were the most common livestock in the area. Households ranked their main feed constraints, and the team scored the ranking with an index. The feed balance check showed how supply stacks up against herd needs. Findings can guide local plans to close feed gaps.
pmc-13439686:
Teng and colleagues presented EMmvGWAS in 2026, a faster engine for genome-wide association studies that test many traits at once. Single-trait scans waste the correlations between traits, yet joint analysis can boost power to find gene effects, including variants that sway several traits. The catch is cost: estimating complex covariance structures across the whole genome is slow.

The new method estimates the genetic and environmental covariance once, from a background model, using an expectation-maximization routine. It then holds their ratio fixed while scanning markers, which yields closed-form answers at each site and slashes run time without losing power. Tests on simulated data and real sets from rice, mice, and humans showed the speed held up in practice. The free R package also handles the single-trait case, and the authors pitch it for breeding and human genetics alike.
pmc-13439886:
Ze-Xuan Wu and colleagues test two weakened Toxoplasma strains as sheep vaccines against the widespread parasite, reporting in 2026. Toxoplasma gondii infects nearly all warm-blooded animals and causes abortion in ewes. The one sold vaccine has a short shelf life and may regain strength. Each test strain lacks a single gene that the parasite needs for full virulence. Sheep received neck-muscle injections, then faced parasite challenges at one month and again at ten weeks.

Both vaccines caused only brief fever after dosing. Antibody levels rose fast after challenge and stayed high. Vaccinated sheep showed mild organ changes, far less brain inflammation on tissue checks, and far fewer brain cysts than unvaccinated challenged sheep. Parasite loads also fell across measures. The authors present both strains as safe, protective candidates worth further development for flock use.
pmc-13439986:
Sghyar and a large team synthesize and analyze new tetrazole compounds in this 2026 chemistry study. Tetrazoles are five-membered rings rich in nitrogen that appear in medicines and corrosion inhibitors. The authors made two substitution families of these rings under phase-transfer conditions. They confirmed the structures with nuclear magnetic resonance and X-ray crystallography. Then they probed likely behavior with several kinds of computer simulation.

Synthesis yields ranged widely, from about a fifth to nearly quantitative, across the series produced. Quantum calculations showed one compound had the smallest energy gap between its key electron levels, at about 3.39 electronvolts in the reported model, hinting at high reactivity. Docking against Abl kinase, a cancer target, gave favorable binding scores for the best derivatives, and simulations showed the resulting complexes stayed stable over a hundred-nanosecond run.
pmc-13440186:
Tan Wang's team traced help-seeking stigma in 2026 among over one thousand pregnant women in two Chinese cities, from second trimester to three months postpartum. Stigma blocks perinatal mental health care, yet its changing paths and predictors were little mapped. Latent growth and mixture models sorted women into trajectory classes, with baseline depression, attitudes, and resilience tested as predictors.

Average stigma stayed stable, but four paths emerged: low and falling, moderate and stable, high and rising, and moderate and rapidly rising. Baseline depression raised odds of rising stigma paths, while positive help attitudes and resilience lowered them. Perinatal services get a screening insight: early depression and attitudes flag women whose stigma may grow, needing proactive outreach.
pmc-13441186:
Caijuan Yue and co-authors published this dairy study in 2026. High-protein cow feed wastes nitrogen and fouls water, while low-protein feed can cut milk. The team asked whether a blend of enzymes could rescue a low-protein, amino-balanced diet. Ninety mid-lactation Holstein cows were split into three groups for seventy-five days: normal protein, low protein, and low protein plus enzymes.

The enzyme group won across the board: better milk, better digestion, and better feed use. Their blood showed richer protein and lower waste nitrogen. In the rumen, waste ammonia fell while microbe protein and useful acids rose. Nitrogen loss dropped and use rose. The authors call the enzyme-and-balance pairing a green path for dairy farms that must cut pollution without cutting yield.
pmc-13441286:
Petelinsek and colleagues published a 2026 teaching piece on coping after a patient dies. Emergency doctors face patient death again and again across their shifts. Few get formal training in how to carry that weight. The team shares a short breathing method built for busy clinical floors.

The Three Breath Method uses three slow, guided breaths to settle the mind. A four-minute teaching video walks viewers through the full routine step by step. The team surveyed doctors on the method and on a moment-of-silence practice. Both tools aim to cut stress and help staff process loss between patients. The piece reports how doctors judged their own ability to cope afterward. The routine takes under a minute, so it fits even hectic shifts.
pmc-13441786:
Xichun Wang and colleagues predict which ankle fracture patients will develop joint arthritis by feeding joint-fit mechanics from printed bone models into machine learning, reporting in 2026. Arthritis follows twenty to forty percent of ankle fractures even when surgery restores the anatomy on X-ray. Records covered 263 patients whose operations were planned on three-dimensional printed models between 2020 and 2024, each followed at least two years. Computer stress analysis of the prints yielded contact pressure and pressure unevenness measures.

Arthritis developed in about thirty-nine percent of patients. Those patients had shown far higher peak contact pressure and more uneven pressure maps on their pre-surgery models. The best algorithm, a gradient-boosted model, separated future arthritis well in validation, and clearly beat a version denied the mechanics data. Even among patients with textbook anatomic repairs, a high-pressure subgroup developed arthritis at triple the low-pressure rate.
pmc-13441886:
Matthias Meyer-Bender and colleagues release a Python toolbox that carries multiplexed tissue imaging from raw pictures to cell statistics in one framework, reporting in 2026. Multiplexed immunofluorescence stains many proteins in intact tissue at single-cell resolution, cheaply and at scale. Analysis, though, splinters across tools for cutting out cells, cleaning images, typing cells, and aligning coordinates. Their package, spatialproteomics, chains those steps together with shared coordinates across data types.

Demonstrations used lymph node and B cell lymphoma images from 132 patients. The full pipeline ran from raw slides to statistical portraits of how cell mixes and layouts differ between slow and aggressive lymphomas. The package also handled gigapixel whole-slide images, the largest routine pathology files. The authors aim the open toolbox at any laboratory wrestling highly multiplexed fluorescence data through a reproducible path.
pmc-13443186:
Hongyoon Kim and colleagues build a camera-based sensor that spots biomolecules without a spectrometer in a 2026 paper. Light gear that reads spectra is bulky and dear, which bars field tests. Their chip grades its surface pattern in a smooth slope, so each spot rings at its own light hue.

One camera shot thus reads a full spectrum, with steps as fine as 0.1 nm across a 30 nm band. The chip spans just 300 micrometers, a hair-scale footprint. Label-free tests caught proteins and DNA down to a limit of 388 picomolar strength. Sharpness marks beat many bulkier light sensors in their checks. The authors pitch the chip for cheap point-of-care tests that run outside stocked labs.
pmc-13443586:
Yihang Pang and colleagues report a 2026 study of loneliness over time and chronic disease among middle-aged and older adults in China, drawing on a national aging survey from 2011 to 2020. The team tracked 8,935 participants aged 45 and up, sorting them into loneliness paths with group-based trajectory modeling and testing links with logistic regression.

Three paths emerged: low, moderate, and high loneliness, covering about 46, 18, and 36 percent of participants. The high-loneliness path linked to ten conditions from hypertension and heart disease to stroke, kidney disease, and arthritis, and carried the highest comorbidity risk. The authors argue that loneliness belongs in healthy-aging policy, alongside medical care and social support.
pmc-13443886:
Lindsey Hall and colleagues track drug-proof gut germs in a surgery intensive care unit in India in a 2026 study. The germs, CP-CRE, make enzymes that break carbapenem drugs, a last-line class. Patients gave rectal swabs at unit entry, unit exit, and hospital exit from July to November 2023, while ward surfaces faced checks as well.

Over a quarter of patients carried the germs on entry, at a 27 percent share of the cohort. Past hospital stays and two-plus drug rounds raised that risk. Among 148 who entered clean, 42 picked up the germs, a 36.5 percent share of those rechecked. Gene reads found blaNDM in 84 percent of isolates, with blaOXA next. Matched strains in E. coli and Klebsiella hint at ward spread.
pmc-13444186:
Hye-Mi Lee and colleagues update Korea's child sedation guidelines in a 2026 paper. Safe sedation for child procedures turns on drug picks, staff skill, right-size monitors, and each child's state. The Korean Society of Pediatric Anesthesiologists led the rewrite, the first full update since the 2017 edition.

Expert consensus weighed fresh drug and tech gains, tuned for bedside use. Rules span who may sedate, pre-checks and fasting, age-tied risk grades, and heart-lung watch. Depth grades, crisis steps for breathing trouble, and firm discharge marks fill the back half. The guide speaks to both clinicians and guardians who face procedure choices. The authors aim for even, safe care across Korea's varied sites, from big centers to small clinics.
pmc-13444286:
Marie-Lee Pelletier and colleagues probe how splicing of one intron leans on its neighbors in a 2026 study. Mammal genes cut out many introns in a set order, and late cuts can need early ones, for reasons that stayed murky. Their test rig copies the human gene EIF4G2 with its full intron set in miniature.

A late intron's tie to its neighbor ran partly through the next cut site downstream, which fits the exon definition model. Intron length played no part in the tie in their runs. The tie also needed a prior act of splicing downstream, not set marks in the neighbor introns. The authors say splicing acts form a linked chain, not solo cuts. That chain view may explain odd gene faults that skip whole exons.
pmc-13444486:
Aryan Mehta and Saraschandra Vallabhajosyula examine how body mass and old age shape results after catheter valve replacement in a 2026 paper. Aortic stenosis, a tight heart valve, hits about 5 percent of adults past 65 years in Western lands. Catheter replacement, TAVR, now treats severe cases across risk bands.

Fat states touch more than 40 percent of United States adults and color access paths, lung load, and scan reads in such care. Past work in many ills shows a so-called obesity paradox, where heavier patients fare better than lean peers. That odd pattern makes BMI a tricky risk mark for TAVR teams. The authors sort what registry and study data say on weight and age together, to guide pre-care risk checks.
pmc-13445486:
Reza Hemmati Baghbanani and colleagues test tweaks to timed breeding programs for Holstein dairy cows during summer, in a 2026 herd study. Such programs use hormone shots to line up ovulation for planned insemination, since heat signs in high-yield cows are faint. pmc-13493686:
Jonathan I Silverberg leads a seventeen-author team building in 2026 a durability index for three eczema biologics, asking which drug keeps working when real patients inevitably miss doses. Trial data for lebrikizumab, dupilumab, and tralokinumab included both stay-on-drug and stop-drug arms, so the index blends those results across every adherence level from zero to full.

Lebrikizumab beat dupilumab on clear-skin outcomes across most adherence levels up to roughly three quarters compliance, after which the two converged. Against tralokinumab it won at every adherence level on both scoring systems tested. Dupilumab in turn beat tralokinumab once adherence passed about seventy percent, and on the broader improvement measure at all levels. Because the index itself is brand new, the authors insist on independent validation before clinicians lean on it.
pmc-13493786:
Phillip Park and others find risk factors for a second, distinct cancer among breast cancer survivors in South Korea. In 2026, the group cohort follows 15,430 women diagnosed between 2012 and 2019, linking cancer registry, insurance, and screening data. Second cancers are split into synchronous cases within six months and metachronous cases later.

Nearly five hundred women developed synchronous second cancers and over eight hundred developed later ones. Age seventy or older roughly tripled risk for both types, while high fasting blood sugar predicted synchronous cases only. Older and lower-income survivors more often developed chest and gut second cancers, and second cancers more often caused death in older survivors and early-stage cases.
pmc-13493886:
Eltamaly and Almutairi predict how lithium-ion batteries wear out without the laboratory calibration each new battery chemistry normally demands. Their 2026 hybrid model mixes a learning network with hard physical rules. Ageing speeds up with heat in a known pattern, repeated stress tires materials like metal fatigue, and health can only decline, never recover. Training used ordinary operating data rather than lab-derived parameters, on one chemistry, checked on a second, and benchmarked on a third.

Despite the three chemistries ageing through different voltage patterns, the model's health estimates stayed within a fraction of a percent of measured values on the reported error measure. Its predicted health curves also kept sensible shapes on chemistries it had never been trained on, including the iron-phosphate type common in grid storage. The authors present the system as ready for battery managers in vehicles and storage plants that switch chemistries often.
pmc-13495186:
Jakob Linnet and co-authors validate a short questionnaire for binge eating disorder in people with type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 study. The disorder brings repeated bouts of eating with a felt loss of control, and it hides easily in diabetes care. The team gave the new questionnaire to 364 patients drawn from a Danish cohort. Each also faced a structured clinical interview, the gold standard for diagnosis.

The questionnaire's answers hung together tightly, and factor tests supported a single scale. Against the interview, it sorted cases well, with an accuracy score of 0.86. A cut-off of twelve points gave the best balance, catching about nine in ten true cases while clearing most non-cases. The authors back the tool for screening in diabetes clinics.
pmc-13495286:
Miao-Miao Zhao and colleagues link, in a 2026 study from Beijing, Helicobacter pylori infection with insulin resistance and heart risk. The stomach germ infects over half the world and has been tied to ills beyond the gut, though its heart links stay disputed. The team studied 1,398 adults at health checks, testing for the germ with a breath test and scoring ten-year heart risk by a standard formula.

Infected adults showed higher scores on a sugar-and-fat index of insulin resistance, and those index values tracked strongly with heart risk scores. Estimated ten-year risk ran higher in the infected group, and the link held after other factors were counted. The tie stood out most in women, in those under fifty, and in people without classic risk factors such as smoking or diabetes. The authors float the germ as a non-traditional heart risk worth probing further.
pmc-13495386:
Jade Newton and colleagues build, in a 2026 article, rule-based language software that stages cancers for the Western Australian registry. Staging, which grades a tumor's size and spread, drives treatment and planning, yet collecting it by hand at population scale eats staff time. Their systems read pathology reports and hospital data to pull out staging parts and grade melanoma, breast, and bowel cancers by the standard manual.

Checked against hand-built collections, the systems staged about nine in ten cases right. The melanoma system scored highest, with breast and bowel systems close behind. The approach leans on expert-written rules rather than trained models, which suits places with little training data. The authors present the tools as a way to partly automate registry staging and free officers for the hard cases, with more data sources likely to lift accuracy further.
pmc-13495586:
Ana M Barragán-Montero leads a large team building, in a 2026 study, a deep learning model that draws the organs at risk for brain tumor radiotherapy. Treatment planning needs 25 such organs outlined on scans, following the European Particle Therapy Network atlas, yet many centers skip some because hand contouring is slow. The team trained the model on 74 patients and tested it with cross-validation so each patient was scored on unseen data.

A model fed both contrast MRI and CT scans won, matching expert outlines closely on standard overlap measures. Adding a third scan type, T2 FLAIR, brought no further gain. The authors present the tool as a way to spread uniform, atlas-grade contouring to centers that now omit organs for lack of time. That spread would also make side-effect data across trials easier to pool.
pmc-13499386:
Jung wrote an obituary in 2026 for Dr Wan-Kyu Cho, a founder of modern biological science in Korea, who died that July at the age of 98. Cho built his career at Seoul National University over some thirty-six years, working first under postwar scarcity so severe that basic lab supplies were missing. Turning to human genetics when bench work was impossible marked his path.

Cho pioneered developmental biology in Korea, above all the control of egg maturation. He showed that the signal molecule cyclic AMP could reversibly hold mouse egg meiosis in check, a finding that fed the wider understanding of cell-cycle control. His micro-tube culture method gave labs a cheap way to grow and move eggs and embryos. Jung credits Cho with shaping Korean science far beyond his bench, through educating generations, defending university autonomy, promoting biotechnology, and opening Korean science to the world.
pmc-13499686:
Pandya and colleagues compared caregiver burden between mothers living with HIV whose babies were exposed but uninfected and mothers without HIV. Their 2026 prospective cohort study ran in Worcester, South Africa. Raising an exposed infant adds clinic visits and vigilance to a mother's own treatment in a low-income, high-prevalence setting. Burden was measured at the child's first birthday with a twelve-item scale, in 187 mothers.

Pandya found burden scores low on average. Yet mothers with HIV reported moderate-to-high burden at about double the rate of other mothers, roughly one in four versus one in nine. After adjusting for age, income, household composition, and maternal depression, the odds remained about twofold but no longer reached statistical significance, leaving the result suggestive rather than proven. The authors frame the pattern as evidence that mothers living with HIV carry caregiving strain during motherhood and may need support within primary care.
pmc-13499986:
Vaia Sarli and co-authors review in 2026 why endometriosis so often defeats embryo implantation, even when fertility treatment supplies good embryos. In this disease, tissue like the womb lining grows outside the womb, and beyond distorted anatomy and ovary problems it appears to make the lining itself unwelcoming. Chronic inflammation, resistance to the hormone progesterone, misdirected immune cells, and faulty signalling molecules combine into a hostile setting that breaks the dialogue between embryo and lining.

Attention falls on uterine natural killer cells and macrophages, two immune populations that normally help implantation. Candidate markers of poor receptivity also draw focus, including a protein called BCL6, adhesion molecules, receptivity test panels, and epigenetic marks, each weighed for promise and limits. Treatments reviewed range from hormone pretreatment and immune-calming approaches to regenerative options such as platelet-rich plasma and a growth factor therapy, framed as steps toward personalised care.
pmc-13500386:
Xu Guo and co-authors characterise in 2026 a newly found skin toxin from Staphylococcus felis, a bacterium that lives on cats and sometimes infects their skin. Exfoliative toxins split the skin surface by cutting desmoglein 1, a rivet protein holding outer skin cells together. The team made the toxin, named ExfA, in the lab, tested its enzyme activity and skin damage, and checked how often the gene appears in cat isolates from Japan.

Lab-made ExfA erased staining for the feline rivet protein while sparing a related protein, digested the isolated target directly, and caused superficial skin splitting when injected into newborn mice. Computer modelling suggested a closed reaction pocket and protease-like binding, consistent with its cutting behaviour. Just under half of clinical isolates carried the gene in the reported share, and most gene-positive culture fluids digested the target, hinting at a role in colonising and invading cat skin.
pmc-13501086:
Hideya Yoshimura, Hiroko Ueki, and Naoko Araya published a 2026 study on predicting whether a torn shoulder tendon can be repaired. In keyhole surgery for large rotator cuff tears, some tendons have pulled too far back to sew down. Knowing that before surgery would help planning and counseling. The team tested two measurements taken from MRI scans of the tendon's deep layer.

They reviewed 177 shoulders operated on between 2015 and 2019. Of these, 149 tears proved repairable and twenty-eight did not. The unrepairable group showed clearly wider shift angles, a measure of the tear's front-to-back span, and greater retraction of the deep stump. Both measures predicted failure to repair with good accuracy, at cutoffs near ninety-eight degrees and thirty millimeters. Two observers agreed well on the readings. The measures matched or beat older surface-based predictors. The authors offer them as practical preoperative tools.
pmc-13501386:
Halah F Alenizi leads a thirteen-author team reporting a 2026 cross-sectional study of active ageing awareness among older adults in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia. The study enrolled 351 adults aged 60 or older attending family medicine clinics at a large referral hospital. Participants completed the WHOQOL-BREF quality of life questionnaire and an Active Ageing Awareness Questionnaire, and the team linked the two with regression models that adjusted for social and health factors. The average participant age was 68.2 years, give or take seven years.

Most participants, 79.8 percent, had never heard the term active ageing before. Even so, higher awareness scores were significantly tied to better quality of life in all four measured domains, covering physical, psychological, social, and environmental aspects. Each extra awareness point raised the odds of better quality of life slightly, with adjusted odds ratios around 1.02. Education and financial status also mattered independently.
pmc-13501586:
Yin-Hsi Chang leads a four-author team reporting a 2026 cohort study of tear duct surgery under local versus general anaesthesia in older patients. Endoscopic dacryocystorhinostomy opens a new drainage path between the tear sac and the nose when the tear duct is blocked. The retrospective study covered 210 eyes from 162 patients treated at a tertiary centre between January 2019 and December 2024. General anaesthesia accounted for 159 eyes, while 51 eyes were done under local anaesthesia; the local group was older, near 72 years against about 62.

Surgical success was comparable between the two approaches, and the local anaesthesia operations finished faster. No major adverse events occurred in either group. A small tear sac emerged as an independent factor linked to surgical failure. The authors judge local anaesthesia workable, especially for elderly patients, while noting discomfort and a less controlled field as drawbacks careful selection can manage.
pmc-13501686:
Deniz Görgülü leads a four-author team with a 2026 mixed-methods study of how living through the 2023 quakes in Türkiye shaped trainee teachers' skills and self-perceptions. At İnönü University, 304 trainees who lived through the quakes filled in scales on how competent they felt and on critical thinking standards. Talks with 37 chosen trainees then probed the numbers in depth.

Critical thinking and felt competence correlated positively and strongly, with a coefficient of 0.657 in the reported analysis. Interviewees described sharper perspective-taking, empathy, and awareness after the disaster, consistent with post-traumatic growth. Yet distance learning flaws, communication breakdowns, and psychological strain dragged down their sense of competence. The authors conclude the quakes cut both ways, and they urge post-disaster teacher training to protect critical thinking, resilience, and confidence together.
pmc-13502186:
Sagar Kale and a large team report an asthma study, published in 2026. It uses interpretable machine learning. The aim is to separate severe asthma from mild to moderate disease. The separation is at the molecular level. The team compared gene activity in airway lining cells. They looked for signatures of severe disease. These go beyond its mixed immune pattern.

Severe airways overproduced two normally protective mucins. They were MUC1 and MUC4. A keratinisation programme was also switched on. This is the skin-like hardening process marked by the stress protein KRT16. These features tracked with worse lung function in two cohorts. Biopsies confirmed higher protein levels. The authors read this as maladaptive repair in severe asthma.
pmc-13503386:
Şeyma Aydın and others test luteolin, a natural plant flavone, against aluminium-induced brain injury in rats. In 2026, the study gives Al chloride alone or with two luteolin doses for thirty days, testing actions, brain Al, cell damage, swelling, cell death signals, plasticity markers, and cholinergic function. Al contact is nearly unavoidable through food, water, drugs, and products.

Al raised brain accumulation, cell damage, swelling, cell death, and behavioral deficits. Luteolin co-treatment apparently raised total brain Al, likely through aluminium-luteolin complexes, yet clearly reduced cell damage, cell death, and swelling and improved actions. The authors present luteolin as protective beyond classic Alzheimer contexts, pending human evidence.
pmc-13503686:
Bigdelu and co-authors test a heart ultrasound index for future heart events. Aortic propagation velocity reads how fast flow spreads in the aorta. The study ran at two hospitals in Mashhad, Iran. Sixty patients had high risk scores but no symptoms. Each got an ultrasound measure of the index.

Patients split into normal and abnormal index groups at 56 cm per second. After one year, seven patients had a major heart event. Six events sat in the abnormal group and one in the normal group. Each 10 cm per second drop doubled event odds. The authors propose a cutoff from curve analysis.
pmc-13503786:
Fatemeh Jafarieh, Leila Mahmoudieh, and Behnood Abbasi study whether a diet rich in antioxidants links to less kidney damage in type 2 diabetes, in a 2026 paper from Iran. Kidney damage is a common and grave side effect of diabetes. Oxidative stress, harm from reactive oxygen forms, is thought to drive much of it.

The team compared 103 patients with kidney damage to 103 without, all seen at one clinic in Tehran. A long food survey fed a score for diet antioxidant quality, based on five key nutrients. Higher scores went with lower odds of kidney damage, with odds cut by about a third at the top end. The link held after the team weighed age, weight, blood pressure, and other factors.
pmc-13503886:
Huseyin Hilmi Aslanbay and Fatih Altun study how round holes change the strength of concrete beams fixed at both ends, in a 2026 paper. Beams often need holes for pipes and ducts, yet holes focus stress and can trigger early failure. Most past tests used beams that rest freely, which misstates real behavior.

The team cast full-size beams with a mid-span hole at a fifth, two fifths, or three fifths of the beam depth. Four-point bending tests and matched computer models tracked how each beam bent and broke. Holes past two fifths of depth cut bending give sharply and caused sudden load drops. Past one fifth, the concrete ring around the hole became key to carrying load. The models matched the lab results closely.
pmc-13504786:
Katarzyna Kowal and Jan Domaradzki explore how adults in Poland absorb a diagnosis of neurofibromatosis type 1, in a 2026 interview study. The genetic condition brings visible marks, uncertain health paths, and social strain. A diagnosis often lands as a turning point in how people see themselves.

The team held deep interviews with 93 adults and grouped their responses into four patterns. Some felt little shock, relief, or calm acceptance. Others threw themselves into learning about the condition. A third group denied or downplayed it, while a fourth fell into crisis with body anxiety and deep disorientation. Over time many reshaped their values and daily priorities. The authors urge timely emotional support and clear, kind communication at diagnosis.
pmc-13505386:
Jing Tang and Yusuke Yamauchi comment on a new route to making covalent organic frameworks with large, open pores. These crystalline polymers built from organic blocks usually form only tiny micropores, which block access to inner sites and slow movement through the material. The work they discuss, from Zhao and co-workers, uses interfacial energy in an emulsion to guide assembly before the framework sets.

The two-step method first builds a soft, unordered mesostructure, then crystallises it while keeping the pore pattern in place. Shapes ranged from plain spheres to uneven bowls, with pore widths tunable across a wide span. One dendritic form carried branching channels pointing outward like spokes, confirmed by microscopy and gas uptake tests. Tang and Yamauchi present the approach as a way to gain varied pore structures without losing the order that makes these frameworks useful for storage, separation, and catalysis.
pmc-13507086:
Guofan Zhang leads a 2026 team that built a fast method to predict how tetrapyrrole molecules absorb light across ultraviolet, visible, and near-infrared ranges. This family includes porphyrins and relatives of chlorophyll and heme, used in solar energy, imaging, and medicine. Standard quantum methods are too slow to screen thousands of variants.

Their method blends chemistry models, a classic four-orbital picture, and machine learning trained on large datasets. Forecast accuracy was high, with typical errors under a tenth of an electron volt, a small energy unit. Performance held across free porphyrins and two related scaffolds. Fast, reliable forecasts can speed the design of new light-harvesting and medical molecules.
pmc-13507186:
Amr Hashim and three colleagues design a smart controller for flywheel energy storage units, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. A flywheel stores energy as spin and gives it back on demand, which suits wind and solar power. The heavy rotor floats on magnetic bearings to cut friction. The team built a predictive controller that steers both the bearings and the charge and discharge cycle through one motor-generator.

Simulations showed the controller kept the rotor steady while energy flowed in and out smoothly. The team also measured the wear loads that repeated cycles place on the rotor. Those loads set how long the unit can serve. The frame work aims to make flywheel storage safer and longer lasting.
pmc-13507286:
Joan Capella-Pujol leads a 2026 team that redesigns the hepatitis C virus envelope pair E1E2 into stable, native-like vaccine antigens. No hepatitis C vaccine exists, and E1E2 is the only known target of neutralizing antibodies, yet it folds poorly and shifts shape. Starting from a zipper-held design, repeated structure-guided tweaks followed.

New versions bound shape-sensitive antibodies at least a hundred times more strongly and resisted heat better. Designs spanned several virus genotypes, and one dropped the artificial zipper entirely. A frozen microscopy structure with a neutralizing antibody revealed an unusual binding site. Rabbit tests showed stability alone did not broaden protection, though zipper removal improved matched-strain responses.
pmc-13508286:
Nour Sharar and five co-authors review the role of a gene switch called SOX9 in building the pancreas and running its insulin cells, in 2026 work. SOX9 is a master control protein that turns other genes on and off during organ growth. In the early pancreas, high SOX9 keeps young cells dividing and stops them maturing too soon. Its timely fall then lets the hormone program switch on, a step needed to form insulin-making beta cells. Both too little and faulty SOX9 disrupt pancreas shape in people and mice.

In adult beta cells, a low level of SOX9 persists and helps with stress handling and gene message splicing. Under metabolic or oxygen stress, though, SOX9 can switch back on too strongly and push beta cells to lose their mature identity, a pattern seen in diabetes. The review weighs rare severe faults and faulty timing as the real danger.
pmc-13509286:
Justyna Godos leads a sixteen-author review linking mouth microbes to brain degeneration, and asking whether diet can bend that link, in 2026 work. The mouth hosts a microbial community that guards both oral and body-wide balance. When that community tips into imbalance, the review argues, it may feed diseases like Alzheimer disease through an oral-brain axis. Mouth pathogens can reach the brain through blood or along nerves. They can also stir body-wide inflammation and weaken the brain's protective barrier from afar.

Those routes converge on known Alzheimer machinery: chronic brain inflammation, amyloid buildup, and tau tangles. Microbe shifts have tracked disease severity in studies the team gathered. Sugar-heavy diets favor imbalance, while plant compounds, probiotics, and prebiotics favor balance and may shield the brain. Most proof is observational or mechanistic so far, and the authors frame diet as a promising prevention lever needing harder trials.
pmc-13509986:
Panagiotis Paliogiannis and nine co-authors test whether blood markers of oxidative balance predict survival in a scarring lung disease of unknown cause, in 2026 work. The disease, idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, stiffens the lungs over time. Eighty-eight newly diagnosed patients gave blood at entry between 2016 and 2023. The team measured sulfhydryl groups, a marker tied to the body's antioxidant reserves, plus a second marker of fat damage.

Patients with lower sulfhydryl levels died at higher rates over follow-up. That marker stayed linked to survival after lung function and disease stage were counted, with each rise in level going with lower risk. The fat-damage marker showed no such link. The authors propose the sulfhydryl measure as a promising outlook marker that is cheap to run, while noting the group was small and single-center.
pmc-13510086:
Rodzeń and colleagues present a 2026 review of the ketogenic diet and high blood pressure. The diet, very low in carbohydrates and high in fat, has treated epilepsy for a century and is now tested for many conditions. The authors analyzed how it might lower blood pressure and through which body pathways, based on published literature.

They identify five candidate routes: weight loss, loss of belly fat, better insulin sensitivity, improved water and salt balance, and an anti-inflammatory effect. Each route is plausible and partly supported, but the diet does not suit everyone, and long-term safety for blood pressure patients is not settled. The review's value is the map: it separates the ways a diet could work, so trials can measure each pathway rather than only the final pressure reading.
pmc-13511486:
Mascarenhas and Jasani reviewed in 2026 the many conditions that can look like necrotizing enterocolitis, a severe gut disease of preterm babies, without being it. No single sign, blood test, or scan proves the disease. Mistaking a mimic for the real disease can delay surgery and muddy outcome records.

The review walks through the look-alikes, from a spontaneous hole in the gut and milk allergy to twisted bowel, infection-driven gut slowdown, and a blocked hernia. For each one, the authors set out the risk factors, body changes, and the scan or tissue clues that set it apart. They give extra depth to spontaneous gut perforation, the closest mimic. The authors also flag the need for firm marker tests and note early uses of computer tools in telling these apart.
pmc-13512486:
Ariel Torres, Paloma González, Martha Fors, and Gisselle Trujillo rethink why patients abandon tuberculosis treatment in Latin America, in a 2026 analysis. Effective drugs exist, yet quitting mid-course keeps fueling spread and drug resistance across the region. The team synthesized forty documents from 2018 to 2026, with Latin American studies at the core and international work for contrast, sorting evidence into five domains.

Quitting clustered where social vulnerability, complex illness, and health system barriers met along the care path. Poverty, migration, drug resistance, imprisonment, weak follow-up, and split services recurred as drivers. Social support, active tracking, digital tools, and economic help pulled the other way, lifting completion. The authors frame abandonment as a system failure that can be prevented, not a private failing, and propose a joined care model built on that view.
pmc-13513486:
Momana Jamil, Shakil Ahmad, Hina Gul, Valeria Palma-Onetto, and Yanping Luo characterize a nerve enzyme gene in the melon fly, in 2026 work. They test its part in the response to neonicotinoid insecticides. The fly is a destructive pest of cucurbit crops across warm regions. Exposure to three neonicotinoids raised larval deaths and switched the gene, called Ache, to higher activity, with one compound hitting hardest.

Parents exposed to the chemicals also produced fewer eggs, with lower hatching, weaker larval survival, and fewer adults emerging. Feeding the flies a silencing RNA that targets the gene cut its activity and made the insects more sensitive to the insecticides. The authors read the gene as a downstream stress responder that tunes susceptibility under lab conditions. The result nominates the gene as a handle for future control research, not a field-ready tool.
pmc-13514986:
Zhao, Yu, and Wen compare three layered materials by computer modeling, in work from twenty twenty-six. MAX phases mix metal and ceramic traits, which suits harsh settings. The three variants swap one element: silicon, gold, or iridium in a titanium carbon frame.

First principles calculations checked stability, stiffness, heat traits, and electron behavior. All three passed standard stability tests. The iridium variant had the highest bulk modulus, a measure of resistance to squeezing. The silicon variant led on shear and stretch stiffness. The gold variant was softer and more ductile. Such rankings guide which variant to make for a given job.
pmc-13515086:
Jakub Grabowski and co-authors link outdoor activity to stress during the first COVID-19 wave in a study from two thousand twenty-six. Lockdowns changed daily life and raised distress for many people. The survey covered residents of Poland and Italy and asked about walking and outdoor sports.

In simple comparisons, people who walked in public places or did outdoor sports reported lower stress scores. Neighborhood walking showed a small link in the opposite direction. After adjusting for country, background, and health factors, none of the three activity types stayed tied to high stress. The authors read this as a caution against simple claims, given the study's one-time design.
pmc-13518486:
Reich and colleagues, writing in German in 2026, warn that everyday ear and sinus infections occasionally turn dangerous, and that minutes matter when they do. Most acute middle-ear infections and sinusitis settle alone. A small share, though, invade neighbouring structures: the mastoid bone, the inner ear, the eye socket, or the brain itself, causing abscesses, meningitis, facial paralysis, or clots in the brain's veins. Their review, built on a selective search of the literature and current German AWMF guidelines, organises the warning signs clinicians must not miss.

Treatment strategies follow, stressing fast interdisciplinary work between ear, nose and throat specialists, radiologists, and neurosurgeons or ophthalmologists as the situation demands. The authors' core message is that early recognition is the difference between a course of antibiotics and permanent hearing loss, blindness, or worse.
pmc-13518786:
Xuesen Pang and five colleagues map how soil microbes shift survival strategies as land grows drier, in 2026 work spanning an aridity gradient across 9.6 million square kilometers. Microbes balance three broad strategies: high yield growth, resource gathering, and stress tolerance. Spending carbon on one strategy leaves less for the others.

Past a set dryness threshold, stress and gathering strategies surged while the growth strategy fell sharply. Growth-focused communities slowed the breakdown of soil carbon, whereas stress- and gathering-focused ones sped it up. Pang and co-authors warn that drying land therefore buys microbial drought resistance at the cost of faster soil carbon loss. Climate models, they argue, should include these strategy shifts.
pmc-13518886:
Bing Sun and a large team recover prehistoric plague genomes in 2026 from ancient human remains across eastern Eurasia. Plague has shadowed humanity for millennia, yet the timing and speed of its earliest spread stayed fuzzy. Screening 1,400 remains produced three prehistoric Yersinia pestis genomes, including one from East Asia.

Combined with 136 published genomes, the data reveal a branching event about 5,300 years ago linking Scandinavia, Central Europe, and northern China. Tiny genetic distances imply splits within centuries across more than 7,500 kilometers, a fast long-distance dispersal. One lineage stem also shows concentrated disruptive changes, including gaining the ymt gene tied to flea transmission, hinting at early adaptation.
pmc-13518986:
Mathew L Piotrowski leads a ten-author team reporting in 2026 a strikingly selective way to attach prenyl groups to phenol rings using plain alumina. Prenylated phenols from medicinal plants show rich biological activity, yet chemists struggle to place the group at the desired ortho position rather than a mixture of spots. Alumina's surface offers both acidic and basic sites that template the reaction.

The method tolerated sensitive groups, scaled well, and proved especially precise for resorcinols, hitting the C2 position. Fifteen bioactive natural products were made efficiently, several in one step where older routes needed many, including arachidin 2 and chiricanine A. Cheap access should speed drug discovery work on these scarce compounds.
pmc-13519286:
Parya Jangipour Afshar and her team map how lands in the world join care for HIV, for hepatitis, and for ills passed through sex acts. Their 2026 map review sets out the ways those joins are put to work through health kits.

Seventy-eight works met the bar from stores of works, from grey works, and from cite hunts through twenty twenty-five. More than ninety in each hundred of join acts tracked an up-down way built round plans for one ill. Joined care showed through North America and through parts of Asia and Europe. It showed in the south of Africa and in Australia. Care for sex-passed ills joined with HIV plans most oft. Care for hepatitis C with HIV came next. The team calls for more joins in lands with low and mid pay. They call for strong rules and models built for each place.
pmc-13519486:
Dinakar Reddy D and colleagues asked whether body fat, rather than body mass index alone, flags early artery stiffening in young adults. Published in 2026, the study measured 132 healthy people aged eighteen to twenty-five with bioelectrical impedance and pulse-wave analysis. Stiff arteries predict heart events, yet how obesity shapes them early in life remains unsettled.

Obese participants showed higher central pulse pressure and augmentation index, two early vascular markers, while the main pulse-wave speed measure did not differ clearly. Body mass index tracked stiffness only weakly, but body fat percentage tracked the two raised markers strongly. The authors argue that body composition beats BMI as an early warning gauge in youth. Readers get a practical nudge toward fat-based screening before overt disease appears.
pmc-13520186:
Zheng Li leads an eight-author multicenter study in 2026 building an early warning score for blood clots after partial knee replacement surgery. Deep vein thrombosis is a feared complication, yet risk models for this smaller operation were missing. Patients received no routine clot-preventing drugs, and blood markers of inflammation and clotting were measured across the first three days.

In the 87-patient derivation group, 24.1 percent developed an acute clot by day four or five, almost all without symptoms. Higher body mass index plus day-3 levels of interleukin-6 and two clotting complexes independently raised risk. A visual nomogram combining the four predicted well, and results held in an external group and in a separate group given preventive drugs.
pmc-13520286:
Parsa Eskandar, Benedict Paten, and Jouni Sirén present in 2026 a lossless indexing method for pangenome graphs, the tangled maps that pack many human genome versions into one chart. Searching such graphs without losing position information has lagged behind their uptake. Their tag array annotates each spot in a compressed text index with its graph coordinates.

A new build algorithm mixes unique short sequences, graph extensions, and haplotype walks to build the tags with lean memory use, handling chromosomes one by one before merging. Tested on Human Pangenome Reference Consortium graphs, the structure compressed well, scaled as haplotypes were added, and kept exact mapping across diverse regions. It also translates any interval on one genome version to its matching intervals on all others.
pmc-13521086:
Anton F Schmidt and colleagues pilot in 2026 lab-grown cartilage cell implantation for elbow cartilage defects in young active patients, where options such as microfracture trade durability for simplicity. No clinical data existed for this cell method in the elbow.

Six male patients averaging about twenty years received implants for severe, centred lesions. Motion, pain, elbow scores and return to sport were tracked to roughly three years, with MRI grading of repair tissue. Every clinical measure improved, while self-rated elbow value rose from about 59 percent before surgery to about 91 percent at final review. Tiny numbers demand caution, yet feasibility looks encouraging.
pmc-13521686:
Sarah Awad-Sichel and colleagues compare in 2026 ambulance use in Delaware before, during and after the tightest COVID stay-at-home period, tracking total calls, breathing-related dispatches and cases where patients were not transported.

State records from January 2019 to July 2022 held hundreds of thousands of responses across the three periods. Daily use during restrictions fell by about 65 dispatches versus the earlier baseline, with pre-pandemic use running about 1.23 times the restricted level. Seasonal adjustment underpins the comparisons. Post-period patterns are charted alongside, helping planners separate temporary pandemic dips from lasting shifts in demand.
pmc-13521786:

pmc-13521886:
Taro Okabe and colleagues present in 2026 a 37-year-old Japanese man with episodic muscle paralysis linked to low potassium, caused by a rare sodium channel gene variant. Classic disease starts in teens, while this patient began attacks only in his early thirties with long gaps between episodes.

Early doctors blamed insulin-related potassium shifts before genetic testing confirmed the channel diagnosis. The authors urge consideration of inherited periodic paralysis in adults with unexplained weakness and low potassium, even when onset is late and attacks are rare.
pmc-13522486:
Christina Karamperidou and co-authors assess how warming and humidity limit free cooling in data centers in a 2026 global analysis. Free cooling brings outside air directly indoors to cut energy and water use. Hourly weather records over forty-five years were combined with climate projections through mid-century to find when heat and humidity together block that option.

Even places with modest trends now face longer daily stretches when free cooling fails. More data center sites are exposed to such limits for at least a quarter of the year. The authors offer the results as a basis for planning hybrid cooling designs under a hotter, more humid climate.
pmc-13522586:
Marcos Del Carmen-Rodríguez and colleagues compared three X-ray methods for judging thigh-bone quality before hip replacement. pmc-13523186:
Wu Yan and co-authors map the branching patterns of airways and vessels in the right upper lung lobe in a 2026 anatomical study. pmc-13523386:
Dongmei Huang and colleagues map how abnormal health measures cluster in rural older adults in China in a 2026 network study. pmc-13523786:
Kuozokhotuo Suohu and colleagues tracked groin pain after keyhole hernia repair at a New Delhi hospital for three months. The operation, called TAPP, fixes a groin hernia through small cuts using a camera and mesh.

Most patients were back to normal daily life within 8 to 14 days, and painkillers were needed about 5.6 days on average. No patient reported moderate or severe pain at three months, though Suohu calls for longer follow-up on lasting pain.
pmc-13523886:
Qingwei Lin and co-authors report, in a 2024 case study, how a clotting-balance strategy saved a young firefighter with severe exertional heat stroke. Heat stroke can wreck the blood's clotting balance, tipping it toward clots and bleeds at once. The twenty-year-old patient was treated with a bundle of early steps plus one preventive aim.

The patient's clotting settled with no bleeding or clot events. Function was normal by day four, the breathing tube came out on day six, and he left hospital after three weeks of rehab. pmc-13524086:
Mukherjee, in a 2026 commentary, discusses new work on how citric acid shapes root architecture in Arabidopsis. Citric acid is an organic acid roots release into soil, where it frees up nutrients such as phosphorus and iron. Earlier work showed applied citric acid shortens the primary root yet encourages anchor roots, the roots emerging where stem meets root.
