Citric acid at 1 to 5 millimolar clearly reduced primary root length while increasing anchor root formation over the same range. Mukherjee highlights the tissue-specific logic: one common soil chemical pushes the plant to invest less in downward growth and more in anchoring roots near the surface. The commentary frames the mechanism as agriculturally relevant for stress-prone soils.
pmc-13524786:
Uroš Vezonik, Giulia Iannelli, Daniel Kaiser, and Nuno Maulide present a 2026 synthetic chemistry method for swapping the alkyl group on secondary N-methylamines, a common building block in medicines. Cleanly editing unprotected amines with simple, unactivated alkenes or alkynes has been a lasting challenge. Editing at a late stage is prized because it can vary a finished drug candidate in one step.

Their swap platform changes the outer parts of the amine while tolerating many functional groups and unprotected amine starting materials. The team shows direct coupling of fully loaded, unprotected building blocks and even complex peptides, a setting usually hostile to such chemistry. Freedom in planning from the swap also allowed several high-selling pharmaceuticals to be made in a single step, showing wide reach.
pmc-13524886:
Qingyang Zhao led a team reviewing two conditions that often occur together in young people in a 2026 paper. Itchy, inflamed skin and attention and hyperactivity problems raise each other's burden. Children with the skin condition face a higher risk of the attention disorder, above all when skin disease starts early, runs severe, or wrecks sleep.

The review pulls together evidence on how common the pairing is and why it may arise. A loop linking inflammation, itching, and behavior is the leading idea. The authors propose early screening for attention problems in these children. Firm control of skin inflammation and itching, they argue, is the key step to break the cycle.
pmc-13525186:
Dollie and co-authors described a 2026 case report of a fifty-one-year-old woman with a huge multinodular goitre, an enlarged thyroid gland full of lumps. She had lived with a painless neck mass for five years, then developed trouble swallowing and breathlessness on effort over five months. Her thyroid hormone levels stayed normal throughout.

Examination and imaging showed the gland bulging down behind the breastbone and squeezing her windpipe sideways. Dollie notes that a raised arms test, called Pemberton's sign, was positive, a warning of airway pressure. A needle sample was bloody and gave no answer, so surgeons removed the whole thyroid because of the airway risk. Tissue tests confirmed benign nodular disease, and the authors warn that normal hormone results never rule out dangerous compression.
pmc-13526786:
Zid and colleagues tested in 2026 whether human choices in uncertain tasks follow the foraging logic of animal behavior rather than the value comparison assumed by psychology. The standard account says people price every option and pick the best. Animal research says decision-makers stick with a current option until its value drops below a threshold, then explore. The team ran classic comparison tasks and fitted both model families to what people actually did.

Signs of threshold computation appeared even in tasks built for comparison. A new foraging model built on that rule fitted behavior better than standard reinforcement learning models, predicted people's tendency to repeat choices. Even predicted held-out participants whose behavior looked almost impossible under the classic account. The authors conclude that threshold-based deciding runs wider in human life than the field assumed, with consequences for how experiments should be designed.
pmc-13527086:
Zhang, Li, and Koh published a 2026 study on deleting one atom to rebuild ring molecules. Oxetanes are four-sided rings with one oxygen, prized in drug design. Pulling the oxygen out shrinks or reshapes the ring in one stroke. The team used light and iodoform, with no catalyst, for the cut.

The reaction first opened the ring into a two-iodine chain piece. That piece then closed into three-sided rings or fused ring systems. The method tolerated many chemical groups used in drug building. It also shortened routes to known medicines in demonstration runs. Atom deletion opens chemical territory that standard building steps skip. Precise oxygen spotting in crowded rings was the key hurdle cleared. Iodoform under light drives the oxygen-removal step in the scheme.
pmc-13527886:
Uchizawa and nine co-authors compare energy use in female distance runners with and without missed periods, in a study from twenty twenty-six. Some runners cut food intake to stay light for races. A theory says total energy use stays capped, so hard training steals energy from rest and sleep. Missed periods may signal that energy is too low.

They studied twenty runners, ten with missed periods and ten without. Total energy use did not differ between the two groups. Longer weekly runs linked to more training burn and less casual movement burn. Links to rest and sleep burn faded once body makeup was weighed. The pattern fits the capped energy theory for both groups alike.
pmc-13527986:
Xinyi Zheng examines in a 2026 paper how managing one's boss can backfire. Managing the boss means shaping your work around a supervisor's priorities. It is usually praised as proactive and helpful. Zheng asked whether some supervisors instead read it as a threat to their rank. The data came from a three-wave survey in China. It covered 452 supervisor and subordinate pairs.

Employees who managed their boss more were linked with supervisors feeling their hierarchy was threatened. That feeling alone did not explain later ostracism of the employee. The chain held only for supervisors with a strong belief in power distance. For them, perceived threat led more often to shutting the employee out. Zheng argues proactive behavior is not always read as loyalty. Context and hierarchy beliefs shape the response.
pmc-13528386:
Hendra Goh and ten colleagues co-design a phone app for maternal and child health in rural Cambodia in a 2026 study. Village health groups and health center staff are the users. Sixteen stakeholders shaped the feature list in early rounds. Ten field users then tested the app. Quick interviews fed each design round.

Offline mode keeps the app alive without signal. Users said the decision aid made care steadier and boosted confidence. Records improved accuracy and quick finding. Staff also saw admin uses, from stock tracking to auto reports. The authors back co-design for tools that must fit poor-connectivity settings.
pmc-13529186: Srikaran Bojja and co-authors present a large colonic perineurioma found during workup for chronic belly pain and constipation, in work from twenty twenty-six. Perineuriomas are rare, benign growths in the colon, called fibroblastic polyps. They most often sit in the lower colon and cause no symptoms. Most turn up by chance on screening scopes. The patient was a forty-four year old woman with long standing pain and constipation. Her scope found a multi lobed polyp five centimetres wide. Tissue tests confirmed the type.
pmc-13529886:

The team mapped the proof with scoping rules and the PRISMA-ScR guide, and searched the health lists and gray works with no date bounds. Of 174 works found, five fit their rules. Win rates ran from 18 to 100 per cent, the low rates from old works with old ways. New works showed high rates and no bone death. In no work was root canal care tied to bone death. pmc-13530186:
Kevin Brown and a team including Joseph Keane show that HIV blocks the fuel switch human macrophages need to fight tuberculosis. Their study was published in twenty twenty-six. TB kills people with HIV at high rates, and failing macrophages are a core reason.

HIV pushed the opposite way, damping sugar enzymes and favoring slow oxygen-based burning. In co-infection, HIV won: the TB-driven shift was suppressed. The work used an HIV-carrying cell line plus human macrophages exposed to an HIV surface protein. The finding names metabolism as a battleground in co-infection.
pmc-13530486:
Nam-Hong Choi and co-authors study knee surgery outcomes in a paper from two thousand twenty-six. Scans six months after surgery split patients into healed and not healed groups. The not healed group had a clearly steeper slope than the healed group. Age and body weight did not differ. pmc-13531186:

pmc-13534486:

pmc-13534586:
Musa Hussain and colleagues present in 2026 a thin, flexible textile antenna that works across three bands for wearable devices. The antenna covers bands suited to 5G wearables, Wi-Fi, and short-range sensing. Bending tests kept key measures close to flat performance, and body phantom tests checked safety exposure and gain. Comparisons with recent designs support its use in clothing-based electronics.
pmc-13534686:
Shuting Bu and colleagues linked relay-hub wiring shifts to Parkinson motor groups and their genes. pmc-13536486:
Shirong Lin, Yufeng Chen, Yadan Chen, and a wider team wrote this research paper, published in 2026. It asks whether a diet that stokes inflammation in the body is linked to cardiorenal anemia syndrome, a condition where heart failure, kidney disease, and anemia occur together.

Higher scores went with higher odds of the syndrome in both countries. Blood markers of inflammation seemed to carry part of the effect. The authors also built prediction models from the survey data. pmc-13536686:
Hancong Li and colleagues examine why a medicinal jujube variety differs in quality across the eastern foothills of the Taihang Mountains in a 2026 study. pmc-13536786:

pmc-13538386:

pmc-13538686:

pmc-13538786:

pmc-13539686:

pmc-13540586:

More than four hundred patients answered a detailed questionnaire. Two service-quality models structured the analysis. Needs formed a clear hierarchy of importance. Informed consent ranked among the strongest concerns. Gap analysis showed where care falls short. Hospitals can use the priorities to improve patient experience.
pmc-13540886:
Siqing Liu and five colleagues pool, in a 2026 meta-analysis, evidence on heart and vessel disease appearing long after treatment for blood cancers. Survival keeps improving, so late effects on the heart matter to a growing population.

Leukaemia survivors faced well over double the overall cardiovascular risk of comparison groups, with heart failure risk about four times higher. Hodgkin and non-Hodgkin lymphoma survivors showed similar positive links. The authors push targeted heart prevention for this group.
pmc-13541786:
Gustavo Delmilho and ten co-authors test a feed swap for finishing lambs in a study from two thousand twenty-six. They replaced half the sugarcane silage with Moringa oleifera silage, a tropical forage tree. Sixteen crossbred lambs were split between the standard and mixed diets for seventy-five days.

Lambs on the mixed diet had lower fasting and hot carcass weights. Fat cover and ribeye area did not differ, and neither did meat protein, fat, or ash. pmc-13541886:

Spin coating gave far more even films than cast films, with much smaller spread in thickness and surface roughness. Two builds gave three clean pulses each, spaced about 16 hours and about 72 hours apart.
pmc-13541986:

pmc-13542086:

They also showed fewer needless transmissions than unprotected control.
pmc-13543386:

pmc-13543486:

Scores also differed by gender, education, chronic disease status, and having a relative in healthcare. pmc-13543586:

pmc-13543886:

pmc-13545186:

China kept the highest rates despite the steepest declines, India improved slowest while its case count nearly doubled, and smoking stayed the leading behavioral risk. The authors argue that aging populations will keep absolute numbers climbing without stronger screening and prevention.
pmc-13545386:

Use before surgery rose from two percent to five percent over that span. Weight change on the drugs varied widely, from large losses to gains, with an average loss of nine pounds. About one in five users lost at least twenty pounds. Drug use showed no clear link to repeat surgery, complications, or emergency visits after the operation.
pmc-13546586:

The cells in question are M2 macrophages, a type linked with poor outcomes. Resistant tumors kept most of these cells in the outer rim, while tumors that responded well showed them flooding into the core. A simple ratio of core to rim density captured the split and tracked the degree of tumor shrinkage. The authors propose the ratio as a new way to gauge likely chemo response before treatment ends.
pmc-13547386:

On hourly data from Jiangsu and half-hourly data from Australia, the hybrid cut average errors by roughly a quarter to a half compared with the untuned model. It lifted a fit score close to perfect on the Australian set. The staged search beat either optimizer used alone. The author presents the hybrid as a robust tool for grid operators.
pmc-13547586:

pmc-13615786:
Lizuiyue Li and co-authors published this study in 2026. It sequences the genomes of two Eremogone species, alpine plants in the pink family. Both genomes were assembled to chromosome scale.

Comparing them revealed a recent genome tripling shared by the whole plant family. The team rebuilt the family's ancestral chromosome set, at nine chromosomes. Which genes survived the tripling was not random. Kept genes skew toward roles that help in alpine life. Reads across tissues showed gene control also drifting between the species. The authors read these two layers, gene keeping and gene tuning, as twin tracks of mountain adaptation.
pmc-13616286:
Charlotte Meyer leads a team introducing an injectable, self-expanding foam to stop bleeding after childbirth, the leading cause of mothers' deaths worldwide. Many current tools are costly, hard to use in rough settings, or hard to remove. Their system stores stable starting materials and a simple applicator that mixes a gel foam inside the womb at the point of care.

The expanding foam presses at 67 to 92 millimetres of mercury, matching standard balloon tamponade, while also backing the blood's own clotting. It then breaks down safely in place, so nothing must be pulled out. Bench, lab-grown tissue, and body-like tests confirmed the pressure range. A treatment that a small clinic can store, mix in minutes, and leave to dissolve could save mothers far from big hospitals.
pmc-13616586:
Ananya Chandra and colleagues report a 2026 case of a temporary heart rhythm block in a fetus, a rare pattern in which only every second atrial beat reached the ventricles. Fetal heart block usually stems from structural heart disease or maternal immune disease. The team looked closely when a 31-year-old pregnant patient was referred at twenty weeks after a slow fetal heart rate was noted. Ultrasound showed a structurally normal heart with normal pumping. Yet the ventricles beat at 75 per minute while the atria beat at 150.

Blood tests, including immune antibodies, thyroid checks, and electrolytes, came back normal. No valve leaks or fluid around the heart were seen. The mother reported regular cannabis use during pregnancy and tested positive for its main active compound, with no other recreational drugs found. Because the heart looked reassuring, the team held off on anti-inflammatory drugs and planned close weekly monitoring.
pmc-13619086:
Elisa Evangelista and colleagues tested whether a brief attention task at waking can objectively flag severe sleep inertia in idiopathic hypersomnia, a 2026 diagnostic study. Sleep inertia, the groggy, impaired state just after waking, is a hallmark of this disorder, yet it is usually judged by self-report. The team gave two five-minute vigilance tests, one in the evening and one at waking, to 350 drug-free patients: 131 with idiopathic hypersomnia and 219 with other sleep disorders.

A cutoff of at least four lapses on the morning test best separated patients with severe inertia from other-disorder patients without inertia, with sensitivity near 73 percent and specificity near 69 percent. A rise of at least four lapses from evening to morning was more specific but less sensitive. More than half of all participants crossed the morning cutoff.
pmc-13623386:
Nair Chase da Silva and colleagues report on teaching the United Nations Sustainable Development Goals to nursing students at the Federal University of Amazonas in Brazil. The goals form a global plan for fairer, greener development by 2030, and health workers meet many of them in daily practice. The experience report covers a third-semester course run from March to July 2025.

Teaching unfolded in four stages: opening theory, building an education project, carrying it out, and sharing results. Students took the goals out of the lecture hall and taught them to school pupils, cleaning and maintenance staff, office workers, and local health council members. Working with such mixed audiences forced the students to translate broad goals into plain, useful messages. The authors conclude that the project trained a critical, reflective style of health education, and they present the format as one other nursing schools could adopt.
pmc-13623786:
Sahaj Grewal leads a mini-review of social robots used with children who have autism spectrum disorder. Friendly robots can coach social and communication skills, and short studies show gains. The authors warn that three fast-moving add-ons are racing ahead of safety proof: robots paired with wearable sensors, robots inside virtual reality, and robots that chat using generative artificial intelligence.

Each add-on carries child-specific risks. Sensors worn on the body may distress children with sensory sensitivities, immersive scenes can overload attention, and constant data collection raises privacy worries. Free-running AI conversation could reinforce unhelpful communication habits. The research base is still small pilots with little follow-up. The authors propose a five-part validation roadmap covering child calibration standards, shared development measures, large multisite trials, long-term monitoring, and human-backed safety design. Their verdict: promising, but not ready as a main therapy.
pmc-13624586:
Nikita Deshmukh and co-authors lay out a trial protocol for migraine care that pairs physio with nerve stimulation. Migraine brings repeat head pain and cuts quality of life for many people. Standard physio helps some, but may miss the brain's pain tuning shift. Two skin-based nerve methods could tune those pain paths from outside the body.

Patients will be split by lot into two arms for the trial. One arm pairs ear vagus nerve stimulation with standard physio. The other pairs brow nerve stimulation with the same physio base. Pain, attack counts, and neck scores will be logged before, after, and at follow-up. The team expects both arms to gain, with one perhaps ahead.
pmc-13625386:
Mohammed Inayatullah and colleagues hunt for a shared program behind chemotherapy resistance across cancers, in this study from twenty twenty-six. Resistance kills more cancer patients than any other treatment failure, yet each cancer was assumed to find its own escape. The team combined single-cell sequencing, spatial mapping, and drug tests across tumor types.

The shared state surprised them. Resistant cells were not the sleepy, shape-shifted cells of textbook accounts. They were dividing fast, with growth genes wide awake and repair crews active. One master switch, the transcription factor MYC, sat at the center, and a helper enzyme, SRM, which builds growth-supporting polyamines, emerged as its effector. Blocking MYC, SRM, or a related growth signal restored drug sensitivity in cell lines, patient tumor organoids, and mice. The authors offer the MYC-SRM axis as a druggable weak point in stubborn cancers.
pmc-13625786:
Srikanth Swamy Swaroop B and co-authors present a 2026 study of a protein tag that feeds breast cancer growth. An enzyme called PAK1 is often overactive in breast and other cancers. It tags partner proteins with phosphate groups to switch them on. The team reports a new target of that tag: ARGLU1, a protein already found at high levels in breast tumors.

Tests with mass tools and labeled cells confirmed the tag lands at one spot, spot 77. Cells with a blocked spot grew, moved, and invaded less, and formed fewer colonies and balls. A mimic of the tagged form restored the push. Tumor samples showed high levels of both the protein and its tagged form, tied to later stage and poorer survival. The tag site could serve as a drug aim or a warning mark.
pmc-13625886:
Jiaqi Wang and others fermented a fish and rice food called Yucha in 2026. Unplanned fermentation makes quality hard to foresee. Three lactic bacteria strains were added on purpose. Each strain rewired food chemistry in its own way. Chemistry mapping charted those shifts. Network methods foretold health effects after that.

Added strains sped fermentation up quickly. Power against oxidation changed by strain choice. Many active compounds were listed. Hundreds of oxygen damage targets were linked. Two signal pathways looked central there. Results remain machine forecasts, not proof. Still, strain choice can steady quality. Health-focused fermented foods may benefit.
pmc-13626586:
Keith Bodger and colleagues asked which bowel-disease patients prefer clinic visits versus remote follow-up in the UK. The pandemic pushed remote care, yet preference drivers were poorly understood. Their secondary analysis surveyed 5,833 inflammatory bowel disease patients with remote-consultation experience, sorting future preference into strong clinic, strong remote, or none.

Two-thirds had no preference, one-quarter strongly preferred remote, and one-tenth strongly preferred clinic visits. Clinic preference tracked with older age, male sex, deprivation, Asian ethnicity, more comorbidities, Crohn's disease, worse symptoms, and dissatisfaction. Bodger and colleagues argue remote care must be fitted equitably, not uniformly.
pmc-13626886:
Pochen Li and five co-authors describe a hard overdose case in this two thousand twenty-six report. A young woman swallowed ninety slow-release valproate tablets with alcohol. Valproate is a drug for seizures and mood. In overdose it can depress the brain, raise ammonia, and harm many organs. Slow-release tablets keep soaking into the body for a long time. That makes such cases hard to treat with standard gut cleaning.

The patient arrived about six hours after the overdose, agitated and delirious. Staff protected her airway with a breathing tube. The tablets had clumped in her stomach into a partial mass. Doctors removed them by endoscopy. Blood-cleaning therapy followed later. The case shows why teams may need to look inside the stomach when slow-release overdoses stay severe.
pmc-13629286:
Ana Gil Méndez and eight colleagues drew together thirteen studies of end-of-life care experience. The studies ran from 2014 to 2024. They asked how people with palliative needs and their families experience care. The 2026 synthesis searched three databases. It re-read findings from wealthy lands through careful theme work.

Care emerged as a shifting, human process, not a straight path. Families carried heavy burdens. Scarce support made them worse. So did limited resources and patchy talk with care teams. Patients judged care by two things. Were their choices and identity respected? Were staff truly present? Dignity ran through all of it. Nursing practice could strengthen or weaken it. So could office systems. The authors argue services must treat the family as a unit of care.
pmc-13629386:
Yi-Hsin Wang, Kang-Yuan Lee, Chung-Hsiang Lin, and Chao-Min Cheng build triangular nanofluidic channels with walls of two semiconductor materials, to study flow driven by capillary force. Using nanoimprint lithography and plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition, they built hollow one-layer and three-layer channels joining gallium nitride and silicon nitride.

The one-layer channels let the team measure flow for liquids in common biological use. Speeds ran from well under one to nearly seventeen micrometers per second. From those speeds the team worked out capillary pressures, pressure drops, and wall shear stresses. The three-layer channels showed the build plan extends to more layers. Liquid thickness and how wet the wall gets proved to rule the flow. The results give designers firm numbers for passive devices.
pmc-13630586:
Finlayson, Gore, and Skelton tested a 2026 feasibility study of prompted voiding for adults with intellectual disability and urinary incontinence. Incontinence affects an estimated quarter to half of this population, yet few interventions aim to build continence skills. Their programme paired wrist worn toilet alarms with individual toileting plans over twelve weeks.

Seventeen adults took part, following personal plans that prompted regular toilet visits for urination at set times. Thirteen participants, seventy-seven percent, followed their plan across the full twelve weeks with staff support provided. Finlayson reports fifteen participants, eighty-eight percent, intended to keep using their plan after the study ended. Personal goal setting was built into each plan alongside the alarm prompts and routines. The authors judge prompted visits feasible for the majority of this sample.
pmc-13631286:
Qianru Zeng and six colleagues release an open dataset for studying focused ultrasound treatment of uterine fibroids. Their study appeared in 2026. The technique cooks fibroid tissue through the skin under imaging guidance. It preserves the uterus. Yet how hard a given case will be varies greatly between patients. That spread resists reproducible study.

The dataset bundles several kinds of data. It holds structured clinical variables and continuous multi-sequence MRI. It holds procedural parameters and precisely defined outcome measures. All are standardised and anonymised. As a proof of use, the team supplies a baseline model. It fuses the imaging with clinical data to predict treatment difficulty. On a held-out test set it classified its recommendations with strong accuracy. The resource targets benchmarking of multimodal medical AI.
pmc-13631686:
Staying in HIV care through pregnancy and after birth is the focus of a systematic review led by Hansen. She and her colleagues gathered studies from high-income countries on women living with HIV, asking how steadily they remained in treatment during pregnancy and in the months after delivery. Keeping appointments and taking antiretroviral therapy matter because steady treatment can suppress the virus and lower the chance of passing HIV to a baby.

Searching three large databases, the team screened more than five thousand records and kept eleven cohort studies for close reading. Retention was stronger during pregnancy than after birth, with drops seen up to two years postpartum, although later studies showed better retention than earlier ones. Women who took antiretroviral therapy and reached viral suppression during pregnancy tended to stay in care afterward with better viral outcomes. Varied outcome definitions kept the authors from pooling the results.
pmc-13632186:
Santiago Leiva and four colleagues published this 2026 study of a fatty tag that helps Zika virus infect human cells. The tag, called S-palmitoylation, attaches a fat molecule to proteins and can change their stability and behavior. The host protein under study is RNAseK, a small part of a cell pump that Zika and related viruses need. The team mapped exactly where the fatty tags sit on this protein.

They found tags on four specific building blocks of the protein. Changing those spots removed the tags entirely. Cells carrying the untaggable version produced less virus and fewer infectious particles than cells with the normal protein. Without its tags, the protein broke down faster inside the cell. The tags also helped keep cell compartments acidic, a step the virus uses. Blocking this tagging could become an antiviral strategy.
pmc-13632786:
Tristan Lilley and four colleagues tested whether emergency doctors in a community hospital could learn ultrasound-guided nerve blocks. Painful arm injuries often need procedures, and full sedation ties up staff and monitoring. A nerve block numbs only the arm. The study ran through 2025 and began with a two-hour class plus hands-on practice. Mentors then coached the doctors during real shifts, and knowledge was tested before and after.

Seventeen physicians finished the training, and their test scores more than doubled on average. During rollout, the doctors performed thirty brachial plexus blocks, which numb the arm through the shoulder's nerve bundle. In nearly all cases the planned procedure finished without sedation. Two cases still needed sedation, and no immediate complications appeared. The authors conclude that a short, structured course can bring this skill into community emergency care.
pmc-13632986:
Ye Sull Kim and three colleagues report a surgical emergency traced to a hormone shortage. A seventy-seven-year-old woman undergoing lower spine fusion developed dangerously low blood pressure during the operation. Fluids and several pressure-raising drugs failed to hold it. Her history held a clue: she had taken steroid medicines for rheumatoid arthritis, stopped nearly three decades earlier. Her skin was also unusually fragile.

The team suspected adrenal insufficiency, a state where the adrenal glands cannot supply enough cortisol for the stress of surgery. After the operation they gave her intravenous hydrocortisone, a lab-made form of that hormone. Her circulation steadied quickly and the pressure drugs could be withdrawn. Blood tests before and after surgery never proved the diagnosis outright. Even so, the pattern and her fast response made the case strong. She left the hospital without complications.
pmc-13634186:
Chuwen Xu and co-authors wrote a practical guide to long-read sequencing for studying the transcriptome, the full set of RNA messages in a cell. Short-read methods count genes but cannot rebuild full-length messages or untangle spliced variants and repetitive regions. Long-read platforms read whole RNA molecules directly. The review walks the workflow: choosing a platform and library strategy, processing noisy reads, and interpreting the results at the level of transcript variants.

Adoption lags because library preparation is demanding and the analysis tools change fast. Their roadmap distills the decisions and offers checklists meant to standardize practice. Emerging frontiers and best-practice advice close the review. The readers are researchers who want isoform-level detail without learning every pitfall by trial and error. A playbook, the authors argue, is what the field needs for results that other labs can reproduce.
pmc-13634586:
Xinmiao Wu and co-authors trace how a gene for a milk protein is switched on in the sheep mammary gland, in this 2026 study. The gene, LALBA, makes a key whey protein, and its control wiring was not mapped. The team compared gland tissue from dairy sheep with high and low milk output. They charted gene activity, open chromatin, and chemical marks across the tissue.

A super-enhancer sits at the LALBA locus, and one segment, E4, is its active core. Blocking E4 cut the gene's output. Capture tests showed E4 physically loops to the gene's promoter. A factor called ELF5 binds both spots and bridges the loop, driving the gene. Oddly, the gene ran higher in low-output sheep, and its activity slowed cell division in lab tests.
pmc-13635186:
Eun-Kyung Hwang and five colleagues study a brain hub for negative feelings during cannabis withdrawal in rats, in a paper dated twenty twenty-six. The hub, the lateral habenula, gathers signals tied to bad mood states. The team gave rats the main active part of cannabis, then stopped it and tested fear learning. Live calcium reads and cell recordings tracked the hub during withdrawal.

Fear responses and hub activity both rose during withdrawal. The hub's brake signals weakened, leaving its output cells overexcited. The brake fault traced to one input path, not another. The authors tie the hub's overdrive to the dread and fear that mark cannabis withdrawal.
pmc-13637286:
Sophie Hilda Lemoupa Makajio and six colleagues published this 2026 systematic review of community health workers in cervical cancer screening across sub-Saharan Africa. The region carries the world's highest rates of this cancer, mostly because screening coverage is thin. Community health workers are lay providers extending the health system's reach. The team searched three databases for controlled studies comparing worker-involved programs with standard approaches, updated in 2025.

Only six studies passed their quality bar. Every one used the workers for health education and counseling. Workers also recruited women through home visits, rebooked follow-up appointments, eased access to clinics, and even watched children during screening. Uptake rose significantly in three of the five studies that made it the main outcome. The one study tracking follow-up visits saw better attendance too. The authors judge the approach promising but uneven, with success hinging on program design and setting.
pmc-13638286:
Mishra and a large team of co-authors build a score that predicts when lung fluid will need draining again, in a study from 2026. In cancer patients, fluid around the lung builds back at varied rates after drainage. Ten British hospitals followed 241 such patients for three months to find what sets the pace.

Three bedside measures predicted the timing: breathing rate, fluid depth on ultrasound, and breathlessness on a simple scale. Combined as the RED score, they forecast timing fairly well in the study group. First checks in two outside groups also looked sound. The score could help plan care and visits.
pmc-13642186:
Ran Duan and four colleagues present a 2026 computational framework, GDMF, for predicting links between genes and observable traits. Such genome-to-phenome prediction helps explain complex traits in crops and human disease, but sparse, noisy data and weak use of network structure limit older methods.

GDMF joins a graph attention network, which weighs connections in a mixed molecular network, with weighted deep matrix factorization that balances global relationship tables. It also borrows meaning from trait vocabulary text to offset scarce plant data. Tests on maize and human datasets beat competing methods clearly, supporting the design for sparse biological prediction tasks.
pmc-13645986:
Rihito Nagata and colleagues report a salvage pancreaticoduodenectomy, the Whipple operation, for a local return of colon cancer. Their patient, a sixty-six-year-old man, had his right colon cut out for ascending colon cancer that grew into the gallbladder. The tumor was far along in its place, with no spread, and carried a KRAS mutation. He got four rounds of chemotherapy after surgery.

Four months later, scans found a mass of about three centimeters, taking in the duodenum and ileum. It was called a local return. Two rounds of chemotherapy shrank it. The team then did the Whipple operation, taking in the bowel parts hit. Tissue tests hinted the cancer came from cells left at the cut plane. The patient turned down more chemotherapy. He has stayed disease-free for over seven years.
pmc-13646086:
Lingxiang Wen and five colleagues test a yogurt starter bacterium that was mutated during a space mission and now makes far more of a natural thickener. The thickener, called EPS, can replace added gums in clean-label foods when bacteria produce it during fermentation. The strain, named LP-Wang25, was compared with its parent strain in growth, genome, and activity tests. Yogurt trials then judged texture, flavor, and panel scores.

The mutant grew faster after a shorter lag and made roughly forty percent more EPS, reaching a level the genome work ties to gene control rather than new machinery. It also showed stronger antioxidant and calming activity in lab assays. Yogurt made with it was thicker, lost less whey, and smelled more milky, with higher sensory scores. The authors offer the strain as a route to better yogurt without added thickeners.
pmc-13647386:
Abdikerim Mohamed Moumin and six colleagues survey 442 mothers in Borama, Somaliland, about depression after childbirth and whether they completed the full chain of maternal care. That chain means enough pregnancy visits, a facility birth, and a postnatal check. Depressive symptoms were self-reported on a simple yes-or-no basis. Models weighed social, structural, clinical, and health-system factors for both outcomes.

About a quarter of the women reported depressive symptoms, and only about a third finished all three care steps. Single mothers, women with labor complications, women rating their own health fair or poor, and, unexpectedly, university-educated women faced higher odds of symptoms. More than a third of suffering women had told no one. Starting pregnancy care early and higher education both raised care completion. The authors urge clinics to ask routinely about mothers' emotional state while strengthening early visits and follow-up.
pmc-13647986:
John C. Sentmanat and Andrei G.
